text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that female-restricted Wieacker-Wolff syndrome (WRWFFR) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ZC4H2 gene ({300897}) on chromosome Xq11.

See also Wieacker-Wolff syndrome (WRWF; {314580}), which is mostly observed in males; carrier females may have mild features. WRWF and WRWFFR represent a phenotypic spectrum of overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Female-restricted Wieacker-Wolff syndrome (WRWFFR) is an X-linked dominant syndromic form of neurogenic arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (AMC) with central and peripheral nervous system involvement. Affected individuals have decreased fetal movements causing the development of contractures in utero and resulting in AMC and diffuse contractures involving the large and small joints apparent at birth. There is global developmental delay with difficulty walking or inability to walk, hypotonia that often evolves to spasticity, and variably impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech and language. Dysmorphic facial features, including hypotonic facies, ptosis, microretrognathia, and small mouth, are seen in most patients. Seizures are uncommon; some patients have evidence of a peripheral motor neuropathy with distal muscle weakness. The level of X inactivation in lymphocytes and fibroblasts is often skewed, but may not predict the severity of the phenotype. Most cases occur sporadically; rare X-linked dominant inheritance has been reported in families (summary by {1:Frints et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Frints et al. (2019)} reported 14 unrelated females (families 2, 8, 10-14, and 20-23) with sporadic occurrence of WRWFFR associated with de novo heterozygous mutations in the ZC4H2 gene. The patients, who ranged in age from 11 months to 23 years/adulthood, showed a wide variation in clinical presentation and severity. Several patients presented in utero with fetal akinesia and AMC with contractures identified on prenatal ultrasound. In general, the patients presented at birth with AMC and joint contractures, including clenched hands, overlapping digits, ulnar or radial deviation of the hands, metacarpophalangeal contractures, flexion contractures of the wrists, elbows, and knees, hip contractures, sometimes with congenital hip dislocation, rocker bottom feet, clubfeet, Achilles tendon contractures, narrow chest with limited shoulder movements, and progressive kyphosis or scoliosis. Many patients had poor overall growth, sometimes with short stature and/or microcephaly. Many patients had oromotor dysfunction with facial weakness, dysarthria, drooling, dysphagia, and poor feeding; some required a feeding tube. All had some degree of global developmental delay with hypotonia and delayed walking or inability to walk; several patients were wheelchair-bound due to hypotonia, spasticity with hyperreflexia, contractures, and/or distal muscle weakness and atrophy. Although a few patients had mild learning disabilities and were able to attend special schools, most had moderately to severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech and language. IQ of 1 patient was 50. Seizures were uncommon, and brain imaging, when performed, showed nonspecific abnormalities, such as delayed myelination, enlarged ventricles, and brain atrophy. Most patients had dysmorphic features, including brachycephaly, high forehead, facial palsy, microretrognathia, low-set or posteriorly rotated ears, deep-set eyes, ptosis, almond-shaped eyes, anteverted nares, long philtrum, downturned corners of the mouth, small or carp-shaped mouth, cleft palate, and short neck. Other variable features included oculomotor apraxia, hypermetropia, widely spaced nipples, and neuropathic bladder with urinary incontinence. One patient (family 22) had EMG and muscle biopsy evidence of chronic denervation and motor neuron dysfunction resulting in Duane syndrome, swallowing abnormalities, and dysarthria. X-inactivation studies in lymphocytes derived from several patients showed skewed patterns (100:0 in family 2, 95:5 in family 13, 80:20 in family 20, 98:2 in family 21, and 83:17 in family 23). The patients were part of a large cohort of 23 newly identified families with WRWF, which also included families with affected males. The detailed review of clinical features included patients who had previously been reported.

{1:Frints et al. (2019)} also reported a family (family 3) in which 2 sibs, male and female, had a severe neonatal lethal form of the disorder. The proband was a female fetus who showed fetal akinesia and severe congenital malformations with diffuse contractures, dysmorphic facial features, and enlarged brain ventricles on prenatal ultrasound. The pregnancy, which was also complicated by polyhydramnios, was electively terminated, and postmortem examination confirmed the prenatal findings. An earlier pregnancy in the family was an affected male infant with AMC and cleft palate who died of respiratory distress 10 hours after birth, and a subsequent pregnancy resulted in early spontaneous miscarriage at 12 weeks' gestation. The unaffected mother in this family was a mosaic carrier (less than 10%) of the mutation. X-inactivation studies of lymphocytes and fibroblasts from the mother and the affected female fetus showed a random pattern in both (78:22 in the mother and 61:39 in the fetus).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the ZC4H2 gene that were identified in most affected female patients with WRWFFR by {1:Frints et al. (2019)} occurred de novo. In 1 family (family 3), the transmission pattern was consistent with X-linked dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 14 unrelated females with WRWFFR, {1:Frints et al. (2019)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations or intragenic deletions in the ZC4H2 gene (see, e.g., {300897.0008}, {300897.0010}, {300897.0012}-{300897.0014}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome, whole-genome sequencing, or CNV analysis and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not found in the 1000 Genomes Project or gnomAD databases. In family 3, a severely affected female fetus carried a heterozygous frameshift mutation ({300897.0009}) that was found in the mosaic state (less than 10%) in the unaffected mother. A male infant with similar features in the same family had died 10 hours after birth, but DNA from that infant was not available. Most of the mutations were predicted to result in a loss of function and haploinsufficiency: there were 7 nonsense, splice site, or frameshift mutations, 5 intragenic deletions affecting only the ZC4H2 gene, and 2 missense variants affecting highly conserved residues. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells besides X-inactivation studies were not performed. The pathogenic mechanism was postulated as haploinsufficiency.

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 85, with or without midline brain defects

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-85 with or without midline brain defects (DEE85) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SMC1A gene ({300040}) on chromosome Xp11.

Mutation in the SMC1A gene can also cause Cornelia de Lange syndrome-2 (CDLS2; {300590}), a milder disorder with some overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-85 with or without midline brain defects (DEE85) is an X-linked neurologic disorder characterized by onset of severe refractory seizures in the first year of life, global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech, and dysmorphic facial features. The seizures tend to show a cyclic pattern with clustering. Many patients have midline brain defects on brain imaging, including thin corpus callosum and/or variable forms of holoprosencephaly (HPE). The severity and clinical manifestations are variable. Almost all reported patients are females with de novo mutations predicted to result in a loss of function (LOF). However, some patients may show skewed X inactivation, and the pathogenic mechanism may be due to a dominant-negative effect. The SMC1A protein is part of the multiprotein cohesin complex involved in chromatid cohesion during DNA replication and transcriptional regulation; DEE85 can thus be classified as a 'cohesinopathy' (summary by {6:Symonds et al., 2017} and {4:Kruszka et al., 2019}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Hansen et al. (2013)} reported an 11-year-old Swiss girl with DEE85. She was born with microcephaly, congenital hip dysplasia, and diaphragmatic hernia. At age 3 months, she developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures associated with EEG abnormalities; the seizures tended to occur in clusters. She had global developmental delay with mildly delayed walking and mild speech delay. Dysmorphic features included a round face with arched eyebrows, short nose, upslanting palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, mild retrognathia, crowded teeth, flattened midface, clinodactyly, and camptodactyly. The authors noted that the report expanded the phenotypic spectrum associated with SMC1A mutations.

{5:Lebrun et al. (2015)} reported a 7-year-old girl, born of unrelated Portuguese parents, with DEE85. She had intrauterine growth retardation and manifested microcephaly and mild dysmorphic facial features at birth. She had synophrys, thin nose and upper lip, retrognathia, triangular face, and small hands and feet. During the first month of life, she developed refractory focal seizures, infantile spasms, and multifocal seizures associated with hypsarrhythmia on EEG. Thereafter she showed severe developmental delay with poor visual contact, impaired intellectual development, absent speech, axial hypotonia, peripheral hypertonia, spastic tetraparesis, scoliosis, and poor overall growth. Other features included gastroesophageal reflux and stereotypic hand movements. Brain imaging showed small frontal lobes and thin corpus callosum.

{1:Goldstein et al. (2015)} reported 2 unrelated girls with DEE85. Patient A was a 4-year-old girl with intractable epilepsy associated with status epilepticus, global developmental delay, severe hypotonia, limb hyperreflexia, and microcephaly. She was able to walk a few steps at age 18 months, but later regressed and was nonambulatory. She was nonverbal and had a feeding tube. Her seizures were refractory to medication and evolved into clusters with a cyclic frequency every 1 to 2 weeks. Other features included long eyelashes, short nose, hirsutism, and small hands and feet. Brain imaging showed nonspecific findings, including mildly enlarged ventricles, mildly rotated hippocampal heads, and some white matter hyperintensities. Patient B was a 3-year-old girl who had mild developmental delay before the onset of seizures at 11 months of age. The seizures were initially refractory, but eventually were controlled. Brain imaging showed mild enlargement of extraaxial spaces and slight thinning of the corpus callosum. Neither patient showed classic dysmorphic features suggestive of CDLS, thus expanding the phenotypic spectrum.

{3:Jansen et al. (2016)} reported 2 unrelated female patients with DEE85. Patient 1 was a 46-year-old woman with severe developmental delay apparent from infancy. She had impaired intellectual development with absent language and inability to crawl or walk. At age 9 months, she developed refractory seizures associated with EEG abnormalities. She also had a history of cleft palate. Physical examination as an adult showed small head circumference (-2.5 SD), short stature, low anterior hairline, flat midface, straight eyebrows with deep-set eyes, long small ears, long nose, short philtrum, disorganized dentition, small hand with tapering fingers, and contractures of the fingers and toes. Other features included axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, visual impairment, myopia, and scoliosis. Brain imaging showed enlarged ventricles and cerebellar hypoplasia. The other patient was a 14-year-old girl who developed refractory generalized seizures at 2 months of age. She had global developmental delay with loss of ambulation in childhood, severely impaired intellectual development with absent speech, hypotonia, poor feeding requiring a G-tube, and poor overall growth with small head circumference (-2.5 SD). Dysmorphic features included trigonocephaly, upslanting palpebral fissures, blepharophimosis, posteriorly rotated ears, full cheeks, full lips, short philtrum gingival hyperplasia, and small hands with slender fingers. {3:Jansen et al. (2016)} concluded that the phenotype in these patients was distinct from CDLS2.

{6:Symonds et al. (2017)} reported 10 unrelated girls with early-onset refractory seizures, 8 of whom were probands identified through the DDD cohort based on exome sequencing. A ninth patient was a sister of one of the 8 probands, and a tenth patient was identified through analysis of a custom gene panel. All presented with drug-resistant epilepsy within the first months of life (median, 4.5 months), although 2 patients eventually became seizure-free. Seizure types were variable, including afebrile motor seizures, tonic-clonic, clonic, focal, myoclonic, absence, and generalized. EEG showed focal or multifocal abnormalities, spike and sharp-wave complexes, and generalized background slowing; some patients had status epilepticus. The seizures tended to occur in clusters in a cyclic pattern. The patients had moderate to profound developmental delay with delayed walking or inability to walk, impaired intellectual development and absent language, hypotonia, and poor growth with short stature and progressive microcephaly. Four patients had congenital cardiac anomalies, mainly septal defects, 2 had cleft palate, and 2 had bifid thoracic vertebrae. Dysmorphic features included flattened midface, short upturned nose, and shallow philtrum. Brain imaging was normal in 5 patients and showed nonspecific anomalies in 2, whereas 3 had variable midline brain defects, including small cavum septum vergae, thin corpus callosum, and semilobar holoprosencephaly, respectively. Of 2 affected sisters, one (patient 9) had semilobar HPE and died at 11 months of age; the other (patient 8), who carried the same mutation, had no structural organ anomalies, no dysmorphic features, and normal brain MRI. None of the patients were considered clinically to have features of CDLS before the genetic analysis, and the authors suggested that the phenotype was not only distinct from, but also more severe than CDLS.

<Subhead> Patients with Significant Midline Brain Defects

{4:Kruszka et al. (2019)} reported 5 unrelated girls (patients 7-11), ranging in age from 15 months to 6 years, with early-onset epileptic encephalopathy and midline brain defects. The patients were ascertained due to holoprosencephaly. Four patients had early-onset seizures; seizures were not reported in a 15-month-old girl. Three patients had semilobar HPE, 1 had triventricular ectasia, and 1 had middle interhemispheric HPE. All had microcephaly, and most had dysmorphic facial features, including brachycephaly, sloping forehead, arched eyebrows, synophrys, midface flattening, bitemporal narrowing, depressed nasal bridge, upslanting palpebral fissures, and single central incisor. Additional common but variable features included growth delay, small hands and feet, and feeding problems. One patient had spina bifida and another had patent foramen ovale.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SMC1A gene that were identified in female patients with DEE85 with or without midline brain defects by {1:Goldstein et al. (2015)}, {3:Jansen et al. (2016)}, and {4:Kruszka et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In an 11-year-old Swiss girl with DEE85, {2:Hansen et al. (2013)} identified a de novo heterozygous mutation (c.1731G-A, E577E) in the SMC1A gene, predicted to result in a splicing defect. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In a 7-year-old girl, born of unrelated Portuguese parents, with DEE85, {5:Lebrun et al. (2015)} identified a de novo heterozygous splice site mutation in the SMC1A gene ({300040.0007}). The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed the presence of only the mutant transcript, which was significantly reduced compared to controls, suggesting nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and a loss of function (LOF).

In 2 unrelated girls with DEE85, {1:Goldstein et al. (2015)} identified de novo heterozygous frameshift mutations in the SMC1A gene ({300040.0008} and {300040.0009}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. X-inactivation studies in peripheral blood cells showed a skewed pattern (93:7) in 1 patient, but a random pattern in the other. Additional functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 2 unrelated females with DEE85, {3:Jansen et al. (2016)} identified de novo heterozygous LOF mutations in the SMC1A gene (see, e.g., {300040.0010}). The mutations were found by whole-genome sequencing. X-inactivation studies in 1 patient showed a random pattern, whereas it was skewed in the other patient (85:15); additional functional studies were not performed. {3:Jansen et al. (2016)} concluded that the de novo LOF mutations in the SMC1A gene in females cause an abnormal dosage effect and that the resulting phenotype is distinct from CDLS2. The authors further suggested that LOF mutations in males may be embryonic lethal.

In 10 unrelated females with DEE85, {6:Symonds et al. (2017)} identified de novo heterozygous nonsense, frameshift, or splice site mutations in the SMC1A gene (see, e.g., {300040.0011}-{300040.0013}). Functional studies of the variants were not performed. X-inactivation studies, performed in some patients, had variable results: some showed a random pattern, whereas others had a skewed pattern. {6:Symonds et al. (2017)} speculated that if SMC1A escapes X inactivation, then haploinsufficiency is unlikely to be the causative mechanism; rather, the authors postulated a dominant-negative effect. The findings also suggested that complete SMC1A deficiency is embryonic lethal, as no males with such mutations have been reported.

In 5 unrelated girls (patients 7-11) with DEE85 and variable midline brain defects, including holoprosencephaly (HPE), {4:Kruszka et al. (2019)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the SMC1A gene (see, e.g., {300040.0014} and {300040.0015}). All mutations except 1 were nonsense, frameshift, or splice site mutations, suggesting a loss-of-function effect; there was 1 missense mutation. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. Knockdown of the SMC1A gene in human neural progenitor cells resulted in upregulation of GLI2 ({165230}), ZIC2 ({603073}), and SMAD3 ({603109}) gene expression. Although the significance of these findings was unclear, they demonstrated that loss of SMC1A perturbs the expression of genes involved in HPE. The patients were part of a cohort of 277 individuals with HPE as well as gathered through collaborative efforts such as GeneMatcher.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that X-linked multiple congenital anomalies-neurodevelopmental syndrome (MCAND) is caused by hemizygous mutation in the OTUD5 gene ({300713}) on chromosome Xp11.

description.title: Description
description.content: X-linked multiple congenital anomalies-neurodevelopmental syndrome (MCAND) is an X-linked recessive congenital multisystemic disorder characterized by poor growth, global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, and variable abnormalities of the cardiac, skeletal, and genitourinary systems. Most affected individuals also have hypotonia and dysmorphic craniofacial features. Brain imaging typically shows enlarged ventricles and thin corpus callosum; some have microcephaly, whereas others have hydrocephalus. The severity of the disorder is highly variable, ranging from death in early infancy to survival into the second or third decade. Pathogenetically, the disorder results from disrupted gene expression and signaling during embryogenesis, thus affecting multiple systems (summary by {2:Tripolszki et al., 2021} and {1:Beck et al., 2021}). {1:Beck et al. (2021)} referred to the disorder as LINKED syndrome (LINKage-specific deubiquitylation deficiency-induced Embryonic Defects).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Tripolszki et al. (2021)} reported a large family in which 13 males spanning 3 generations were affected with a severe multisystemic developmental disorder. All but one were deceased: most died in utero, infancy, or early childhood, although 1 patient died at age 37 years. Clinical details were available for 6 patients. They presented in infancy with hypotonia, respiratory insufficiency, and poor growth and feeding difficulties, followed by global developmental delay. Common dysmorphic features included macrocephaly often associated with hydrocephalus, craniosynostosis, deep-set eyes, hypertelorism, large forehead, flat nasal bridge, low-set ears, nystagmus, and strabismus. Most patients had hypospadias and cryptorchidism, limb or hand contractures, foot deformities, and short stature. More variable features included congenital cardiac defects, such as septal defects or pulmonary stenosis, renal anomalies including hydronephrosis, seizures, and visual impairment. Brain imaging showed enlarged ventricles and dysgenesis of the corpus callosum. No clinical information was available for the other affected males in the family who died in infancy or early childhood, but they were reported to have been small, hypotonic infants with poor feeding, developmental delay, micropenis, and impaired vision.

{1:Beck et al. (2021)} reported 10 patients from 7 unrelated families with a developmental disorder associated with multiple congenital anomalies. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts. Four patients (P1-P4) from 2 families (F1 and F2) had a severe phenotype resulting in death in infancy. Six patients (P5-P10) from 5 additional families (F3-F7) had a somewhat attenuated phenotype and were alive between 2 and 14 years of age. Common features among all patients included intrauterine growth retardation, poor postnatal growth, microcephaly, hypotonia, and global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development. Six patients had cardiac defects, including septal defects, double outlet right ventricle, pulmonary stenosis, and pulmonary atresia. Genitourinary abnormalities were also commonly observed; these included micropenis, cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and vesicoureteral reflux. Many patients had variable limb or skeletal anomalies, such as clubfeet, rocker-bottom feet, postaxial polydactyly, overlapping fingers, and butterfly vertebrae. Notable dysmorphic features included craniosynostosis, midface hypoplasia, retrognathia, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, hypermetropia, strabismus, nystagmus, astigmatism, and depressed nasal bridge. More variable features included hirsutism, nonspecific renal anomalies, and feeding difficulties, sometimes requiring tube feeding. Brain imaging showed enlarged ventricles and thin or absent corpus callosum; one patient each had pontocerebellar hypoplasia and polymicrogyria.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MCAND in the families reported by {2:Tripolszki et al. (2021)} and {1:Beck et al. (2021)} was consistent with X-linked recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 affected males from a large multigenerational family with MCAND, {2:Tripolszki et al. (2021)} identified a hemizygous missense mutation in the OTUD5 gene (E200K; {300713.0001}). The mutation, which was found by genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database (v2.1.1). The variant segregated with the disorder in the family; there were 4 unaffected female carriers. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 10 patients from 7 unrelated families with MCAND, {1:Beck et al. (2021)} identified 7 different hemizygous mutations in the OTUD5 gene (see, e.g., {300713.0002}-{300713.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families except the patient in family 2 who had a de novo mutation. There were 5 missense mutations, 1 splice site, and 1 in-frame deletion. None were present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional studies of some of the mutations showed that they resulted in a loss of function by various effects, including a reduction in protein levels, mislocalization of the protein, or disruption of K48- or K63-linked ubiquitin chain cleavage. Induced pluripotent stem cells derived from 1 patient showed defects in neuroectodermal differentiation compared to controls. Cellular knockdown of OTUD5 resulted in similar differentiation abnormalities that could not be rescued by mutant OTUD5. Expression of some of the variants in mice resulted in lethality. Detailed proteomic experiments using mass spectrometry identified chromatin remodelers as substrates of OTUD5, suggesting that OTUD5 controls neuroectodermal cell fate by regulating chromatin accessibility, which enables activation of transcriptional networks that drive differentiation. {1:Beck et al. (2021)} concluded that OTUD5 regulates cell fate decisions during embryogenesis by cleaving K48-ubiquitin linkage on substrates. Reduction of this activity through mutation results in defective embryogenesis and leads to a multiple congenital anomaly syndrome. Thus, aberrant degradation of chromatin regulators is a major disease mechanism, similar to the pathogenetic mechanisms of Coffin-Siris syndrome (see, e.g., CSS1, {135900}) and Cornelia de Lange syndrome (see, e.g., CDLS1, {122470}), both of which show some overlapping clinical features.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-90 (DEE90) is caused by hemizygous or heterozygous mutation in the FHF2 gene (FGF13; {300070}) on chromosome Xq26.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-90 (DEE90) is an X-linked neurologic disorder characterized by onset of refractory seizures in the first days or months of life. Although most patients have focal seizures associated with oromotor automatisms and apnea, various seizure types may occur, including epileptic spasms, generalized tonic-clonic, and absence. EEG shows multifocal discharges; hypsarrhythmia, intermittent burst suppression, and slow spike-wave background resembling Lennox-Gastaut syndrome may also be observed. Affected individuals have global developmental delay with variable severity, but it is usually profound or severe. Some are unable to walk or speak, whereas others may achieve some milestones and show autistic features (summary by {1:Fry et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Fry et al. (2021)} reported 7 patients, including 6 males and 1 female, from 5 unrelated families with a similar developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. The patients, who ranged in age from 2 to 19 years, presented between day 1 and 6 months of age with seizure-like behavior, including apnea, lip smacking, repetitive swallowing, eye deviation, facial twitching, and autonomic features, such as drooling and vomiting. The seizures, which were mostly resistant to medication, were consistent with focal seizures, often with secondary generalization. Other seizure types, including epileptic spasms, absence, tonic, and myoclonic, were also observed. EEG showed multiple epileptogenic foci and was sometimes consistent with a clinical diagnosis of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Two sibs from family B had hypsarrhythmia and the patient from family E had atypical hypsarrhythmia and an intermittent burst-suppression pattern. All patients had severe to profound developmental delay with delayed walking or inability to walk, poor or absent speech, and poor communication. Three patients were diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Other more variable features included hypotonia, unstable gait, abnormal movements, hyperreflexia, scoliosis, feeding problems, cortical visual impairment, and constipation. Some patients had nonspecific dysmorphic facial features with hypotonia, coarse facies, and strabismus. Brain imaging was normal in most patients, but cerebral atrophy was present in 2 patients, and hippocampal white matter abnormalities and thin corpus callosum in another. The only affected girl, P2, who was the sister of P1 (family A), had a similar phenotype, with onset of seizures on day 11 of life and severely impaired psychomotor development. Although she had undergone left anterior temporal lobectomy and partial amygdalohippocampectomy at age 7 years, seizures persisted. She achieved walking and was able to attend a special school, showing a slightly less severe phenotype compared to her brother.

{2:Narayanan et al. (2022)} described a 16-month-old girl with DEE90. Her head circumference was more than 2 SD below the median at birth, and her weight and length were at -1 SD. She was noted to have excessive crying from age 3 months and regression of milestones at age 8 months. At 5 months of age she developed tonic-clonic seizures of left upper and lower limbs. She had microcytic hypochromic anemia and elevated lactate level. An EEG showed sleep activation of occasional left temporal spikes, and MRI showed prominent frontotemporal subarachnoid spaces, thin corpus callosum, and mild delayed myelination. She continued to have focal seizures despite treatment. At 1 year of age, a repeat EEG showed focal epileptiform abnormalities over the left frontocentral region consistent with the diagnosis of left frontocentral focal epilepsy, and a repeat MRI showed prominent frontotemporal subarachnoid spaces without cerebral atrophy and thin corpus callosum; myelination was normal. On examination, she was nondysmorphic except for medial flaring of eyebrows and tented upper lip vermilion. She had generalized hypotonia. At 2 years of age, she was noted to have focal seizures despite treatment. She also had chronic constipation.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE90 in the families reported by {1:Fry et al. (2021)} was consistent with X-linked inheritance. Of 7 patients with the disorder, 6 were males and 1 was a female. There was also evidence of mutations occurring de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 7 patients, including 6 males and 1 female, from 5 unrelated families with DEE90, {1:Fry et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous or hemizygous missense mutations in exon 1A of the FGF13 (FHF2) gene (R11C, {300070.0001}; R14T, {300070.0002}; and R11P {300070.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Segregation studies, when possible, suggested de novo occurrence, although there were 2 families (A and B) with 2 affected sibs, consistent with maternal mosaicism. In vitro electrophysiologic studies in transfected neuronal cells showed that the R11C mutation reduced long-term inactivation of sodium channels compared to wildtype, whereas R14T was completely incapable of promoting long-term inactivation. The sodium channels in cells expressing R11C recovered from long-term activation by 200 ms, compared to 1 s in cells with wildtype FGF13. Sodium channels in cells expressing R14T showed no evidence of long-term inactivation, as channels fully recovered as quickly as in cells lacking FGF13. The mutations did not affect protein expression or binding of FGF13 to the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain of sodium channels. The findings indicated that the mutations disrupted the ability of the FGF13 N-terminal inactivation particle to cause long-term inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels. {1:Fry et al. (2021)} concluded that the mutations have a gain-of-function effect that is likely to increase neuronal excitability.

In a 16-month-old girl with DEE90, {2:Narayanan et al. (2022)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the FGF13 gene (I5S; {300070.0004}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database or in an in-house database. The authors noted that all reported mutations in the FGF13 gene in patients with DEE90 involved exon 1. Exon 1A codes for the highly conserved N-terminal domain of isoform A of the FGF13 protein and has both proexcitatory and inhibitory effects on voltage-gated sodium channels.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder, X-linked syndromic, with pigmentary mosaicism and coarse facies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that X-linked syndromic intellectual developmental disorder with pigmentary mosaicism and coarse facies (MRXSPF) is caused by hemizygous or heterozygous mutation in the TFE3 gene ({314310}) on chromosome Xp11.

description.title: Description
description.content: X-linked syndromic intellectual developmental disorder with pigmentary mosaicism and coarse facies (MRXSPF) is characterized by a phenotypic triad of severe developmental delay, coarse facial dysmorphisms, and Blaschkoid pigmentary mosaicism. Additional clinical features may include epilepsy, orthopedic abnormalities, hypotonia, and growth abnormalities. The disorder affects both males and females ({2:Villegas et al., 2019}; {1:Diaz et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Villegas et al. (2019)} reported 5 patients, including 4 females, aged 3 to 20 years, and 1 male, aged 5 years, with severely impaired intellectual development. One patient (patient 5) walked at age 40 months and spoke a few words, whereas the other patients did not walk or have speech. Four of the patients had epilepsy. Brain MRIs were normal in all 5 patients. Facial features included hypertelorism (4/5), cleft lip and palate (1/5), flat nasal bridge (3/5), bifid nose (1/5), coarse facial features (4/5), hypertrichosis (2/5), and thick lips (2/5). Four of 5 patients had hypopigmentation on Blaschko lines. Skeletal features included flat feet (3/5), hyperlordosis (2/5), and clubfeet (1/5). Two patients had an umbilical hernia and 2 patients had strabismus.

{1:Diaz et al. (2020)} reported 2 female patients, aged 11 and 5 years, with severe developmental delay, including impaired intellectual development, and autism spectrum disorder. Both patients had a history of developmental regression and hand stereotypies. Both patients were able to walk and speak a few words. One of the patients had epilepsy, and both had hypotonia. Brain MRI was normal in both patients. Other features shared by the patients included Blaschkoid pigmentary mosaicism, hepatomegaly, and recurrent otitis media.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MRXSPF in the patients reported by {2:Villegas et al. (2019)} and {1:Diaz et al. (2020)} was consistent with X-linked inheritance. The heterozygous mutations in the TFE3 gene that were found in females occurred de novo. The mutation in the male reported by {2:Villegas et al. (2019)} was de novo mosaic.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 5 unrelated patients with MRXSPF, {2:Villegas et al. (2019)} identified mutations in the TFE3 gene, including de novo hemizygous mutations in 4 females ({314310.0001}-{314310.0004}) and a de novo mosaic mutation in 1 male ({314310.0005}). The mutations occurred in exons 3 and 4, which are predicted to form a domain containing 2 stable alpha helices and to form a RAG-binding fold that is crucial for cytoplasmic TFE3 inactivation.

In 2 unrelated females with MRXSPF, {1:Diaz et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in exon 3 and a de novo splice site mutation in intron 4 of the TFE3 gene ({314310.0006}-{314310.0007}), respectively. The mutations were found by trio whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies were not performed.

clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, mild to profound
Contiguous gene syndrome caused by 390kb-1.7Mb duplication of Xq13 encompassing at least SLC16A2 () and RLIM ()

Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, mild to profound
Molecular Basis: Contiguous gene syndrome caused by 390kb-1.7Mb duplication of Xq13 encompassing at least SLC16A2 () and RLIM ()

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that it represents a contiguous gene syndrome on chromosome Xq13.2-q13.3 that involves the RLIM ({300379}) gene in all patients and variably includes the NEXMIF ({300524}), SLC16A2 ({300095}), and FTX ({300936}) genes. Increased dosage of the RLIM gene is believed to be primarily responsible for the phenotype ({1:Palmer et al., 2020}).

Point mutations in the RLIM, NEXMIF, and SLC16A2 genes have been found to cause Tonne-Kalscheuer syndrome ({300978}), XLID98 ({300912}), and Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome ({300523}), respectively.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Palmer et al. (2020)} reported 14 males from 8 families with an age range of 3 to 60 years. Twelve of the patients had mildly to severely impaired intellectual development. Two patients had speech delay. One patient had epileptic encephalopathy, 2 patients had possible afebrile seizures, and 1 patient had febrile seizures. Three patients had autism spectrum disorder, 4 patients had some features of autism spectrum disorder, and 1 patient had a pervasive developmental disorder. Six patients had disordered sleep. Musculoskeletal features included hypotonia in 5 patients, pes planus in 3 patients, and hypermobility of small joints/fingers in 3 patients. Variable facial features included short palpebral fissures, straight and medially flared eyebrows, and a flat midface.

cytogenetics.title: Cytogenetics
cytogenetics.content: Using chromosome microarray analysis, {1:Palmer et al. (2020)} identified overlapping duplications of Xq13.2-q13.3 in 14 males from 8 families with X-linked impaired intellectual development and distinctive facial features. All of the duplications were inherited from an unaffected mother. In all tested carrier mothers, X-chromosome inactivation was moderately to severely skewed. The minimal overlapping region in the patients contained only the RLIM gene. Flanking genes that were duplicated in some patients included NEXMIF, SLC16A2, and FTX, a long noncoding RNA gene. Studies in lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) from 5 patients demonstrated increased RLIM gene expression compared to controls, and FTX expression was increased in the 3 males in whom this gene was fully or partially duplicated. NEXMIF gene expression was variable in both patients and controls. RLIM protein expression was increased in the 5 patient LCL lines, and downstream expression of the target protein MDM2 ({164785}) was decreased, but expression of the MDM2 target TP53 ({191170}) was unchanged. SLC16A2, which is not expressed in LCLs, was tested in fibroblasts from one patient, and its gene expression was not changed compared to controls. {1:Palmer et al. (2020)} concluded that the most likely gene duplication responsible for the main phenotype was RLIM, but contributions from FTX, SLC16A2, and NEXMIF could not be excluded.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder, X-linked syndromic, Pilorge type

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that the Pilorge type of X-linked syndromic intellectual developmental disorder (MRXSP) is caused by heterozygous or hemizygous mutation in the GLRA2 gene ({305990}) on chromosome Xp22.

description.title: Description
description.content: The Pilorge type of X-linked syndromic intellectual developmental disorder (MRXSP) is characterized by global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, speech delay, and behavioral abnormalities, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD). More variable features include motor incoordination, seizures, and ocular abnormalities (summary by {1:Marcogliese et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Pilorge et al. (2016)} reported 2 unrelated male patients with autism spectrum disorder and other neurologic deficits associated with hemizygous mutations in the GLRA2 gene. Patient 1 had language delay, low-average IQ of 82, and some motor coordination difficulties. He had no dysmorphic features or seizures. As a young adult, he lived with his parents and worked in a sheltered environment. Patient 2 had severe language delay, mild intellectual disability (IQ of 63), and onset of generalized tonic-clonic seizures starting at 18 years of age. He lived by himself in a sheltered home environment and could care for personal needs. Patient 2 had a sister, who did not carry the GLRA2 mutation, with autism, more severe intellectual disability, and an episode of psychosis.

{3:Piton et al. (2011)} reported a girl with autism, loss of acquired words, seizures, mild motor developmental delay, macrocephaly, and hypothyroidism associated with a heterozygous variant in the GLRA2 gene. The variant was inherited from her unaffected mother.

Using online matchmaking software, including GeneMatcher, {1:Marcogliese et al. (2022)} identified 13 patients with variable developmental delay who had mutations in the GLRA2 gene. The authors had identified the GLRA2 gene through studies in Drosophila as having a role in behavior, which they postulated could extend to humans. Eight females (patients 1-8) all had de novo heterozygous mutations, and 5 males (patients 9-13) had hemizygous mutations. The 8 females, who ranged from 6 months to 6.7 years of age, had developmental delay with intellectual disability. Some had hypotonia or incoordination. One was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, 1 had psychosis, 4 had inattention/hyperactivity, and 3 had sleep disturbances. Four had early-onset seizures with EEG abnormalities and 1 had EEG abnormalities suggestive of epilepsy. Patient 2 had early-onset epileptic encephalopathy between ages 6 months and 2 years when the seizures remitted, patient 4 had infantile spasms and seizures and died at age 7 months secondary to complications of COVID-19, patient 6 had infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia on EEG, consistent with a diagnosis of West syndrome, and patient 7 had infantile spasms that evolved to atonic and tonic-clonic seizures. The severity of neurologic impairment was variable: some patients (patients 1 and 8) were able to attend school, although they had learning difficulties. Other patients had severe speech delay or absent speech, poor concentration, and ataxic gait. Four had microcephaly and 1 had borderline microcephaly. Ocular features included nystagmus, myopia, astigmatism, exotropia, strabismus, and oculomotor apraxia. Brain imaging was normal in 4 patients and showed variable nonspecific abnormalities in the others, including cortical atrophy, delayed myelination, thin corpus callosum, and white matter abnormalities. Some had nonspecific dysmorphic facial features. All the females carried de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the GLRA2 gene.

The 5 males reported by {1:Marcogliese et al. (2022)} ranged from 11 months to 35 years of age and had developmental delay with mildly delayed walking, motor difficulties such as hypotonia and incoordination, variable intellectual disability, and speech delay. Three patients had ASD and 1 was suspected to have autism; the fifth patient, at 11 months old, was too young for evaluation. Some patients had inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, agitated behavior, or anxiety. A few patients were able to attend school with special aids and therapies. The 35-year-old had cognitive and social difficulties, but no seizures, and was able to complete high school. Three patients had various types of seizures, including generalized tonic-clonic, absence, and myoclonic. One patient showed developmental regression after seizure onset at age 2.5 years. Ocular abnormalities, including myopia, strabismus, astigmatism, and reduced visual acuity were also observed. Three patients were noted to have variable dysmorphic features, including long face, high anterior hairline, epicanthal folds, downslanting palpebral fissures, broad eyebrows, long eyelashes, bulbous nose, and broad nasal tip. Brain imaging, performed in 4 patients, was normal in 2 patients and showed T2-weighted signal abnormalities in the other 2 patients. Four patients inherited a hemizygous GLRA2 mutation from an unaffected mother, whereas 1 (patient 12) inherited the mutation from a mildly affected mother who had skewed X inactivation (60:40). The unaffected mother of patient 9 also had skewed X inactivation (82%).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The transmission pattern of MRXSP in a family reported by {2:Pilorge et al. (2016)} was consistent with X-linked recessive inheritance. Hemizygous mutations in the GLRA2 gene that were identified in 2 additional male patients with MRXSP occurred de novo.

The transmission pattern of MRXSP in the families of affected males reported by {1:Marcogliese et al. (2022)} was consistent with X-linked recessive inheritance. Heterozygous mutations in the GLRA2 gene that were identified in females with MRXSP occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
{2:Pilorge et al. (2016)} reported 3 different hemizygous mutations in the GLRA2 gene ({305990.0001}-{305990.0003}) in 3 male patients with MRXSP. The patients were ascertained from large cohorts of males with autism spectrum disorder who underwent genetic analysis. There were 2 missense variants and 1 small intragenic deletion. Two mutations occurred de novo and the third was inherited from an unaffected mother. In vitro functional expression studies showed that the mutations interfered with GLRA2 localization and/or function, resulting in absent or impaired glycine receptor activation, which is consistent with a loss of function. The overall findings supported a role for glycinergic transmission in neurocognitive development. No other pathogenic GLRA2 mutations were identified in over 4,000 males with autism spectrum disorder or other neurodevelopmental disorders, suggesting that they are very rare events.

In a girl with MRXSP, {3:Piton et al. (2011)} identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the GLRA2 gene (R350L; {305990.0004}). The patient was ascertained from a cohort of 142 patients with autism spectrum disorder who underwent direct sequencing of 111 X-linked synaptic genes, including GLRA2. The variant was inherited from the patient's unaffected mother; X-inactivation studies were not performed. {4:Zhang et al. (2017)} performed detailed electrophysiologic studies in HEK293 cells, which showed that the R350L mutation caused altered glycine receptor channel properties and kinetics, with increased inhibitory postsynaptic current (IPSC) rise and decay times. The slowed decay times, longer duration of active periods, and increased conductance of the mutant channel indicated that the mutation results in a gain-of-function effect.

In 8 unrelated females (patients 1-8) with MRXSP, {1:Marcogliese et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the GLRA2 gene. Six patients carried the same variant in the GLRA2 gene (T296M; {305990.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies were performed only for the T296M variant. {1:Marcogliese et al. (2022)} found that expression of high levels of T296M caused lethality in Drosophila, whereas low levels of T296M expression caused the formation of melanized nodules in the thorax. Electroretinogram studies in mutant Drosophila suggested that the T296M variant increases synaptic transmission when expressed in postsynaptic neurons, but not at presynaptic neurons. These findings suggested that T296M may act as a gain-of-function allele. Studies of patient cells were not performed. {1:Marcogliese et al. (2022)} also identified 5 different hemizygous missense variants (see, e.g., R252C; {305990.0006}) in 5 unrelated male patients with MRXSP. All were maternally inherited: 4 of the mothers were unaffected, whereas 1 mother with skewed X-inactivation (60:40) was mildly affected. Functional studies were performed only for the R252C variant. Viability studies in mutant Drosophila indicated that the R252C variant was a loss-of-function allele. Electroretinogram studies in mutant flies suggested that the R252C variant decreases synaptic transmission when expressed in synaptic neurons, further suggesting that it causes a loss of GLRA2 function. Studies of patient cells were not performed. The authors concluded that the recurrent de novo T296M mutation in females acts as a gain-of-function allele and that the rare GLRA2 variants found in males behave as loss-of-function alleles.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Pilorge et al. (2016)} found that morpholino knockdown of the glra2 ortholog in zebrafish led to hyperbranching of spinal motor axons compared to controls. These abnormalities could be rescued by expression of the wildtype gene, but not by mutations found in humans. Glra2-null mice had no abnormalities in social behavior, but showed short and long-term learning and memory deficits for novel objects; spatial learning was similar to wildtype. This was associated with impaired long-term potentiation in vitro in cortical slices from Glra2-null mice. These findings suggested that defective glycinergic signaling results in abnormal plasticity in the prefrontal cortex, a region implicated in autism spectrum disorder.

phenotypes.phenotype: Epilepsy, X-linked 2, with or without impaired intellectual development and dysmorphic features

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that X-linked epilepsy-2 with or without impaired intellectual development and dysmorphic features (EPILX2) is caused by hemizygous or heterozygous mutation in the GABRA3 gene ({305660}) on chromosome Xq28.

description.title: Description
description.content: X-linked epilepsy-2 with or without impaired intellectual development and dysmorphic features (EPILX2) is a neurologic disorder characterized by the onset of seizures usually in the first years of life, although later onset may also occur. Most individuals also have developmental delay, speech delay, and intellectual disability or learning difficulties. Some patients have dysmorphic facial features or mild skeletal anomalies. The severity of the disorder and accompanying features are highly variable, even within the same family. In general, males are more severely affected than females, although there is evidence for incomplete penetrance in both sexes ({1:Niturad et al., 2017}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Niturad et al. (2017)} reported 3 unrelated families (families 1, 2, and 3) with various forms of epilepsy associated with a range of neurologic defects, including impaired intellectual development and learning difficulties, segregating in an X-linked pattern of inheritance. Two brothers from family 1, of Israeli descent, developed seizures at 3 years of age and showed global developmental delay with moderate to severe intellectual disability. The older brother had refractory seizures and was diagnosed with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. At age 18 he was nonverbal, had poor eye contact, and was living in an institution. The younger brother died of choking during a seizure at 10 years of age. Their 14-year-old sister and 42-year-old mother, who also carried the mutation, were less severely affected. The sister had developmental delay with mildly impaired intellectual development and learning disabilities. She developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures at age 7 years that were mostly controlled by medication. The mother had developmental delay, learning disabilities, and experienced 4 isolated generalized tonic-clonic seizures from 21 years of age. Additional notable features in the affected members of family 1 included cleft palate, micrognathia, horizontal nystagmus, sloping shoulders, short stature, short neck, and scoliosis. Family 2, of Polish descent, demonstrated more intrafamilial phenotypic variability. There were 4 female mutation carriers: 2 had absence seizures with mild learning difficulties, and 2 had learning difficulties without seizures. Of the 4 male mutation carriers, 2 showed mild developmental delay with learning difficulties and onset of absence seizures in their teens. Both were able to graduate from special schooling. A third male mutation carrier did not have seizures, but showed mild intellectual disability, learning disabilities, hyperactivity, and speech defects. These individuals also had dysmorphic features of variable severity, including micrognathia, small mouth, large ears, tall stature, tapering fingers, cleft palate, and horizontal nystagmus. The remaining male mutation carrier in family 2 was unaffected and finishing higher education at 25 years of age; this was an example of incomplete penetrance. An Italian boy in family 3 presented with seizures at 3 years of age; he had borderline intellectual functioning. His mother, who also carried the mutation, was unaffected. This boy had a sister who had a single febrile seizure at 10 months of age, but she did not carry the mutation, indicating a phenocopy. {1:Niturad et al. (2017)} also identified 2 unrelated girls (families 4 and 5) with epilepsy who were found to carry a de novo heterozygous mutation in the GABRA3 gene; neither had a family history of a similar disorder. Both had mild speech delay and developed seizures in the first years of life. They had mildly impaired intellectual development and behavioral abnormalities, including anxiety in 1 and autistic features in the other.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of EPILX2 in some of the families reported by {1:Niturad et al. (2017)} was consistent with X-linked inheritance with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. However, heterozygous mutations in the GABRA3 gene that were identified in 2 female patients with EPILX2 occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In affected members of 2 unrelated families (families 1 and 2) with EPILX2, {1:Niturad et al. (2017)} identified hemizygous or heterozygous missense mutations in the GABRA3 gene ({305660.0001}-{305660.0002}). Another boy (family 3) carried a heterozygous intragenic deletion ({305660.0004}) that was inherited from his unaffected mother. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families, although there was variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance. Two additional girls with the disorder carried a de novo heterozygous missense variant (Y474C; {305660.0003}). Most of the mutations were absent from the gnomAD database; 1 variant was present once in gnomAD. In vitro electrophysiologic studies in Xenopus oocytes showed that the mutations resulted in a significant reduction in GABA-evoked current amplitudes compared to controls, consistent with a loss of function. X-inactivation studies, performed in several individuals, did not show significant skewing patterns. {1:Niturad et al. (2017)} identified 2 additional variants in the GABRA3 gene in 2 more families (families 6 and 7), but these variants did not segregate with the disorder in the families. The proband in family 6 was a boy with speech delay and autism spectrum disorder, but no seizures, associated with a hemizygous G47R variant. He had a similarly affected brother who did not carry the variant. The proband in family 7 was a girl with onset of seizures at 8 years of age associated with a heterozygous T336M variant that was inherited from her unaffected mother. Her sister and father both had seizures, but did not carry the GABRA3 variant.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Hijazi-Reis syndrome (HIJRS) is caused by hemizygous or heterozygous mutation in the TCEAL1 gene ({300237}) on chromosome Xq22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Hijazi-Reis syndrome (HIJRS) is an X-linked dominant disorder characterized by global developmental delay with hypotonia, motor delay, impaired intellectual development, and speech and language delay. Affected individuals also have dysmorphic facial features, gastrointestinal issues, and ocular anomalies. Rare patients have seizures ({1:Hijazi et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Hijazi et al. (2022)} reported 4 unrelated males (individuals 1, 2, 3, and 4) and 2 unrelated females (individuals 5 and 7) with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder who were ascertained through collaborative research efforts after exome sequencing identified hemizygous or heterozygous mutations in the TCEAL1 gene. The patients, who ranged from 5 to 17 years of age, had global developmental delay with hypotonia, delayed walking with an unsteady gait, ataxia, or inability to walk, and impaired intellectual development with particular deficits in expressive language. The males were more severely affected cognitively than the females. Behavioral abnormalities, including autistic features, outbursts, repetitive behavior, and tics, were common. Three patients had seizures, including 1 patient with a single seizure. A few had feeding problems, constipation, gastroesophageal reflux, or dysmotility issues; 1 was tube-fed at 10 years of age. Most had variable ocular abnormalities, including astigmatism, strabismus, and myopia/hyperopia; 1 patient had nystagmus and another had iris coloboma. Common dysmorphic features included broad forehead, low-set ears, deep-set eyes, telecanthus, and bow-shaped upper lip. Several patients had recurrent infections. Brain imaging was normal in some, but abnormal in 3 patients who were found to have myelination defects and possible shortening of the corpus callosum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The hemizygous and heterozygous mutations in the TCEAL1 gene that were identified in patients with HIJRS by {1:Hijazi et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 unrelated patients, including 4 males (individuals 1-4) and 1 female (individual 7), with HIJRS, {1:Hijazi et al. (2022)} identified de novo hemizygous or heterozygous mutations in the TCEAL1 gene ({300237.0001}-{300237.0005}). Three males and the female carried nonsense or frameshift mutations, predicted to result in a loss of function, and 1 male carried a hemizygous missense variant (C90Y; {300237.0004}). Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors suggested that the truncating variants may escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay because all occurred in the final and only-coding exon 3. A 17-year-old girl (individual 5) with a similar phenotype was found to have a de novo heterozygous 14-kb deletion on chromosome Xq22 (chrX:102,879,326-102,893,312) (GRCh37/hg19) encompassing only the TCEAL1 gene that was identified through high-density aCGH. This finding suggested that a loss of TCEAL1 function and haploinsufficiency for the gene underlies the human neurologic disease traits. {1:Hijazi et al. (2022)} also identified a 12-year-old boy (individual 8) with a distinct phenotype (normal intellectual development and spasticity) who carried a hemizygous missense variant (D116N) of uncertain significance in the TCEAL1 gene that was inherited from his unaffected mother. Functional studies of this variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that X-linked intellectual developmental disorder-111 (XLID111) is caused by hemizygous or heterozygous mutation in the SLITRK2 gene ({300561}) on chromosome Xq27.

description.title: Description
description.content: X-linked intellectual developmental disorder-111 (XLID111) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by different degrees of impaired intellectual development associated with motor, speech, and behavioral impairments ({1:El Chehadeh et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:El Chehadeh et al. (2022)} described 8 patients, 7 males and 1 female from 7 unrelated families, with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients ranged in age from 8 to 30 years. Seven patients had developmental delay and 1 patient (patient 3) had developmental regression. All of the patients had impaired intellectual development, which was borderline in 1, mild in 2, moderate to severe in 3, and severe in 2. Neuropsychiatric features included anxiety (7/8), autism spectrum disorder (4/8), attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (2/8), and aggression (2/8). Four patients had an unsteady gait, 3 had spasticity and/or dystonia, and 3 had seizures. Other features included feeding difficulties in 4 patients, kyphoscoliosis in 4 patients, macrocephaly in 2 patients, and microcephaly in 1 patient. Brain MRI was abnormal in 4 patients, including white matter abnormalities in 3 patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of XLID111 in the family reported by {1:El Chehadeh et al. (2022)} was consistent with X-linked inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: By whole-exome sequencing in 8 patients, including 2 sibs, from 7 unrelated families with XLID111, {1:El Chehadeh et al. (2022)} identified hemizygous or heterozygous mutations in the SLITRK2 gene ({300561.0001}-{300561.0006}). The mutation arose de novo in the 1 female patient (patient 4), was inherited from the mother in 5 patients, and was inherited in the 2 sibs (patients 1 and 2) from a mother who was assumed to have germline mosaicism because the mutation was absent in her blood. Expression of SLITRK2 with the E461X ({300561.0001}) mutation in cultured neurons resulted in abnormal dendritic branching and abnormal protein localization. Expression of SLITRK2 with the L74S, P374R ({300561.0004}), or R426C ({300561.0005}) mutation in HEK293 cells resulted in proteins with reduced surface expression compared to wildtype protein and were present in only an immature, nonglycosylated form.

phenotypes.phenotype: Hemolytic uremic syndrome, atypical, 8, with rhizomelic short stature

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome-8 with rhizomelic short stature (AHUS8) is caused by hemizygous mutation in the C1GALT1C1 gene ({300611}) on chromosome Xq23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome-8 with rhizomelic short stature (AHUS8) is an X-linked disorder with variable manifestations. The age at onset of renal symptoms is variable, ranging from infancy to the early twenties. Features of atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) include acute renal dysfunction with proteinuria, thrombotic microangiopathy, anemia, thrombocytopenia, increased serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and schistocytes on peripheral blood smear. Affected individuals also have short stature with short limbs. More variable features include immunodeficiency with recurrent infections, developmental delay, and dysmorphic features. Treatment with C5 inhibitors results in improvement of renal function. Female carriers may show an attenuated phenotype ({2:Hadar et al., 2023}; {1:Erger et al., 2023}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of aHUS, see AHUS1 ({235400}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Hadar et al. (2023)} reported a 3-year-old boy, born of unrelated Jewish-Moroccan parents, with aHUS and mutation in the C1GALT1C1 gene. He presented soon after birth with transient hypoglycemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia, all of which resolved spontaneously. He had short limbs and long eyelashes; polyhydramnios and shortened long bones had been observed on prenatal ultrasound. By 2 weeks of age, anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and increased serum LDH were present; schistocytes were found on peripheral blood smear. Renal function was abnormal, with increased creatinine, urea, uric acid, and proteinuria, and renal ultrasound showed increased echogenicity and mildly enlarged kidneys. Infection and fever were not present, and he was diagnosed with aHUS. Treatment with the C5 inhibitor eculizumab resulted in rapid clinical improvement. At 3 years of age, he still had mild proteinuria that was treated with ravulizumab, another C5 inhibitor. He had normal cognitive and motor development with minor language impairment; he also had rhizomelic short stature.

{1:Erger et al. (2023)} reported 2 German half brothers (M1 and M2) with a complex multisystemic disorder associated with aHUS who carried mutation in the C1GALT1C1 gene. Both presented in infancy with thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia, and recurrent infections. They also had disproportionate short stature with short limbs and variable global developmental delay. M1, a 7-year-old boy, had pulmonary hypertension and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy at birth, subaortic stenosis, neonatal seizures, and recurrent infections with hypogammaglobulinemia. At age 5, he presented with acute kidney injury with proteinuria and edema requiring dialysis. Laboratory studies showed thrombotic microangiopathy, hemolytic anemia, schistocytosis, thrombocytopenia, increased LDH, and dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, consistent with aHUS. Treatment with C5 inhibitors resulted in clinical improvement of renal function. M1 also had hypotonia and global developmental delay, including impaired intellectual development (IQ less than 55 at age 6), poor speech, and delayed walking with an ataxic gait. M2 had a history of anemia, leukopenia, and neutropenia since infancy and recurrent infections in childhood that decreased in adolescence. At age 21, he developed severe acute kidney injury with similar laboratory findings as his brother. He also had acute pancreatitis and elevated lipase. Treatment with a C5 inhibitor improved kidney function and lipase levels. M2 had developmental delay and speech delay, attended a special school, and worked in a manual job. Both M1 and M2 showed variable dysmorphic features, including high forehead, flattened nasal bridge, prominent nasal tip, short philtrum, posteriorly rotated ears, retrognathia, prominent nasolabial folds, open mouth, and downturned corners of the mouth. Family history revealed that a maternal half brother from a third partnership developed renal failure and died 3 days after birth, but autopsy was not performed and tissue was not available for study. Both the mother and maternal grandmother of M1 and M2 showed some similar but milder features, including borderline short stature, learning disabilities, mild transient anemia or thrombocytopenia, and mild dysmorphic features. The grandmother had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The hemizygous mutation in the C1GALT1C1 gene that was identified in a patient with AHUS8 by {2:Hadar et al. (2023)} occurred de novo.

The transmission pattern of AHUS8 in the family reported by {1:Erger et al. (2023)} was consistent with X-linked inheritance, with males showing a more severe phenotype and females an attenuated phenotype.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 3-year-old boy, born of unrelated Jewish-Moroccan parents, with AHUS8, {2:Hadar et al. (2023)} identified a de novo hemizygous missense mutation in the C1GALT1C1 gene (T89I; {300611.0006}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. No mutations in other aHUS-associated genes were found. In vitro studies of patient erythrocytes showed that the Tn antigen was not exposed, but there was striking agglutination in the presence of peanut agglutinin (PNA) lectin, indicating constant exposure of the T antigen (the Core-1 disaccharide). {2:Hadar et al. (2023)} suggested that Core-1 was malformed due to the C1GALT1C1 mutation, preventing the addition of further sugars and leaving the T antigen exposed. They speculated that this may activate the lectin pathway-mediated complement cascade via recognition by ficolin proteins (see, e.g., FCN1; {601252}).

In 2 maternal half brothers of German origin with AHUS8, {1:Erger et al. (2023)} identified a hemizygous missense mutation in the C1GALT1C1 gene (A20D; {300611.0007}). The mutation was found in the heterozygous state in the mother and maternal grandmother who had very mild symptoms of the disorder and showed skewed X-inactivation favoring expression of the mutant allele. C1GALT1C1 protein levels were undetectable in lymphoblastoid cells derived from the boys, and protein levels and activity of T synthase (C1GALT1; {610555}) were markedly reduced to less than 5% of controls. Cells transfected with the A20D mutation showed lower protein levels, although the mutation was able to partially rescue loss of C1GALT1 activity in C1GALT1C1-null cells. Patient fibroblasts showed higher expression of the A20D and C1GALT1 proteins and higher C1GALT1 activity compared to patient lymphoblastoid cells, suggesting cell- and tissue-specific effects. Further studies demonstrated that the mutant A20D protein was degraded by the proteasome pathway. Overall, the findings indicated that the A20D mutant protein is functionally active, and that decreased expression of the mutant chaperone protein is responsible for decreased C1GALT1 activity. Although patient lymphoblastoid cells showed increased expression of the Tn antigen compared to controls, consistent with altered O-glycosylation, the majority of glycoproteins showed normal T antigen expression, indicating that the Core-1 O-glycan is present. The authors designated the disorder COSMC-CDG.
