phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and cortical atrophy

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and cortical atrophy (NDMSCA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the VARS gene (VARS1; {192150}) on chromosome 6p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and cortical atrophy (NDMSCA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe global developmental delay with poor motor and intellectual function apparent soon after birth, as well as postnatal progressive microcephaly. Most patients develop early-onset, frequent, and often intractable seizures, compatible with an epileptic encephalopathy. Other features include poor feeding, poor overall growth, absent speech, poor or absent eye contact, inability to achieve walking, hypotonia, and peripheral spasticity. Brain imaging usually shows progressive cerebral atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and abnormalities in myelination. Death in childhood may occur (summary by {4:Siekierska et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Karaca et al. (2015)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families (HOU1242 and HOU2294) with a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by severe developmental delay, intellectual disability, severe microcephaly, and cortical atrophy. No additional clinical details were provided. {4:Siekierska et al. (2019)} provided follow-up of the families reported by {2:Karaca et al. (2015)}, who were of Turkish origin. None of the patients were able to walk or speak, and all had early-onset generalized seizures.

{5:Stephen et al. (2018)} reported 2 brothers, born of unrelated parents of Indian descent, with NDMSCA. The elder brother was born with microcephaly (-6 SD), small anterior fontanel, prominent sutural ridging, and weak cry. He developed seizures in the first month of life and did not acquire any developmental milestones. Brain imaging at 4 months of age showed diffuse cerebral atrophy with thinning of the corpus callosum, and ophthalmologic examination showed myopic astigmatism. He died at age 1 year due to a severe respiratory infection. The proband was a 3-year-old boy with global developmental delay, progressive microcephaly (-9 SD), no head control, no speech, and generalized hypotonia with contractures of the ankles and fingers. He developed refractory seizures at 2 months of age. He also had swallowing difficulties and was tube-fed. Both patients had dysmorphic facial features, including low-set ears, long eyelashes, sloping forehead, micrognathia, and short nose with flat nasal bridge. Brain imaging showed progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, decreased white matter, subcortical white matter hyperintensities, and thinning of corpus callosum. Karyotype analysis showed increased chromosomal breakage.

{3:Okur et al. (2018)} reported 2 brothers of European descent, 10 and 15 years of age, with NDMSCA. Both were born prematurely at 31 and 27 weeks' gestation, respectively; alpha-fetoprotein was increased during 1 of the pregnancies. They had hypotonia, global developmental delay with inability to walk or speak, spasticity, and postnatal microcephaly. Both patients had transient elevation of liver enzymes in infancy. Neither had seizures, and brain imaging in 1 patient was normal.

{1:Friedman et al. (2019)} reported 7 patients from 5 unrelated families with NDMSCA. Three of the families (2937, 3308, and 3439) were consanguineous and of Egyptian origin, another family (3007) was Syrian with remote consanguinity, and the fifth family (GB31) was Caucasian. Four patients died between 2.5 months and 10 years of age; the living patients ranged from 10 months to 5 years of age. All patients presented within the first days, weeks, or months with generalized or myoclonic seizures, often associated with hypsarrhythmia on EEG; seizures could be controlled in only some patients. All had severe to profound global developmental delay with axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, hyperreflexia, feeding difficulties, and absent language. Some patients had extrapyramidal signs. All but 1 had severe postnatal microcephaly (down to -8.2 SD). Two patients had transient elevation of liver enzymes and 1 had hepatomegaly. Brain imaging was normal in 1 patient, but showed progressive cortical atrophy and hypoplastic corpus callosum in the others; 1 patient had abnormal gyration and another had abnormal myelination. Neuropathologic examination of 1 child showed a reduction in cerebral white matter volume, gliosis, and decreased myelination, but preserved axonal density. In the Caucasian family (GB31), the mother had a history of recurrent pregnancy loss, often associated with neural tube defects.

{4:Siekierska et al. (2019)} reported 10 patients from 7 unrelated families, including 2 consanguineous Turkish families (families 4 and 5) that had previously been reported by {2:Karaca et al. (2015)}, with NDMSCA. The patients ranged from 11 months to 14 years of age. All had global developmental delay apparent in the first months of life, severe to profound impaired intellectual development with absent speech, and most were unable to walk independently. All except 2 sibs (family 3) developed various types of refractory seizures in infancy, consistent with epileptic encephalopathy. The patients had poor overall growth and microcephaly. More variable features included hypotonia, spasticity, and sleep problems. Most had abnormal brain imaging, showing cerebral atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and myelination defects. The patients were identified through international collaboration or via GeneMatcher.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NDMSCA in the families reported by {2:Karaca et al. (2015)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with NDMSCA, {2:Karaca et al. (2015)} identified homozygous missense mutations in the VARS gene (L885F, {192150.0001} and R1058Q, {192150.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but {2:Karaca et al. (2015)} noted that mutations in other genes involved in various other aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (see, e.g., DARS, {603084}) have been identified in neurologic disorders. The families were part of a cohort of 128 mostly consanguineous families with neurogenetic disorders, often including brain malformations, that underwent whole-exome sequencing.

In a boy, born of unrelated parents of Indian origin, with NDMSCA, {5:Stephen et al. (2018)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the VARS gene ({192150.0003} and {192150.0004}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The patient had a brother with a similar phenotype who died at age 12 months; DNA from the affected brother was not available. Studies of patient-derived fibroblasts showed about 50% decreased VARS mRNA, severely decreased VARS protein levels, and about a 4-fold decrease in aminoacylation activity of VARS compared to controls. The findings suggested that the mutations resulted in a loss of function with a negative impact on protein synthesis and cellular metabolism.

Using exome sequencing in 2 brothers with NDMSCA, {3:Okur et al. (2018)} identified compound heterozygous missense variants in the VARS gene (A22D and F1072L) that segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, and the variants were classified as variants of uncertain significance.

In 7 patients from 5 families with NDMSCA, {1:Friedman et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the VARS gene (see, e.g., {192150.0005} and {192150.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Most were missense mutations, although 1 patient with a very severe phenotype was compound heterozygous for a missense and a nonsense mutation. Fibroblasts derived from several patients with different mutations showed significantly decreased VARS enzymatic activity, about 20%, compared to wildtype, consistent with a partial loss of function.

In 10 patients from 7 unrelated families with NDMSCA, including the 2 families previously reported by {2:Karaca et al. (2015)}, {4:Siekierska et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the VARS gene (see, e.g., {192150.0007}-{192150.0011}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. Affected members in all but 1 family carried biallelic missense mutations; 2 sibs in family 3 were compound heterozygous for a frameshift and a missense mutation ({192150.0009} and {192150.0010}). All missense variants occurred at conserved residues in or close to the catalytic or anticodon-binding domains, and could be broadly categorized into 2 groups based on molecular modeling: one group was predicted to have an adverse effect on protein structure, and the other was predicted to interfere with tRNA binding. Various studies were performed on the missense mutations, including enzymatic activity, yeast complementation studies, and zebrafish rescue. Analysis of cells derived from some patients showed significantly decreased VARS enzymatic activity compared to controls (at least 50%, but usually less than 25% residual activity). Some of the mutant proteins were able to restore growth in yeast complementation studies, but 3 were unable to fully rescue defects in zebrafish with knockdown of the vars gene. The findings overall indicated that the mutations result in a loss-of-function effect, and that VARS is a critical gene for neuronal development.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: In wildtype zebrafish, {4:Siekierska et al. (2019)} found that vars was strongly and selectively expressed in the developing brain, eye, and other organs during embryogenesis. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of the vars gene in zebrafish resulted in increased lethality, loss of posture, abnormal behavior with jerky spasmodic movements, progressive microcephaly with head abnormalities, increased apoptosis in the head, microphthalmia, and pericardial edema. Electrophysiologic studies on mutant fish also showed epileptiform activity.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH VARIABLE MOTOR AND LANGUAGE IMPAIRMENT; NEDMIAL
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the DExH-box helicase 30 gene (DHX30,)

Head: Small head circumference
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the DExH-box helicase 30 gene (DHX30,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with variable motor and speech impairment

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with variable motor and language impairment (NEDMIAL) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the DHX30 gene (DHX30; {616423}) on chromosome 3p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: NEDMIAL is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by delayed psychomotor development and hypotonia apparent from early infancy, resulting in feeding difficulties, ataxic gait or inability to walk, delayed or absent speech development, and impaired intellectual development, sometimes with behavioral abnormalities, such as hand-flapping. Additional common features may include sleep disorder, nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, and joint hyperlaxity (summary by {2:Lessel et al., 2017} and {3:Mannucci et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Lessel et al. (2017)} reported 12 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 3 to 17 years, with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder apparent from early infancy. Most of the patients were Caucasian of European descent, although 2 were of Hispanic descent, 1 was Turkish, and 1 was of Yemenite/Tripolitan Jewish descent. The patients presented in infancy with delayed psychomotor development, hypotonia, and feeding difficulties. All had severe intellectual disability. Many had behavioral abnormalities, including autistic features, aggressive behavior, low frustration tolerance, and stereotypies, although some were described as pleasant or smiling. All but 2 patients were nonverbal and had very poor or absent communication skills, although a few had some nonverbal gestures and sounds. Six patients never achieved independent ambulation and 4 walked with an ataxic gait. Three patients had seizures and 1 had hearing loss. Brain imaging was normal in some patients, but showed nonspecific abnormalities in others, including cerebral atrophy, cerebellar atrophy, enlarged ventricles, and delayed myelination. Additional common features included sleep abnormalities, bruxism, joint hypermobility, persistent fingerpads, tapering fingers, flat feet, poor fine motor skills, and involuntary movements, such as dystonia or chorea. Many patients had variable dysmorphic facial features, such as small head, strabismus, epicanthal folds, synophrys, high palate, low-set ears, orofacial hypotonia, full eyelids, and eversion of the lower lip. The patients were severely disabled; none attended school, many had no purposeful hand movements and had impaired fine motor skills, and at least 1 patient was noted to be doubly incontinent at age 13 years. Two of the patients (probands F and G) had previously been reported by {1:Eldomery et al. (2017)} as part of a large study of patients who underwent exome sequencing.

{3:Mannucci et al. (2021)} described 25 patients with variants in the DHX30 gene. Among 19 patients with a heterozygous missense variant within a highly conserved motif in the helicase core domain (including 1 with mosaicism), all had a phenotype consistent with NEDMIAL: all had global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, severe speech impairment (14 were nonverbal and the others had speech delay), and gait abnormalities (only 9 learned to walk, all with an ataxic gait). Other findings included muscular hypotonia in 18, feeding difficulties in 16, microcephaly in 13, joint hypermobility in 14, structural brain anomalies in 11, sleep disturbances in 9, strabismus in 8, autistic features in 5, and seizures in 4. One of these patients (individual 6), who was mosaic for a missense variant, had a milder clinical course, with ability to walk at age 2 years 8 months and to talk in simple sentences at the age of 15 years. Four patients with heterozygous haploinsufficiency or protein-truncating variants (frameshift or nonsense, whole-gene deletion, or in-frame deletion) had a milder form of the NEDMIAL phenotype with mild muscular hypotonia, the ability to walk in the second year of life, and at least 20 words by 3 years of age. (The patient with a whole-gene deletion (individual 24) had a large deletion encompassing 9 other genes.) Two patients (individuals 21 and 4) had distinctly different phenotypes. Individual 21, who had a heterozygous variant outside the helicase core domain, had unremarkable psychomotor development until the age of 8 years when she presented with truncal ataxia. She had regression in motor skills and developed cognitive problems with reduced concentration. Individual 4, who had a homozygous variant classified as a variant of unknown significance, had early-onset infantile epileptic encephalopathy and died at 11 months of age.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous DHX30 mutations in all 12 patients with NEDMIAL reported by {2:Lessel et al. (2017)} occurred de novo. {3:Mannucci et al. (2021)} reported a patient who inherited the mutation from a mosaic mother.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 12 unrelated patients with NEDMIAL, {2:Lessel et al. (2017)} identified 6 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the DHX30 gene ({616423.0001}-{616423.0006}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. All mutations occurred within the helicase core region, which is predicted to mediate either ATP binding/hydrolysis or RNA recognition. In vitro cellular expression studies showed that all 5 variants that occurred in the ATP binding motifs II or VI ({616423.0002}-{616423.0006}) showed markedly reduced ATPase activities compared to wildtype. The 1 remaining variant (R493H; {616423.0001}), located in the putative RNA-binding motif Ia, did not alter RNA-dependent activity of DHX30, but did interfere with the binding capacity toward some target RNAs. Transfection of the mutations into a human cell line (U2OS) showed that the mutant proteins accumulated abnormally in cytoplasmic stress granules, which was associated with a global decrease in protein synthesis. {2:Lessel et al. (2017)} hypothesized that the DHX30 variants generate a chronic stress condition whereby pervasive and pronounced stress granule assembly induces impairments in the local regulation of translation, thus adversely affecting neurodevelopmental processes.

{3:Mannucci et al. (2021)} identified 23 patients with NEDMIAL and variants in the DHX30 gene, 10 of which were novel. These included 19 with heterozygous missense variants within a helicase core motif (including 1 with mosaicism) predicted to be responsible for ATP binding or hydrolysis, and 4 with heterozygous haploinsufficiency or protein-truncating variants (see, e.g., {616423.0007}). Two additional patients (individuals 21 and 4) with variants in DHX30 had strikingly different phenotypes; individual 21 had a heterozygous missense variant outside of the helicase core motif and individual 4 had a homozygous variant (R725H) within the helicase core region but the variant was classified as a variant of uncertain significance. None of these DHX30 variants was present in the gnomAD database (v2.1.1).

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: Based on their 25 patients and the patients reported by {2:Lessel et al. (2017)} with mutations in the DHX30 gene, {3:Mannucci et al. (2021)} suggested a genotype/phenotype correlation. The 18 patients with heterozygous missense variants within a helicase core motif had a severe phenotype consistent with patients previously reported with NEDMIAL by {2:Lessel et al. (2017)}. The 4 patients with heterozygous haploinsufficiency or protein-truncating variants and the patient with mosaicism had a milder form of NEDMIAL, leading the authors to suggest 2 DHX30-associated neurodevelopmental disorder subtypes. Two patients had distinct phenotypes; patient 21 with a heterozygous variant outside the helicase core motif showed late-onset progressive ataxia, and patient 4 with a variant of unknown significance had early-lethal infantile epileptic encephalopathy.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with ataxic gait, absent speech, and decreased cortical white matter

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with ataxic gait, absent speech, and decreased cortical white matter (NDAGSCW) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RAB11B gene ({604198}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: NDAGSCW is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by severely delayed psychomotor development apparent from infancy. Affected individuals have delayed and difficulty walking, intellectual disability, absent speech, and variable additional features, including hip dysplasia, tapering fingers, and seizures. Brain imaging shows decreased cortical white matter, often with decreased cerebellar white matter, thin corpus callosum, and thin brainstem (summary by {1:Lamers et al., 2017}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Lamers et al. (2017)} reported 5 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 4.5 to 13 years, with severely delayed psychomotor development and severe to profound intellectual disability with absent speech. The patients were ascertained through several different research centers. Most patients had hypotonia and delayed walking (after the age of 3 years) with difficulty walking or with ataxic gait; 2 also showed spasticity and dystonia. Three patients had childhood-onset epilepsy that was well-controlled, 1 had a single seizure, and 1 did not have seizures. Ophthalmologic abnormalities included nystagmus (2), hypermetropia (2), strabismus (2), and optic atrophy/impaired vision (3). All patients had tapering fingers, 4 had hip dysplasia, and 2 had pes cavus or clubfoot; other skeletal anomalies included clinodactyly, overriding toes, and simian crease. Some patients had dysmorphic facial features, such as facial hypotonia, deep-set eyes, upslanting palpebral fissures, full upper eyelids, and dysplastic ears. Three patients had mild microcephaly (-3 to -4 SD). Brain imaging, performed in 4 patients, showed similar abnormalities, including markedly decreased cortical white matter, thin corpus callosum, less severely decreased cerebellar white matter, and enlarged ventricles. Other brain abnormalities observed in several patients included cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, thin brainstem, delayed myelination, and optic nerve hypoplasia. One patient appeared to have atypical partial rhombencephalosynapsis, and 2 other patients had decreased width of the cerebellar vermis. The patients were severely disabled and did not attend school, but some were noted to have simple comprehension and the ability to perform simple tasks. Some had behavior abnormalities, including stereotypic behavior, bruxism, drooling, and hand-flapping; at least 1 child had a happy demeanor. One patient was incontinent at age 6 years; details on continence were not provided for the other patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The RAB11B mutations identified in all 5 unrelated patients with NDAGSCW reported by {1:Lamers et al. (2017)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 unrelated patients with NDAGSCW, {1:Lamers et al. (2017)} identified 2 recurrent de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the RAB11B gene (V22M, {604198.0001} and A68T, {604198.0002}). The patients were ascertained from several different research cohorts, and the mutations were identified by trio-based whole-exome sequencing. In vitro cellular transfection studies showed that both mutant proteins had homogeneous localization in the cytoplasm, decreased association with vesicular membranes, no association with the pericentrosomal region, and colocalization with a Golgi marker, all of which were different from wildtype and similar to that observed in studies of a known inactive mutant (S25N) that is GDP-bound. Molecular modeling suggested that both the V22M and A68T variants affect the GDP/GTP binding pockets, resulting in a nucleotide-free inactive state, with V22M showing a stronger disruptive effect than A68T. Both V22M and A68T showed increased interaction with SH3BP5 ({605612}) compared to wildtype RAB11B, with V22M showing a stronger affinity compared to A68T. {1:Lamers et al. (2017)} concluded that the mutations act in a dominant-negative manner to alter GDP/GTP binding, thus inactivating the protein and causing alterations in binding to certain guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), as well as protein mislocalization, which may have additional adverse cellular effects.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that glycosylphosphatidylinositol biosynthesis defect-15 (GPIBD15) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GPAA1 gene ({603048}) on chromosome 8q24.

description.title: Description
description.content:
GPIBD15 is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by delayed psychomotor development, variable intellectual disability, hypotonia, early-onset seizures in most patients, and cerebellar atrophy, resulting in cerebellar signs including gait ataxia and dysarthria. The disorder is caused by a defect in glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) biosynthesis (summary by {1:Nguyen et al., 2017}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of GPI biosynthesis defects, see GPIBD1 ({610293}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Nguyen et al. (2017)} reported 10 patients from 5 unrelated families with GPIBD15. The families were ascertained from several research studies and were of various origins, including Caucasian, Hispanic, Egyptian, Pakistani, and Finnish. The patients ranged in age from 3.8 to 30 years. All patients showed global developmental delay with mild to moderate intellectual disability, hypotonia, delayed sitting, severely delayed speech, and cerebellar atrophy. The patients had very poor speech with dysarthria and all except 2 were unable to walk or could only walk with support due to ataxic gait and gait instability; the 2 who could walk achieved the skill around age 3 years. Two older sibs in their thirties were wheelchair-bound. Three patients from a Pakistani family were noted to have frank spasticity, whereas others had brisk reflexes. Cerebellar signs included dysarthria, dysmetria, uncoordinated eye movements with ocular ataxia and apraxia, nystagmus, and tremor. Intellectual disability varied; a few patients had moderate cognitive impairment (e.g., IQ of 50 in 1 patient) and could only say a few words, whereas some patients were able to play on a computer and understand most conversation. Three children from a Pakistani family (family 4) could attend normal school with help; these children did not have seizures. The older sibs in their thirties (family 5, Finnish) lived in a sheltered housing with daily assistance, although they were able to eat and dress independently. One patient had cortical visual impairment, 3 had myopia, and 1 had optic atrophy. Seven patients from 4 families had onset of generalized seizures within the first 2 years of life that were only partially or not well controlled by medication and associated with generalized polyspike discharges on EEG. One patient had a history of status epilepticus. Brain imaging showed cerebellar atrophy or hypoplasia, which was progressive in some patients. Common dysmorphic features, seen in one-third to one-half of the patients, included bitemporal narrowing, prominent forehead, widely spaced eyes, broad nasal root, and anteverted nares. Eight patients had osteopenia or osteoporosis, and a ninth had hip dysplasia; however, plasma alkaline phosphatase was normal.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of GPIBD15 in the families reported by {1:Nguyen et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 10 patients from 5 unrelated families with GPIBD15, {1:Nguyen et al. (2017)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the GPAA1 gene (see, e.g., {603048.0001}-{603048.0007}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. There were 6 missense mutations, 2 frameshift mutations, and 1 splicing mutation, but none of the patients carried 2 frameshift mutations. Cells derived from several of the patients showed variably decreased amounts of GPI-anchored proteins at the cell surface, including CD16 (FCGR3A; {146740}), CD24 ({600074}), CD109 ({608859}), and CD73 ({129190}). These defects could be partially rescued by expression of wildtype GPAA1. Transfection of plasmids containing the mutations into GPAA1-deficient HEK293 cells showed that some of the missense variants had decreased activity, whereas others had residual activity. The findings indicated that the mutations caused a defect in the biosynthesis of GPI-anchored proteins, and highlighted the role of this transamidase complex in the development and function of the cerebellum and the skeletal system.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that glycosylphosphatidylinositol biosynthesis defect-16 (GPIBD16) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PIGC gene ({601730}) on chromosome 1q24.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Glycosylphosphatidylinositol biosynthesis defect-16 (GPIBD16) is an autosomal recessive severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by moderate to profoundly impaired motor and intellectual development with axial hypotonia, peripheral hypertonia, inability to walk, and absent speech. Affected individuals develop seizures within the first year of life that may be refractory to treatment. Dysmorphic facial features, microcephaly, and variable brain imaging abnormalities are usually present. Death in childhood may occur ({1:Bayat et al., 2025}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of GPI biosynthesis defects, see GPIBD1 ({610293}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Edvardson et al. (2017)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with GPIBD16. Two sibs were born of consanguineous Arab parents (family A), and an unrelated patient was born of nonconsanguineous Sephardic Jewish parents (family B). The patients presented with epilepsy and severe global developmental delay between 3 and 12 months of age. The sibs from family A had relatively rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures that responded to antiepileptic drugs. The patient from family B had seizures that were unresponsive to several antiepileptic drugs, but they remitted after several months. In family A, the oldest sib walked at age 6 years and could say a few words at age 9; the younger sib started walking at age 2 and could speak short sentences at age 6. Both were toilet-trained. The child from family B did not achieve any developmental milestones beyond 1 year of age. Other organ systems were not involved, hearing and vision were intact, and there were no dysmorphic features. Brain imaging was normal except for 1 patient who had an arachnoid cyst that was asymptomatic. Serum alkaline phosphatase was normal.

{3:Pons et al. (2020)} reported 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Algerian parents, with GPIBD16. Both presented soon after birth with axial hypotonia, limb hypertonia, hepatosplenomegaly, and poor ocular fixation. The older sib developed subcortical myoclonic jerks at 12 months of age, and later had febrile tonic seizures. At age 5 years, he had a large head circumference (+2 SD), severe global developmental delay with unstable walking, absent language, and no eye contact. Recurrent respiratory infections and asthma were also noted. Dysmorphic features included pectus excavatum, supernumerary nipple, short limbs, coarse facial features, depressed nasal bridge, low-set ears with large earlobes, wide mouth, and dystrophic hair. Brain MRI was normal. The younger sib had similar and somewhat more severe clinical features, with hypomyelination on brain imaging; she died at 20 months of age.

{1:Bayat et al. (2025)} reported 18 patients from 10 unrelated families with GPIBD16 associated with biallelic mutations in the PIGC gene. Six families were consanguineous. Most of the patients were children between 40 days and 7 years of age, although 1 (P14 from family 7) was 26 years old and had the mildest phenotype. Eleven patients died between 40 days and 7 years of age. There was a discrepancy in the number of deceased patients between figure 1A and Table 1 of the report. All patients except P14 had severe to profound global developmental delay with hypotonia, limited movements, inability to walk, and impaired intellectual development with absent speech. Most had poor overall growth with short stature and microcephaly (down to -6.25). The patients had onset of focal and generalized refractory seizures within the first year of life associated with variable EEG abnormalities, including multifocal discharges, generalized spike waves, and polyspike waves; 1 patient had hypsarrhythmia. Over half of patients had episodes of status epilepticus. Most had brain imaging abnormalities, including cerebellar hypoplasia, cortical and subcortical volume loss, enlarged ventricles, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, and hypomyelination. Dysmorphic facial features were common, including high forehead, long face, malar hypoplasia, retrognathia, short philtrum, pointed chin, low-set ears, deep-set eyes, depressed or wide nasal bridge, and wide mouth. Additional more variable features included strabismus, scoliosis, pectus defects, clinodactyly, and arachnodactyly.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of GPIBD16 in the families reported by {2:Edvardson et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with GPIBD16, {2:Edvardson et al. (2017)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PIGC gene ({601730.0001}-{601730.0003}). The mutations, which were found by exome analysis, segregated with the disorder in both families. Flow cytometric analysis of patient leukocytes showed variably decreased expression of GPI-anchored proteins, including CD16 (FCGR3A; {146740}) and CD55 ({125240}). Transfection of the mutations into PIGC-null cells showed that the mutations were unable to rescue cell surface expression of GPI-anchored proteins, consistent with a partial or almost complete loss-of-function effect.

In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Algerian parents, with GPIBD16, {3:Pons et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous truncating mutation in the PIGC gene ({601730.0004}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. RT-PCR of patient cells showed the presence of an elongated PIGC transcript. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In 18 patients from 10 unrelated families with GPIBD16, {1:Bayat et al. (2025)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PIGC gene (see, e.g., {601730.0005}-{601730.0009}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were all inherited from the unaffected parents. There were 5 missense variants, 2 nonsense mutations, an in-frame deletion, a frameshift, and a disruption of the initiation codon. The variants were either absent from gnomAD (v4.1.0) or found at a very low frequency. The mutations occurred throughout the gene, with variants occurring in both the transmembrane domains and in the catalytic domain, with no apparent genotype/phenotype correlations. Flow cytometric analysis of fibroblasts or granulocytes derived from some of the patients showed decreased cell surface expression of GPI-anchored proteins, such as FLAER, CD16 (see {146740}), CD24 ({600074}), and CD55 ({125240}). In vitro functional studies of the PIGC variants found in family 8 showed absent (Cys265PhefsTer11) or no (G96R) catalytic activity compared to wildtype. Overall, the findings suggested that disease-causing PIGC mutations cause encephalopathy due to decreased GPI cellular signaling.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without hyperkinetic movements and seizures, autosomal recessive

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with or without hyperkinetic movements and seizures (NDHMSR) is caused by homozygous mutation in the GRIN1 gene ({138249}) on chromosome 9q34.

Homozygous mutation in the GRIN1 can also cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-101 (DEE101; {619814}), and heterozygous mutation in the GRIN1 gene can cause autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder with or without hyperkinetic movements and seizures (NDHMSD; {614254}).

description.title: Description
description.content: NDHMSR is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by severely delayed psychomotor development, severely impaired intellectual development, and involuntary movements, including stereotypic movements, spasticity, and dystonia. Affected individuals are usually unable to walk independently and have poor or absent speech. Some patients may have seizures (summary by {1:Lemke et al., 2016}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Lemke et al. (2016)} reported 2 brothers, born of consanguineous parents (family 1), with severe developmental delay, impaired intellectual development with absent speech, and autistic features. They also had hypotonia, spasticity, involuntary movements such as dystonia and restless movements, and self-injurious behavior. Neither patient had clinical seizures, but both showed abnormal EEG with spikes or spike-wave discharges during sleep in infancy. At age 11, 1 the EEG of 1 patient showed left temporal spikes. Brain imaging was normal.

{2:Rossi et al. (2017)} reported 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Moroccan parents, with neurodevelopmental delay and hyperkinetic movements without seizures. The patients presented in the first months of life with hypotonia, severe developmental delay, and involuntary stereotypic movements. One achieved standing with support at age 3.5 years, and the other was able to sit with support, but not stand, at age 3 years. One patient had poor eye contact, and in the other eye contact was present. Neither patient could speak. Neither patient had seizures; EEG was normal in 1 and not performed in the other. Dysmorphic features included frontal bossing and mild midface hypoplasia; one child had strabismus. Brain imaging in one patient showed mild cerebral atrophy and thin corpus callosum; brain imaging in the other patient was normal.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NDHMSR in the families reported by {1:Lemke et al. (2016)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous parents (family 1), with NDHMSR, {1:Lemke et al. (2016)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the GRIN1 gene (R217W; {138249.0008}). The mutation, which was found by next-generation sequencing approaches, segregated with the disorder in the family. In vitro functional expression studies showed that the R217W mutation did not affect channel current, but resulted in a significant increase in zinc inhibition when coexpressed with wildtype GRIN2A ({138253}). The carrier parents were unaffected, suggesting that haploinsufficiency for GRIN1 can be tolerated and is not pathogenic.

In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Moroccan parents, with NDHMSR, {2:Rossi et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the GRIN1 gene (D227H; {138249.0010}). The mutation, which was found by massive parallel sequencing of a gene panel and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but {2:Rossi et al. (2017)} hypothesized that missense variants in the amino-terminal domain of the protein may be hypomorphic and pathogenic in the homozygous state, whereas the functionality of 1 allele, as observed in the parents, is sufficient to avoid clinical expression in heterozygous carriers.

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: Four sibs from 2 unrelated consanguineous families ({1:Lemke et al., 2016}; {2:Rossi et al., 2017}) with NDHMSR carried homozygous missense mutations in the GRIN1 gene (R217W, {138249.0008} and D227H, {138249.0010}). Both mutations occurred in the amino terminus of the protein. In both families, the heterozygous parents were unaffected. {1:Lemke et al. (2016)} and {2:Rossi et al. (2017)} postulated that homozygosity for a mutation that results in a hypomorphic or complete loss-of-function allele results in clinical manifestations, whereas possession of 1 functional allele is sufficient to avoid clinical manifestations. This is in contrast to patients with heterozygous missense mutations in the GRIN1 gene that have a dominant-negative effect ({614254}).

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Alkuraya-Kucinskas syndrome (ALKKUCS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the KIAA1109 gene ({611565}) on chromosome 4q27.

description.title: Description
description.content: ALKKUCS is an autosomal recessive severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by arthrogryposis, brain abnormalities associated with cerebral parenchymal underdevelopment, and global developmental delay. Most affected individuals die in utero or soon after birth. Additional abnormalities may include hypotonia, dysmorphic facial features, and involvement of other organ systems, such as cardiac or renal. The few patients who survive have variable intellectual disability and may have seizures (summary by {2:Gueneau et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Alazami et al. (2015)} reported a fetus (family 13DG1900) with hydrocephalus, micrognathia, clubfeet, arthrogryposis with flexion deformity, pleural effusion, and Dandy-Walker malformation who died 1 hour after birth.

{2:Gueneau et al. (2018)} reported 13 individuals from 10 unrelated families with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder, including the fetus reported by {1:Alazami et al. (2015)}, who was born of consanguineous Saudi parents. Among the 13 patients reported by {2:Gueneau et al. (2018)}, only 3 patients from 2 families were alive at 7, 11, and 13 years of age. Seven patients died between birth and the first months of life, and 3 affected pregnancies were terminated due to detection of the condition on prenatal ultrasound. In addition, 3 families had a history of recurrent miscarriages. The 3 living children (2 Lithuanian sibs and a girl from the UK) had global developmental delay from infancy and variable intellectual disability. The least severely affected patient was an 11-year-old girl from the UK with behavioral problems and learning disabilities who was able to walk and attend school. Prenatal ultrasound showed severe microcephaly (-5 SD) and reduced white matter volume. She had dysmorphic features, including hypertelorism, upslanting palpebral fissures, and high-arched palate, as well as a complex congenital heart disorder with tetralogy of Fallot. The 2 Lithuanian sibs had severe intellectual disability with absent language and hypotonia resulting in inability to stand without support, as well as early-onset epilepsy, plagiocephaly, and cerebral parenchymal rarefaction and ventriculomegaly on brain imaging. These 3 children had eye movement abnormalities, including oculomotor apraxia, hypermetropia, and strabismus, as well as mild joint contractures and foot deformities. The more severely affected 10 deceased infants and fetuses showed abnormalities on prenatal ultrasound, mainly arthrogryposis with flexion deformities, edema, and abnormal brain imaging. The patients had joint contractures, adducted thumbs, camptodactyly, clinodactyly, clenched hands, clubfoot, and overlapping fingers and toes. There were variable dysmorphic features, including macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, hypotelorism, hypertelorism, small eyes, low-set ears, posteriorly rotated ears, short nose, flattened nasal bridge, anteverted nares, retrognathia, cataracts, cystic hygroma, and webbed neck. Pre- and postnatal brain imaging showed multiple variable severe abnormalities in all patients. Abnormalities included enlarged ventricles, hypoplasia or absence of the corpus callosum, cortical lamination or migration defects, thin parenchymal mantle, gyral abnormalities, lissencephaly, neuronal heterotopia, prominent germinal matrix, and brainstem and cerebellar hypoplasia or dysplasia, often with a kinked brainstem. Additional congenital abnormalities were variable, but included pericardial or pleural effusions, heart or kidney abnormalities, and scrotum or penis hypoplasia. The infants that were born had hypotonia and breathing difficulties.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of ALKKUCS in the families reported by {2:Gueneau et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a female infant, born of consanguineous Saudi parents, with ALKKUCS, {1:Alazami et al. (2015)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the KIAA1109 gene (Y519X; {611565.0001}). The patient was part of a large cohort of 143 multiplex consanguineous families with various neurodevelopmental disorders who underwent whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In 12 patients from 9 unrelated families with ALKKUCS, {2:Gueneau et al. (2018)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the KIAA1109 gene (see, e.g., {611565.0002}-{611565.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families from whom parental DNA was available. Functional studies of the KIAA1109 variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but {2:Gueneau et al. (2018)} noted that the only individuals who survived beyond infancy had biallelic missense mutations. Knockdown of the gene in zebrafish resulted in head defects and abnormal body curvature (see ANIMAL MODEL).

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{3:Verstreken et al. (2009)} found that deletion of the KIAA1109 ortholog 'tweek' in Drosophila resulted in larval lethality. Rare homozygous flies that survived to adulthood were unable to walk or stand upright for long periods and exhibited seizures. The authors named the gene tweek after the cartoon character 'Tweek' from the television series 'South Park,' because the behavior of the adult mutant flies reminded them of the character. Tweek mutation resulted in NMJ synaptic vesicles that were reduced in number, but increased in size, with increased neurotransmitter release during spontaneous vesicle fusion events. The basal content of PI(4,5)P2 was reduced at tweek mutant NMJs, with altered PI(4,5)P2 distribution during neuronal activity and altered synaptic vesicle recycling.

{2:Gueneau et al. (2018)} noted that Kiaa1109-null mice show embryonic lethality, but that some Drosophila with complete loss of Kiaa1109 can survive; the surviving animals present with severe neurologic defects, such as seizures and inability to stand or walk (tweek phenotype). {2:Gueneau et al. (2018)} found that morpholino knockdown of the kiaa1109 gene in zebrafish resulted in increased frequency of hydrocephalus or other head defects and increased body curvature compared to controls. However, unlike in mice, homozygosity for disruption of the kiaa1109 gene did not appear to result in lethality.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-92 (DEE92) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GABRB2 gene ({600232}) on chromosome 5q34.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-92 (DEE92) is characterized in most patients by onset of seizures in infancy or childhood and associated with global developmental delay and variable impairment of intellectual development. The seizure type and severity varies, and seizures may be intractable in some patients. Some patients are severely affected, unable to walk or speak, whereas others show some development. Additional neurologic features, including cortical blindness, dystonia, and spasticity, may occur. Mutations occur de novo (summary by {1:Hamdan et al., 2017}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Srivastava et al. (2014)} reported a 12-year-old Spanish girl with intellectual disability and epilepsy. At age 9 months, she developed febrile seizures, and she eventually developed nonfebrile tonic-clonic and subtle seizures that could be controlled with medication. Her development slowed during childhood, but she was able to attend regular school where she received special tutoring. Neurologic examination showed clumsy fine motor movements, difficulty heel-walking, and brisk reflexes. Brain MRI was normal.

{2:Ishii et al. (2017)} reported a 2-year-old boy with severe early-onset myoclonic encephalopathy. Immediately after birth, the boy presented with poor feeding, lethargy, weak crying, and eyelid and limb myoclonus. He then developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures associated with a suppression-burst pattern on EEG. He continued to have daily seizures with poor or absent response to medication. He was bedridden and had a feeding tube.

{1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} reported 10 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 15 days to 15 years, with DEE92. The patients were ascertained from several large cohorts of patients who underwent whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing, or who were screened with a targeted gene panel. There was clinical variability regarding seizure type and severity of neurologic dysfunction. All but 1 patient had global developmental delay, although that patient had early-onset seizures and language delay, and all but 1 patient had seizures, although that patient had severe psychomotor delay. Seizure onset occurred between birth and 6 years, and seizure types included febrile, absence, myoclonic, atonic, focal, multifocal, and generalized tonic-clonic. EEG was normal in some patients, but showed variable abnormalities in others, including background slow waves, spike waves, and burst suppression patterns; at least 1 patient had hypsarrhythmia. Seizures were manageable in some patients and intractable in others. Six patients had acquired microcephaly and 1 had congenital microcephaly. Several patients were unable to walk or speak, whereas a few achieved some developmental milestones. Other features observed in several patients included hypotonia, dyskinesia, spasticity, dystonia, ataxia, and cortical visual impairment. Brain imaging was normal in most patients, but showed mild nonspecific white matter abnormalities in other patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the GABRB2 gene that were identified in patients with DEE92 by {3:Srivastava et al. (2014)} and {2:Ishii et al. (2017)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 12-year-old Spanish girl with DEE92, {3:Srivastava et al. (2014)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GABRB2 gene (M79T; {600232.0001}). The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In a 2-year-old boy with DEE92, {2:Ishii et al. (2017)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GABRB2 gene (T287P; {600232.0002}). The mutation, which was found by gene panel sequencing of 214 patients with epileptic disorders, was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells showed that the mutation resulted in decreased total GABRB2 expression and caused a 66% decrease in cell surface expression. GABA receptors containing the mutant beta-2 subunit were retained within the cell. Peak amplitudes of currents from GABA receptors containing the mutant subunit were decreased by 96.4%, indicating significant Cl- channel dysfunction. {2:Ishii et al. (2017)} postulated that the mutation caused a dominant-negative effect when expressed with other receptor subunits.

In 10 unrelated patients with DEE92, {1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the GABRB2 gene (see, e.g., {600232.0003}-{600232.0005}). The mutations were found by whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing, or by screening of a targeted gene panel. Functional studies of the variants were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-58 (DEE58) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the NTRK2 gene ({600456}) on chromosome 9q21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-58 (DEE58) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by the onset of infantile spasms and refractory seizures in the first days or months of life. Affected individuals have global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, usually with absent speech and inability to walk. Additional features include optic atrophy with poor or absent visual fixation, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and spasticity (summary by {1:Hamdan et al., 2017}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} reported 4 unrelated children with the onset of infantile spasms and seizures in the first days or months of life. The patients had moderately to severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech; 2 had autistic features, mainly stereotypic behaviors. The patients were severely disabled with difficulty walking or inability to walk and poor or absent eye contact with optic nerve hypoplasia or cortical visual impairment. Seizures were generalized infantile spasms, focal or of multiple types, and were difficult to control. At least 1 patient had status epilepticus. EEG abnormalities included diffuse slowing, multifocal spikes, and hypsarrhythmia. Brain imaging showed optic nerve hypoplasia in all patients. Additional features included acquired microcephaly, feeding difficulties with poor overall growth, hypotonia, spasticity, hyperreflexia, nystagmus, and poor fine or voluntary movements.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the NTRK2 gene that were identified in patients with DEE58 by {1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 unrelated patients with DEE58, {1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the NTRK2 gene (Y434C; {600456.0003}). The mutations were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant were not performed. The patients were ascertained from several large cohorts of patients with seizures and developmental delay who underwent genetic studies.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal dominant 55, with seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-55 with seizures (MRD55) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the NUS1 gene ({610463}) on chromosome 6q22.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} reported 3 unrelated patients with onset of myoclonic seizures in the first years of life. The most severely affected patient (indvKW) was an 8-year-old boy with global developmental delay, moderately impaired intellectual development, speech delay, and ataxic gait. He developed myoclonic seizures, which could be controlled with medication, at age 12 months. The second patient (HSJ0623) was a 15-year-old boy who presented at age 10 months with myoclonic seizures and mild motor delay. He later developed frequent atonic seizures that were refractory between ages 2 and 7, but were finally controlled with medication. EEG showed diffuse background slowing and high or small amplitude spikes. He was able to run, climb stairs, and play sports, attended special education school, and could speak, but he was clumsy on fine motor tasks. He had a mild tremor without other cerebellar signs, and was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. The third patient (HSJ0627) was a 29-year-old woman who presented at 2.5 years of age with febrile myoclonic status epilepticus. She then developed myoclonic absence seizures and drop attacks that eventually were well-controlled with multiple medications. EEG showed generalized spike-wave and polyspike-wave activity. She had mild motor delay and could jump and run, but was unable to ride a bicycle. She could speak and read at a first grade level and had mild dysarthria and tremor, but no ataxia. Brain imaging in all patients was normal.

{2:Yu et al. (2021)} described 3 patients, aged 5, 14, and 35 years, with developmental delay or impaired intellectual development, seizures, and ataxia. Patient 1, a 14-year-old girl, presented at age 12 with a history of borderline impaired intellectual development, seizures, and tremor since age 3 years, ocular flutter, and gait ataxia. Her early developmental milestones were normal. She had a history of 2 motor seizures and occasional absence seizures. On examination, she had a fine tremor with mild gait ataxia. She had a normal brain MRI. Patient 2, a 35-year-old woman, was initially evaluated at age 30 years. She had a history of moderately impaired intellectual development, seizures, tremor, and gait ataxia. Early developmental milestones were delayed. She had an absence seizure at age 4 years, a grand mal seizure at age 14 years, and 3 subsequent seizures associated with medication changes. At age 22, she developed a tremor in her hands and feet. She had a normal brain MRI at age 31. Patient 3, a 5-year-old boy, was initially evaluated at age 3 years due to developmental delay, seizures, and tremor. He had mild to moderate motor delays related to balance issues and moderate to severe speech delay. He developed seizures and an upper extremity tremor at age 2 years. He had dysarthria but he did not have ataxia. Subcortical parietal gliosis was seen on brain MRI. EEG revealed abnormal epileptiform discharges.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 unrelated patients with MRD55 with seizures, {1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} identified 3 different de novo heterozygous mutations in the NUS1 gene ({610463.0002}-{610463.0004}). Two of the mutations were truncating, and 1 was an intragenic deletion encompassing all of exon 2. Two patients were found by whole-genome sequencing of 197 individuals with developmental epileptic encephalopathy; the third patient was found by clinical exome sequencing from another patient cohort. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patients cells were not performed, but {1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} postulated haploinsufficiency as the pathogenic mechanism.

In 3 patients with MRD55 with seizures, {2:Yu et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the NUS1 gene ({610463.0004}-{610463.0007}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Yu et al. (2021)} developed a zebrafish morpholino knockdown for the nus1 gene. At 4-5 days postfertilization (dpf), the fish morphants demonstrated abnormal swimming, including short bursts of high-speed swim events compared to wildtype fish. Npc2 ({601015}) protein expression was decreased in morphant embryos at 1-4 dpf, and abnormal cholesterol accumulation, particularly in hindbrain, spinal cord and neurons, was seen by filipin staining. Decreased Lamp1 ({153330}) proteolysis was also seen in the morphant fish, indicating impaired lysosomal degradation. Treatment of the fish with 2-hydroxypropyl-beta-cyclodextrin to facilitate cholesterol efflux from lysosomes resulted in improved swimming parameters, reduced cholesterol storage, and improved lysosomal function.

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay and seizures with or without movement abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay and seizures with or without movement abnormalities (DEDSM) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the DHDDS gene ({608172}) on chromosome 1p36.

description.title: Description
description.content: DEDSM is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay, variable intellectual disability, and early-onset seizures with a myoclonic component. Most patients have delayed motor development and show abnormal movements, including ataxia, dystonia, and tremor (summary by {1:Hamdan et al., 2017}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} reported 5 unrelated patients with global developmental delay and seizures. Four of the patients were between 5 and 7 years of age, and 1 was 35. All had global developmental delay, with moderate to severe intellectual disability. Four patients had mildly delayed walking and all had delayed speech; 1 girl was nonverbal at age 4. One patient showed normal early development with only hypotonia until about 2 years of age when global delay became apparent. The patients had onset of variable myoclonic seizures in the first decade of life (between 1 and 7 years). Seizure types included absence, eyelid myoclonus, isolated cortical myoclonus, and others. The seizures were difficult to control in most patients, and EEG, when performed, usually showed generalized spike-wave discharges. Two unrelated patients showed seizure sensitivity to light and fever. Additional more variable features included hypotonia, ataxia, tremor, dystonia, and short stature. The 35-year-old man had abnormal movements, including myokymia, bradykinesia, hypomimia, rigidity, freezing, and impaired postural reactions. Brain imaging was normal, except in 1 patient who had a Chiari I malformation. Two patients specifically studied had normal glycosylation assays.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 unrelated patients with DEDSM, {1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} identified 2 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the DHDDS gene (R37H, {608172.0002} and R211Q, {608172.0003}). The mutations were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing of several cohorts of patients with developmental delay and epilepsy. Studies of patient cells and functional studies of the variants were not performed, but {1:Hamdan et al. (2017)} postulated a gain-of-function or dominant-negative effect.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-56 (MRD56) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CLTC gene ({118955}) on chromosome 17q23.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:DeMari et al. (2016)} reported a 3.5-year-old girl, conceived through in vitro fertilization, with global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, absent language, hypotonia, and inability to walk. Her neonatal period was notable for hypoglycemia, apnea, bradycardia, hyperbilirubinemia, subdural hematoma, laryngomalacia, and feeding difficulties requiring admission to the NICU for a month. She also had hydrocephalus, hypothyroidism, and vitamin K-dependent clotting factor deficiency, and she developed a mediastinal ganglioneuroblastoma. Dysmorphic features included low-set ears, depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nares, and widely spaced and inverted nipples. She did not have seizures; brain imaging and EEG were normal. At age 3.5 years, she was socially alert and interactive and was making some developmental progress.

{3:Hamdan et al. (2017)} reported 12 unrelated patients with MRD56. The patients ranged in age from 3 to 30 years. All had global developmental delay of varying degree and impaired intellectual development that ranged from borderline to severe. Most had hypotonia, delayed walking, poor fine motor skills, clumsiness, and poor or absent speech. Several patients were able to attend special schools, whereas a few patients had more significant disability, never achieving ambulation or speech. Several patients had nonspecific and variable dysmorphic features, such as upslanting palpebral fissures, long philtrum, thin upper lip, open mouth, high-arched palate, and prominent ears. Four patients had seizures with onset in the first years of life, and a fifth patient had 1 seizure at age 14 years without recurrence. Two patients had had pharmacoresistant epilepsy with a preponderance of myoclonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, whereas 2 had seizures that could be controlled. Other more variable features included ataxia, spasticity, paraparesis, acquired microcephaly, oral and motor apraxia, and behavioral abnormalities, such as impulsivity and attention deficits. Brain imaging was normal in most patients, but showed nonspecific abnormalities in others, including pontocerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, delayed myelination, and abnormal T2-weighed signals.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{2:DeMari et al. (2016)} reported a 3.5-year-old girl, conceived through in vitro fertilization, with global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, absent language, hypotonia, and inability to walk. Her neonatal period was notable for hypoglycemia, apnea, bradycardia, hyperbilirubinemia, subdural hematoma, laryngomalacia, and feeding difficulties requiring admission to the NICU for a month. She also had hydrocephalus, hypothyroidism, and vitamin K-dependent clotting factor deficiency, and she developed a mediastinal ganglioneuroblastoma. Dysmorphic features included low-set ears, depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nares, and widely spaced and inverted nipples. She did not have seizures; brain imaging and EEG were normal. At age 3.5 years, she was socially alert and interactive and was making some developmental progress. Exome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation in the CLTC gene ({118955.0001}). Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors postulated haploinsufficiency of CLTC as the pathogenetic mechanism. {2:DeMari et al. (2016)} noted that CLTC is highly expressed in the brain and plays a role in neuronal transmission by facilitating the recycling and/or release of vesicles at the presynaptic termini of neurons.

{1:Balci et al. (2020)} studied the patient reported by {2:DeMari et al. (2016)}, who was then aged 6 years. She had lymphadenopathy, a mediastinal mass, and hypercalcemia, and was diagnosed with T-cell lymphocytic leukemia. She was found to have a recurrent heterozygous mutation in the DNMT3A gene (R882C; {602769.0007}) seen in patients with Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS; {615879}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CLTC gene that were identified in patients with MRD56 by {3:Hamdan et al. (2017)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 12 unrelated patients with MRD56, {3:Hamdan et al. (2017)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the CLTC gene (see, e.g., {118955.0002}-{118955.0006}). The mutations were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing of several cohorts of patients with developmental delay and epilepsy. There were 5 truncating mutations, 2 small in-frame deletions, 1 splice site mutation, and 3 missense mutations, 1 of which was recurrent and found in 3 unrelated patients. Individuals with refractory epilepsy were found to carry variants in the first section of the clathrin light chain-binding domain, whereas truncating mutations affecting the C terminus tended to be associated with hypotonia, global developmental delay, and impaired intellectual development. Studies of patient cells and functional studies of the variants were not performed. {3:Hamdan et al. (2017)} noted that CLTC is involved in endocytosis, intracellular trafficking, and synaptic recycling.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH MICROCEPHALY, EPILEPSY, AND BRAIN ATROPHY; NEDMEBA

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, epilepsy, and brain atrophy

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, epilepsy, and brain atrophy (NEDMEBA) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TRAPPC6B gene ({610397}) on chromosome 14q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: NEDMEBA is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by global developmental delay, severe intellectual disability with poor or absent speech and autistic stereotypic behaviors, microcephaly, early-onset generalized seizures, and hypotonia (summary by {2:Marin-Valencia et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Marin-Valencia et al. (2018)} reported 6 patients from 3 unrelated consanguineous families of Egyptian origin with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder apparent since infancy. Four of the patients from 2 families were children, aged 2 to 10 years, whereas 2 sibs from the third family were in their early twenties. Features included global developmental delay, severe intellectual disability with poor or absent speech, and autistic features, such as poor social interaction and hand flapping. The patients had poor growth with microcephaly (-4 to -7 SD) and short stature (-2 to -3 SD). They all developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures in the first years of life. None had obvious facial dysmorphism, but strabismus was common. Brain imaging, available for 4 patients, showed cortical atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and cerebellar and brainstem atrophy. The 2 older patients lost the ability to eat by themselves and became overall more dependent at 23 and 21 years of age, respectively, suggesting a slowly progressive course with a neurodegenerative component.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMEBA in the families reported by {2:Marin-Valencia et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 6 patients from 3 consanguineous Egyptian families with NEDMEBA, {2:Marin-Valencia et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the TRAPPC6B gene ({610397.0001}). The mutation, which was found by homozygosity mapping and candidate gene analysis, segregated with the disorder in the families. Haplotype analysis suggested a founder effect. Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed an abnormal shorter transcript resulting from the skipping of exon 2, confirming the splice site abnormality. However, patient fibroblasts did not show obvious endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or Golgi morphologic changes or defects in intracellular trafficking.

In 2 patients from a consanguineous family (IDH3) with intellectual disability, {1:Harripaul et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous truncating mutation in the TRAPPC6B gene (R42X; {610397.0002}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. No additional clinical information was provided, and no functional studies of the variant or studies of patient cells were reported. The patients were ascertained from a cohort of 192 consanguineous families from Pakistan and Iran with autosomal recessive intellectual disability who underwent whole-exome sequencing.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Marin-Valencia et al. (2018)} found that morpholino knockdown of the trappc6b gene in zebrafish embryos resulted in decreased survival and decreased head size with evidence of increased apoptosis. Trappc6b morphants also showed a decreased seizure threshold, with increased spontaneous neuronal firing, and more frequent and longer calcium currents, consistent with neuronal hyperexcitability.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without seizures and gait abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with or without seizures and gait abnormalities (NEDSGA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GRIA4 gene ({138246}) on chromosome 11q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without seizures and gait abnormalities (NEDSGA) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy or early childhood, resulting in variably impaired intellectual development that can range from profound with absent speech to mild with an ability to attend special schools. Most affected individuals show irritability, stiffness, and hypertonia early in life, which progresses to spasticity and impaired gait later. Some patients may develop seizures of variable severity early in life (summary by {1:Martin et al., 2017}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Martin et al. (2017)} reported 5 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 4 to 21 years, with a neurodevelopmental disorder apparent from early infancy or childhood. Three patients showed irritability, stiffness, hypertonia, and/or increased startle reflex in the neonatal period. The patients had mild to severe developmental delay with intellectual disability and poor or absent speech. The most severely affected patient (patient 2) was a 21-year-old man who developed intractable seizures at age 5 weeks and had spastic quadriplegia with inability to walk, absent speech, inability to follow commands, nystagmus, strabismus, contractures, choreiform movements, short stature, and microcephaly. He also had brain abnormalities on imaging, including cortical atrophy and thin corpus callosum. The 4 other patients were less severely affected and could walk, although most had a clumsy or stiff gait. Two of these 4 patients had spasticity, including 1 with disabling hyperekplexia, and a third had hypotonia in the neonatal period. Three of these 4 patients had seizures of variable severity, including 1 with status epilepticus. The least severely affected child (patient 5) had normal motor development and no seizures; she could attend special school at age 4, although she was intellectually disabled. Dysmorphic features were mild or absent among the patients, with the only common feature being large ears. More variable additional features included sleeping problems, feeding difficulties, optic nerve hypoplasia, and stereotypic hand movements.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the GRIA4 gene that were identified in patients with NEDSGA by {1:Martin et al. (2017)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 unrelated patients with NEDSGA, {1:Martin et al. (2017)} identified 5 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the GRIA4 gene ({138246.0001}-{138246.0005}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Four of the mutations occurred in the highly conserved SYTANLAAF motif, which plays an important role in channel activation and gating. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but molecular modeling suggested that the location of 3 of the variants in the SYTANLAAF motif oriented toward the center of the pore region would most likely lead to disturbance of the gating mechanism allowing leakage or an open state, whereas the fourth variant in that motif likely results in reduced channel permeability. The fifth variant (R697P; {138246.0005}), in the extracellular domain, was predicted to interfere with the binding between monomers. The least affected child (patient 5) carried the R697P variant, suggesting some degree of genotype/phenotype correlation. The mutations were predicted to have a dominant functional effect rather than to cause a loss of function.
