phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 31

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 31 (MC1DN31) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TIMMDC1 gene ({615534}) on chromosome 3q13.

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex I deficiency, see {252010}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Kremer et al. (2017)} reported 3 unrelated patients (35791, 66744, and 96687) with mitochondrial complex I deficiency. All patients had severe neurologic dysfunction manifest as infantile-onset hypotonia, failure to thrive, and delayed or minimal psychomotor development. Additional more variable features included sensorineural deafness, dysmetria, dyskinetic movements, peripheral neuropathy, and nystagmus. One patient had brain imaging results consistent with Leigh syndrome, and another patient developed refractory seizures. Two patients died at ages 30 and 20 months; the third patient was alive at age 6 years, but had 2 older sibs who died young from a neurodegenerative disorder with severe epilepsy. The patients, from Greece, Northern Africa, and Germany, were of differing ethnic descent.

{1:Boutaud et al. (2023)} reported 2 sib fetuses in each of 2 families (families A and B); the parents in family A were consanguineous. All 4 patients had agenesis of the corpus callosum, 2 had lissencephaly, and 2 had a gyration delay. All 4 patients had hypoplasia of the basal ganglia nuclei, 2 had pons hypoplasia, 1 had vermis hypoplasia. Two patients had germinolytic cysts and 3 had frontal paraventricular cysts. One patient had gonadal dysgenesis and one had micropenis and hypospadias.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC1DN31 in the families reported by {2:Kremer et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 unrelated patients (35791, 66744, and 96687) with mitochondrial complex I deficiency, {2:Kremer et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous mutation in the TIMMDC1 gene ({615534.0001}).

{1:Boutaud et al. (2023)} identified a homozygous mutation (R137H; 615534.0002) in the TIMMDC1 gene in 2 sib fetuses in each of 2 families (families A and B) with MC1DN31. The parents in family A were consanguineous. The mutation was identified by whole-exome sequencing and segregated with disease in the families. TIMMDC1 protein expression was reduced in muscle tissue from the patients in both families. Expression of 3 subunits of respiratory chain complex I (NDUFA9, {603834}; NDUFB8, {602140}; and NDUFA13, {609435}) were also reduced in muscle tissue from the patients.

preferredTitle: MITOCHONDRIAL COMPLEX I DEFICIENCY, NUCLEAR TYPE 32; MC1DN32
clinicalSynopsis: White matter abnormalities consistent with Leigh syndrome seen on brain imaging
Mitochondrial complex I deficiency in various tissues
Two unrelated patients have been reported (last curated January 2019)
Caused by mutation in the NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase subunit B8 gene (NDUFB8,)

Neurologic - CNS: White matter abnormalities consistent with Leigh syndrome seen on brain imaging
Laboratory Abnormalities: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency in various tissues
Miscellaneous: Two unrelated patients have been reported (last curated January 2019)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase subunit B8 gene (NDUFB8,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 32

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 32 (MC1DN32) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the NDUFB8 gene ({602140}) on chromosome 10q24.

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex I deficiency, see {252010}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Piekutowska-Abramczuk et al. (2018)} reported 2 unrelated children with mitochondrial complex I deficiency. One child presented at 3 months of age with respiratory failure, seizures, and increased serum and CSF lactate. He had hypotonia, failure to thrive, and severely delayed psychomotor development with limited contact with his environment. He also developed left ventricular cardiac hypertrophy. Brain imaging showed signal alterations in the midbrain, putamen, and thalamus, consistent with Leigh syndrome (see {256000}) with later development of supratentorial and brainstem atrophy and cystic lesions. The patient was ventilator-dependent and fully dependent for all daily life activities. The other child was born at term and needed immediate resuscitation. He had poor growth, hypotonia, and delayed development. Laboratory studies showed increased serum and CSF lactate and lesions in the basal ganglia and internal capsule, consistent with Leigh syndrome. He died at age 15 months.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC1DN32 in the families reported by {1:Piekutowska-Abramczuk et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated children with mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 32 manifest as Leigh syndrome, {1:Piekutowska-Abramczuk et al. (2018)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the NDUFB8 gene ({602140.0001}-{602140.0004}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or targeted exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families.

preferredTitle: ARTHROGRYPOSIS, CLEFT PALATE, CRANIOSYNOSTOSIS, AND IMPAIRED INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENT; ACCIID
clinicalSynopsis: Generalized seizures, tractable (seen at 9 months in 1 patient)
Two unrelated patients have been reported (last curated January 2019)
One patient had more severe skeletal manifestations
Caused by mutation in the protein phosphatase 3, catalytic subunit, alpha isoform gene (PPP3CA,)

Head: Plagiocephaly
Trigonocephaly
Neurologic - CNS: Generalized seizures, tractable (seen at 9 months in 1 patient)
Miscellaneous: Two unrelated patients have been reported (last curated January 2019)
One patient had more severe skeletal manifestations
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the protein phosphatase 3, catalytic subunit, alpha isoform gene (PPP3CA,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Arthrogryposis, cleft palate, craniosynostosis, and impaired intellectual development

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that arthrogryposis, cleft palate, craniosynostosis, and impaired intellectual development (ACCIID) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PPP3CA gene ({114105}) on chromosome 4q24.

Heterozygous mutation in the PPP3CA gene can also cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-91 (DEE91; {617711}).

description.title: Description
description.content: ACCIID is characterized by arthrogryposis, cleft palate, craniosynostosis, micrognathia, short stature, and impaired intellectual development. Seizures and bony abnormalities (severe slenderness of the ribs and tubular bones and perinatal fractures) have been observed ({1:Mizuguchi et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Mizuguchi et al. (2018)} reported 2 unrelated patients with arthrogryposis, cleft palate, craniosynostosis, micrognathia, short stature, and impaired intellectual development. One patient (patient 5) was a 5-year-old female who had severe hydrops fetalis with ascites and right hydronephrosis on fetal ultrasonography. She had severe feeding difficulties and respiratory distress requiring tube feedings and mechanical ventilation. She had coronal craniosynostosis, hypertelorism, short nose, cleft palate, micrognathia, and arthrogryposis with bilateral talipes equinovalgus. Radiologic examination showed severe slenderness of tubular bones and ribs (gracile bones) with bowing of the radii and delayed calvarial ossification. She also developed several fractures during the neonatal period. She had a hypoplastic left kidney with severe vesicoureteral reflux and severe developmental delay. No seizures were observed. The other patient (patient 6) was a 7-year-old boy who had pedal edema at birth, as well as trigonocephaly, cleft palate, micrognathia, retrognathia, ptosis, arthrogryposis, and brachydactyly. He had significant developmental delay and developed generalized seizures with fever in infancy, which were mild and responsive to treatment. Brain MRI showed periventricular white matter changes with asymmetric ventriculomegaly.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations that were identified in 2 patients with ACCIID by {1:Mizuguchi et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 patients with ACCIID, {1:Mizuguchi et al. (2018)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the autoinhibitory domain of the PPP3CA gene ({114105.0007}-{114105.0008}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Using a yeast model, the mutations were found to be constitutively activating.

preferredTitle: MEGA-CORPUS-CALLOSUM SYNDROME WITH CEREBELLAR HYPOPLASIA AND CORTICAL MALFORMATIONS; MCCCHCM
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase 1 gene (MAST1,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase 1 gene (MAST1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Mega-corpus-callosum syndrome with cerebellar hypoplasia and cortical malformations

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mega-corpus-callosum syndrome with cerebellar hypoplasia and cortical malformations (MCCCHCM) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the MAST1 gene ({612256}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Mega-corpus-callosum syndrome with cerebellar hypoplasia and cortical malformations (MCCCHCM) is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, and characteristic brain abnormalities on brain imaging. Affected individuals have enlargement of the corpus callosum, enlarged ventricles, and cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia. Other features may include lack of speech development, gait instability, and seizures. Some patients with MAST1 mutations may have impaired intellectual development and/or autism spectrum disorder without significant findings on brain imaging (summary by {1:Tripathy et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Tripathy et al. (2018)} reported 6 unrelated children with characteristic brain malformations, including enlargement of the corpus callosum, enlarged ventricles, and cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia. Four patients had gyral simplification, 3 had dysplastic longitudinal gyri, and 1 had periventricular white matter nodules. The patients had variable motor and cognitive impairment, ranging from intellectual disability to severe encephalopathy; 5 were nonverbal. The patients had hypotonia and unsteady gait or only the ability to sit. Less common features included seizures (in 2 patients), short stature, strabismus, and oculomotor apraxia.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

Through the GeneMatcher program, {1:Tripathy et al. (2018)} identified 4 additional unrelated children with developmental delay and impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech associated with de novo missense variants in the MAST1 gene. Two of the patients had autism spectrum disorder and 2 had mild microcephaly. Brain imaging showed a small brainstem, cerebellum, and enlarged ventricles in 1 patient and dorsal hypoplasia of the corpus callosum in another patient, but the other 2 patients had normal brain imaging. More variable features included gait instability, hypotonia, esotropia, dysmorphic features, and seizures. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the variants were not found in the dbSNP, 1000 Genomes Project, or ExAC databases, {1:Tripathy et al. (2018)} speculated that these variants had a deleterious effect on protein function and may contribute to a phenotypic spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the MAST1 gene that were identified in patients with MCCCHCM by {1:Tripathy et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 unrelated patients with MCCCHCM, {1:Tripathy et al. (2018)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the MAST1 gene ({612256.0001}-{612256.0004}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Three patients carried in-frame deletions of single residues in a hydrophobic core of a 4-helix bundle in the domain of unknown function (DUF1908), and 3 patients carried the same missense variant in the kinase domain (G517S; {612256.0004}). In vitro functional studies showed that 1 of the variants (lys276del; {612256.0002}) increased MAST1 binding to microtubules compared to controls. Mutant mice heterozygous for a Mast1 leu278del allele ({612256.0003}) showed a thicker corpus callosum compared to wildtype, which was due to an increase in the number of myelinated axons crossing the midline. Mutant mice also had an overall reduction in cortical volume and thickness and decreased cerebellar volume and number of granule and Purkinje cells due to increased apoptosis compared to controls.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Tripathy et al. (2018)} used CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to generate a mutant Mast1 mouse strain with heterozygous expression of a leu278del allele, to recapitulate the mutation identified in a patient with MCCCHCM ({612256.0003}). Mutant mice showed a thicker corpus callosum compared to wildtype, which was due to an increase in the number of myelinated axons crossing the midline. Mutant mice also had an overall reduction in cortical volume and thickness and decreased cerebellar volume and number of granule and Purkinje cells due to increased apoptosis compared to controls. The deletion of leu278 was associated with decreased levels of other MAST protein family members, whereas complete loss of Mast1 was associated with increased levels of other MAST proteins, likely a compensatory effect. These findings suggested that the leu278 allele acts in a dominant-negative manner. There was no evidence of abnormal activation of the AKT3 ({611223})/mTOR (see {601231}) pathway.

preferredTitle: FIBROSIS, NEURODEGENERATION, AND CEREBRAL ANGIOMATOSIS; FINCA
clinicalSynopsis: Increased latencies on visual evoked potentials
Giant responses on visual evoked potentials
Over-inflated lungs seen on chest x-ray
Onset of symptoms at 2 months of age
Death in second year of life due to respiratory failure
Caused by mutation in the NHL repeat-containing protein 2 gene (NHLRC2,)

Eyes: Increased latencies on visual evoked potentials
Giant responses on visual evoked potentials
Lung: Over-inflated lungs seen on chest x-ray
Miscellaneous: Onset of symptoms at 2 months of age
Death in second year of life due to respiratory failure
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the NHL repeat-containing protein 2 gene (NHLRC2,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that fibrosis, neurodegeneration, and cerebral angiomatosis (FINCA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NHLRC2 gene ({618277}) on chromosome 10q25.

description.title: Description
description.content: Fibrosis, neurodegeneration, and cerebral angiomatosis (FINCA) is characterized by severe progressive cerebropulmonary symptoms, resulting in death in infancy from respiratory failure. Features include malabsorption, progressive growth failure, recurrent infections, chronic hemolytic anemia, and transient liver dysfunction. Neuropathology shows increased angiomatosis-like leptomeningeal, cortical, and superficial white matter vascularization and congestion, vacuolar degeneration and myelin loss in white matter, as well as neuronal degeneration. Interstitial fibrosis and granuloma-like lesions are seen in the lungs, and there is hepatomegaly with steatosis and collagen accumulation ({4:Uusimaa et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{4:Uusimaa et al. (2018)} studied 2 Finnish brothers and an unrelated Finnish boy with a multiorgan syndrome, which the authors designated 'FINCA' for the features of fibrosis, neurodegeneration, and cerebral angiomatosis. All 3 children appeared healthy at birth, but presented at age 2 months with irritability, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, diarrhea, and growth failure. During the following months, they exhibited delayed development, reduced vision, recurrent infections, transient hepatic dysfunction, and chronic hemolytic anemia. The 2 brothers developed dystonic tetraplegia, and the other boy was dystonic as well. One patient exhibited cardiomegaly. All had progressive respiratory difficulties that culminated in death from respiratory failure in the second year of life. At autopsy, all 3 brains were atrophic and showed increased angiomatosis-like leptomeningeal, cortical, and superficial white matter vascularization and congestion, as well as white matter degeneration and variable neuronal degeneration. Lung biopsies showed severe interstitial fibrosis, with no normal lung tissue in 2 of the patients. In addition, unusual granuloma-like lesions were observed, which were enriched with myofibroblasts. All 3 patients had hepatomegaly; transmission electron microscopy of a biopsy from 1 of the patients showed steatosis and accumulation of collagen bundles.

{1:Brodsky et al. (2020)} reported a patient who presented at 4 hours of life with indirect hyperbilirubinemia, leukocytosis, bilateral pneumonia, and hemolytic anemia. He also had cardiomegaly and hepatosplenomegaly. Echocardiogram at 6 weeks of age showed ventricular hypertrophy. Lung CTs at 1.5, 2, and 5 months of age showed bilateral consolidation and atelectasis. He had recurrent infections, and laboratory testing showed decreased serum IgG, and decreased CD3, CD4, and CD8 cells. He had a pectus excavatum, which was surgically corrected at 1 year and 8 months of age, and a lung biopsy at that time demonstrated pulmonary fibrosis. He had dystonia and delayed motor activity starting at 2 months of age. At 21 months of age he developed epileptogenic myoclonus. Brain MRI showed a thin corpus callosum, moderate atrophy of the frontotemporal area, and ventriculomegaly. There was no evidence of cerebral angiomatosis. Although his condition stabilized until the age of 2 years and 3 months, he developed an acute illness and died at age 2 years and 5 months from respiratory failure.

{2:Rapp et al. (2021)} reported 6 patients from 3 families of various ethnic origin with disease onset between 0 to 12 months of age. Two of the patients had an overall progressive disease course, 2 patients had a stable disease course, and 2 patients had an intermediate disease course. Four of the patients had exacerbations of respiratory disease, and chest CTs performed in 3 patients showed ground glass opacities with patchy consolidations in 2 and subpleural cyst formation in 1. Neurologic features included developmental delay in 5 patients, irritability in 5, axial hypotonia in 5, and dystonia in 6. Three patients had episodic diarrhea, 4 had feeding problems, and 3 had failure to thrive. One patient had hepatosplenomegaly and 2 patients had transient liver dysfunction. None of the patients had angiomatosis. Two patients died of respiratory distress, at ages 17 and 22 months.

{3:Sczakiel et al. (2023)} reported 15 patients, ranging in age from 22 months to 19 years, from 12 families with FINCA syndrome. All of the patients had moderate to severe global developmental delay and neuromuscular symptoms. Neurologic findings included seizures or EEG abnormalities (11/15), axial hypotonia (12/15), dystonia or spasticity (4/14), gait disturbances (5/9), brain abnormalities (7/15), and speech or motor regression (6/10). Four of 10 patients had borderline microcephaly (less than -2 SD), 9 had decreased body weight, and 7 had short stature. Pulmonary findings included 2 patients with respiratory distress in infancy. Other findings included 2 patients with anemia, 3 with strabismus, 2 with diarrhea, and 1 with hepatomegaly.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of FINCA in the families reported by {4:Uusimaa et al. (2018)}, {1:Brodsky et al. (2020)}, and {2:Rapp et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 Finnish male infants from 2 unrelated families with fibrosis, neurodegeneration, and cerebral angiomatosis, {4:Uusimaa et al. (2018)} performed whole-exome sequencing and identified compound heterozygosity for a missense mutation (D148Y; {618277.0001}) and a 2-bp deletion ({618277.0002}) in the NHLRC2 gene. Genealogy traced back 7 to 9 generations, to the 1750s, did not show common ancestors for the 2 families, and consanguinity within the families could not be confirmed because their ancestors were born in northern Finland at least 150 miles apart.

By whole-exome sequencing in a 2-year-old Ukrainian boy with FINCA, {1:Brodsky et al. (2020)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the NHLRC2 gene ({618277.0001} and {618277.0003}). Functional studies were not performed.

In 5 patients with FINCA, including 2 sets of sibs, {2:Rapp et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the NHLRC2 gene ({618277.0001}; {618277.0004}-{618277.0005}). The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing and segregated with disease in each family.

In 15 patients from 12 families with FINCA, {3:Sczakiel et al. (2023)} identified biallelic mutations in the NHLRC2 gene, including the recurrent D148Y mutation ({618277.0001}) and 9 novel mutations (see, e.g., {618277.0006}-{618277.0009}). The novel mutations included 1 start-loss mutation, 3 missense mutations, 2 in-frame deletions, 2 nonsense mutations, and 1 C-terminal frameshift mutation. Expression of the novel mutations in HEK293 cells showed varying levels of reduced expression compared to wildtype.

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: {3:Sczakiel et al. (2023)} expressed 9 NHLRC2 mutations identified in patients with FINCA in HEK293 cells and found that the mutations showed varying levels of reduced expression compared to wildtype. {3:Sczakiel et al. (2023)} then added the expression levels for each mutation in the biallelic combinations identified in the patients and compared the total calculated expression with the patient phenotypes. Patients with the lowest calculated total NHLRC2 expression were more likely to have pulmonary involvement compared to patients with higher calculated total expression.

clinicalSynopsis: Most patients have onset of seizures in the first months of life
Later onset of seizures in the first year of life may also occur
Topiramate may have a favorable response on seizures
Caused by mutation in the calcium channel, voltage-dependent, alpha-1E subunit gene (CACNA1E,)

Head: Macrocephaly (in some patients)
Miscellaneous: Most patients have onset of seizures in the first months of life
Later onset of seizures in the first year of life may also occur
Topiramate may have a favorable response on seizures
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the calcium channel, voltage-dependent, alpha-1E subunit gene (CACNA1E,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-69 (DEE69) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1E gene ({601013}) on chromosome 1q25.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-69 (DEE69) is an autosomal dominant severe neurodevelopmental encephalopathic disorder characterized by early-onset refractory seizures, hypotonia, and profoundly impaired development often associated with macrocephaly, hyperkinetic movements, and contractures. The disorder can sometimes result in early death. Some patients may have a favorable seizure response to topiramate medication (summary by {1:Helbig et al., 2018}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Helbig et al. (2018)} reported 30 unrelated patients with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by early-onset intractable seizures, severe hypotonia, and severe or profound global developmental delay with absent or very poor speech and inability to sit or walk. Most of the patients were children in the first decade, although there were several teenagers and 1 patient who died at age 25 years. Six further patients died in the first years of life. Most patients presented with various types of seizures in the first months of life, although 2 patients had onset of seizures at 3 years of age and 2 had not had seizures by age 4 years. EEG in those with seizures showed multifocal discharges, polyspike slow-wave discharges, and sometimes hypsarrhythmia or burst-suppression patterns. Some patients showed developmental regression after onset of seizures. Additional common features included spastic quadriplegia, hyperreflexia, hyperkinetic movements, dystonia, myoclonus, clonus, poor or absent eye contact, nystagmus, cortical visual impairment, and loss of head control. Thirteen patients had congenital contractures and 13 had macrocephaly. Brain imaging was normal in many and showed nonspecific white matter volume loss, atrophy of the corpus callosum, or cortical atrophy in a few patients. Three patients (27, 28, and 29) had a slightly milder phenotype, including 2 who had not developed seizures by age 4 years and 1 who had been seizure-free and was off medication at age 6. These 3 patients were able to achieve walking and a few words.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{2:Royer-Bertrand et al. (2021)} described 7 patients, aged 18 months to 31 years, with de novo mutations in the CACNA1E gene, only one of whom (patient 4) had seizures (infantile spasms), which began at 6.5 months of age and responded to topiramate. Of 3 other patients tested, 2 had an abnormal EEG and 1 was normal. All 7 patients had global developmental delay and/or intellectual disability. Four patients showed developmental regression and 3 showed motor stereotypies. Symptom onset/parental concern was shortly after birth to 24 months of age.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CACNA1E gene identified in patients with DEE69 by {1:Helbig et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: Five patients with DEE69 reported by {1:Helbig et al. (2018)} showed a favorable seizure response to treatment with topiramate, which blocks R-type calcium channels. However, topiramate had no effect on seizure control in 10 of 18 (56%) patients.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 30 unrelated patients with DEE69, {1:Helbig et al. (2018)} identified 14 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the CACNA1E gene (see, e.g., {601013.0001}-{601013.0005}). The variants, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, occurred throughout the gene, although most clustered in the cytoplasmic ends of S6 segment transmembrane domains that line the inner pore of the channel and form the activation gate. All mutations were classified as pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines, and none were found in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. There were several recurrent mutations. In vitro functional expression studies of some of the mutations in human tsA201 transformed kidney cells showed that they resulted in consistent gain-of-function effects, including facilitated voltage-dependent channel activation, slowed inactivation, and increased current density compared to wildtype. The findings indicated that the mutations perturb the gating properties of the channel, resulting in increased inward calcium currents that may affect neuronal excitability and synaptic transmission. Three additional patients (31, 32, and 33) with a milder neurologic phenotype were found to carry heterozygous frameshift or nonsense mutations in the CACNA1E gene that were predicted to result in a loss of function and haploinsufficiency. Functional studies of these variants were not performed. One of these patients inherited the mutation from an apparently unaffected father, another was somatic mosaic for the mutation, and parental DNA from the third was unavailable. Thus, the significance of these loss-of-function mutations was unclear. The patients were ascertained though international collaboration between research and diagnostic sequencing laboratories.

{2:Royer-Bertrand et al. (2021)} described 7 patients, aged 18 months to 31 years, with de novo heterozygous mutations in the CACNA1E gene, including 6 missense and 1 splicing. None of the mutations were found in the gnomAD database. No functional evidence was provided for any of the mutations, but codon 702 appeared to be a hotspot. The only patient (patient 4) who had seizures (infantile spasms) had an ala702-to-ser substitution ({601013.0006}).

preferredTitle: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER, AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE 67; MRT67
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3, subunit F gene (EIF3F,)

Head: Microcephaly
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3, subunit F gene (EIF3F,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder-67 (MRT67) is caused by homozygous mutation or compound heterozygous mutation in the EIF3F gene ({603914}) on chromosome 11p15.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Martin et al. (2018)} reported 9 patients, 4 to 48 years of age, with intellectual developmental disorder from 7 nonconsanguineous families of European ancestry. All were homozygous for the same mutation in EIF3F (see MOLECULAR GENETICS). All patients were born at term with average growth parameters, and all had normal growth. There were no specific facial dysmorphic features and no structural brain abnormalities on MRI. Impaired intellectual development ranged from specific learning disability to severe ID. Six had seizures, one of these with infantile spasms. Three had sensorineural hearing loss. One of these patients also had bilateral cleft lip and palate. One other patient had anal stenosis, cryptorchidism, and small hands and feet. One patient had wasting of thenar and hypothenar eminences, which was noted because EIF3F had been shown to play a role in regulating skeletal muscle size via interaction with the mTOR ({601231}) pathway ({1:Csibi et al., 2010}).

Through GeneMatcher and internal communications, {2:Huffmeier et al. (2021)} collected 21 previously unreported patients from 16 families with MRT67 and mutation in the EIF3F gene. Global developmental delay was present in all patients. Hearing loss was found in 57% of patients, behavioral problems in 57%, muscular hypo- or hypertonia in 48%, short stature in 40%, microcephaly at the last physical examination in 32%, ophthalmologic findings in 38%, sleep issues in 24%, and epilepsy in 15%. Developmental regression was observed in 3 of 21 individuals at the age of 2.5 years (P11.1), 21 years (P4.1), and in adulthood (P14). Dysmorphic features were subtle and nonspecific.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MRT67 in the families reported by {3:Martin et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
{3:Martin et al. (2018)} reported homozygosity for a phe232-to-val variant in EIF3F (F232V; {603914.0001}) in 9 patients from 7 families with MRT67, all of European descent and participants in the Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) study. This variant, {dbSNP rs141976414}, is one of the most common protein-altering variants in the gene and is present at an allele frequency of 0.12%, never in homozygosity, in non-Finnish Europeans in gnomAD.

In 21 newly reported patients from 16 families with MRT67 who were found through GeneMatcher and internal communications, {2:Huffmeier et al. (2021)} identified the previously reported F232V mutation in the EIF3F gene in homozygosity in 20 patients and in compound heterozygosity with a novel 1-bp duplication (c.861dup, {603914.0002}) in 1. Haplotype analysis showed that the F232V variant was on an identical haplotype in 15 affected individuals of all tested families, suggesting a founder effect. The c.861dup variant was not present in the gnomAD database. The patient (P3) with the c.861dup mutation had motor and speech development and postnatal growth on the severe end of the spectrum compared to patients with homozygosity for the F232V variant, suggesting the possibility of genotype-phenotype correlation.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-70 (DEE70) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PHACTR1 gene ({608723}) on chromosome 6p24.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-70 (DEE70) is neurologic disorder characterized by the onset of epileptic spasms or seizures in the first months of life. EEG may show hypsarrhythmia, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of West syndrome. Affected individuals show severely delayed psychomotor development with impaired or absent walking and language skills; intellectual impairment ranges from moderate to severe (summary by {2:Hamada et al., 2018}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:De Ligt et al. (2012)} reported a 28-year-old woman with DEE70. She had her first seizures at 3 weeks of age and thereafter showed severely delayed psychomotor development. She learned to sit and could speak a few words, but later lost these skills. Epilepsy could be relatively controlled with medication. As an adult, she had low normal height, small head circumference (-2.5 SD), spastic tetraparesis with joint contractures, and scoliosis.

{2:Hamada et al. (2018)} reported 2 unrelated Japanese children, aged 4 and 5 years, with DEE70. They presented with seizures in the first months of life and also showed global developmental delay. EEG showed hypsarrhythmia in both patients, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of West syndrome. One patient was more severely affected, with poor seizure response to medication and no head control. Brain imaging showed cortical atrophy and delayed myelination. He also had cryptorchidism. The other patient had favorable seizure response to ACTH and normal brain imaging; he walked at 18 months and had a few words at 24 months. He was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. This patient had mild dysmorphic facial features.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the PHACTR1 gene that were identified in patients with DEE70 by {2:Hamada et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 28-year-old woman (trio 90) with DEE70, {1:de Ligt et al. (2012)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the PHACTR1 gene (R521C; {608723.0001}). The mutation was found by exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. The patient was ascertained from a larger cohort of 100 patients with severe intellectual disability who underwent exome sequencing.

In 2 unrelated patients with DEE70, {2:Hamada et al. (2018)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the PHACTR1 gene (L500P, {608723.0002} and N479I, {608723.0003}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing. In vitro functional expression studies showed that these mutations interrupted actin binding, whereas R521C interrupted PP1 (see {176875}) binding. The mutations were unable to rescue the neuronal migration defects in Phactr1-null mice (see ANIMAL MODEL), suggesting that they are pathogenic. In addition, expression of the mutations in mice induced migration defects and caused abnormal cortical architecture in a dominant-negative manner.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Hamada et al. (2018)} found that knockdown of the Phactr1 gene in embryonic mouse brain resulted in neuronal migration defects and abnormal cortical architecture.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-68 (MRT68) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TRMT1 gene ({611669}) on chromosome 19p13.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Najmabadi et al. (2011)} reported a consanguineous Iranian family (M300) in which 5 individuals had nonsyndromic moderate to severe impaired intellectual development. Clinical details were limited. A subsequent report by {2:Davarniya et al. (2015)} included the clinical features of 2 patients in family M300, noting that they had mild dysmorphic facial features with protruding ears, narrow palpebral fissures, and broad eyebrows. They also had involvement of the extremities, with pes planus and onset of progressive spasticity in the lower limbs during adolescence. Brain imaging reportedly showed cerebellar atrophy and an enlarged fourth ventricle.

{2:Davarniya et al. (2015)} reported 3 adult brothers, born of consanguineous Iranian parents (family 9000114), with MRT68. They had low birth weight and overall poor growth, global developmental delay with delayed walking, moderately delayed intellectual development (IQ range 55-70), and delayed speech until 4 to 6 years of age. Mild dysmorphic features, such as synophrys, broad nasal bridge, and hypoplastic maxilla, were also present. One patient had hearing loss. All also had muscle weakness in the upper and lower limbs. Brain imaging did not reveal significant abnormalities.

{1:Blaesius et al. (2018)} reported 4 patients from 2 unrelated Pakistani families with MRT68. The patients presented at birth with microcephaly and later showed impaired intellectual development. Three adult sibs from 1 family did not have motor involvement, whereas the single patient from the second family was more severely affected with motor and speech delay and hypotonia. Two of the adult sibs and the singleton patient had progressive microcephaly (-4 to -4.9 SD). All had seizures. Brain imaging of the singleton patient showed generalized white matter volume loss, periventricular leukomalacia, and isolated inferior vermis hypoplasia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MRT68 in the family reported by {2:Davarniya et al. (2015)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In affected members of a consanguineous Iranian family (M300) with MRT68, {3:Najmabadi et al. (2011)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the TRMT1 gene ({611669.0001}). The family was part of a large cohort of 136 consanguineous families with intellectual disability who underwent genetic analysis. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In 3 adult brothers, born of consanguineous Iranian parents (family 9000114), with MRT68, {2:Davarniya et al. (2015)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the TRMT1 gene ({611669.0003}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of linkage analysis and whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not found in 100 Iranian controls. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the variant was predicted to result in a loss of function.

In 4 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous Pakistani families with MRT68, {1:Blaesius et al. (2018)} identified homozygous loss of function mutations in the TRMT1 gene ({611669.0001} and {611669.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

preferredTitle: HYPOMAGNESEMIA, SEIZURES, AND IMPAIRED INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENT 2; HOMGSMR2
clinicalSynopsis: Persistent seizure activity despite amelioration of magnesium levels
Caused by mutation in the Na+/K+ transporting ATPase, alpha-1 polypeptide gene (ATP1A1,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the Na+/K+ transporting ATPase, alpha-1 polypeptide gene (ATP1A1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Hypomagnesemia, seizures, and impaired intellectual development 2

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hypomagnesemia, seizures, and impaired intellectual development-2 (HOMGSMR2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP1A1 gene ({182310}) on chromosome 1p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Hypomagnesemia, seizures, and impaired intellectual development-2 (HOMGSMR2) is characterized by generalized seizures in infancy, severe hypomagnesemia, and renal magnesium wasting. Seizures persist despite magnesium supplementation and are associated with significantly impaired intellectual development ({1:Schlingmann et al., 2018}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of hypomagnesemia, seizures, and impaired intellectual development, see HOMGSMR1 ({616418}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Schlingmann et al. (2018)} studied 3 infants who presented between 6 days and 6 months of age with generalized convulsions and severe hypomagnesemia due to massive renal magnesium wasting. Despite treatment with antiepileptic drugs and intravenous magnesium followed by oral supplementation, seizure activity persisted. Brain MRI in 2 of the patients showed cerebral volume loss, and all 3 had significant global developmental delay, displaying limited motor skills and speaking only in single words at ages 4 years, 6 years, and 10 years, respectively. In addition, 2 patients showed clinical features compatible with an autism spectrum disorder. All 3 patients were normotensive, and cardiac evaluation was unremarkable. Significant polyuria was observed in 2 patients, but renal concentrating ability remained at least partially intact, with random urine osmolalities of greater than 400 mosmol/L. Although laboratory analyses did not show renal salt wasting or significant activation of the renin-aldosterone system, all affected individuals exhibited intermittent episodes of significant hypokalemia due to renal potassium wasting. The parents of all 3 children were clinically unaffected and had normal serum magnesium levels.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the ATP1A1 gene that were identified in patients with HOMGSMR2 by {1:Schlingmann et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: From a cohort of 7 children with hypomagnesemia and intractable seizures associated with severely impaired intellectual development, who were negative for mutation in the CNNM2 ({607803}) and TRPM6 ({607009}) genes, {1:Schlingmann et al. (2018)} identified 3 who were heterozygous for missense mutations in the ATP1A1 gene ({182310.0006}-{182310.0008}). All 3 variants were shown to have arisen de novo and were not found in public variant databases.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with cardiac defects and dysmorphic facies (IDDCDF) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TMEM94 gene ({618163}) on chromosome 17q25.

description.title: Description
description.content: IDDCDF is an autosomal recessive syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by globally impaired development with intellectual disability and speech delay, congenital cardiac malformations, and dysmorphic facial features. Additional features, such as distal skeletal anomalies, may also be observed ({2:Stephen et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Stephen et al. (2018)} reported 10 patients from 6 unrelated families with a similar syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. The families were of different ethnic origins, but most were consanguineous and of Middle Eastern descent. The patients ranged in age from 3 to 24 years, and all had global developmental delay apparent from infancy or early childhood, with mild to moderate impaired intellectual development, learning disabilities, speech delay, and mildly delayed walking. Many attended special schools; IQ of 1 patient at age 16 was 58. All but 1 of the patients presented in infancy with variable congenital heart defects, including tetralogy of Fallot, atrial and ventricular septal defects, patent foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus, hypoplastic pulmonary valve or pulmonary atresia, and double outlet right ventricle. Dysmorphic features included triangular face with pointed chin, short nose with anteverted nares, flat nasal bridge, deep-set eyes, hypertelorism, long philtrum, thin upper lip, low-set or dysmorphic ears, highly arched eyebrows, and synophrys or hypertrichosis. Some patients had mild myopia or strabismus, and some had somatic overgrowth and large head circumference. About half of patients had skeletal anomalies, such as long or overlapping fingers or toes, cutaneous syndactyly, and scoliosis. Less common features observed in only 1 or 2 patients included seizures, pectus abnormalities, hypotonia, feeding or respiratory difficulties, hypospadias, and cryptorchidism. Brain imaging, performed in a few patients, showed nonspecific abnormalities, such as Chiari I malformation (1 patient), delayed myelination, and white matter signal abnormalities.

{1:Al-Hamed et al. (2020)} reported prenatal and postnatal clinical features in patients from 2 unrelated patients, conceived of consanguineous Saudi Arabian parents. In the first family, a fetus was found to have generalized skin edema, ascites, unilateral hydrothorax, and polyhydramnios on prenatal ultrasound at 26 weeks' gestation. A fetal echocardiogram was normal. The infant was delivered at 28 weeks' gestation by cesarean section due to severe maternal preeclampsia and died immediately after delivery. In the second family, a fetus had a thick nuchal fold, micrognathia, bilaterally clenched hands, and an abdominal cyst on prenatal ultrasound at 29 weeks' gestation. Prenatal echocardiogram showed a large atrial septal defect and small ventricular septal defects. After birth, the infant had dysmorphic facial features and birth weight greater than normal for gestational age. The infant died at 6 months of age following cardiac surgery. A sib of this patient was found to have a thick nuchal fold on prenatal ultrasound, and the pregnancy was terminated after confirmation of homozygous mutation in the TMEM94 gene.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IDDCDF in the families reported by {2:Stephen et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 10 patients from 6 unrelated families with IDDCDF, {2:Stephen et al. (2018)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous nonsense, frameshift, or splice site mutations (see, e.g., {618163.0001}-{618163.0005}). All the mutations were predicted or demonstrated to result in truncated proteins lacking the highly conserved C-terminal domain including cation P-type ATPase domains. Analysis of cells from patients from 2 unrelated families showed significantly decreased TMEM94 expression, consistent with a loss of function. Global transcriptome profiling of cells from 1 family showed dysregulation of genes involved in cell growth, proliferation, and survival that were predicted to affect several organ systems involved in the phenotype. The patients were ascertained through collaborative research efforts and matchmaking platforms, and the mutations, which were found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Several of the affected individuals were found to have homozygous variants of unknown significance in other genes, including those known to cause recessively inherited neurodevelopmental disorders, but these variants were not considered to be the primary genetic cause of the disorder.

{1:Al-Hamed et al. (2020)} reported 3 patients with IDDCDF from 2 unrelated Saudi Arabian consanguineous families with homozygous mutations in the TMEM94 gene ({618163.0006}-{618163.0007}, respectively). The mutations were identified prenatally by whole-exome sequencing and were present in heterozygous state in the parents. Mutation testing was performed because of detection of fetal anomalies.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Stephen et al. (2018)} found that homozygous loss of Tmem94 in mice was embryonic lethal and led to craniofacial defects, cardiac abnormalities, and abnormal neuronal migration in the central nervous system.

phenotypes.phenotype: Encephalopathy, progressive, early-onset, with brain edema and/or leukoencephalopathy, 2

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that early-onset progressive encephalopathy with brain edema and/or leukoencephalopathy-2 (PEBEL2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NAXD gene ({615910}) on chromosome 13q34.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Early-onset progressive encephalopathy with brain edema and/or leukoencephalopathy-2 (PEBEL2) is an autosomal recessive severe neurometabolic disorder characterized by rapidly progressive neurologic deterioration that is usually associated with a febrile illness. Affected infants tend to show normal early development followed by acute psychomotor regression with ataxia, hypotonia, and sometimes seizures, resulting in death in the first years of life. Brain imaging shows multiple abnormalities, including brain edema and signal abnormalities in the cortical and subcortical regions (summary by {3:Van Bergen et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of PEBEL, see PEBEL1 ({617186}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Van Bergen et al. (2019)} reported 6 unrelated children with a similar multisystem disorder resulting in early death in the first years of life. The patients presented in the first months or years with episodic neurologic deterioration and developmental regression, often associated with acute illness, fever, or mild trauma. Almost all had normal development prior to disease onset, although some had mild speech delay. Features at disease onset included lethargy, irritability, gait ataxia, loss of speech, and abnormal movements, including dystonia and chorea. Some had recurrent vomiting and diarrhea, seizures, ophthalmoplegia, and/or hearing loss. Brain imaging showed edema, frontal lobe atrophy, diffusion abnormalities throughout the brain, white matter abnormalities, signal abnormalities in the striatum and basal ganglia, and volume loss. Brain biopsy performed on 1 patient showed extensive neuronal damage and reactive gliosis. Most patients also developed skin lesions in the groin and axillae consistent with epidermal necrosis, several patients developed pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow, and 1 patient had severe cardiomyopathy.

{1:Borna et al. (2020)} reported a 7-year-old boy with PEBEL2 who was developmentally typical until the age of 1 year when he developed bronchitis, hypotonia, and elevated creatine kinase. At that time he was also found to have mild anemia and elevated liver transaminases, lactate dehydrogenase, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Hemophilus influenzae and Corynebacterium were detected. At age 4 years, he had poor communication skills, clumsiness, and repetitive behaviors. A diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder was suspected, although he had an average score on a full-scale IQ assessment. He was admitted to the hospital with gastroenteritis and dehydration at age 7. Laboratory investigations revealed elevated liver transaminases, lactate dehydrogenase, lactate, creatine kinase, and glucose as well as metabolic acidosis. During his hospitalization, he had a sudden deterioration and died. Postmortem evaluation showed thickening of the myocardial wall and gross hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Acute inflammation of the digestive tract, acute myocarditis, acute tubular necrosis, and congestion of various organs were also seen.

{5:Zhou et al. (2020)} reported a patient who presented at 2 years and 10 months of age with skin lesions and involuntary movements that began in the context of a febrile respiratory tract illness. Brain MRI initially showed mild cerebellar edema. A follow-up MRI 2 weeks later demonstrated abnormal signal in the basal ganglia and cerebellar hemispheres. A skin biopsy of one of the lesions showed necrosis of the epidermis. He had a complete neurologic recovery and improvement of skin lesions 2 months after initiation of antioxidant vitamin supplements. At 3 years and 10 months of age he had a similar episode in the setting of a febrile illness, and brain MRI showed edema of the basal ganglia, which eventually improved. After whole-exome sequencing demonstrated mutations in the NAXD gene, therapy with niacin was initiated when he had another recurrence of skin lesions. Niacin treatment resulted in improvement of the lesions, and at 5 years of age, he had no further occurrences.

{2:Manor et al. (2022)} reported a patient who presented at 2 years of age with gait abnormalities in the setting of respiratory failure. Laboratory testing demonstrated an elevation in creatine kinase. He developed a gradual recovery to baseline but had progressive muscle weakness. At 13 years of age, he was evaluated for a 4-month episode of weight loss and was found to have hip flexor weakness. At 16 years of age, he had a myoencephalopathic crisis with respiratory failure. A muscle biopsy showed ragged-blue fibers and COX-negative fibers with increased lipid droplets. After genetic testing demonstrated biallelic mutations in NAXD, treatment with niacin was started and the patient had improvement in his creatine kinase level. Plasma metabolomic studies showed depletion of nicotinamide metabolites during metabolic crisis, which normalized after niacin supplementation.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PEBEL2 in the families reported by {3:van Bergen et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content:
{5:Zhou et al. (2020)} reported a patient who had improvement in skin lesions and cessation of episodic neurologic deterioration after initiation of niacin therapy.

{2:Manor et al. (2022)} reported a patient who had improvement in creatine kinase level after initiation of niacin therapy.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 6 unrelated probands with PEBEL2, {3:Van Bergen et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the NAXD gene (see, e.g., {615910.0001}-{615910.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Patient cells showed abnormal accumulation of the damaged toxic cofactors S-NADHX, R-NADHX, and cyclic NADHX, which could be rescued by wildtype NAXD. Patient cells and muscle biopsies also showed impaired mitochondrial function, higher sensitivity to metabolic stress, and decreased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production. In vitro functional cellular studies of 2 missense variants (R308C, {615910.0001} and G63S, {615910.0003}) showed that the mutant proteins were thermolabile and had altered functional properties resulting in decreased overall enzymatic activity. The findings suggested that NAXD deficiency can be classified as a metabolite repair disorder in which accumulation of damaged metabolites likely triggers devastating effects in tissues such as the brain and the heart, eventually leading to early childhood death.

In a 7-year-old boy with PEBEL2, {1:Borna et al. (2020)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the NAXD gene: a 4-bp deletion (c.51_54delAGAA; {615910.0005}) previously identified by {3:Van Bergen et al. (2019)}, and a 1-bp deletion (c.44delG; {615910.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Both mutations are located in the mitochondria-targeted isoform of NAXD. Overexpression of either mutation in HEK293FT cells showed loss of protein expression compared to wildtype.

{4:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} observed that the 3 patients with PEBEL2 reported by {3:Van Bergen et al. (2019)} and {1:Borna et al. (2020)} who were homozygous or compound heterozygous for NAXD mutations predicted to cause loss of the mitochondrial NAXD isoform but not the cytosolic NAXD isoform (c.51_54delAGAA and c.44delG) did not have the characteristic skin findings seen in the other reported PEBEL2 patients. Furthermore, lower NADHX levels were detected in fibroblasts from the patient who was homozygous for the c.51_54delAGAA mutation compared to patients with other mutations, as reported in {3:Van Bergen et al. (2019)}. {4:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} therefore hypothesized that a loss of only the mitochondrial isoform of NAXD, as compared to the loss of both the cytosolic and mitochondrial isoforms, may lead to differences in disease development due to residual cytosolic repair of damaged NAD(P)H.

By whole-exome sequencing in a Chinese boy with PEBEL2, {5:Zhou et al. (2020)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the NAXD gene: a 2-bp deletion ({615910.0007}) and a missense mutation (I106M; {615910.0008}).

In a patient with PEBEL2, {2:Manor et al. (2022)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the NAXD gene ({615910.0009} and {615910.0010}). The mutations were identified by a combination of chromosome array and whole-exome sequencing. Because exon 1 contains the mitochondrial propeptide and the cytosolic form is encoded starting in exon 2, the V16I mutation may affect only the mitochondrial isoform.

Two unrelated patients have been reported (last curated February 2019)

phenotypes.phenotype: Congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation 2

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital disorder of glycosylation with defective fucosylation-2 (CDGF2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the FCSK gene ({608675}) on chromosome 16q22.

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of CDGF, see {618005}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Ng et al. (2018)} reported 2 unrelated children, aged 6 and 7 years, with a severe multisystem disorder apparent from early infancy. One patient was born prematurely at 25 weeks' gestation. As infants, they had hypotonia, poor feeding necessitating tube feeding, and severely delayed psychomotor development. Both developed intractable seizures with epileptic encephalopathy; EEG in 1 patient showed hypsarrhythmia. Ocular features included maculopathy, visual impairment, cortical blindness, optic atrophy, strabismus, and nystagmus. Both patients had respiratory difficulty with frequent infections, as well as contractures. Both were nonambulatory and had severely impaired intellectual development. Brain imaging showed cerebellar and brainstem atrophy (pontocerebellar hypoplasia), hypoplasia or agenesis of the corpus callosum, and white matter abnormalities including periventricular leukomalacia, consistent with a destructive process. One patient had serum metabolic abnormalities of methylmalonic acid and B12 metabolism; serum transferrin analysis performed in this patient showed normal results.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDGF2 in the families reported by {1:Ng et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated patients with CDGF2, {1:Ng et al. (2018)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations in the FUK gene ({608675.0001}-{608675.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Immunoblot analysis of cells derived from patient 1 showed a 60 to 80% reduction in FUK levels and severely decreased FUK activity compared to controls, which could be rescued by wildtype FUK. Cell lines were not available from patient 2. The findings were consistent with a loss of function.

Deep ventral cleft in the pons

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that lissencephaly-9 with complex brainstem malformation (LIS9) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the MACF1 gene ({608271}) on chromosome 1p34.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Lissencephaly-9 with complex brainstem malformation (LIS9) is an autosomal dominant neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent since infancy, impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, and sometimes abnormal or involuntary movements associated with abnormal brain imaging that typically shows pachygyria, lissencephaly, and malformation of the brainstem consistent with a neuronal migration defect (summary by {1:Dobyns et al., 2018}).

For a general description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of lissencephaly, see LIS1 ({607432}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Irahara et al. (2014)} reported a 5-year-old Japanese girl with global developmental delay, poor speech, no social gestures, and stereotypic movements. Brain imaging showed several abnormalities, including pontine hypoplasia with a vertical split in the pons, impaired decussation fibers across the midline, and partial thickening of the cerebral cortex.

{1:Dobyns et al. (2018)} reported 9 children, including a pair of monozygotic twin sisters and a previously reported Japanese girl ({2:Irahara et al., 2014}), with a severe neurologic disorder associated with similar abnormalities of neuronal migration on brain imaging. The patients were unrelated, except for the twin sisters, and were ascertained from several clinical or research centers. All had cortical malformations on brain imaging, including posterior predominant lissencephaly, diffuse pachygyria with thick cortex, and thin anterior commissure. Additional imaging findings included midline crossing defects, small or absent pontine crossing fibers, mildly dysplastic hippocampi, thin corpus callosum, narrowing of the brainstem with small pons and midbrain, widening of the medulla, and small cerebellum. A deep ventral cleft was noted in the pons. The patients had global developmental delay, severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, axial hypotonia, delayed walking or inability to walk, and early-onset seizures. More variable features included spasticity, involuntary movements, dysphagia, strabismus, and cortical visual impairment. One patient each had asymmetric facial movements, limited ocular adduction, optic nerve hypoplasia, poor temperature regulation, and ventricular septal defect that closed spontaneously. The twin girls, who were the most severely affected, also had microcephaly (-4 to -5 SD) and short stature.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the MACF1 gene that were identified in patients with LIS9 by {1:Dobyns et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

cytogenetics.title: Cytogenetics
cytogenetics.content: {3:Jorgensen et al. (2014)} reported a family in which 3 sibs and their mother had hypotonia of variable severity. The 2 most severely affected patients had onset of generalized muscle weakness from birth, delayed motor development, easy fatigability, facial weakness, and contractures. Genetic analysis identified a duplication of chromosome 1p34.3 that included the MACF1 gene. The deletion, which was found by array CGH analysis, most likely occurred de novo in the mildly affected mother. Muscle biopsy from 2 patients showed reduced expression of MACF1 compared to controls, as well as subtle nonspecific changes on electron microscopy, including membrane folding and electron dense membrane structures. RNAi-based knockdown of the macf1 ortholog in C. elegans resulted in decreased motility compared to controls.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 9 patients, including a pair of monozygotic twin sisters and a Japanese patient reported by {2:Irahara et al. (2014)}, with LIS9, {1:Dobyns et al. (2018)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the MACF1 gene ({608271.0001}-{608271.0006}). The mutations were identified by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing. There were 5 missense mutations and 1 intragenic deletion. Four of the missense mutations found in 7 patients occurred at highly conserved zinc-binding residues in or near the GAR domain, all of which were predicted by molecular modeling to alter the configuration of the domain and likely abrogate microtubule binding. One patient (LR16-412) had a missense mutation in the spectrin repeat domain (G4706R; {608271.0006}); the authors noted that this patient had only subtle brainstem dysplasia compared to patients with mutations in the GAR domain. Cells derived from 2 patients showed an increased number of shortened cilia compared to wildtype. Otherwise, functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. {1:Dobyns et al. (2018)} noted that Macf1-null mice have been shown to have disrupted neuronal migration via disruption of microtubule dynamics, including abnormal axonal extension and guidance with defects in midline crossing.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-71 (DEE71) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the glutaminase gene (GLS; {138280}) on chromosome 2q32.

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-71 (DEE71) is characterized by early neonatal refractory seizures, respiratory failure, structural brain abnormalities and cerebral edema, with death within weeks after birth. Glutamine levels are significantly increased (z score 3.2-11.7). Three patients have been described (summary by {1:Rumping et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Rumping et al. (2019)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated families who presented soon after birth with severe hypotonia and respiratory insufficiency requiring mechanical ventilation. The patients developed early-onset refractory seizures associated with a burst-suppression pattern on EEG, and brain imaging showed a simplified frontal gyral pattern with an anterior-to-posterior gradient and deep and subcortical white matter involvement. Gliosis, loss of basal ganglia volume, and cerebral edema were also present. All patients died within the first weeks of life. In 1 of the families, a sib had previously died of a similar disorder. Glutamine levels were significantly increased in the affected individuals (z scores 3.2 and 11.7).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE71 in the families reported by {1:Rumping et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with DEE71, {1:Rumping et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the GLS gene ({138280.0001}-{138280.0003}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The mutations were predicted to result in a loss of function, and newborn Guthrie cards from affected individuals in 1 family (family 2) showed significantly increased glutamine, consistent with a loss of GLS function.
