text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with progressive movement abnormalities, cognitive decline, and brain abnormalities (NEDMCB) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ZBTB11 gene ({618181}) on chromosome 3q12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with progressive movement abnormalities, cognitive decline, and brain abnormalities (NEDMCB) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay and developmental regression resulting in variably impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, difficulty walking or inability to walk, and various movement abnormalities, including spasticity, hypertonia, dystonia, tremor, and myoclonus. Affected individuals usually show poor overall growth, often with microcephaly, hypotonia, limb contractures, and cataracts. Most have progressive brain imaging abnormalities, including enlarged ventricles, white matter loss, and cerebellar atrophy. A subset of patients have combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (CMAMMA), although this is not a reliable biomarker ({2:Ortigoza-Escobar et al., 2024}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Fattahi et al. (2018)} reported 2 consanguineous families in which several members had impaired intellectual development. Clinical details were limited. Family A, of Iranian origin, contained 3 affected individuals ranging in age from 14 to 27 years. They had mild microcephaly (-2.6 to -3 SD), mildly delayed walking and speech by age 2 to 3 years, and IQ between 40 and 45. Other variable features included facial hypotonia with drooling, maxillary hyperplasia, spasticity, ataxia, and dysarthria. Brain imaging showed cerebellar hypoplasia in 1 patient and enlarged ventricles in another. Family B, of Pakistani origin, contained 6 patients ranging in age from 7 to 20 years. Only 1 had mild microcephaly (-3.1 SD), and all had cognitive impairment with moderate intellectual disability and poor or absent speech. One patient had seizures in childhood that later dissipated.

{4:Stromme et al. (1995)} reported 2 sibs, a 23-year-old man and a 10-year-old girl, born of unrelated parents from a remote part of Western Norway, who presented in infancy or the first year of life with global developmental delay, poor overall growth with small head circumference, and developmental regression. Other features included athetosis, spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses, and dystonic posturing. The brother was mute and unresponsive to external stimuli; he had neck and limb contractures. The sister had 1 episode of seizures at 7 years of age. Both had severely impaired intellectual development with absent language. They also had bilateral cataracts and increased urinary methylmalonic acid. Brain imaging showed partial agenesis of the cerebellar vermis and enlarged ventricles due to white matter atrophy; the sister had signal abnormalities in the basal ganglia.

{5:Sumathipala et al. (2022)} reported 5 patients, aged 7 to 50 years, from 3 unrelated families with a progressive neurodevelopmental disorder beginning in early childhood. One sib pair (family A) was previously reported by {4:Stromme et al. (1995)}. Follow-up of these sibs indicated that the brother had severe contractures and was wheelchair-bound; the sister also had multiple joint contractures, but could walk some steps with support. They had profound intellectual disability and were nonverbal. Both had microcephaly, receding forehead, deep-set eyes, and prominent lower jaw. Brain imaging showed progressive loss of white matter; there was a molar tooth-like sign in the sister. They had elevated urinary and serum methylmalonic acid and elevated urinary malonic acid. The 3 additional patients reported by {5:Sumathipala et al. (2022)} had global developmental delay with developmental regression. An 8-year-old boy (family B) had loss of speech and ambulation, hypotonia, and profoundly impaired intellectual development. Urinary methylmalonic and malonic acid were increased. Two sisters in family C, born of consanguineous parents, showed poor overall growth with microcephaly, hypotonia, dysarthria with chewing difficulties, drooling, and delayed walking. One showed developmental regression and the other had ataxia. They had mildly impaired intellectual development. Dysmorphic features included long face, malar flattening, broad nasal bridge, long philtrum, thick lips, and short neck. Brain imaging in 1 showed thin corpus callosum without cerebellar anomalies. Urinary analysis in these sisters showed normal malonic and methylmalonic acid levels.

{2:Ortigoza-Escobar et al. (2024)} reported 29 patients, ranging from 2 to 50 years of age (median age of 17 years), with NEDMCB. Thirteen patients from 10 families were newly identified, and 16 had previously been reported in the literature. The families were of various ethnic origins, and most were consanguineous. The phenotype was variable, but all had neurodevelopmental delay/regression of varying severity. Common features included impaired intellectual development (95%), motor delay (71%) with median sitting and walking at 10.6 and 17.35 months, and language delay (95%). Intellectual disability was mild in 8, moderate in 10, and severe to profound in 6. Neurodevelopmental regression was noted in 48%; cognitive decline was observed in 28%. Five (45%) of 11 had failure to thrive, and 11 (48%) of 23 had microcephaly. Early-onset cataracts were observed in 10 (42%) of 24 patients. Abnormal movements were commonly observed, including spasticity (82%), ataxia (60%), orofacial and limb dystonia (57%), myoclonus (46%), tremor (28%), stereotypies (21%), chorea (14%), and tics. The older patients tended to show dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, and tremor, whereas pediatric cases had ataxia. About 40% had muscle weakness, many had hypertonia, 67% had limb contractures, and 6 (37%) of 16 patients had seizures (3 with isolated seizures, 3 with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 2 with focal seizures). Of 5 individuals with brain MRI, 4 showed hypoplastic corpus callosum, 4 had T2 hyperintensities predominantly in the posterior thalami and periventricular white matter, 2 had white matter volume loss, and 2 had cerebellar volume loss. Abnormalities in the basal ganglia were rarely observed. Biochemical studies showed CMAMMA in 8 (53%) of 15 patients examined, suggesting limited utility of that biomarker. One patient with severe dystonia and myoclonus received bipallidal deep brain stimulation with a favorable response.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{3:Scala et al. (2023)} reported a 13-year-old boy with a complex neuropsychiatric phenotype, including speech abnormalities (single words with dyslalia), complex motor tics, and psychomotor agitation consistent with Tourette syndrome ({137580}) associated with biallelic missense mutations in the ZBTB11 gene and a de novo heterozygous 22q11.21 duplication involving at least 12 genes. He had normal early development, but was diagnosed with ADHD at age 2, had an IQ of 88, and showed behavioral abnormalities, including oppositional behavior, aggressive outburst, selective eating, and occasional enuresis and encopresis. EEG showed spike-wave complexes. Plasma methylmalonic acid was normal. Functional studies of the variants were not performed. The authors suggested that the phenotype of NEDMCB may be more heterogeneous than previously described, but noted that the 22q11.21 duplication may also contribute to the manifestations in this patient.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMCB in the families reported by {1:Fattahi et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In affected members of 2 unrelated consanguineous families with NEDMCB, {1:Fattahi et al. (2018)} identified homozygous missense mutations in the ZBTB11 gene (H729Y, {618181.0001} and H880Q, {618181.0002}). The mutations, which were found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and subsequent sequencing of the candidate interval, segregated with the disorder in the families. Neither mutation was found in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells showed that the mutant proteins were excluded from the nucleolus, where the wildtype protein is predominantly localized. Molecular modeling suggested that the mutation may affect zinc binding and proper protein folding, resulting in adverse effects on DNA-binding specificity. The findings were consistent with a loss of function.

In 5 patients, including 2 sib pairs, from 3 unrelated families with NEDMCB, {5:Sumathipala et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the ZBTB11 gene ({618181.0003}-{618181.0007}). The disorder was confirmed to segregate with the disorder in 2 of the families. ChIP-seq, which was performed on fibroblasts from 3 patients, identified reduced binding of ZBTB11 to genes involved in RNA processing and mitochondrial function, including ACSF3 ({614245}), MTHFD2L ({614047}), AGK ({610345}), and MCAT ({614479}), compared to control fibroblasts. Reduced binding of mutant ZBTB11 to ACSF3 led to decreased ACSF3 transcript level, explaining the combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria identified in some patients.

In 13 patients from 10 unrelated families, 5 of which were consanguineous, with NEDMCB, {2:Ortigoza-Escobar et al. (2024)} identified biallelic mutations in the ZBTB11 gene (see, e.g., {618181.0008}-{618181.0009}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families (except for family 10 in which the proband was adopted). There were 10 missense and 4 frameshift variants that occurred throughout the gene with no apparent genotype/phenotype correlations. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-74 (DEE74) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GABRG2 gene ({137164}) on chromosome 5q34.

Heterozygous mutation in the GABRG2 gene can cause a spectrum of seizure phenotypes, including some with more benign outcomes (see {607681}).

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-74 (DEE74) is neurologic disorder characterized by the onset of refractory seizures in the first months of life. Seizure types are variable and include infantile spasms, myoclonic, tonic, atonic, and absence, often with secondary generalization. Affected individuals have severe global developmental delay with hypotonia, severe motor impairment, roving eye movements, and absent language (summary by {1:Shen et al., 2017}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Shen et al. (2017)} reported 8 unrelated children of European descent, ranging in age from 3 to 10 years, with DEE. Onset of variable intractable seizure types occurred in the first year of life, and included tonic-clonic, tonic, partial with secondary generalization, febrile, and myoclonic. The seizures progressed in most patients to include other types. All patients had severe global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, absent speech, and severe hypotonia with motor disabilities. Additional features included roving or abnormal eye movements, such as nystagmus, and choreiform movements. Brain imaging was normal in most, but 2 patients had volume loss and delayed myelination.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the GABRG2 gene that were identified in patients with DEE74 by {1:Shen et al. (2017)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 unrelated children with DEE74, {1:Shen et al. (2017)} identified 6 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the GABRG2 gene (see, e.g., {137164.0006}; {137164.0008}-{137164.0009}). The mutations, which were found by exome or genome sequencing or by sequencing of an epilepsy candidate gene panel, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The mutations occurred throughout the gene in different structural domains. Accordingly, in vitro functional expression studies showed variable effects: the variants decreased GABA-evoked currents to different extents and some variants altered zinc sensitivity. Some variants caused reduced potency to GABA stimulation, whereas others caused kinetic abnormalities of the channel. Mutant proteins were stable in transfected HEK293 cells, but showed variably decreased surface and intracellular expression, suggesting impaired trafficking and abnormal retention of some of the mutants in the endoplasmic reticulum. For example, the R323Q mutation ({137164.0006}), which occurred at an invariant residue in the pore-forming M2 domain, decreased channel current by about 50%, increased zinc inhibition by about 25%, had reduced surface expression (about 50%), and had decreased response to GABA compared to wildtype. The A106T mutation ({137164.0007}), which occurred in the N-terminal domain, decreased channel current by about 30%, had mildly decreased surface expression (about 75%), slowed deactivation of the channel, and had decreased response to GABA compared to wildtype.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-39 (COXPD39) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GFM2 gene ({606544}) on chromosome 5q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-39 (COXPD39) is an autosomal recessive multisystem disorder resulting from a defect in mitochondrial energy metabolism. Affected individuals show global developmental delay, sometimes with regression after normal early development, axial hypotonia with limb spasticity or abnormal involuntary movements, and impaired intellectual development with poor speech. More variable features may include hypotonia, seizures, and features of Leigh syndrome ({256000}) on brain imaging. There are variable deficiencies of the mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme complexes in patient tissues (summary by {3:Glasgow et al., 2017}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Dixon-Salazar et al. (2012)} reported 2 sibs, born of consanguineous parents, with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients had microcephaly, simplified gyral pattern and pachygyria on brain imaging, and insulin-dependent diabetes. One of the affected sibs had died, but the age at death and cause of death were not provided. The patients were part of a large cohort of 188 probands from consanguineous unions with genetic forms of neurodevelopmental disorders who underwent exome sequencing.

{2:Fukumura et al. (2015)} reported 2 Japanese sisters with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. Both patients were born with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and showed severe hypotonia. The older sib had enlarged lateral ventricles and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, but no cortical malformations. She developed refractory seizures with hypsarrhythmia at age 3 months, and died at age 13 months after showing no developmental progress. Brain imaging of the younger sib showed progressive cerebellar atrophy and abnormal signals restricted to the midbrain suggestive of Leigh syndrome. By age 7 years, she was ventilator-dependent and bedridden with spasticity, bradycardia, and lack of developmental progress. Laboratory studies, including serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) lactate, were normal, but magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) showed a lactate peak. Fibroblasts from the second patient showed approximately 50% decreased activities of mitochondrial complexes III and IV compared to controls, but normal complexes I and II.

{3:Glasgow et al. (2017)} reported 2 unrelated patients with COXPD39. Both were noted to have developmental delay and regression of developmental milestones around 2 years of age after normal early development. They acquired some speech, but later lost language skills and developed dysarthria (patient 1) or loss of language (patient 2). Both had loss of motor skills and lost the ability to walk in childhood. Patient 1 had intrauterine growth retardation and asymptomatic hypoglycemia in the newborn period. He was able to walk at 14 months and run at age 5, but developed dystonia and spasticity in the lower limbs. Patient 2 developed a severe seizure disorder and had myopathic facies with drooling, axial hypotonia with hypertonic limbs, and dystonic involuntary movements. Brain imaging in both patients showed T2-weighted abnormalities in the basal ganglia, consistent with Leigh syndrome, as well as abnormalities in other brain regions, including volume loss in the corpus callosum and cerebellum. Laboratory studies showed increased serum and CSF lactate. Analysis of patient fibroblasts and skeletal muscle showed variable decreases in several mitochondrial respiratory complexes, most notably complexes I and IV. These findings were consistent with tissue-specific manifestations.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of COXPD39 in the families reported by {3:Glasgow et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous parents, with a neurodevelopmental disorder consistent with COXPD39, {1:Dixon-Salazar et al. (2012)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the GFM2 gene (D576E; {606544.0001}). The mutation, which was identified by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family and was not found in 200 controls. The mutation occurred at a highly conserved residue and was predicted to damage the protein, but functional studies were not performed.

In 2 Japanese sisters with COXPD39, {2:Fukumura et al. (2015)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the GFM2 gene ({606544.0002} and {606544.0003}). Studies of patient cells confirmed that both mutations resulted in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, consistent with a loss of function. The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family.

In 2 unrelated patients with COXPD39, {3:Glasgow et al. (2017)} identified biallelic mutations in the GFM2 gene ({606544.0004}-{606544.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. In vitro functional expression studies in patient fibroblasts did not show a defect in translation of mitochondrial proteins, but {3:Glasgow et al. (2017)} postulated that GFM2 acts later in the process. Patient skeletal muscle and fibroblasts showed variable decreased levels and activities of several subunits of mitochondrial complexes I, III, and IV.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-70 (MRT70) is caused by homozygous mutation in the RSRC1 gene ({613352}) on chromosome 3q25.

description.title: Description
description.content: MRT70 is characterized primarily by impaired intellectual development. Mild facial dysmorphism, febrile seizures, and behavioral abnormalities have been reported in some patients ({1:Maddirevula et al., 2018}; {2:Perez et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Maddirevula et al. (2018)} described 3 affected children from a consanguineous Malaysian family with cognitive impairment, no dysmorphic features, and normal brain MRIs. One sib was reported to have had febrile seizures.

{2:Perez et al. (2018)} described a consanguineous Bedouin kindred with 5 children who presented with apparently autosomal recessive severe global developmental delay with no regression, impaired intellectual development with speech delay, aberrant behavior, and mild generalized hypotonia. All patients had mild to moderate intellectual disability with walking at age 3 to 4 years and verbal expression of only a few single words even in adolescence. These patients had mild facial dysmorphisms described as a broad nasal bridge, slight hypertelorism, and retrognathia with an open mouth and drooling. All children had febrile seizures during childhood, and one developed focal seizures with impaired awareness that occasionally progressed to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures that were effectively treated with valproic acid. While all affected individuals had deficits in fine motor skills and incontinence, none had abnormalities in coordination. Behavioral abnormalities included temper tantrums, self-harm infliction, and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). One of the 5 sibs had autistic features. The remainder of physical and neurologic exams, ophthalmologic and hearing tests, and brain MRIs were normal.

{3:Scala et al. (2020)} identified 17 patients from 7 consanguineous families with impaired intellectual development, behavioral abnormalities, and dysmorphic facial features. All patients had global developmental delay and mildly to moderately impaired intellectual development. No developmental regression was observed. Twelve patients had variable behavioral disorders, including autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder, and aggressive behaviors. All patients showed generalized hypotonia, with decreased deep tendon reflexes in 6 patients. Five patients had gait ataxia, with truncal ataxia in 1. Six patients had seizures, including 2 patients with febrile seizures only. Dysmorphic features consisted of deep-set eyes, broad nasal base, and a high-arched palate, although a consistent facial gestalt could not be recognized.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MRT70 in the families reported by {1:Maddirevula et al. (2018)} and {2:Perez et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
{1:Maddirevula et al. (2018)} reported 3 sibs with MRT70 with a homozygous nonsense mutation in the RSRC1 gene (R90X; {613352.0001}). {2:Perez et al. (2018)} reported 5 sibs with MRT70 with a homozygous nonsense mutation in the RSRC1 gene (R69X; {613352.0002}).

{3:Scala et al. (2020)} reported 17 patients from 7 consanguineous families with MRT70 and homozygous loss-of-function variants in the RSRC1 gene. The patients were of different ancestries collected through GeneMatcher. The variants that were identified by exome sequencing were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. In 1 family of Amish ancestry in which no single-nucleotide variant was identified by exome sequencing, comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) array identified an 81-kb deletion encompassing exons 9-10 of RSRC1 and the entire adjacent gene, MLF1 ({601402}). In another family, of Pakistani origin, a 500-bp deletion involving exon 2 of RSRC1 was identified. Among the 7 families, 5 sequence variants (including an intragenic duplication and 2 partial deletions) were identified (see, e.g., {613352.0003}-{613352.0005}). All variants fully segregated with the phenotype.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-18 (HLD18) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the DEGS1 gene ({615843}) on chromosome 1q42.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-18 (HLD18) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by onset of global developmental delay usually in early infancy. Affected individuals have very poor psychomotor development, including inability to sit or walk independently in the more severe cases, as well as poor or absent speech, dystonia, and spasticity. A subset of patients may develop seizures. Brain imaging shows hypomyelinating leukodystrophy affecting various brain regions; some patients may also have progressive atrophy of the corpus callosum, thalami, and cerebellum (summary by {3:Pant et al., 2019}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, see {312080}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Karsai et al. (2019)} reported a 22-year-old man, born of consanguineous Turkish parents, with HLD18. At age 6 months, he presented with delayed motor development. Over the next 2 decades, he showed progressive and severe spasticity, resulting in flexion contractures with extensor plantar responses and the inability to walk. Additional features of neurologic dysfunction included impaired intellectual development with absent speech, poor overall growth with mild microcephaly (-2.5 SD), progressive scoliosis, neurogenic bladder, and gastroesophageal reflux with feeding difficulties necessitating gastrostomy. He also developed seizures at age 5 years that were controlled with medication. Consecutive brain imaging showed general hypomyelination, thinning of the brainstem and occipital white matter, reduced thalamic volume, thin corpus callosum, and progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. Sural nerve biopsy showed thin myelin sheaths, moderate myelin folding, widening of the endoplasmic reticulum of Schwann cells, and autophagic vacuoles in the cytoplasm of Schwann cells. Nerve conduction velocities were slowed, consistent with a demyelinating neuropathy, and muscle biopsy showed neurogenic atrophy. Central visual and auditory evoked potentials had prolonged latency. Analysis of plasma lipids showed increased levels of dihydrosphingolipid species compared to controls. Treatment with a special diet to increase sphingolipid consumption had no notable effects.

{3:Pant et al. (2019)} reported 19 patients from 13 unrelated families with HLD18. Eight families were consanguineous, of Egyptian, Moroccan, Indian, Pakistani, or Middle Eastern descent. Most patients were children in their first decade, although 2 were 18 and 20 years of age, respectively. The patients had a similar phenotype with onset of symptoms in early infancy, although 2 sibs in 1 family (family 5) presented at 2 years of age. There was variable severity of the disorder, fitting mainly into 2 groups. The majority (15 patients, 79%) had a severe form characterized by failure to thrive sometimes necessitating tube feeding, irritability, and poor psychomotor development, often with absent or minimal motor development and no language acquisition. Additional features included dystonia, spasticity, dysarthria, dysmetria, abnormal eye movements or nystagmus, and contractures or scoliosis. Most (80%) developed resistant seizures in the first years of life. Three patients had acquired microcephaly (down to -4.8 SD). Four patients died at a mean age of 4.6 years. A somewhat milder disease course was observed in 4 patients, (patients 3, 7, 8, and 14), including 2 sibs who acquired the ability to sit or walk unassisted and could use some words. Five of 14 patients analyzed also had decreased nerve conduction velocities, consistent with a peripheral demyelinating process, and all 5 patients tested showed prolonged latencies in central conduction pathways. Brain imaging in all patients showed hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, mainly in the periventricular white matter, often with abnormalities of the corpus callosum and basal ganglia. Progressive thalamic and cerebellar atrophy was also commonly observed. The brain abnormalities correlated with the severity of the disorder.

{1:Dolgin et al. (2019)} reported a large consanguineous Arab Israeli family in which 2 sibs in each of 2 branches had HLD18. The patients, who ranged in age from 17 to 24 years, had normal development to age 8 to 18 months. All had mildly to severely impaired intellectual development; one patient attended regular high school and could speak 2 languages, whereas the other 3 had little or no speech. Three patients had epilepsy, which was controlled by medication. All had spastic quadraplegia and sustained clonus in the Achilles tendons. Brain imaging, performed in 2 sibs, showed moderate dilatation of the lateral ventricles with abnormal hyperintense signal in the periventricular perioccipital region, as well as thinning of the corpus callosum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HLD18 in the families reported by {3:Pant et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 22-year-old man, born of consanguineous Turkish parents, with HLD18, {2:Karsai et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the DEGS1 gene (A280V; {615843.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed decreased expression of the mutant protein (about 80% decrease), as well as decreased enzyme activity (about 20% residual activity) compared to wildtype. This was associated with increased levels of the DEGS1 substrate dihydroceramide (DhCer). In vitro cellular expression of the mutation resulted in decreased protein levels compared to controls, suggesting instability of the mutant protein. Analysis of patient plasma showed an abnormal sphingolipid profile with increased dihydrosphingolipid species compared to controls, as well as a potentially novel toxic sphingoid base.

In 19 patients from 13 unrelated families with HLD18, {3:Pant et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the DEGS1 gene (see, e.g., {615843.0002}-{615843.0007}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all 4 families for whom parental DNA was available. There were 3 frameshift, 4 nonsense, and 6 missense mutations. Twelve of the 13 variants were located in the fatty acid desaturase (FAD) domain, and all missense mutations occurred at highly conserved residues. Eight variants were not found in control populations, whereas the others had a minor allele frequency less than 0.0001 in large databases, including gnomAD and 1000 Genomes Project. None were found in the homozygous state in control databases. Patients with homozygous loss-of-function mutations tended to have a more severe course, although some patients with missense mutations also had a severe disease course. Analysis of fibroblasts or skeletal muscle, available from 4 patients (patients 3, 4, 7, and 9), showed accumulation of the DEGS1 substrate DhCer and an increased DhCer/Cer ratio, consistent with impaired enzyme activity. Fibroblasts from patients 4, 7, and 9 also showed increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) compared to controls. Additional functional studies or studies of patient cells were not performed. {3:Pant et al. (2019)} postulated that DhCer may be toxic or destabilizing for myelinating oligodendrocytes or for the biogenesis of the myelin sheath and even neurons. Disruption of DEGS1 also likely results in a broader imbalance of overall sphingolipid metabolism, which has structural and signaling functions. The patients were identified through collaborative efforts, including GeneMatcher.

In affected members of a large consanguineous Arab Israeli family with HLD18, {1:Dolgin et al. (2019)} identified homozygosity for a missense mutation in the DEGS1 gene (N255S; {615843.0003}). The mutation segregated with the disorder in the family.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: In zebrafish, {3:Pant et al. (2019)} found that the degs1 ortholog was expressed in the dorsal region of the brain. Morpholino knockdown of the gene resulted in locomotor disability, impaired movement, impaired myelination, and an increased DhCer/Cer ratio. Treatment of mutant fish with fingolimod, an inhibitor of ceramide synthase (CERS1; {606919}), the enzyme prior to DEGS1, resulted in improved mobility, improved myelination, amelioration of the ceramide species, and decreased ROS.

phenotypes.phenotype: Global developmental delay, progressive ataxia, and elevated glutamine

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that global developmental delay, progressive ataxia, and elevated glutamine (GDPAG) is caused by homozygosity or compound heterozygosity for a triplet repeat expansion upstream of the GLS gene ({138280}) on chromosome 2q32.

description.title: Description
description.content: Patients with global developmental delay, progressive ataxia, and elevated glutamine (GDPAG) present in early childhood with delay of both gross and fine motor skills and delayed speech. Ataxia develops by mid- to late childhood, necessitating use of a walker or wheelchair. Plasma glutamine is persistently elevated by a factor of 2.5 despite normal plasma ammonia levels. Residual glutaminase (GLS) activity can be detected in fibroblasts and lymphocytes. One or both alleles of the GLS gene carry an expanded GCA trinucleotide repeat in the 5-prime untranslated region (UTR); the repeat expansion may be found in compound heterozygosity with another GLS mutation. Three patients have been reported (summary by {1:van Kuilenburg et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Van Kuilenburg et al. (2019)} described 3 unrelated probands from nonconsanguineous families who presented with early-onset delay in both gross and fine motor skills, as well as delayed speech. Ataxia developed in all 3 patients, and all showed progressive neurologic deterioration. Patient 1 sat unsupported at 11 months and crawled at 18 months. At 3 years of age she had a broad-based ataxic gait with hands held. At the most recent examination at age 7 years, she relied on a wheelchair due to ataxic gait. Patient 2 sat at 13 months and crawled at 17 months. When first assessed at just under 3 years of age, he could walk only with support. At age 6 years his gait had become ataxic. Patient 3 sat and crawled at the usual time, but did not stand until age 3 years. She had a febrile seizure at 3 years of age. At age 12 years she required a walker and had hypotonia, tremor, and dysarthria with severe ataxia. Initial brain MRI revealed no diagnostic abnormality in all 3 patients. Brain MRI of patient 3 at age 12 years showed cerebellar atrophy. Metabolic investigation in all patients revealed persistently and significantly elevated plasma glutamine (1800-2209 micromol/l, normal 405-781 micromol/l), but normal urinary organic acids, including orotic acid.

No patient had hyperammonemia or any history of hyperammonemic decompensation. The presence of urea cycle disorders had previously been excluded.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The pattern of transmission in the families reported by {1:van Kuilenburg et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: Using exome sequencing in 2 patients with progressive neurodegeneration and glutaminase deficiency, {1:van Kuilenburg et al. (2019)} identified heterozygosity for a paternally inherited missense mutation in the GLS gene (P313L; {138280.0006}) in 1 patient. No candidate variant was identified in the other patient. In a third patient, analyzed separately, a maternally inherited 1-bp duplication ({138280.0007}) was identified. Hypothesizing that the missing heritability in these 3 patients was due to variation at the GLS locus refractory to detection by exome sequencing, {1:van Kuilenburg et al. (2019)} performed genome sequencing and triplet repeat-primed PCR assays and identified a GCA repeat expansion ({138280.0005}) in the 5-prime untranslated region of the GLS gene in all 3 patients.

phenotypes.phenotype: Metabolic crises, recurrent, with variable encephalomyopathic features and neurologic regression

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that recurrent metabolic crises with variable encephalomyopathic features and neurologic regression (MECREN) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SLC25A42 gene ({610823}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Recurrent metabolic crises with variable encephalomyopathic features and neurologic regression (MECREN) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder with a highly variable phenotype. Most affected individuals present in the first years of life with episodic lactic acidosis associated with illness or stress, resulting in transient or permanent neurologic dysfunction. Some patients may recover, whereas others show subsequent variable developmental regression of motor and cognitive skills. Other features may include dystonia, hypotonia with inability to sit or walk, seizures, and abnormal signals in the basal ganglia. There is significant phenotypic heterogeneity, even among patients with the same mutation (summary by {1:Almannai et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Shamseldin et al. (2016)} reported a 16-year-old boy, born of consanguineous Saudi parents, with mitochondrial myopathy. He had delayed motor development with frequent falls early in life. At age 16, he was mobile, but unable to run. Symptoms included muscle weakness, aching, and fatigue, as well as facial muscle weakness with dysarthria. He was not cognitively impaired; he was in tenth grade and doing well academically. Laboratory studies showed increased serum lactate, and muscle biopsy showed ragged-red-like fibers, subsarcolemmal mitochondrial accumulation, and decreased COX activity.

{1:Almannai et al. (2018)} reported 12 patients from 8 unrelated consanguineous families, mostly of Middle Eastern descent, with a highly variable childhood-onset disorder consistent with mitochondrial dysfunction. Most patients came to attention due to episodic lactic acidosis associated with an illness, and 4 patients showed subsequent developmental regression of both motor and cognitive skills. At the mildest end of the spectrum, 4 affected sibs (family 4) had normal psychomotor development and developed intermittent lactic acidosis in childhood, often requiring hospitalization, but not affecting development. Only 1 of these 4 sibs had significant disability: he presented at age 10 years with lactic acidosis and subsequently developed choreoathetosis and dystonia, progressive renal insufficiency resulting in renal failure and hemodialysis at age 22, and reduced systolic function with dilated left ventricle. Cognition in this patient and in all his sibs was normal. His affected sister had recurrent hospitalizations for acidosis, but later gave birth to a healthy child without complications. In another family (family 6), which was distantly related to family 4, 2 sisters were much more severely affected. They presented in the first 6 months of life with metabolic acidosis and thereafter showed significant developmental regression with hypotonia, inability to sit without support, absent speech, and intellectual disability. One had dystonia. The other 6 children were the only affected patients in their respective families. The phenotype among these children ranged from considerable developmental regression after episodic lactic acidosis, resulting in the inability to sit, roll over, or speak, whereas others had only mild developmental delay, sometimes with ataxia or dystonia. At least 2 of these 6 patients (patients 3 and 12) had normal psychomotor development at age 3 years. Brain imaging was abnormal in 5 patients, showing hyperintensities in the basal ganglia; 1 patient (patient 2) had iron deposition in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra. Two patients (patients 2 and 11) had seizures. Aside from increased serum lactate, there were no consistent biochemical abnormalities, and treatment with several vitamins and cofactors did not result in clinical improvement. All patients were homozygous for the same missense mutation in the SLC25A42 gene (N291D; {610823.0001}), and {1:Almannai et al. (2018)} emphasized the phenotypic heterogeneity even within families.

{2:Iuso et al. (2019)} reported 2 unrelated boys, one born of consanguineous Saudi parents and the other of unrelated German parents, with MECREN. The Saudi child presented soon after birth with respiratory insufficiency and thereafter had recurrent respiratory infections and gastroesophageal reflux. He started crawling at age 24 months, but made no real developmental progress. At age 6 years, he had dystonia, profound hypotonia, was unable to sit or walk, and had severe cognitive impairment with absent speech. Brain imaging showed hyperintensities in the putamen; serum lactate was increased. The German child presented with an acute metabolic crisis and rhabdomyolysis at age 1 year. Laboratory studies showed increased serum creatine kinase and lactate, hyperammonemia, metabolic acidosis, and abnormal liver enzymes. He later developed seizures, and had recurrent episodes of fever and seizures associated with delayed psychomotor development by age 9 years. Brain imaging showed signal alterations in the caudate.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MECREN in the families reported by {1:Almannai et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 16-year-old boy, born of consanguineous Saudi parents, with MECREN, {3:Shamseldin et al. (2016)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SLC25A42 gene (N291D; {610823.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome analysis, segregated with the disorder in the family and was not found in the ExAC database or in 700 in-house control exomes. Molecular modeling suggested that the N291 residue faces the interior of the substrate-binding groove. The mutation was unable to rescue the motor-deficit phenotype in zebrafish with morpholino knockdown of the slc25a42 gene, suggesting that the mutation resulted in a loss of function.

{1:Almannai et al. (2018)} identified homozygosity for the N291D mutation in the SLC25A42 gene in 12 patients from 8 unrelated consanguineous families with MECREN. The phenotype was highly variable, even within families, and the authors suggested that exogenous factors and stressors can modulate disease severity. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

{2:Iuso et al. (2019)} identified homozygosity for the N291D mutation in the SLC25A42 gene in a Saudi boy with MECREN. An unrelated German boy with the disorder was homozygous for a splice site mutation in SLC25A42 ({610823.0002}). Analysis of cells from the German patient did not show the canonical SLC25A42 transcript, but instead showed 3 abnormal transcripts. Total cellular CoA was reduced by about 20% in patient fibroblasts compared to controls. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were found in heterozygous state in all unaffected parents, confirming segregation.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Shamseldin et al. (2016)} found that morpholino knockdown of the slc25a42 gene in zebrafish resulted in defects in early motor development, muscle weakness, and bent tails. Mutant animals also had severe muscle disorganization with mitochondrial abnormalities, including fragmented inner mitochondrial membrane and absence of the dense membranous network observed in controls.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that myoectodermal gonadal dysgenesis syndrome (MEGD) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PPP2R3C gene ({615902}) on chromosome 14q13.

Heterozygous PPP2R3C mutations in males cause teratozoospermia with reduced fertility (SPGF36; {618420}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Myoectodermal gonadal dysgenesis syndrome (MEGD) is characterized by 46,XY complete or partial gonadal dysgenesis, or 46,XX gonadal dysgenesis, in association with extragonadal anomalies, including low birth weight, typical facies, rod and cone dystrophy, sensorineural hearing loss, omphalocele, anal atresia, renal agenesis, skeletal abnormalities, dry and scaly skin, severe myopathy, and neuromotor delay. Dysmorphic facial features along with muscular habitus are the hallmarks of the syndrome. Abnormal hair patterning with frontal upsweep and additional whorls, eyebrow abnormalities comprising broad, arched, and sparse or thick eyebrows, underdeveloped alae nasi, smooth philtrum, and low-set ears with overfolded helices facilitate a gestalt diagnosis. ({4:Guran et al., 2019}; {1:Altunoglu et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Brosnan et al. (1980)} described two 46,XY sisters from Texas, aged 1.5 and 8.5 years, with peculiar facies; cardiac, renal, musculoskeletal, and ectodermal anomalies; short stature; streak gonads; and mild developmental delay. Abnormalities included cleft lip and palate, preauricular pits, acromelia with broad hands and feet, and a hypermuscular appearance. Ectodermal defects included 'punched out scalp defects' and unusual position of hair whorls. The nose had a 'squashed down' appearance because of a short columella and small nares. Ears appeared low-set because of extreme hypoplasia of the upper pinnae with heavily overfolded helices. Bone age radiographs showed marked delay. The labia and vagina appeared to be normal in both sisters; at laparotomy, both were found to have a primitive bicornuate uterus, with long primitive fallopian tubes and streak gonads. Both sisters also had ventricular septal defects, and the older sister had right renal agenesis. {1:Altunoglu et al. (2022)} noted the overlapping features of these sisters with those of patients with PPP2R3C-associated gonadal dysgenesis; unfortunately the sisters had been lost to follow-up and further evaluation was not possible.

{5:Kennerknecht et al. (1995)} reported the cases of 12- and 14-year-old Turkish sisters with a 46,XY chromosome constitution, normal female external genitalia, and absence of gonadal tissue. Except for omphalocele, right renal agenesis, and malrotation of the colon in the older sister, internal organs were normal. Both were mentally retarded and of short stature, with markedly retarded bone age. They had an almost identical pattern of minor anomalies: peculiar face, abnormally modeled ears with very broad helices, hypodontia, short neck, inverted nipples, thoracolumbar scoliosis, 'dysplastic' hips (left pelvic muscles were noted to be absent in the younger sister), and partial clino-/syndactyly of the toes. The parents were related as first cousins. In the elder sib, sequencing of the conserved region of the SRY gene ({480000}), i.e., the high mobility group (HMG) box, showed no abnormality. {5:Kennerknecht et al. (1995)} suggested that the disorder in the 2 sisters represented a new autosomal recessive syndrome.

{4:Guran et al. (2019)} reported 4 unrelated 46,XY females from consanguineous Turkish families with syndromic complete gonadal dysgenesis and mutation in the PPP2R3C gene. The genital phenotype was female with hypoplastic labia majora; uterus was present in 3 patients and a primitive bicornuate uterus was detected in the fourth patient. All 4 exhibited similar facial dysmorphism, with flat face, sparse arched eyebrows, epicanthal folds, beaked nose with hypoplastic alae nasi, long smooth philtrum, thin lips with narrow mouth opening, and low-set, posteriorly rotated ears with overfolded helix. They had unruly hair with frontal upsweep and unusual hair whorls, and skin was dry and scaly. All 4 had lacrimal puncta hypoplasia and rod-cone dystrophy. Of 3 patients who had auditory testing, 2 showed sensorineural hearing loss. All exhibited severe myopathy with thick, stiff muscles; patients 2 and 3 underwent electromyography that revealed severe diffuse myopathy. Skeletal findings included short stature, delayed bone age, and limited elbow extension, and all 4 exhibited neuromotor delay. Patients 2 and 4 underwent gonadectomy; histologic analysis showed few to no Leydig cells and peripherally located Mullerian-like tubular structures in loose connective tissue containing vessels and peripheral nerve bundles. Patient 3 was a 19-year-old woman who had no gonads seen on laparoscopy at age 13.75 years and was given estrogen replacement therapy starting at age 14; she had Tanner stage 2 breast development at age 14.5, Tanner stage 2 pubic hair at age 17.5, and underwent menarche at age 18. All of the families had a history of multiple infertile couples, and semen analysis in 3 of the probands' fathers revealed teratozoospermia (see SPGF36; {618420}). The fourth father did not undergo testing, and other relatives were unavailable for testing. One heterozygous mother reported oligomenorrhea and hypomenorrhea with normal pelvic ultrasound, and another mother underwent menopause at age 44 years. The authors proposed the designation 'myo-ectodermal-gonadal dysgenesis (MEGD)' for the phenotype.

{1:Altunoglu et al. (2022)} reported 8 patients from 4 families with 46,XX or 46,XY syndromic gonadal dysgenesis and mutation in the PPP2R3C gene, including 2 Turkish sisters (family 3) originally described by {5:Kennerknecht et al. (1995)}. All affected individuals displayed consistent findings of either XX or XY gonadal dysgenesis, short stature, muscular habitus, mild global developmental delay and/or intellectual deficit, and recognizable facial gestalt comprising broad eyebrows, underdeveloped alae nasi, thin vermilion of the lips, and small low-set protruding ears with overfolded helices. The 2 XX individuals presented as cases of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with nonvisualization of gonadal structures, suggestive of gonadal dysgenesis, whereas the 6 XY individuals exhibited a phenotypic spectrum, ranging from normal female-appearing external genitalia in 3 cases, to ambiguous genitalia consisting of pseudovaginal perineoscrotal hypospadias with micropenis and single urogenital opening in 3 cases. Mullerian remnants were observed in all 6 XY individuals. {1:Altunoglu et al. (2022)} noted that funduscopy and optical coherence tomography did not reveal any evidence of retinal dystrophy in the 4 affected individuals of families 1 and 2. In addition, serum creatine kinase measurements and electromyography in patients from those families excluded the presence of myopathy. The authors concluded that retinal dystrophy and myopathy are not universal findings in patients with PPP2R3C-associated gonadal dysgenesis, and suggested an eponymous designation, 'Brosnan-Kennerknecht-Guran-Koc (BKGK) syndrome,' for the disorder.

{3:Cicek et al. (2022)} studied 4 children from 3 unrelated consanguineous Turkish families with MEGD and mutation in the PPP2R3C gene. In family 1, a 9-year-old 46,XX girl (P1) had primary gonadal insufficiency with short stature, high gonadotropin and low AMH ({600957}) levels, and gonads that could not be visualized on pelvic ultrasound. She also had visual impairment due to rod-cone dystrophy, left renal agenesis, epilepsy, and showed high serum creatine kinase concentrations. The two 46,XY sisters in family 2 (P2a and P2b), ages 8 and 6, had complete gonadal dysgenesis, with normal-appearing female external genitalia and low levels of adrenal and gonadal androgens and AMH, and high gonadotropin levels. In family 3, the proband was an undervirilized 10.5-year-old boy (P3) with partial gonadal dysgenesis. He was born with ambiguous genitalia and had micropenis, left cryptorchidism, penoscrotal hypospadias with chordee, bifid scrotum, and agenesis of the ductus deferens on the right. Histopathology of the left gonad revealed immature testis at age 8 months. All 4 children exhibited the common facial characteristics of MEGD syndrome, and all had short broad hands with a single horizontal crease and cutaneous syndactyly. All had myopathy and significant muscular build with thick and stiff muscles, particularly in the neck, and showed significantly delayed bone ages. The patients in families 1 and 2 also had developmental delay, whereas the proband in family 3 had normal neuromotor development. Other variable features included gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiac anomalies.

{6:Zhang et al. (2022)} reported a 24-year-old 46,XY Chinese woman with complete testicular dysgenesis and mutation in the PPP2R3C gene. She presented at age 18 years with primary amenorrhea, poor development of secondary sexual characteristics, and short stature with delayed bone age. Laparoscopy revealed uterine dysgenesis, bilateral oviduct-like structures, and streak ovaries; histopathology of the gonadectomy material showed an oviduct-like structure bilaterally. She exhibited the typical facial gestalt of MEGD, with flat face, hypoplastic alae nasi, thin lips, low-set ears, and mandibular retrusion. Because studies in mice had shown that PPP2R3C is highly expressed in lymphocytes and plays a role in B-cell survival, the authors analyzed B- and T-cell subsets in the proband and found a decreased number of CD19+ B cells and CD4+ T cells, a previously unreported feature of MEGD.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MEGD in the families reported by {4:Guran et al. (2019)} and {1:Altunoglu et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

mapping.title: Mapping
mapping.content: {1:Altunoglu et al. (2022)} performed SNP array analysis in 2 Turkish sisters, one 46,XX and one 46,XY, and their 46,XY nephew with syndromic gonadal dysgenesis (family 1) and identified a 6.7-Mb region of homozygosity (ROH) on chromosome 14q, between basepairs 33,387,288 and 40,096,985. The authors concluded that the candidate gene resided within this shared ROH, since the pedigree data were suggestive of autosomal recessive inheritance, with consanguinity in 2 generations and affected status of both XX and XY individuals.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 4 unrelated 46,XY females from consanguineous Turkish families with syndromic complete gonadal dysgenesis, {4:Guran et al. (2019)} identified homozygosity for 3 different missense mutations in the PPP2R3C gene ({615902.0001}-{615902.0003}) that segregated with disease in each family and were not found in ethnically matched controls or in public variant databases. The heterozygous fathers exhibited morphologic abnormalities of spermatozoa and reduced fertility (SPGF36).

In 2 Turkish sisters, one 46,XX and one 46,XY, and their 46,XY nephew (family 1) with syndromic gonadal dysgenesis, and 2 affected 46,XY Turkish sisters (family 3) who were originally described by {5:Kennerknecht et al. (1995)}, {1:Altunoglu et al. (2022)} identified homozygosity for a previously reported missense mutation in the PPP2R3C gene (L193S; {615902.0002}). In a 4-year-old 46,XX Turkish girl (family 2) with syndromic gonadal dysgenesis, they identified homozygosity for another previously reported missense mutation in PPP2R3C (L103P; {615902.0003}). In addition, 2 affected 46,XY Indian sisters (family 4) were homozygous for a 9-bp in-frame duplication ({615902.0004}). The unaffected parents in each family were heterozygous for the respective mutations. {1:Altunoglu et al. (2022)} noted that XY patients with the L193S variant presented inter- and intrafamilial differences in the severity of the genital phenotype, suggesting the possibility of additional individual or environmental factors on gonadal development. In addition, the authors noted that 5 couples from the 4 families in their study conceived a total of 14 pregnancies without assisted reproductive techniques, and 8 heterozygous females had normal menarche and menopause, suggesting that reduced male or female fertility and/or premature ovarian failure are not common findings in PPP2R3C heterozygotes.

In 4 children with MEGD from 3 unrelated Turkish families, including a 46,XX girl (P1) with primary gonadal insufficiency, two 46,XY sisters (P2a and P2b) with complete gonadal dysgenesis, and an undervirilized 10.5-year-old boy (P3) with partial gonadal dysgenesis, {3:Cicek et al. (2022)} sequenced the PPP2R3C gene and identified homozygosity for the previously reported L193S missense mutation. All parents were heterozygous carriers of the variant.

By whole-exome sequencing in a 24-year-old 46,XY Chinese woman with complete testicular dysgenesis, {6:Zhang et al. (2022)} identified compound heterozygosity for a 3-bp in-frame deletion ({615902.0005}) and a missense mutation (G417E; {615902.0006}) in the PPP2R3C gene, for which her unaffected parents were heterozygous. The missense mutation was not found in public variant databases, but the deletion was present at very low minor allele frequency in the ExAC and gnomAD databases.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired speech and hyperkinetic movements

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired speech and hyperkinetic movements (NEDISHM) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ZNF142 gene ({604083}) on chromosome 2q35.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired speech and hyperkinetic movements (NEDISHM) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent in infancy. Most patients have mildly delayed walking, speech and language delay, and a hyperkinetic movement disorder with dystonia, tremor, ataxia, or chorea. Some may develop seizures that tend to abate (summary by {3:Khan et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Khan et al. (2019)} reported 7 patients from 4 unrelated families with NEDISHM. The patients ranged in age from 10 to 35 years. Two families were consanguineous, of Turkish (family B) and Pakistani (family C) origin. All patients presented with global developmental delay in infancy, and most had mildly delayed walking by 2 years of age, although 1 child from family B never achieved walking and was wheelchair-bound. The patients had moderately to severely impaired intellectual development (IQ range, 40-78) with speech delay and dysarthria and/or impaired language initiation and expression. One patient (family B) was nonverbal, and another (family D) was diagnosed with childhood apraxia of speech. At least 2 patients were able to attend school. Most patients had variable involuntary hyperkinetic movements, including segmental dystonia affecting the neck (torticollis), face, and upper limbs, as well as tremor, ataxia, chorea, spastic diplegia, and hyperreflexia. The dystonia became generalized in the patient from family B, who had the most severe phenotype. Five patients had seizures, although 2 had only 1 generalized tonic-clonic seizure around 1 to 2 years of age. The other 3 patients had earlier onset of tonic-clonic seizures that tended to abate or responded to medication. Four patients had dolichocephaly. Brain MRI, performed in 2 patients, showed nonspecific hyperintensities and thin corpus callosum. In family C, a presumably affected sib had died of seizures at age 9 years.

{1:Christensen et al. (2022)} described 26 patients from 16 families with NEDISHM. The major features in this cohort included intellectual disability (23/26), language impairment (26/26), developmental delay (22/26), seizures (17/26), hypotonia (10/19), behavioral issues (12/22), and movement disorders (10/19). Brain imaging, which was performed in 22 patients, showed no structural changes. Shared facial features included thick lips and eyebrows, epicanthus, and a broad nasal bridge.

{2:Kamal et al. (2022)} reported a 5-year-old boy with NEDISHM who presented with developmental delay in the second year of life. He developed seizures at 2 years of age. At age 5 years he was not able to walk or speak in complete sentences. He also had impaired intellectual development and hypotonia. A brain MRI was normal.

{4:Proskorovski-Ohayon et al. (2024)} reported NEDISHM in 2 females from a consanguineous Bedouin family. Patient IV3 had typical early development until 8 months of age when she developed seizures. A brain MRI was normal. She had delayed motor development and walked at 30 months of age. At 10 to 15 years of age, she had severely impaired intellectual development and profound speech delay. Patient III9 had normal development until 3 years of age when she developed seizures and intellectual and motor developmental regression. At 40 to 50 years of age, she had medication-resistant seizures, was wheelchair dependent and unable to speak, and needed support with feeding.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDISHM in the families reported by {3:Khan et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 7 patients from 4 unrelated families with NEDISHM, {3:Khan et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the ZNF142 gene ({604083.0001}-{604083.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Four of the 6 mutations identified were frameshift or nonsense, consistent with a loss of function. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, although {3:Khan et al. (2019)} noted that mutations in similar zinc finger family genes have been identified in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders.

{2:Kamal et al. (2022)} identified compound heterozygous mutations (Q9X, {604083.0007} and R581C, {604083.0008}) in the ZNF142 gene in a 5-year-old boy, born of consanguineous Iranian parents, with NEDISHM. The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

In 35 patients (9 previously reported) from 21 unrelated families (5 previously reported) segregating NEDISHM, {1:Christensen et al. (2022)} identified biallelic mutations in the ZNF142 gene, including 27 different mutations, 18 of which were novel. Twenty-one patients had a homozygous mutation and 14 patients had compound heterozygous mutations. One patient (individual 23) had a homozygous single nucleotide deletion due to maternal uniparental disomy of an 8.5-kb region including the ZNF142 gene. Twenty-three of the mutations were predicted to result in a truncated protein and 4 were missense mutations. The 3 patients who had compound heterozygosity for 1 or 2 missense mutations had a somewhat milder phenotype compared to those with 2 truncating mutations.

In 2 females with NEDISHM from closely related consanguineous Bedouin families, {4:Proskorovski-Ohayon et al. (2024)} identified a homozygous mutation in the ZNF142 gene (c.4002delG; {604083.0009}) that was predicted to result in a frameshift and premature termination. Functional studies in patient cells were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that susceptibility to acute infection-induced encephalopathy-9 (IIAE9) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NUP214 gene ({114350}) on chromosome 9q34.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Susceptibility to acute infection-induced encephalopathy-9 (IIAE9) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by episodic acute neurodegeneration and developmental regression associated with infections and febrile illness. Patients present in the first months or years of life, often after normal or only mildly delayed early development. Some patients may have partial recovery between episodes, such as transient ataxia, but the overall disease course is progressive, resulting in global developmental delay, abnormal movements, refractory seizures, microcephaly, and cerebellar atrophy (summary by {1:Fichtman et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of susceptibility to acute infection-induced encephalopathy, see {610551}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Shamseldin et al. (2019)} reported 3 sisters, born of consanguineous Saudi parents, with a severe encephalopathy. The patients presented in infancy with recurrent admissions due to breathing difficulties, suspected to be related to gastroesophageal reflux, poor feeding, hypotonia, failure to thrive, vomiting, and recurrent infections. All also had persistent hyponatremia. All developed seizures in the first months of life and thereafter showed further neurodegeneration with loss of developmental skills. A fever as a trigger was specifically noted in 1 of the patients, but could not be excluded in the others. They had poor overall growth with microcephaly and profound developmental delay; all died by 15 months of age. Brain imaging, performed in 2 patients, showed diffuse atrophic changes.

{1:Fichtman et al. (2019)} reported 4 children from 2 unrelated families with a similar neurodegenerative disorder associated with febrile illnesses. The episodes, which first occurred between 5.5 and 30 months of age, were characterized by developmental stagnation or regression, partially reversible ataxia, seizures or myoclonic jerks, and altered muscle tone. All patients had hyponatremia upon acute presentation. Only 1 of the patients, from a consanguineous Palestinian family (family A), had mild global developmental delay prior to acute neurodegeneration. He was able to run and speak at age 3, but had lost voluntary movements, was nonverbal, and required a feeding tube by age 11, when he died of sepsis. The other patients had a similar disease course, with recurrent episodes of fever-induced neurodegeneration with refractory seizures and abnormal movements, although not resulting in death. Additional features included hypotonia, hyperkinetic movements, and progressive microcephaly. Brain imaging showed progressive cerebellar atrophy and cerebral atrophy; 1 patient also had T2-weighted abnormalities in the thalami, hippocampi, and brainstem. A viral trigger was identified in 3 of the 4 cases, and the authors suggested that the trigger was the febrile episode itself rather than a specific pathogen.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IIAE9 in the families reported by {1:Fichtman et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 sisters, born of consanguineous Saudi parents, with IIAE9, {2:Shamseldin et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the NUP214 gene (D154G; {114350.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of linkage analysis and exon sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not found in the gnomAD database. Patient fibroblasts showed a dysmorphic phenotype of nuclei with an abnormal surface morphology and dramatic disruption of NUP214 localization similar to that observed in cells with knockdown of the NUP214 gene. These findings suggested that the mutation resulted in a loss of function.

In 4 patients from 2 unrelated families with IIAE9, {1:Fichtman et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the NUP214 gene ({114350.0002}-{114350.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed about a 50% decrease in NUP214 and NUP88 ({602552}) levels compared to controls, and immunoblot analysis showed decreased nuclear rim localization of these proteins. The findings suggested that the mutations destabilize NUP protein interactions. Functional studies in patient fibroblasts showed impaired, although not abolished, activity of nuclear transport pathways, including protein import and mRNA export. Direct surface imaging of fibroblast nuclei by scanning electron microscopy revealed a large increase in the presence of central particles ('plugs') in the nuclear pore channels of affected cells. Treatment with a transcription inhibitor reduced these 'plugs,' suggesting that many of the particles may be messenger RNA complexes. Exposure of fibroblasts from affected individuals to heat shock resulted in a marked delay in their stress response, followed by increased apoptotic cell death. These abnormalities could be partially rescued with transfection of wildtype NUP214 and NUP88. The results suggested a mechanistic link between decreased cell survival in cell culture and severe fever-induced neurodegeneration in affected individuals.

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay with variable intellectual impairment and behavioral abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay with variable intellectual impairment and behavioral abnormalities (DDVIBA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TCF20 gene ({603107}) on chromosome 22q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay with variable intellectual impairment and behavioral abnormalities (DDVIBA) is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder. Most patients have impaired intellectual development with speech difficulties, and many have behavioral abnormalities, most commonly autism spectrum disorder (ASD), defects in attention, and/or hyperactivity. Many patients have dysmorphic features, although there is not a consistent gestalt. Additional more variable features may include hypotonia, somatic overgrowth with macrocephaly, mild distal skeletal anomalies, sleep disturbances, movement disorders, and gastrointestinal issues, such as constipation. The phenotype is highly variable (summary by {5:Vetrini et al., 2019} and {4:Torti et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Babbs et al. (2014)} reported a 25-year-old woman (family 6) with moderate intellectual disability (IQ of 45) and ASD who carried a de novo frameshift mutation in the TCF20 gene ({603107.0001}). She also had craniosynostosis, but this feature was also present in her mother, who did not carry the TCF20 mutation, suggesting it was a coincidental finding.

{3:Schafgen et al. (2016)} reported 2 unrelated boys, both 14 years of age, with global developmental delay with mildly delayed walking, speech delay, and impaired intellectual development (IQ of 54 and 62). Only patient 2 had features consistent with autism, although patient 1 had stereotypic movements. Both also had features of somatic overgrowth, including macrocephaly, obesity, and tall stature, as well as mild movement abnormalities, including hypotonia, ataxic movements, and problems with writing and coordination. Both had inverted nipples. Patient 1 had mild dysmorphic features, including prominent forehead, downturned corners of the mouth, and prominent lower lip, as well as scoliosis. Patient 2 had sleep disturbances and onset of seizures at age 10 years.

{5:Vetrini et al. (2019)} reported 31 unrelated families, including a family with a set of affected monozygotic twins, with an overlapping neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through research protocols involving several centers. Five individuals (patients 2, 8, 10, 19, and 26) had previously been reported in the {2:Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study (2017)}. Common core features among all patients included developmental delay/impaired intellectual development, variable additional neurologic abnormalities, and dysmorphic features. Most had motor and language delay, as well as hypotonia (66%) and ASD (66%). Other features included movement disorder (44%), such as ataxia or spasticity, sleep disturbances (38%), seizures (25%), structural brain abnormalities (22%), growth delay (13%), macrocephaly (25%), digital anomalies (34%), somatic overgrowth (28%), and inverted nipples (13%). Dysmorphic facial features were common, although variable, and included tented upper lip, brachycephaly, midface hypoplasia, and low-set ears; there was no recognizable gestalt. In addition to the monozygotic twins (patients 27 and 28), there were 3 families in which a less severely affected parent carried the same heterozygous mutation as the proband (patients 1, 5, and 7).

{4:Torti et al. (2019)} reported 27 patients from 24 unrelated families with DDVIBA. Common features included global developmental delay with intellectual disability (mean IQ of 69), autistic features (69%), attention disorders or hyperactivity (67%) or other behavioral abnormalities (85%), and hypotonia (63%). Patient had mild motor delay, with an average age at walking around 20 months and spoken words around 23 months, although most had speech difficulties. Most were able to attend special schools, and some young adults needed help with self-care. More variable features included ataxia, gait disturbance, balance issues, and spasticity. Only 3 patients had seizures. Brain imaging was normal in most patients, although a few had nonspecific abnormalities, such as thick corpus callosum. Less common features included gastrointestinal problems (mainly constipation), skeletal problems such as scoliosis and foot deformities, and ocular abnormalities including strabismus and myopia. Many had dysmorphic facial features, but there was not a specific gestalt. There were 2 families (sibs 10a/b and sibs 17a/b/c) with evidence of germline mosaicism.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: Although the vast majority of TCF20 mutations occur de novo, {5:Vetrini et al. (2019)} observed 4 unrelated families with DDVIBA who showed autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 25-year-old woman (family 6) with DDVIBA, {1:Babbs et al. (2014)} identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation in the TCF20 gene ({603107.0001}). Analysis of patient cells showed that the mutation escaped nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and would likely produce a truncated protein. Five patients from 4 additional families with ASD were found to carry heterozygous missense variants affecting conserved residues in the TCF20 gene (K512E and P1557L); the P1557L variant was present in unaffected parents, and functional studies of these missense variants were not performed.

In 2 unrelated boys with DDVIBA, {3:Schafgen et al. (2016)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the TCF20 gene ({603107.0002} and {603107.0003}). One was a nonsense mutation and the other was a frameshift; functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. The mutations were found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The patients were ascertained from a cohort of 313 individuals with intellectual disability who underwent trio-based whole-exome sequencing.

In 28 patients from 27 unrelated families, including a set of monozygotic twins (patients 27 and 28), with DDVIBA, {5:Vetrini et al. (2019)} identified 25 heterozygous mutations in the TCF20 gene (see, e.g., {603107.0004}-{603107.0006}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing; none were found in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. Most of the mutations were predicted to result in a loss of function: there were 18 frameshifts, 5 nonsense, 1 splice site, and 1 missense (K1710R). Most of the mutations occurred de novo, although there were 4 families in which the pathogenic mutation was inherited from an affected parent; the parents tended to have a milder phenotype. Four additional patients carried heterozygous deletions ranging from 128 kb to 2.64 Mb that disrupted the TCF20 gene. A few patients carried additional variants in other genes, which may have contributed to the phenotype. Functional studies of the variants and studies of most patient cells were not performed. However, RNA studies of 3 of the variants that were predicted to cause premature termination showed that they escaped nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. No genotype/phenotype correlations were observed.

In 27 patients from 24 families with DDVIBA, {4:Torti et al. (2019)} identified heterozygous mutations in the TCF20 gene (see, e.g., {603107.0007}-{603107.0009}). The patients were ascertained from several clinical and research centers, and the mutations were found by exome sequencing with Sanger confirmation. Almost all mutations occurred de novo; germline mosaicism was demonstrated or predicted in 2 familial cases. There were 23 frameshift or nonsense mutations, all predicted to result in a loss of function, and 1 missense mutation. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but none of the variants were present in large population cohorts. Several patients carried possible pathogenic variants in other genes, which may have contributed to the phenotype.
