text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Snijders Blok-Fisher syndrome (SNIBFIS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the POU3F3 gene ({602480}) on chromosome 2q12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Snijders Blok-Fisher syndrome (SNIBFIS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia, variable impaired intellectual development, and specifically impaired speech and language acquisition. Patients achieve independent ambulation and most have mildly to moderately impaired cognition with autistic features, although a few may develop seizures and have a more severe phenotype. Dysmorphic features include abnormal, cupped, or prominent ears and ocular anomalies. Mutations usually occur de novo, although 1 family with autosomal dominant inheritance has been reported (summary by {1:Snijders Blok et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Snijders Blok et al. (2019)} reported 18 unrelated patients with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. Most of the patients were children, although there were several adults. Only 1 patient had a family history of the disorder; the patient's similarly affected mother carried the same mutation. The patients, who were ascertained through matchmaking initiatives, had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development and notable speech and language delay, particularly affecting expressive speech and often associated with oromotor problems, word-finding difficulties, and social communication issues. Two individuals were nonverbal at age 20 (patient 1) and 5 years (patient 5), respectively, although it was noted that both patients had a more severe phenotype associated with early-onset epilepsy. Many individuals had autistic features, and a formal diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) was made in 37%. Sleep disturbances were observed in several patients. Many (56%) had hypotonia, and many had delayed fine and motor development, although all achieved independent walking in the first years of life. About half (53%) had visual defects, usually strabismus or refraction errors; 1 patient had impaired hearing. There was an overlap in dysmorphic facial features, with most patients having cupped, prominent, and low-set ears (84%). Other common features included open-mouth appearance with full lips, broad and depressed nasal bridge with bulbous nasal tip, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, periorbital fullness, small or slanted palpebral fissures, and smooth philtrum. Some patients had distal skeletal anomalies, such as broad thumbs, short digits, and flat feet. Brain imaging showed variable abnormalities, such as delayed myelination, cerebral atrophy, and corpus callosum abnormalities, in 7 (64%) of 11 patients in whom studies were performed. Epilepsy was present only in 2 unrelated patients (patients 1 and 2), who had a severe seizure disorder as well as capillary hemangiomas, and carried the same missense mutation (R362L; {602480.0001}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of Snijders Blok-Fisher syndrome in 1 family reported by {1:Snijders Blok et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. However, the vast majority of affected individuals carried de novo heterozygous mutations.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 19 patients with SNIBFIS, {1:Snijders Blok et al. (2019)} identified heterozygous mutations in the POU3F3 gene (see, e.g., {602480.0001}-{602480.0006}). Mutations occurred de novo in 17 patients, whereas 1 variant was shared by a similarly affected mother and daughter (patients 18 and 19). Mutations occurred throughout the gene, and mutation types included nonsense and frameshift variants, 4 missense variants affecting highly conserved residues in functional domains, and an in-frame deletion of 5 amino acids. The mutations were found by exome sequencing; none of the mutations was found in the gnomAD database. Functional expression studies of selected variants (4 protein-terminating, 4 missense, and the in-frame deletion) showed that all mutant proteins were expressed, as expected since intronless genes are insensitive to nonsense-mediated decay. The missense variants showed normal cellular localization, whereas the others showed aberrant localization in the cytoplasm, sometimes associated with protein aggregates. In vitro functional expression studies showed that the 4 protein-terminating mutations had severely impaired transcriptional activation function, as measured by luciferase activity. Two missense (R362L, N456S) and the in-frame deletion showed partially impaired transcriptional activity compared to wildtype. In contrast, the R407L variant showed an increase in luciferase activity, whereas the R407G variant (affecting the same codon) was similar to wildtype. A construct containing a conserved transcriptional binding site from FOXP2 ({605317}) was used in the studies. The mutant proteins had variably impaired dimerization capacity: in general, the truncating proteins had impaired dimerization, whereas the missense variants were able to dimerize. {1:Snijders Blok et al. (2019)} concluded that disruptions of POU3F3 function result in a characteristic neurodevelopmental disorder.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 13 (PCH13) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the VPS51 gene ({615738}) on chromosome 11q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 13 (PCH13) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development with absent speech, microcephaly, and progressive atrophy of the cerebellar vermis and brainstem. Additional features, including seizures and visual impairment, are variable (summary by {2:Uwineza et al., 2019}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of PCH, see PCH1A ({607596}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Gershlick et al. (2019)} reported a 6-year-old Caucasian girl, born of unrelated parents, with a severe multisystemic disorder with prominent neurodevelopmental abnormalities. She presented in early infancy with feeding difficulties and failure to thrive associated with chronic cholestatic hepatitis. She had hypotonia, global developmental delay with an inability to sit or speak, nystagmus, seizures, status epilepticus during sleep, frequent body movements, cortical visual impairment, and was tube-fed. Dysmorphic features included brachycephaly, epicanthal folds, strabismus, long eyelashes, ptosis, overfolded ears, upturned nasal tip, facial hypotonia with full cheeks and open mouth, thin upper lip, high and narrow palate, low posterior hairline, and mild clubbing of the fingernails. Additional features included sleep apnea, gastric volvulus, constipation, asthma, recurrent respiratory infections, and lower extremity edema. Brain imaging was normal at age 4 months, but showed pontocerebellar hypoplasia, evidence of a Dandy-Walker variant, small hippocampus, thin corpus callosum, and periventricular white matter abnormalities at 4 and 6 years of age. Laboratory studies showed hypoglycosylation of serum transferrin and abnormal O- and N-linked glycosylation, suggesting a possible congenital disorder of glycosylation (see, e.g., CDG1A; {212065}).

{2:Uwineza et al. (2019)} reported 2 sisters, born of distantly related parents from Rwanda, with variable manifestations of PCH13. The older 9-year-old sister had severely impaired global development with absent speech and walking achieved with an ataxic gait after 5 years of age. She had microcephaly (-3.23 SD) and dysmorphic features, including hypertelorism, upturned nasal tip, short philtrum, open mouth with thick vermilion of the upper lip, high-arched palate, large teeth with dental caries, strabismus, and pes planus. Brain imaging at age 5 years showed a Dandy-Walker anomaly and enlarged ventricles, whereas brain imaging at age 9 showed cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and mega cisterna magna. The younger 30-month-old sister had early normal development until about 12 months of age, when she showed stagnation associated with a febrile illness. She had feeding problems, inability to walk, no language, poor overall growth, and microcephaly (-4.56 SD). Dysmorphic features included upturned nasal tip and strabismus. Brain imaging showed reduced white matter volume and a thin corpus callosum; the authors suggested that cerebellar atrophy may progress with age. Neither patient had nystagmus, optic impairment, edema, pyramidal signs, or hepatic involvement; seizures were not noted. Serum transferrin was normal.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PCH13 in the family reported by {1:Gershlick et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 6-year-old Caucasian girl, born of unrelated parents, with PCH13, {1:Gershlick et al. (2019)}, identified compound heterozygous mutations in the VPS51 gene (c.2232delC, {615738.0001} and R490C, {615738.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were each inherited from an unaffected parent, confirming segregation. Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed decreased levels of VPS51 (about 25% of controls), as well as decreased levels of certain other VPS proteins (all about 50% of controls) associated with decreased levels of the GARP and EARP complexes (see {615738}) and abnormal localization of the complexes in the cytosol rather than to the trans-Golgi network. Other abnormalities included altered levels and distribution of the cation-independent mannose 6-phosphate receptor (CIMPR; IGF2R; {147280}) and TGN46 ({603062}), indicative of a recycling defect, and lysosomal swelling.

In 2 sisters, born of related parents from Rwanda, with PCH13, {2:Uwineza et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous mutation in the VPS51 gene ({615738.0003}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, arthrogryposis, and structural brain anomalies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, arthrogryposis, and structural brain anomalies (NEDMABA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the SMPD4 gene ({610457}) on chromosome 2q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, arthrogryposis, and structural brain anomalies (NEDMABA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe global developmental delay, usually with hypotonia and absence of spontaneous movements other than head control, impaired intellectual development with absent speech, distal contractures, progressive microcephaly, dysmorphic features, and distal skeletal abnormalities, such as rocker-bottom feet and clenched hands with camptodactyly. Brain imaging tends to show a simplified gyral pattern of the cerebral cortex, delayed myelination, thin corpus callosum, and hypoplasia of the brainstem and cerebellum. The disorder may be complicated by feeding and/or breathing difficulties, often resulting in death in infancy (summary by {1:Magini et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Magini et al. (2019)} reported at least 23 affected individuals from 12 unrelated families with a severe congenital neurodevelopmental disorder resulting in death before 12 months of age in about 33% of patients. Several families had single or recurrent miscarriages of possibly affected fetuses who did not undergo genetic testing, raising the number of likely affected to 32. The patients were ascertained from various networks and through collaborative sharing of information, with variable clinical information; many families were consanguineous. The majority of affected infants presented with intrauterine growth retardation, congenital microcephaly, neonatal respiratory distress, and arthrogryposis of the hands and feet. Preterm birth and low birth weight were common. Those who survived the neonatal period had severe global developmental delay with limited spontaneous movement, often only achieving head control, and virtually no cognitive or speech development. Microcephaly was progressive, up to -9 SD; most patients had hypo- or hypertonia, and several had breathing or swallowing difficulties due to laryngomalacia, sometimes requiring tube feeding or mechanical ventilation. Seizures occurred in about 60% of patients, as did congenital heart defects, including septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, dilated cardiomyopathy, and congestive heart failure. Neuroimaging, available for 9 patients, showed microcephaly and a simplified gyral pattern with thin corpus callosum, delayed myelination, and mild cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia in some patients. Neuropathologic examination of 1 affected fetus at age 22 weeks' gestation showed disorganization of the cerebral cortex and evidence consistent with abnormal neuronal migration. Variable dysmorphic features, when noted, included receding forehead, short or downslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, large ears with simple helices, low-set ears, smooth or short philtrum, depressed nasal bridge, thin lips, cleft lip, short neck, simian creases, clenched hands with camptodactyly, rocker-bottom feet, and clubfeet. Two sets of brothers from 2 unrelated families (families 9 and 11) had the least severe phenotype and were able to achieve delayed independent walking and some words or speech. Both boys in family 9 had seizures and developed dilated cardiomyopathy, resulting in death at about 12 years of age. The boys in family 11 were monochorionic diamniotic twins who were 47,XYY. These boys were alive and did not have seizures, but both had congenital heart defects and dysmorphic features; they had IQ of 59 and 55.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMABA in the families reported by {1:Magini et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 23 affected members of 12 unrelated families with NEDMABA, {1:Magini et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the SMPD4 gene (see, e.g., {610457.0001}-{610457.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, or by a combination of linkage analysis and RNAseq analysis of patient transcripts, segregated with the disorder in the families. The vast majority of mutations were nonsense, frameshift, or splice site mutations, suggesting a loss-of-function effect. Two sibs with a milder phenotype carried a homozygous missense variant (P446L; {610457.0005}), suggesting that this variant protein retained some residual function. Analysis of patient fibroblasts from 2 families with splice site mutations showed significantly decreased SMPD4 mRNA and protein levels compared to controls, consistent with a loss of function. Gene expression profiling of fibroblasts derived from patients of 1 family ({610457.0001}) showed differentially expressed genes that fell into clusters involved in protein secretory pathways and other cellular activities, including movement, signaling, growth, proliferation, development, death, and survival. Ultrastructural analysis of patient fibroblasts showed dilated cisternae of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER), as well as accumulation of abnormal protein aggregates and evidence of increased autophagy, suggesting increased ER stress compared to controls. However, there was no evidence of activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR). Patient cells and control cells with siRNA-mediated knockdown of the SMPD4 gene showed a reduced percentage of cells in the G2/M phase with a milder increase of cells in the G1 phase, suggesting impairment of the cell cycle, as well as increased susceptibility to apoptosis under stress conditions compared to controls.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Siddiqi syndrome (SIDDIS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the FITM2 gene ({612029}) on chromosome 20q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Siddiqi syndrome (SIDDIS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay, early-onset progressive sensorineural hearing impairment, regression of motor skills, dystonia, poor overall growth, and low body mass index (BMI). More variable features may include ichthyosis-like skin abnormalities or sensory neuropathy (summary by {3:Zazo Seco et al., 2017}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Zazo Seco et al. (2017)} reported 6 sibs, born of consanguineous Pakistani parents (family W09-1008), with a syndromic developmental disorder. The patients were between 6 and 26 years of age at the time of the report. The presenting symptom, at about 6 months of age, was sensorineural hearing impairment that progressed to profound hearing loss by about 10 years of age. The patients also had global developmental delay with mildly delayed walking initially, inability to run, and lack of independent ambulation by age 9 (1 patient). The 3 older patients had progressive loss of ambulation and head control by age 10 years. Three patients developed dystonic limb and trunk movements after 2 years of age; fine motor skills were impaired due to hand involvement. Cognition was impaired, but the patients were able to feed themselves. Other features included contractures, pes cavus, muscle atrophy, and ichthyosis-like skin abnormalities, mainly at the shins. Although most complained of paresthesias, burning, or pain sensation, suggesting abnormal sensory function or small-fiber neuropathy, nerve conduction studies in 1 patient were normal. One patient had onset of daily seizures at age 15. Brain imaging performed in 2 patients, including the patient with seizures, was normal. The patients had failure to thrive with low weight, but no features of lipodystrophy. The authors suggested that the disorder be called Siddiqi syndrome after the physician who studied the family.

{2:Shakir et al. (2018)} reported a 4-year-old boy, born of unrelated parents, with Siddiqi syndrome. At birth, he showed intrauterine growth retardation, hypoplastic adducted thumbs, planovalgus foot deformities, and borderline low-set ears. He had global developmental delay with poor head control, delayed motor milestones, lower extremity hypotonia, dystonic movements of the trunk and limbs, and profound sensorineural hearing loss. Brain imaging showed Dandy-Walker malformation. He also had gastrointestinal problems, but did not have sensory or skin abnormalities.

{1:Riedhammer et al. (2018)} reported an 8-year-old girl, born of consanguineous parents, with SIDDIS. She had global developmental delay with poor fine motor skills, ataxic gait, impaired intellectual development (IQ of 58), sensorineural hearing loss, and poor speech. Other features included short stature and hyperkeratosis mainly at the shins. She did not have dysmorphic features or polyneuropathy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SIDDIS in the family reported by {3:Zazo Seco et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 5 sibs, born of consanguineous Pakistani parents (family W09-1008), with SIDDIS, {3:Zazo Seco et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the FITM2 gene (E2X; {612029.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping, linkage analysis, and whole-exome sequencing, was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The variant segregated with the disorder in the family and was not found in the ExAC database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the mutation was predicted to result in a complete loss of function.

In a 4-year-old boy with SIDDIS, {2:Shakir et al. (2018)} identified compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the FITM2 gene ({612029.0002} and {612029.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were each inherited from an unaffected parent. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In an 8-year-old girl, born of consanguineous parents, with SIDDIS, {1:Riedhammer et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the FITM2 gene (G232R; {612029.0004}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based exome sequencing, was found in the heterozygous state in each unaffected parent. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Zazo Seco et al. (2017)} determined that Drosophila have a single Fitm gene that is widely expressed throughout developmental states and in many tissues. RNAi-induced gene downregulation of Fitm in Drosophila resulted in severely impaired and uncoordinated locomotion, as well as evidence of a sensory neuropathy associated with abnormal dendrite branching of sensory neurons and a reduction in dendritic field coverage in some mutant flies. Mutant flies also had hearing impairment and a progressive decrease in lipid droplet size in the fat body compared to controls. The findings recapitulated the phenotypic features of Siddiqi syndrome.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Halperin-Birk syndrome (HLBKS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SEC31A gene ({610257}) on chromosome 4q21. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content: Halperin-Birk syndrome (HLBKS) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by structural brain defects, spastic quadriplegia with multiple contractures, profound developmental delay, seizures, dysmorphism, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy. Death occurs in early childhood ({1:Halperin et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Halperin et al. (2019)} reported 2 sibs, born of a highly consanguineous Bedouin family, with a severe congenital neurodevelopmental disorder resulting in death at 4 and 2 years of age, respectively. Microcephaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and mildly impaired intrauterine growth retardation were apparent in utero by ultrasound. After birth, the patients had failure to thrive and subsequently had almost no developmental progress. They had no visual or verbal communication, were unable to walk, had only minimal nonpurposeful movements, and had spastic quadriplegia with hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and contractures. Other features included pseudobulbar palsy associated with gastroesophageal reflux and recurrent aspiration, congenital cataracts, optic atrophy, and hearing impairment. Both developed focal and generalized seizures soon after birth, and EEG showed disorganized background activity with sharp spike-wave discharges. Dysmorphic features included abnormal skull shape, pointed triangular face, micrognathia, high-arched palate, thick lips, long eyelashes, and dislocation of the hips. One patient had clubfoot, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, umbilical and inguinal hernia, and perimembranotic ventricular septal defect (VSD). Brain imaging in both showed severe structural abnormalities, including semilobar holoprosencephaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, enlarged ventricles, and colpocephaly.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HLBKS in the family reported by {1:Halperin et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Bedouin parents, with HLBKS, {1:Halperin et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the SEC31A gene ({610257.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Analysis of parental cells carrying the mutation showed that it resulted in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and a complete loss of function. Knockdown of the gene in Drosophila recapitulated the phenotype (see ANIMAL MODEL). CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of the SEC31A gene in human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells resulted in failure of the cells to expand to generate viable clones. Knockdown of the gene in HEK293 cells resulted in increased susceptibility to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress compared to controls.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Halperin et al. (2019)} found that complete loss of sec31a in Drosophila was embryonically lethal and associated with defects in eye and brain development, consistent with abnormal neurodevelopment.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurooculocardiogenitourinary syndrome (NOCGUS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the WDR37 gene ({618586}) on chromosome 10p15.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurooculocardiogenitourinary syndrome (NOCGUS) is a multisystem disorder characterized by poor growth and anomalies of the ocular, craniofacial, neurologic, cardiovascular, genitourinary, skeletal, and gastrointestinal systems. Lethality before 2 years of age has been observed ({2:Reis et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Kanca et al. (2019)} studied 5 patients with overlapping ocular and neurologic phenotypes and mutations in the WDR37 gene. All exhibited eye anomalies, including colobomas and microphthalmia; dysmorphic features, including prominent forehead, broad nasal bridge, wide downturned mouth, excessive nuchal skin, and widely spaced nipples; seizures; and feeding difficulties. Developmental delay and severe intellectual disability, with no verbal development, was present in 4 of the patients; the fifth was an infant too young for evaluation. Most patients had hypotonia, postnatal microcephaly, and congenital cardiac defects, and sensorineural hearing loss was present in 2 of them. Both male probands had micropenis and undescended testes, and the oldest patient, a 19-year-old woman, had delayed thelarche and menarche. Brain malformations were similar among the 5 probands, and key features from brain imaging included diffuse gyral hypoplasia, due to thin or narrow gyri with reduced white matter; mildly small and dysplastic hippocampi; diffusely reduced volume of white matter; mildly enlarged lateral ventricles; diffusely thin corpus callosum, with callosal lipoma in 1 patient; unusually thin anterior commissure; mild diffuse brainstem hypoplasia, most obvious in the pons; diffuse, mild to moderate cerebellar hypoplasia, with diffuse and strikingly abnormal foliar pattern; and mildly enlarged posterior fossa in some patients. Brain MRI also revealed retinal colobomas and optic nerve hypoplasia. The authors noted that despite the similarities among the patients, some features were not present in all patients or were specific to a single proband; for example, the oldest patient developed spastic quadriplegia, whereas the others exhibited hypotonia, and only 1 proband showed significant neuroregression.

{2:Reis et al. (2019)} reported 4 unrelated patients with mutations in the WDR37 gene and overlapping multisystem phenotypes consisting of severe complex ocular anomalies, dysmorphic craniofacial features, hearing loss with recurrent otitis media, excess nuchal skin or cystic hygroma, structural brain anomalies with severe neurologic impairment, congenital heart defects, genitourinary anomalies, feeding disorders with postnatal growth deficiency, structural gastrointestinal anomalies, and skeletal anomalies, including scoliosis, hip dysplasia, syndactyly, and contractures. The 2 patients who were alive at age 30 years and 8 years were nonverbal with limited to no ambulation; another patient died at age 22 months from respiratory failure due to pneumonia and cardiac anomalies. Limited clinical information was available for the fourth patient.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the WDR37 gene that were identified in patients with NOCGUS by {1:Kanca et al. (2019)} and {2:Reis et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 5 unrelated probands with overlapping ocular and neurologic phenotypes, {1:Kanca et al. (2019)} identified heterozygosity for 4 different de novo missense mutations in the WDR37 gene ({618586.0001}-{618586.0004}). The variants were not present in the ExAC or gnomAD databases.

In 4 unrelated patients with poor growth and overlapping anomalies of the ocular, craniofacial, neurologic, cardiovascular, genitourinary, skeletal, and gastrointestinal systems, {2:Reis et al. (2019)} identified heterozygosity for the same 4 de novo missense mutations in the WDR37 gene that were identified by {1:Kanca et al. (2019)}.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH DYSMORPHIC FACIES AND DISTAL SKELETAL ANOMALIES; NEDDFSA

Caused by mutation in the zinc finger MIZ-domain containing 1 gene (ZMIZ1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and distal skeletal anomalies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and distal skeletal anomalies (NEDDFSA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ZMIZ1 gene ({607159}) on chromosome 10q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and distal skeletal anomalies (NEDDFSA) is a global neurodevelopmental disorder with highly variable features. Patients often show poor feeding, poor overall growth, and hypotonia from early infancy, followed by mildly delayed motor development, poor language acquisition, and behavioral abnormalities. Intellectual development varies from severe with absent speech to mild with the ability to attend special schools. Common features include dysmorphic facial features with notable eye anomalies, joint hypermobility, and mild skeletal anomalies of the hands and feet (summary by {1:Carapito et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Carapito et al. (2019)} reported 14 unrelated patients and 3 sibs with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who ranged in age from 1.5 to 20 years, were ascertained through a transatlantic collaborative effort to share information about patients who were found by genetic analysis to have mutations in the ZMIZ1 gene. All patients came to attention for global developmental delay, although the severity was variable: only 2 patients were noted to have severe intellectual disability, including a 19-year-old woman who was nonverbal (patient 10), but many had mild to moderately impaired intellect, and several were able to attend special schools. Most patients had mildly delayed walking, delayed speech, and behavioral abnormalities, such as autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or aggression; about half had hypotonia. Many patients had feeding difficulties and constipation with poor overall growth. Variable craniofacial abnormalities were apparent in almost all patients. These included facial hypotonia, midface hypoplasia, prominent or deep-set eyes, hypertelorism, up- or downslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, prominent or broad nasal bridge, anteverted nares, prominent columella, large or low-set ears, long smooth philtrum, micrognathia, cupid's bow, and wide or small mouth. Four patients had hearing loss and 12 had variable ocular anomalies, including ptosis, Duane syndrome, hypermetropia, glaucoma, astigmatism, coloboma, and amblyopia, but each feature was only seen in 1 or 2 patients. About half of the patients had joint hypermobility, 3 had scoliosis, and at least 12 had some type of hand or foot anomaly, mainly brachydactyly, tapered fingers, fifth finger clinodactyly, camptodactyly, long or wide halluces, hallux valgus, and/or 2-3 toe syndactyly. Two had clubfoot. The few patients who got radiographs showed coned epiphyses of the phalanges. Many patients had other mild congenital cardiac or urogenital malformations, but these were seen only in 1 or 2 patients each and did not form a consistent pattern. The malformations included ventricular septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, atrophic kidney, vesicoureteral reflux, hypospadias, and cryptorchidism. Three patients had seizures. Brain imaging, when performed, was normal in some patients, but showed variable nonspecific abnormalities in others, including enlarged ventricles, cerebral atrophy, delayed myelination, thin corpus callosum, and cerebellar atrophy; 2 patients had nodular heterotopia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the ZMIZ1 gene that were identified in patients with NEDDFSA by {1:Carapito et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 14 unrelated patients with NEDDFSA, {1:Carapito et al. (2019)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the ZMIZ1 gene (see, e.g., {607159.0001}-{607159.0005}). Three adopted sibs with a similar phenotype and a heterozygous mutation were also identified ({607159.0006}). The patients were ascertained through a transatlantic collaborative effort; the mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. None of the variants were found in available public databases, including gnomAD. The mutations, which included missense, frameshift, and splice site defects, were scattered throughout the gene, although there was a cluster of variants affecting a conserved alanine-rich region (residues 280-305) thought to have important functions. Analysis of peripheral blood from 5 patients showed normal mRNA levels, even for a patient with a splice site mutation, and expression of 3 missense variants into HeLa cells showed proper nuclear localization. Transfection of 3 variants (T300M, {607159.0001}; c.3112dupA, {607159.0002}; K91R, {607159.0003}) into HEK293T cells resulted in decreased induction of luciferase activity compared to wildtype (although the change for K91R was not statistically significant), suggesting impaired coactivation activity of the mutant proteins. Electroporation of these 3 mutants into progenitor cells in the ventricular zone of embryonic mice cortices resulted in defective neuronal migration to the cortex, as well as morphologic abnormalities of the neurons manifest as rounded cells with aberrantly oriented processes. These findings suggested that the ZMIZ1 mutations disrupted proper neuronal polarization and neuronal migration in the developing cortex. Functional studies of the other variants and additional studies of patient cells were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-81 (DEE81) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the DMXL2 gene ({612186}) on chromosome 15q21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-81 (DEE81) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder typically characterized by onset of severe refractory seizures soon after birth or in the first months of life. Affected individuals show little developmental progress with no eye contact and no motor or cognitive development. Other features may include facial dysmorphism, such as hypotonic facies and epicanthal folds, as well as sensorineural hearing loss and peripheral neuropathy. Brain imaging shows cerebral atrophy, impaired myelination, thin corpus callosum, and progressive leukoencephalopathy (summary by {1:Esposito et al., 2019}; {2:Maddirevula et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Maddirevula et al. (2019)} reported a 3-year-old boy (patient 17-4220), born of consanguineous parents, who developed focal seizures at 3 months of age. He then showed global developmental delay, no eye contact, and macrocephaly. Dysmorphic features included long face, high forehead, short philtrum, and low-set ears. Brain imaging showed cerebral atrophy and atrophy of the brainstem.

{1:Esposito et al. (2019)} reported 6 children from 3 unrelated families with DEE81, who were clinically diagnosed with Ohtahara syndrome. Each family contained 2 affected sibs; 2 families were consanguineous and of Israeli Arab (family 2) and Turkish descent (family 3). The patients presented soon after birth with either respiratory distress or refractory focal, myoclonic, or tonic seizures. EEG showed disorganized background activity, multifocal spike discharges, and a burst-suppression pattern. The patients showed almost no developmental progress, with poor visual fixation, quadriplegia with inability to walk, hypotonia, absent spontaneous movements, and almost no cognitive, motor, communicative, or language development. Five patients died within the first 9 years of life. Brain imaging showed thin corpus callosum, hypomyelination, and progressive leukoencephalopathy. The 2 sibs from family 3 also had a simplified gyral pattern. Other features included sensorineural hearing loss, mild peripheral polyneuropathy, and dysmorphic features, such as myopathic facies, downslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, short forehead, saddle nose, and high-arched palate. The 2 sibs from family 1 had microcephaly (-3.6 SD), whereas the other patients had a large head size. Some patients had nonpitting limb edema.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE81 in the families reported by {1:Esposito et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 3-year-old boy (patient 17-4220), born of consanguineous parents, with DEE81, {2:Maddirevula et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the DMXL2 gene ({612186.0003}). The variant, which was found by exome sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 6 patients from 3 unrelated families with DEE81, {1:Esposito et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the DMXL2 gene ({612186.0004}-{612186.0007}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. None of the variants were present in the gnomAD database. Fibroblasts from all 3 probands showed almost no DMXL2 protein, suggesting degradation or instability and a loss-of-function effect. Patient fibroblasts also showed lysosomal abnormalities, particularly decreased LAMP1 ({153330}), decreased pH within acidic organelles, impaired lysosomal degradative capacity, and defective autophagy with abnormal accumulation of autophagy receptors and substrates compared to controls. Ultrastructural analysis showed vacuolization and accumulation of atypical fusion-like structures. The abnormalities could be rescued by expression of wildtype DMXL2. Knockdown of Dmxl2 using shRNA in cultured mouse hippocampal neurons resulted in similar lysosomal abnormalities and defective autophagy, as well as a significant decrease in neurite complexity, consistent with impaired synaptic connections.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-72 (MRT72) is caused by homozygous mutation in the METTL5 gene ({618628}) on chromosome 2q31.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-72 (MRT72) is characterized by moderately to severely impaired intellectual development, microcephaly, and facial dysmorphism. Some patients may have seizures ({2:Hu et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Richard et al. (2019)} reported 7 patients from 2 unrelated families (family PKMR43M of Pakistani descent and consanguineous family F47949 of Yemenite descent) with a similar intellectual developmental disorder and mutation in the MRT72 gene. The patients ranged in age from 7 to 31 years; 2 affected individuals from family PKMR42M were deceased. Globally impaired development was apparent from infancy or early childhood and included delayed walking by a few years, delayed fine motor skills, poor or absent speech acquisition, and moderate to severe cognitive deficits. The patients had poor overall growth, microcephaly (-2.8 to -5 SD), and dysmorphic facial features, including prominent nose with broad nasal base and overhanging nasal tip, large ears, posteriorly rotated ears, and variable dysplastic teeth. Brain imaging of 1 patient showed no abnormalities other than microcephaly. None of the patients had hearing impairment, visual defects, or seizures.

{2:Hu et al. (2019)} reported 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Iranian parents (family M8600616), with a phenotype consistent with MRT72. The brothers were 10 and 5 years of age. They had normal early development, with walking and first words at 12 months of age, although the parents noted learning difficulties since infancy. One sib, who had no history of seizures, was able to walk and spoke with slurred speech. The other sib developed seizures in infancy and walked with an unbalanced gait. They had microcephaly (-7 to -8 SD), strabismus, narrow nasal base, broad nasal ridge, long philtrum, thin upper lip, and large ears. IQs were 25 and 26, indicating severe impairment. Both sibs had aggressive behavior with short temper.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MRT72 in the families reported by {3:Richard et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In the supplemental material of their article, {1:Anazi et al. (2017)} reported a 1.9-year-old girl (11DG1842) with a mutation in the METTL5 gene that 'potentially explained her phenotype.' She had impaired intellectual development, oligodactyly, aplasia cutis congenita, posteriorly rotated ears, prominent nose, and micrognathia. Her growth parameters were all below the 3rd percentile. No functional studies were reported.

In affected members of 2 unrelated families with MRT72, {3:Richard et al. (2019)} identified homozygous frameshift mutations in the METTL5 gene ({618628.0001} and {618628.0002}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families. In vitro cellular studies in COS-7 and HEK293T cells transfected with constructs containing the mutations showed that both frameshift mutations resulted in significantly decreased levels of the protein compared to wildtype, suggesting that the mutant proteins were unstable and degraded by the proteosome. {3:Richard et al. (2019)} also performed similar functional studies of a missense METTL5 variant (G61D; {618628.0003}) reported by {2:Hu et al. (2019)}. G61D had normal levels of expression. Transfection of the 3 variants into COS-7 cells showed that all had cellular localization similar to that of wildtype, with accumulation in the nucleus and formation of aggregates in the cytoplasm. In addition, none of the 3 variants adversely affected cellular localization or synapse morphology when transfected into cultured rat hippocampal cells.

In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Iranian parents, with a phenotype consistent with MRT72, {2:Hu et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous missense variant in the METTL5 gene (G61D; {618628.0003}). The variant, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. The family was part of a large cohort of 404 consanguineous families, mostly Iranian, in which 2 or more offspring had impaired intellectual development. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Richard et al. (2019)} found that morpholino-based knockdown of the mttl5 gene in zebrafish embryos resulted in decreased head size, reduction in the forebrain and midbrain, and curved tails, suggesting that the gene has an important role in brain development.

clinicalSynopsis: Three unrelated families have been reported (last curated November 2019)
Caused by mutation in the tripartite motif-containing protein 71 gene (TRIM71,)

Miscellaneous: Three unrelated families have been reported (last curated November 2019)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the tripartite motif-containing protein 71 gene (TRIM71,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital hydrocephalus-4 (HYC4) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TRIM71 gene ({618570}) on chromosome 3p22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Congenital hydrocephalus-4 (HYC4) is characterized by inadequate passage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from its point of production to its point of absorption, in the absence of obstruction (communicating hydrocephalus). Patients undergo surgical shunting at birth because of extreme ventriculomegaly. Patients have neurodevelopmental delay and epilepsy ({2:Furey et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Furey et al. (2018)} reported 3 unrelated patients with congenital communicating hydrocephalus that was diagnosed prenatally. One of the patients was a woman (102-1) who had a similarly affected son. The other 2 patients had sporadic occurrence of the disorder with no other family members affected. Although clinical details were limited, the patients were noted to have neurodevelopmental delay and epilepsy. Brain imaging confirmed communicating hydrocephalus and enlarged ventricles; the mother and son also had open schizencephalic clefts.

{1:Duy et al. (2024)} identified 20 unrelated patients with congenital hydrocephalus-4. Ventricular dilatation was seen in 17 patients, and 11 required cerebrospinal diversion treatment. Eleven patients had corpus callosum defects, 11 had developmental or cognitive issues, 5 had seizures/epilepsy, and 4 had hearing problems. Craniofacial abnormalities (including unilateral coronal craniosynostosis in 1 patient) were seen in 7 patients, limb anomalies in 5, and congenital heart defects in 3.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HYC4 in the family reported by {2:Furey et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 unrelated patients with HYC4, {2:Furey et al. (2018)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the TRIM71 gene (R608H, {618570.0001} and R796H, {618570.0002}). Both mutations occurred at highly conserved residues in the NHL domain. One of the patients transmitted the mutation to an affected child who was diagnosed prenatally. The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not found in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors suggested that this form of hydrocephalus is related to impaired neurogenesis rather than active CSF accumulation. The patients were part of a cohort of 88 probands with communicating hydrocephalus and 89 probands with hydrocephalus associated with aqueductal stenosis who underwent whole-exome sequencing.

Among a large cohort of patients (a total of 2,697 parent-proband trios and 8,091 exomes) with cerebral ventriculomegaly, {1:Duy et al. (2024)} identified 13 unrelated patients with de novo heterozygous variants in the TRIM71 gene ({618570.0001}-{618570.0004}) and 7 patients with rare, damaging heterozygous variants in highly conserved N-terminal domains of the TRIM71 gene, 3 of whom inherited the variant from a parent, and 4 for whom the inheritance was unknown. The phenotype was consistent with HYC4, a syndromic form of hydrocephalus that includes cerebral ventriculomegaly, often requiring neurosurgical diversion of cerebrospinal fluid, developmental delay or other neurobehavioral abnormalities, and other structural defects. The 13 de novo variants included 2 missense variants that had previously been reported ({618570.0001}-{618570.0002}), each seen in 3 patients in this cohort, 4 other missense variants that occurred in 1 patient each, a nonsense mutation ({618570.0003}), a 7-bp duplication resulting in a frameshift and premature termination ({619570.0004}), and a splice site mutation. None of the de novo variants were seen in 1,798 controls, and all of the identified variants 'had a very low allele frequency' in gnomAD (v2.1.1). Functional studies showed that some TRIM71 variants disrupted TRIM71 binding to canonical mRNA targets, whereas others disrupted localization of TRIM71 to processing bodies. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of human embryos demonstrated expression of TRIM71 in early embryonic neural stem cells.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{4:Schulman et al. (2008)} found that loss of Lin41 led to embryonic lethality after embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) in mice. Lin41 -/- embryos had defects in anterior neural tube closure, resulting in exencephaly. Open neural folds were everted, enlarged, and failed to fuse, and brain tissue was exposed.

{3:Mitschka et al. (2015)} confirmed that loss of Trim71 resulted in 100% embryonic lethality in mice. Starting from E9.5, Trim71 -/- mice exhibited a severe neural tube closure defect characterized by an open cranial neural tube extending from forebrain to hindbrain. At later stages, Trim71 -/- mice showed general growth retardation of the trunk, and all embryos were dead by E14.5.

preferredTitle: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH SPEECH DELAY, AUTISM, AND DYSMORPHIC FACIES; IDDSADF
clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, mild to severe

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with speech delay, autism, and dysmorphic facies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with speech delay, autism, and dysmorphic facies (IDDSADF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CNOT3 gene ({604910}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with speech delay, autism, and dysmorphic facies (IDDSADF) is a developmental disorder with the most highly consistent features of hypotonia, relatively small stature, developmental delay, behavioral problems, and impaired intellectual development. Variable dysmorphic facial features are present, without a consistent pattern. A predisposition to moyamoya angiopathy has been observed ({2:Martin et al., 2019}, {3:Pinard et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Martin et al. (2019)} reported 8 unrelated patients (patients 9-16) with an intellectual developmental disorder associated with de novo heterozygous mutations in the CNOT3 gene that were predicted to result in premature termination of the protein. The patients were ascertained from several large cohorts of patients who underwent diagnostic exome sequencing. Seven patients were between 4 and 19 years of age; 1 patient was 55 years old. The patients had delayed walking (up to 5 years), variable hypotonia, fine motor delay, and delayed or absent speech. Five had autistic features, several had learning difficulties, and 1 had severe intellectual disability. The 55-year-old man was unable to read or write. All had dysmorphic features, although there was no consistent recognizable pattern. Variable features included prominent forehead, flat nasal bridge, anteverted nares, long columella, deep-set eyes, upslanting palpebral fissures, prominent or low-set eyebrows, short philtrum, thin upper lip, small chin, and strabismus. Some patients had tapering fingers, small feet, and/or short hands, and there was a trend toward short stature. Brain imaging, performed in most patients, was normal, although 2 had minor anomalies, including occipital atrophy and partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. Additional rare features, such as foot deformities, kyphosis, scoliosis, and skin pigmentation anomalies, were also observed. Patient 12 had temporal lobe epilepsy diagnosed at age 13 years. {2:Martin et al. (2019)} also identified 8 additional unrelated patients (patients 1-8) with de novo heterozygous missense variants in the CNOT3 gene. These patients had similar clinical features, including mildly delayed walking, hypotonia, delayed or absent language, intellectual disability, learning difficulties, and autism. Four of these patients were able to attend mainstream school with special assistance. Variable dysmorphic features and brain imaging abnormalities were present in some patients; 3 had seizures.

From a cohort of 197 probands with moyamoya disease (see {252350}), {3:Pinard et al. (2020)} reported 4 unrelated patients with mutation in the CNOT3 gene. Moyamoya angiopathy was bilateral in 2 patients and unilateral in 2 patients; 3 had ischemic stroke and the remaining patient had moyamoya-related facial and upper extremity numbness. Other features were variable, and the authors concluded that rare variants in the CNOT3 gene predispose to moyamoya disease in the presence or absence of developmental delay.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CNOT3 gene that were identified in patients with IDDSADF by {2:Martin et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 unrelated patients with IDDSADF, {2:Martin et al. (2019)} identified de novo heterozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations in the CNOT3 gene (see, e.g., {604910.0001}-{604910.0005}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing; functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. Eight additional patients with a similar disorder carried de novo missense variants in the CNOT3 gene; functional studies of these variants were not performed. The patients were ascertained from over 13,000 individuals from the {1:Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study (2017)} as well as from large-scale sequencing work performed by other groups. {2:Martin et al. (2019)} concluded that haploinsufficiency of CNOT3 was the likely mechanism of action given the 8 cases with variants predicted to result in premature termination. The authors noted that data from databases such as ExAC indicated that CNOT3 is highly intolerant of loss-of-function variation.

phenotypes.phenotype: Cortical dysplasia, complex, with other brain malformations 10

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations-10 (CDCBM10) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the APC2 gene ({612034}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations-10 (CDCBM10) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by severely impaired global development associated with abnormalities on brain imaging, including lissencephaly, cortical dysplasia, subcortical heterotopia, and paucity of white matter. The disorder results from defective neuronal migration during brain development. Affected individuals often develop seizures, are unable to walk, and do not acquire language (summary by {2:Lee et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of CDCBM, see CDCBM1 ({614039}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Lee et al. (2019)} reported 12 patients, aged 7 months to 15 years, from 8 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients presented within the first months or years of life with severe global developmental delay. Eight patients developed myoclonic and generalized seizures in infancy or early childhood. Some patients had refractory seizures, whereas others had controllable seizures. EEG in these patients showed generalized epileptic activity; 1 patient had hypsarrhythmia. Most patients had axial hypotonia, and some had peripheral hypertonia or spasticity. Development was severely impaired: none of the patients were able to walk and none had language acquisition. Brain imaging in all patients showed lissencephaly in a posterior-predominant to anterior gradient and thickening of the cerebral mantle. Additional more variable abnormalities included enlarged ventricles, thin corpus callosum, posterior subcortical heterotopia, ribbon heterotopia, and paucity of white matter. A few patients had brainstem and/or cerebellar hypoplasia. Detailed imaging, performed in some patients, showed areas of pachygyria, agyria, and cortical dysplasia with in-folding of gyri in the mesial occipital cortex. {2:Lee et al. (2019)} suggested that the neuroimaging features may be distinctive for this disorder. These features were suggestive of a malformation of cortical development likely due to defective neuronal migration during brain development.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDCBM10 in the families reported by {2:Lee et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 12 patients from 8 unrelated families with CDCBM10, {2:Lee et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the APC2 gene (see, e.g., {612034.0002}-{612034.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families; none of the variants were found in the 1000 Genomes Project or gnomAD databases. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but all of the variants were predicted to result in a loss of function. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts focusing on patients with confirmed lissencephaly. Seven of the families were consanguineous and of Middle Eastern origin.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{1:Almuriekhi et al. (2015)} found that Apc2-null mice had impaired learning and memory associated with an abnormal head shape, dilated ventricles, and thin corpus callosum. Knockdown of Nsd1 ({606681}) significantly reduced the expression of Apc2, indicating that Apc2 is a downstream effector of Nsd1. Nsd1 knockdown also caused impaired cerebral neuronal migration and layering defects similar to that observed in Apc2-null mice, and expression of Apc2 in Nsd1-null cells rescued the defect. The findings indicated that expression of NSD1 controlled neuronal migration through the induction of APC2.

By immunostaining of the developing mouse cortex, {3:Shintani et al. (2012)} found expression of the Apc2 gene in postmitotic migrating neuronal cells, but not in glial cells. Apc2-null mice showed severe defects in neuronal lamination in the cortex, hippocampus, cerebellum, and olfactory bulb, consistent with impaired directional neuronal migration. In vitro functional studies in isolated cerebellar granule cells showed abnormal actin reorganization after stimulation with BDNF ({113505}), which was associated with attenuated signaling through Rac1 ({602048}), TrkB ({600456}), and Cdc42 ({116952}). The findings suggested that Apc2 is a mediator of the cytoskeletal regulation at the leading edge of migrating neurons in response to extracellular guiding molecules during brain development.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with short stature and behavioral abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with short stature and behavioral abnormalities (IDDSSBA) is caused by homozygous mutation in the IQSEC1 gene ({610166}) on chromosome 3p25.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Ansar et al. (2019)} reported 5 living patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with a similar developmental disorder. Two sibs in family 1 (F208), of Pakistani descent, were 36 and 23 years of age. They had global developmental delay with delayed motor milestones, severely impaired intellectual development, and aphasia. Other features included short stature, small head circumference, facial dysmorphism, and aggressive behavior. One had poor vision, and neither had seizures. Two other similarly affected sibs had died. Two brothers in family 2, of Saudi descent, were 6 and 11 years of age; a 6-year-old relative was similarly affected. These patients developed refractory seizures at about 2 months of age. Seizure types included febrile, generalized tonic-clonic, and absence, with frequent episodes of status epilepticus. They had global developmental delay with severely impaired intellectual development, but were able to walk independently at age 3 and had a few words at age 4. Other features included short stature, hypotonia, ataxic gait, and behavioral abnormalities, including inattention, hyperactivity, and aggression. Brain imaging in the 2 brothers was normal; EEG showed slowed background activity and low-amplitude sharp discharges.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IDDSSBA in the families reported by {1:Ansar et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In affected individuals from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with IDDSSBA, {1:Ansar et al. (2019)} identified homozygous missense mutations in the IQSEC1 gene (T343M, {610166.0001} and R321Q, {610166.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. {1:Ansar et al. (2019)} found that ubiquitous overexpression of IQSEC1 in Drosophila was lethal, whereas expression of either of the identified mutations was not lethal, suggesting that the variants caused a loss of function. Targeted disruption of the gene in Drosophila and mice resulted in axonal guidance defects.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Ansar et al. (2019)} noted that the Drosophila homolog of the 3 IQSEC genes is a single gene, 'schizo.' Schizo is broadly expressed in the central and peripheral nervous systems of Drosophila embryos, including neurons, neuropil, cell bodies, and glia. Schizo regulates axonal growth cone guidance via the Slit (see, e.g., SLIT1, {603742})-ROBO (see, e.g., ROBO1, {602430}) pathway and plays a role in midline commissure formation. {1:Ansar et al. (2019)} found that flies with mutant Schizo had commissural, axonal, and dendritic defects, as well as deficits in the retinal photoreceptors, suggesting abnormal axonal guidance. Targeted deletion of the Iqsec1 gene in mouse cortical neurons early in development resulted in an increased density of dendritic spines that had small heads, consistent with immature development.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with absent language and variable seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with absent language and variable seizures (NEDALVS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the WASF1 gene ({605035}) on chromosome 6q21.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Ito et al. (2018)} reported 5 unrelated adult patients, ranging in age from 21 to 30 years, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts and the GeneMatcher database. All had severe to profoundly impaired intellectual development with autistic features and absent language, although some could speak a few words. Four patients had delayed motor skills and delayed walking (up to 10 years of age), whereas 1 was nonambulant at age 23 years. Most had hypotonia and an abnormal gait with poor balance. Four patients developed variable types of seizures in childhood, both generalized and focal, and some patients had an abnormal pain threshold with automutilation. The affected individuals had midfacial hypoplasia and mild ocular anomalies, such as strabismus, deep-set eyes, gray sclera, and exophthalmia, but there was no recognizable phenotype. One patient had vision loss. Additional more variable features included skeletal anomalies, such as joint hypermobility, ankle valgus, pes planus, short toes, and long tapered fingers, widely spaced or inverted nipples, feeding difficulties, constipation, and recurrent urinary tract infections. Brain imaging showed enlarged ventricles in 2 patients and mild Sylvian atrophy in a third, but was normal in 2.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the WASF1 gene that were identified by {1:Ito et al. (2018)} in patients with NEDALVS occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 unrelated adults with NEDALVS, {1:Ito et al. (2018)} identified de novo heterozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations in the WASF1 gene ({605035.0001}-{605035.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. The variants all clustered around the C-terminal WH2 domain in the highly conserved WCA region of the WASF1 protein that is important for actin binding and subsequent polymerization. Western blot analysis of fibroblasts derived from 2 patients with the R506X mutation ({605035.0001}) showed 50% residual wildtype WASF1 protein and a variable lesser amount of a truncated protein. These findings suggested that the variants likely result in altered function of the mutant protein rather than complete protein loss or haploinsufficiency. The fibroblasts showed abnormal lamellipodia formation at the cell periphery and defective actin remodeling, as well as elongated mitochondria, compared to controls, suggesting altered actin polymerization and defects in the normal mitochondrial fission/fusion balance. {1:Ito et al. (2018)} suggested that altered actin regulation resulting from mutations in the WASF1 gene, which is highly and specifically expressed in the brain, may adversely impact synaptic formation and/or plasticity. Three patients had variants of unknown significance in other genes that most likely did not contribute to the phenotype, although that possibility could not be excluded.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with nonspecific brain abnormalities and with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with nonspecific brain abnormalities and with or without seizures (NEDBAS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the DLL1 gene ({606582}) on chromosome 6q27.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with nonspecific brain abnormalities is a highly variable syndrome characterized by impaired intellectual development and behavioral abnormalities associated with structural changes on brain imaging. Some patients have seizures, hypotonia, and scoliosis/kyphosis. Cognitive function ranges from severely impaired to the ability to attend schools with special assistance (summary by {1:Fischer-Zirnsak et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Fischer-Zirnsak et al. (2019)} reported 14 patients from 11 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative research efforts and GeneMatcher. Most were children, although 1 was 16 and another was 35; an affected mother was also reported (without an exact age). All individuals had some sort of developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, often accompanied by autism spectrum disorder, autistic features, attention deficit, stereotypic behavior, and/or structural brain abnormalities on imaging. Clinical details of many patients were limited, but some had speech delay, patient 6 had an IQ of 55, patient 10 had an IQ of 91, and a few were able to attend school. Five patients had seizures. All 11 patients who underwent brain imaging showed nonspecific and variable abnormalities, including hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly, thin, short, or dysplastic corpus callosum, subtle cortical dysplasia, and small cerebellum or pons. One patient had periventricular nodular heterotopia. Dysmorphic features were noted in many patients, mainly upslanting palpebral fissures, although there was not a consistent recognizable phenotype. Additional common features included hypotonia, hyperextensible joints, ataxia, and kyphosis/scoliosis. Less common features included neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, sacral dimple, syringomyelia, and eye movement abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDBAS in some of the families reported by {1:Fischer-Zirnsak et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. However, mutations occurred de novo in many patients.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 14 patients from 11 unrelated families with NEDBAS, {1:Fischer-Zirnsak et al. (2019)} identified heterozygous mutations in the DLL1 gene (see, e.g., {606582.0001}-{606582.0005}). None of the mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were present in the gnomAD database. All but 1 of the mutations were nonsense, frameshift, or splicing; the 1 missense variant (C179F) occurred at a conserved residue. The mutations occurred throughout the gene, and there were no apparent genotype/phenotype correlations. The variants occurred de novo in 6 patients and were inherited from an affected parent in 4 patients from 2 families; the transmission pattern was unknown in the other 4 individuals. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, except to confirm the splicing defect, but all variants were predicted to result in haploinsufficiency. An additional patient (patient 15) had a de novo deletion encompassing both the DLL1 and FAM120B ({612266}) genes. {1:Fischer-Zirnsak et al. (2019)} noted that DLL1 plays an important role in NOTCH signaling, with a particular role in neuronal differentiation during development of the central nervous system.
