text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with behavioral abnormalities, absent speech, and hypotonia (NEDBASH) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NTNG2 gene ({618689}) on chromosome 9q34.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with behavioral abnormalities, absent speech, and hypotonia (NEDBASH) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severely impaired intellectual and motor development, axial and peripheral hypotonia usually with inability to walk, and significant behavioral abnormalities consistent with autism spectrum disorder and reminiscent of Rett syndrome (RTT; {312750}), such as poor communication, stereotypic or repetitive behaviors, hand-wringing, bruxism, and sleep disturbances. Other features include poor overall growth, and joint hypermobility. Rare features include seizures, dystonia, spasticity, and nonspecific brain abnormalities (summary by {1:Abu-Libdeh et al., 2019} and {2:Dias et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Abu-Libdeh et al. (2019)} reported 8 individuals from 4 consanguineous families of Arab Muslim descent residing in the Jerusalem and Hebron areas with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who ranged in age from 4 to 12 years, presented with global developmental delay between 3 and 6 months of age. The patients had poor overall growth with failure to thrive and small head circumference; 3 had frank microcephaly (-3.2 to -4.1 SD). The affected children were able to sit, although briefly for some, but they had no expressive verbal language, had poor eye contact, and did not use their hands purposefully. Most showed repetitive stereotypies of the hands and bruxism. Other features included truncal and appendicular hypotonia and joint laxity. Brain MRI, when performed, was normal; none of the patients had seizures. Some had minor dysmorphic features, such as beaked nose, pectus excavatum, or fifth finger clinodactyly.

{2:Dias et al. (2019)} reported 16 individuals from 7 unrelated families with NEDBASH. The families were of different ethnic origins, including Turkish, Iranian (Persian, Bakhtiari, Kurdish), Mexican, Egyptian, and Bangladeshi; 5 families were consanguineous. The patients, who ranged in age from 1.25 to 21 years, had global developmental delay with severe to profoundly impaired intellectual development and significant behavioral abnormalities, including autistic features, autism spectrum disorder, hyperactivity, mood disorders, aggression, hand and face stereotypies, sleep disturbances, laughing/screaming spells, anxiety, self-injurious behavior, and bruxism. The behavioral phenotype was reminiscent of Rett syndrome. IQ, assessed in a few patients, ranged from 12 to 30. Most patients were nonambulatory, although a few achieved delayed walking by age 3 years, and all were nonverbal or could only speak a few words. Additional common features included hypotonia in infancy, muscle weakness and atrophy, and hyporeflexia. Some patients had dystonia and/or spasticity, tremor, ataxia, and/or nystagmus. Five patients had seizures associated with abnormal EEG; some were responsive to medication, although 1 patient had poorly controlled myoclonic seizures. Variable dysmorphic features were common, including low-set ears, esotropia, strabismus, frontal bossing, hypotelorism, deep-set eyes, anteverted nares, and downturned mouth. Most had poor overall growth, and gastrointestinal symptoms, such as drooling, constipation, and bloating, were common. Brain imaging, when performed, was usually normal, but some patients had variable and nonspecific abnormalities, including cortical atrophy, enlarged ventricles, cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, poor myelination, and white matter abnormalities.

{3:Heimer et al. (2019)} reported 3 girls from 2 unrelated consanguineous Arab families with a phenotype reminiscent of Rett syndrome. The girls ranged in age from 6.5 to 12 years. They presented in the first months of life with axial and peripheral hypotonia, areflexia, and severe global developmental delay. They were unable to stand or crawl, had poor functional hand use, absent speech, and Rett-like features, including stereotypic midline hand wringing, hand chewing, bruxism, shrieking or laughing episodes, sleep disturbances, and constipation, and were not toilet-trained. Other features included poor overall growth with joint hyperlaxity and dysmorphic features, including brachycephaly, wide forehead, low hairline, sunken eyes, and small, cold hands and feet. All had good visual pursuit with intense eye contact. None of the patients had seizures, and brain imaging was normal.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDBASH in the families reported by {1:Abu-Libdeh et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 8 patients from 4 consanguineous Arab Muslim families with NEDBASH, {1:Abu-Libdeh et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the NTNG2 gene (c.376dupT; {618689.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. Haplotype analysis indicated a founder effect. The mutation was not found in the gnomAD database, but the heterozygous variant was found in 2 of about 3,500 individuals in an in-house database of mainly Arab Muslim individuals. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the variant was predicted to result in a loss of function.

In 16 patients from 7 unrelated families with NEDBASH, {2:Dias et al. (2019)} identified homozygous missense mutations in the NTNG2 gene (see, e.g., {618689.0002}-{618689.0006}). The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts and the GeneMatcher/Matchmaker programs. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. All mutations affected conserved residues in either the laminin-like or EGF domains; none of the mutations were found in the Exome Variant Server or gnomAD databases, or in large in-house databases. Three of the mutations involved cysteine residues putatively involved in disulfide bridge formation. Molecular modeling predicted that these mutations would disrupt a disulfide bridge and have a negative effect on protein stability. Other mutations were predicted to cause protein misfolding. Transfection of all mutations into HeLa cells resulted in variably decreased protein expression at the cell surface compared to wildtype, suggesting a loss-of-function effect. Knockdown of the Ntng2 gene in murine N2A neuronal cells using siRNA resulted in decreased neurite number, decreased neurite length, and decreased dendritic field compared to controls. These findings suggested that appropriate expression of NTNG2 plays an important role in neurodevelopment and possibly synaptic plasticity.

In 3 girls from 2 consanguineous Arab Muslim families with NEDBASH, {3:Heimer et al. (2019)} identified homozygosity for the previously reported c.376dupT mutation in the NTNG2 gene. The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the mutation was predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and a loss of function. Knockdown of Ntng2 in murine primary hippocampal neurons caused reduced neurite length and dendritic arborization compared to controls. The authors noted the significant phenotypic overlap with Rett syndrome, suggesting functional similarities between the NTNG2 and MECP2 ({300005}) genes.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{4:Zhang et al. (2016)} found that Ntng2-null mice had impaired visual, auditory, and motor coordination abilities, as well as reduced anxiety levels and possible spatial learning and memory deficits, compared to wildtype. Cellular studies of mutant mice showed aberrant localization of the postsynaptic Ngl2 receptor, which resulted in abnormal synapse formation and function.

{3:Heimer et al. (2019)} found that shRNA-mediated knockdown of either the Ntng1 ({608818}) or Ntng2 genes in murine embryos resulted in striking neuronal migration defects in the brain, with about 50% of cells failing to reach the cortical plate by postnatal day 1; these deficits remained at postnatal day 7.

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase, mitochondrial gene (GOT2,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-82 (DEE82) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GOT2 gene ({138150}) on chromosome 16q21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-82 (DEE82) is an autosomal recessive mitochondriopathy manifest as early-onset metabolic epileptic encephalopathy. Soon after birth, affected individuals exhibit hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and global developmental delay even before the onset of seizures in the first year of life. The severity is variable, but all patients have severely impaired intellectual development with absent speech and spastic tetraplegia. Other features include poor overall growth with microcephaly and recurrent infections. Brain imaging shows cerebral atrophy, thin corpus callosum, cerebellar hypoplasia, and white matter abnormalities. Laboratory studies show increased serum lactate and ammonia. Importantly, treatment with combined pyridoxine and serine can result in significant improvement in seizures as well as some mild developmental progress (summary by {1:van Karnebeek et al., 2019}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Van Karnebeek et al. (2019)} reported 4 children, ranging in age from 4 to 10 years, from 3 unrelated families with DEE82. Two families were consanguineous and of Egyptian descent, and 1 family was Romanian. The patients presented soon after birth or in the first months of life with feeding difficulties, respiratory insufficiency, drooling, hypotonia, and developmental delay. Patient 1 had abdominal spasms and disturbed sleep. All developed severe and frequent seizures between 4 and 9 months of age. Seizure types included febrile, afebrile, myoclonic, tonic, and generalized tonic-clonic; the seizures were refractory in patients 1 and 4, but could be controlled with antiepileptic medication in patients 2 and 3, who were sisters. The patients had failure to thrive with poor overall growth and progressive microcephaly, and frequent infections. They had severely impaired psychomotor development with profoundly impaired intellectual development, absent speech, and spastic para- or quadriplegia with brisk reflexes. Only 1 patient could walk short distances with support; the other 3 patients were wheelchair-bound. More variable features included nystagmus and scoliosis, and the sisters had acrocyanosis and chilblains in winter. Laboratory investigations showed increased serum lactate and ammonia in all patients; patient 1 also had decreased serine and increased citrulline. Urinary organic acids and acylcarnitines were unremarkable. Brain imaging showed cerebral atrophy and white matter abnormalities in all patients; other findings were enlarged ventricles, thin corpus callosum, and cerebellar vermis atrophy. Patient 1 also had periventricular leukomalacia and multicystic encephalomalacia. Each family had another affected fetus or child who died of the disorder. Treatment with pyridoxine and serine resulted in clinical improvement and amelioration of the seizure frequency (see CLINICAL MANAGEMENT).

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: {1:Van Karnebeek et al. (2019)} found that supplementation with pyridoxine and serine resulted in clinical improvement in 2 patients (patients 1 and 4) with DEE82 confirmed by genetic analysis. Both patients had refractory seizures that could be fully controlled by treatment with both pyridoxine and serine; these patients also made some minor developmental progress.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE82 in the families reported by {1:van Karnebeek et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients from 3 unrelated families with DEE82, {1:van Karnebeek et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the GOT2 gene ({138150.0001}-{138150.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. Three mutations were missense, and 1 was an in-frame deletion of a conserved residue. All mutations occurred at highly conserved residues in the aminotransferase catalytic domain. Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed variably decreased protein levels and activity compared to controls. Patient cells and GOT2-knockdown HEK293 cells had impaired de novo serine synthesis compared to controls, and HEK293 cells also had impaired glycine synthesis; the defects could be rescued by transfection with wildtype GOT2 as well as by supplementation with pyruvate. These findings were interpreted as aiding the pathway of reoxidation of cytosolic NADH by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; {150000}). The authors concluded that defective intracellular redox homeostasis is the underlying basis of the disorder.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Van Karnebeek et al. (2019)} found that mice with GOT2 homozygous mutations found in humans with DEE82 and mice homozygous for a complete loss of Got2 died in utero, consistent with embryonic lethality. Heterozygous mice were viable and healthy. Morpholino knockdown of the got2a gene in zebrafish resulted in variable severity of developmental brain defects, small head, round or bent bodies, deformed tail, and low circulation with pericardial edema, as well as embryonic death. Mutant zebrafish also developed seizure-like episodes with EEG abnormalities in the forebrain. Treatment with pyridoxine and serine, and with pyruvate to a lesser extent, ameliorated the phenotype; pyridoxine and serine had a synergistic effect.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with behavioral abnormalities and craniofacial dysmorphism with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with behavioral abnormalities and craniofacial dysmorphism with or without seizures (IDDBCS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PHF21A gene ({608325}) on chromosome 11p11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Patients with intellectual developmental disorder with behavioral abnormalities and craniofacial dysmorphism with or without seizures (IDDBCS) have impaired intellectual development or developmental delay of varying severity with impaired motor skills and language delay. Macrocephaly, obesity, and overgrowth are frequently seen. Approximately half of patients experience seizures, and neurobehavioral disorders including autism are usually present ({1:Hamanaka et al., 2019}; {2:Kim et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Hamanaka et al. (2019)} reported 3 boys with impaired intellectual development, 2 of whom had macrocephaly and overgrowth. Patient 1, a Japanese boy, was macrosomic and macrocephalic. He developed infantile spasms at age 7 months and at age 18 months was diagnosed with West syndrome due to hypsarrhythmia on EEG. His development was severely delayed; at age 3, he could not understand speech or communicate. He remained macrosomic, and head CT showed metopic synostosis at age 18 months. Dysmorphic features included brachycephaly, frontal bossing, depressed nasal bridge, small nose with anteverted nares, downturned mouth with tented upper lip, and tapering fingers. Patient 2 was a 5-year-old Japanese boy in whom developmental delays were noted after 1 year of age. He walked independently at age 2 years. At evaluation at age 5, he was irritable and hyperactive with features of autism, including head banging, body shaking, and self-injurious behaviors. Smiling and eye contact were absent. The K-form developmental test found moderate to severe deficits in both cognitive-adaptive and language-social areas. Head circumference was at the 90th to 97th percentile, and head CT showed a metopic ridge. Patient 3 was a 9.5-year-old Norwegian boy identified through DECIPHER and referred at age 2 for developmental delay and macrosomia. He had mild hypotonia, decreased balance and coordination, and walked at 18 months of age. Fine motor skills were delayed, but he played rugby and swam daily. He was easily fatigued and required much sleep. Language development was markedly delayed, especially regarding expressive language and articulation. However, the authors commented that at home he spoke 2 languages and had no difficulty with social interactions. Extensive neuropsychological testing showed performance in the severe learning disability/mild intellectual impairment range. Dysmorphic features included macrocephaly, downslanting palpebral fissures, mild hypertelorism, a slightly broad nasal bridge, smooth philtrum, and downturned corners of the mouth. Brain MRI was normal at age 4 years. Due to overgrowth, advanced bone age, and mildly impaired intellectual development, the initial diagnosis considered was Weaver syndrome ({277590}).

{2:Kim et al. (2019)} reported 7 individuals with a syndromic intellectual developmental disorder. The 3 females and 4 males ranged in age from 3 years 4 months to 18 years. All had developmental delay and/or impaired intellectual development with language delay and impaired motor skills. Four of 5 had attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, and/or hypotonia. Two of 7 had macrocephaly. Three of 6 were described as autistic. Four had epilepsy or infantile spasms. Four of 7 were obese; 1 other had height and weight greater than the 97th percentile, and another had height +1 SD and weight +2.5 SD. Of the 7, 3 had tapering fingers, 2 had syndactyly, and 4 had clinodactyly. Six of 7 had variable facial dysmorphisms with no consistent gestalt.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the PHF21A1 gene that were identified in patients with IDDBCS by {1:Hamanaka et al. (2019)} and {2:Kim et al. (2019)} were shown to have occurred de novo in all but one case ({2:Kim et al., 2019}), for whom DNA from both parents could not be obtained.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 children with intellectual developmental disorder and craniofacial anomalies, {1:Hamanaka et al. (2019)} identified heterozygous de novo truncating variants in the PHF21A1 gene ({608325.0001}-{608325.0003}).

{2:Kim et al. (2019)} identified 7 heterozygous coding mutations (e.g., {608325.0002}, {608325.0004}), 6 of which were shown to be de novo, in 7 patients with a syndromic intellectual developmental disorder with craniofacial anomalies and neurobehavioral problems. A C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) was truncated in 6 of the patients, suggesting that this domain may play an important role in PHF21A1 function.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Liang-Wang syndrome (LIWAS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KCNMA1 gene ({600150}), which encodes the BK potassium channel, on chromosome 10q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Liang-Wang syndrome (LIWAS) is a polymalformation syndrome apparent from birth that shows large phenotypic variability and severity. However, all patients have some degree of neurologic dysfunction. The most severely affected individuals have severe global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech, marked craniofacial dysmorphism, and visceral and connective tissue abnormalities affecting the bones and vessels. The least severely affected individuals lack seizures, significant dysmorphism, and visceral involvement; they come to attention for neurologic signs and symptoms, including developmental delay with speech delay, strabismus, and/or ataxia. About half of patients have brain imaging anomalies, notably cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and thin corpus callosum, whereas the other half have normal brain imaging (summary by {1:Liang et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Liang et al. (2019)} reported 3 unrelated patients, aged 3, 12, and 21 years, with a severe multisystem disorder. The patients presented in infancy with global developmental delay and impaired intellectual development, poor speech, delayed walking with ataxia or inability to walk, and axial hypotonia. Two patients had absence seizures, and brain imaging showed cerebellar and cerebral atrophy in only 1 patient. All had similar and significant coarse craniofacial abnormalities, including gingival hypertrophy, synophrys, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, broad nasal root, wide mouth with downturned corners, thin upper lip and everted lower lip, abnormal tongue, frontal hemangioma, and strabismus. One patient also had nystagmus and laryngomalacia. Significant visceral anomalies were also observed in these patients, including intestinal atresia, dilatation, and malrotation, patent ductus arteriosus, and tortuosity of large and medium-sized arteries, including an aortic aneurysm in 1 patient. Two patients had an enlarged bladder. Radiographs also showed bony anomalies, such as bone thickening, abnormal ribs, sclerosis, and dysplasia. All 3 patients carried the same missense mutation in the KCNMA1 gene (G375R; {600150.0007}), suggesting a possible genotype/phenotype correlation.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{1:Liang et al. (2019)} also identified 5 additional unrelated patients with a milder form of Liang-Wang syndrome. These patients, all under 10 years of age, had developmental delay with speech delay, dysarthria or speech dyspraxia, as well as impaired intellectual development; the least impaired patient had an IQ of 85. Other rare variable features in this group of patients included ataxia, tremor, distal hand and foot anomalies, and axial hypotonia. Only 1 patient (patient 9) had severe generalized epilepsy with status epilepticus, and 2 patients had dyskinetic movements: patient 5 had dystonia and patient 7 had torticollis. Brain imaging was abnormal in 3 patients. None had visceral malformations or dysmorphic facial features, although 1 had hypertelorism and another had strabismus with left sensorineural deafness.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the KCNMA1 gene that were identified in patients with LIWAS by {1:Liang et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 unrelated patients with various forms of LIWAS, {1:Liang et al. (2019)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations affecting highly conserved residues in the KCNMA1 gene (see, e.g., {600150.0007}-{600150.0011}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, were not found in multiple public databases, including gnomAD. The mutations occurred throughout the gene and impacted the transmembrane regions, the pore region, and the RCK1 or RCK2 domains. In vitro functional electrophysiologic expression studies in transfected HEK293 cells showed that all the mutations resulted in a loss of the BK potassium current: most (S351Y, G356R, G375R, and I663V) resulted in complete loss of current, whereas others (P805L and D984N) resulted in decreased protein expression and/or decreased channel conductivity compared to wildtype. {1:Liang et al. (2019)} noted that the KCNMA1 gene plays a role not only in neuronal tissues, where it is involved in neurotransmitter release and membrane repolarization, but also in osteoclasts and smooth muscle, which may explain the variable features observed in some of the patients. Noting other reports of homozygous truncating mutations with a slightly different phenotype (CADEDS; {617643}), {1:Liang et al. (2019)} suggested that there may be a difference between truncating variants causing haploinsufficiency and missense variants, with missense variants possibly interfering with other subunits and binding proteins, thus causing a dominant-negative effect.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{3:Sausbier et al. (2004)} developed Bk -/- mice by targeted disruption of the Kcnma1 gene. Mutant mice had normal life expectancy compared with wildtype littermates, but showed obvious ataxia. Very young Bk -/- mice were small, but length and weight became normal at 12 weeks of age. Mutant mice showed moderate vascular dysfunction due to lack of BK channels in vascular smooth muscle. Independent neurologic deficits associated with loss of BK channels included cerebellar dysfunction in the form of abnormal conditioned eye-blink reflex, abnormal locomotion, and pronounced deficiency in motor coordination, likely due to cerebellar learning deficiency. At the cellular level, Bk -/- mice showed a dramatic reduction in spontaneous activity in cerebellar Purkinje neurons due to depolarization-induced inactivation of the action potential mechanism.

{2:Meredith et al. (2004)} obtained Slo -/- mice at an approximately normal mendelian ratio. Slo -/- mice were smaller than wildtype at birth, but they gained normal size by 5 weeks of age. All organs appeared normal in Slo -/- mice, but both male and female Slo -/- mice were subfertile. Slo -/- mice displayed moderate ataxia and showed weak motor performance, coordination, and grip strength compared with wildtype. Motor learning was not impaired. Slo -/- mice demonstrated elevated urination frequency. Slo -/- urinary bladder smooth muscle lacked voltage-activated BK currents and showed enhanced contractility.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cortical malformations, and spasticity

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cortical malformations, and spasticity (NEDMCMS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TMX2 gene ({616715}) on chromosome 11q12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cortical malformations, and spasticity (NEDMCMS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe to profound global developmental delay, early-onset seizures, microcephaly, and polymicrogyria and/or cerebral atrophy on brain imaging. Most affected individuals are unable to walk or speak and have profoundly impaired intellectual development, as well as axial hypotonia and peripheral spasticity. Rare individuals may be less severely affected (summary by {2:Vandervore et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Vandervore et al. (2019)} reported 14 patients from 10 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were gathered through international collaborative networks such as GeneMatcher, and genetic studies were performed by 9 different laboratories. Most patients ranged in age from 1.5 to 13 years, although 2 Puerto Rican sibs (P4 and P5 from family 4) were aged 25 and 28 years at the time of the report. Family 5 was previously reported by {3:Zillhardt et al. (2016)}. Three patients in the report of {2:Vandervore et al. (2019)} had died: 2 in the first weeks of life and the third at age 6 years. Twelve patients (P1-P12) had severe to profound global developmental delay with inability to walk or speak, microcephaly (-2.5 to -6.7 SD), and onset of seizures in infancy or the first years of life. Most, but not all, had drug-resistant epilepsy characterized by apnea, epileptic spasms, myoclonic seizures, focal seizures sometimes with secondary generalization, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Other common features included axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity with hyperreflexia consistent with cerebral palsy, and an overall progressive neurodegenerative disease course. Two unrelated patients (P13 and P14) had a less severe form of the disorder without microcephaly and were able to achieve walking and some language; P14 had normal brain imaging and did not have seizures. Seven of the 12 patients who underwent brain imaging showed cortical malformations, including diffuse polymicrogyria (5 patients), pachygyria (2 patients), and/or cerebral atrophy (5 patients). Postmortem examination, performed on 2 patients, showed extensive unlayered polymicrogyria throughout the cortex and undulating bands of neurons extending deep into the cortex. The transition from normal cortex to polymicrogyric cortex was abrupt, the molecular layer appeared fused between adjacent gyri, and the gray-white matter junction was blurred. Leptomeninges over the abnormal areas was focally thickened. A few patients had nonspecific dysmorphic features, such as hypertelorism, myopia, upslanting palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, wide nasal base, broad nasal bridge, thin upper lip, everted lower lip, widely spaced teeth, gum hypertrophy, and pigeon chest with scoliosis, but there was no overall gestalt.

{1:Ghosh et al. (2020)} reported 8 children from 4 unrelated consanguineous families of Middle Eastern or Central Asian descent (Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Egypt, Kuwait) with NEDMCMS. Two patients had died at 4 and 5 years of age. The patients presented soon after birth with progressive microcephaly (eventually reaching -3 to -4 SD) and achieved almost no developmental milestones. They had spastic tetraplegia with hyperreflexia, were unable to walk, had no fine motor skills, absent language, and profoundly impaired intellectual development with lack of social interaction. All developed refractory generalized tonic-clonic seizures in the first days or weeks of life; EEG showed multifocal spike-wave discharges. Brain imaging, performed in 6 patients, showed lissencephaly, cerebral atrophy with enlarged ventricles, and reduced white matter volume with hypogenesis of the corpus callosum. More variable features included cerebral mantle thickening and cerebellar/brainstem hypoplasia. Dysmorphic features were not noted.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: {2:Vandervore et al. (2019)} and {1:Ghosh et al. (2020)} confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance of NEDMCMS.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 14 patients from 10 unrelated families with NEDMCMS, {2:Vandervore et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the TMX2 gene (see, e.g., {616715.0001}-{616715.0007}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families from whom parental or sib DNA was available. Mutation types included missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splice site, and the mutations were predicted to result in a loss of function. Detailed in vitro functional studies were performed on fibroblasts derived from 2 unrelated patients (P1 and P2; see {616715.0001}-{616715.0003}). Gene ontology analysis using RNA-seq data of these fibroblasts showed differentially expressed genes involved in posttranslational modifications, postsynaptic membrane function, calcium ion channels, and neuronal growth. These patient cells showed impaired mitochondrial respiratory reserve capacity and lower ability to cope with oxidative stress compared to wildtype, which may have resulted from calcium flux. Patient cells also had higher levels of the TMX2 dimer and higher rates of polymerization compared to controls, suggesting that these mutations induce constitutive TMX2 polymerization, mimicking an increased oxidative state. There was no evidence of activation of the ER-stress unfolded protein response.

In 8 affected patients from 4 unrelated consanguineous families of Middle Eastern or Central Asian descent (Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Egypt, Kuwait) with NEDMCMS, {1:Ghosh et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous mutation in the TMX2 gene ({616715.0003}); the variant was the same as one identified by {2:Vandervore et al. (2019)}. Analysis of patient cells showed that TMX2 mRNA levels were reduced to 15 to 50% of controls, suggesting that the mutation affects splicing or mRNA stability, resulting in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Abnormal transcripts were not detected, and additional functional studies were not performed. The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Haplotype analysis did not indicate a common founder, suggesting that the mutation arose independently in the families. The mutation was not found in a control database of 2,397 Middle Eastern individuals. Patient cells showed no evidence of abnormal repeat expansion of C9ORF72 ({614260}), with which TMX2 has been associated.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with brain anomalies and with or without vertebral or cardiac anomalies (NEDBAVC) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the DHX37 gene ({617362}) on chromosome 12q24.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Paine et al. (2019)} reported 5 patients with a neurodevelopmental disorder and brain anomalies with or without vertebral or cardiac anomalies. Patients were ascertained through the Baylor-Hopkins Center for Mendelian Genomics and GeneMatcher. Individual 1, initially reported by {1:Karaca et al. (2015)} as patient BAB4434, had developmental disability (DD) and impaired intellectual development (ID). Brain MRI revealed cortical volume loss, severe dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, colpocephaly, delayed myelination, thickened sulci, polymicrogyria, and cerebellar volume loss. Individual 2 was a 19-year-old Italian woman with asymmetric cerebellar hypoplasia, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, bilateral ophthalmoplegia, and severe scoliosis. She presented at age 5 months with developmental delay and hypotonia. At 6 years, she developed generalized epilepsy and muscle spasms that were only partially controlled. She never walked, could not manipulate objects, and did not have any language. Brain MRI showed hypoplasia of the right cerebellar hemisphere and asymmetric posterior cranial fossa. Orbital MRI showed hypoplasia of extraocular muscles. Visual evoked potentials were markedly altered. Individual 3 was initially identified by ultrasound at 6 weeks' gestation when no heart beat was detected. A perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) and secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) required surgical correction at age 6 months. A skeletal survey showed segmentation anomalies at T3 and L5 and 13 pairs of ribs; the vertebral bodies at C3 and C4 were flattened and dysplastic. The patient had plagiocephaly, facial asymmetry, telecanthus, epicanthal folds, and pectus excavatum. At age 1 year, he was short, with normal head circumference. He was hypotonic, but he could roll over. Abdominal ultrasound showed an intramural thrombus of the inferior vena cava. Individual 4 had been diagnosed with Aicardi syndrome (see {304050}). She was noted to have enlarged brain ventricles in utero. She had infantile spasms, which were not diagnosed until 2 months of age. Brain MRI at 2 days of age showed complete agenesis of the corpus callosum; repeat MRI at 2 months of age showed ventriculomegaly, colpocephaly, cerebellar dysplasia, intracranial cysts, polymicrogyria, and heterotopia. Ophthalmologic examination at age 2 months revealed bilateral chorioretinal lacunae and right optic nerve coloboma. She developed choreoathetosis and silent aspiration requiring gastrostomy tube. At age 4 years and 10 months, she presented with scoliosis involving T8-L4 with a 62 degree angle impacting respiratory function. She had dysmorphic features, including short philtrum, large eyes, anteverted nares, macrodontia, downturned corners of the mouth, protruding ears with abnormal pinna and broad neck. She also had precocious puberty with advanced bone age (bone age of 15 years at age 9 years 5 months). Individual 5 presented at age 15 months with developmental delay and hypotonia; he babbled but had no words and could not yet pull to stand. His growth parameters were at the 10th to 15th percentile. At age 10 years, his delay persisted and he had dysmorphic features including hypertelorism, a pointed chin, midface hypoplasia, tooth agenesis, and hypoplastic nails. He also had Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (see {194200}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: {2:Paine et al. (2019)} confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance of NEDBAVC syndrome.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: By whole-exome sequencing, {1:Karaca et al. (2015)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the DHX37 gene (N419K; {617362.0001}) in a boy with NEDBAVC syndrome. By exome sequencing, {2:Paine et al. (2019)} identified 2 additional patients (individuals 2 and 3) with NEDBAVC who were compound heterozygous for mutations in the DHX37 gene ({617362.0002}-{617362.0005}). In 2 other patients (individuals 4 and 5), {2:Paine et al. (2019)} identified heterozygous mutations in the DHX37 gene; one mutation was proven to be de novo and the other was not found in the patient's mother but no sample from the father was available for study.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Poirier-Bienvenu neurodevelopmental syndrome (POBINDS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CSNK2B gene ({115441}) on chromosome 6p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Poirier-Bienvenu neurodevelopmental syndrome (POBINDS) is a neurologic disorder characterized in most cases by early-onset seizures and variably impaired intellectual development (ID). The severity of neurologic impairment is highly variable: some patients may have refractory seizures and be bedridden with no meaningful speech, whereas others may have treatment-responsive seizures and achieve normal psychomotor development (summary by {1:Li et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Poirier et al. (2017)} reported 2 unrelated male patients, aged 10 and 19 years, with POBINDS. Both had mild early developmental delay with delayed walking and walking difficulties, as well as learning difficulties with significant speech delay. One patient had attention deficit and autistic features, but no seizures. The other patient developed refractory myoclonic epilepsy at 18 months of age; EEG showed generalized spike/wave discharges and slowed background activity. Both patients were noted to have variable dysmorphic features around adolescence, including prognathism, open mouth with protruding tongue, bushy eyebrows, flat philtrum, dental anomalies, strabismus, and downturned corners of the mouth. Brain imaging was normal in the patient without seizures, but showed white matter hyperintensities in the patient with seizures.

{4:Sakaguchi et al. (2017)} reported a 21-month-old Japanese boy with POBINDS. He presented in early infancy with mild developmental delay and daily myoclonus. At age 10 months, he developed complex partial seizures. EEG was consistent with cortical origin of the myoclonus; brain imaging was normal. He was able to speak a few words and walk by himself, but had impaired intellectual development.

{2:Nakashima et al. (2019)} reported 2 unrelated children of Malaysian (patient 3) and Japanese (patient 4) origin with a severe form of POBINDS. Both presented in the first 2 months of life with refractory seizures, including focal, focal evolving to generalized tonic-clonic, and evolution to epileptic encephalopathy in 1 patient. At 15 and 7 years of age, both patients had profoundly impaired global development: they were bedridden with no speech and had not achieved sitting. Brain imaging showed cerebellar atrophy in 1 patient and mega cisterna magna in the other.

{1:Li et al. (2019)} reported 9 unrelated Chinese children, ranging in age from 6 months to 6 years, with POBINDS. All had onset of generalized tonic-clonic seizures before 12 months of age, including 8 with onset before 6 months of age. One patient also had myoclonus. EEG was normal in 5 patients, and brain imaging was normal in 7, whereas 2 patients showed nonspecific poor myelination and enlarged subarachnoid space, respectively, on imaging. Four patients became seizure-free after monotherapy, and 3 became seizure-free with polytherapy. The most severely affected patient (patient 1) was a 6-year-old boy with profoundly impaired ID, inability to walk, and absent language. He had refractory myoclonic and generalized epilepsy with multiple spikes on EEG. By contrast, 4 patients had mildly impaired ID, 1 had moderate ID, and 3 of the 7 patients who became seizure-free had normal intelligence and acquired normal developmental milestones. The findings suggested that impaired intellectual development is a common finding in this disorder, even if seizures are well-controlled.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CSNK2B gene that were identified in patients with POBINDS by {3:Poirier et al. (2017)} and {2:Nakashima et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 unrelated patients with POBINDS, {3:Poirier et al. (2017)} identified de novo heterozygous splice site mutations in the CSNK2B gene ({115441.0001} and {115441.0002}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not found in the 1000 Genomes Project or ExAC databases. Analysis of patient cells showed decreased mRNA levels compared to controls, and RT-PCR showed that the mutations resulted in exon skipping and premature termination, consistent with haploinsufficiency and a loss of function. However, the authors noted that the mutations may induce the production of an aberrant truncated protein. {3:Poirier et al. (2017)} postulated that the mutations may cause abnormal dopamine signaling.

In a 21-month-old Japanese boy with POBINDS, {4:Sakaguchi et al. (2017)} identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation in the CSNK2B gene ({115441.0003}). The mutation was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the variant was predicted to result in haploinsufficiency.

In a 15-year-old Malaysian girl (patient 3) with POBINDS, {2:Nakashima et al. (2019)} identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation in the CSNK2B gene ({115441.0004}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was classified as pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines. Transfection of the mutation into HEK293 cells showed that the mutant protein was expressed, but was unable to bind with CSNK2A1 ({115440}), which may induce instability of the CK2 holoenzyme. A missense variant (H165R) at a highly conserved residue was identified in another unrelated patient (patient 4) with a similar disorder, but limited functional studies did not indicate a pathogenic effect, and the variant was classified as 'likely pathogenic' according to ACMG guidelines.

In 9 unrelated patients with POBINDS, {1:Li et al. (2019)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the CSNK2B gene (see, e.g., {115441.0005}-{115441.0007}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing of a cohort of 816 probands with epilepsy, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The mutations occurred throughout the gene and comprised 4 missense variants, 3 frameshifts, and 1 splice site mutation. None of the variants were found in the 1000 Genomes Project or gnomAD databases; all were predicted to be pathogenic (8) or likely pathogenic (1) by ACMG criteria, but only 4 had predictive evidence of 'very strong' pathogenicity. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. Five variants occurred in the zinc-binding domain, suggesting a hotspot; patients with these variants responded to antiepileptic treatment. However, patients with missense mutations could have a severe phenotype and those with frameshift mutations could have a mild phenotype, precluding establishment of a definitive genotype/phenotype correlation.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neuromuscular disease and ocular or auditory anomalies with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neuromuscular oculoauditory syndrome (NMOAS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the DHX16 gene ({603405}) on chromosome 6p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neuromuscular oculoauditory syndrome (NMOAS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder with variable features including hypotonia, nonspecific developmental delay, and ear deformity or sensorineural deafness. Features may be reminiscent of Aicardi syndrome (see {304050}), with chorioretinal lacunae, infantile spasms, and agenesis of the corpus callosum ({1:Paine et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Paine et al. (2019)} reported 4 patients with a neuromuscular syndrome. The first patient (individual 6) presented at age 10 weeks with infantile spasms following an uneventful birth. Brain MRI at age 2 months showed agenesis of the corpus callosum and subependymal heterotopia. At age 5 months, her head circumference was at the 10th to 25th percentile and she had hypotonia, poor head control, poor visual tracking, and slow social smile. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed chorioretinal lacunae and areas of depigmentation around the optic nerve. She was given a clinical diagnosis of Aicardi syndrome (see {304050}). The second patient (individual 7) was delivered by emergency cesarean section at 32 weeks' gestation due to nonreassuring fetal heart tones. Her birth length was at the 5th percentile and her limbs appeared short. She had bilateral epicanthal folds and posteriorly rotated, simple auricles. Brain ultrasound was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged kidneys with poor corticomedullary differentiation and multiple cysts. She died 16 days after birth. No autopsy was performed. The third patient (individual 8) presented with severe congenital hypotonia, bilateral talipes equinovarus, and flexion contractures of the hands and knees. He suffered poor postnatal growth and required nasogastric feeding. He had recurrent choking and aspiration of oral secretions. He had diminished nerve conduction velocities and absent sensory nerve action potentials confirming an axonal sensory and denervating motor neuropathy as well as sensorineural deafness. He also manifested a high-frequency, low-amplitude horizontal nystagmus. Brain MRI was normal. At age 4 months, he was admitted to hospital in respiratory failure in the setting of coronavirus and died despite intensive care. Autopsy revealed normal central cerebral myelination, and in the sural nerve, a paucity of large myelinated axons rimmed only by thin myelin sheaths or completely lacking myelin with atrophic myofibers in the quadriceps. The fourth patient (individual 9) presented at age 10 months with a febrile seizure, which recurred at 15 and 17 months. He could stand without support at 11 months and walked at 13 months. By 20 months, he had an unsteady gait and hypertrophic calf muscles and then stopped walking. Creatine kinase was normal and a muscle biopsy showed myopathy with atrophy of type I fibers and mild signs of inflammation. He was diagnosed with myositis, which was treated with cortisol. At age 4 years, he developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures. At age 5, his gait was broad-based and ataxic; he could not jump and had no deep tendon reflexes. Repeat muscle biopsies showed degenerative myopathy. Ophthalmologic evaluation at age 7 showed pale pupils, shrunken vessels, and pigmentary changes. Neurophysiologic investigation showed extensive myopathic changes on EMG and pathologic visual and auditory evoked potentials; the EEG showed severe signs of generalized and multifocally diminished seizure threshold. At age 9 years, sensorineural deafness was diagnosed but IQ was normal. Vision progressively deteriorated. At age 34 years, he was wheelchair-bound, blind, deaf, and seizure-free.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the DHX16 gene that were identified in patients with NMOAS by {1:Paine et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: By trio exome sequencing, {1:Paine et al. (2019)} identified heterozygous de novo mutations in the DHX16 gene ({603405.0001}-{603405.0004}) in 4 unrelated patients with NMOAS. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation in 2 families. The mutations were not found in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. No functional studies were reported.

phenotypes.phenotype: Pachygyria, microcephaly, developmental delay, and dysmorphic facies, with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations-15 (CDCBM15) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TUBGCP2 gene ({617817}) on chromosome 10q26.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations-15 (CDCBM15) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by progressive microcephaly associated with abnormal facial features, hypotonia, and variable global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development. Brain imaging shows variable malformation of cortical development on the lissencephaly spectrum, mainly pachygyria and thin corpus callosum (summary by {2:Mitani et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of CDCBM, see CDCBM1 ({614039}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Mitani et al. (2019)} reported 5 children, ranging in age from 3 to 7 years, from 4 unrelated families with CDCBM15. Two of the families, of Turkish (family 1) and Iranian (family 3) descent, were consanguineous; the other 2 families, of Indian (family 2) and Polish (family 4) descent, were not consanguineous. Two individuals from families 2 and 3 were born prematurely at 31 and 27 weeks' gestation, respectively, and died around 3 years of age. All patients presented in infancy with hypotonia, global developmental delay with delayed walking, progressive microcephaly (down to -5.5 SD in 3 living patients and down to -9.0 SD in one of the premature infants who later died). All had similar dysmorphic features, including narrow or sloped forehead, up- or downslanting palpebral fissures, thick eyebrows, bulbous nose, prominent ears, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, thick lips, and retro/micrognathia. Four patients had generalized seizures and/or abnormal EEG suggestive of seizures. They had variably impaired intellectual development with poor or absent language. However, the least affected individual, who did not have seizures and had normal motor development, was able to attend a regular school with special help at age 7. Variable ocular anomalies were noted in the 4 more severely impaired patients, including cortical blindness, astigmatism, myopia, and optic atrophy. Brain imaging in all 5 patients showed features consistent with malformations of cortical development, including pachygyria (5/5), thin corpus callosum (4/5), cerebellar volume loss (3/5), subcortical band heterotopia (2/5), delayed myelination (2/5), and thin brainstem (2/5). The 2 patients born prematurely had additional imaging anomalies, including subependymal cysts and periventricular leukomalacia, that may have been related to prematurity. One of the patients from family 1, who had a more severe phenotype with some additional features, including pectus excavatum, broad toes, widely spaced teeth, and autistic behavior, also carried a de novo duplication of 2q23.1 (see {156200}), consistent with a dual genetic diagnosis.

{1:Gungor et al. (2021)} reported 2 sibs with CDCBM15, who were born to first-cousin Turkish parents. The older sib, a 10-year-old girl, presented with severe developmental delay, hypotonia, and intractable epilepsy at the age of 6 months and lost all motor and cognitive abilities by age 4 years. Dysmorphic features included narrow forehead, thick eyebrows, bulbous nose, prominent ears, widely spaced teeth, retrognathia, and maxillary hypoplasia. Neurologic exam showed microcephaly, atrophy and contractures of the extremities with brisk reflexes and spasticity. Brain MRI showed pachygyria, cerebellar parenchymal atrophy, bilateral volume loss in cerebral white matter, cystic foci with increased intensity in neighboring white matter, and thinning of the corpus callosum. Her affected 8-year-old brother had normal developmental milestones until the age of 8 months when developmental delay was noted. At age 3 years, he began to have intractable seizures. Neurologic exam at age 8 years showed microcephaly, atrophy and contractures of the extremities, increased reflexes, and spasticity. Brain MRI showed cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, decreased white matter volumes, cystic foci with neighboring hyperintensities at the centrum semiovale, and thin corpus callosum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDCBM15 in the families reported by {2:Mitani et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 4 unrelated patients with CDCBM15, {2:Mitani et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the TUBGCP2 gene ({617817.0001}-{617817.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts and GeneMatcher. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but analysis of patient fibroblasts derived from the patient with a splice site mutation demonstrated the production of several abnormal transcripts that were predicted to result in a loss of function. The 3 other variants, all missense, occurred at highly conserved residues in the important Grip1 and Grip2 ({621438}) functional domains. The authors hypothesized that the role of TUBGCP2 in microtubules could explain neuronal migration abnormalities observed in these patients.

In 2 sibs with CDCBM15, who were born to first-cousin Turkish parents, {1:Gungor et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous mutation in the TUBGCP2 gene (E311K; {617817.0005}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was present in heterozygous state in the parents and a healthy sib. The variant was not present in the gnomAD database or in a cohort of 1,182 Turkish controls. The variant, which is predicted to disrupt the electrostatic interaction between the GCP2 and GCP3 proteins, was shown not to affect GCP2 protein levels, but a delocalization of gamma-tubulin was noted. Using mass spectrometry, dysregulation of multiple proteins that are important to the development and maintenance of the nervous system was noted. {1:Gungor et al. (2021)} stated that these results suggest that axon and neurite outgrowth/elongation might also be altered, along with perturbed neuronal differentiation, migration, and synaptic plasticity. In addition, the results could explain the findings of brainstem atrophy and disturbed myelination seen in some patients as well as abnormalities in neuronal migration.

Caused by mutation in the trafficking protein particle complex, subunit 4 gene (TRAPPC4,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, spasticity, and brain atrophy

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, spasticity, and brain atrophy (NEDESBA) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TRAPPC4 gene ({610971}) on chromosome 11q23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, spasticity, and brain atrophy (NEDESBA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severely impaired global development apparent soon after birth. Affected individuals develop seizures in the first year of life and achieve almost no psychomotor progress, resulting in feeding difficulties and an inability to walk or speak. Other features include hypotonia, peripheral spasticity with contractures, cortical visual impairment, and dysmorphic features, including microcephaly. Death in childhood may occur (summary by {5:Van Bergen et al., 2020}).

{5:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} noted that the molecular mechanism of this disorder can be classified into a group of similar phenotypes resulting from mutations in genes associated with transport protein particles, sometimes referred to as 'TRAPPopathies' (review by {4:Sacher et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{5:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} reported 8 children from 3 unrelated families of Caucasian, Turkish, and French-Canadian descent with a similar syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Four of the patients died in the first years of life. The remaining patients, who ranged in age from 17 months to 17 years, had a severe phenotype with hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, almost no psychomotor development, and inability to walk or speak. They had severe feeding difficulties, necessitating tube-feeding in most. Symptom onset was soon after birth, when delayed milestones were first observed. All developed early-onset seizures of various types within the first year of life, which were often associated with EEG abnormalities, such as slow background and multifocal epileptic discharges. Most had cortical visual impairment and/or poor visual tracking, and 2 also had impaired hearing. All had dysmorphic features, including microcephaly (down to -7 SD), bitemporal narrowing, full cheeks, prominent nasal tip, long philtrum, wide open mouth with thin tented upper lip, and pointed chin. More variable features included progressive scoliosis, contractures, congenital hip dislocation, osteopenia, abnormal dentition, dystonia, and tremor. Brain imaging, performed in 4 patients, showed progressive cortical and cerebellar atrophy. There was no evidence of iron deposition.

{1:Ghosh et al. (2021)} reported 23 patients from 17 unrelated families. who developed a severe and progressive encephalopathy with developmental stagnation in the first few months of life. Some of the patients also had psychomotor regression. The patients all developed microcephaly and all developed seizures in the first 6 months of life. Neurologic examination in the patients showed spastic tetraplegia and hyperreflexia in all patients, and abnormal movements including ataxia and dystonia in some patients. Three patients had bilateral cataracts, and visual pursuits were absent in all patients. Two patients had hearing loss. Brain MRI demonstrated cerebral atrophy in all patients. In many patients, MRI also demonstrated white matter loss, ventriculomegaly, and cerebellar atrophy. Facial dysmorphisms in the patient cohort included bitemporal narrowing, thick eyebrows, full cheeks, a long philtrum, wide mouth, thick and tented upper lip, and pointed chin.

{2:Kaur et al. (2020)} reported a 1 year 7 month old girl, born to parents of Indian descent, with progressive encephalopathy consistent with NEDESBA. Findings included growth delay and microcephaly, bitemporal narrowing, prominent nasal tip, full cheeks, long philtrum, tented and thin upper lip, open and wide mouth, and pointed chin. She had progressive dystonia and spasticity in all 4 limbs and clonus. Brain imaging at 6 months of age showed significant cerebral atrophy, white matter volume loss, and thinning of the corpus callosum. Hearing testing was unremarkable and eye examination showed the possibility of cortical visual impairment. She was noted at age 1 year 7 months to have markedly elevated plasma lactate and creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels, suggesting muscle involvement. At 2 years 3 months of age, her CPK levels were lower, leading the authors to suggest the possibility of episodic rhabdomyolysis.

{3:Majethia et al. (2022)} reported 3 children from 2 unrelated families of Indian descent with NEDESBA. The child from the first family had a classic clinical presentation, whereas the 2 children in the second family had a milder phenotype with later onset. The first child was noted to have delayed crying and regurgitation of feeds in the newborn period, with developmental delay, growth delay, and microcephaly noted at age 8 months. He had marked spasticity in all limbs, and hearing response was nonrecordable bilaterally. Ophthalmologic examination was unremarkable. Brain MRI showed delayed myelination, dilated ventricles, thin corpus callosum, cerebral atrophy, and white matter volume loss. Creatine phosphokinase and serum lactate levels were elevated at 8 months of age. At 1 year of age, the child had a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure. On evaluation at 14 months, he had failure to thrive, dystonia, spasticity, and brisk deep tendon reflexes. The 2 brothers in the second family, age 15 and 10 years, attained age-appropriate motor milestones, but speech delay was noted by age 3 years. They had generalized tonic-clonic seizures at 7 years of age. Motor regression with abnormal movements and unsteadiness of gait was noted in the older sib and behavior abnormalities (e.g., aggression and hyperactivity) were noted in the younger sib. Growth delay and microcephaly were noted in both sibs, but was more mild than that seen in previously reported patients. Facies were nondysmorphic. CPK levels were found to be elevated in one of the brothers at age 10 years. Brain MRI of the younger sib showed mildly prominent ventricles, mild cerebral atrophy, white matter volume loss, and subtle hyperintensities in the periventricular white matter.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDESBA in the families reported by {5:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 7 children from 3 unrelated families with NEDESBA, {5:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the TRAPPC4 gene ({610971.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. It was found at a low frequency (0.0002419) in only heterozygous state in the gnomAD database. Analysis of fibroblasts derived from 1 patient confirmed the splicing defect, and Western blot analysis showed some production of the wildtype protein, but at significantly decreased levels compared to controls; a truncated protein was not detected, consistent with nonsense-mediated mRNA decay of the mutant transcript. Fibroblasts derived from 1 patient showed overall decreased levels of fully-assembled TRAPP complexes compared to controls. Haplotype analysis was not consistent with a founder effect, but rather suggested a mutational hotspot. Detailed functional studies of patient fibroblasts showed ER/Golgi secretory defects that could be rescued by transfection of wildtype TRAPPC4, as well as defects in autophagy and autophagosome formation. Similar defects, including decreased levels of the assembled TRAPP complex and secretion and autophagy defects, were observed in a yeast trs23 temperature-sensitive mutant with decreased levels of the Trappc4 ortholog. The findings suggested that the pleiotropic effects of the phenotype resulted from defects in both cellular trafficking and autophagy. ({6:Van Bergen (2020)} noted that several errors appeared in the pedigrees in Figure 2A of their article; correct information appears in their Supplementary Table 1. One of the deceased patients in Family 2 (2-II-1) is not listed in Supplementary Table 1 because DNA from this patient was not available for testing.)

In 23 patients from 17 unrelated families with NEDESBA, {1:Ghosh et al. (2021)} identified homozygosity for the recurrent splice site mutation in the TRAPPC4 gene (c.454+3A-G; {610971.0001}) that had previously been identified by {5:Van Bergen et al. (2020)}. The mutation was identified by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing. RNA sequencing in skin fibroblasts from 1 patient (patient 15) revealed partial exon 3 skipping of TRAPPC4 due to use of a cryptic splice donor site, which was predicted to result in a premature stop and nonsense-mediated decay. {1:Ghosh et al. (2021)} reported that the c.454+3A-G mutation was relatively common across populations worldwide, and that it was unlikely that the variant was derived from a shared common ancestor because a shared haplotype was not identified.

In a girl, born of Indian parents without reported consanguinity, with neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, spasticity, and brain atrophy, {2:Kaur et al. (2020)} identified homozygosity for the c.454+3A-G mutation in exon 3 of the TRAPPC4 gene. The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing, was present in heterozygous state in the parents. The variant was not present in an in-house exome sequencing database of 693 individuals. Autozygosity mapping demonstrated a 123-Mb region of homozygosity by descent, with the variant found in a 2.24 Mb region of homozygosity.

In 3 children with NEDESBA from 2 unrelated families of Indian descent, {3:Majethia et al. (2022)} identified homozygosity for missense mutations in the TRAPPC4 gene (L64P, {610971.0002}; P93L, {610971.0003}). Parents in both families were heterozygous for the variant.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-83 (DEE83) is caused by homozygous mutation in the UGP2 gene ({191760}) on chromosome 2p14.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-83 (DEE83) is a severe autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by onset of frequent seizures in the first days to months of life that are usually refractory to medical treatment and are associated with significant EEG abnormalities. Affected individuals have profoundly impaired development, with no motor or language skill acquisition, poor or absent visual tracking, and poor oromotor function necessitating tube feeding. Many patients die in the first years of life (summary by {1:Perenthaler et al., 2020}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Perenthaler et al. (2020)} reported 20 children from 13 unrelated families with DEE83. Most children were under age 3.5 years, although 4 patients ranged in age from 6 to 13 years. Of the 20 children, 11 died between 2 months and 13 years of age. In addition, there were at least 7 deceased, similarly affected sibs of the patients who were not available for study. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts and the GeneMatcher database; most of the families were consanguineous. The affected infants presented in the first days, weeks, or months of life with frequent, usually multiple daily, seizures that were mostly refractory to treatment. The seizures were associated with significant EEG abnormalities, including multifocal discharges, generalized spike-wave discharges, and polyspike discharges. Some patients showed hypsarrhythmia on EEG, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of West syndrome. All patients had profoundly impaired global development with head lag, inability to roll over or sit, absent speech, poor or absent visual tracking, and severe oromotor hypotonia necessitating tube feeding. They had axial hypotonia with peripheral spasticity and/or hyperreflexia, and a few had dystonia. Ocular anomalies, such as hypermetropia, foveal hypoplasia, and pale optic discs, were sometimes observed; nystagmus was uncommon. Other features included constipation and recurrent infections, mainly respiratory. Variable dysmorphic features were sometimes observed and included microcephaly or small head circumference, sloping forehead, elongated head, high anterior hairline, arched eyebrows, flat nasal bridge, low-set ears, prominent philtrum, small mouth, and brachydactyly or genu valgum. However, dysmorphic features were not present in many of the patients. Brain imaging, performed in most patients, showed nonspecific generalized anomalies, such as cortical, cerebral, and cerebellar atrophy, delayed myelination, reduced white matter, and thin corpus callosum. Two other patients with a similar phenotype from 2 additional unrelated families were reported, but detailed clinical features were not provided.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE83 in the families reported by {1:Perenthaler et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 20 patients from 13 unrelated families with DEE83, {1:Perenthaler et al. (2020)} identified the same homozygous c.34A-G transition at a highly conserved nucleotide in the UGP2 gene ({191760.0001}). The mutation was predicted to result in a met12-to-val (M12V) substitution in the longer isoform (isoform 1) and to disrupt a translational start site (c.1A-G) in the shorter isoform (isoform 2), which is highly expressed in brain and neural stem cells. The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. The variant was not present in several large control databases, including the Exome Variant Server and Iranone databases, but was found at a low frequency (5.3 x 10(-5)) in only heterozygous state in the gnomAD database (15 of 280,902 alleles). Western blot analysis of fibroblasts from 1 patient showed absent expression of the UGP2 short isoform, with upregulation of the long isoform harboring the M12V substitution. Whereas the 2 isoforms were equally expressed in wildtype fibroblasts, the expression of the shorter isoform was diminished to 25% of total UGP2 in heterozygous patients. These findings indicated that the long isoform carrying the M12V variant is upregulated when the short isoform is missing. The M12V long isoform showed normal cellular localization and enzymatic activity in patient cells, which may explain the survival of the patients. In vitro functional cellular expression studies showed that expression of the mutation in the short UGP2 isoform and complete knockdown of the short UGP2 isoform in human embryonic stem cells resulted in disrupted programmed differentiation into neural cells. Transcriptome analysis of the mutant cells showed a signature suggesting a tendency to differentiate prematurely, as well as changes in the expression of several specific genes implicated in pathways involved in neurodevelopmental disorders. The metabolic profile of mutant cells was also abnormal, showing reduced ability to produce UDP-glucose and synthesize glycogen, impaired protein glycosylation, and increased activation of the unfolded protein response. These defects could be restored by expression of wildtype UGP2. {1:Perenthaler et al. (2020)} concluded that disruption of the brain-specific UGP2 isoform resulted in the neurologic phenotype with viability of the patients. The authors further suggested that total loss of function or complete absence of UGP2 in all cells would be embryonic lethal. The findings highlighted the emerging role of tissue-specific isoforms as a disease mechanism in genetic disorders.

populationGenetics.title: Population Genetics
populationGenetics.content: The families with DEE83 reported by {1:Perenthaler et al. (2020)} were of Middle Eastern descent, including Pakistani, Iranian, Saudi Arabian, Indian, and Omani, and haplotype analysis of several individuals suggested a founder effect. Although 1 family (family 1) was Dutch, the authors noted that Dutch traders settled in the region around Balochistan in the 17th century. The mutation was estimated to have originated about 26 generations or 600 years ago.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Perenthaler et al. (2020)} found that knockdown of zebrafish UGP2 orthologs resulted in decreased ability to produce UDP-glucose, reduced global neural activity, abnormal movements, decreased spontaneous visual movements, and possibly increased susceptibility to seizures.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with hypotonia and behavioral abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with hypotonia and behavioral abnormalities (IDDHBA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CDK8 gene ({603184}) on chromosome 13q12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with hypotonia and behavioral abnormalities (IDDHBA) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by onset of hypotonia and variably impaired global developmental delay in infancy. Affected individuals tend to have learning disability, usually requiring special schooling, as well as behavioral abnormalities, such as autistic features and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Additional more variable features may include nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, congenital heart defects, visual or ocular movement anomalies, and poor feeding and/or gastroesophageal reflux (summary by {1:Calpena et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Calpena et al. (2019)} reported 12 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 6 months to 16 years, with IDDHBA. Soon after birth or during early infancy, the patients presented with hypotonia, feeding difficulties with episodic vomiting, sometimes requiring tube feeding, and global developmental delay. Six patients had congenital heart defects, including septal defects, valvular anomalies, hypoplastic aortic arch or coarctation, and tetralogy of Fallot. A few patients needed cardiac surgery soon after birth. The patients had delayed motor development with delayed walking, speech delay, and impaired intellectual development ranging from mild to severe. The IQ of patient 3 at age 8 years was 55, and most patients had concurrent diagnoses of autism and/or ADHD as well as other behavioral anomalies, although most were able to attend special schooling; patient 11 attended a mainstream school at age 7. Only 2 patients had well-controlled seizures, and 3 had sensorineural hearing loss. Ocular anomalies, such as strabismus, exotropia, ptosis, and nystagmus, and impaired vision, were often observed. Brain imaging, performed in 9, was normal in 4 patients, but showed agenesis or thin corpus callosum in 4 others; 1 patient had hippocampal asymmetry. Most patients had dysmorphic features, although there was not a common gestalt: these included brachycephaly, arched eyebrows, epicanthal folds, prominent eyes, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, low-set or prominent ears, prognathism, long philtrum or columella, broad nasal base with small tip, wide or open mouth, and mild distal anomalies of the hands and feet, such as broad thumbs, hypoplastic phalanges, planovalgus feet, and joint hypermobility.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CDK8 gene that were identified in patients with IDDHBA by {1:Calpena et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 12 unrelated patients with IDDHBA, {1:Calpena et al. (2019)} identified 8 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the CDK8 gene (see, e.g., {603184.0001}-{603184.0005}). The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts, and the mutations were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing. All the variants occurred at highly conserved residues in the functional kinase domain, and none were present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies in transfected human colorectal cancer cells (SW620) showed that all the mutations strongly attenuated CDK8 kinase activity toward STAT1 ({600555}) compared to controls, consistent with a specific loss-of-function effect; 2 variants retained partial activity. All of the variants were able to bind ATP and cyclin C. Studies of patient cells were not performed. {1:Calpena et al. (2019)} concluded that haploinsufficiency was an unlikely disease mechanism, and they postulated a dominant-negative effect. However, there was no reduction in CDK8 phosphorylation activity when the S62L mutation ({603184.0001}) was mixed with wildtype CDK8.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA AND AUTISTIC FEATURES WITH OR WITHOUT HYPERKINETIC MOVEMENTS; NEDHAHM
