text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that genitourinary and/or brain malformation syndrome (GUBS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PPP1R12A gene ({602021}) on chromosome 12q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Genitourinary and/or brain malformation syndrome (GUBS) is characterized by variable genitourinary anomalies, including disorders of sex differentiation, and brain abnormalities ranging from agenesis of the corpus callosum to anencephaly. Other variable congenital anomalies have been observed, including omphalocele and gastrointestinal tract atresia with aberrant vessels ({1:Hughes et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Hughes et al. (2020)} reported 12 unrelated individuals with genitourinary and/or brain malformations and mutations in the PPP1R12A gene. Midline brain malformations were present in 5 patients, with 2 exhibiting holoprosencephaly; the most severe brain finding was anencephaly. Genitourinary anomalies were observed in 9 patients, including 4 who were 46,XY individuals with female external genitalia. Three patients showed both brain and genitourinary anomalies. Patients exhibited a wide spectrum of genitourinary phenotypes, ranging from partial gonadal dysgenesis with micropenis, hypospadias, and ambiguous genitals with Mullerian duct remnants, to complete gonadal dysgenesis in a genotypic 46,XY individual with female external genitalia. Other congenital anomalies included omphalocele, jejunal and ileal atresia with aberrant mesenteric blood supply, and syndactyly. Noting that all 9 of the 46,XY individuals had urogenital anomalies, including 3 who also exhibited brain abnormalities, whereas the 3 patients who were 46,XX only showed severe brain anomalies, the authors suggested a possible sex-influenced mechanism. However, 2 of the 46,XX patients were 'not evaluated' for genitourinary malformations; in the third 46,XX individual, genitourinary malformation was listed as 'not described on autopsy'; and 3 of the 46,XY patients were 'not evaluated' for brain malformations.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the PPP1R12A gene that were identified in affected members of the families with GUBS reported by {1:Hughes et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 12 unrelated patients with genitourinary and/or brain malformations, {1:Hughes et al. (2020)} identified heterozygosity for de novo premature termination codon (PTC) variants in the PPP1R12A gene (see, e.g., {602021.0001}-{602021.0003}). The authors noted that the patients exhibited a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, and that the PPP1R12A variants occurred across multiple exons and 1 intron, with no clear genotype-phenotype correlation observed with specific variants.

preferredTitle: BASAL GANGLIA CALCIFICATION, IDIOPATHIC, 8, AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE; IBGC8
clinicalSynopsis: Onset of symptoms usually in adulthood
Caused by mutation in the junctional adhesion molecule 2 gene (JAM2,)

Miscellaneous: Onset of symptoms usually in adulthood
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the junctional adhesion molecule 2 gene (JAM2,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Basal ganglia calcification, idiopathic, 8, autosomal recessive

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive idiopathic basal ganglia calcification-8 (IBGC8) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the JAM2 gene ({606870}) on chromosome 21q21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal recessive idiopathic basal ganglia calcification-8 (IBGC8) is a progressive neurologic disorder with insidious onset of motor symptoms in adulthood. Affected individuals develop gait difficulties, parkinsonism, pyramidal signs, and dysarthria. Some may demonstrate cognitive decline or memory impairment. Brain imaging shows extensive calcifications in various brain regions including the basal ganglia, thalamus, and cerebellum. Because serum calcium and phosphate are normal, the disorder is thought to result from defects in the integrity of the neurovascular unit in the brain (summary by {2:Schottlaender et al., 2020}).

For a phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of IBGC, see IBGC1 ({213600}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Cen et al. (2020)} reported 4 patients from 3 unrelated Chinese families, 2 of which were consanguineous, with IBGC8. Family 1 had previously been reported by {3:Wang et al. (2015)}. The patients, who ranged in age from 35 to 50 years, presented in their twenties or thirties with insidious onset of slowly progressive dysarthria, slurred speech, and parkinsonism, including bradykinesia, rigidity, and dystonic gait. One patient had onset of tonic-clonic seizures at age 8 months, but the seizures were mostly controlled by medication. Brain imaging in all patients showed severe calcifications in the cerebral cortex, as well as extensive calcifications in multiple additional brain regions, including the lenticular and caudate nuclei, thalamus, and cerebellar hemispheres. Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid levels were normal.

{2:Schottlaender et al. (2020)} reported 7 patients from 4 unrelated families with IBGC8. Three families, including 2 large consanguineous families from Traveller communities in England and Northern Ireland (families 1 and 2), and a nonconsanguineous family from the US (family 3), were identified using the GeneMatcher program. The fourth patient was a singleton from a consanguineous Turkish family (family 4). Family 2 had 4 affected individuals who ranged in age from 39 to 49 years, whereas the other 3 unrelated patients were aged 24, 15, and 7 years. The age at symptom onset ranged from early childhood to the late thirties, although most had onset of significant symptoms as adults. Initial symptoms included progressive walking difficulties, coordination problems, ataxia, severe depression, cognitive decline, and dysarthria. The older individuals had pyramidal signs with increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses, extrapyramidal features, and parkinsonism with bradykinesia, rigidity, bradykinesia, and hypomimia. These patients also had ophthalmoplegia and/or gaze palsies, abnormal visual pursuit with saccadic intrusions, and limb dystonia, as well as orofacial dyskinesia with poor tongue control and dysphagia, requiring feeding tube placement in 2. The proband in family 2 died in his late forties. Most patients had cognitive involvement, including 3 with severe cognitive decline, 1 with memory decline, and 1 with progressive impaired intellectual development and autism spectrum disorder. The 7-year-old presented with seizures at age 18 months, but these were well-controlled and she showed normal intellectual development with no neurologic signs; the disorder in that patient was found by brain imaging and confirmed by genetic testing. Brain imaging in all patients showed significant calcifications in the basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum, and deep gray matter.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IBGC8 in the families reported by {1:Cen et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 4 patients from 3 unrelated Chinese families with IBGC8, {1:Cen et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the JAM2 gene ({606870.0001}-{606870.0004}). The mutation in the first family, which was consanguineous, was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Mutations in the subsequent 2 unrelated patients were found by Sanger sequencing of the JAM2 gene in a cohort of 398 probands with a similar disorder. The mutations, which segregated in the families in the available parental DNA, were not found in the gnomAD database. Two mutations resulted in a complete loss of function, as demonstrated by lack of protein expression in transfected CHO cells, whereas 2 mutations were expressed but were predicted to interfere with proper protein function. The authors speculated that the mutations impaired cell-cell adhesion functions and reduced integrity of the neurovascular unit in the brain.

In 7 patients from 4 unrelated families with IBGC8, {2:Schottlaender et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the JAM2 gene ({606870.0005}-{606870.0008}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the 3 families from whom parental DNA was available. Studies of patient cells with a homozygous nonsense mutation (R229X) showed a reduction of mutant mRNA compared to controls, consistent with nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, and absence of the JAM2 protein, consistent with a loss of function. The authors hypothesized that the mutations caused defects in cell-to-cell adhesion and dysfunction of the movement of solutes in the neurovascular unit in the brain, resulting in the disorder.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Schottlaender et al. (2020)} found that Jam2-null mice developed age-dependent significant walking and gait abnormalities compared to controls. Neuropathologic brain analysis showed age-dependent progressive prominent vacuolization in the midbrain, thalamus, and cerebral and cerebellar cortices. These changes were associated with reactive astrogliosis, microglial activation, and a reduced neuronal density. Similar findings were observed in spinal cord sections. However, there was no evidence of mineralization or calcification in the brain or spinal cord of mutant mice.

preferredTitle: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER, AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT 63, WITH MACROCEPHALY; MRD63
clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, moderate to severe
Caused by mutation in the triple functional domain gene (TRIO,)

Head: Macrocephaly (+2 to +4.7 SD) (in most patients)
Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, moderate to severe
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the triple functional domain gene (TRIO,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal dominant 63, with macrocephaly

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-63 with macrocephaly (MRD63) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TRIO gene ({601893}) on chromosome 5p15.

Heterozygous mutation in the TRIO gene can also cause a similar disorder with microcephaly (MRD44; {617061}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Barbosa et al. (2020)} reported 9 unrelated patients with MRD63. One of the patients (patient 9) had previously been reported by {2:Pengelly et al. (2016)}. Most of the patients ranged in age from 3 to 19 years; 1 was 40 years old. All had global developmental delay with delayed walking usually by 3 to 5 years of age, although 3 younger patients were unable to walk independently. They had moderate (2 patients) or severe (7 patients) impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, expressive and comprehensive language delay, and variable behavioral abnormalities, such as stereotypies. Two patients had seizures and 1 had possible EEG abnormalities. Overall growth was generally poor, and many had early feeding difficulties, although all except 2 had relative macrocephaly (+2 to +4.7 SD). About half of the patients had variable dysmorphic features, including high forehead with frontal bossing, arched eyebrows, long or downslanting palpebral fissures, low hanging columella, high nasal bridge, hypoplastic or anteverted nares, large earlobes, large mouth, and thin upper lip. Less common features included dental anomalies, short tapering digits, small hands and feet, and scoliosis.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the TRIO gene that were identified in patients with MRD63 by {1:Barbosa et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 9 unrelated patients with MRD63, {1:Barbosa et al. (2020)} identified 5 different heterozygous missense mutations in the TRIO gene (see, e.g., {601893.0007}-{601893.0010}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were confirmed to occur de novo in 8 patients; inheritance was unknown in the ninth patient. All mutations occurred at highly conserved residues in the seventh spectrin repeat, and none were present in the gnomAD database. Three mutations, found in 6 unrelated patients, affected the same residue (R1078W, R1078G, and R1078Q). Molecular modeling predicted that the mutations could cause steric hindrance and alter the structural organization of the protein or interfere with protein folding. Expression of the mutations into HEK293 cells resulted in increased RAC1 ({602048}) activation, as measured by increased PAK1 ({602590}) phosphorylation, compared to wildtype. Transfection of the mutations into neuroblastoma cells caused enhanced neurite outgrowth and increased lamellipodia formation compared to controls. The findings were consistent with a gain-of-function effect.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Nabais Sa-de Vries syndrome type 2 (NSDVS2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SPOP gene ({602650}) on chromosome 17q21.

Heterozygous mutation in the SPOP gene can also cause the related disorder NSDVS1 ({618828}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Nabais Sa-de Vries syndrome type 2 (NSDVS2) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent from birth and distinctive dysmorphic facial features. Most patients have additional anomalies, including congenital heart defects, sleep disturbances, hypotonia, and variable endocrine abnormalities, such as hypothyroidism (summary by {1:Nabais Sa et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Nabais Sa et al. (2020)} reported 5 unrelated patients (patients 3-7) with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. Four patients were between 15 and 20 years of age, whereas the fifth patient was 10 months old. The patients were ascertained by clinical exome sequencing, and thereafter reviewed for reverse phenotyping. Three patients had neonatal difficulties, including hypotonia, swallowing or breathing difficulties, failure to thrive, and bradycardia due to congenital heart disease. The patients had global developmental delay, with mildly delayed walking by 2-3 years, severe speech delay, and impaired intellectual development (IQ range, 45-53). Two patients had seizures, including 1 with hemiparesis, dystonia, and chorea. Brain imaging, performed in 3 patients, showed enlarged ventricles in 2 and slightly small corpus callosum in 1. Dysmorphic facial features included relative or absolute macrocephaly (+2.5 to +4 SD in most), large forehead, high anterior hairline, small low-set ears, protruding ears, hypertelorism, deep-set eyes, long palpebral fissures, sparse and thin eyebrows, prominent broad or low nasal bridge with bulbous nasal tip, low-hanging columella, micrognathia, and pointed chin. One patient had a high-arched palate and another had a cleft/lip palate. Four of the patients had congenital heart disease, including septal defects, pulmonary stenosis, patent ductus arteriosus, and hypoplastic left heart syndrome with outflow obstruction. Cardiac information for the fifth patient was not available. Three patients had endocrine abnormalities, including hypogonadism in 1 and hypothyroidism in 2. Information from 1 of the older patients (patient 6) was not available, and the 10-month-old patient had no endocrine findings. Less common features included strabismus, ocular refraction anomalies, gastroesophageal reflux, and sleep apnea.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SPOP gene that were identified in patients with NSDVS2 by {1:Nabais Sa et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 unrelated patients with NSDVS2, {1:Nabais Sa et al. (2020)} reported 4 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the SPOP gene ({602650.0004}-{602650.0007}). The patients were ascertained by clinical exome sequencing or through large datasets, including cohorts of over 1,000, over 4,000, and over 14,000 patients with various neurodevelopmental disorders; they were gathered via collaborative efforts such as the GeneMatcher or GeneDx programs. All but 1 of the variants occurred in the MATH domain, all affected highly conserved residues, and all were absent from the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies in an endometrial cancer cell line and in patient cells showed that the mutations resulted in upregulation of BRD2, BRD3, and BRD4, consistent with decreased SPOP activity and a dominant-negative effect causing reduced ubiquitination and degradation of these proteins compared to controls. The authors postulated that increased BET protein activity may stimulate growth, resulting in macrocephaly, since BET proteins are involved in cell cycle progression.

preferredTitle: EPILEPSY, EARLY-ONSET, 2, WITH OR WITHOUT DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY; EPEO2
clinicalSynopsis: Brain abnormalities on imaging (patients A and B)
Onset in the first days or years of life
One Chinese family and 3 unrelated patients have been reported
Caused by mutation in the SET domain-containing protein 1A gene (SETD1A,)

Neurologic - CNS: Brain abnormalities on imaging (patients A and B)
Miscellaneous: Onset in the first days or years of life
One Chinese family and 3 unrelated patients have been reported
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the SET domain-containing protein 1A gene (SETD1A,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Epilepsy, early-onset, 2, with or without developmental delay

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that early-onset epilepsy-2 with or without developmental delay (EPEO2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SETD1A gene ({611052}) on chromosome 16p11.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Early-onset epilepsy-2 with or without developmental delay (EPEO2) is an autosomal dominant neurologic disorder characterized by the onset of generalized tonic-clonic seizures in the first days, months, or years of life. The severity is highly variable: some patients have normal psychomotor development and normal brain imaging, whereas others may show developmental delay associated with abnormalities on brain imaging (summary by {1:Yu et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of EPEO, see {617290}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Yu et al. (2019)} reported a 4-generation Chinese family in which 4 individuals had early-onset seizures. The proband (patient 1) was a 15-month-old girl who presented on day 2 of life with frequent tonic-clonic seizures associated with sharp wave and sharp slow wave discharges on EEG. Seizure frequency decreased with medication; she had normal development. Family history revealed that her father had a history of seizures after birth, and her paternal grandfather and great-grandmother had seizures during childhood, but clinical details were limited. The authors also reported an unrelated girl with a similar disorder (patient 2). She developed twitching and occasional loss of consciousness at 2 years of age. EEG showed paroxysmal sharp waves and sharp slow waves on both sides. She had normal development (DQ of 110) and brain imaging was essentially normal.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{1:Yu et al. (2019)} reported 2 additional unrelated Chinese children (patients 3 and 4) with onset of tonic-clonic seizures at 9 months and day 1 of life, respectively. EEG showed sharp waves and spike wave discharges. Both patients had a more complicated course with developmental delay in at least 1. Patient 3 had s history of hypoglycemia, hypothyroidism, and growth retardation. Brain MRI showed cerebral dysplasia, decreased myelinated white matter, and mild ventriculomegaly. Patient 4 had lung dysplasia, patent foramen ovale, and sepsis, and signal abnormalities in the cerebral occipital areas on brain imaging. An older brother reportedly had neonatal seizures and died at around 1 month of age; patient 4 was lost to follow-up.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of EPEO2 in the family reported by {1:Yu et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. Heterozygous mutations in 3 other patients occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 members of a 4-generation Chinese family with EPEO2, {1:Yu et al. (2019)} identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the SETD1A gene (R913C; {611052.0002}). Three additional patients with a similar disorder, with or without developmental delay, were subsequently found to carry de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the SETD1A gene (Q269R, {611052.0003}; G1369R, {611052.0004}; and R1392H, {611052.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in 1 family; in the other 3 patients, the mutations occurred de novo. The mutations were either not present or found at low frequencies in the gnomAD database. Studies of patient cells were not performed. Expression of wildtype SETD1A and constructs of the 4 mutations into mouse cortical primary neurons showed that the mutations were associated with decreased density of mushroom-like spines on the secondary branches of dendrites, which represent excitatory synapses. In contrast, the mutations had no effect on axon length. The findings suggested that the SETD1A mutations do not affect axon growth or general neuronal morphology, whereas they may have an adverse effect on the normal development of synapses. Studies in mouse brain also suggested that the mutations disrupt normal neuronal development, which may lead to epilepsy (see ANIMAL MODEL).

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Yu et al. (2019)} used electroporation to introduce the R913C SETD1A mutation into E14.5 mouse fetuses. Postmortem examination indicated that neurons expressing the R913C mutation migrated faster than controls, suggesting that the mutation disturbs the normal process of cortical development. Transcriptome analysis of cortical neuron samples from fetal mice transfected with wildtype SETD1A or with the R913C, Q269R, G1369R, or R1392H mutations showed that the G1369R and R1392H mutations were associated with significant downregulation of Neurl4 ({615865}) and Usp39 ({611594}) compared to controls. Changes in Neurl4 expression due to R913C and Q269R did not reach statistical significance. In contrast, shRNA knockdown of the murine Setd1a gene resulted in increased expression levels of Neurl4 and Usp39. Both of these genes are associated with the ubiquitin ligase pathway.

clinicalSynopsis: Nonspecific white matter abnormalities seen on MRI (in some patients)
Caused by mutation in the lanosterol synthase gene (LSS,)

Head: Microcephaly (in some patients)
Neurologic - CNS: Nonspecific white matter abnormalities seen on MRI (in some patients)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the lanosterol synthase gene (LSS,)

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that alopecia-intellectual disability syndrome-4 (APMR4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the LSS gene ({600909}) on chromosome 21q22.

Mutation in the LSS gene can also cause nonsyndromic hypotrichosis (HYPT14; {618275}).

description.title: Description
description.content:
Alopecia-intellectual disability syndrome-4 (APMR4) is characterized by alopecia universalis, scaly skin, and psychomotor retardation of varying degrees ({1:Besnard et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of alopecia-intellectual disability syndrome, see APMR1 ({203650}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Romano et al. (2018)} reported 2 sibs with congenital alopecia and impaired intellectual development from a nonconsanguineous family from Switzerland. Clinical examination in adolescence showed sparse lanugo-like scalp hair, sparse and brittle eyebrows, sparse and thinned eyelashes, sparse hair on the extremities, and an absence of axillary and pubic hair.

{1:Besnard et al. (2019)} studied 11 patients from 7 families with congenital alopecia and developmental delay. Complete alopecia was observed at birth in all patients, and 8 of the patients also exhibited ichthyosis and/or erythroderma. Intellectual development was mildly to severely impaired, and 3 patients showed microcephaly. Epilepsy was present in 8 patients, with onset ranging from birth to 10 weeks. Neurodevelopmental abnormalities included absent or very limited speech in 9 patients and hypotonia in 7 patients, with delayed or absent walking in 7 patients. Brain MRI was performed in 9 patients; 2 had normal findings and 7 showed nonspecific abnormalities. Cholesterol levels were normal in 4 of 5 individuals tested, and the fifth had a low level. Various genital abnormalities were observed in 4 of 6 male patients. The authors noted that inter- and intrafamilial clinical variability was present.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of APMR4 in the family reported by {2:Romano et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 Swiss sibs with congenital alopecia and impaired intellectual development, {2:Romano et al. (2018)} identified compound heterozygosity for mutations in the LSS gene ({600909.0008}-{600909.0009}). Their unaffected parents were each heterozygous for 1 of the mutations. The intellectual impairment in the Swiss sibs was considered to be coincidental by {2:Romano et al. (2018)}, but {1:Besnard et al. (2019)} noted that the data from their study did not support that conclusion, because all of their patients had intellectual impairment as well as alopecia.

In 11 patients from 7 unrelated families with complete alopecia and psychomotor retardation, {1:Besnard et al. (2019)} identified homozygosity or compound heterozygosity for mutations in the LSS gene (see, e.g., {600909.0010}-{600909.0014}) that segregated with disease.

clinicalSynopsis: Attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD, in some patients)
Caused by mutation in the lysine demethylase 3B gene (KDM3B,)

Neurologic - Behavioral/Psychiatric: Attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD, in some patients)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the lysine demethylase 3B gene (KDM3B,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Diets-Jongmans syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KDM3B gene ({609373}) on chromosome 5q31.

description.title: Description
description.content: Diets-Jongmans syndrome (DIJOS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by mild to moderately impaired intellectual development with a recognizable facial gestalt (summary by {1:Diets et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Diets et al. (2019)} reported 17 patients (9 males, 8 females) ranging in age from 9 months to 42 years with a syndrome characterized by mild to moderate intellectual impairment in all affected individuals. Patients were characterized as having a recognizable facial gestalt; among 16 patients characterized, long ears were present in 9, broad nasal tip in 14, thin upper vermilion in 12, wide mouth in 12, and prominent or pointed chin in 13. The majority of patients also had nonneutral palpebral fissures, with 4 of 16 having upslanted and 5 of 16 downslanted palpebral fissures. Ptosis and low columella were also frequently reported. The majority (8 of 15) of patients had behavioral problems, including ADHD, and autism; 2 patients had both. Nine of 16 patients were short, with a height below 2.5 SD; two-thirds had height below 1.5 SD. Eight of 13 had neonatal feeding difficulties. Three of 17 patients were reported with epilepsy, 4 of 17 with hearing loss, and 5 of 17 with childhood hypotonia. Interestingly, 2 of these patients (patient 2 and patient 11) were previously reported by {2:Diets et al. (2018)} in a cohort of children with cancer. Patient 2, a 16-year-old female, developed acute myeloid leukemia at age 14 and was born with congenital hypothyroidism and hip dysplasia. Patient 11, a 17-year-old male, developed Hodgkin lymphoma at age 14, and also had umbilical and inguinal hernias and cryptorchidism. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia was reported in 2 patients and heterotaxy in 1. Two patients had strabismus and 1 had low vision and nystagmus.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DIJOS in 3 of the families studied by {1:Diets et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. In other affected individuals de novo occurrence was confirmed.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: {1:Diets et al. (2019)} reported 17 patients with DIJOS with 14 novel heterozygous mutations in the KDM3B gene (e.g., {609373.0001}-{609373.0005}). In 10 individuals de novo occurrence was confirmed, and in 3 the mutations were inherited from a similarly affected parent. Four of the mutations were nonsense mutations, leading the authors to posit haploinsufficiency as the mechanism for the disorder.

clinicalSynopsis: Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency in skeletal muscle
T2-weighted abnormalities in the basal ganglia
Increased serum and CSF lactate (in some patients)
Later onset has been reported in 1 patient
Caused by mutation in the fast kinase domains 2 gene (FASTKD2,)

Muscle/Soft Tissue: Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency in skeletal muscle
Neurologic - CNS: T2-weighted abnormalities in the basal ganglia
Laboratory Abnormalities: Increased serum and CSF lactate (in some patients)
Miscellaneous: Later onset has been reported in 1 patient
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the fast kinase domains 2 gene (FASTKD2,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-44 (COXPD44) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the FASTKD2 gene ({612322}) on chromosome 2q33.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-44 (COXPD44) is an autosomal recessive mitochondrial disorder with multisystemic manifestations. Most affected individuals present in infancy or early childhood with global developmental delay, hypotonia, and abnormal movements. Most patients develop seizures, often associated with status epilepticus, and some patients may have optic atrophy. One patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has been reported. Serum lactate may be increased, although that finding is inconsistent. Detailed biochemical analysis shows variable combined deficiencies of mitochondrial oxidative complexes that appear to be tissue-specific (summary by {2:Wei et al., 2020}).

For discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Ghezzi et al. (2008)} reported 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Bedouin parents, with a mitochondrial encephalomyopathy. The first child was born with bilateral congenital hip dislocation, but showed normal development until about 7 months of age when she presented with refractory generalized tonic-clonic convulsions associated with a febrile illness. She subsequently showed global developmental delay and left-sided hemiplegia with spastic paraplegia and decreased muscle strength. At 14 years of age, she was able to obey simple commands in 2 languages, could recognize colors, and had a 20-word vocabulary. She could sit herself up, but was never able to stand or walk. She also had optic atrophy and cerebral atrophy on brain imaging. Her brother presented with subacute neurologic deterioration with muscle hypotonia with extrapyramidal movements after a febrile illness. He developed refractory seizures associated with status epilepticus. Brain MRI showed increased signal intensities on the left caudate nucleus, globus pallidus, and crus cerebri. A brain CT scan at 30 months revealed generalized and white matter atrophy, more pronounced on the left basal ganglia, with bilateral dilatation of the ventricles and basal cysternae. At 4 years he was bedridden with no communication and no voluntary activity, and he was tube-fed. He had bilateral optic atrophy, strabismus, hyperreflexia, and dystonic posturing. Plasma lactate was mildly increased in the first patient, but not in the second; CSF lactate was increased in the second patient. Biochemical assays on isolated mitochondria from skeletal muscle of the first patient showed reduced activity of cytochrome C oxidase (21% of controls), consistent with complex IV deficiency, and decreased activity of NADH-ferricyanide reductase (58% of controls) (MTND1; {516000}), possibly suggesting decreased complex I activity. Other mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex were within normal limits. Neither patient had cardiac, liver, or renal involvement.

{2:Wei et al. (2020)} reported 3 unrelated Chinese patients, between 3 and 12 years of age, with COXPD44. The patients presented between age 6 months and 2 years with delayed psychomotor development, mildly delayed walking, and variable additional neurologic abnormalities, including axial hypotonia and dyskinetic movements. Two patients had seizures associated with status epilepticus, 1 patient had optic atrophy, stroke-like episodes, dysarthria, and nystagmus, and the 12-year-old developed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Serum lactate was mildly increased in 2 patients. Brain imaging in all patients showed T2-weighted hyperintensities in the basal ganglia, globus pallidus, caudate, putamen, and brainstem.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{3:Yoo et al. (2017)} reported a 33-year-old Korean man, born of unrelated parents, who presented at age 15 years with generalized tonic-clonic seizures after normal earlier development. After the first seizure episode, he presented again with status epilepticus and a left visual defect associated with right occipital lobe infarction on brain imaging. Serum lactate was mildly increased, and he was diagnosed with MELAS ({540000}) based on suspicion of a mitochondrial disorder and the stroke-like presentation. He had EEG abnormalities and bilateral optic atrophy, but other organ systems were not involved. Muscle biopsy showed type II fiber predominance, but immunostaining for mitochondrial complexes II and IV were normal. Analyses of respiratory chain complexes in muscle homogenate were not performed. {3:Yoo et al. (2017)} noted the later onset and milder disease in this patient compared to the patients reported by {1:Ghezzi et al. (2008)}, and suggested that phenotypic variability may be dependent on the type and location of mutations. The patient was compound heterozygous for a missense and a nonsense mutation in the FASTKD2 gene ({612322.0002} and {612322.0003}). Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of COXPD44 in the families reported by {2:Wei et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Bedouin parents, with COXPD44, {1:Ghezzi et al. (2008)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the FASTKD2 gene (R416X; {612322.0001}). The mutation, which was found by linkage analysis and candidate gene sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The mutation was predicted to result in premature termination with loss of the 2 transmembrane domains as well as the FAST kinase domain, resulting in loss of function. Functional studies of the variant and studies of the variant in patient cells were not performed.

In a 33-year-old Korean man with a mild form of COXPD44, {3:Yoo et al. (2017)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the FASTKD2 gene: a nonsense mutation (R205X; {612322.0002}) and a missense mutation (L255P; {612322.0003}). The mutations, which were found by targeted sequencing of a panel of genes involved in mitochondrial function and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variants and studies of the variant in patient cells were not performed, but immunostaining for COX was normal in patient skeletal muscle biopsy.

In 3 unrelated Chinese children with COXPD44, {2:Wei et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations in the FASTKD2 gene ({612322.0004}-{612322.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. All the mutations were predicted to result in truncated proteins lacking the C-terminal RNA-binding domain. Analysis of immortalized lymphocytes derived from 2 patients showed barely detectable FASTKD2 protein as well as significantly decreased (30-40% lower than controls) mRNA levels of the mitochondrial ribosomal 16S subunit (MTRNR2; {561010}). Immunoblotting of patient cells using specific antibodies indicated combined deficiencies of mitochondrial complex I (GRIM19, NDUFA13; {609435}), complex III (UQCRC2;{191329}), complex IV (COX4I1; {123864}), and complex V (ATP5A; {164360}); levels of complex II (SDHA; {600857}) were normal. In vitro studies of patient cells also showed a decrease in basal cellular respiration and mitochondrial OXPHOS-coupled respiration, manifest as a dramatic decrease in ATP production and increased extracellular lactate, compared to controls. Knockdown of FASTKD2 in human muscle cells impaired the assembly of multiple OXPHOS complexes, but did not affect nuclear-encoded complex II. Expression of the mutations into FASTKD2-null HEK293 cells were unable to rescue the combined OXPHOS defect, suggesting that the proteins were not functional. Overall, the results suggested that FASTKD2 causes defective mitochondrial RNA translation.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Wei et al. (2020)} found that knockdown of fastkd2 in zebrafish resulted in combined OXPHOS dysfunction and increased lethality. Mutant animals also had a decreased heart rate and increased sensitivity to touch compared to controls, suggesting tissue-specific defects in heart and neurologic function.

Growth - Other: Postnatal catch-up growth (patients without neurologic abnormalities)
Head: Prominent metopic suture
Miscellaneous: Mean age of diagnosis, 7 weeks (range birth-26 weeks) Two patient subsets, (1) permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus 2 and (2) developmental delay, epilepsy, and neonatal diabetes (DEND syndrome)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the potassium channel, inwardly rectifying, subfamily J, member 11 gene (KCNJ11,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Diabetes, permanent neonatal 2, with or without neurologic features

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus-2 (PNDM2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KCNJ11 ({600937}) gene on chromosome 11p15.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus-2 (PNDM2) is characterized by onset of insulin-requiring hyperglycemia within the first months of life that requires insulin therapy throughout life. Some patients additionally have marked developmental delay, muscle weakness, and epilepsy ({4:Gloyn et al., 2004}). The triad of developmental delay, epilepsy, and neonatal diabetes is known as DEND ({10:Shimomura et al., 2007}).

{9:Proks et al. (2006)} stated that heterozygous activating mutations in KCNJ11 are the most common cause of PNDM and account for 26 to 64% of cases, and that neurologic features are found in 20% of patients with KCNJ11 mutations.

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus, see PNDM1 ({606176}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
Permanent diabetes of infancy is primarily characterized by onset of hyperglycemia within the first 6 months of life. Among 12 patients with PNDI and mutation in the KCNJ11 gene, {4:Gloyn et al. (2004)} reported a mean age of 7 weeks at diagnosis (range birth to 26 weeks). All affected patients had hyperglycemia (270 to 972 mg/dl), and 3 had ketoacidosis. None of the patients had pancreatic autoantibodies associated with type 1 diabetes. Patients did not secrete insulin in response to glucose or glucagon but did secrete insulin in response to tolbutamide. All patients had low birth weight. Three of 12 patients had similar neurologic abnormalities, including developmental delay, muscle weakness, and epilepsy. All 3 patients with neurologic abnormalities had dysmorphic features, including prominent metopic suture, a downturned mouth, bilateral ptosis, and limb contractures.

{3:Gloyn et al. (2006)} reported 4 unrelated patients with developmental delay, epilepsy, and neonatal diabetes (DEND) associated with mutations in the KCNJ11 gene. All had infantile-onset of diabetes without pancreatic autoantibodies (diagnosed from day 1 of life to 3 months) with hyperglycemia, polydipsia, polyuria, and ketoacidosis in some. The most severely affected child had seizures with hypsarrhythmia, neurologic deterioration with social withdrawal, and mild dysmorphic features, including prominent metopic suture, downturned mouth, and bilateral ptosis. She died from aspiration pneumonia at age 6 months; genetic analysis revealed a novel mutation in the KCNJ11 gene (C166F; {600937.0015}). {3:Gloyn et al. (2006)} considered the phenotype of this patient a case of DEND. Two other patients had developmental delay and axial hypotonia, but only 1 of these also had dysmorphic features and seizures. The fourth child, who had no dysmorphic or neurologic features, had a diabetic mother who also had no neurologic involvement. {3:Gloyn et al. (2006)} noted the phenotypic variability between patients, even between those with the same mutation.

{10:Shimomura et al. (2007)} reported a patient with neonatal diabetes who had had persistent hyperglycemia from birth and developed refractory neonatal seizures with hypsarrhythmia. By age 3.5 years, psychomotor retardation was severe, with hypotonia, athetotic movements, inability to roll over or sit without support, decreased eye contact, and inability to speak. {10:Shimomura et al. (2007)} stated that this patient was the sixth case of DEND (developmental delay, epilepsy, and neonatal diabetes) reported to that time.

Using a battery of targeted neuropsychological and behavioral assessments, {1:Carmody et al. (2016)} evaluated 23 patients with KCNJ11 mutations, 9 with and 14 without global developmental delay, all successfully treated with sulfonylurea, and 20 healthy sib controls, The patients without global developmental delay had significant differences compared with sib controls on a range of assessments, including IQ, measures of academic achievement, and executive function. KCNJ11 patients with global delay exhibited significant differences in behavioral symptoms, with a tendency to avoid social contact, and displayed a reduced ability to adapt to new circumstances. Parents reported more immature behavior, gross mood swings, bizarre thoughts, and other unusual and severe behaviors, and there were also significant deficits in all subdomains of daily living skills.

{5:Landmeier et al. (2017)} reported that while 25% of patients with KCNJ11 have obvious neurologic dysfunction, less was known about those with milder problems. They compared 30 probands from one center with 25 sibs and found that 13 (43%) of probands had ADHD versus 2 (8%) of sibs (p less than 0.05). They also noted significant differences in behavior difficulties, social awareness, and academic achievement. Sleep disorders were also much more prevalent among KCNJ11 mutation carriers (p less than 0.01).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PNDM in families studied by {4:Gloyn et al. (2004)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. Additionally, de novo occurrence was demonstrated.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content:
{13:Zung et al. (2004)} reported an infant with PNDM due to a mutation in the KCNJ11 gene (R201H; {600937.0002}) who showed a better response to oral sulfonylurea (glibenclamide) treatment than to insulin pump therapy.

{8:Pearson et al. (2006)} assessed glycemic control in 49 diabetic patients with known heterozygous mutations in the KCNJ11 gene; 44 (90%) successfully discontinued insulin after receiving appropriate doses of sulfonylureas. The extent of tolbutamide blockade of K(ATP) channels in vitro reflected the response seen in patients. Glycosylated hemoglobin levels improved significantly in patients who switched to sulfonylurea therapy, and improved glycemic control was sustained at 1 year.

{11:Stanik et al. (2007)} also reported patients with PNMD due to mutation in the KCNJ11 gene who were successfully transferred from insulin to sulfonylurea therapy with dramatic improvement in diabetes control and quality of life.

The patient of {10:Shimomura et al. (2007)} showed a good response to sulfonylurea treatment, with both improved glycemic control without insulin and neurologic improvement. {10:Shimomura et al. (2007)} noted that this was the first report of a child with severe DEND who had clinical improvement of both diabetes as well as neurologic features after sulfonylurea therapy.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 10 of 29 patients with permanent neonatal diabetes, {4:Gloyn et al. (2004)} identified 6 novel, heterozygous missense mutations in the KCNJ11 gene (see, e.g., {600937.0002}-{600937.0003}). In 2 patients the diabetes was familial, and in 8 it arose from a spontaneous mutation. In 4 of the 10 families, the mutation was an arg201-to-his substitution (R201H; {600937.0002}). When the most common mutation, R201H, was coexpressed with SUR in Xenopus oocytes, the ability of ATP to block mutant ATP-sensitive potassium channels was greatly reduced.

{2:Edghill et al. (2007)} noted that the majority of KCNJ11 mutations resulting in neonatal diabetes mellitus occur de novo. They found that germline mosaicism was indicated by pedigree analysis in 2 of 18 families in which neither parent was affected and in 1 of 12 additional parents tested for somatic mosaicism. {2:Edghill et al. (2007)} concluded that de novo KCNJ11 mutations can arise during gametogenesis or embryogenesis, thus increasing the risk of neonatal diabetes for subsequent sibs.

{10:Shimomura et al. (2007)} reported an Italian boy with severe neonatal diabetes with neurologic features (DEND) caused by a de novo mutation in the KCNJ11 gene (I167L; {600937.0016}).

{6:Mannikko et al. (2010)} reported 2 novel mutations on the same haplotype (cis), F60Y ({600937.0023}) and V64L, in the slide helix of Kir6.2 (KCNJ11) in a patient with neonatal diabetes, developmental delay, and epilepsy. Functional analysis revealed that the F60Y mutation increased the intrinsic channel open probability, thereby indirectly producing a marked decrease in channel inhibition by ATP and an increase in whole-cell potassium-ATP currents. When expressed alone, the V64L mutation caused a small reduction in apparent ATP inhibition, by enhancing the ability of MgATP to stimulate channel activity. The V64L mutation also ameliorated the deleterious effects on the F60Y mutation when it was expressed on the same, but not a different, subunit. The authors concluded that F60Y is the pathogenic mutation and that interactions between slide helix residues may influence KATP channel gating.

populationGenetics.title: Population Genetics
populationGenetics.content: Of 31 Japanese patients with NDM, including 15 with PNDM and 16 with transient NDM (TNDM), {12:Suzuki et al. (2007)} identified a 6q24 abnormality (see {601410}) in 11, a KCNJ11 mutation in 9, and an ABCC8 ({600509}) mutation in 2. Seven patients with a KCNJ11 mutation, including 2 with DEND and the 2 with an ABCC8 mutation, had PNDM. All of the patients with the 6q24 abnormality and 2 patients with a KCNJ11 mutation had TNDM. {12:Suzuki et al. (2007)} concluded that the 6q abnormality and KCNJ11 mutations are major causes of NDM in Japanese.

nomenclature.title: Nomenclature
nomenclature.content: {7:Massa et al. (2005)} noted that the diagnostic time limit for PNDM has changed over the years, ranging from onset within 30 days of birth to 3 months of age. However, as patients with the clinical phenotype caused by mutation in the KCNJ11 gene have been identified with onset up to 6 months of age, {7:Massa et al. (2005)} suggested that the term 'permanent diabetes mellitus of infancy' (PDMI) replace PNDM as a more accurate description, and include those who present up to 6 months of age. The authors suggested that the new acronym be linked to the gene product (e.g., GCK-PDMI, KCNJ11-PDMI) to avoid confusion with patients with early-onset, autoimmune type I diabetes.

clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the ATP-binding cassette, subfamily C, member 8 gene (ABCC8,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the ATP-binding cassette, subfamily C, member 8 gene (ABCC8,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus-3 (PNDM3) is caused by heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the ABCC8 ({600509}) gene on chromosome 11p15.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus-3 (PNDM3) is characterized by the onset of mild to severe hyperglycemia within the first months of life, and requires lifelong therapy (summary by {1:Babenko et al., 2006}). Some patients also have neurologic features, including developmental delay and epilepsy ({3:Proks et al., 2006}; {1:Babenko et al., 2006}). The triad of developmental delay, epilepsy, and neonatal diabetes is known as DEND.

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus, see PNDM1 ({606176}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Proks et al. (2006)} described a patient with PNDM3 in whom the first indication of hyperglycemia was mild glycosuria without ketonuria on the seventh day of life. Birth weight was 2200 g. Hyperglycemia gradually increased until it was 20g/24h at the age of 13 weeks. At that time a formal diagnosis of diabetes was made on the basis of an oral glucose tolerance test, on which insulin values were less than the detection limits of the assay. Other laboratory values were normal. At age 13 weeks the patient weighed 3400 g (less than -2 SD), with a length of 53 cm (less than -2 SD) and a head circumference of 34.2 cm (less than -2 SD). Insulin treatment was started at age 15 weeks in single or multiple dosages of 0.7 U/kg/day, using mixtures of short- and intermediate-acting insulin; glycemic control was poor. The patient showed marked motor and social developmental delay, with muscle weakness with hypotonia apparent by 1 year. During his second year, there were intermittent fine distal and athetoid involuntary movements with the later development of severe muscle spasms. Electroencephalography revealed nonspecific generalized epileptiform activity. Brain CT scan was normal. At age 27 years the patient remained on insulin treatment and high doses of anticonvulsive medication, had never achieved speech, and had difficulty standing unaided owing to muscle spasms in his limbs.

{4:Stanik et al. (2007)} studied a patient with PNDM3 who was born at 40 weeks' gestation at a normal weight. He developed diabetes in his second month of life as manifested with polyuria, polydipsia, and failure to thrive during a respiratory tract infection. Hyperglycemia reached 28 mmol/liter without changes in acidobasic balance. Axial hypotonus required rehabilitation lasting for 36 months.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: {4:Stanik et al. (2007)} reported a patient with PNDM due to mutation in the ABCC8 gene who was successfully transferred from insulin to sulfonylurea therapy, with achievement of normoglycemia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PNDM3 in families studied by {2:Ellard et al. (2007)} was consistent with autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive inheritance. In other cases, de novo occurrence was demonstrated.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 27-year-old man who had permanent neonatal diabetes, severe developmental delay, and generalized epileptiform activity on EEG, {3:Proks et al. (2006)} identified heterozygosity for a de novo missense mutation (F132L; {600509.0016}) in the ABCC8 gene. Functional studies showed that F132L markedly reduced the sensitivity of the K(ATP) channel to inhibition by MgATP, thereby increasing the whole-cell K(ATP) current; the authors noted that the functional consequence of the F132L mutation mirrors that of mutations in KCNJ11 ({600937}) causing neonatal diabetes.

From a group of 73 patients with neonatal diabetes, {1:Babenko et al. (2006)} screened the ABCC8 gene in 34 who did not have alterations in chromosome 6q or mutations in the KCNJ11 or GCK genes. In 2 PNDM patients, they identified heterozygosity for a mutation ({600509.0017} and {600509.0018}, respectively). They also identified heterozygosity for 5 different mutations (see, e.g., {600509.0019} and {600509.0020}) in 7 patients with transient neonatal diabetes (TNDM2; {610374}). Mutant channels in intact cells and in physiologic concentrations of magnesium ATP had markedly higher activity than did wildtype channels. These overactive channels remained sensitive to sulfonylurea, and treatment with sulfonylureas resulted in euglycemia. The mutation-positive fathers of 5 of the probands with transient neonatal diabetes developed type II diabetes mellitus ({125853}) in adulthood; {1:Babenko et al. (2006)} proposed that mutations of the ABCC8 gene may give rise to a monogenic form of type II diabetes with variable expression and age at onset. The authors noted that dominant mutations in ABCC8 accounted for 12% of cases of neonatal diabetes in the study group.

populationGenetics.title: Population Genetics
populationGenetics.content: Of 31 Japanese patients with NDM, including 15 with PNDM and 16 with transient NDM (TNDM), {5:Suzuki et al. (2007)} identified a 6q24 abnormality (see {601410}) in 11, a KCNJ11 mutation in 9, and an ABCC8 mutation in 2. Seven patients with a KCNJ11 mutation, including 2 with DEND and the 2 with an ABCC8 mutation, had PNDM. All of the patients with the 6q24 abnormality and 2 patients with a KCNJ11 mutation had TNDM. {5:Suzuki et al. (2007)} concluded that the 6q abnormality and KCNJ11 mutations are major causes of NDM in Japanese.

Caused by mutation in the neurooncologic ventral antigen 2 gene (NOVA2,)

Head: Small head circumference

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without autistic features and/or structural brain abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with or without autistic features and/or structural brain abnormalities (NEDASB) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the NOVA2 gene ({601991}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without autistic features and/or structural brain abnormalities (NEDASB) is an early-onset neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay, poor or absent speech and language development, and behavioral abnormalities reminiscent of autism spectrum disorder (ASD; {209850}) or Angelman syndrome (AS; {105830}). Additional features may include poor overall growth with small head circumference, axial hypotonia, spasticity, and seizures. Some patients have abnormal findings on brain imaging, including cerebral atrophy, cerebellar atrophy, and/or thin corpus callosum (summary by {1:Mattioli et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Mattioli et al. (2020)} reported 6 unrelated patients, ascertained through the collaborative efforts of several international diagnostic laboratories or research centers performing exome sequencing in patients with intellectual disability, who carried de novo heterozygous frameshift mutations in the NOVA2 gene. Five patients were between 3 and 9 years of age, and 1 was 22 years old; none had a family history of a similar disorder. These individuals presented in the first months or years of life with global developmental delay, delayed motor milestones, hypotonia, and/or feeding difficulties. Most achieved walking by age 4 years, although 1 was unable to walk at age 9, and all had impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech and language acquisition. Behavioral abnormalities were common: most patients had autistic features, including stereotypic movements, body rocking, and poor social interaction, and several demonstrated inappropriate laughter and/or hand flapping, suggestive of Angelman syndrome. More variable features included spasticity, hyperreflexia, and/or ataxic gait. Two patients had seizures: myoclonic seizures in 1 and refractory myoclonic/absence seizures in the other. All patients had poor overall growth with borderline or small head circumference (-1 to -2.5 SD), and a few had mild dysmorphic features, such as brachycephaly, deep-set eyes, downslanting palpebral fissures, downturned mouth, anteverted nares, and deep philtrum. Two patients had normal brain imaging, but the others showed variable structural abnormalities, including thin corpus callosum, cortical atrophy, white matter loss, cerebellar volume loss, and type 1 Chiari malformation.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the NOVA2 gene that were identified in patients with NEDASB by {1:Mattioli et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 unrelated patients with NEDASB, {1:Mattioli et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous frameshift mutations in the NOVA2 gene ({601991.0001}-{601991.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing through different laboratories, were not found in public databases, including gnomAD. All the mutations occurred in the last exon, exon 4, and were predicted to escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), although studies of patient cells were not performed. Expression of 1 of the mutations (Mut1) ({601991.0001}) in HeLa cells showed that the mutant protein was expressed at normal levels and showed normal nuclear localization, consistent with escape from NMD. All the mutations, which clustered near one another, resulted in frameshifts leading to the same alternative frame, and the resulting truncated proteins shared a common region of 133 residues before premature termination between residues 394-401. The full-length protein contains 492 residues. The mutations were predicted to remove the third KH domain (residues 406-473), which binds RNA loops composed of the tetranucleotide YCAY. SiRNA-mediated knockdown of NOVA2 in human neuronal cells resulted in an increase in the proportion of cells with multiple neurites and a decrease in the proportion of undifferentiated cells compared to controls. The abnormalities in neurite outgrowth could be rescued by wildtype NOVA2, but not by the Mut1 mutation. Transcriptome analysis of human neural stem cells treated with siRNA causing a 50% reduction in NOVA2 expression showed that a set of genes had differences in alternative splicing. Gene ontology analysis showed that the affected genes were related to transmembrane proteins, the extracellular matrix, cytoskeleton organization, and neuron projection/dendrite development. Genes affected included several that have been shown to undergo alternative splicing in the mouse cortex, such as SGCE ({604149}), NEO1 ({601907}), SORBS1 ({605264}), and DAB1 ({603448}). In vitro studies showed that Mut1 had a reduction in RNA binding capacity for the YCAY motif compared to wildtype, and expression of Mut1 in HeLa cells resulted in abnormal regulation of splicing of certain genes, although the findings were more consistent with a partial loss of function than a complete loss of function. There was no evidence of a dominant-negative effect.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Mattioli et al. (2020)} found that knockdown of the nova2 ortholog (nova1a) in zebrafish resulted in a reduction in the number of axonal tracts formed between optic tecta, as well as a reduction in tecta size. The morpholino phenotype could be rescued by wildtype NOVA2 mRNA, but not by NOVA2 mutant (Mut1) mRNA. However, injection of either wildtype or Mut1 NOVA2 alone did not significantly affect axonal tracts.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, MICROCEPHALY, AND SEIZURES; NEDHYMS
clinicalSynopsis: Four unrelated patients have been reported (last curated April 2020)
Caused by mutation in the adenosine deaminase, RNA-specific, B1 gene (ADARB1,)

Head: Microcephaly, progressive (down to -4.4 SD)
Brachycephaly
Plagiocephaly
Miscellaneous: Four unrelated patients have been reported (last curated April 2020)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the adenosine deaminase, RNA-specific, B1 gene (ADARB1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, microcephaly, and seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, microcephaly, and seizures (NEDHYMS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ADARB1 gene ({601218}) on chromosome 21q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, microcephaly, and seizures (NEDHYMS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay with axial hypotonia, inability to sit or walk, and severely impaired intellectual development with absent language. Most patients develop early-onset intractable seizures that prevent normal development. Additional features include feeding difficulties with poor overall growth and microcephaly. Some patients may have spastic quadriplegia, poor eye contact due to cortical blindness, variable dysmorphic features, and nonspecific abnormalities on brain imaging (summary by {3:Tan et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Tan et al. (2020)} reported 4 unrelated children, ranging from 2 to 11 years of age, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were evaluated by exome sequencing at different centers and ascertained through the GeneMatcher or Matchmaker Exchange programs. The patients presented in the first year of life with failure to thrive, developmental delay, and axial hypotonia. Three patients presented with early-onset intractable seizures, often associated with status epilepticus. The fourth patient (patient 1) had a slightly less severe seizure disorder with onset of staring spells and likely generalized tonic-tonic seizures at age 5 years, although EEG showed no epileptiform activity and he was not on seizure medication. All patients had global developmental delay with inability to stand or walk, severe to profoundly impaired intellectual development, poor or absent eye contact, often associated with cortical visual blindness, and absent language. Some failed to achieve developmental milestones or showed developmental stagnation. Two patients had peripheral spasticity. Additional features included feeding difficulties and poor overall growth; 2 patients were tube-fed. All patients had microcephaly (-3.3 to -4.4 SD), and some had nonspecific dysmorphic features, including plagiocephaly, brachycephaly, round or oval face, upslanting palpebral fissures, thin upper lip, and high-arched palate. Brain imaging showed variable anomalies, including thin corpus callosum, brain atrophy, and delayed myelination. Patient 2 died of epilepsy at 2 years of age. Patient 3 had a family history, including 5 first trimester spontaneous abortions in the mother and several relatives with intellectual disability, although detailed genetic testing was not available.

{2:Maroofian et al. (2021)} reported 3 patients from 2 families with developmental delay and encephalopathy. Patient 1 presented at 2 weeks of age with infantile spasms and myoclonic jerks, which progressed to generalized seizures. Brain MRI at 3 months of age showed mild cerebral atrophy and white matter abnormalities. At 5 years of age she had profound developmental delay and impaired intellectual development. On examination, she had microcephaly, strabismus, axial hypotonia, appendicular spasticity, and contractures. Brain MRI at the age of 5.6 years showed cerebral atrophy, corpus callosum hypoplasia, and ventricular enlargement. Patients 2 and 3 were sibs who had normal psychomotor development until the ages of 2 and 4 months, respectively. Afterwards, they both had severe developmental delay and developed seizures at 4 to 5 months of age. Neurologic examination in both sibs revealed microcephaly, axial hypotonia, progressive spastic tetraplegia, and hyperreflexia. Brain MRI in patient 2 at 4 years of age demonstrated cerebral atrophy, corpus callosum hypoplasia, and abnormal signal in the lentiform nucleus. Brain MRI in patient at 11 months of age showed cortical and subcortical atrophy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDHYMS in the families reported by {3:Tan et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 4 unrelated patients with NEDHYMS, {3:Tan et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations in the ADARB1 gene ({601218.0001}-{601218.0005}). The patients were evaluated by exome sequencing at different centers and ascertained through the GeneMatcher or Matchmaker Exchange programs. The mutations occurred throughout the gene, and molecular modeling showed that they were situated in or around the deaminase domain or the dsRBD1 domain. In vitro functional expression assays in HEK293 cells showed that 4 of the 5 variants caused variable decreases in the RNA editing activity of ADARB1 compared to controls. Some of the variants also impaired ADARB1 RNA editing of the mouse Gria2 ({138247}) Q/R site. The authors hypothesized that the mutations had adverse effects on RNA editing of target substrates, although the precise molecular effects remained to be clarified.

In 3 children from 2 consanguineous families with NEDHYMS, {2:Maroofian et al. (2021)} identified homozygous mutations in the ADARB1 gene (R630Q, {601218.0006}; c.1245_1247+1del, {601218.0007}). The mutations, which were identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in each family. Expression of the R630Q mutation in HEK293 cells resulted in decreased RNA editing activity. Expression of the c.1245_1247+1del mutation in a minigene assay resulted in abnormal splicing, with skipping of exon 4, and was predicted to result in nonsense-mediated decay.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Higuchi et al. (2000)} studied ADAR2-mediated RNA editing by generating mice that were homozygous for a targeted functional null allele. Editing in Adar2 -/- mice was substantially reduced at most of 25 positions in diverse transcripts; the mutant mice became prone to seizures and died young. The impaired phenotype appeared to result entirely from a single underedited position, since it reverted to normal when both alleles for the underedited transcript were substituted with alleles encoding the edited version exonically. The critical position specifies an ion channel determinant, the Q/R site, in AMPA receptor GluRB premessenger RNA. {1:Higuchi et al. (2000)} concluded that this transcript is physiologically the most important substrate of ADAR2.

clinicalSynopsis: Onset of seizures in the first decade
Caused by mutation in the CEP85-like protein gene (CEP85L,)

Miscellaneous: Onset of seizures in the first decade
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the CEP85-like protein gene (CEP85L,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that lissencephaly-10 (LIS10) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CEP85L gene ({618865}) on chromosome 6q22.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Lissencephaly-10 (LIS10) is a neurologic disorder characterized by variably delayed development with mildly to moderately impaired intellectual development and language delay, as well as seizures, which are often intractable. There is a spectrum of severity, with some patients having normal early development and only borderline to mild cognitive impairment. Brain imaging shows features consistent with neuronal migration defects, including posterior-predominant lissencephaly, pachygyria, agyria, and subcortical band heterotopia (summary by {2:Tsai et al., 2020}).

For a general description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of lissencephaly, see LIS1 ({607432}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Tsai et al. (2020)} reported 13 patients from 9 unrelated families with LIS10. Most of the patients were adults ranging in age from 19 to 52 years, although there were 2 children who were 3 and 5 years old. A father and daughter (family VIII) had previously been reported by {1:Deconinck et al. (2003)}. The patients were ascertained due to brain imaging findings of lissencephaly and/or subcortical band heterotopia. Between early infancy and 14 years of age, the patients presented with variable seizure types, including focal impaired awareness, absence, tonic, clonic, myoclonic, and generalized. Seizures were often intractable, although they could be controlled with medication in some patients. EEGs showed variable abnormalities, such as background slowing, sharp and slow waves, and/or spike-wave complexes; both focal and multifocal or diffuse spike discharges were observed. Most patients showed developmental delay with delayed language and speech development, impaired intellectual development, and mildly delayed walking, although some had normal early development with regression after seizure onset. In addition, a few patients had borderline or mild cognitive impairment and were able to attend special schools; at least 1 patient was able to attend college. IQ, measured in 4 patients, ranged between 58 and 84. Four patients had notable visual problems, including cortical visual impairment, visual agnosia, and myopia. Three adult patients in family V had psychiatric abnormalities, including depression, bipolar disorder, hallucinations, aggressive behavior, and suicide attempts. Brain imaging in all patients showed posterior-predominant lissencephaly, pachygyria, and/or subcortical band heterotopia; 2 patients had agyria.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: LIS10 often occurs sporadically due to de novo mutations, although rare autosomal dominant inheritance has been reported ({2:Tsai et al., 2020}).

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 13 patients from 9 unrelated families with LIS10, {2:Tsai et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous mutations in the CEP85L gene (see, e.g., {618865.0001}-{618865.0005}). The mutations occurred de novo in 4 patients, were inherited in 2 families (families V and VIII), and occurred de novo in 2 sisters (family IX) likely due to parental gonadal mosaicism; the inheritance pattern was unknown in 2 patients. Mutations in the first 5 probands were found by genome or exome sequencing; mutations in the remainder of the patients were identified by targeted sequencing of the CEP85L gene in 31 individuals with a similar phenotype and in 1 from a search of the literature. Six patients from 4 families had missense variants affecting a highly conserved 15-residue coding region in exon 2 (S58C, D65N, I68T, and E69R), suggesting that it is an important functional domain. Three families had splice site mutations resulting in the skipping of exon 2, and 2 families had mutations affecting the translation initiation codon; the latter mutations were demonstrated to result in decreased protein levels compared to controls. Functional studies of the variants and additional studies of patient cells were not performed. {2:Tsai et al. (2020)} noted that truncating variants in CEP85L are observed in healthy controls, suggesting that haploinsufficiency may not be the pathogenic mechanism. The authors hypothesized that the pathogenicity results from disruption of a conserved region, perhaps through a dominant-negative model.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: Using RNA interference, {2:Tsai et al. (2020)} found that knockdown of Cep85l in mouse caused a neuronal migration defect.

clinicalSynopsis: Caused by duplication of 1.5Mb duplication of chromosome 17q11

Head: Microcephaly
Molecular Basis: Caused by duplication of 1.5Mb duplication of chromosome 17q11

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because the NF1 microduplication syndrome is a contiguous gene duplication syndrome within chromosome 17q11.2 involving the NF1 gene ({613113}).

For a discussion of the clinical features and cytogenetics of the reciprocal 17q11.2 deletion, see {613675}.

description.title: Description
description.content: The NF1 microduplication syndrome is characterized by mild to moderate impairment of intellectual development and mild facial dysmorphisms, with variable other features including early-onset baldness, tooth enamel hypoplasia, seizures, and macro- or microcephaly. Neurofibromas have not been reported (summary by {3:Moles et al., 2012}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Grisart et al. (2008)} reported a large family segregating a microduplication of the NF1 microdeletion syndrome region. Two adult brothers had developmental delay and mild mental retardation associated with early onset of baldness around 14 to 15 years of age, mild facial dysmorphism with sparse eyelashes and eyebrows, long midface, malar hypoplasia, nasal deviation, bifid nose tip, flared nares, thin upper lip, dental enamel hypoplasia, and large testes. Family history included a similarly affected father with 3 mentally retarded half sisters and a mentally retarded half brother. The deceased grandmother was also reportedly affected. Two carriers of the microduplication were reportedly unaffected. Neurofibromas were not reported in any individual.

{3:Moles et al. (2012)} reported 7 additional patients with chromosome 17q11 microduplications that included the NF1 gene. Six patients were male and 1 was female. They ranged in age from newborn to 21 years old. Inheritance was unknown for 4, de novo for 1, and maternal or paternal for 1 each. All patients except for the newborn and 2 month old were noted to have developmental delay or intellectual disability. Three of 7 had seizures. Five patients had facial dysmorphisms, including some undescribed. One patient had microcephaly, and 1 had macrocephaly. One patient had bilateral cleft lip and palate and unilateral iris coloboma as well as polymicrogyria. One was reported to have a normal brain MRI. None of the patients had neurofibromas. None of the patients reported in this study had dental enamel hypoplasia or premature balding, as reported by {1:Grisart et al. (2008)}.

{1:Grisart et al. (2008)} and {3:Moles et al. (2012)} noted that {2:Lu et al. (2007)} had reported a patient with NF1 microduplication (V4-36). The individual had been referred for developmental delay/impaired intellectual development, failure to thrive, and microcephaly.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NF1 microduplication syndrome in the family reported by {1:Grisart et al. (2008)} and in 2 families reported by {3:Moles et al. (2012)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. De novo occurrence of a heterozygous microduplication was also confirmed by {3:Moles et al. (2012)}.

cytogenetics.title: Cytogenetics
cytogenetics.content:
Using microarray CGH, FISH analysis, and multiple ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) in a family with mild intellectual impairment, early-onset baldness, and dental enamel hypoplasia,, {1:Grisart et al. (2008)} detected a 1.5- to 1.6-Mb duplication on chromosome 17q11 (chr17:25,964,192-27,475,624, NCBI36) that corresponded perfectly to the NF1 microdeletion syndrome region (see {613675}). This duplication was found in all affected individuals studied, as well as in 2 unaffected family members, indicating reduced penetrance. {1:Grisart et al. (2008)} noted that the same mechanism, nonallelic homologous recombination, underlies both microdeletion and microduplication.

{3:Moles et al. (2012)} reported 7 additional patients with chromosome 17q11 microduplications identified among 48,817 probands undergoing chromosome microarray in 1 large laboratory. All 7 microduplications spanned the entire NF1 gene, and the authors stated that 5 might represent the reciprocal duplications of the more common 1.4-Mb type 1 or 1.2-Mb type 2 NF1 microdeletions.
