phenotypes.phenotype: Seizures, early-onset, with neurodegeneration and brain calcification

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that early-onset seizures with neurodegeneration and brain calcifications (SENERAC) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NRROS gene ({615322}) on chromosome 3q29.

description.title: Description
description.content: Early-onset seizures with neurodegeneration and brain calcifications (SENEBAC) is an autosomal recessive encephalopathy characterized by onset of refractory seizures in the first year of life. Affected individuals tend to have normal or mildly delayed development early in life, but show significant and progressive developmental regression associated with seizure onset. Features include hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, poor eye contact, and absent speech. Most require tube feeding; death in childhood may occur. Brain imaging shows cerebral atrophy, loss of white matter, and punctate calcifications, suggestive of abnormal neuroinflammation (summary by {2:Smith et al., 2020} and {1:Dong et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Smith et al. (2020)} reported 3 children from 2 unrelated families with a similar neurodegenerative disorder. After normal early development, all patients developed refractory seizures between 14 and 18 months, and thereafter showed regression of motor skills ultimately resulting in death by age 3 years. Features included inability to sit, progressive spasticity (in 1 patient), and a progressive decline in head circumference. Brain imaging showed progressive brain atrophy, diffuse signal changes in the cerebral and cerebellar white matter, and calcifications. Neuropathologic examination of patient 3 showed brain atrophy, cortical atrophy with enlarged ventricles, thin corpus callosum, atrophy of the brainstem, and shrunken white matter with cystic degeneration. Histologic studies showed neuronal loss, reactive gliosis, and diffuse and extensive abnormal accumulation of foamy macrophages in a perivascular distribution. These foamy cells immunoreacted with CD68 ({153634}), MHC class II molecules, and p22-phox (CYBA; {608508}), but not NRROS. There was also reduced MBP ({159430}) expression in the white matter compared to controls.

{1:Dong et al. (2020)} reported 6 children from 4 unrelated families with SENEBAC. The patients were between 20 months and 9 years of age; 3 died between 2 and 4 years. All were hypotonic early in life, but only some demonstrated global developmental delay. All had onset of seizures in the first year of life and thereafter showed significant and rapid developmental regression. Seizure types were variable, including febrile, infantile spasms, focal, tonic, complex partial, tonic-clonic, and myoclonic seizures. The seizures occurred daily with a high frequency and were refractory to medication. All required tube feeding; most had recurrent aspiration and some needed a tracheostomy. Five patients developed peripheral hypertonia with significant spasticity and hyperreflexia; other features included visual inattention, poor head control, absent language, and inability to walk. Brain imaging showed marked cerebral atrophy and delayed myelination in all patients, and the findings were progressive in those who had serial imaging. About half the patients also had hypoplasia of the corpus callosum. All 3 patients who had CT scans showed punctate calcifications in the periventricular and subcortical cerebral white matter. Two families had a notable history, with several children dying young from a similar neurodegenerative disorder.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SENEBAC in the families reported by {2:Smith et al. (2020)} and {1:Dong et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 patients from 2 unrelated families (F1442 and F2382) with SENEBAC, {2:Smith et al. (2020)} identified homozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations ({615322.0001}, {615322.0002}) in the NRROS gene, predicted to result in truncated proteins and a loss of function. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 6 patients from 4 unrelated families with SENEBAC, {1:Dong et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the NRROS gene ({615322.0003}-{615322.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. None were present in the gnomAD database. Five patients from 3 families carried homozygous frameshift mutations, and 1 patient (family 4) was compound heterozygous for a frameshift mutation and a missense variant. In vitro functional expression studies of 2 of the frameshift mutations ({615322.0003} and {615322.0004}), which occurred in the last exon (exon 3), showed that both mutant truncated proteins were expressed and localized properly to the ER in transfected HEK293 cells. They interacted with latent TGFB1 ({190180}) similar to wildtype, although the mutant proteins formed aggregates in the cell, whereas wildtype NRROS did not. Flow cytometric analysis showed that cells transfected with the mutations had decreased TGFB1 on the cell surface compared to wildtype, suggesting improper folding or intracellular sequestration of latent TGFB1; these defects could be rescued by expression of wildtype NRROS. The findings were consistent with a loss of function. {1:Dong et al. (2020)} hypothesized that the NRROS mutations impaired the ability to anchor latent TGFB1 on the cell surface, which is required for activation of TGFB1 signaling. This disruption may result in uncontrolled microglial activation owing to the loss of TGFB1 inhibitory activity, resulting in the downstream effects of a disordered response to inflammation, causing abnormal neuroinflammation and neuronal cell death.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Wong et al. (2017)} found that Nrros-null mice developed progressive neurodegeneration around 6 to 8 weeks of age. Features included tremor, unstable gait, hunched posture, and eventual hind-limb paralysis and urinary incontinence. Most died by 6 months of age. Postmortem examination of the brain did not show an inflammatory infiltrate, although there was abnormal accumulation of nonparenchymal perivascular macrophage-like cells and evidence of astrogliosis. Immunostaining of the CNS of wildtype mice showed localization of Nrros mainly in microglia and CNS-resident macrophages. Further detailed studies suggested that Nrros is important for the early development and homeostatic maintenance of microglia in the prenatal and early developing brain.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that progressive myoclonic epilepsy-11 (EPM11) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SEMA6B gene ({608873}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Progressive myoclonic epilepsy-11 (EPM11) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by onset of developmental regression and various types of seizures around 2 years of age after relatively normal early development. The seizures are usually refractory to treatment and are associated with multiple abnormalities on EEG. During the first and second decades, affected individuals develop additional neurologic signs and symptoms, including pyramidal, extrapyramidal, and cerebellar signs such as spasticity, loss of independent ambulation, myoclonus, tremor, and ataxia. Cognitive impairment is severe, and patients can speak only a few words or are non-verbal (summary by {1:Hamanaka et al., 2020}).

For discussion of genetic heterogeneity of progressive myoclonic epilepsy, see EPM1A ({254800}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Hamanaka et al. (2020)} reported 4 unrelated patients, ranging from 11 to 28 years of age, with EPM11. Two were Japanese, 1 was Israeli, and 1 was Malaysian. The patients had mostly normal early development, although some had delayed speech and/or mildly delayed motor milestones with walking around 2 years of age. However, beginning around age 2 years, all showed significant developmental regression and stagnation. Between 18 months and 6 years, the patients developed various forms of epilepsy, which was refractory to treatment in 3 of the patients. Seizure types included atonic seizures with drop attacks, absence seizures, complex partial, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures; the types of seizures varied over time, even in the same individual. One patient developed daily repetitive atonic seizures thought to be negative myoclonus. EEG showed multiple abnormalities, including focal discharges, multifocal spikes, diffuse irregular spike-wave discharges, diffuse slow waves of high amplitude, and spike and polyspike slow-wave discharges during sleep. Later during the disease course, patients developed cerebellar ataxia as well as pyramidal and extrapyramidal/parkinsonian features, including shaking hands, intention tremor, myoclonus, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and muscle rigidity. Myoclonic episodes gradually increased over time. Somatosensory evoked potential (SEP) findings, performed in 2 patients, showed prolonged latency and high amplitudes compared to normal, suggesting cortical disturbance. At last examination, all patients had severe cognitive impairment with poor or absent speech; IQ measured in 2 patients was 25. All had significant walking difficulties: 3 were wheelchair-bound and the fourth could walk only with support. Brain imaging was normal in 2 patients, but showed mild cerebellar atrophy in the other 2. Three patients had a small head circumference (down to -2.5 SD), but none had dysmorphic features. {1:Hamanaka et al. (2020)} concluded that the phenotype, which included pyramidal signs indicating involvement of excitatory neurons in layer 5 of the cerebral cortex, SEP anomalies involving neurons in the somatosensory cortex, and cerebellar abnormalities, was consistent with involvement of several brain regions.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SEMA6B gene that were identified in patients with EPM11 by {1:Hamanaka et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 unrelated patients with EPM11, {1:Hamanaka et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous frameshift mutations in the last exon of the SEMA6B gene ({608873.0001}-{608873.0003}). The mutations, which were found by a sequencing technique using enrichment analysis for mutations predicted to escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The mutations were predicted to result in the production of truncated proteins lacking the intracellular domain. Truncating variants in this region of the gene were not observed in the gnomAD database, although truncating variants in other regions of the gene were observed in gnomAD. RNA analysis of lymphoblastoid cells derived from 1 patient showed that a truncated protein was produced. Cells from the other patients were not available, and functional studies of the variants were not performed. The authors postulated a dominant-negative or gain-of-function effect rather than haploinsufficiency. The patients were ascertained from several large cohorts of patients, totaling over 6,000 individuals, with variable developmental disorders who underwent genetic testing.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Hamanaka et al. (2020)} found that zebrafish with distal truncating variants affecting the intracellular domain of sema6b orthologs which escaped nonsense-mediated mRNA decay had defective brain development and were more susceptible to seizures compared to wildtype. In addition, zebrafish with loss-of-function mutations had less severe abnormalities compared to those with distal truncating mutations, indicating that the truncating mutations exert a more detrimental toxic effect than loss-of-function mutations.

phenotypes.phenotype: Leukoencephalopathy, developmental delay, and episodic neurologic regression syndrome

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that leukoencephalopathy, developmental delay, and episodic neurologic regression syndrome (LEUDEN) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the EIF2AK2 gene ({176871}) on chromosome 2p22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Leukoencephalopathy, developmental delay, and episodic neurologic regression syndrome (LEUDEN) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent in early childhood, followed by episodic neurologic regression or decompensation associated with systemic stress, such as febrile infection. Affected individuals have hypotonia, gait difficulties or ataxia, poor or absent speech with dysarthria, and variable motor abnormalities, including spasticity, dystonia, extrapyramidal signs, and tremor. Many patients have seizures. Brain imaging shows diffuse white matter abnormalities, poor myelination, thin corpus callosum, and generalized cerebral atrophy with enlarged ventricles. The clinical features of the disorder and the abnormal brain imaging findings are progressive (summary by {1:Mao et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Mao et al. (2020)} reported 8 unrelated children, between 18 months and 13 years of age, with LEUDEN syndrome. The patients presented in infancy with global developmental delay, often associated with additional neurologic signs, including nystagmus, seizures, and hypotonia. Most had poor overall growth, mildly delayed walking by 2 years of age, and delayed speech with dysarthria, although patient 9 was nonambulatory and nonverbal at age 4 years. The patients showed progressive loss of developmental milestones associated with fever and illnesses, suggesting neurologic decompensation during stress. The disorder was progressive, and the regression often occurred abruptly, including loss of speech, poor eye contact, postural instability, and a decline in motor skills. Common persistent features included dystonia, truncal or gait ataxia, hypotonia, hypertonia with spasticity and hyperreflexia, tremor, bradykinesia, and parkinsonism. All patients had cognitive impairment, although the older ones were able to attend special schools. One patient had severe involuntary motor abnormalities, including myoclonus, hemiballismus, and choreoathetosis. Four patients had seizures, including focal complex and generalized, and a few had progressive microcephaly (down to -3 SD). A few had nonspecific dysmorphic features, including short philtrum, retrognathia, hypotelorism, fifth finger or toe clinodactyly, esotropia, astigmatism, strabismus, and progressive contractures. Brain imaging in all patients showed T2-weighted hyperintensities in the subcortical white matter, periventricular white matter, and sometimes in the brainstem or spinal cord, consistent with diffuse leukoencephalopathy. Other brain imaging findings included diffuse hypomyelination, thin corpus callosum, cerebellar atrophy, and generalized cerebral atrophy with enlarged ventricles. One patient had polymicrogyria.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in EIF2AK2 gene that were identified in patients with LEUDEN syndrome by {1:Mao et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 unrelated children with LEUDEN syndrome, {1:Mao et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the EIF2AK2 gene (see, e.g., {176871.0001}-{176871.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. The mutations were spread throughout the gene, but most occurred in the kinase or double-stranded RNA-binding motif (DSRM) domains. Studies of fibroblasts derived from 3 patients showed that the mutant proteins were stably expressed, but had decreased kinase activity toward EIF2S1 ({603907}) compared to wildtype. Patient cells also showed decreased levels of the downstream regulator ATF4 ({604064}), and 2 of the cell lines showed impaired response to stress induced by poly(I:C) treatment. {1:Mao et al. (2020)} concluded that reduced EIF2S1 phosphorylation would interfere with downstream molecular pathways critical for responding to cellular stressors, which may lead to neurologic decompensation and damage. These downstream effects may impact the EIF2B protein complex, which activates the stress response: biallelic mutations in related EIF2B genes, including EIF2B1 ({606686}) and EIF2B2 ({606454}), are associated with an overlapping phenotype (see VWM, {603896}). Given that EIF2AK2 requires dimerization for the kinase to function, the authors postulated a dominant-negative effect as the pathogenetic mechanism, rather than haploinsufficiency or a gain-of-function effect.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and cerebellar atrophy, with or without seizures (NEDHCAS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PIGK gene ({605087}) on chromosome 1p31.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and cerebellar atrophy, with or without seizures (NEDHCAS) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, delayed motor skills, and poor or absent speech. Most patients develop early-onset seizures and demonstrate cerebellar ataxia or dysmetria associated with progressive cerebellar atrophy on brain imaging. The disorder is caused by a defect in glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) biosynthesis (summary by {2:Nguyen et al., 2020}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of GPI biosynthesis defects, see GPIBD1 ({610293}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Nguyen et al. (2020)} reported 12 patients from 9 unrelated families with NEDHCAS. Most of the patients were under 10 years of age, but 2 Italian sibs (family 2) were 19 and 27 years old. The patients, who were identified through whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. Four families were consanguineous: F2 of Italian descent, F5 of Egyptian descent, and F8 and F9, both of Pakistani descent. The parents in F4 (Egyptian) and F6 (Nigerian) came from the same village. The patients presented in infancy or early childhood with global developmental delay and hypotonia; some had poor feeding and poor overall growth. Five patients had delayed walking, up to 7 or 8 years in some, and often with an ataxic or unsteady gait, whereas 7 patients were not able to walk independently, even as late as 8 years (patient 1a). Intellectual disability was variable, ranging from mild to severe, but all had poor language development and several were nonverbal. IQ was 58 and 60 in the 2 patients who were tested. Other neurologic features included poor fine motor coordination, dysmetria, nystagmus, abnormal saccades, mild spasticity with hyperreflexia, and abnormal involuntary movements. Seven patients developed variable types of seizures associated with EEG abnormalities between birth and 2 years of age; most were well-controlled by medication. Dysmorphic features, which were variable and nonspecific, included long face, triangular face, myopathic face, plagiocephaly, small head circumference, prominent forehead, high anterior hairline, long philtrum, synophrys, sparse lateral eyebrows, hypotelorism, strabismus or esotropia, squint, broad nose, low-set ears, abnormal ear shape, thin upper lip, dental crowding or tooth anomalies, and brachydactyly. Brain imaging showed progressive cerebellar atrophy or hypoplasia in 10 patients, sometimes with other nonspecific findings, such as decreased white matter and thin corpus callosum.

{1:Chen et al. (2021)} described 2 Chinese sibs with NEDHCAS. The older sib (patient 1) had recurrent seizures starting at 4 months of age, and severe hypotonia, lack of head control, strabismus, and nystagmus. At age 14 months, he was found to have microcephaly. Brain MRI at age 2 years and 8 months demonstrated progressive global brain atrophy and delayed myelination. Physical examination demonstrated dysmorphic facial features, including high-arched eyebrows, epicanthus, short anteverted nose, high-arched palate, tented lip, and retrognathia. He died at the age of 3 years and 4 months due to respiratory complications. The younger sib (patient 2) had a similar clinical course, including acquired microcephaly, hypotonia, dysmorphic features, and similar brain MRI findings. He died at age 1 year due to respiratory complications.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDHCAS in the families reported by {2:Nguyen et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 12 patients from 9 unrelated families with NEDHCAS, {2:Nguyen et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PIGK gene (see, e.g., {605087.0001}-{605087.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. There were missense, nonsense, and splice site mutations, although none of the patients were homozygous for a nonsense or splice site mutation. Flow cytometric analysis of available patient peripheral blood cells showed variably decreased cell surface expression (5 to 35% of controls) of GPI-anchored proteins, particularly CD16 (see {146740}), as well as decreased cell-surface expression of FLAER, a marker for all GPI-anchored proteins. Expression of wildtype PIGK rescued the GPI protein defect in cells derived from patient 1a. In vitro functional expression studies in PIGK-deficient CHO cells showed that 2 of the missense variants (C275R, {605087.0001} and S53F, {605087.0002}) were unable to fully rescue the GPI-anchor defect, suggesting that they are loss-of-function or hypomorphic alleles.

By whole-exome sequencing in 2 Chinese sibs with NEDHCAS, {1:Chen et al. (2021)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the PIGK gene ({605087.0007}-{605087.0008}). In lymphoblastoid cell lines from both patients, PIGK mRNA expression was increased, but protein was expression decreased. PIGK protein expression was also reduced in both carrier parents, indicating that both mutations lead to decreased protein abundance. Flow cytometry showed reduced abundance of FLAER, a marker for GPI-anchored proteins, on the surface of lymphoblastoid cells from both sibs. Homozygosity for either mutation in PIGK was embryonic lethal in knock-in CRISPR-edited mice.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that familial isolated hypoparathyroidism-2 (FIH2) is caused by homozygous mutation in the glial cells missing transcription factor-2 gene (GCM2; {603716}) on chromosome 6p24. Some patients have been reported with heterozygous mutations in the GCM2 gene.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Patients with familial isolated hypoparathyroidism-2 (FIH2) usually present with seizures, caused by hypocalcemia, in early life. Serum parathyroid hormone (PTH; {168450}) levels are low to undetectable. Hyperphosphatemia is present, and levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D may be within the normal range. Development can be normal if hypocalcemia is treated with calcium and vitamin D supplementation ({5:Ding et al., 2001}). Some patients have been found to lack parathyroid glands ({8:Thomee et al., 2005}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of familial isolated hypoparathyroidism, see FIH1 ({146200}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{5:Ding et al. (2001)} studied a large 4-generation Central American family in which 3 individuals had isolated hypoparathyroidism. The proband was a 32-month-old female who had presented with seizures at 5 weeks of age. Serum calcium was 5.1 mg/dl, serum phosphorus was 9.8 mg/dl, and serum concentration of intact PTH was undetectable. Serum concentration of 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 7 ng/ml (normal range 5-42), and of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D was 34 pg/ml (normal range 8-72). The diagnosis of hypoparathyroidism, presumably congenital, was made, and after treatment with calcitriol and supplemental calcium she experienced no further seizures. She reached all cognitive and developmental milestones appropriately. Serum concentration of PTH at 8 months of age was below the detectable limit, with corresponding serum calcium concentrations 7.0 and 8.0 mg/dl. At 19 months of age serum concentration of intact PTH was 10 pg/ml (normal range 10-65) with a corresponding serum calcium concentration of 9.6 mg/dl. Physical examination was normal and growth was parallel but below the second percentile, consistent with predicted adult height reflecting her unaffected parents' short stature. The proband's 22-year-old uncle had experienced seizures at 2 months of age and was presumed to have hypoparathyroidism. He resided in a chronic care facility and was unable to walk, talk, or attend to daily needs. A 24-year-old female cousin developed seizures at 2 weeks of age with low serum calcium and received a diagnosis of hypoparathyroidism; she was treated with vitamin D and calcium and was attending college.

{1:Baumber et al. (2005)} studied a consanguineous 5-generation Pakistani family with 4 individuals presenting in early life with isolated hypoparathyroidism. Three individuals presented in infancy with seizures; hypocalcemia and low PTH levels were detected, and treatment with vitamin D and calcium supplementation was initiated. Due to family history the fourth individual was screened for hypocalcemia shortly after birth, enabling diagnosis and treatment.

{8:Thomee et al. (2005)} studied 2 sibs, the children of first-cousin Moroccan parents, with isolated hypoparathyroidism and low but clearly detectable PTH levels. The proband was a boy who presented at the age of 5 years with a 3-day history of episodic falls, generalized stiffness, pallor, ocular revulsion, and loss of consciousness lasting less than 1 minute. He was positive for the Chvostek sign bilaterally. Hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia were present. Levels of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D were normal, but 25-hydroxyvitamin D was low. Calcemia and phosphatemia returned to normal after calcium and calcitriol treatment, but serum PTH decreased, and increased to low-normal values after treatment was stopped. The proband's 8-year-old sister presented with cardiorespiratory arrest associated with profound hypocalcemia at age 10 months. Investigation showed inappropriately normal serum PTH and normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Treatment with calcium and calcitriol was initiated, but compliance was poor, and the patient experienced repeated episodes of severe hypocalcemia with low but near normal serum PTH and hypocalciuria. Epilepsy, progressive microcephaly, and severe neurologic impairment followed, which were ascribed to the initial anoxic episode. Ultrasound failed to detect parathyroid glands in either child.

{2:Bowl et al. (2010)} studied 8 families from the Indian subcontinent with FIH2. Most patients presented with seizures in the first days or weeks of life, although one patient presented at 1 year of age and another at age 25 years. Serum PTH was undetectable in 4 patients.

{7:Mannstadt et al. (2008)} described 2 families with autosomal dominant hypoparathyroidism. The proband in family A, originally reported as family H by {4:D'Souza-Li et al. (2002)}, had low total serum calcium detected on routine blood testing. Retrospectively, she had experienced episodic carpopedal spasms and perioral tingling for the 5 years preceding the diagnostic workup. Further laboratory investigations revealed hyperphosphatemia and an inappropriately low intact PTH. She gave birth to a son who had a hypocalcemic seizure on day 3 of life. The index case in family B presented at age 35 years with muscle cramps, tetany, and psychiatric symptoms. Laboratory evaluation revealed biochemical findings typical for hypoparathyroidism. Family history revealed 9 additional family members treated with vitamin D supplementation and calcium because of hypocalcemia. Three of the symptomatic family members had clinical manifestations of hypocalcemia before age 10, including seizures in 2 subjects.

{3:Canaff et al. (2009)} also reported an update on the family (family H) originally reported by {4:D'Souza-Li et al. (2002)}. Following the hypocalcemic seizure experienced by the proband on day 3 of life, treatment was initiated with calcitriol. After 12 days his serum calcium normalized and treatment was discontinued. At 8 years of age, he began experiencing multiple episodes of muscle cramps and was found to be hypocalcemic with an inappropriately low serum PTH. All other family members were normocalcemic.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The transmission pattern of FIH2 in the families studied by {5:Ding et al. (2001)}, {1:Baumber et al. (2005)}, {8:Thomee et al. (2005)}, and {2:Bowl et al. (2010)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

The transmission pattern of FIH2 in 2 families reported by {7:Mannstadt et al. (2008)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: Hypocalcemia resulting in seizures can be corrected by calcium and vitamin D supplementation ({5:Ding et al., 2001}, {1:Baumber et al., 2005}).

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In the proband of an extensive kindred with familial isolated hypoparathyroidism, {5:Ding et al. (2001)} identified homozygosity for a large intragenic deletion in the GCM2 gene ({603716.0001}). The nonconsanguineous, asymptomatic parents were heterozygous for the deletion. Haplotype analysis revealed shared genotypes that flanked the GCM2 gene over 5 cM, suggesting a founder effect with homozygosity by descent of the chromosomal segment containing the GCM2 deletion. {5:Ding et al. (2001)} concluded that homozygous loss of function of the GCM2 gene impairs normal parathyroid gland embryology and is responsible for isolated hypoparathyroidism in a subset of patients.

In affected members of a consanguineous Pakistani family with familial isolated hypoparathyroidism, {1:Baumber et al. (2005)} identified homozygosity for a missense mutation in the GCM2 gene (R47L; {603716.0002}).

In 2 sibs from a consanguineous Moroccan family with FIH2, {8:Thomee et al. (2005)} detected homozygosity for a missense mutation in the DNA-binding GCM domain of the GCM2 protein (G63S; {603716.0003}).

{2:Bowl et al. (2010)} identified 4 different homozygous mutations in the GCM2 gene in 8 families with FIH2 from the Indian subcontinent (e.g., {603716.0002}, {603716.0004}).

In 2 families with FIH2, {7:Mannstadt et al. (2008)} detected heterozygous frameshift mutations in the last exon of the GCM2 gene (c.1389delT, {603716.0007}; c.1399delC, {603716.0008}). The mutant GCM2 proteins were well expressed, and both showed dose-dependent inhibition of the transactivation capacity of wildtype protein in luciferase reporter assays.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: Glial cells missing-2 (Gcm2), a mouse homolog of Drosophila Gcm, is the only transcription factor with expression restricted to the parathyroid glands (see {603716}). {6:Gunther et al. (2000)} generated mice deficient in Gcm2 by targeted disruption. The Gcm2-deficient mice lacked parathyroid glands but, unlike PTH-receptor-deficient mice, were viable and fertile and had only a mildly abnormal bone phenotype. The conditionally deleted mice exhibited hypocalcemia associated with hyperphosphatemia and increased calcium elimination in the urine without evidence of renal failure, features characteristic of hypoparathyroidism. Despite their lack of parathyroid glands, the Gcm2-deficient mice had PTH serum levels identical to those of wildtype mice, as did parathyroidectomized wildtype mice. Expression and ablation studies identified the thymus, where Gcm1 ({603715}), another Gcm homolog, is expressed, as an additional, downregulatable source of PTH. Thus, Gcm2 deletion uncovered an auxiliary mechanism for the regulation of calcium homeostasis in the absence of parathyroid glands. {6:Gunther et al. (2000)} suggested that this backup mechanism may be a general feature of endocrine regulation.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIt (CDG2t) is caused by homozygous mutation in the GALNT2 gene ({602274}) on chromosome 1q41.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIt (CDG2t) is an autosomal recessive multisystemic metabolic disorder characterized by global developmental delay, poor overall growth, severely impaired intellectual development with absent language, and behavioral abnormalities. Most patients develop early-onset seizures; brain imaging tends to show white matter abnormalities. Variable dysmorphic features, including long face, almond-shaped eyes, protruding maxilla, and short philtrum, are also present. The disorder, which is associated with low levels of HDL cholesterol, results from defective posttranslational O-linked glycosylation of certain plasma lipids and proteins (summary by {2:Zilmer et al., 2020}).

For an overview of congenital disorders of glycosylation, see CDG1A ({212065}) and CDG2A ({212066}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Khetarpal et al. (2016)} reported 2 unrelated patients with low levels of HDL cholesterol associated with loss-of-function mutations in the GALNT2 gene. Clinical details were limited, but the first patient, a 25-year-old woman of Moroccan descent, had 'neurologic traits,' and the second patient, a 6-year-old boy of Pakistani descent, had 'intellectual disability.'

{2:Zilmer et al. (2020)} reported 7 patients, ranging in age from 4 to 20 years, from 4 unrelated families with CDG2T. Family 1, a consanguineous family of Pakistani descent, had previously been reported by {1:Khetarpal et al. (2016)}. Families 2 (Italian) and 3 (Syrian) both had parents or grandparents from the same geographic region, and family 4 was a consanguineous Egyptian family. The patients presented in early infancy with global developmental delay, hypotonia, delayed walking between 13 months and 6 years, and severely impaired intellectual development with poor speech and absent language. They had poor overall growth, sometimes with feeding difficulties and constipation. Three had short stature and 2 had microcephaly. Most had poor eye contact and behavioral problems, such as autistic features, stereotypic movements, poor communication, and chronic insomnia. Most were incontinent and dependent for activities of daily living. All but 1 (patient F) developed multifocal seizures in the first years of life. Three patients had refractory seizures, but the others had response to medication. A few had eye problems, such as strabismus, myopic astigmatism, and nystagmus. Brain imaging showed diffuse nonspecific subcortical white matter lesions in most patients. The patients also had dysmorphic facial features, including elongated face, high forehead, almond-shaped eyes, protruding maxilla, short philtrum, low-set, posteriorly rotated ears, and full lips with tented upper lip. More variable findings included downslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, abnormal eyebrows, high nasal bridge, and large mouth with macrodontia. Several patients had small hands and small feet with sandal gap. Brain imaging showed diffuse nonspecific subcortical white matter lesions. Laboratory studies showed decreased levels of HDL cholesterol, variably decreased fasting triglycerides, iron deficiency anemia in 4 patients, and low vitamin D in 6.

diagnosis.title: Diagnosis
diagnosis.content: {2:Zilmer et al. (2020)} demonstrated that lack of O-glycosylation of APOC3 ({107720}) is an accurate biomarker of CDG2T.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDG2T in the families reported by {2:Zilmer et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 unrelated probands with CDG2T associated with decreased plasma HDL cholesterol, {1:Khetarpal et al. (2016)} identified 2 homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the GALNT2 gene (F104S, {602274.0001} and Q289X, {602274.0002}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families; neither was present in public population databases, including ExAC. Recombinant protein containing the F104S mutation was unable to O-glycosylate apoC-III (APOC3; {107720}) or IgA1, 2 targets of the wildtype protein. {1:Khetarpal et al. (2016)} also showed that GALNT2 SNP alleles identified in genomewide association studies as being associated with lower HDL-C reduce hepatic GALNT2 gene expression.

In 5 patients from 3 unrelated families (families 2-4) with CDG2T, {2:Zilmer et al. (2020)} identified homozygous mutations in the GALNT2 gene ({602274.0003}-{602274.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Plasma analysis showed that all patients had loss of O-glycosylation of APOC3, consistent with a loss-of-function effect of the mutations.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{1:Khetarpal et al. (2016)} showed in mouse, rat, and cynomolgus monkey that knockout or knockdown of GALNT2 results in reduced HDL-C.

{2:Zilmer et al. (2020)} found that complete knockdown of Galnt2 in mice resulted in significant embryonic lethality. The animals that survived had poor overall growth, abnormal craniofacial features with decreased snout length, and behavioral abnormalities, such as increased activity, poor motor skills, disrupted responses to acoustic stimuli, and impaired social skills.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that pseudo-TORCH syndrome-3 (PTORCH3) is caused by homozygous mutation in the STAT2 gene ({600556}) on chromosome 12q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Pseudo-TORCH syndrome-3 (PTORCH3) is an autosomal recessive disorder of immune dysregulation and neuroinflammation apparent from early infancy. Affected individuals have developmental delay with acute episodes of fever and multisystemic organ involvement, including coagulopathy, elevated liver enzymes, and proteinuria, often associated with thrombotic microangiopathy. Brain imaging shows progressive intracranial calcifications, white matter abnormalities, and sometimes cerebral or cerebellar atrophy. Laboratory studies show abnormal elevation of interferon (IFN)-stimulated gene (ISG) transcripts consistent with a type I interferonopathy. The phenotype resembles the sequelae of intrauterine infection, but there is usually no evidence of an infectious agent. The disorder results from defects in negative regulation of the interferon immunologic pathway. Death in early childhood is common (summary by {1:Duncan et al., 2019} and {2:Gruber et al., 2020}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of PTORCH, see PTORCH1 ({251290}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Duncan et al. (2019)} reported 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Pakistani parents, with onset of a severe multisystemic inflammatory disorder soon after birth. Both infants were born prematurely, at 32 and 34 weeks' gestation, due to premature rupture of membranes. The first brother had transient neonatal thrombocytopenia without evidence of infection, and was later noted to have neurodevelopmental delay, poor growth, and thyroid dysfunction around 6 months. At 8 months, he presented with the first of 3 episodes of marked systemic and neuroinflammatory disease manifest as generalized tonic-clonic seizures, lethargy, and developmental regression. He was found to be septic with pneumococcal blood infection and multiorgan dysfunction, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, increased D-dimers, thrombocytopenia, raised ferritin and LDH, elevated liver enzymes, and acute kidney injury with hypertension and nephrotic range proteinuria. He recovered from this episode and showed mild developmental progress, but had additional similar episodes with seizures, developmental regression, and multisystem involvement without evidence of infection; autoantibody screening was normal. He met the diagnostic criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and had features of renal thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA). Brain imaging showed progressive diffuse intracranial calcification, white matter disease, and intracranial hemorrhage. He died of infection during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation at age 20 months. His younger brother had similar disease course characterized by abnormal neurodevelopment apparent from early infancy. At about 3 weeks of age, he developed apneic episodes, anemia, coagulation anomalies, and proteinuria associated with brain imaging anomalies, such as intracranial parenchymal calcifications and hemorrhage, abnormal cerebral white matter, and brainstem and cerebellar atrophy. There was no evidence of infection. He continued to have neurologic regression and showed dystonia and EEG abnormalities, consistent with severe neurologic damage. He died at 14 weeks of age. Blood analysis in both patients showed an elevation in IFN-stimulated gene (ISG) transcripts, which partially responded to treatment with ruxolitinib.

{2:Gruber et al. (2020)} reported a boy, born of consanguineous Moroccan parents who presented with an early-onset, severe autoinflammation syndrome consistent with type I interferonopathy. After birth, he received the BCG vaccine without secondary effects. At age 15 days, he presented with diarrhea, oral thrush, and adenitis associated with Klebsiella and Pseudomonas infection. Antibiotic treatment resulted in clinical improvement, but he was noted to have bronchiolitis and seizures unrelated to the fever. Brain imaging showed bilateral cerebral calcifications. At age 5 months, he presented again with acute respiratory distress in the absence of infection; he died soon thereafter of respiratory failure. Two sibs had previously died from complications that appeared infectious in origin, but without an identified pathogen. Detailed studies of blood from the proband showed increased levels of ISGs, including IFIT1 ({147690}), IFI27 ({600009}), RSAD2 ({607810}), and ISG15 ({147571}), all of which were elevated nearly 1,000-fold in the patient as compared with healthy donors or the heterozygous mother. Patient plasma also showed very high levels of IFN-alpha, confirming a type I interferonopathy, as well as low frequencies of natural killer (NK) cells and monocytes, and elevations in T cells, suggesting a dysregulated immunophenotype.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PTORCH3 in the family reported by {1:Duncan et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Pakistani parents, with PTORCH3, {1:Duncan et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the STAT2 gene (R148W; {600556.0003}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was found only in the heterozygous state at a very low frequency in the gnomAD database. STAT2 protein expression was unaffected in patient cells. RNA and RT-PCR analysis of patient blood showed increased IFN-stimulated gene (ISG) gene expression, consistent with a type I interferonopathy. Basal and induced production of beta-interferon (IFNB1; {147640}) and alpha-interferon (IFNA1; {147660}) were similar to controls, although these samples were acquired during treatment. Patient cells and STAT2-null cells transduced with the mutation showed a similar heightened sensitivity to IFNA1, consistent with an abnormally enhanced response upon exposure to interferon, rather than constitutive activation of STAT2. The abnormalities were associated with prolonged IFNAR ({107450}) signaling in patient cells, but not in parental cells carrying the heterozygous mutation, which the authors noted is unusual for gain-of-function mutations. Further in vitro studies showed that the R148W mutation impaired the interaction of STAT2 with the negative regulator USP18 ({607057}), resulting in desensitization to the negative regulation normally conferred by USP18. Knockdown of USP18 in control cells resulted in prolonged STAT2 phosphorylation, recapitulating the phenotype of patient cells. In contrast, USP18 was unable to suppress IFN-alpha signaling in patient cells; knockdown of USP18 in patients cells also had no effect, indicating insensitivity to USP18. The findings were consistent with an inability of patient cells to properly restrain IFNAR signaling, which results in an inflammatory disease consistent with a type I interferonopathy. {1:Duncan et al. (2019)} noted that the loss of negative regulation of IFNAR signaling, due to the STAT2 mutation, behaves as a recessive trait with an overall gain-of-function effect on the IFN signaling pathway.

In a boy, born of consanguineous Moroccan parents, with PTORCH3, {2:Gruber et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the STAT2 gene (R148Q; {600556.0004}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was found in the heterozygous state in the unaffected mother; paternal DNA was not available. The authors noted that the R148 residue is highly conserved in mammals, but not in rodents. Prolonged IFN1 stimulation of patient cells and of STAT2-null cells transduced with the mutation resulting in increased expression of ISGs compared to controls, consistent with a gain-of-function effect. Notably, expression of wildtype STAT2 resulted in normalization of the defects, showing that biallelic mutation is required for the effect. Immunoprecipitation studies in patient fibroblasts showed reduced ability of R148Q STAT2 to recruit USP18 to the IFNAR2 ({602376}) receptor complex, although affinity between mutant STAT2 and USP18 appeared to be normal. Patient cells were unable to attenuate signaling in response to IFN1 even in the presence of USP18, suggesting that USP18 was functionally null, perhaps due to a trafficking defect of USP18 to the IFNAR receptor. {2:Gruber et al. (2020)} noted that homozygous gain-of-function mutations are rare, and suggested that they must disrupt negative regulatory processes to be pathogenic, as in this case.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Liberfarb syndrome (LIBF) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PISD gene ({612770}) on chromosome 22q12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Liberfarb syndrome (LIBF) is a progressive disorder involving connective tissue, bone, retina, ear, and brain. Patients exhibit severe short stature and scoliosis with thoracic kyphosis and lumbar hyperlordosis. Severe joint laxity results in dislocations of elbows, hips, and knees. Eye findings are consistent with early-onset retinal degeneration, and there is moderate to severe early-onset hearing loss. Microcephaly is apparent by school age, and patients exhibit developmental delay and intellectual deficits ({3:Peter et al., 2019}). Clinical variability has been observed, with some patients presenting differences in the severity and location of skeletal dysplasia involvement as well as variation in other features of the syndrome ({1:Girisha et al., 2019}; {4:Zhao et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Liberfarb et al. (1986)} described an 11-year-old girl with severe pigmentary degeneration of the retina associated with severe musculoskeletal abnormalities, growth failure, recurrent respiratory problems, sensorineural hearing loss, and mental retardation. The musculoskeletal abnormalities included short long bones, hyperextensible joints, scoliosis, lordosis, spina bifida occulta, dislocated radial heads, dislocated hips, and valgus deformities of the knees with laterally dislocated patellae. At 9.3 years of age, she exhibited severe short stature and low weight, with height of 87.5 cm and weight of 10 kg (average for a 25-month-old and 15-month-old child, respectively). Subglottic stenosis, discovered during an episode of croup at age 7 years, persisted despite multiple tracheal revisions. The proband developed difficulties with night vision at age 7.5 years; at age 11, she had visual acuity of 20/80 bilaterally that did not improve with pinhole. Fundus examination showed pale optic discs and extremely attenuated retinal vessels. The entire circumference of the retina appeared atrophic, and there was heavy pigment deposition in the macula and circumferential periphery bilaterally. Electroretinographic (ERG) responses were reduced or nonrecordable, indicating widespread impairment of retinal function. Electrooculogram showed low amplitudes, suggesting impaired retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function, and pattern reversal visual evoked response showed severe impairment of the macula. Taken together, the electrophysiologic data indicated diffuse retinal dysfunction consistent with tapetoretinal degeneration. Hearing evaluation at age 10.5 years showed moderate to profound sensorineural hearing loss bilaterally. She had minimal receptive and expressive spoken language skills in English and in Portuguese, and was diagnosed with mild to moderate mental retardation. The authors designated the skeletal findings as a spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, but suggested that the severe ligamentous laxity rather than any primary abnormality might have caused the developmental malformations of the epiphyses and vertebrae. There was no family history of a similar phenotype and her parents were unaware of consanguinity; however, both of their families originated from the Azores.

{3:Peter et al. (2019)} followed up on the patient of {2:Liberfarb et al. (1986)}, noting that she had died at age 35 years of cardiac arrest and anoxic encephalopathy. They also noted that the parents were consanguineous.

{3:Peter et al. (2019)} reported 2 sets of brothers from 2 unrelated consanguineous families, from continental Portugal (family 1) and Brazil (family 2), who exhibited early-onset retinal degeneration, sensorineural hearing loss, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and skeletal dysplasia with progressive short stature and scoliosis. The authors noted that the phenotype of both sets of brothers was similar to that of the female patient reported by {2:Liberfarb et al. (1986)}. None of the patients had scoliosis or overt joint dislocations at birth, but the combination of epiphyseal dysplasia and joint laxity resulted in hip dislocation and severe genua valga as well as progressive, severe spinal deformation, with thoracic kyphosis, lumbar hyperlordosis, and a variable degree of scoliosis. There was markedly delayed ossification of all epiphyses, contributing to joint instability and retarded bone age, and fine metaphyseal striations were also observed in childhood. The authors classified this as a spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with predominant epiphyseal involvement, but noted that the severe joint instability and progressive severe spinal deformation were clinically more significant than the skeletal dysplasia. Another major feature was childhood-onset retinal degeneration, with pale optic discs, RPE mottling, severely reduced caliber of retinal vessels, and areas of bone-spicule pigment deposition. Microcephaly was not present at birth but was apparent by school age, at which time developmental delay was noted to be significant. Hearing loss also did not seem to be congenital but rather to develop in childhood. The authors designated the disorder Liberfarb syndrome.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{1:Girisha et al. (2019)} reported a 3-year-old girl (P1) and 9-year-old boy (P2) from unrelated Indian families with an 'unclassifiable' form of spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia and mutations in the PISD gene. The probands exhibited short stature, microcephaly, mild facial dysmorphism, platyspondyly, large epiphyses, metaphyseal dysplasia, and hallux valgus. The girl had kyphosis in infancy; additional features at 3 years of age included broad wrists and limited extension in both elbows. X-rays at 9 months of age showed platyspondyly with anterior beaking of the vertebrae, large epiphyses with serrated outlines of the proximal and distal femora and proximal tibiae, and generalized metaphyseal irregularities of the long bones; these features improved by 3 years of age. In addition, the iliac crests were irregular and lace-like. X-rays in the boy showed platyspondyly with wedge-shaped vertebrae, mildly large capital femoral epiphyses with coxa vara, and mild metaphyseal dysplasia of the long bones. The authors noted that the patients appeared to exhibit age-dependent differences, with metaphyseal dysplasia and megaepiphysis becoming less conspicuous with advancing age, and coxa vara becoming manifest at an older age. Vision and hearing were reported to be normal, and both had normal psychomotor development.

{4:Zhao et al. (2019)} studied 2 sisters with short stature and skeletal dysplasia and mutations in the PISD gene. Both had congenital cataracts and multiple respiratory illnesses in early childhood, as well as progressive short stature, sensorineural hearing loss, and mild global developmental delay. They exhibited a distinctive facial appearance with depressed nasal bridge and midface hypoplasia. Both had subglottic stenosis, which required tracheostomy in the older sister, who had residual stridor at age 28 years; the younger sister was also diagnosed with tracheomalacia and experienced respiratory decompensation at age 25 years. Skeletal survey in childhood was similar in both, and showed delayed bone age, mild thoracic platyspondyly, metaphyseal striations, and brachydactyly. Serial brain MRIs showed progressive volume loss and hypomyelination of the corpus callosum. {4:Zhao et al. (2019)} noted phenotypic similarities between the affected sisters and the 2 patients reported by {1:Girisha et al. (2019)}.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of LIBF in the families reported by {3:Peter et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

mapping.title: Mapping
mapping.content: In 2 unrelated consanguineous families with Liberfarb syndrome, from continental Portugal (family 1) and Brazil (family 2), negative for mutation in the KIF22 gene ({603213}), {3:Peter et al. (2019)} performed homozygosity mapping and identified a 3.36-Mb region on chromosome 22, which was not only fully homozygous in the 3 patients analyzed, but also showed the same haplotype in all 3 (chr22:29,456,733-32,811,952; GRCh37). The authors calculated that the size of the haplotype corresponded to approximately 9.92 meioses, suggesting that the Portuguese and Brazilian patients had a common ancestor about 5 generations earlier.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sets of brothers from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with Liberfarb syndrome mapping to chromosome 22, {3:Peter et al. (2019)} identified homozygosity for a 10-bp deletion in the PISD gene ({612770.0001}) that segregated with disease in both families. Targeted Sanger sequencing of DNA from the patient originally reported by {2:Liberfarb et al. (1986)} (LIB-001), extracted from a paraffin-embedded surgical biopsy of the esophagus, confirmed the presence of the same 10-bp deletion.

In an affected girl (P1) and boy (P2) from unrelated Indian families with an 'unclassifiable' form of spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, who were negative for mutation in known skeletal dysplasia-associated genes, {1:Girisha et al. (2019)} identified homozygosity for a missense mutation in the PISD gene (C266Y; {612770.0002}) that segregated with disease and was not found in controls or the gnomAD database. Analysis of regions of homozygosity indicated remote consanguinity between the 2 families.

In 2 sisters with progressive short stature and skeletal dysplasia, {4:Zhao et al. (2019)} identified compound heterozygosity for a missense mutation (R277Q; {612770.0003}) and a splicing mutation ({612770.0004}) in the PISD gene.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder and structural brain anomalies with or without seizures and spasticity

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder and structural brain anomalies with or without seizures and spasticity (NEDBASS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PTPN23 gene ({606584}) on chromosome 3p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder and structural brain anomalies with or without seizures and spasticity (NEDBASS) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent from early infancy, poor overall growth often with microcephaly, impaired intellectual development with delayed or absent speech, axial hypotonia, and peripheral spasticity. Additional common but variable features include early-onset seizures, optic atrophy with poor visual fixation, and dysmorphic facial features. Brain imaging shows cerebral atrophy, poor or absent myelination with loss of white matter volume, and often hypoplasia of the corpus callosum and/or cerebellum. Early death may occur (summary by {2:Bend et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Alazami et al. (2015)} reported a 5-year-old boy, born of consanguineous Saudi Arabian parents (family 08DG-00322), with developmental delay, seizures, and diffuse brain atrophy on MRI. {4:Sowada et al. (2017)} provided more detailed clinical features of this patient and family. The boy had profound global developmental delay, onset of mostly refractory seizures around 6 months of age, and cortical blindness with poor visual attention. He did not attain developmental milestones and was wheelchair-bound with spasticity, hypertonia, absent speech, lack of purposeful hand movements, and progressive microcephaly (-6 SD). Other features included scoliosis, failure to thrive, and severe hip dysplasia. EEG showed sharp waves, spikes, and slow waves with occasional polyspikes. Brain imaging showed enlarged ventricles, cerebellar hypoplasia, thin corpus callosum, progressive brain atrophy, and a severe reduction of white matter volume. He died of a chest infection at age 9 years. The family history was significant for 7 affected deceased sibs with a similar phenotype through 2 marriages of the father.

{5:Trujillano et al. (2017)} reported a child with global developmental delay, poor speech and language, motor delay, spasticity, seizures, microcephaly, and brain atrophy. He was also noted to have developmental regression. The patient was identified from a large study of 1,000 patients referred for genetic analysis of a suspected mendelian disorder; clinical details were limited.

{4:Sowada et al. (2017)} reported a girl, born of unrelated German parents, who presented in the first months of life with microcephaly (-2.6 SD), lack of visual fixation, axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, and poor feeding. She developed refractory severe seizures at 5 months of age, followed by developmental arrest. Seizures occurred daily and included myoclonic, tonic, and focal motor; EEG showed background slowing, frequent multifocal spikes, and hypsarrhythmia. She was tube-fed and had poor overall growth. Brain imaging showed reduced brain volume, particularly of the white matter, absent myelination, enlarged ventricles, hypoplastic optic nerves, and hypoplastic corpus callosum. She died of pneumonia just before 5 years of age.

{3:Smigiel et al. (2018)} reported a 6-year-old girl, born of unrelated Polish-Belarussian parents, with NEDBASS. She showed intrauterine growth retardation, hypotonia, and feeding problems at birth. She later had global developmental delay, severe spasticity, and onset of mostly refractory multifocal seizures around 2 years of age. She was microcephalic, deaf, and blind with optic nerve atrophy, thus having no visual contact and no verbal communication. At age 6, she could not walk, sit, or speak. Brain imaging showed severely impaired myelination, progressive cortical/subcortical atrophy, reduced white matter volume, enlarged ventricles, and cerebellar atrophy.

{2:Bend et al. (2020)} reported 7 unrelated patients, ranging from 14 months to 13 years of age, with NEDBASS. The patients, who were identified by whole-exome sequencing and multicentral international collaboration, presented in the first months or years of life with global developmental delay, variably delayed walking, sometimes with unsteady gait, and variably impaired intellectual development with speech and language delay or inability to verbalize. Most had abnormal muscle tone with spasticity: 2 were wheelchair-bound and unable to walk, and 3 had significant contractures. One patient had tremor and another had apraxia. Only 2 patients had seizures, in contrast to earlier reports. More variable features included axial hypotonia, optic atrophy, and visual impairment. Variable dysmorphic features were observed in most patients, including brachycephaly, prominent forehead, long face, malar hypoplasia, micrognathia, smooth or long philtrum, synophrys, thin eyebrows, strabismus, low-set or prominent ears, prominent nasal root, full or thin lips, broad mouth, and high-arched palate. Brain imaging was abnormal in all but 1 patient (patient 3), showing enlarged ventricles, brain atrophy, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, and delayed myelination. The most severely affected patient (patient 4) was a 7-year-old Syrian girl with microcephaly (-3 SD), spastic quadriparesis with multiple small and large joint contractures, no language, abnormal eye movements, and profound developmental delay. Brain imaging reportedly showed brain atrophy and lissencephaly. The least severely affected patient (patient 5), was a 10-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish girl with mild intellectual disability and difficulty in social interactions. She had hypoplasia of the optic nerves and dysmorphic features. Another child (patient 2) was able to attend special schooling.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDBASS in the families reported by {1:Alazami et al. (2015)} and {2:Bend et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 5-year-old boy, born of consanguineous Saudi Arabian parents with NEDBASS, {1:Alazami et al. (2015)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the PTPN23 gene (R1332L; {606584.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The family was part of a large cohort of 143 multiplex consanguineous families with various neurodevelopmental disorders who underwent whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In a patient with NEDBASS, {5:Trujillano et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the PTPN23 gene (M302V; {606584.0002}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. The patient was part of a large cohort of 1,000 patients from 54 countries with suspected mendelian diseases who were referred for exome sequencing.

In a 4.9-year-old girl, born of unrelated German parents, with NEDBASS, {4:Sowada et al. (2017)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the PTPN23 gene (R1196X, {606584.0003} and P532L, {606584.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were either very rare or absent in the gnomAD database. The nonsense mutation was inherited from the unaffected father, whereas the missense mutation could not be detected in the mother, suggesting that it occurred de novo or was low-grade mosaic. Structural modeling of the variants predicted that the R1196X variant would lead to a truncated protein lacking most of the phosphatase domain, and that the P532L variant would induce structural changes and cause instability of an important functional domain.

In a 6-year-old girl, born of unrelated parents from Poland and Belarusse, with NEDBASS, {3:Smigiel et al. (2018)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the PTPN23 gene (N634K, {606584.0005} and c.2974delC, {606584.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Neither variant was present in the gnomAD database. Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed loss of a slower migrating form of SMN1 ({600354}) compared to controls and to cells derived from the heterozygous father who carried the c.2974delC mutation. {3:Smigiel et al. (2018)} postulated that the slower SMN1 may have represented a phosphorylated form of the SMN1 protein, which was absent in the patient. In addition, patient cells showed decreased amounts of SMN1 that localized to Cajal bodies in the nucleus (22% of patient cells) compared to the amount of SMN1 that localized to Cajal bodies in control or the father's cells (50%). This abnormality was associated with increased nucleoplasmic SMN1 in patient cells. The findings suggested that the PTPN23 mutations may adversely affect UsnRNP assembly, which may affect mRNA splicing patterns of various genes.

In 7 unrelated patients with NEDBASS, {2:Bend et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PTPN23 gene (see, e.g., {606584.0007}-{606584.0009}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. There were 8 missense mutations, 1 frameshift, and 3 in-frame deletion variants. The mutations occurred throughout the gene and there was no apparent genotype-phenotype correlation, although the authors postulated that patients with 2 missense mutations may have a less severe phenotype than those with a complete loss-of-function mutation on 1 allele. None of the patients carried 2 complete loss-of-function alleles, suggesting that these may be embryonic lethal. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: Microcephaly, developmental delay, and brittle hair syndrome

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that microcephaly, developmental delay, and brittle hair syndrome (MDBH) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CARS1 gene ({123859}) on chromosome 11p15.

description.title: Description
description.content: Microcephaly, developmental delay, and brittle hair syndrome (MDBH) is a multisystem disorder with clinical variability. Affected individuals show cognitive and motor disabilities, as well as some degree of fine, brittle hair with microscopic shaft abnormalities. Other shared features include failure to thrive in early childhood and short stature, with some patients exhibiting feeding difficulties and hepatic steatosis ({1:Kuo et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Kuo et al. (2019)} reported 4 patients from 3 unrelated families who exhibited overlapping phenotypes and had biallelic mutations in the CARS1 gene. Shared features included short stature, failure to thrive, and developmental delay with motor, language, and cognitive disabilities, as well as an ataxic, wide-based gait. Some patients also exhibited behavioral issues such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, restlessness, and irritability. All 4 had thin, sparse, brittle hair with tiger-tail patterning on polarized light microscopy; some showed trichoschisis and/or trichorrhexis nodosa of the hair shafts, and some also had brittle or fragile nails. Hepatic steatosis was diagnosed in 3 patients, with 2 showing hepatomegaly, and 1 having cholestasis and fat malabsorption in infancy. Two patients were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes in the third decade of life. Two exhibited microcephaly. Findings on brain MRI included mild cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, delayed myelination, and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MDBH in the families reported by {1:Kuo et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients from 3 unrelated families with microcephaly, developmental delay, and brittle hair syndrome, {1:Kuo et al. (2019)} reported homozygosity or compound heterozygosity for mutations in the CARS1 gene ({123859.0001}-{123859.0005}). Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed significantly reduced CARS activity, consistent with a loss-of-function effect for the variants.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with autistic features and language delay, with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with autistic features and language delay, with or without seizures (IDDALDS), is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TANC2 gene ({615047}) on chromosome 17q23.

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with autistic features and language delay, with or without seizures (IDDALDS), is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay, variable intellectual disability, impaired speech development, and behavioral abnormalities, most commonly on the autism spectrum. About half of patients develop seizures; brain imaging is typically normal. Additional features are highly variable, but may include chronic constipation, walking difficulties, and dysmorphic facial features (summary by {3:Guo et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {3:Guo et al. (2019)} reported 20 unrelated probands with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. Two families (families NN2 and CF) contained 2 or 3 affected sibs, but most of the patients were singleton cases. The patients were ascertained through genetic analysis from several international collaborators; many were identified in large cohorts of patients with autism spectrum disorder. The patients, who ranged in age from childhood to adult, had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development and poor speech and language acquisition; a few were nonverbal. IQ, formally measured in some patients, ranged from about 40 to 90, and a few patients were noted to attend special schools. Many had mildly delayed early motor development, but they were able to walk independently, sometimes with a wide-based or unsteady gait. Almost all patients had behavioral abnormalities, most commonly autism or features of autism, such as stereotypic/repetitive movements and poor social skills. Aggression was rarely observed. About half of patients had seizures, with variable onset, type, and severity. Significant poor growth and/or feeding problems were not reported, but many had chronic constipation. Less common findings included hypotonia, ataxia, spasticity, sleep disturbances, foot deformities, scoliosis/kyphosis, and joint hypermobility. Dysmorphic features were sometimes observed, particularly in the more severely affected individuals. These included large ears with thick helices, thick eyebrows with synophrys, deep-set eyes, strabismus, large nose with high nasal bridge, short and flat philtrum, large mouth with thin upper lip and thick everted lower lip, widely spaced teeth, tongue protrusion, and low hairline. Brain imaging was essentially normal. In 4 families (SS2, GU, NN2, and CF), an affected parent with neuropsychiatric and/or behavioral abnormalities was found to carry a heterozygous TANC2 mutation. Features in these individuals included learning difficulties, ADHD, PTSD, and bipolar disorder.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: Most of the heterozygous mutations in the TANC2 gene that were identified in patients with IDDALDS by {3:Guo et al. (2019)} occurred de novo. However, there were rare instances of autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 20 unrelated probands with IDDALDS, {3:Guo et al. (2019)} identified heterozygous nonsense, frameshift, or splice site mutations, or intragenic deletions in the TANC2 gene (see, e.g., {615047.0001}-{615047.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, targeted sequencing, and array-based CGH, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing; none were present in the ExAC database. The patients were ascertained through a network of international collaborators and the GeneMatcher database. Eleven of the patients had de novo point mutations, and 5 probands inherited point mutations (from a mildly affected parent in 4 of those cases); the inheritance pattern could not be determined in 1 patient. Two affected sibs had an intragenic deletion inherited from their mosaic father, and 2 unrelated patients had de novo intragenic deletions. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors postulated a loss-of-function effect. {3:Guo et al. (2019)} also identified 5 unrelated individuals with overlapping phenotypes who were found to carry de novo heterozygous missense variants in the TANC2 gene. Three variants (R755H, R961Q, and H1689R) were found in 3 patients with a primary diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. Another variant (R760C) was found in a patient with impaired intellect and speech delay ({1:de Ligt et al., 2012}), and the last (A794V) was found in a patient with schizophrenia ({2:Fromer et al., 2014}). The R755H, R760C, and A794V variants occurred in the ATPase regulatory domain, and R961Q was in 1 of the ANK domains. H1689R, R760C, and A794V and were not found in the ExAC nonpsychiatric samples, whereas R755H and R961Q were both reported 4 times in ExAC. Functional studies of these missense variants were not performed. All mutations occurred throughout the gene and there were no apparent genotype/phenotype correlations, although all the disruptive mutations occurred before the PDZ interacting motif.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-86 (DEE86) is caused by homozygous mutation in the DALRD3 gene ({618904}) on chromosome 3p21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-86 (DEE86) is a neurologic syndrome characterized by severe and persistent seizures associated with EEG abnormalities beginning in the first few months of life, global developmental delay, severe motor deficits, dystonic movements, and dysmorphic facial features ({1:Lentini et al., 2020}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Lentini et al. (2020)} reported 2 sibs, born of consanguineous parents, with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Both pregnancies were complicated by oligohydramnios and placental insufficiency. The patients presented with severe and persistent seizures, including myoclonic seizures, in the first 6 or 7 months of life. These were associated with EEG abnormalities, including multifocal epileptic discharges, slowed background, and slow generalized polyspike and wave activity. While the epilepsy in 1 patient could be controlled by medication, the epilepsy in the other patient was poorly controlled. The patients had profound global developmental delay, severe motor deficits, hypotonia with muscle wasting, dystonic movements, and subtle dysmorphic facial features. Brain imaging in 1 patient showed diffuse brain parenchymal volume loss and poor myelination. More variable features included poor feeding, optic disc pallor, microcephaly, and poor or absent visual tracking. At ages 11 and 7, the sibs were immobile and nonverbal; 1 had a feeding tube.

{2:Zhang et al. (2025)} reported a patient with DEE86 who developed epilepsy at 4 years of age and then had regression of his psychomotor skills. At 15 years of age he had progressive immobility, limited speech, myoclonus, increased upper extremity tone, and ataxia. A brain MRI showed thin corpus callosum, widening of the sulci and ventricular system, and cerebellar arteriovenous malformation.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE86 in the family reported by {1:Lentini et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous parents, with DEE86, {1:Lentini et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the DALRD3 gene (Y417X; {618904.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of autozygosity mapping and exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The mutation was predicted to result in loss of the DALR tRNA anticodon-binding domain. Studies of patient-derived lymphocytes showed decreased levels of the full-length DALRD3 protein, suggesting nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. There was also a substantial reduction of m3C modification in tRNA-arg-CCU and tRNA-arg-UCU in patient cells compared to control cells, indicating that the mutation results in a partial loss of function.

{2:Zhang et al. (2025)} identified a homozygous mutation in the DALRD3 gene (R517C; {618904.0002}) in a Sudanese patient with DEE86. DALRD3 protein expression was reduced in patient fibroblasts compared to controls, suggesting that the mutation results in decreased protein stability. Functional studies in patient fibroblasts showed decreased m3C modification of arginine tRNAs. Cotransfection and immunoprecipitation assays in HEK293T cells demonstrated that the mutant DALRD3 had impaired associations with METTL2 and tRNAs.
