text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-87 (DEE87) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CDK19 gene ({614720}) on chromosome 6q21.

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-87 (DEE87) is a neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia, and onset of frequent refractory seizures or infantile spasms between 6 and 15 months of age. Affected individuals have severely impaired motor and cognitive development with little or absent speech and poor visual tracking. More variable features include facial dysmorphisms, joint laxity, and nonspecific brain imaging findings (summary by {1:Chung et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Chung et al. (2020)} reported 3 unrelated patients with a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. The first patient, who was 25 years of age, presented in infancy with global developmental delay, including sitting at 9 months, 3 words by 12 to 15 months, and walking with a wide-based gait at age 5. At age 15 months, she developed refractory generalized tonic-clonic seizures that led to neurologic regression with loss of speech. Additional features included hypotonia, joint laxity, mild scoliosis, pica, and hand-flapping. The other 2 patients, who were under 3 years of age, developed severe refractory seizures associated with hypsarrhythmia on EEG between 6 and 9 months of age. Both were of Chinese descent. At age 2 years, patient 2 was able to lift his head, but could not roll, sit, crawl, speak, or track objects. Brain imaging showed mild cerebral atrophy. Patient 3 also had global developmental delay. At age 18 months, he had hypotonia and was only able to crawl; brain imaging showed delayed myelination. All patients had dysmorphic facial features, including hypotelorism, straight eyebrows, prominent nose with bulbous tip, midface hypoplasia, large mouth with widely spaced teeth, and arched upper lip.

{2:Sugawara et al. (2020)} reported a 7-year-old girl with global developmental delay from early infancy and onset of epileptic spasms and tonic seizures at 6 months of age. An interictal EEG showed hypsarrhythmia, confirming a diagnosis of infantile spasms. Her epilepsy was refractory to conventional treatment and ketogenic diet. At 12 months of age, her length was at the 99th centile, weight was at the 88th centile, and head circumference was at the 33rd centile. Facial features included hypertelorism, a prominent nose with a bulbous tip, and a large mouth with widely spaced teeth. On neurologic examination, she had severe developmental delay and global hypotonia. Brain MRI showed brain atrophy and white matter abnormalities. She had an elevated total protein content in her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Glycine concentrations in her CSF and plasma were moderately elevated, but the CSF/plasma glycine ratio was normal. Nonketotic hyperglycinemia was ruled out based on genetic testing. Oral dextromethorphan treatment was unsuccessful. At age 7 years of age, she was profoundly disabled and continued to have seizures.

{3:Yang et al. (2021)} reported a 10-month-old boy with onset of infantile spasms at 4 months of age that occurred shortly after falling asleep or soon after waking up. Before seizure onset, development was normal; however, by age 10 months, developmental delay was noted with an overall development quotient of 43. His head circumference was at the 3rd centile, with weight at the 99th centile (length not provided). Facial features included hypertelorism, prominent nose with a bulbous tip and low nasal bridge, and high-arched palate. Neurologic examination was significant for hypotonia. Brain MRI showed that part of the cerebral gurus of the cerebral lobe was widened, sulci was deepened, and both lateral ventricles and the bilateral frontotemporal subarachnoid space were enlarged. Video EEG showed interictal hypsarrhythmia with diffuse and multifocal sharp wave discharges and frequent spikes with slowing in the background during sleep and wake. Laboratory examinations, including amino acid screening, were normal.

{4:Zarate et al. (2021)} reported 11 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 9 months to 14 years, with DEE87 and reviewed their clinical findings along with findings of the 3 patients reported by {1:Chung et al. (2020)}. All 14 patients had developmental delay, 11/14 had hypotonia, 9/14 had epilepsy, and 5/9 had autism or autistic features. Brain imaging was abnormal in 8/14 patients. Dysmorphic features were seen in all 14 patients. Eye findings included myopia, strabismus, cortical blindness, and optic disc atrophy in 9/14 patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CDK19 gene that were identified in patients with DEE87 by {1:Chung et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 unrelated patients with DEE87, {1:Chung et al. (2020)} identified 2 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the CDK19 gene (T196A, {614720.0001} and Y32H, {614720.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Studies of patient cells were not performed. However, in vivo functional expression studies in Drosophila showed that the mutant proteins localized normally to the perinuclear region in neurons, and that the mutations resulted in a loss-of-function effect acting in a dominant-negative manner (see ANIMAL MODEL).

By trio whole-exome sequencing, {2:Sugawara et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the CDK19 gene (Y32H; {614720.0002}) in a 7-year-old girl with DEE87.

By trio whole-exome sequencing, {3:Yang et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the CDK19 gene (T31N; {614820.0003}) in a 10-month-old boy with DEE87.

{4:Zarate et al. (2021)} reported 11 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 9 months to 14 years, with DEE87 and de novo missense mutations in the kinase domain of CDK19, including recurrent changes at residues Gly28 ({614720.0004} and {614720.0005}) and Tyr32 ({614720.0002}). Using in vitro autophosphorylation and substrate phosphorylation assays to examine the impact of these variants, {4:Zarate et al. (2021)} found that kinase activity was lower for G28R and higher for Y32H when compared to wildtype protein activity. Injection of CDK19 mRNA with either Y32H or G28R in an in vivo zebrafish model significantly increased the percentage of embryos with morphologic abnormalities compared to injection with wildtype CDK19 mRNA.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Chung et al. (2020)} found that overexpression of human wildtype CDK19 in wildtype Drosophila did not affect viability, but expression of either the human T196A or Y32H mutants ({614720.0001}, {614720.0002}) resulted in decreased viability (53 to 69%), suggesting a dominant effect. The sole homolog of CDK19 in Drosophila is Cdk8 ({603184}). Wildtype CDK19 was able to rescue larval lethality in Cdk8-null Drosophila, whereas neither T196A nor Y32H was able to rescue lethality, suggesting that each mutation causes a loss of function. Neuronal-specific knockdown of Cdk8 in Drosophila caused increased lethality, as well as increased sensitivity to seizures, as demonstrated by the 'bang sensitivity' assay. These phenotypic defects could be rescued by expression of wildtype CDK19, but not mutant T196A or Y32H. Immunostaining of adult Drosophila CNS showed that both wildtype and mutant CDK19 localized to the perinuclear space and cytoplasm of most neurons, with some nuclear localization. Neuronal-specific knockdown of Cdk8 in Drosophila caused a significant decrease in boutons at the neuromuscular junction, suggesting that Cdk8 plays a role in synaptic development.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with language impairment and behavioral abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with language impairment and behavioral abnormalities (NEDLIB) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GRIA2 gene ({138247}) on chromosome 4q32.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with speech impairment and behavioral abnormalities (NEDLIB) is characterized by impaired intellectual development or developmental delay, behavioral abnormalities including autistic features, and language impairment. Other features include seizures and developmental regression ({1:Salpietro et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Salpietro et al. (2019)} reported 25 unrelated patients, ranging from 3 months to 31 years of age, with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through collaboration of several research centers who shared data from whole-exome, whole-genome, or targeted sequencing that identified GRIA2 mutations. The phenotype represented a spectrum of neurologic deficits, including global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, and behavioral abnormalities, such as autism spectrum disorder, repetitive behaviors, stereotypic movements including hand-flapping, obsessive-compulsive traits, and hyperactivity. Some patients had normal early development, but then showed regression with impaired social and language skills. About half of patients developed early-onset focal or tonic-clonic seizures, most of which were refractory to treatment. Several patients had head growth deceleration, 4 patients were unable to walk, several had gait abnormalities, incoordination, ataxia, or dystonia, and about half were nonverbal. Brain imaging tended to be normal, although some patients had nonspecific abnormalities, such as cerebral atrophy, cerebellar atrophy, and white matter changes. Two patients died in infancy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the GRIA2 gene that were identified in patients with NEDLIB by {1:Salpietro et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 25 unrelated patients with NEDLIB, {1:Salpietro et al. (2019)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the GRIA2 gene (see, e.g., {138247.0001}-{138247.0006}). There were 15 missense, 2 splice site, and 1 nonsense mutation, 1 in-frame deletion, and 2 frameshift variants; mutations occurred throughout the gene. The mutations, which were found by whole-genome, whole-exome, or targeted sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. The mutations were predicted to result in a loss of function. In vitro functional expression studies in transfected HEK293T cells showed variable effects of the mutations. Seven of 11 mutations caused a decreased agonist-induced current compared to wildtype, 3 mutations had normal current amplitudes, and 1 resulted in an increase in current amplitude. When coexpressed with GRIA1 ({138248}), most of the mutant proteins showed a decreased current amplitude compared to wildtype, and some affected rectification. Some mutations reduced the GRIA2 surface expression, suggesting that defects in heteromerization or cell surface trafficking may be another important pathogenic mechanism. Overall, most of the mutations appeared to result in a loss of function. No clear genotype/phenotype correlations emerged, although 2 patients who died in infancy both carried the same variant (A639S; {138247.0005}). {1:Salpietro et al. (2019)} emphasized the biologic diversity of the tested mutants, and suggested that phenotypic differences may arise from different effects of distinct mutations. The report implicated GRIA2 dysfunction and disruption of glutamatergic synaptic transmission in neurodevelopmental disorders.

clinicalSynopsis: Dysmorphic facial features (noted in patient A)
Periventricular nodular heterotopia (PVNH), frontal predominant, seen on brain imaging
Caused by mutation in the microtubule-associated protein 1B gene (MAP1B,)

Head: Microcephaly (patient A)
Face: Dysmorphic facial features (noted in patient A)
Neurologic - CNS: Periventricular nodular heterotopia (PVNH), frontal predominant, seen on brain imaging
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the microtubule-associated protein 1B gene (MAP1B,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that periventricular nodular heterotopia-9 (PVNH9) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the MAP1B gene ({157129}) on chromosome 5q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Periventricular nodular heterotopia-9 (PVNH9) is an autosomal dominant neurologic disorder characterized as a malformation of cortical development. Anterior predominant PVNH, thin corpus callosum, and decreased white matter volume are found on brain imaging, but the clinical effects are variable. Most patients have impaired intellectual development and cognitive defects associated with low IQ (range 50 to 80), learning disabilities, and behavior abnormalities. Some patients develop seizures that tend to have a focal origin. However, some mutation carriers may be less severely affected with borderline or even normal IQ, suggesting incomplete penetrance of the phenotype (summary by {1:Heinzen et al., 2018}, {3:Walters et al., 2018}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of periventricular nodular heterotopia, see {300049}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Heinzen et al. (2018)} reported 4 unrelated probands who were found to have PVNH on brain imaging. The PVNH was mainly anterior predominant; in addition, perisylvian polymicrogyria was observed in 1 patient and suspected in another. Clinical details were limited, but 2 patients had childhood-onset focal seizures and another had some EEG abnormalities without overt seizures. Cognitive difficulties were noted in 3 patients, including IQ of 55 in 1, early language delay in another, and mild global developmental delay with comprehension anomalies in the third. The patient with early language delay was able to attend college, but did not graduate. The mother of 1 of the patients, who also carried a MAP1B mutation, also had brain imaging abnormalities that were less severe than in her affected child. Findings in the mother included PVNH, polymicrogyria, and thin dysmorphic corpus callosum; she did not have seizures or cognitive deficits. This family also had a history of psychiatric disease, and both the mother and her affected child had 'collapsing' episodes of uncertain etiology. Two additional parents who carried the mutation were clinically unaffected, although brain imaging was not performed.

{3:Walters et al. (2018)} reported a 5-generation Icelandic family (family 1) in which 8 individuals had variable cognitive deficits associated with PVNH on brain imaging. Four affected individuals were clinically diagnosed with impaired intellectual development (IQ range 58-71), and 3 affected family members without a clinical diagnosis were found to have low IQ ranging from 56 to 63. The eighth patient from the oldest generation, who was deceased, reportedly had a history of poor learning and Alzheimer disease. There was 1 family member clinically diagnosed with intellectual disability (IQ of 57) who did not carry the mutation, and another member who married into the family who had cognitive impairment (IQ of 71), but was not tested for the mutation. Two additional smaller Icelandic families were subsequently identified. In family 2, 3 sibs were variably affected with low IQ (range 67-79), autism, attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and learning difficulties; their affected mother had an IQ of 77 with dyslexia and dyscalculia. In family 3, a carrier mother was unaffected (IQ of 92), but showed PVNH on brain imaging. Her daughter had autism spectrum disorder, learning disability, and an IQ of 76. Overall, common features included intellectual disability, learning disabilities such as dyslexia and dyscalculia, speech delay, and behavioral problems, including ADD/ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), autism spectrum disorder, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. Brain imaging performed in 9 patients with a mutation from the 3 families showed PVNH and thin corpus callosum, whereas 6 family members without mutations did not have PVNH on brain imaging. The affected individuals had decreased white matter and a decrease in fractional anisotropy compared to controls, suggesting disordered or compromised axons.

{2:Julca et al. (2019)} reported a 7-year-old African-American boy with PVNH9. Prenatal history was remarkable for daily exposure to alcohol, phencyclidine, and cigarettes. The patient presented at 30 months of age with global developmental delay, poor overall growth with microcephaly, and a diagnosis of fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS). He had speech delay, delayed walking with toe walking and wide-based gait, impaired intellectual development, and behavioral problems such as ADHD. EEG showed some focal abnormalities, suggesting subclinical seizures. Dysmorphic features included prominent metopic ridge, long and upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, synophrys, small philtrum, gingival hypertrophy, everted upper lip, high-arched palate, small and posteriorly rotated ears, tapered fingers, left single palmar crease, fetal finger pads, bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly, and hirsutism. Brain imaging showed PVNH and thin corpus callosum. He also had mild unilateral conductive hearing loss. Family history was significant for a mother with mild intellectual disability and history of drug and alcohol abuse. Two maternal half brothers of the proband had learning difficulties, speech delay, and behavioral abnormalities, including ADHD, and 2 maternal half sibs of the mother had learning disabilities. The father of the proband was healthy with normal development.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PVNH9 in the families reported by {1:Heinzen et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance. The mutation in 1 case occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 4 unrelated probands with PVNH9, {1:Heinzen et al. (2018)} identified heterozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations in the MAP1B gene (see, e.g., {157129.0001}-{157129.0003}). One patient had a de novo mutation, 2 unrelated patients inherited the variants from clinically unaffected fathers who did not undergo brain imaging, and the last patient inherited the mutation from a mother who had similar, but milder, structural abnormalities on brain imaging. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not found in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but all were predicted to cause premature termination and a loss of function (LOF). {1:Heinzen et al. (2018)} noted that while MAP1B is very intolerant to functional variation, LOF variants have rarely been observed in the ExAC and gnomAD databases. The patients were ascertained from a cohort of 202 individuals with PVNH who underwent exome sequencing.

In affected members of 3 Icelandic families with PVNH9, {3:Walters et al. (2018)} identified 3 different heterozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations in exon 5 of the MAP1B gene ({157129.0004}-{157129.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families, although there was variable expressivity of the phenotype. None of the variants were present in public databases, including gnomAD. Expression of the mutations into HeLa cells showed that truncated proteins of the expected size were produced. {3:Walters et al. (2018)} stated that all the mutations resulted in absence of the LC1 domain of the protein.

In a 7-year-old boy with PVNH9, {2:Julca et al. (2019)} identified a de novo heterozygous nonsense mutation in the MAP1B gene (E679X; {157129.0007}). The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing; functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, hypotonia, and brain abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, hypotonia, and brain imaging abnormalities (NEDSHBA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GRM7 gene ({604101}) on chromosome 3p26.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, hypotonia, and brain imaging abnormalities (NEDSHBA) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay, severe to profound intellectual impairment, early-onset refractory seizures, hypotonia, failure to thrive, and progressive microcephaly. Brain imaging shows cerebral atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and myelination defects. Death in childhood may occur (summary by {2:Marafi et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Charng et al. (2016)} reported 4 patients from 2 unrelated families (families 014 and BMGL) with NEDSHBA. Clinical details were limited, but the patients had global developmental delay, microcephaly, seizures, and hypotonia. Brain imaging showed cortical atrophy, thin and short corpus callosum, and cerebellar volume loss; imaging in 3 patients showed hypomyelination. The patients were ascertained from a larger cohort of individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders who underwent exome sequencing.

{3:Reuter et al. (2017)} reported 2 sibs, born of consanguineous parents (family MR005), with NEDSHBA. Clinical details were limited, but features included microcephaly, short stature, global developmental delay with profoundly impaired intellectual development, seizures, limb hypertonia, lipodystrophy, and recurrent infections. Brain imaging showed cerebral atrophy and leukodystrophy. The patients were part of a large study of 152 consanguineous families with neurodevelopmental disorders who underwent exome sequencing.

{2:Marafi et al. (2020)} reported 5 patients from 3 additional consanguineous families (families 4, 5, and 6) with NEDSHBA. They also reviewed the clinical features of the patients previously reported by {1:Charng et al. (2016)} and {3:Reuter et al. (2017)}. Five of the 6 families were consanguineous and from the Middle East; family 2 was nonconsanguineous and from the United States. The patients ranged in age from 2 to 15 years; 5 had died between 45 days and 13 years of age, most commonly of respiratory failure. Several of the pregnancies were complicated by polyhydramnios, and several patients had perinatal complications, mostly respiratory. All presented in the first year of life with severe to profound global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, and seizures that were often refractory. Seizure types included myoclonic, focal, multifocal, and generalized tonic-clonic; 4 patients had status epilepticus. Other common features included progressive microcephaly (down to -3.8 SD), hypotonia, peripheral hypertonia, hyperreflexia, short stature, failure to thrive, and recurrent infections. Dysmorphic facial features noted in some patients included hypotonic facies, wide mouth, prominent nose, low anterior hairline, prominent teeth, and thick lips. Three patients had cortical visual impairment and 4 had hormonal abnormalities, such as panhypopituitarism, hypothyroidism, and growth hormone deficiency in the absence of structural pituitary abnormalities. Neuroimaging studies, performed in most patients, showed variable abnormalities, including cerebral atrophy, hypomyelination, thin corpus callosum, and cerebellar atrophy. Serial imaging in 2 sibs suggested that the disorder was progressive in the first 2 years of life, followed by a static course.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSHBA in the families reported by {1:Charng et al. (2016)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 4 patients from 2 unrelated families with NEDSHBA, {1:Charng et al. (2016)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations in the GRM7 gene ({604101.0001}-{604101.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Syrian parents, with NEDSHBA, {3:Reuter et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the GRM7 gene (W586X; {604101.0004}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The patients were part of a large study of 152 consanguineous families with neurodevelopmental disorders who underwent exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. {2:Marafi et al. (2020)} noted that this mutation occurs before the transmembrane domain and is predicted to result in a loss of function.

In 3 unrelated probands, born of consanguineous parents (families 4, 5, and 6), with NEDSHBA, {2:Marafi et al. (2020)} identified homozygous mutations in the GRM7 gene ({604101.0005}-{604101.0007}). There were 2 missense mutations and 1 nonsense mutation. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. None of the variants, including the ones previously reported by {1:Charng et al. (2016)} and {3:Reuter et al. (2017)} were found in the homozygous state in the gnomAD database. Although functional studies of the variants and studies of patients cells were not performed, the authors predicted a loss-of-function effect. {2:Marafi et al. (2020)} hypothesized that loss of GRM7 function would result in loss of inhibition of the glutamatergic pathway, excess glutamate release, and neuronal hyperexcitability, as well as a possible direct neurotoxic effect of increased glutamate.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that episodic ataxia type 9 (EA9) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN2A gene ({182390}) on chromosome 2q23.

Heterozygous mutation in the SCN2A gene can cause the less severe phenotype benign familial infantile seizures-3 (BFIS3; {607745}) and the more severe phenotype developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-11 (DEE11; {613721}). SCN2A mutations result in a clinical spectrum of neurologic abnormalities that show overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Episodic ataxia type 9 (EA9) is a neurologic disorder characterized by onset of ataxic episodes in the first years of life. Features may include difficulty walking, dizziness, slurred speech, headache, vomiting, and pain. The ataxic episodes vary in frequency and duration; most tend to occur every few weeks or months and last minutes to hours. Prior to the EA, most patients have neonatal- or infantile-onset tonic or generalized tonic-clonic (GTC) seizures that may be severe and refractory to medication, but remit later in infancy or early childhood, either spontaneously or concurrently with medication. Some patients have mildly delayed development with speech delay and/or autistic features or mildly impaired intellectual development. However, others show normal psychomotor development. Treatment of the ataxic episodes with acetazolamide is effective in about 50% of patients (summary by {8:Schwarz et al., 2019}).

For a phenotypic description and discussion of genetic heterogeneity of episodic ataxia, see EA1 ({160120}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{6:Liao et al. (2010)} reported an 11-year-old boy with neonatal onset of hypomotor seizures followed by tonic-clonic movements on alternating sides. Hypomotor, focal, and bilateral motor seizures continued weekly to monthly until 1.3 years. Beginning at this time, he developed ataxic episodes with poor balance, ataxia, slurred speech, intermittent myoclonic jerks, and severe distress with headache, back pain, hypermotor activity, hyperventilation, and retching or vomiting. Mild motor dyspraxia, but no ataxia, was present between the episodes. After numerous medications that were ineffective, he became seizure-free on acetazolamide. Neuropsychologic testing showed normal intelligence, but specific problems in visual processing, fine motor function, and tactile sensation. MRI showed mild cerebellar atrophy at age 5 years.

{11:Touma et al. (2013)} reported a pair of monozygotic twin boys who carried the same de novo heterozygous A263V mutation identified in the patient reported by {6:Liao et al. (2010)}. On the first day of life, both boys developed refractory seizures (up to 60 per day) associated with a burst-suppression pattern on EEG. One twin died on day 19 from iatrogenic cardiopulmonary arrest. The other twin became seizure-free on medication at age 8 months, and seizure-free without medication at age 2 years; this corresponded to improvement of the EEG abnormalities. The surviving twin showed global developmental delay; he could say short sentences but had head lag, axial hypotonia, and inability to crawl. Brain imaging of the surviving twin showed diffuse signal abnormalities in the basal ganglia and brainstem suggestive of cytotoxic edema; these abnormalities improved with age. The phenotype overlapped with DEE11.

{3:Howell et al. (2015)} reported 2 unrelated girls (patients 8 and 9) with a phenotype consistent with EA9. Both were 3 years of age and presented at 10 days and 6 weeks of age, respectively, with focal seizures and multifocal spikes on EEG. Both patients were classified as having epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (EIMFS). The seizures remitted at 3.5 months and 2 years of age, respectively. The patient with earlier seizure remission had normal development, whereas the other had language delay and anxiety. Both developed dystonia and axial hypotonia. One had frank episodic ataxia, whereas the other had early handedness and episodic breath-holding.

{9:Schwarz et al. (2016)} reported 3 unrelated patients with EA9 and provided follow-up of the patient reported by {6:Liao et al. (2010)}. Although the phenotype was heterogeneous, all patients presented in the first weeks of life with tonic or generalized tonic-clonic seizures that remitted by the first year of life, although the patient reported by {6:Liao et al. (2010)} had a few isolated seizures later in childhood. Between 15 months and 4 years of age, the patients developed features of episodic ataxia, including impaired balance, dizziness, slurred speech, headache, and vomiting. The frequency of the ataxic episodes varied from 1 or 2 per month to 1 to 10 per week, and the duration from a few minutes to several hours. Other more variable features included hypotonia, persistent ataxia, clonus, and dyspraxia. Treatment of the EA was difficult: 2 of the patients did not respond to acetazolamide. Two patients had mild global developmental delay with mild intellectual disability (IQ range 67-76).

{4:Johannesen et al. (2016)} reported a 19-month-old girl with EA9. She had onset of tonic and GTC seizures on the first day of life with remission at age 7 months, despite several hospitalizations with status epilepticus. At age 15 months, she developed episodic ataxia with dizziness, poor balance, and motor disturbances. The episodes occurred in 2-hour clusters, lasted a few minutes, and occurred several times a week. Triggers included stress and sleep deprivation. Otherwise, neurodevelopment was normal. {2:Gorman and King (2017)} reported a 3-year-old boy with a similar phenotype. He had onset of tonic seizures in the first days of life followed by remission of seizures around 18 months and onset of ataxic episodes around 20 months of age. Phenytoin reduced the seizures in the neonatal period, and carbamazepine later reduced the frequency of the ataxic events. He had normal development.

{5:Leach et al. (2016)} reported a 5-year-old boy with EA9. He presented at 11 and 17 months of age with episodes of acute encephalopathy precipitated by minor falls and head injury. Features included decreased consciousness, vomiting, intermittent limb stiffness, dystonic posturing, hypotonia, nystagmus, ataxia, and 'possible seizures.' He reportedly had mildly delayed global development prior to the first episode. EEG was normal, thus excluding seizures. Brain imaging showed cerebellar edema with T2 hyperintensities and arachnoid cysts. The neurologic symptoms subsided over the following days, but he did not return to baseline. Brain imaging at 2.5 years of age showed cerebellar atrophy that stabilized. The patient also had autism spectrum disorder and global developmental delay with mild intellectual disability. He did not have overt seizures. Treatment with acetazolamide was effective in controlling the ataxic episodes.

{1:Fazeli et al. (2018)} reported a family in which a mother and her 2 sons had EA9 associated with impaired speech development. One of the sons presented between 12 and 36 months of age with recurrent subacute cerebellar ataxia, manifest as unstable posture, wobbly head, and intention tremor. The first 2 episodes occurred after vaccination; the latter 2 had no obvious possible trigger. Recovery took about 3 weeks after the episodes. Brain imaging showed a stable circumscribed lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere, but no cerebellar atrophy. He also had delayed speech development with mild motor and cognitive delay (IQ of 88). His mother had mildly impaired cognitive development and speech delay in early childhood (IQ of 71 as an adult). She had a history of several episodes of EA in childhood without seizures similar to her son; the last episode was at 18 years of age. Brain imaging was normal. The younger son, who was 13 months of age, had 1 episode of mild ataxia that resolved, and normal psychomotor development at that time. None of the patients had seizures; the authors noted the rare familial occurrence of the disorder and the absence of seizures.

{8:Schwarz et al. (2019)} reported 21 patients with EA9, including 9 newly identified individuals and 12 previously reported patients. The phenotype was variable, but a common disease course and clinical pattern could be observed. Most patients developed seizures in the first days or months of life, followed by onset of ataxic episodes in the first years of life, all after at least 10 months of age. During the ataxic episodes, features included dizziness, vertigo, gait instability, dysarthria, dystonia, hypotonia, headache, pain, tremor, vomiting, and nystagmus. The frequency was most commonly weekly to monthly, although some experienced daily occurrence or only had episodes several times a year. Similarly, the duration usually lasted minutes to hours, although some lasted days or weeks. Some triggering factors were noted, such as minor head injuries, sleep deprivation, alcohol ingestion, photostimulation, and sudden sensory input, such as noise. Early-onset seizures were usually treated with a sodium channel blocker, commonly phenytoin, with variable success, and the ataxic episodes responded to acetazolamide in about half of cases. Rare patients responded to other antiepileptic medication. Development and cognitive abilities also varied: many had normal development, whereas others had mild developmental delay with motor delay, speech delay, learning difficulties, and/or autistic features. Severely impaired intellectual development was rare.

{7:Passi and Mohammad (2021)} reported a 15-month-old boy who presented with episodic ataxia after normal early neurologic development. He showed neurologic deterioration with subsequent episodes, but responded well to medication. Eleven months after the first episode, he could walk well, speak several words, had good eye contact, and interacted well socially. Family history revealed that his father had episodic hemiplegia which began at 18 months of age and lasted until 9 years of age. He did not have seizures and brain imaging was normal. After age 9, he developed normally, was able to run a business, and was intellectually and neurologically normal. Clinical exome panel sequencing identified a heterozygous missense variant in the SCN2A gene in both individuals (L1650P; {182390.0016}). Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{10:Suddaby et al. (2019)} reported a 38-year-old patient with a complex neurologic phenotype associated with a de novo heterozygous missense variant in the SCN2A gene (S1656P) identified through whole-exome sequencing. From childhood, she exhibited autistic features, such as poor social skills and stereotypical behavior, although she did not have developmental delay or learning difficulties. She had episodes of limb rigidity and dysarthria in infancy, diagnosed as an atypical seizure disorder. The seizures recurred at age 9 years, were consistent with episodic ataxia, and responded to treatment. At age 36 years, she developed psychotic symptoms, including paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, disordered speech, and lack of self-care, resulting in multiple psychiatric hospitalizations and treatment with various psychiatric medications. She then showed delayed learning, blunted affect, grossly impaired cognition, poor insight, and slowed speech, some of which may have been secondary to medication. Other features included ptosis, wide mouth, facial asymmetry, increased muscle tone, and brisk reflexes. Additional systemic findings included chronic temporomandibular joint pain, headaches, overactive bladder, immune neutropenia, rheumatoid arthritis, gastroesophageal reflux, and Raynaud phenomenon. {10:Suddaby et al. (2019)} emphasized that the patient had psychiatric features on the schizophrenia spectrum, expanding the phenotypic spectrum associated with SCN2A mutations. Functional studies of the S1656P variant were not performed, and the authors noted that she carried variants of uncertain significance in other genes that may have contributed to the phenotype.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The transmission pattern of EA9 in the family reported by {1:Fazeli et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

The heterozygous mutations in the SCN2A gene that were identified in most of the patients reported by {8:Schwarz et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a boy with EA9, {6:Liao et al. (2010)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the SCN2A gene (A263V; {182390.0011}). Electrophysiologic studies showed that the A263V mutation resulted in a 3-fold increase in persistent sodium current, indicating a profound gain of function. Other changes including slowed fast inactivation and accelerated recovery of slow inactivation. These findings were consistent with a gain-of-function effect and neuronal hyperexcitability.

{3:Howell et al. (2015)} reported 2 unrelated girls, each with a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the SCN2A gene (A240S and F928C). Functional studies of the variants were not performed.

{4:Johannesen et al. (2016)} and {2:Gorman and King (2017)} independently identified de novo A263V mutations in the SCN2A gene in a 19-month-old girl and a 3-year-old boy with EA9, confirming the association of the phenotype with this specific mutation. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In 3 unrelated patients with EA9, {9:Schwarz et al. (2016)} identified heterozygous mutations in the SCN2A gene ({182390.0011}, {182390.0013}, {182390.0014}). In vitro functional electrophysiologic studies in transfected cells showed that the newly reported mutations resulted in a gain-of-function effect with increased cell membrane excitability, although the studies suggested that there were different molecular mechanisms.

In a 5-year-old boy with EA9, {5:Leach et al. (2016)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the SCN2A gene (G1634D; {182390.0015}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not found in the ExAC database. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In a woman and her 2 sons with EA9, {1:Fazeli et al. (2018)} identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the SCN2A gene (L1650P; {182390.0016}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not found in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In 9 patients from 8 unrelated families with EA9, {8:Schwarz et al. (2019)} identified heterozygous missense mutations in the SCN2A gene (see, e.g., {182390.0011}). Most of the variants occurred de novo, but 2 sibs (patients 3 and 4) inherited an A263V mutation from an unaffected father. Functional studies of the variants were not performed. In combination with previous reports, {8:Schwarz et al. (2019)} concluded that EA9-associated mutations occur throughout the SCN2A gene, although the A263V variant was a recurrent mutation, and there appeared to be a hotspot region around S4 segment in domain IV. {8:Schwarz et al. (2019)} noted that there is time-dependent divergent expression of SCN2A during development, with early expression in the CA1 region of the hippocampus and later postnatal expression in the cerebellum, which may correlate with the phenotype.

phenotypes.phenotype: Agenesis of corpus callosum, cardiac, ocular, and genital syndrome

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that agenesis of corpus callosum, cardiac, ocular, and genital syndrome (ACOGS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CDH2 gene ({114020}) on chromosome 18q12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Agenesis of corpus callosum, cardiac, ocular, and genital syndrome (ACOGS) is a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay and/or intellectual disability, corpus callosum agenesis or hypoplasia, craniofacial dysmorphisms, and ocular, cardiac, and genital anomalies ({1:Accogli et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Accogli et al. (2019)} reported 9 individuals with mutations in the CDH2 gene, who exhibited a strikingly similar clinical and radiologic phenotype, including developmental delay/intellectual disability, callosal malformations, cardiac and ocular abnormalities, and characteristic facial dysmorphisms. One patient (patient 2) had been previously studied by {4:Uccella et al. (2019)}. All patients exhibited developmental delay, and half had mild to moderate intellectual impairment. Two individuals met diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder, 1 displayed self-injurious behaviors, and another had several neuropsychiatric issues, including auditory hallucinations. Seven of 9 patients had agenesis of the corpus callosum, and 1 had corpus callosum hypoplasia; brain imaging was not reported for the remaining patient. Hypothalamic adhesion was identified in 5 patients, periventricular nodular heterotopia in 4, and 2 individuals had an interhemispheric cyst communicating with the third ventricle. Four patients had hypoplastic or dysplastic tentorium, 2 patients had megacisterna magna, and another showed an atretic parietal cephalocele. A wide range of congenital cardiac defects were present, including defects of the atrioventricular canal in 2 patients, aortic coarctation in 2, dextrocardia with right pulmonary artery hypoplasia in 1, and tricuspid regurgitation in 1. Two individuals developed seizures, which were focal in 1 and infantile spasms in the other. Half of the cohort exhibited congenital eye defects, including Peters anomaly in 2 patients, unilateral ptosis with Duane anomaly in 1, congenital cataracts in 1, and strabismus in 3 patients, all requiring surgical intervention. Hyposmia was reported in 3 patients, 1 of whom also had hypogeusia. One patient exhibited congenital mirror movements. Shoulder deformities were present in 3 patients, with 2 showing Sprenger deformity and 1 having absence of shoulder muscles. Four of 5 male patients had genital anomalies, including cryptorchidism in 3 and micropenis in 1. Four patients had macrocephaly, and 1 had relative macrocephaly at last evaluation. Craniofacial dysmorphisms observed included broad and prominent forehead, downslanting palpebral fissures, deep-set eyes, low-set posteriorly rotated ears with thick helices and earlobes, thin upper lip, and pointed chin.

{2:Reis et al. (2020)} described 4 children with agenesis of the corpus callosum, Peters anomaly, dysmorphic features, and developmental delays, who had mutations in the CDH2 gene. One of the patients (patient 2) had previously been studied as patient 6 by {3:Reis et al. (2008)}. Dysmorphic features in these children included hypertelorism, flat nasal bridge, low-set or posteriorly rotated ears, upturned earlobes, thin upper lip, small mouth with downturned corners, and low anterior hairline. Neurologic features included cognitive delays and mild hypotonia with hypertonic extremities; additional brain malformations included hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, incomplete hippocampal rotation, and absent septum pellucidum. One patient (patient 4) was reported to have Peters anomaly and umbilical hernia, but no other syndromic features were noted at age 18 months; also, an older brother was reported to have Peters anomaly, but the family was lost to follow-up.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The heterozygous mutations in the CDH2 gene that were identified in patients with ACOGS by {1:Accogli et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

The transmission pattern in 1 family reported by {2:Reis et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance; in 1 patient the mutation was shown to have occurred de novo; and in the remaining 2, inheritance could not be established.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 9-year-old boy (patient 2) with agenesis of the corpus callosum, mild intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder, Duane anomaly, craniofacial dysmorphisms, tricuspid regurgitation, and cryptorchidism, previously reported by {4:Uccella et al. (2019)}, {1:Accogli et al. (2019)} identified heterozygosity for a de novo missense mutation in the CDH2 gene (D597N; {114020.0003}). From the GeneMatcher database, the authors ascertained 8 additional cases with overlapping phenotypes and heterozygous de novo mutations in the CDH2 gene (see, e.g., {114020.0004}-{114020.0007}). Noting the neurodevelopmental features observed in the affected individuals, including agenesis of the corpus callosum, periventricular nodular heterotopias, hyposmia, mirror movements, and Duane anomaly, the authors suggested that CDH2 plays a critical role in neuronal migration and axon pathfinding.

In a male patient (patient 1) with agenesis of the corpus callosum, Peters anomaly, dysmorphic features, and cognitive delay, {2:Reis et al. (2020)} performed trio analysis of exome data and identified heterozygosity for a de novo splicing variant in the CDH2 gene ({114020.0008}). Review of exome data from 145 additional probands with developmental ocular anomalies identified 3 more patients with Peters anomaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and other syndromic features who had heterozygous missense mutations in the CDH2 gene, including a boy (patient 2) who previously had been studied as patient 6 by {3:Reis et al. (2008)} (V162D; {114020.0009}). In 1 patient (patient 4), a P603S mutation was inherited from an apparently unaffected mother who had not undergone formal eye exam; however, the family was lost to follow-up.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Suleiman-El-Hattab syndrome (SULEHS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TASP1 gene ({608270}) on chromosome 20p12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Suleiman-El-Hattab syndrome (SULEHS) is an autosomal recessive multisystem developmental disorder characterized by hypotonia and feeding difficulties soon after birth, global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor expressive speech, and a general happy demeanor. There is a distinctive facial appearance with microcephaly, thick arched eyebrows with synophrys, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, low-set ears, broad nasal bridge, and thin upper lip. Additional more variable features include recurrent respiratory infections, cardiovascular malformations, cryptorchidism, seizures, and distal anomalies of the hands and feet (summary by {2:Suleiman et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Suleiman et al. (2019)} reported 4 unrelated children, ranging from 1 to 4 years of age, with a similar syndromic developmental disorder. Patient 2 had previously been reported by {1:Suleiman et al. (2018)}. All patients were placed in the NICU soon after birth, due to hypotonia, respiratory insufficiency, and/or poor feeding with failure to thrive. They had significant global developmental delay with poor expressive speech. The 3 older patients achieved walking by age 3, often with difficulties, had poor motor skills, and were essentially nonverbal. The patients had limited ability to follow commands, indicating cognitive impairment, although visual tracking and attempts at communication were observed in some; a happy demeanor was noted. Other features included respiratory infections, cardiovascular malformations, mainly septal defects, cryptorchidism, and single palmar crease. Distinctive facial features included microcephaly (down to -5 SD), excessive forehead hair, arched and thick eyebrows with synophrys, epicanthus, hypertelorism, thick eyelids with periorbital fullness, broad nasal bridge, long smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and low-set prominent ears with overfolded helices. Less common features included hirsutism, preauricular skin tag, webbed neck, microretrognathia, wide mouth, and downslanted palpebral fissures. Two patients had drooling, 2 had seizures, and 1 each had short stature, brachycephaly, polydactyly, clinodactyly, hydronephrosis, hearing impairment, and eye anomalies, including hyperopia, strabismus, amblyopia, and pale optic discs.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SULEHS in the families reported by {2:Suleiman et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 unrelated children with SULEHS, {2:Suleiman et al. (2019)} identified homozygous mutations in the TASP1 gene ({608270.0001}-{608270.0003}). There was 1 intragenic deletion predicted to result in a frameshift, 1 missense mutation, and 1 nonsense mutation. The mutations, which were found by chromosome microarray analysis or whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by breakpoint mapping or Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Three of the families were consanguineous. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but all were predicted to result in a loss of function. Patient 2 had previously been reported by {1:Suleiman et al. (2018)}. {2:Suleiman et al. (2019)} commented that the phenotype overlapped somewhat with Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome (WDSTS; {605130}), caused by mutation in the KMT2A gene ({159555}), and Kabuki syndrome ({147920}), caused by mutation in the KMT2D gene ({602113}). Both of these genes encode substrates of TASP1 that activate HOX and cyclin genes downstream; KMT2A and KMT2D also play a role in histone modification.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-45 (COXPD45) is caused by homozygous mutation in the MRPL12 gene ({602375}) on chromosome 17q25. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-45 (COXPD45) is an autosomal recessive multisystem disorder characterized by poor overall growth apparent from infancy, global developmental delay, seizures, and acute progressive neurologic deterioration with loss of skills. Other features may include dysmorphic facies and lesions on brain imaging. Laboratory studies show increased serum lactate and COXPD in patient tissues, consistent with a mitochondrial defect (summary by {1:Serre et al., 2013}).

For discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Serre et al. (2013)} reported a boy, born of consanguineous Roma Gypsy parents, with COXPD45. He presented at birth with severe hypotrophy and later showed failure to thrive with poor overall growth. He had mild muscle weakness, but started walking with aid at 12 months. Increased plasma lactate prompted analysis of mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme activity, which demonstrated a combined OXPHOS deficiency in muscle, liver, and skin fibroblasts. Complexes I and IV were particularly affected. At age 2, he developed seizures and had rapid neurologic deterioration associated with an acute infection and fever. He then showed psychomotor retardation, severe trunk hypotonia, inability to sit or stand unaided, no speech, intermittent horizontal nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia, and tremor. Brain imaging showed white matter abnormalities and lesions in the basal ganglia. His condition continued to deteriorate and he died after cardiac arrest. Mild facial dysmorphisms were noted, including round face, epicanthic folds, arched palate, short neck, low-set ears, and median palmar crease. During the next pregnancy, the mother expected dizygotic twins, but prenatal diagnosis based on assessment of respiratory chain enzyme activities showed a severe complex IV deficiency in fetal cells, leading to termination of the pregnancy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of COXPD45 in the family reported by {1:Serre et al. (2013)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a boy, born of consanguineous Roma Gypsy parents, with COXPD45, {1:Serre et al. (2013)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the MRPL12 gene (A181V; {602375.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and candidate gene sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The mutation was not found in the dbSNP database or in 100 ethnically matched controls. In a subsequent pregnancy, affected dizygotic twin fetuses were also found to carry this homozygous mutation; the pregnancy was terminated. The steady-state level of MRPL12 in patient fibroblasts was reduced to 30% of control values, and there was altered integration into the large ribosomal subunit. In vitro translation studies showed a reduction in the synthesis of subunits in mitochondrial complexes I, II, and III, but no aberrant translation products were identified.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-88 (DEE88) is caused by homozygous mutation in the MDH1 gene ({154200}) on chromosome 2p15. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-88 (DEE88) is an autosomal recessive severe neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay, early-onset epilepsy, and progressive microcephaly. Brain MRI findings may include corpus callosum abnormalities, prominent ventricles, and mild hypoplasia of the inferior vermis and pons ({1:Broeks et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Broeks et al. (2019)} reported 2 affected first cousins, a 25-month-old boy and a 4-year-old girl, from a consanguineous Saudi family with early-onset epileptic encephalopathy. The boy was born prematurely at 32 weeks' gestation and spent 3 weeks in the neonatal intensive care unit for weight management. At 13 months of age, he was diagnosed with global developmental delay and progressive microcephaly. Seizure-like activity was also described. At 14 months of age, he had microcephaly, poor growth, and facial dysmorphisms, including a tall forehead, prominent infraorbital creases, a depressed nasal bridge, and an everted lower lip. He also had axial hypotonia and appendicular hypertonia. An EEG showed hypsarrhythmia. Brain MRI showed partial agenesis of the corpus callous, predominantly in the splenium, prominent ventricles, and mild hypoplasia of the inferior vermis and pons. His 4-year-old cousin had severe developmental delay, epilepsy, microcephaly, and similar facial dysmorphisms. Her brain MRI showed mild shortening of the corpus callosum and normal pons and ventricles. Plasma amino acids, acylcarnitines, lactic acid, and urine organic acids were normal in both patients. Nontargeted metabolomics on blood spots from both patients showed increased glutamate and glycerol-3-phosphate.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE88 in the family reported by {1:Broeks et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 first cousins from a consanguineous Saudi family with DEE88, {1:Broeks et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous mutation in the MDH1 gene (A138V; {154200.0001}). The mutation, which was identified by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family and was not found in the gnomAD database or in a local database of approximately 2,300 ethnically matched exomes. MDH1 protein levels were reduced in lymphoblastoid cells and fibroblasts from the patients. {1:Broeks et al. (2019)} noted that the neurologic phenotype in these patients resembled the phenotype in other patients with defects in the malate-aspartate shuttle (see, e.g., DEE51, {617339}).

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Mitchell syndrome (MITCH) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ACOX1 gene ({609751}), which encodes straight-chain acyl-CoA oxidase, on chromosome 17q25.

Homozygous mutation in the ACOX1 gene causes peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase deficiency ({264470}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Mitchell syndrome (MITCH) is a progressive disorder characterized by episodic demyelination, sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and hearing loss ({1:Chung et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Chung et al. (2020)} reported 3 unrelated patients with a progressive disorder including episodic demyelination, sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and hearing loss. Patient 1 presented at age 12 years with clumsiness and mild hearing loss. He had mild leg weakness, lower limb areflexia, and upper limb hyporeflexia. A spine MRI showed T2 hyperintensities in the dorsal columns of the cervical and thoracic cord, and nerve conduction studies showed a sensory axonal polyneuropathy. He had a waxing and waning course, and was treated intermittently with immunomodulation therapies. His hearing loss progressed and he received a cochlear implant. At age 19, he developed respiratory muscle weakness, dysphagia, and altered mental status. A brain MRI showed development of central lesions. The patient died following removal of life support. Patient 2, identified through GeneMatcher, presented at age 9 years with hearing loss and lower limb weakness. A spine MRI showed T2 hyperintensities from the cervical to lumbar spine and focal enhancement with nerve root enhancement. Nerve conduction studies showed a sensorimotor polyneuropathy. She was treated with immunomodulatory therapy, but repeat brain MRI 2 months later showed new T2 hyperintense lesions in the bilateral occipital lobes with meningeal and parenchymal enhancement. She developed an ascending paralysis leading to respiratory failure, encephalopathy, and seizures. With further immunomodulatory therapy, she recovered some respiratory function and motor skills. After 2 years of clinical stability, she developed autonomic dysfunction, rash, and another episode of respiratory failure, seizures, and encephalopathy. At age 14 she had severely impaired cognition and required a tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation as well as a gastric feeding tube. Patient 3, identified from a large database, presented at age 3 years with a diffuse desquamatory rash. Two months later he developed difficulty walking, hyporeflexia, and respiratory distress. He had full recovery after rehabilitation. At age 4 he developed another rash, followed by gait difficulties and bilateral hearing loss. A brain MRI showed enhancement of multiple cranial nerves, and spine MRI showed enhancement of thoracic and cauda equina roots. He was started on immunomodulatory therapy but he continued to have episodic neuroregression and rash. At age 7, brain MRI showed confluent periventricular, deep and subcortical white matter signal abnormalities with cystic leukomalacia, and a repeat MRI at age 8 showed progression of the white matter signal abnormality with sparing of u-fibers, multiple cystic foci, and areas of diffusion restriction. At age 9, he was nonambulatory and nonverbal with some spontaneous extremity movements.

nomenclature.title: Nomenclature
nomenclature.content: {1:Chung et al. (2020)} proposed the name Mitchell syndrome for this disorder to honor their patient 1.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the ACOX1 gene that were identified in patients with Mitchell syndrome by {1:Chung et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 unrelated patients with Mitchell syndrome, {1:Chung et al. (2020)} identified the same heterozygous de novo missense mutation in the ACOX1 gene (N237S; {609751.0008}). The mutations were found by trio exome sequencing. Studies in flies carrying the human ACOX1 N237S mutation showed increased protein dimerization that appeared to be resistant to protein turnover. The mutant protein was also shown to have increased enzyme activity compared to the wildtype protein, suggesting a gain-of-function effect.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome-19 (MTDPS19) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the SLC25A10 gene ({606794}) on chromosome 17q25. One such patient has been reported.

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of autosomal recessive mtDNA depletion syndromes, see MTDPS1 ({603041}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Punzi et al. (2018)} reported a 9-year-old boy, born of unrelated Italian parents, with a complex multisystem disorder. He presented at birth with hypospadias, bilateral hydrocele, and unilateral hearing loss. At age 3 months, he developed daily infantile spasms associated with multifocal epileptiform discharges and a suppression burst pattern on EEG. The seizures were refractory to treatment. He had severe hypotonia, absent eye tracking, and poor spontaneous movements that evolved to spastic quadriparesis and dyskinesias after the onset of seizures. MRI was initially normal, but later showed white matter abnormalities and thin corpus callosum. Growth parameters were normal, and neuropsychiatric evaluations revealed normal to high intellectual ability. Laboratory studies showed iron-deficient anemia, increased lactate, and reduced mitochondrial respiratory complex I activity (27% of controls) and decreased mtDNA content (40% lower than controls) in muscle.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MTDPS19 in the family reported by {1:Punzi et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a 9-year-old boy with MTDPS19, {1:Punzi et al. (2018)} identified compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SLC25A10 gene ({606794.0001} and {606794.0002}). The mutations were found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and segregated with the disorder in the family. Patient fibroblasts showed a 10-fold decrease in SLC25A10 transcripts compared to controls, and Western blot analysis did not detect the SLC25A10 protein. In vitro functional expression studies showed negligible, if any, transport activity for malate/phosphate exchange, consistent with a loss of function. In addition, patient cells showed a decrease in both the NADPH/NADP+ and GSH/GSSG ratios as well as a growth defect under stress conditions. Studies in yeast lacking the Slc25a10 ortholog showed impaired growth, impaired mitochondrial respiration, decreased mtDNA, and increased vulnerability to oxidative stress compared to controls. {1:Punzi et al. (2018)} postulated that the loss of SLC25A10 function causes disturbances in respiratory-demanding conditions and oxidative stress vulnerability, which may induce mitochondrial defects.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter deficiency (SMVTD) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the SLC5A6 gene ({604024}) on chromosome 2p23.

Biallelic mutation in the SLC5A6 gene can also cause biotin-responsive childhood-onset peripheral motor neuropathy (COMNB; {619903}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter deficiency (SMVTD) is an autosomal recessive multisystemic metabolic disorder with highly variable manifestations. Affected individuals usually present at birth or in infancy with severe feeding problems, gastrointestinal reflux, cyclic vomiting, and diarrhea associated with failure to thrive. Gastrointestinal hemorrhage may occur; tube-feeding is often required for a short time. The course and severity of the disease varies: some patients have episodes of acute metabolic decompensation during infection that respond well to treatment, whereas others show more permanent neurologic regression with loss of early motor and cognitive milestones in the first year or so of life. Less severely affected patients have normal development or mild growth and motor delays, whereas more severely affected individuals may have seizures, ataxia, spasticity, peripheral neuropathy, immune defects, and osteopenia. In severely affected patients, brain imaging shows cerebral, cerebellar, and brainstem atrophy and thin corpus callosum. Treatment with biotin, pantothenic acid, and alpha-lipoic acid has been shown to result in significant clinical improvement ({1:Byrne et al., 2019}; {2:Hauth et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{5:Subramanian et al. (2017)} reported a boy, born of unrelated parents, who presented in early infancy with feeding difficulties requiring gastrostomy tube placement, increased muscle tone, and multiple infections associated with hypogammaglobulinemia. At age 15 months, he demonstrated delayed development with poor head control, inability to sit, spastic cerebral palsy, and impaired intellectual development with language delay. Other features included poor growth with acquired microcephaly, nystagmus, and osteopenia and bone fractures associated with hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and increased alkaline phosphatase. Brain imaging showed thin corpus callosum, brain atrophy, and pontine hypoplasia. Treatment with biotin, pantothenic acid, and lipoate resulted in developmental progress and resolution of the immunoglobulin and bone defects.

{1:Byrne et al. (2019)} reported 2 sibs who had normal early development until about 12 to 14 months of age, and thereafter showed developmental regression with loss of motor, cognitive, and language skills. They also had progressive decline in head circumference centile, truncal ataxia, and dyskinetic appendicular movements. One sib died at 2.7 years of age due to acute gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Neuropathologic examination showed a small cerebrum and cerebellum, as well as the presence of axonal spheroids and reactive gliosis. There were also variable axonal abnormalities of the peripheral nerves. The surviving sib developed mixed types of seizures associated with multifocal spike-wave discharges on EEG; he also had cyclic vomiting. The seizures were controlled by medication. Other features included decreased IgG and a mixed demyelinating and axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Brain imaging showed cerebral, cerebellar, and brainstem atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and nonspecific white matter abnormalities. At 7 years of age, the surviving sib was treated with biotin, dexpanthenol, and alpha-lipoic acid, which resulted in the patient achieving developmental process, seizure control, attenuation of cyclic vomiting, and resolution of peripheral neuropathy.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{4:Schwantje et al. (2019)} reported a 3-year-old girl who presented around 10 months of age with severe feeding difficulties, poor growth, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and persistent vomiting with traces of blood. She also showed mild motor delay; speech was normal. At age 17 months, she developed metabolic acidosis and acute neurologic and cardiorespiratory decompensation associated with gastroenteritis. Laboratory studies showed hypoglycemia and hyperammonemia, and biochemical features suggesting biotin deficiency. She required tube-feeding for several months and was started on biotin supplementation, although she continued to have vomiting and diarrhea. After the genetic diagnosis was established, the biotin dose was increased and pantothenic acid was added, resulting in resolution of the diarrhea and improved growth, although gross motor delay was still noted. {4:Schwantje et al. (2019)} emphasized that infection may unmask this metabolic disorder.

{2:Hauth et al. (2022)} reported a 5-year-old girl, small for gestational age, who presented soon after birth with recurrent vomiting, gastroesophageal reflux, and failure to thrive. She continued to have vomiting and diarrhea, necessitating tube feeding for several months. At age 2 years, she was admitted for acute metabolic decompensation during a gastrointestinal viral illness. She recovered, but had subsequent periods of cyclic vomiting with a tendency to ketoacidosis. Psychomotor development was age-appropriate, although she was clumsy. Other features included low energy, very dry eczematous skin, and mild osteopenia. After the genetic diagnosis was established, she was started on biotin, pantothenic acid, and lipoic acid with resolution of vomiting, no more episodes of metabolic decompensation, and improved growth, development, and exercise capability.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: In patients with SMVTD, {1:Byrne et al. (2019)} and {5:Subramanian et al. (2017)} reported clinical improvement after treatment with biotin, pantothenic acid, and alpha-lipoic acid.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SMVTD in the family reported by {1:Byrne et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a boy with SMVTD, {5:Subramanian et al. (2017)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in exon 3 of the SLC5A6 gene (R94X, {604024.0001} and R123L, {604024.0002}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing. In vitro functional expression studies in HeLa cells transfected with the mutations showed no induction in biotin uptake compared to controls, consisted with a loss of function.

In 2 sibs with SMVTD, {1:Byrne et al. (2019)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC5A6 gene: a frameshift ({604024.0003}) and a missense mutation (R400T; {604024.0004}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Expression of the frameshift transcript was decreased compared to controls, suggesting nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, whereas R400T was expressed normally. In vitro studies of patient fibroblasts showed decreased biotin uptake compared to the parents, although the change was not statistically significant compared to controls. However, HeLa cells transfected with the mutations showed impaired biotin uptake compared to controls, consistent with a loss of function.

In a 3-year-old girl with SMVTD, {4:Schwantje et al. (2019)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC5A6 gene ({604024.0003} and c.1865_1866del, {604024.0005}). The c.1865_1866del mutation occurred in the last exon and was predicted to result in a frameshift (Gln622fs) and extension of the protein by 37 amino acids. The mutations, which were found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing, were each inherited from an unaffected parent. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In a patient with SMVID, {2:Hauth et al. (2022)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC5A6 gene, c.1865_1866del ({604024.0005}) and a splice site mutation ({604024.0006}). Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but the authors postulated that c.1865_1866del may encode a protein with residual catalytic activity since it appears to affect only the extreme C terminus.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Sabui et al. (2018)} found that Slc5a6-null mice exhibited growth retardation, developed chronic active intestinal inflammation, and died early. Treatment of pregnant mothers and of the mutant mice themselves with biotin and pantothenic acid prevented early death and normalized the growth rate and intestinal inflammation. The findings indicated that biotin and/or pantothenic acid play a role in maintaining normal intestinal integrity and health.
