text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Li-Ghorbani-Weisz-Hubshman syndrome (LIGOWS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KAT8 gene ({609912}) on chromosome 16p11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Li-Ghorbani-Weisz-Hubshman syndrome (LIGOWS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay, mild to moderately impaired intellectual development with language delay, and mild dysmorphic features. Affected individuals may have behavioral abnormalities and difficulties with numbers and understanding certain concepts, such as money. Some patients have seizures. Brain imaging often shows enlarged ventricles, thin corpus callosum, and gray matter nodular heterotopia, suggesting abnormal cortical brain development. More variable additional features may be present (summary by {1:Li et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Li et al. (2020)} reported 8 unrelated patients, ranging from 2 to 18 years of age, with a syndromic form of impaired intellectual development. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts and query of databases, such as GeneMatcher and DECIPHER. The patients had global developmental delay with walking in the first few years of life, often with an unsteady gait, fine motor delay, and impaired intellectual development with language delay. Cognitive impairment ranged from mild to moderate: IQ measured in 2 patients was 50 and 55. Many had difficulties with numbers or the value of money; 1 patient had ADHD and another had autism. Five patients had seizures and a sixth had a single febrile seizure. Brain imaging showed abnormalities in 5 of 7 patients who underwent studies. These included enlarged ventricles, decreased white matter volume, thin corpus callosum, and subependymal gray matter nodular heterotopia, suggestive of a neuronal migration defect. One patient had possible polymicrogyria. Most had nonspecific and variable dysmorphic features, such as hypotelorism, telecanthus, epicanthal folds, upslanted palpebral fissures, fullness of the upper lids, esotropia, low-set or dysplastic ears, high or depressed nasal bridge, full lips, downturned corners of the mouth, open mouth, fifth finger clinodactyly, and overlapping toes. A few had vision problems, mostly hyperopia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the KAT8 gene that were identified in 8 patients with LIGOWS by {1:Li et al. (2020)} occurred de novo. An additional patient (T9) carried compound heterozygous variants in the KAT8 gene that were inherited from unaffected parents; this suggested possible rare autosomal recessive inheritance and incomplete penetrance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
<Subhead> De Novo Heterozygous Mutations

In 8 unrelated patients with LIGOWS, {1:Li et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the KAT8 gene (see, e.g., {609912.0001}-{609912.0004}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. In vitro functional expression studies showed that the mutations were expressed at normal levels and could promote expression of MSL proteins (see MSL1, {614801}) similar to wildtype, but all mutants caused impaired acetylation of histone 4 lysine-16 (H4K16) compared to controls. The findings implicated a role for epigenetic regulation in cerebral cortical development.

<Subhead> Associations Pending Confirmation

{1:Li et al. (2020)} reported a 4-year-old girl (T9) with a similar but more severe neurodevelopmental disorder, who was compound heterozygous for a nonsense and a missense mutation in the KAT8 gene (K175X and R325C). Each unaffected parent was heterozygous for one of the mutations. In vitro studies showed that the R325C mutation impaired acetylation of H4K16; the nonsense mutation was difficult to express, but showed abnormal nuclear localization and was unable to promote expression of MSL proteins. The truncated protein was predicted to lack the catalytic domain, likely resulting in a loss of function. The authors postulated incomplete penetrance of the variants, as well as a possible different pathogenic mechanism for these mutations.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: In mice, {1:Li et al. (2020)} found that cerebrum-specific knockout of the Kat8 gene resulted in impaired postnatal growth, hyperactive behavior, and early death. Analysis of mutant mice at various stages of embryonic development showed cerebral hypoplasia with defects in neocortical lamination, abnormal neuronal differentiation with decreased neuronal progenitor cells, and aberrant neuronal migration. These defects were associated with impaired cell proliferation, increased apoptosis, defective neurosphere formation in vitro, and decreased H4K16 propionylation and acetylation in the cerebrocortical neuroepithelium.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy with impaired intellectual development (type B, 15; MDDGB15) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the DPM3 gene ({605951}) on chromosome 1q22. One such patient has been reported.

Biallelic mutation in the DPM3 gene can also cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy with cardiomyopathy without central nervous system involvement (MDDGC15; {612937}).

description.title: Description
description.content:
Congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy with impaired intellectual development (MDDGB15) is characterized by elevated serum creatine kinase, developmental delay, epilepsy, impaired intellectual development, and brain abnormalities ({1:Fu et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy type B, see MDDGB1 ({613155}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Fu et al. (2019)} reported an 8-year-old Chinese girl with congenital muscular dystrophy with central nervous system involvement. She had delayed motor development with ability to stand at age 30 months and walking at age 3 years. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated serum creatine kinase without obvious muscle symptoms. At age 6, she developed frequent absence seizures and showed mildly impaired intellectual development and learning difficulties. Brain imaging showed mild white matter abnormalities around the lateral ventricles. At age 8, she had normal muscle strength, but muscle biopsy showed myopathic features with increased fiber size variability and a few central nuclei. Immunoblotting indicated severely decreased alpha-dystroglycan (DAG1; {128239}). She did not have dilated cardiomyopathy; N-glycosylation studies were not performed.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MDDGB15 in the family reported by {1:Fu et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a Chinese girl with MDDGB15, {1:Fu et al. (2019)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the DPM3 gene (P42A, {605951.0003} and L85X, {605951.0004}). The mutations, which were found by next-generation sequencing of a targeted gene panel, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variants were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with seizures and language delay

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with seizures and language delay (IDDSELD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SETD1B gene ({611055}) on chromosome 12q24.

Patients with a microdeletion of chromosome 12q24 including the SETD1B gene have similar and overlapping features ({5:Palumbo et al., 2015}; {4:Labonne et al., 2016}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with seizures and language delay (IDDSELD) is characterized by global developmental delay with speech and language impairment and onset of seizures usually in the first few years of life. Seizures tend to be myoclonic, although variable types have been reported. Many patients have accompanying behavioral abnormalities, most commonly autism spectrum disorder and anxiety. Additional features, such as facial dysmorphism, tapering fingers, and pigmentary skin changes may also be observed (summary by {6:Roston et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Hiraide et al. (2018)} reported a 12-year-old Japanese girl (patient 1) with early-onset myoclonic seizures and impaired intellectual development. At 2 years, 9 months of age, she developed refractory myoclonic seizures with neck anteflexion and rolling of the eyes, which later evolved to frequent myoclonic absence seizures. EEG showed diffuse 2-3 Hz spike-wave discharges on a slow wave background. The seizures were eventually controlled with multiple medications, and she was seizure-free at 6 years of age. She had global developmental delay with walking at age 20 months and meaningful words at 14 months. At age 10 years, 9 months, she had mildly impaired intellectual development (IQ of 64), normal language, and autism spectrum disorder. Brain imaging was normal. An unrelated 34-year-old Japanese man (patient 2) with a similar but more severe disorder was also reported. He had onset of myoclonic seizures at age 4 years and generalized tonic seizures at age 6. EEG showed spike- and polyspike-slow wave complexes. The seizures were partially responsive to medication. This patient had global developmental delay with profoundly impaired intellectual development (IQ of 10), language delay, anxiety, and autism spectrum disorder. He also had dysmorphic features, including square face, thick eyebrows, downslanting palpebral fissures, flat occiput, full cheeks, full lower lip, and mildly tapered fingers. Brain imaging was normal. Patient 2 developed sigmoid adenocarcinoma at age 30.

{1:Den et al. (2019)} reported a Japanese girl with IDDSELD. At 2 years of age, she developed jerks associated with fever, followed by daily myoclonic seizures with EEG abnormalities, including diffuse spike and slow wave complexes with a background activity of occipital 5-6 Hz theta waves. She had developmental delay, language delay, and autistic behavior. Brain imaging was normal, and she did not have dysmorphic features.

{3:Krzyzewska et al. (2019)} reported 3 unrelated patients (patients 1, 2, and 5), aged 7 to 16 years, with IDDSELD. They were able to walk without support, but had impaired intellectual development and language delay. Two had documented seizures (the information was not available for the third patient), and 1 had autism. Two patients had dysmorphic features, including upslanting palpebral fissures, proptosis, hypertelorism, sunken eyes, short palpebral fissures, thick eyebrows, full cheeks, cleft lip/palate, and oligodontia.

{6:Roston et al. (2021)} reported 4 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 3.5 to 19 years, with IDDSELD. The patients had global developmental delay with mildly delayed walking, mildly to moderately impaired intellectual development, and speech impairment. Three patients had onset of seizures between 2 and 3 years of age, whereas 1 had onset of seizures at age 12. Seizure types included myoclonus, eyelid myoclonus, facial twitching, and absence and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. EEG abnormalities were variable; the seizures were difficult to control in some patients. Two patients had autism and 1 had attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Growth parameters and brain imaging were essentially normal. Other more variable features included joint laxity, lumbar lordosis, inguinal hernia, eczema or pigmentary skin abnormalities, and periodic shaking of the hands. One patient had subtle dysmorphic features, including downslanting palpebral fissures, small ears, midface hypoplasia, small nose, smooth philtrum, full cheeks, thin upper lip, fifth finger clinodactyly, and persistent fingertip pads.

{7:Weerts et al. (2021)} reported clinical features in 28 patients with IDDSELD, including 17 males and 11 females, with pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutations in the SETD1B gene. Features included seizures (20/28), which were generalized at onset in 16 patients; developmental delay (26/28); intellectual disability (21/25); autism spectrum disorder (18/28); and sleep disturbances (6/25). Dysmorphic facial features seen in the cohort included a high anterior hairline, thick arched or straight eyebrows, deep-set eyes, thin lips, and a prominent nose.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SETD1B gene that were identified in patients with IDDSELD by {2:Hiraide et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 unrelated Japanese patients with IDDSELD, {2:Hiraide et al. (2018)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the SETD1B gene (R1842W, {611055.0001}; R1859C, {611055.0002}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in several public databases, including dbSNP (build 137), 1000 Genomes Project, and ExAC. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. The patients were part of a cohort of 337 individuals with childhood-onset epilepsy who underwent trio-based whole-exome sequencing. In addition to the mutation in the SETD1B gene, patient 2, who had a more severe phenotype, carried additional variants in 4 other genes that may have contributed to the disorder. These included a de novo A9V variant in the KCNH7 gene ({608169}), a hemizygous L185I variant in the CNKSR2 gene ({300724}), a Y80C variant in the TBX22 gene ({300307}), and a D740E variant in the PCDH19 gene ({300460}).

In a Japanese girl with IDDSELD, {1:Den et al. (2019)} identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift in the last exon of the SETD1B gene ({611055.0003}) that was demonstrated to escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and predicted to produce a truncated protein. Additional functional studies were not performed, but the findings suggested a possible gain-of-function effect. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing; it was not present in multiple public databases, including gnomAD.

In 3 unrelated patients with IDDSELD, {3:Krzyzewska et al. (2019)} identified heterozygous mutations in the SETD1B gene ({611055.0001}-{611055.0002}; R1301X, {611055.0004}). Two of the mutations occurred de novo; the inheritance pattern in the third patient was unknown. The mutations were detected by whole-exome sequencing, and some of the patients were gathered through the GeneMatcher program. Using differential analysis to study patient DNA, {3:Krzyzewska et al. (2019)} found a shift of the genomewide methylation status toward hypermethylation compared to controls. This 'episignature' was unique to patients with SETD1B mutations when compared to patients with other neurodevelopmental disorders associated with methylation changes. The authors postulated a loss-of-function effect of the mutations.

{7:Weerts et al. (2021)} identified mutations in the SETD1B gene in 36 patients with neurodevelopmental disorders. Thirty-two patients had heterozygous mutations, 28 of which were shown to be de novo, 1 was inherited from an affected parent, and 1 was inherited from an unaffected parent. Of the heterozygous mutations, 14 were considered to be pathogenic (see, e.g., {611055.0008}-{611055.0012}) and 10 were considered to be likely pathogenic. Four patients (patients 3, 4, 11, and 12) from 3 families had biallelic variants of unknown significance in the SETD1B gene, which were inherited from unaffected carrier parents.

clinicalSynopsis: Global developmental delay, moderate to severe
Caused by mutation in the MAP kinase-activating death domain gene (MADD,)

Neurologic - CNS: Global developmental delay, moderate to severe
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the MAP kinase-activating death domain gene (MADD,)

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that DEEAH syndrome (developmental delay with endocrine, exocrine, autonomic, and hematologic abnormalities) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MADD gene ({603584}) on chromosome 11p11.

Biallelic mutation in the MADD gene can also cause a less severe neurodevelopmental disorder with some overlapping features (NEDDISH; {619005}).

description.title: Description
description.content: DEEAH syndrome is an autosomal recessive multisystemic disorder with onset in early infancy. Affected individuals usually present in the perinatal period with respiratory insufficiency, apneic episodes, and generalized hypotonia. The patients have failure to thrive and severely impaired global development with poor acquisition of motor, cognitive, and language skills. Other common features include endocrine, pancreatic exocrine, and autonomic dysfunction, as well as hematologic disturbances, mainly low hemoglobin. Patients also have dysmorphic and myopathic facial features. Additional more variable features include seizures, undescended testes, and distal skeletal anomalies. Death in early childhood may occur (summary by {2:Schneeberger et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Anazi et al. (2017)} reported a female infant, born of consanguineous Saudi parents, with a severe multisystemic disorder resulting in death at 14 months of age. The pregnancy was complicated by decreased fetal movements. She was hypoglycemic on the first day of life and developed seizures on day 20, despite glycemic control. She had profound developmental delay with poor eye contact, poor overall growth, and dysmorphic features, including downslanting palpebral fissures, depressed nasal bridge, posteriorly rotated ears, long philtrum, small mouth, micrognathia, short neck, widely spaced nipples, and overriding toes. Brain imaging at 5 months showed delayed myelination and T2-weighted hyperintensities in the basal ganglia.

{2:Schneeberger et al. (2020)} reported 14 patients (patients 1-14) from 11 unrelated families (families 1-11) with a severe multisystemic disorder apparent from early infancy. Six patients died before the third year of life and 1 died at age 7; the other patients ranged from 4 months to 12 years of age. Ten patients presented with perinatal complications, including apnea, respiratory distress, and generalized hypotonia. They showed failure to thrive with poor overall growth and hypotonia. All showed severely delayed motor development with limited spontaneous movement; most were unable to roll over or sit, although 2 patients could stand or walk with support. They had severe to profoundly impaired intellectual development mostly with absent speech, although a few patient could say single words. Nine patients had seizures, often associated with fever or hypoglycemia; EEG abnormalities were also observed. Brain imaging showed enlarged ventricles (5 patients), delayed myelination (1 patient), and pituitary hypoplasia (2 patients). Four patients had hearing loss and 8 had ocular findings such as esotropia, strabismus, myopia, or hyperopia. Almost all patients had features of peripheral or autonomic neuropathy, manifest as reduced pain sensation with self-mutilation, absent tears, apneic episodes, reduced heart rate, decreased sweating, and temperature dysregulation. The patients had additional systemic involvement, most notably endocrine abnormalities, such as hypoglycemia, thyroid dysfunction, growth hormone deficiency, and panhypopituitarism. Thirteen patients had low hemoglobin and 5 had thrombocytopenia. The patients had feeding problems with distended abdomen, gastroesophageal reflux, diarrhea or obstipation, hepatosplenomegaly, and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Skeletal anomalies included overlapping toes and fingers, cutaneous syndactyly, contractures, and variable radiographic findings such as reduced bone age, scoliosis, and hip dysplasia. Male patients had small penis and undescended testes. The patients had common dysmorphic features such as high, broad forehead, bitemporal narrowing, depressed nasal bridge, short nose with hypoplastic alae, small mouth, high palate, short palpebral fissures, micro- or retrognathia, low-set ears, short or long philtrum, and short neck.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEEAH syndrome in the families reported by {2:Schneeberger et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 14 patients from 11 families (families 1 to 11) with DEEAH syndrome, {2:Schneeberger et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the MADD gene (see, e.g., {603584.0005}-{603584.0008}). The families were of various ethnic descents, including Arab, Pakistani, South American, and Caucasian, and the patients were ascertained through international collaboration. The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Most were absent from the gnomAD database, but a few were present at a low frequency. Most patients carried a nonsense, frameshift, or splice site mutation on at least 1 allele, but 2 patients had homozygous missense mutations. In vitro functional expression studies of some of the mutations showed impaired TNFA-induced activation of the MAPK signaling pathway compared to controls. Patient cells showed enhanced susceptibility to TNFA-dependent apoptosis as well as other cellular stressors that resulted in activation of the intrinsic apoptosis pathway. Finally, patient cells showed decreased internalization of EGF compared to controls, which suggested a defect in the activation of small GTPase proteins and a disruption of vesicle trafficking, such as exocytosis. Overall, these data were consistent with a loss-of-function or hypomorphic effect of the mutations on MADD function. {2:Schneeberger et al. (2020)} noted that while there were no apparent genotype/phenotype correlations, mutation-specific disruption of the various MADD functions may underlie the clinical variability observed in the patients.

{2:Schneeberger et al. (2020)} noted that {1:Anazi et al. (2017)} had identified a homozygous missense mutation (variously reported as V977G, L977R, and L1040R) in the MADD gene in 14-month-old girl (17DG0771), born of consanguineous parents, with a similar disorder resulting in early death. {1:Anazi et al. (2017)} did not perform functional studies of the variant.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies, impaired speech and hypotonia

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies, impaired speech, and hypotonia (NEDDISH) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MADD gene ({603584}) on chromosome 11p11.

Biallelic mutation in the MADD gene can also cause a more severe neurodevelopmental disorder with some overlapping and additional systemic features (DEEAH; {619004}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies, impaired speech, and hypotonia (NEDDISH) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay and mildly to severely impaired intellectual development with poor speech and language acquisition. Some patients may have early normal development with onset of the disorder in the first years of life. More variable neurologic abnormalities include hypotonia, seizures, apnea, mild signs of autonomic or peripheral neuropathy, and autism. Aside from dysmorphic facial features and occasional findings such as scoliosis or undescended testes, other organ systems are not involved (summary by {3:Schneeberger et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Anazi et al. (2017)} reported a 6-year-old girl (17DG0770), conceived via IVF, with NEDDISH. She had normal early development until about 15 months of age when she showed speech delay, poor eye contact, and impaired social interaction compared to her unaffected dizygotic twin brother. She was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and continued to show speech delay, sleep disturbances, and behavioral abnormalities. Her twin brother was also mildly delayed, but not studied further.

{2:Hu et al. (2019)} reported 2 adult sisters, born of unrelated Iranian parents (family M135) with NEDDISH. Early development was normal, and both learned to walk and talk at 12 months of age. At 22 and 30 years of age, they showed impaired intellectual development (IQs of 50 and 60) and could build 2-word phrases, count money, and follow simple commands. Neither had seizures, spasticity, or behavioral abnormalities. Both had macrocephaly (+4 SD) and a long face or square mandible.

{3:Schneeberger et al. (2020)} reported 9 patients (patients 15-23) from 6 families (families 12-17) with NEDDISH. The patients, who ranged from 1 month to 19 years of age, all had global developmental delay, although the severity was highly variable. Two sibs (family 14) had mild intellectual disability at 13 and 19 years of age, whereas the rest of the patients had moderate to severe impairment. A few had behavioral abnormalities, such as ADHD or autistic features. Most had mildly delayed walking, sometimes with a dystonic gait, and all except 1 had impaired speech, including 2 patients who were nonverbal. Five patients had seizures, including 2 with absence and 2 with generalized; the fifth patient had only 1 episode of seizures. Other common features included hypotonia and nonspecific dysmorphic features, such as dolichocephaly, plagiocephaly, high or broad forehead, broad nasal bridge, full cheeks, low-set ears, small mouth, high palate, and dental crowding. Brain imaging was essentially normal, although 2 patients showed delayed myelination. Affected males had small penis and undescended testes. Less common features included kyphosis/scoliosis, apneic episodes in the neonatal period, and reduced pain sensation, suggesting neuropathy. None had endocrine abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDDISH in the families reported by {3:Schneeberger et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 6-year-old girl (17DG0770) with NEDDISH, {1:Anazi et al. (2017)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the MADD gene (R198H, {603584.0001} and R327X, {603584.0002}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing of 68 families with intellectual disability, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the nonsense mutation was predicted to disrupt the DENN domain including the GTPase binding site.

In 2 adult sisters, born of unrelated Iranian parents (family M135), with NEDDISH, {2:Hu et al. (2019)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the MADD gene ({603584.0003} and {603584.0004}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The family was part of a large cohort of 404 consanguineous families, mostly Iranian, in which 2 or more offspring had impaired intellectual development. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 9 patients (patients 15-23) from 6 families (families 12-17) with NEDDISH, {3:Schneeberger et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the MADD gene (see, e.g., {603584.0004} and {603584.0009}). The families were of various ethnic descents, including Persian and Caucasian, and the patients were ascertained through international collaboration. The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Most were absent from the gnomAD database, but 1 was present at a low frequency. Missense, nonsense, and frameshift mutations were identified. In vitro functional expression studies of fibroblasts derived from 1 patient (patient 18) showed disruption of several MADD functions compared to controls (see {603584.0009}), consistent with a loss-of-function or hypomorphic effect.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-48 (COXPD48) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the NSUN3 gene ({617491}) on chromosome 3q11.

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Van Haute et al. (2016)} reported a male infant who presented at around 3 months of age with failure to thrive, microcephaly, developmental delay, muscle weakness, external ophthalmoplegia, and convergent nystagmus associated with increased plasma lactate levels. Skeletal muscle analysis identified combined OXPHOS deficiency with normal mtDNA levels.

{1:Paramasivam et al. (2020)} reported an 8-month-old boy, born of consanguineous parents of East Asian origin, with a complex encephalomyopathic disorder. He presented at 4 months of age with global developmental delay, hypotonia, muscle weakness, and seizures associated with lactic acidosis. Brain imaging showed cerebral atrophy and white matter hyperintensities in both cerebral hemispheres. The patient's older sister, who had died, had lactic acidosis. Skeletal tissue and fibroblasts were not available from either patient.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of COXPD48 in the family reported by {2:Van Haute et al. (2016)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a male infant with COXPD48, {2:Van Haute et al. (2016)} identified compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the NSUN3 gene ({617491.0001} and {617491.0002}). Each unaffected parent was heterozygous for one of the mutations. Western blot analysis of patient-derived fibroblasts showed absence of the full-length NSUN3 protein, consistent with a loss of function. Patient fibroblasts also showed impaired mitochondrial respiratory chain activity, reduced oxygen consumption, impaired growth under galactose conditions, and defective mitochondrial translation and protein synthesis compared to controls. These defects could be restored by expression of wildtype NSUN3. More detailed analysis of patient cells showed methylation abnormalities affecting the anticodon of mt-tRNA(Met), which was responsible for impaired mitochondrial translation and a combined OXPHOS deficiency.

In an 8-month-old boy, born of consanguineous East Asian parents, with COXPD48, {1:Paramasivam et al. (2020)} identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the NSUN3 gene (C152S, {617491.0003} and A141P, {617491.0004}). The mutations, which were found by targeted sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Both occurred at highly conserved residues in the protein and neither were present in several public databases, including gnomAD. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with progressive spasticity and brain white matter abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with progressive spasticity and brain white matter abnormalities (NEDSWMA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the HPDL gene ({618994}) on chromosome 1p34.

Biallelic mutation in the HPDL gene can also cause the less severe disorder spastic paraplegia-83 (SPG83; {619027}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with progressive spasticity and brain white matter abnormalities (NEDSWMA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by impaired psychomotor development apparent in infancy. Affected individuals show poor overall growth, progressive microcephaly, and axial hypotonia, with later onset of spasticity. The disorder is progressive. Some patients show normal early development, but later have regression of motor, cognitive, and language skills. More variable features include seizures, joint contractures, ocular disturbances, episodic respiratory failure, and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features. The intellectual impairment is variable, ranging from poor visual contact with inability to walk or speak to milder intellectual disability with the ability to say some words. Brain imaging shows variable white matter abnormalities, including thin corpus callosum and poor myelination (summary by {2:Husain et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{5:Mitchell and Bundey (1997)} and {4:McHale et al. (1999)} reported a consanguineous family of Pakistani origin in which 4 sibs presented in infancy with a phenotype consistent with spastic cerebral palsy. All had moderately to severely impaired intellectual development. All had spasticity affecting predominantly the lower limbs, although 2 also had mild hypertonia and ataxia of the upper limbs. Spastic features included hypertonicity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses. Two older sibs had contractures. One patient had bilateral dislocated hips and another had microcephaly and scoliosis. Cranial nerve abnormalities, nystagmus, and seizures were not present. {6:Morgan et al. (2021)} provided follow-up of this kindred and identified 3 additional affected individuals. The patients had onset of mildly delayed walking in the first years of life with spasticity of the lower limbs, hyperreflexia, and increased tone. Some patients had upper limb ataxia and facial hypotonia. The disorder was progressive, and most patients became wheelchair-bound in the second or third decades. Five patients were noted to have learning disabilities; none had seizures.

{2:Husain et al. (2020)} reported 12 patients from 9 unrelated families with global developmental delay apparent in infancy. The patients were ascertained through international collaboration and the GeneMatcher program. There was clinical heterogeneity regarding the age at onset and severity. Two sibs, born of unrelated Algerian parents (family 1), were the most severely affected. They presented at birth with hypotonia, poor feeding, failure to thrive, and severe global developmental delay. They developed spastic tetraparesis, axial dystonia, progressive microcephaly (-5 SD), seizures, and joint contractures. One sib was noted to be nonverbal and to have poor visual function. Dysmorphic features included hypertelorism, long eyelashes, anteverted nostrils, high-arched palate, short neck, and retrognathia. Brain imaging in both patients showed white matter defects and thin corpus callosum, as well as T2-weighted signal abnormalities in the central white matter. Nine additional patients (families 2-8) had onset of neurologic signs and symptoms between 1 week and 12 months of age: some showed normal early development and subsequent regression with loss of skills. The last patient (family 9), who had a milder phenotype, presented at 5 years of age with progressive spasticity and brain imaging abnormalities, with subsequent loss of independent ambulation and dysarthria. Common features among all patients included progressive spasticity, often resulting in inability to walk, contractures, hypotonia, muscle weakness, ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, visual disturbances, poor or absent speech, dysphagia, and progressive microcephaly. Most patients developed seizures, and 3 had electrophysiologic evidence of a peripheral neuropathy. Five patients had episodes of acute respiratory failure necessitating hospitalization. Muscle biopsy, when performed, showed fiber size variation; a few samples had increased or decreased activities of mitochondrial respiratory enzymes, suggesting mitochondrial dysfunction, although there was no consistent signature of OXPHOS deficiency. Several patients had mildly increased lactate. Brain imaging in most patients revealed white matter pathology. {2:Husain et al. (2020)} delineated 3 MRI patterns observed in the patients. Pattern I was characterized by T2-weighted multifocal striatal signal changes, reduction of white matter volume, thin corpus callosum, and deficient myelination. U-fibers were often affected, although the cerebellum was not. Pattern II was characterized by white matter abnormalities affecting the thalami, brainstem, and cerebellum. Pattern III was not related to clear pathology, although some patients had evidence of white matter changes. There tended to be a correlation between the severity of the disorder and the MRI pattern, such that patients with pattern I had the most severe phenotype. The MRI abnormalities were progressive in some and improved over time in others.

{8:Wiessner et al. (2021)} reported a cohort of 34 individuals with biallelic mutations in the HPDL gene. The patients were categorized has having mild disease (10 patients), intermediate disease (9 patients), or severe disease (15 patients). The 10 patients with mild disease had SPG83 ({619027}). The 15 patients with severe disease had an age of onset between 0 and 12 months. All 15 had global developmental delay and infantile-onset spasticity, which affected all 4 limbs in 14 patients. None of the patients were ambulatory. Other clinical features included seizures in 11 patients, episodic encephalopathy in 6 patients, and oculomotor abnormalities in 4 patients. MRI abnormalities, reported in 14 patients, included corpus callosum abnormalities in 11, generalized white matter changes in 11, abnormal gyration in 4, and global cerebral atrophy in 7. The 9 patients with intermediate disease presented between 3 and 7 years of age, and all 9 achieved independent walking. Other features in these 9 patients included upper limb involvement in 7, ataxia in 6, oculomotor abnormalities in 6, and seizures in 2. One patient had an encephalopathic episode. Of the 8 patients with intermediate disease for whom MRI findings were reported, 5 had cerebellar atrophy, 4 had corpus callosum abnormalities, and 5 had olival hyperintense lesions.

{1:Ghosh et al. (2021)} reported 16 patients with NEDSWMA from 7 unrelated consanguineous families from Egypt, Pakistan, and Iran. The patients, who ranged from 1 month to 14 years of age, had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, poor social skills, and delayed or absent acquisition of gross and fine motor skills. Eight patients died between 2 months and 13 years of age, most commonly from epilepsy. Most, but not all, had onset of myoclonic or focal epilepsy in the first days or months of life; the seizures in these patients were mostly intractable. The patients also had lower limb spasticity with hypertonia and hyperreflexia with Babinski sign. Extrapyramidal signs, such as dystonia, tremor, and rigidity, were also observed in some patients. Many had impaired vision, including cortical blindness, poor tracking, and nystagmus. Brain imaging in the more severely affected patients showed cortical atrophy, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, brainstem hypoplasia, ventriculomegaly, and white matter defects. About half the patients had poor growth with microcephaly (down to -6 SD); a few had nonspecific dysmorphic features.

{7:Shi et al. (2025)} reported a boy with NEDSWMA who developed normally until 8 years of age, when he presented with rapidly progressing spasticity over 2 to 3 months, requiring use of a wheelchair. Two younger sibs had developed rapidly progressing and catastrophic encephalopathy and seizures and had died in infancy. The second sib had the same compound heterozygous HPDL variants as the proband. Administration of oral CoQ10 had no effect over 6 weeks. Given the availability of pure 4-hydroxybenzoate (4-HB), {7:Shi et al. (2025)} obtained approval for administration of a single-patient investigational new drug (IND) and started treatment with initial updosing over 4 days to 100 mg/kg for 30 days, then 50 mg/kg for 95 days, then 25 mg/kg. There was some emesis during the initial high-dose high-volume treatment, but no further emesis. Remarkably, the boy regained motor skills and was able to run by day 54 and ride a bicycle by day 124. There was no toxicity during 8 months of treatment. The authors concluded that treatment with CoQ10 headgroup intermediates can restore CoQ10 synthesis and modify the course of mitochondrial encephalopathy driven by HPDL variants.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSWMA in the families reported by {2:Husain et al. (2020)} and {6:Morgan et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 12 patients from 9 unrelated families (families 1-9) with NEDSWMA, {2:Husain et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the HPDL gene (see, e.g., {618994.0001}-{618994.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families and were not present in the gnomAD database. There were nonsense, frameshift, and missense mutations. Western blot analysis of fibroblasts derived from some of the patients showed significantly reduced HPDL protein levels compared to controls, suggesting that the mutations result in a loss-of-function effect. Additional functional studies of the variants were not performed. The patients were ascertained from several medical centers through international collaborative efforts and GeneMatcher.

In affected members of a consanguineous Pakistani kindred reported by {5:Mitchell and Bundey (1997)} and {4:McHale et al. (1999)} to have a cerebral palsy phenotype, {6:Morgan et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the HPDL gene (L176P; {618994.0007}) on chromosome 1p34. The mutation, which was found by a combination of linkage analysis and whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both branches of the kindred. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. One branch of the family had previously been reported by {3:Lynex et al. (2004)} as having a homozygous missense variant in the GAD1 gene (S12C; {605363.0001}), but the updated report by {6:Morgan et al. (2021)} noted that the GAD1 variant did not segregate in the family; the findings established that the HPDL mutation is actually the cause of the disorder in this family.

{8:Wiessner et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the HPDL gene in 34 individuals from 25 unrelated families, including 24 patients with NEDSWMA and 10 with autosomal recessive SPG83. Twenty-eight mutations were identified in the 25 families, 12 of which were consanguineous. {8:Wiessner et al. (2021)} noted that truncating mutations in the HPLD gene tended to be more frequent in patients with severe disease compared to those with mild or intermediate disease, suggesting a correlation between residual enzymatic activity and phenotypic severity.

In 16 patients from 7 unrelated consanguineous families with NEDSWMA, {1:Ghosh et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the HPDL gene (see, e.g., {618994.0006}, {618994.0010}-{618994.0013}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. All mutations occurred in one of the VOC domains and were predicted to affect enzyme function. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but knockdown of the HPDL gene in a cell line resulted in up- and downregulation of metabolites compared to controls, although tyrosine catabolism appeared to be unaffected. Additional studies of HPDL-null cells showed reduced oxygen consumption, suggesting an effect on mitochondrial metabolism. The authors concluded that the disorder is not only a mitochondrial neurodegenerative condition, but also likely a neurometabolic condition, and results from a loss of HPDL function.

{7:Shi et al. (2025)} reported an 8-year-old boy with NEDSWMA who was compound heterozygous for mutations in the HPDL gene (see {618994.0014}). Two younger sibs, 1 of whom was shown to carry the same mutations, had developed rapidly progressing and catastrophic encephalopathy and seizures and had died in infancy. Oral administration of the CoQ10 headgroup intermediate 4-hydroxybenzoate (4-HB) stabilized and improved the neurologic symptoms of the patient, with no toxicity during 8 months of treatment. The authors concluded that treatment with CoQ10 headgroup intermediates can restore CoQ10 synthesis and modify the course of mitochondrial encephalopathy driven by HPDL variants.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{1:Ghosh et al. (2021)} found that Hpdl-null mice developed seizures, had poor overall growth, and died before day 15 of life. Brains from mutant mice were smaller than those of controls and showed cellular apoptosis. There was no evidence of abnormalities in tyrosine catabolism.

{7:Shi et al. (2025)} found that that supplementation with the CoQ10 headgroup intermediates 4-hydroxymandelate (4-HMA) or 4-HB improved the neurologic symptoms of Hpdl -/- mice and extended their lifespan to the average lifespan of a mouse. Both 4-HMA and 4-HB crossed the blood-brain barrier and restored CoQ synthesis in brain. Moreover, 4-HMA improved mitochondrial and cerebellar morphology of Hpdl -/- brain, improved mitochondrial electron transport chain activity and Purkinje cell function, and alleviated deficits in motor function.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that coenzyme Q10 deficiency-9 (COQ10D9) is caused by homozygous mutation in the COQ5 gene ({616359}) on chromosome 12q24. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Coenzyme Q10 deficiency-9 (COQ10D9) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by onset of cerebellar ataxia associated with cerebellar atrophy in the first decade of life. Some patients may have additional neurologic signs and symptoms, including intellectual disability and seizures. Treatment with CoQ10 may offer clinical benefit (summary by {1:Malicdan et al., 2018}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency, see COQ10D1 ({607426}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Malicdan et al. (2018)} reported 3 sisters, born of unrelated parents of Iraqi-Jewish descent, with onset of cerebellar ataxia and variable additional neurologic features in the first decade of life. The 17-year-old proband, who was the most severely affected, presented in early childhood with short stature and a moderate delay in motor and cognitive milestones, followed by nonprogressive cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, myoclonic jerks, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures that could be controlled. She had mild-to-moderate intellectual disability with impulsivity, short attention span, and other behavioral problems. Neurologic examination showed mild horizontal nystagmus, slow saccades with saccadic pursuit and apraxic gaze, dysmetria, mild tremor, ataxic gait, and mild lower limb spasticity with brisk reflexes. Brain imaging showed nonprogressive cerebellar atrophy. Her 2 sisters, who were 22 and 14 years of age, had mild motor delay and mild cerebellar ataxia associated with variable cerebellar signs, such as nystagmus, oculomotor apraxia, dysarthria, and mild dysmetria. Brain imaging in the older sister showed mild cerebellar atrophy. The older sister had myoclonic jerks and a single seizure at age 22 that could be controlled; the younger sister had no seizures. Both sisters had mild learning disabilities but attended school. The older sister also gave birth to a healthy boy and had no signs of deterioration during the pregnancy. Skeletal muscle biopsy showed increased type 2C muscle fibers (about 34% compared to less than 7% in controls), but there were no signs of myopathy, ragged red fibers, mitochondrial dysfunction, or structural defects. The patients showed favorable response to treatment with CoQ10 supplementation.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of COQ10D9 in the family reported by {1:Malicdan et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 sisters with COQ10D9, {1:Malicdan et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous 9.6-kb duplication in the COQ5 gene ({616359.0001}). The duplication, which was found by detailed genetic analysis and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Homozygosity for the variant was not found in 92 healthy individuals from the same ethnic background; however, there were 3 heterozygous carriers, yielding a minor allele frequency of about 1.5%. Patient fibroblasts, leukocytes, and skeletal muscle tissue had significantly decreased COQ5 mRNA and protein levels compared to controls. Cultured fibroblasts from 1 patient showed a defect in mitochondrial complex II+III activity and abnormal oxygen consumption, suggesting that the mutation had an adverse effect on mitochondrial respiration.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with epilepsy, behavioral abnormalities, and coarse facies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with epilepsy, behavioral abnormalities, and coarse facies (IDDEBF) is caused by homozygous mutation in the ALG14 gene ({612866}) on chromosome 1p21. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content: IDDEBF is a severe disorder characterized by impaired intellectual development, epilepsy, behavioral abnormalities, and coarse facies. Brain MRI findings may include delayed myelination in the deep parietal lobes ({1:Kvarnung et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Kvarnung et al. (2018)} reported a brother and sister from a consanguineous family from Afghanistan (family 9) who presented in early infancy with infantile spasms and developmental delay. At ages 18 and 21 years, both sibs had severely impaired intellectual development, autism, epilepsy, anxiety, and behavioral problems, including aggression, hyperactivity, and self-injurious behaviors. Both had coarse features and prognathism. Neither sib had speech. Brain MRI in the sister at age 12 years showed delayed myelination in the deep parietal lobes.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IDDEBF in the family reported by {1:Kvarnung et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 adult sibs from a consanguineous family from Afghanistan (family 9) with IDDEBF, {1:Kvarnung et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous deletion in intron 2 of the ALG14 gene ({612866.0003}). The mutation, which was identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The mutation was not present in the gnomAD database. Analysis of RNA from patient fibroblasts showed 2 transcripts: a transcript with aberrant in-frame skipping of exon 3 and the full-length ALG14 transcript with significantly reduced expression compared to controls. Analysis of RNA from the father showed expression of both transcripts, but normal expression of the full-length transcript.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Vissers-Bodmer syndrome (VIBOS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CNOT1 gene ({604917}) on chromosome 16q21.

Heterozygous mutation in the CNOT1 gene also causes holoprosencephaly-12 with or without pancreatic agenesis (HPE12; {618500}), which shows some overlapping neurologic features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Vissers-Bodmer syndrome (VIBOS) is characterized by global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, speech delay, motor delay, and behavioral abnormalities apparent from infancy. The phenotype is highly variable: some individuals have only mild learning difficulties, whereas others have severe cognitive impairment with IQ in the 50s. Many patients have behavioral abnormalities, including autism spectrum disorder, ADD, ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and impulsivity. Other common features include growth impairment abnormalities, hypotonia, and distal skeletal defects, such as foot and hand deformities. Less common features include seizures, brain abnormalities on MRI, feeding problems, and joint hypermobility. Most individuals have dysmorphic facial features, but there is no recognizable gestalt (summary by {3:Vissers et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {3:Vissers et al. (2020)} reported 39 individuals from 37 unrelated families with a similar developmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts facilitated by the MatchMaker Exchange program. Five of the patients (patients 20-24), previously reported as having HPE12 ({1:De Franco et al., 2019} and {2:Kruszka et al., 2019}), were also included in the paper by {3:Vissers et al. (2020)}. The patients, who ranged from infancy to 22 years of age, had global developmental delay, usually with impaired intellectual development, speech delay, and hypotonia. There was variability in the presence of these features as well as in the severity of disability: some patients were reported not to have intellectual disability, but they had learning difficulties or speech or motor delay. Most patients had variable nonspecific additional features, including abnormal growth (74%), behavioral problems (65%), brain abnormalities (65%), and anomalies of the skeletal system or soft tissue system. These included decreased stature and head circumference, clinodactyly, brachydactyly, foot deformities, and scoliosis. Brain imaging findings, when present, were nonspecific: white matter abnormalities, thin corpus callosum, and enlarged ventricles. Behavioral problems, such as autism spectrum disorder, poor attention, and obsessive-compulsive behavior, were observed in most patients. Most patients (over 90%) had dysmorphic facial features, but there was no gestalt or recognizable pattern. Features included hypertelorism, straight eyebrows, strabismus, low nasal bridge, and thick lips. None of the patients reported for the first time by {3:Vissers et al. (2020)} had holoprosencephaly or pancreatic agenesis, suggesting that HPE12 is a distinct clinical entity.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CNOT1 gene that were identified in most patients with VIBOS by {3:Vissers et al. (2020)} occurred de novo. In 2 families, the inheritance pattern was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with variable or incomplete expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 39 patients from 37 unrelated families with VIBOS, {3:Vissers et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous mutations in the CNOT1 gene (see, e.g., {604917.0002}-{604917.0006}). The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts facilitated by MatchMaker Exchange. Most of the mutations occurred de novo, although 2 were inherited from mildly affected parents, and 1 was inherited from a somatic mosaic parent. There were nonsense, frameshift, splice site, and missense mutations, with no obvious genotype/phenotype correlations. The missense mutations affected conserved residues in functional domains of the protein. In vitro functional studies of some of the variants that were transfected into COS1 cells showed that the mutant proteins were still able to interact with partner proteins of the CCR4-NOT complex. The mutations also did not increase apoptosis in transfected cells, and there were no differences in endonucleolytic nonsense-mediated mRNA decay components compared to controls. These findings suggested that the mutations were hypomorphic, rather than dominant-negative. None of the mutations were able to fully rescue memory deficits in Cnot1-null Drosophila, although some showed partial rescue. {3:Vissers et al. (2020)} noted that their functional studies were unable to reveal the pathophysiologic mechanisms resulting from the CNOT1 mutations, but concluded that knockdown and rescue experiments in Drosophila supported the plausibility that the mutations contributed to the neurodevelopmental disorder observed in the patients.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Vissers et al. (2020)} found that knockdown of the Cnot1 gene in Drosophila was associated with impaired learning and memory compared to wildtype. Expression of the human CNOT1 gene was able to rescue the memory phenotype.

phenotypes.phenotype: Myopathy, epilepsy, and progressive cerebral atrophy

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that myopathy, epilepsy, and progressive cerebral atrophy (MEPCA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ALG14 gene ({612866}) on chromosome 1p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Myopathy, epilepsy, and progressive cerebral atrophy (MEPCA) is a severe autosomal recessive disorder with onset in utero or at birth. Affected individuals have hypotonia with respiratory or feeding difficulties apparent from birth and often associated with contractures of the large joints. There is little spontaneous movement: skeletal muscle biopsy and electrophysiologic studies are consistent with a myopathy or myasthenic disorder. Patients also develop refractory seizures with burst-suppression pattern or hypsarrhythmia on EEG. Brain imaging shows progressive cerebral atrophy and myelination defects. All patients reported to date died within the first year of life (summary by {1:Schorling et al., 2017}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Schorling et al. (2017)} reported 5 infants from 3 unrelated families with a neurodegenerative disorder resulting in death in the first year of life. The patients presented at birth with severe muscular hypotonia, respiratory insufficiency and feeding problems necessitating support or intervention, and joint contractures. Some had foot deformities and high-arched palate. In some cases, the pregnancies were complicated by polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movements. All patients developed refractory seizures with burst suppression or hypsarrhythmia on EEG. Serial brain imaging showed progressive and severe supratentorial atrophy, as well as delayed myelination. Muscle biopsy revealed variation in fiber diameter, type II fiber predominance, fiber atrophy, and nonspecific myopathic changes. Mitochondrial respiratory chain studies were normal. Nerve conduction studies performed in 2 patients showed decremental responses after repetitive stimulation, consistent with a myasthenic disorder. Pyridostigmine treatment was initially successful, but only temporary. EMG in 1 patient showed denervation and reinnervation, suggestive of anterior horn cell disease. Neuropathologic studies, performed in 2 patients, showed neurodegenerative changes with reactive astrocytosis, microglia, and decreased myelination. There was no evidence for neuronal migration defects or cortical dysplasia. Dysmorphic features included turricephalus, scaphocephalus, micrognathia, and high-arched palate. Isoelectric focusing of serum transferrin was performed in 2 patients, but showed only mild abnormalities in 1.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MEPCA in the families reported by {1:Schorling et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 infants from 3 unrelated families with MEPCA, {1:Schorling et al. (2017)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations in the ALG14 gene (D74N, {612866.0004}; V141G, {612866.0005}; and R109Q, {612866.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. All were found at low frequencies in the ExAC database (less than 0.02%). Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. The patients presented at birth with severe hypotonia; all died within the first year of life. Based on the known gene function, the authors postulated that a glycosylation defect was the cause of this multisystem disorder, although there was not clear laboratory evidence of a glycosylation defect.

phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 3

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 3 (MC4DN3) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COX10 gene ({602125}) on chromosome 17p12.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 3 (MC4DN3) is an autosomal recessive multisystem metabolic disorder with a highly variable phenotype. Some patients present with encephalomyopathic features in early infancy, whereas others may present later in infancy or the first years of life after normal early development. Affected individuals show hypotonia, failure to thrive, and developmental delay or regression with poor eye contact and loss of motor skills with ataxia. Additional features observed in some patients include proximal renal tubulopathy, macrocytic anemia, sensorineural hearing loss, nystagmus, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, consistent with systemic involvement. Brain imaging in most patients shows lesions consistent with Leigh syndrome (see {256000}). Laboratory studies show increased serum lactate and decreased levels and activity of mitochondrial respiratory complex IV. Most patients die in infancy (summary by {3:Valnot et al., 2000} and {1:Antonicka et al., 2003}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency, see {220110}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Valnot et al. (2000)} reported a boy with unremarkable development until the age of 18 months when he developed ataxia. At 2 years of age he presented with poor eye contact, severe muscle weakness, hypotonia, ataxia, ptosis, pyramidal syndrome, and status epilepticus. Increased urinary amino acids were suggestive of a proximal tubulopathy. Isolated cytochrome c oxidase (COX) deficiency in muscle, lymphocytes, and fibroblast cultures was demonstrated. He died at 2 years of age. An older sister had died at 5 years of age of a mitochondrial encephalopathy ascribed to COX deficiency. A younger sister had progressive neurologic deterioration with similar biochemical anomalies at the age of 2 years and died at the age of 3 years.

{1:Antonicka et al. (2003)} reported 2 unrelated patients with COX deficiency caused by mutations in the COX10 gene. The first patient (patient D) presented in the first week of life with hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, hypotonia, and poor feeding. He also had profound sensorineural hearing loss, severe biventricular hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and macrocytic anemia. He died at age 5 months. Skeletal muscle mitochondrial COX activity was less than 5% of control values, and COX activity in the patient's fibroblasts was decreased to approximately 40% of control values. The second patient (patient S) presented at 6 weeks of age with hypotrophy, anemia, hypotonia, and lactic acidosis. Brain imaging showed symmetric basal ganglia lesions consistent with Leigh syndrome (see {256000}). She died at age 4 months. Skeletal muscle and fibroblast COX activity were 16% and 18% of normal controls, respectively. The authors noted the different clinical presentations.

{2:Coenen et al. (2004)} reported a patient who developed failure to thrive, hypotonia, delayed motor development, and motor agitation at 5 months of age. Other features included head lag, ataxia, nystagmus, slow saccades, and poor visual fixation. He had metabolic acidosis and hyperintense lesions in the thalamus, consistent with Leigh syndrome. COX activity was significantly reduced in patient muscle and fibroblasts. The patient died at 9 months of age.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC4DN3 in the family reported by {3:Valnot et al. (2000)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

mapping.title: Mapping
mapping.content: {3:Valnot et al. (2000)} performed a genetic linkage study of a consanguineous family with an isolated cytochrome c oxidase defect and mapped the disease locus to chromosome 17p13.1-q11.1, near COX10, a gene that encodes a complex IV assembly protein.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In affected members of a consanguineous family with an isolated cytochrome c oxidase defect, {3:Valnot et al. (2000)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the COX10 gene ({602125.0001}). The mutation segregated with the phenotype in the family. Western blot analysis of patient fibroblasts revealed almost undetectable levels of COX subunit II, and the mutant allele failed to correct a yeast cox10 mutant strain, thus confirming the biochemical effects of the mutation.

{1:Antonicka et al. (2003)} reported 2 unrelated patients with COX deficiency caused by compound heterozygous mutations in the COX10 gene ({602125.0002}-{602125.0005}). The mutations segregated with the phenotype in both families.

In a patient with COX deficiency, {2:Coenen et al. (2004)} identified a homozygous mutation in the COX10 gene ({602125.0006}). Residual COX activity in skeletal muscle was 29% of controls. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation.

phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 7

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC4DN7) is caused by homozygous mutation in the COX6B1 gene ({124089}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC4DN7) is an autosomal recessive metabolic encephalomyopathic disorder with highly variable manifestations. Only a few patients have been reported. Some patients have normal early development then show rapid neurodegeneration with progressive muscle weakness, gait disturbances, and cognitive decline in mid to late childhood. Other features may include seizures and visual impairment. Brain imaging shows progressive leukodystrophy with cystic lesions. In contrast, at least 1 patient has been reported who presented in the neonatal period with metabolic acidosis, hydrocephalus, hypotonia, and cortical blindness. This patient developed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy resulting in early death. All patients had increased serum lactate and decreased levels and activity of mitochondrial respiratory complex IV (summary by {2:Massa et al., 2008} and {1:Abdulhag et al., 2015}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency, see {220110}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Massa et al. (2008)} reported 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Saudi Arabian parents, with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency. After normal development, the boys had onset of muscle weakness and pain or unsteady gait and visual disturbances at ages 8 and 6 years, respectively. The older boy had rapidly progressive neurologic deterioration with leukodystrophic brain changes and seizures and died at age 10 years. The younger boy had ataxia, muscle weakness, cognitive decline, decreased visual acuity, and leukodystrophic changes in the brain. Both had increased serum and CSF lactate and decreased COX activity (20% of normal) in muscle biopsy.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{1:Abdulhag et al. (2015)} reported a male infant, born of consanguineous Palestinian parents, who presented in the neonatal period with lactic acidosis and left ventricular hypertrophy. He developed encephalomyopathy with hydrocephalus, cortical blindness, and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy; he died at age 30 months.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC4DN7 in the family reported by {2:Massa et al. (2008)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
{2:Massa et al. (2008)} identified a homozygous mutation in the COX6B1 gene (R19H; {124089.0001}) in 2 Saudi Arabian sibs with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency. In vitro studies showed that the mutant COX6B1 subunit resulted in a decrease of fully assembled COX.

In a male child, born of consanguineous Palestinian parents, with COX deficiency, {1:Abdulhag et al. (2015)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the COX6B1 gene (R20C; {124089.0002}). Western blot analysis of patient muscle mitochondria showed isolated undetectable complex IV activity and barely detectable residual amount of mutant protein (11% of control), suggesting that the mutant protein is unstable. Transfection of wildtype COX6B1 into patient fibroblasts restored COX activity. {1:Abdulhag et al. (2015)} stated that the R20C residue was the same residue as that reported by {2:Massa et al. (2008)}.

phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 12

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 12 (MC4DN12) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PET100 gene ({614770}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 12 (MC4DN12) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder characterized by the onset of neurologic dysfunction in early infancy. Affected individuals demonstrate hypotonia with poor head control, profoundly delayed global development with inability to fix and follow, poor overall growth, abnormal spasms or myoclonus, and seizures. Most patients die in the first years of life; those that survive have spastic quadriplegia, feeding difficulties necessitating tube feeding, and profoundly impaired intellectual development with poor or absent communication. More variable features include cortical blindness, nystagmus, scoliosis, and hearing impairment. Brain imaging shows abnormalities consistent with Leigh syndrome (see {256000}), as well as cystic cavitation. Laboratory studies show lactic acidosis, increased serum creatine kinase, and decreased levels and activity of mitochondrial respiratory complex IV (summary by {1:Lim et al., 2014}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency, see {220110}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Lim et al. (2014)} reported 10 patients from 8 families with mitochondrial complex IV deficiency. All of the patients were of Lebanese descent living in Australia, and 6 of the families were consanguineous. The patients had a severe neuromuscular disorder, with profoundly delayed psychomotor development since early infancy, seizures, hypotonia, and brain abnormalities consistent with Leigh syndrome. Many of the patients died in the first years of life.

{2:Olahova et al. (2015)} reported a newborn girl, born of consanguineous British Pakistani parents, with MC4DN12. The patient had intrauterine growth retardation and was delivered by cesarean section at 34 weeks' gestation. She had severe lactic and metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, increased serum creatine kinase, and intraventricular cysts on brain ultrasound. She developed seizures at 48 hours of age and died at 55 hours of age.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC4DN12 in the families reported by {1:Lim et al. (2014)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 10 patients from 8 Lebanese families living in Australia with mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, {1:Lim et al. (2014)} identified a homozygous mutation in the PET100 gene (M1?; {614770.0001}). The mutation, which was found by homozygosity mapping combined with targeted sequencing of the candidate region, segregated with the disorder in all the families. The variant was not found in the dbSNP (build 132) or 1000 Genomes Project databases. Patient fibroblasts showed a significant loss of the complex IV holoenzyme, although the subunits were translated, suggesting an assembly defect. Overexpression of the wildtype gene in patient cells restored COX2 levels and complex IV assembly.

In a newborn girl, born of consanguineous British Pakistani parents, with MC4DN12, {2:Olahova et al. (2015)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the PET100 gene (Q48X; {614770.0002}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Patient fibroblasts and skeletal muscle showed isolated impaired complex IV activity and a profound defect in COX assembly with decreased steady-state levels of complex IV proteins and decreased amounts of fully assembled complex IV.
