text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with speech impairment and dysmorphic facies (NEDSID) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SETD1A gene ({611052}) on chromosome 16p11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with speech impairment and dysmorphic facies (NEDSID) is characterized by developmental delay associated with mild to moderately impaired intellectual development or learning difficulties, behavioral or psychiatric abnormalities, and delayed speech and language acquisition. Additional features include dysmorphic facies, distal limb anomalies, gastrointestinal problems or feeding difficulties, and hypotonia. The phenotypic features and severity of the disorder are variable (summary by {3:Kummeling et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Kummeling et al. (2021)} reported 15 unrelated patients with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder who were ascertained from several different clinical or research centers through the GeneMatcher program. Twelve patients were between 34 months and 10 years of age, 2 were in their teens, and 1 was 23 years old. One boy (patient 5) died at 4 years of age. The patients had global developmental delay with mild motor delay, mild to moderately impaired intellectual development, learning difficulties, and poor speech and language acquisition. One girl (patient 14) was specifically noted to have speech apraxia. Most had behavioral or psychiatric abnormalities, including aggressive behavior, short attention span, anxiety, sleep disturbances, overfriendliness, and autistic features. Two older patients had features of a psychotic disorder. All patients had dysmorphic facial features, although the features were somewhat variable. Common findings included high forehead, downslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, deep-set eyes, wide nose with anteverted nares and broad tip, full cheeks, low-set ears, microtia, full cheeks, everted upper lip, wide mouth, and widely spaced teeth. Many patients also had distal limb anomalies, such as pes planus, broad fingers, or long tapered fingers; joint hypermobility was often present. Additional features present in some patients included gastrointestinal problems, recurrent infections, skin abnormalities, visual impairment, and hypotonia. Three patients had seizures and 4 had nonspecific findings on brain imaging, such as abnormal corpus callosum or white matter abnormalities.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{1:Eising et al. (2019)} reported a 6-year-old girl (patient 04) who presented with speech delay and childhood apraxia of speech (CAS). Clinical details were limited, but she was noted to have poor oral and listening skills, dysarthria, and motor impairment. IQ was in the average range. Genetic analysis identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation in the SETD1A gene: functional studies of the variant were not performed. The patient was part of a cohort of 19 probands diagnosed with CAS who underwent genetic studies.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SETD1A gene that were identified in patients with NEDSID by {3:Kummeling et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 15 unrelated patients with NEDSID, {3:Kummeling et al. (2021)} identified 14 different de novo heterozygous mutations in the SETD1A gene (see, e.g., {611052.0001}; {611052.0006}-{611052.0008}). The mutations were found by routine diagnostic testing and the patients were ascertained from several different places through the GeneMatcher program. There were 5 nonsense, 6 frameshift, 1 missense, and 2 splice site mutations. All variants were predicted to disrupt or delete the SET catalytic domain. Five patients carried additional variants of uncertain significance affecting other genes. Analysis of fibroblasts derived from 3 patients, including the patient with the only SETD1A missense variant (Y1499D; {611052.0006}), showed elevated activation of the DNA damage response and increased DNA degradation under stress conditions compared to controls. These data indicated that the mutations likely caused a loss-of-function effect and SETD1A haploinsufficiency. {3:Kummeling et al. (2021)} concluded that the findings were consistent with a possible role of H3K4 methylation and other epigenetic changes in regulating the function of adult neurons post development.

{4:Singh et al. (2016)} reported 7 patients with schizophrenia (SCZD; {181500}) and learning difficulties who had heterozygous loss-of-function variants in the SETD1A gene (see, e.g., {611052.0001}). The mutations were found to occur de novo when parental DNA was available. No loss-of-function variants were found in controls (p = 3.3 x 10 (-9)). The patients were part of a cohort of 4,264 patients with schizophrenia, 9,343 controls, and 1,077 trios who underwent genetic studies. Including 3 previously reported patients ({5:Takata et al., 2014}; {2:Guipponi et al., 2014}), 7 of 10 individuals with schizophrenia reported by {4:Singh et al. (2016)} who carried SETD1A variants also had learning difficulties. Metaanalysis results showed that SETD1A disruptions are rare in schizophrenia, occurring in about 0.13% of cases. {4:Singh et al. (2016)} also found heterozygous loss-of-function variants in the SETD1A gene in 4 of 4,281 children with severe neurodevelopmental disorders and in 2 individuals from a sample of 5,720 Finnish exomes, both of whom had neuropsychiatric phenotypes. The findings suggested that loss-of-function variants in the SETD1A gene can cause a range of neurodevelopmental disorders, and that epigenetic dysregulation of the histone H3K4 methylation pathway may play a role in the pathogenesis of schizophrenia.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Kummeling et al. (2021)} found that knockdown of the Drosophila SETD1A ortholog Set1 in terminally differentiated postmitotic neurons of the mushroom body (MB), the primary memory and learning center of the fly brain, resulted in memory deficits as assessed by the courtship conditioning assay. Histologic studies of mutant fly brains did not show morphologic abnormalities in the MB. The authors concluded that this gene is required for normal functioning of adult MB neurons during memory formation, rather than during development.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-51 (COXPD51) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the PTCD3 gene ({614918}) on chromosome 2p11.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-51 (COXPD51) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a Leigh syndrome phenotype (see {256000}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Borna et al. (2019)} reported a Japanese infant, born of unrelated parents, who was delivered by emergency cesarean section due to intrauterine growth retardation. Her growth parameters at birth were below the standard measurements. The neonatal period was complicated by respiratory insufficiency requiring ventilatory support. She developed progressive limb rigidity, myoclonus, and nystagmus, and showed delayed psychomotor development. She also required tube feeding. Analysis of cultured fibroblasts showed a severe reduction in mitochondrial respiratory complexes I and IV. Brain imaging showed lesions in the medulla, cerebral peduncle, thalamus, and basal ganglia, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of Leigh syndrome. She also had optic atrophy and severe bilateral hearing loss. She died of respiratory failure at 1 year, 4 months of age. She was found to have a mutation in the PTCD3 gene.

{2:Finsterer et al. (2019)} commented that the phenotype of the patient reported by {1:Borna et al. (2019)} was not consistent with Leigh syndrome, but rather a 'Leigh-like disorder.' These authors delineated subtle differences between the clinical features in the Japanese girl and typical features of Leigh syndrome, including lack of hypotonia, ataxia, and lactic acidosis.

{3:Munoz-Pujol et al. (2023)} reported 3 patients from 2 families, including a sib pair, with COXPD51. Patient 1 presented at 10 months of age with developmental delay and hypertonia. At 2 years of age, he had pale optic nerves and an akinetic-rigid syndrome. At 2.5 years of age, he developed acute episodic respiratory symptoms with neurologic decline, chronic respiratory failure, and dysphagia necessitating a gastrostomy. At 3 years of age, he had spastic and dystonic tetraparesis, optic atrophy, and absent visual evoked potential responses. At 4 years of age, he was found to have a sensory and motor axonal neuropathy and bilateral hearing loss. He died at 11 years of age from pneumonia. A muscle biopsy at 3.5 years of age showed mixed COX-negative fibers with increased amounts of lipid material. Patient 2.1, a 19-year-old female, had severe developmental delay and abnormal eye movements recognized in the first year of life. She had 2 seizures, at age 6 and 10 years. At 12 years of age, she developed dystonia and scoliosis. On examination at age 18 years, she had no language development and had generalized dystonia and spasticity. A brain MRI at 15 years of age showed optic nerve atrophy and volume loss of the thalamus. Her twin sister, patient 2.2, had severe early developmental delay and abnormal eye movements noted from 3 months of age. She was diagnosed with dystonia and scoliosis at 4 to 5 months of age. At 17 years of age, she presented with seizures and acute respiratory insufficiency. She died 1 month later.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of COXPD51 in the family reported by {1:Borna et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a Japanese infant with lethal COXPD51, {1:Borna et al. (2019)} identified compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the PTCD3 gene ({614918.0001} and {614918.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Patient fibroblasts showed decreased levels of the PTCD3 protein compared to controls, as well as variably decreased protein and activity levels of mitochondrial respiratory complexes I and IV. Proteomic analysis of patient cells showed decreased levels of the small mitoribosomal subunits (mt-SSU), which play a role in mitochondrial translation. Further analysis of patient cells demonstrated reduced mitochondrial protein synthesis and defective mitochondrial metabolism with reduced ATP production and cellular respiration compared to controls, leading to a combined OXPHOS deficiency. Expression of wildtype PTCD3 in patient cells rescued the mitochondrial defects, confirming the pathogenicity of the variants.

In 3 patients from 2 families with COXPD51, {3:Munoz-Pujol et al. (2023)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the PTCD3 gene ({614918.0003}-{614918.0006}). The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed with Sanger sequencing. Studies in fibroblasts from patient 1 and patient 2.1 demonstrated reduced PTCH3 protein, reduced maximum respiratory capacity, and reduced expression of the complex I subunit NDUFB8 ({602140}) and the complex IV subunit MTCO2 ({516040}). Patient 1 also had reduced expression of the complex III subunit UQCRC2 ({191329}). Expression of wildtype PTCD3 rescued the abnormal respiratory capacity and subunit expression in fibroblasts from both patients.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 15 (MC4DN15) is caused by homozygous mutation in the COX8A gene ({123870}) on chromosome 11q13. One such patient has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 15 (MC4DN15) is an autosomal recessive multisystem metabolic disorder characterized by the onset of symptoms in infancy. Affected individuals show global developmental delay, poor feeding, short stature with microcephaly, proximal muscle weakness, and distal spasticity. Other manifestations include scoliosis, primary pulmonary hypertension, childhood-onset refractory seizures, and inability to walk. Brain imaging shows features consistent with Leigh syndrome (see {256000}) and enlarged ventricles. Laboratory studies show increased serum and CSF lactate, as well as decreased levels and activity of mitochondrial respiratory complex IV (summary by {1:Hallmann et al., 2016}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency, see {220110}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Hallmann et al. (2016)} reported a 12.5-year-old girl, born of likely related Turkish parents, with mitochondrial complex IV deficiency. She presented at birth with scoliosis, thoracolumbar kyphosis, and pes planovalgus. At 6 months, she had global developmental delay and primary pulmonary hypertension. She also had poor feeding necessitating a feeding tube, short stature, microcephaly, proximal hypotonia, distal spasticity, and onset of severe refractory epilepsy at age 8 years. She had bilateral hip dislocation and was wheelchair-bound. Laboratory studies showed increased serum and CSF lactate. EEG showed generalized slowing and continuous multifocal spike-wave discharges; brain imaging showed T2-weighted hyperintensities in the cerebellum and periventricular areas, suggestive of Leigh syndrome. Additional findings included ventricular enlargement, cystic defects, and pigmentary retinopathy. The patient died at age 12.5 years from cardiopulmonary failure associated with infection and metabolic crisis.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC4DN15 in the patient reported by {1:Hallmann et al. (2016)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a 12.5-year old girl, born of Turkish parents who were likely distantly related, with mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, {1:Hallmann et al. (2016)} identified homozygosity for a splice site mutation in the COX8A gene ({123870.0001}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Patient fibroblasts showed decreased steady-state levels (about 50%) of COA3 protein, no detectable COX14 ({614478}), and decreased synthesis of complex IV. Transfection of wildtype COA3 rescued the complex IV assembly defect.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 16 (MC4DN16) is caused by homozygous mutation in the COX4I1 gene ({123864}) on chromosome 16q24.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 16 (MC4DN16) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder with highly variable manifestations. Common features include failure to thrive with poor overall growth, short stature, and microcephaly. Some patients additionally have neurologic involvement, including developmental regression with severe hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and seizures. Brain imaging in the more severely affected patients shows cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and abnormal lesions in the basal ganglia. In all cases, patient tissues show variably decreased levels and activity of mitochondrial respiratory complex IV (summary by {2:Pillai et al., 2019}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency, see {220110}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Abu-Libdeh et al. (2017)} reported a 5-year-old girl with mitochondrial complex IV deficiency. She presented at age 3 years with failure to thrive, but she had normal psychomotor development and normal brain imaging. Laboratory studies showed mild red blood cell macrocytosis, delayed bone age, and mildly increased chromosomal breakage, reminiscent of Fanconi anemia (see, e.g., FANCA, {227650}). Additional clinical features included frontal bossing, prominent nasal bridge, and short fifth fingers; neurologic examination was normal. Lactic and organic acid levels were normal.

{2:Pillai et al. (2019)} reported 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Iraqi parents, who had normal early development, but showed developmental regression in the first year of life manifest as loss of motor skills and severe hypotonia with inability to sit unsupported. They had short stature and poor overall growth; both required a feeding tube. Both boys developed seizures associated with hypsarrhythmia on EEG in early childhood. Brain imaging showed cerebral and cerebellar atrophy as well as abnormal signals in the basal ganglia consistent with Leigh syndrome (see {256000}). Laboratory studies of 1 patient showed increased serum and CSF lactate and fumarate, suggestive of mitochondrial encephalopathy. Coenzyme Q therapy was started with anecdotal mild clinical improvement. Neither patient had anemia or evidence of increased chromosomal breakage.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC4DN16 in the family reported by {2:Pillai et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 5-year-old girl with MC4DN16, {1:Abu-Libdeh et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous mutation in the COX4I1 gene ({123864.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Patient fibroblasts showed decreased COX4I1 mRNA and protein levels, decreased complex IV activity (66% decrease compared to wildtype), impaired ATP production (40% decrease compared to wildtype), and increased levels of reactive oxygen species. These defects could be rescued by expression of the wildtype gene.

In 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Iraqi parents, with MC4DN16, {2:Pillai et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous missense variant in the COX4I1 gene (P152T; {123864.0002}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The variant was not found in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. Analysis of skeletal muscle biopsy from one of the brothers showed severely decreased complex IV activity (16% residual activity).

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 17 (MC4DN17) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COA8 gene ({616003}) on chromosome 14q32.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 17 (MC4DN17) is an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder with somewhat variable clinical manifestations and severity. Most affected individuals present in early childhood with motor and gait difficulties after normal early development. These motor abnormalities progress to spastic tetraparesis, sometimes resulting in loss of ambulation. Many patients also show episodic developmental regression: some have impaired cognition and dysarthria, although others have normal speech and cognition. More variable features include seizures and sensorimotor polyneuropathy. The clinical features tend to stabilize over time. Brain imaging shows a cavitating leukodystrophy, and laboratory studies show variably decreased levels and activity of mitochondrial respiratory complex IV in patient tissues ({1:Melchionda et al., 2014}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency, see {220110}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Melchionda et al. (2014)} identified 6 individuals from 5 unrelated families with mitochondrial complex IV deficiency. The patients ranged from 4 to 26 years of age. Five patients presented in late infancy or early childhood with evidence of complex IV deficiency, but the phenotype varied. These 5 probands had episodes of neurologic regression manifest as gait difficulties and spastic tetraparesis, sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and dysarthria that in some cases improved over time. The sixth patient, who had an affected sister, never developed neurologic signs. Three patients had normal cognition and 3 had impaired cognition. Brain imaging showed a cavitating leukodystrophy, predominantly affecting the posterior cerebral white matter and corpus callosum, that stabilized or even improved over time.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC4DN17 in the families reported by {1:Melchionda et al. (2014)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 individuals from 5 unrelated families with MC4DN17, {1:Melchionda et al. (2014)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the COA8 gene (see, e.g., {616003.0001}-{616003.0004}). Patient muscle and fibroblasts showed severely decreased complex IV activity (5-61% of normal) and decreased levels of the COX holocomplex; some patients also showed partial decreases of complex I or II. Fibroblasts isolated from 1 of the patients showed increased reactive oxygen species under oxidative stress compared to controls, which was rescued by expression of wildtype APOPT1.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 21 (MC4DN21) is caused by homozygous mutation in the COXFA4 gene (NDUFA4; {603833}) on chromosome 7p21. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 21 (MC4DN21) is an autosomal recessive multisystem metabolic disorder characterized by the onset of symptoms in infancy. Affected individuals present with congenital lactic acidosis and later show global developmental delay with delayed speech and learning disabilities. Additional features include motor dysfunction manifest as spasticity, dystonia, and pyramidal tract signs. Ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, and seizures may also occur. Brain imaging shows T2-weighted hyperintensities in subcortical regions, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of Leigh syndrome (see {256000}). Patient tissues show variably decreased levels and activity of mitochondrial respiratory complex IV ({1:Pitceathly et al., 2013}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency, see {220110}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Pitceathly et al. (2013)} reported 4 members of a consanguineous Pakistani kindred with a complex neurologic disorder associated with isolated mitochondrial complex IV deficiency. Two patients died at 8 and 26 years of age, and 2 were alive at 32 and 34 years of age. All presented in infancy with lactic acidosis, which was treated with sodium bicarbonate. They subsequently showed language delay and variable motor delay, which progressed to learning difficulties and unsteady gait. Additional variable neurologic features included ataxia, dystonia, spasticity, and pyramidal signs; 1 patient had onset of seizures and myoclonus at age 13 years. Two patients had a sensory axonal peripheral neuropathy confirmed by nerve conduction studies. Muscle biopsy showed increased lipid content and isolated COX deficiency. Brain imaging showed T2-weighted hyperintensities in the deep white matter, basal ganglia, thalami, and brainstem, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of Leigh syndrome (see {256000}). One patient had recurrent encephalopathic episodes with neurologic regression and progressive loss of skills, resulting in death at age 8.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC4DN21 in the family reported by {1:Pitceathly et al. (2013)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 members of a consanguineous Pakistani family with MC4DN21, {1:Pitceathly et al. (2013)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the COXFA4 gene ({603833.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. PCR analysis of patient cells demonstrated the production of an abnormal transcript, and Western blot analysis of patient muscle tissue and fibroblasts showed undetectable levels of the COXFA4 protein. The findings were consistent with a loss-of-function effect. The COXFA4 gene was screened in 20 additional probands with isolated COX deficiency, but no further variants were identified.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-20 (HLD20) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CNP gene ({123830}) on chromosome 17q21. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-20 (HLD20) is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of developmental milestones at about 12 to 16 months of age after normal early development. Patients lose motor, language, and cognitive skills and show poor overall growth with microcephaly. The disorder is progressive, resulting in feeding difficulties and spastic quadriplegia. Some patients may have seizures. Brain imaging shows subcortical white matter abnormalities and a thin corpus callosum, suggesting a myelination defect. Death usually occurs in childhood ({1:Al-Abdi et al., 2020}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of HLD, see {312080}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Al-Abdi et al. (2020)} reported a 5-year-old boy (15DG2109), born of consanguineous Omani parents, with a neurodegenerative disorder. He had normal early development until about 16 months of age when he showed irritability and loss of acquired motor and language skills, as well as swallowing and feeding problems with constipation. Physical examination at age 3 years showed an irritable child with dystonic movements, poor overall growth with progressive microcephaly, and mild dysmorphism, including ptosis, hirsutism, and coarse facial features. He had generalized hypertonia with brisk tendon reflexes and extensor plantar responses that progressed to spastic quadriplegia with torticollis and an arching back with scoliosis. Head circumference was -3 SD. Brain imaging showed abnormal hyperintense T2-weighted signals in the deep and periventricular white matter with involvement of subcortical white matter. There was a reduction in white matter volume and thinning of the corpus callosum. Mild cerebellar atrophy was also observed. MR spectroscopy showed a reduced NAA peak and increased choline. The boy died at age 5 years from aspiration pneumonia. Family history revealed 2 older similarly affected brothers who died in childhood. They had normal early development with regression around 12 months of age. One brother had seizures. Brain imaging in one showed abnormal white matter signals and enlarged ventricles.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HLD20 in the family reported by {1:Al-Abdi et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a boy with HLD20, {1:Al-Abdi et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the CNP gene (S82L; {123830.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of autozygosity mapping and exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Patient fibroblasts showed defects in cytoskeletal organization with abnormal F-actin structure. The authors noted that CNP encodes a major component of myelin and is expressed in myelin-forming oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: Myelination of axons by oligodendrocytes enables rapid impulse propagation in the central nervous system. {2:Lappe-Siefke et al. (2003)} showed that Cnp1 is essential for axonal survival but not for myelin assembly. In the absence of glial cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase, mice developed axonal swellings and neurodegeneration throughout the brain, leading to hydrocephalus and premature death. But, in contrast to previously studied myelin mutants, the ultrastructure, periodicity, and physical stability of myelin were not altered in these mice. Therefore, by genetic means, the chief function of glia in supporting axonal integrity can be completely uncoupled from its function in maintaining compact myelin. Oligodendrocyte dysfunction, such as that in the lesions of multiple sclerosis, may suffice to cause secondary axonal loss.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and brain atrophy

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and brain atrophy (NEDSEBA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the EXOC7 gene ({608163}) on chromosome 17q25.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and brain atrophy (NEDSEBA) is an autosomal recessive disorder with highly variable manifestations and severity of these core features. The most severely affected individuals develop symptoms in utero, which may lead to spontaneous abortion or planned termination. Those that survive may present with severe seizures at birth, have poor overall growth with small head circumference, achieve no developmental progress, and show significant brain atrophy and other brain abnormalities. Patients at the mildest end of the phenotypic spectrum have onset of seizures later in childhood and show developmental delay with mildly impaired intellectual development and minimal brain atrophy (summary by {1:Coulter et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Coulter et al. (2020)} reported 8 patients from 4 unrelated families with a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with biallelic mutations in the EXOC7 gene identified through exome sequencing. The severity of the phenotype was highly variable. The most severely affected patients were 2 fetuses from family III who were found to have mild microcephaly, dysmorphic features, and brainstem and cerebellar hypoplasia on prenatal examination. The pregnancies were terminated, and postmortem examination confirmed the abnormal brain findings. Two sisters, born of consanguineous parents (family I), presented at birth with myoclonic seizures, arthrogryposis multiplex, and poor overall growth with small head circumference (-0.5 to -2.6 SD). Brain imaging showed a thin cortex with simplified gyral pattern, thin corpus callosum, and small cerebellum and brainstem. One sib had absent basal ganglia and small thalami. They did not achieve any developmental milestones and died at ages 5 days and 7 months. A 2-year-old boy, born of consanguineous parents (family II), had severe developmental delay, mild hypertonia, poor overall growth with small head circumference (-2.6 SD), and onset of myoclonic and focal seizures at 6 months of age. Brain imaging showed central and cortical atrophy, particularly of the temporal lobe. Three sibs, born of consanguineous parents (family IV), had the least severe phenotype. They had mild to moderate developmental delay, normal head circumference, and no or mild nonspecific dysmorphic features. Brain imaging showed nonspecific atrophy in 2 and was normal in the third. These sibs were 3.5, 6, and 9 years of age, and all developed seizures between age 3 and 6 years.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSEBA in the families reported by {1:Coulter et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 patients from 4 unrelated families with NEDSEBA, {1:Coulter et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the EXOC7 gene ({608163.0001}-{608163.0004}). The mutations, which were found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There was 1 splice site mutation, 2 in-frame deletions, and 1 missense mutation; all were predicted to yield hypomorphic alleles. The authors postulated that the variable severity observed in the patients reflected the extent of EXOC7 loss conferred by specific mutations, with the missense mutation having the mildest phenotypic effect.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Coulter et al. (2020)} noted that homozygosity for an Exoc7 null allele is embryonic lethal in mice. Zebrafish with homozygous loss of exoc7 showed head edema, microcephaly, and small eyes, as well as increased neuronal apoptosis in the developing telencephalon. These findings suggested that the microcephaly and brain atrophy in human with NEDSEBA results from loss of proliferating progenitor cells and postmitotic neurons, consistent with a neurodegenerative process.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and brain atrophy (NEDMISB) is caused by homozygous mutation in the EXOC8 gene ({615283}) on chromosome 1q42. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and brain atrophy (NEDMISB) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe global developmental delay, developmental regression with loss of milestones, severe microcephaly, and brain abnormalities, primarily cerebral atrophy and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum. Affected individuals develop seizures in the first year of life; eventually they are unable to sit, feed, or communicate, and may be unresponsive to stimuli. Other features include muscle weakness, spasticity with hyperreflexia, irritability, and contractures ({1:Coulter et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Coulter et al. (2020)} reported 3 sibs, born of consanguineous parents (family V), with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. One patient died at 14 years of age; the others were alive at 14 years and 11 months, respectively. They had poor overall growth with significant microcephaly (-4.7 to -12.9 SD) and severe global developmental delay with regression and loss of milestones. All had onset of seizures around the first year of life, including 1 patient with febrile, myoclonic, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures associated with hypsarrhythmia on EEG. The patients were unable to sit, feed, or communicate. Additional features included hypotonia, hypertonia, muscle weakness, spasticity, and hyperreflexia. The 2 older patients had excessive crying and irritability, flexion contractures, and poor growth with overall wasting. One had vision loss, optic disc pallor, and nerve degeneration. Two patients had dysmorphic features, including exotropia, round face, and long eyelashes. All patients had abnormalities on brain imaging, including brain atrophy, dilated ventricles, hypogenesis of the corpus callosum, and delayed myelination or white matter abnormalities. The patients did not have signs of Joubert syndrome.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMISB in the family reported by {1:Coulter et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 sibs, born of consanguineous parents, with NEDMISB, {1:Coulter et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the EXOC8 gene ({615283.0002}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Noonan syndrome-13 (NS13) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the MAPK1 gene ({176948}) on chromosome 22q11.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Noonan syndrome-13 (NS13) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by developmental delay and impaired intellectual development of variable severity, associated with behavioral problems. Affected individuals also exhibit reduced postnatal growth and craniofacial anomalies, including ptosis, hypertelorism, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, and short webbed neck. Other features include congenital heart defects and mild skeletal defects ({1:Motta et al., 2020}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of Noonan syndrome, see NS1 ({163950}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Motta et al. (2020)} reported 7 unrelated children with a neurodevelopmental disorder and mutations in the MAPK1 gene. Although the phenotype was variable in terms of severity, it consistently included developmental delay and impaired intellectual development, as well as behavioral problems such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, reduced stress tolerance, and aggressive behavior. Postnatally reduced growth was documented in approximately half of affected individuals. Craniofacial anomalies were also common, including ptosis (6/7 patients), hypertelorism (5/7 patients), downslanting palpebral fissures (3/7 patients), low-set and posteriorly rotated ears (6/7 patients), wide nasal bridge (3/7 patients), and dental anomalies (4/7 patients). Most patients shared a distinctive ear morphology with prominent antitragus and earlobes with central depression; also common was a long deep philtrum, marked upper lip vermilion, and everted lower lip. The authors noted that the craniofacial appearance in association with a short/webbed neck, low posterior hairline, and skin features such as multiple lentigines and cafe au lait spots, as well as reduced growth, substantiated a clinical suspicion of Noonan syndrome or a clinically related disorder in most patients. Congenital heart defects, consisting of atrial septal defects and mitral valve insufficiency, were reported in 4 patients, but none had cardiomyopathy. Hypotonia and EEG anomalies unmasking potential seizure activity were noted, and minor skeletal defects were also a common finding. Bleeding diathesis and lymphedema occurred in 1 patient each. None of the patients was diagnosed with cancer.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the MAPK1 gene found by {1:Motta et al. (2020)} in patients with NS13 occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: By whole-exome sequencing, networking, and connection via GeneMatcher, {1:Motta et al. (2020)} identified 7 unrelated children who exhibited clinically heterogeneous phenotypes with features suggestive of Noonan syndrome or overlapping RASopathies but were negative for mutation in known RASopathy-associated genes, who were heterozygous for de novo private missense mutations in the MAPK1 gene (see, e.g., {176948.0001}-{176948.0004}). All 7 mutations showed gain-of-function effects. Screening of the MAPK1 gene in an additional 267 individuals with a clinically suspected diagnosis of RASopathy, who were negative for mutation in known RASopathy-associated genes, did not reveal other pathogenic variants.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, impaired language, and gait abnormalities (NEDMILG) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NARS1 gene ({108410}) on chromosome 18q21.

Heterozygous mutation in the NARS1 gene causes a similar neurodevelopmental disorder with overlapping features (NEDMILEG; {619092}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, language delay, and gait abnormalities (NEDMILG) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent in infancy. Affected individuals have delayed walking with variable gait abnormalities, impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech and language, and progressive microcephaly. More variable features include hypotonia, early-onset seizures, and a peripheral demyelinating or axonal peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy. The disease follows a neurodegenerative course in many patients; clinical features suggest involvement of both the central and peripheral nervous systems ({1:Manole et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Manole et al. (2020)} reported 24 patients from 13 unrelated families (families 9-21) with a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with biallelic mutations in the NARS1 gene. The patients were ascertained through an international collaborative network of research and diagnostic gene sequencing laboratories. Eight families were consanguineous and of various origins, including Pakistani, Indian, and Libyan. The patients, who ranged in age from 2 to 33 years, presented in infancy with global developmental delay, delayed walking, moderately to severely impaired intellectual development, and poor or absent language development. They had a small head circumference, with most having frank microcephaly (range -2.0 to -8.7 SD). More than half had onset of partial or generalized seizures in the first months or years of life. More variable features included hypotonia, reduced muscle power, broad-based or ataxic gait, spasticity, scoliosis, and clinodactyly. Five patients had a demyelinating or axonal sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy manifest as pes cavus, distal muscle weakness and atrophy, impaired sensation, and decreased or absent reflexes. Brain imaging, when performed, was often normal, although some patients had nonspecific abnormalities, including cerebral atrophy, delayed myelination, thin corpus callosum, and decreased white matter volume. Several patients or their similarly affected sibs died in childhood. Three of the families (families 9, 17, and 19) were also reported by {2:Wang et al. (2020)}, who noted that the patients had a degenerative disease course. {1:Manole et al. (2020)} emphasized the involvement of both the central and peripheral nervous system in this disorder.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMILG in the families reported by {2:Wang et al. (2020)} and {1:Manole et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 24 patients from 13 unrelated families with NEDMILG, {2:Wang et al. (2020)} and {1:Manole et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the NARS1 gene (see, e.g., {108410.0001}-{108410.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Most of the mutations were missense, although 2 families carried a nonsense or frameshift mutation on 1 allele. Affected members of 7 consanguineous families (families 9-15) carried the same homozygous R545C mutation ({108410.0004}). Fibroblasts derived from 3 unrelated patients with different mutations showed variably decreased NARS1 protein levels, impaired homodimerization, reduced cytoplasmic transferase activity, and decreased global protein synthesis compared to controls. These findings suggested that the mutations resulted in a loss of function. Induced neuronal progenitor cells derived from 2 unrelated patients were used to generate cultures of 3D cortical brain organoids (CO). Mutant organoids became progressively smaller with decreased diameter compared to controls beginning around division 52, modeling the microcephaly observed in the patients. Patient CO showed reduced generation of radial glial cells with abnormal neural rosette structure, depletion of rosettes and postmitotic neurons, and decreased proliferation and viability of progenitor cells compared to wildtype. RNA-seq analysis of patient cells detected abnormalities in cell cycle control and neuronal progenitor cell fate differentiation, suggesting a role for NARS1 in these processes.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, impaired language, epilepsy, and gait abnormalities (NEDMILEG) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the NARS1 gene ({108410}) on chromosome 18q21.

Biallelic mutation in the NARS1 gene causes a similar neurodevelopmental disorder with overlapping features (NEDMILG; {619091}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, impaired language, epilepsy, and gait abnormalities (NEDMILEG) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent in infancy. Affected individuals have delayed walking with variable gait abnormalities, including ataxia and spasticity, impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech and language, and progressive microcephaly. Dysmorphic facial features may also be observed. Most patients have early-onset seizures; some may develop a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy. The clinical features suggest involvement of both the central and peripheral nervous systems ({1:Manole et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Manole et al. (2020)} reported 6 unrelated patients (patients 1-6) with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder associated with the same de novo heterozygous nonsense mutation in the NARS1 gene (R534X; {108410.0006}). The patients, who ranged in age from 6 to 22 years, were ascertained through an international collaborative network of research and diagnostic gene sequencing laboratories. They presented in infancy with global developmental delay, mildly delayed walking, usually with an ataxic or broad-based gait, severe to profound impaired intellectual development, and dramatic speech and language impairment associated with a nasal pitch. Some showed stereotypic behavior. Most patients had progressive microcephaly (-2.2 to -5.5 SD), but brain imaging tended to be normal. All but 1 developed early-onset generalized tonic-clonic or myoclonic seizures. Three patients had a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy associated with distal muscle weakness, foot drop, pes cavus, and hyporeflexia, whereas others demonstrated spasticity with hypertonia and hyperreflexia. Less common features included tremor and dysarthria without evidence of cerebellar atrophy, scoliosis, kyphosis, and pectus abnormalities. There were variable dysmorphic features, such as sloping forehead, broad jaw, retrognathia, midface hypoplasia, upslanting palpebral fissures, low-set or dysmorphic ears, hypertelorism, short or long philtrum, upturned nose, wide mouth with thin upper lip and everted lower lip, wide-spaced teeth, long slender fingers, clinodactyly, and syndactyly.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the NARS1 gene that were identified in patients with NEDMILEG by {1:Manole et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 unrelated patients (patient 1-6) with NEDMILEG, {1:Manole et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous nonsense mutation in the NARS1 gene (R534X; {108410.0006}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Cells derived from 1 patient showed a dramatic decrease in enzyme activity compared to wildtype. Expression of this mutation in zebrafish caused cyclopia and gastrulation defects. The authors postulated a toxic gain-of-function dominant-negative effect on NARS1 function. Two additional patients (patients 7 and 8) with a similar disorder but without microcephaly carried de novo heterozygous missense variants in the NARS1 gene (G509S and R322L) that were not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of these variants were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies, sleep disturbance, and brain abnormalities (NEDFASB) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KAT5 gene ({601409}) on chromosome 11q23.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies, sleep disturbance, and brain abnormalities (NEDFASB) is a syndromic disorder with multisystemic involvement. Affected individuals have severe global developmental delay with severely impaired intellectual development, poor or absent language, behavioral abnormalities, seizures, and sleep disturbances. Craniofacial dysmorphisms, while variable, include round face, prognathism, depressed nasal bridge, and cleft or high-arched palate. Brain imaging shows dysgenesis of the corpus callosum and progressive cerebellar atrophy. Additional features may include genitourinary tract anomalies, hearing loss, and mild distal skeletal defects (summary by {1:Humbert et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Humbert et al. (2020)} reported 3 unrelated patients with a similar syndromic disorder identified through GeneMatcher after exome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the KAT5 gene. The patients were 30 years, 13 years, and 2 years of age; none were born of consanguineous parents. Common features included severe global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, behavioral abnormalities, and sleep disturbances. IQ, measured in 2 patients, ranged from 20 to 40. Behavioral features included perseverative language, disruptive behavior, attention deficit, hyperactivity, and stereotypies. The patients also had severe sleep anomalies, including early offset, nighttime awakenings, and daytime sleepiness. All patients developed seizures, although age at onset and seizure type varied. Two patients had mild hearing loss and 1 had hyperacusis. Craniofacial features, while variable, showed some overlap. The patients tended to have a small head with round face, flat facial profile, prognathism, almond-shaped eyes, strabismus, epicanthal folds, depressed nasal bridge, bulbous or upturned nose, low-set ears, downslanting corners of the mouth, and thick lower lip. One had a cleft lip and palate, and another had a high-arched palate. There were variable genitourinary anomalies, including recurrent urinary tract infections (patient 1), cryptorchidism, horseshoe kidney, and vesicoureteral reflux (patient 2), and hypospadias and cryptorchidism (patient 3). Additional variable features included myopia, hyperacusis, brachydactyly, single palmar crease, fifth finger clinodactyly, and feeding difficulties with dysphagia, gastroesophageal reflux, and constipation. Brain imaging showed nonspecific abnormalities: patient 1 had thin corpus callosum, patient 2 had progressive cerebellar atrophy, dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, and small anterior pituitary gland associated with growth hormone deficiency, and patient 3 had cerebellar atrophy and polymicrogyria of the right sylvian fissure.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the KAT5 gene that were identified in patients with NEDFASB by {1:Humbert et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 unrelated patients with NEDFASB, {1:Humbert et al. (2020)} identified 3 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the KAT5 gene: R53H ({601409.0001}), C369S ({601409.0002}), and S413A ({601409.0003}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and the patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. None of the mutations were present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies showed that the mutations resulted in variably decreased histone acetyltransferase (HAT) activity compared to controls. The C369S variant showed the most dramatic effect, being unable to acetylate free histones and chromatin. The complexes containing R53H and S413A were mostly defective in their HAT activity toward chromatin, not free histones. The findings suggested haploinsufficiency; however, a dominant-negative effect could not be excluded. Transcriptome analysis of patient cells showed dysregulation of several genes involved in development, which the authors suggested led to the neurodevelopmental syndrome observed in the patients.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene ({605363}) on chromosome 2q31.

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is a severe autosomal recessive disorder characterized by profound global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, absent speech, inability to sit or walk due to axial hypotonia and spastic quadriparesis, and onset of seizures in the first days or months of life. EEG shows suppression-burst pattern or hypsarrhythmia, consistent with DEE or a clinical diagnosis of West syndrome. More variable features include joint contractures with foot deformities, dysmorphic facial features with cleft palate, and omphalocele. Affected individuals have poor motor skills, poor eye contact, and lack of language development; some die in infancy or early childhood. Brain imaging may be normal or show nonspecific abnormalities (summary by {2:Chatron et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Chatron et al. (2020)} reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who were of Algerian (family A), Egyptian (family B), Turkish (families C and E), Iranian (family D), and Brazilian (family F) origin, were identified through the GeneMatcher program after whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the GAD1 gene. Four of the patients died in infancy or early childhood: the remaining patients ranged from 15 months to 12 years of age. All had onset of seizures in the first days or weeks of life. Seizure types included epileptic spasms, eye twitches, and myoclonic seizures. EEG showed suppression-burst pattern, consistent with neonatal DEE, or hypsarrhythmia, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of West syndrome. Seizures were eventually controlled by antiepileptic drugs in 6 patients. The patients had profoundly impaired development with intellectual disability, absent speech, axial hypotonia, and peripheral spasticity with muscle hypertonia and hyperreflexia. Some had dystonic movements. Other more variable features included scoliosis, pes equinovarus, joint contractures, omphalocele, and cleft palate with dysmorphic facial features. However, not all patients showed these additional features. The 2 Egyptian sibs had the most severe dysmorphic features. Brain imaging was normal in 4 patients, but showed mild variable abnormalities in 5 patients. These included progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, hypoplastic corpus callosum, and posterior cervical junctional notch. Two patients (patients 2 and 4) did not have brain imaging performed. Detailed case descriptions revealed that the patients had profound developmental delay sometimes with regression, poor or absent visual contact, absent speech, poor head control, inability to sit or walk due to spastic quadriparesis, impaired gross and fine motor skills, and poor overall growth.

{3:Neuray et al. (2020)} reported 6 patients, aged 18 months to 10 years, from 6 unrelated families. All of the patients had infantile seizures, predominantly focal motor, beginning between 2 and 6 months of age. Brain MRI was normal in 4 patients and showed slight ventricular enlargement in 1 patient and moderate global atrophy in 1 patient. Five patients had severely impaired intellectual development; 1 patient, who had moderately impaired intellectual development, achieved simple speech and basic perceptive language skills. Five of 6 patients had hypotonia, which was mild in 1 patient and severe in 4. Skeletal findings, each seen in 1 patient, included lower limb arthrogryposis, short arms, scoliosis and pes planus, and congenital hip dislocation. One patient had a cleft palate, and 1 patient had hydronephrosis nephrocalcinosis and bilateral kidney stones. Dysmorphic facial features were seen in 4 patients.

{4:Von Hardenberg et al. (2020)} reported an infant with cleft soft palate, contractures of the fingers and knees, pes equinovarus on the right, and pes adductus on the left. She developed infantile spasms at 5 days of life. An EEG showed a burst suppression pattern. Ophthalmologic examination and MRI were normal. L-glutamate in the patient's urine, plasma, and CSF were in the high-normal range. Seizures were refractory to multiple different antiepileptic therapies. However, after initiation of a ketogenic diet and vigabatrin, she experienced cessation of seizures. At 7 months of age, her psychomotor development, growth, and head circumference were normal.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content:
{2:Chatron et al. (2020)} found that treatment with vigabatrin, which decreases the catabolism of GABA, resulted in seizure control in some patients with DEE89. However, these individuals still had severely impaired global development.

{4:Von Hardenberg et al. (2020)} treated an infant with DEE89 with a ketogenic diet, which was thought to increase GABA synthesis, and vigabatrin, which inhibits the degradation of GABA. This therapy resulted in cessation of seizures in the patient, who had normal development and growth at 7 months of age.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE89 in the families reported by {2:Chatron et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 11 patients from 5 unrelated consanguineous families of various ethnic origins with DEE89, {2:Chatron et al. (2020)} identified homozygous mutations in the GAD1 gene ({605363.0002}-{605363.0006}). The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing identified biallelic GAD1 mutations. The mutations, which were confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were 2 nonsense, 1 frameshift, 1 splice site, 1 in-frame deletion, and 1 missense mutation. Studies of the splice site and in-frame deletion showed that the former altered splicing and the latter was expressed at normal levels. Additional functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but all the variants were predicted to result in a loss of function. {2:Chatron et al. (2020)} noted that since the GAD1 gene is involved in inhibitory synaptic transmission in the nervous system, a loss of function could lead to excessive excitatory drive on motor neurons, resulting in seizures and hypertonia, which was observed in the patients.

In 6 unrelated patients of different ethnicities with DEE89, {3:Neuray et al. (2020)} identified biallelic mutations in the GAD1 gene (see, e.g., {605373.0005} and {605363.0007}-{605363.0009}). The mutations, which were identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the phenotype in all families except one in which the father was not sequenced. Functional studies were not performed.

In a patient with DEE89, {4:von Hardenberg et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous splicing mutation in the GAD1 gene ({605363.0010}), resulting in the skipping of exon 11. The deletion affects the pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase domain of GAD1, including deletion of an active site residue (tyr347) and a functional residue (asp373) involved in pyridoxal 5-prime phosphate binding.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: In addition to its role as an inhibitory neurotransmitter, GABA is presumed to be involved in the development and plasticity of the nervous system. {1:Asada et al. (1997)} found that Gad67 -/- mice were born at the expected frequency but died of severe cleft palate during the first morning after birth. GAD activities and GABA contents were reduced to 20% and 7%, respectively, in the cerebral cortex of the newborn Gad67 -/- mice. Their brains, however, did not show any discernible defects. Previous pharmacologic and genetic investigations suggested the involvement of GABA in palate formation, but this was the first demonstration of a role for GAD67-derived GABA in the development of nonneural tissue.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Kaya-Barakat-Masson syndrome (KABAMAS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the YIF1B gene ({619109}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Kaya-Barakat-Masson syndrome (KABAMAS) is a severe autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by profoundly impaired global development with variable motor abnormalities, such as axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, dystonia, and poor coordination, resulting in the inability to sit or walk. Affected individuals have impaired intellectual development with absent speech, poor eye contact, and feeding difficulties, resulting in poor overall growth, sometimes with microcephaly. Dysmorphic features are generally not present. Additional more variable features include early-onset seizures, ocular anomalies, foot deformities, and nonspecific brain imaging findings, such as thin corpus callosum and cerebral, cerebellar, or pontine atrophy. Some patients may die in infancy or early childhood (summary by {1:AlMuhaizea et al., 2020} and {2:Diaz et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:AlMuhaizea et al. (2020)} reported 6 children from 5 unrelated families, 4 of which were consanguineous, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who ranged in age from 4 to 11 years, had severely impaired psychomotor development with axial hypotonia and inability to sit, walk, or, in some cases, roll over, lack of head control, poor fine motor skills, absent language, and irritability. Most had poor eye contact and only achieved social smiling. Other motor abnormalities included limb dystonia, spasticity, choreiform movements, and dyskinesia. The patients had feeding difficulties and dysphagia, necessitating tube-feeding in 2 patients, and poor overall growth with short stature and microcephaly. Two patients developed seizures at 6 to 8 months of age that could be controlled; 1 patient had cortical blindness. Three patients had nonspecific brain imaging findings, including hypomyelination, thin corpus callosum, and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. Dysmorphic features were not noted, although 2 patients had hip dislocation/dysplasia and 1 patient had foot deformities.

{2:Diaz et al. (2020)} reported 10 patients from 6 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder associated with YIF1B mutations identified through the GeneMatcher program. Four patients in 2 families (families 1 and 2) died between 7 and 15 months of age. Four living patients from 3 families (families 3, 5, and 6) were between 4 and 11 years of age, and 2 sibs (family 4) were 25 and 35 years of age. The families originated from France, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Canada, and Italy; several were consanguineous. The patients presented in infancy with severely impaired psychomotor development. None of the patients, except the adult sibs from family 4, achieved sitting, walking, or head control. All had profoundly impaired intellectual development with absent speech and poor eye contact. Most had feeding difficulties and axial hypotonia, and some had peripheral hypertonia or spasticity with hyperreflexia; a few patients had choreoathetosis or dystonia. Three patients had central hypoventilation: 1 died and the other 2 required ventilatory assistance. More than half of patients had variable ocular abnormalities, including strabismus, optic atrophy, nystagmus, and abnormal visual evoked potentials, suggesting retinal dysfunction. Almost all developed infantile spasms or myoclonic seizures in the first months of life, which were often refractory to treatment. The 2 sibs from family 4, who carried a missense mutation (see MOLECULAR GENETICS), had a slightly less severe phenotype. They began walking at 4 to 5 years of age with a spastic gait and started speaking with a few words at 7 to 8 years. They had severely impaired intellectual development with IQ ranging from 45 to 48. These sibs had onset of tonic-clonic seizures at 20 and 7 years, respectively. Other features observed in the cohort included talipes varus and scoliosis. Brain imaging in some patients showed cerebral, cerebellar, or pontine atrophy, or nonspecific white matter abnormalities, although many patients had normal brain imaging.

{3:Medico Salsench et al. (2021)} described 8 new patients with KABAMAS due to biallelic pathogenic variants in the YIF1B gene and reviewed the literature on previously reported cases. The disorder was characterized by severe to profound neurodevelopmental delay, cognitive impairment, neurologic sequelae, seizures, and microcephaly. All patients presented early in life with a progressive encephalopathy with global developmental delay and cognitive impairment. Almost all had feeding problems, axial hypotonia, and limb spasticity, with seizures in 14 of 22 (64%) patients from whom information was available. Microcephaly was seen in 15 of 23 (65%) patients. About half of the patients showed signs of dystonia, dyskinesia, or microcephaly. Hypoventilation was seen in 5 of 18 (23%) patients and appeared to be associated with brainstem atrophy. Brain imaging abnormalities were seen in about two-thirds of patients. The ability to meet limited developmental milestones (e.g., head control, independent sitting, limited speech) was seen only in patients with missense mutations, suggesting that residual YIF1B activity is present in these patients, consistent with in vitro data.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of KABAMAS in the families reported by {1:AlMuhaizea et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 6 patients from 5 unrelated families with KABAMAS, {1:AlMuhaizea et al. (2020)} identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the YIF1B gene ({619109.0001}-{609109.0003}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families that could be studied. None were present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but all were predicted to result in a complete loss of protein function.

In 10 patients from 6 unrelated families with KABAMAS, {2:Diaz et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the YIF1B gene (see, e.g., {619109.0001}, {619109.0003}-{619109.0006}). The patients, who originated from various countries, including France, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Canada, and Italy, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher database after whole-exome sequencing identified biallelic YIF1B mutations. All but one mutation were nonsense, splice site, or frameshift; the exception was a missense variant (K123Q; {609109.0005}) found in 2 sibs from family 4 who had a slightly less severe phenotype. Western blot analysis of some of the mutations showed decreased protein levels, and most were predicted to lack all or most of the transmembrane domains, consistent with a putative loss of function. Patient-derived fibroblasts showed reduced and shortened cilia compared to controls, suggesting ciliary anchoring defects (see ANIMAL MODEL). These findings, together with mouse studies, implicated several cellular processes that were disrupted by the YIF1B mutation, collectively resulting in a neurodevelopmental disorder.

{3:Medico Salsench et al. (2021)} described 8 new patients with KABAMAS due to biallelic pathogenic variants in the YIF1B gene and reviewed the literature on previously reported cases. Among the total of 24 cases from 19 families, 18 (75%) mutations were truncating or whole gene deletion and 6 (25%) were missense variants. All YIF1B missense variants were located in or close to the transmembrane domains and were absent from gnomAD, except for 1 that was found once in heterozygous state. All changed highly conserved residues. Based on introduction of missense variants into an YIF1B expression plasmid, missense variants did not result in significantly reduced YIF1B protein levels.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Diaz et al. (2020)} found that knockdown of the Yif1b gene in mice did not cause ventilatory defects or increased susceptibility to seizures, although mutant mice showed impaired visual perception associated with retinal dysfunction and optic atrophy. Basal locomotion was normal, but there were some deficits in fine motor skills and coordination. Mutant mice had delayed cerebral myelination, enlarged ventricles, and cerebellar atrophy associated with a reduction in the number of Purkinje cells due to neurodegeneration and necrosis rather than apoptosis. There were disorganized dendritic trees and the presence of microglia cells. Electron microscopic studies of Purkinje cells showed abnormal fragmentation of the Golgi apparatus, large autophagosome-like vacuoles, and aberrant configuration of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) with dilated cisterns compared to controls. Male Yif1b-null mice were infertile due to abnormal spermatozoa flagella, which showed microtubule disorganization. Ciliary abnormalities were also observed in cerebellar Purkinje cells, hippocampal pyramidal cells, and fibroblasts. These findings, together with the human results, suggested that YIF1B is essential not only for Golgi and ER morphology and function, but also for primary ciliary integrity. Loss of YIG1B function leads to altered myelination, neuronal death, and Golgi, ER, and ciliary defects with pathology related to disrupted trafficking of proteins, ultimately resulting in neurodevelopmental abnormalities.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome-3 (RTSC3) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the VPS35L gene ({618981}) on chromosome 16p12.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome-3 (RTSC3) is characterized by craniocerebellocardiac anomalies and severe postnatal growth restriction, as well as complicated skeletal malformations, including vertebral body hypoossification, sternal aplasia, and chondrodysplasia punctata. Other features include developmental delay, ocular anomalies, periventricular nodular heterotopia, and proteinuria ({1:Kato et al., 2020}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome, see RTSC1 ({220210}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Kato et al. (2020)} studied a Japanese sister and brother who exhibited features consistent with RTSC. The sibs presented mostly overlapping multiple congenital anomalies of the craniofacial, ophthalmologic, cardiac, skeletal, and central nervous systems. Craniofacial dysmorphisms included dilated anterior fontanel, prominent forehead, arched eyebrows, downslanting palpebral fissures, upturned nose, thin upper lip, and micrognathia. Other features in the sister included bilateral buphthalmos, left choroidal coloboma, atrioventricular septal defect, brachytelephalangic chondrodysplasia punctata with first metacarpal and metatarsal shortening, and vermian hypoplasia. She died at 28 days of life. Examination of the brother at age 3 years showed severe postnatal growth retardation. Skeletal abnormalities included short limbs, vertebral body hypoossification, sternal aplasia, shortened ulnae with radial bowing, and chondrodysplasia punctata with brachytelephalangy and first metacarpal and metatarsal shortening. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed left microphthalmia and right choroidal coloboma, and orbital MRI showed atrophy of the optic nerve. Brain MRI showed vermian hypoplasia and bilateral periventricular nodular heterotopia (PNH). He developed focal-onset impaired-awareness seizures at 18 months of age, which were controlled by medication. He had 3+ proteinuria on urine test strip, but renal evaluation was not undertaken. Global development was severely delayed, with inability to sit, and speech limited to a few words. The authors noted that the craniofacial, cardiac, and cerebellar anomalies present in the 2 sibs were typical features of RTSC, although the postnatal growth retardation and skeletal anomalies observed in patient 2 seemed to be more severe than those previously documented in RTSC, and additional features such as microphthalmia, PNH, and proteinuria had not been reported in patients with RTSC.

{2:Otsuji et al. (2023)} identified 3 unrelated patients with Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome-3 and reviewed data on their 2 previously reported patients. The patients had features similar to those previously reported, including global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, short stature, findings on brain imaging, dysmorphic facial features, ophthalmologic abnormalities, skeletal complications, and cryptorchidism. Craniofacial features included relative macrocephaly, large anterior fontanelle, hypertelorism, and arched eyebrows. One of the 3 patients was more severely affected, with profoundly impaired intellectual development and severe short stature (-6.5 SD), compared with mild to moderate developmental delay and milder short stature (-2 to -3 SD) in the other 2 patients. Two of the newly reported patients and 1 previously reported patient had low serum IgG levels. The other newly reported patient was diagnosed with common variable immunodeficiency. One patient also had intestinal lymphangiectasia. Proteinuria was seen in 2 newly reported patients and 1 previously reported patient. Elevated LDL levels were also seen in 2 newly reported patients and 1 previously reported patient.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of RTSC3 in the family reported by {1:Kato et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a Japanese sister and brother with an RTSC-like disorder, {1:Kato et al. (2020)} performed exome sequencing and identified compound heterozygosity for a missense mutation (A919T; {618981.0001}) and a 1-bp duplication ({618981.0002}) in the VPS35L gene. The authors noted that all 3 RTSC-associated genes, WASHC5 ({610657}), CCDC22 ({300859}), and VPS35L, are members of the retriever-CCC-WASH axis, which plays a pivotal role in the endosomal membrane recycling system.

In 3 unrelated patients with RTSC3, {2:Otsuji et al. (2023)} identified compound heterozygosity or homozygosity for mutations in the VPS35L gene (see, e.g., {618981.0003}-{618981.0005}). The mutations were identified by exome sequencing. Protein expression was shown to be relatively higher in patients with milder phenotypes compared with those with more severe phenotypes. Ablation of the VPS35L protein decreased the cell surface level of lipoprotein receptor-related protein-1 and low-density lipoprotein receptor, resulting in lower low-density lipoprotein cellular uptake; these studies suggested a mechanism for the hypercholesterolemia seen in patients with RTSC3.
