text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cardioacrofacial dysplasia-2 (CAFD2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PRKACB gene ({176892}) on chromosome 1p31.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Cardioacrofacial dysplasia-2 (CAFD2) is characterized by congenital cardiac defects, primarily common atrium or atrioventricular septal defect; limb anomalies, including short limbs, brachydactyly, and postaxial polydactyly; and dysmorphic facial features. Developmental delay of variable severity has also been observed ({1:Palencia-Campos et al., 2020}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of CAFD, see CAFD1 ({619142}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Palencia-Campos et al. (2020)} reported 4 unrelated probands from Denmark (P4), France (P5 and P6), and Australia (P7) who exhibited congenital cardiac defects, including single atrium in 3 and atrioventricular septal defect in 1. Three patients had valvular defects, and 1 had persistent left superior vena cava draining into the coronary sinus. In addition, all showed postaxial polydactyly of the hands, with 3 also having involvement of the feet. Long narrow thorax was present in 2 of the patients, who also showed short broad hands and feet; other variable bone anomalies were also observed in the 4 patients. Facial dysmorphisms included long face with prominent nose and chin, oral frenula, and dental anomalies, including hypodontia, supernumerary teeth, and conical teeth. Developmental delay was observed in 3 of the 4 patients (P4, P6, and P7), with severe intellectual disability in 1 (P7), who also showed autistic features and focal seizures. Two of the patients (P4 and P5) were clinically diagnosed with Ellis-Van Creveld syndrome (EVC; {225500}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CAFD2 in the families studied by {1:Palencia-Campos et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 unrelated probands with CAFD2, {1:Palencia-Campos et al. (2020)} identified heterozygosity for de novo missense mutations in the PRKACB gene ({176892.0001}-{176892.0004}) that were not found in the gnomAD database. In 1 patient (P5), the mutation was present at a variant allele fraction (VAF) of 0.32, and electropherograms confirmed mosaicism.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that infantile-onset progressive leukoencephalopathy with or without deafness (LEPID) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the KARS1 gene ({601421}) on chromosome 16q23.

Biallelic mutation in the KARS1 gene can also cause congenital deafness with adult-onset progressive leukoencephalopathy (DEAPLE; {619196}), a similar disorder with overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Infantile-onset progressive leukoencephalopathy with or without deafness (LEPID) is an autosomal recessive complex neurodegenerative disorder with onset of symptoms in infancy or early childhood. Most patients present with sensorineural deafness or hypoacousia and global developmental delay. Affected individuals show episodic regression with progressive motor deterioration resulting in spastic tetraplegia and loss of ambulation, as well as impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech. Additional more variable features may include poor overall growth with microcephaly, seizures, visual loss, microcytic anemia, and hepatic enlargement or abnormal liver enzymes. Brain imaging shows deep white matter abnormalities consistent with a progressive leukoencephalopathy. The brain and spinal cord are usually both involved; calcifications of these regions are often observed. Laboratory studies show increased serum lactate and deficiencies of mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes, consistent with global mitochondrial dysfunction. Early death often occurs (summary by {2:Itoh et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{6:Orcesi et al. (2011)} reported a male infant, born of unrelated Italian parents, with a complex neurodegenerative disorder resulting in death at 20 months of age. He was diagnosed with cochlea-based hearing loss associated with absent otoacoustic emissions at 3 months of age. Brain imaging at 5 months showed periventricular intracranial calcifications. At 12 months of age, he had marked developmental delay with severe spastic tetraplegia, microcephaly, and mild visual impairment. Laboratory studies showed microcytic anemia. Brain MRI at that time showed T2-weighted hyperintensities in the cerebral white matter that also affected the internal and external capsules, brainstem, and cerebellum. Serial imaging showed extensive and progressive calcifications in the cerebral white matter, cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord. At age 17 months, he developed hypertonic seizures and thereafter showed further neurodegeneration with spasticity, absence of voluntary movements, and visual fixation without tracking. Muscle biopsy showed a mild reduction in the activities of several mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes, suggesting a mitochondrial defect, and laboratory studies showed microcytic anemia. The boy died of cardiorespiratory arrest at 20 months of age.

{5:McMillan et al. (2015)} reported 2 sibs with a complex neurologic disorder apparent from infancy. Both presented in the first weeks of life with visual impairment, poor fixation, and nystagmus. They showed a progressive decline in head circumference, as well as global developmental delay with mildly delayed walking, cognitive impairment, and language delay. Hearing was normal. Between 2 and 4 years of age, the patients developed seizures characterized by behavioral arrest and blank stares; the seizures could be controlled with medication. Brain imaging in both patients showed abnormal subcortical white matter lesions, loss of subcortical white matter volume, and thinning of the corpus callosum.

{1:Ardissone et al. (2018)} reported 2 unrelated Italian children (patients B and C) with progressive leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord calcifications. Patient B was a 7-year-old boy who had normal early development until about 6 months of age when he developed febrile seizures and thereafter showed psychomotor regression. At 3 years, 10 months of age, he had poor growth with microcephaly, poor eye contact and sound response, nystagmus, absence of spontaneous movements, spastic tetraparesis with extrapyramidal signs, and no language. Detailed examinations showed optic atrophy, absence of visual evoked potentials, profound sensorineural hypoacousia, and hepatomegaly. EEG showed multifocal abnormalities and poor organization of cerebral activity, although seizures were not reported. Patient C was an 18-month-old girl who was noted to have sensorineural hearing impairment in the first months of life. At age 12 months, she had microcephaly, spastic tetraplegia with poor spontaneous movements, and slightly delayed visual evoked potentials. EEG showed poor background organization with abnormal spikes. Serial imaging in both patients showed progressive white matter abnormalities involving subcortical regions, the brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord. There was also diffuse cerebral atrophy and calcifications of the periventricular white matter, cerebellum, and lateral columns of the spinal cord. Laboratory studies in both patients showed hypochromic microcytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and increased plasma lactate and pyruvate. Liver biopsy of patient C suggested a vascular disturbance with nodular regenerative hyperplasia. A mitochondrial disease was suspected, but muscle biopsies were not performed.

{7:Ruzzenente et al. (2018)} reported a French girl who presented in infancy with failure to thrive and congenital sensorineural deafness. She had developmental delay, disorganized movements, dysmorphic features, hypothyroidism, and increased serum lactate. Brain imaging showed hyperintensities in the deep white matter. She died at 20 months of age during an acute infection. Patient fibroblasts showed deficiencies of multiple OXPHOS enzymes, consistent with a mitochondrial disease.

{2:Itoh et al. (2019)} reported 7 children, ranging from 2 to 12 years of age, from 5 unrelated Japanese families with early-onset progressive leukoencephalopathy. Five died between 2 and 12 years of age. Three of the patients, including 2 sibs and an unrelated boy, had previously been reported by {9:Yoshimura et al. (1997)} and {4:Kuki et al. (2011)}. They had congenital deafness, hypotonia, global developmental delay with delayed walking or inability to walk, impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, nystagmus, and intractable seizures. Most had episodic regression associated with infection, sometimes with hemiplegia, quadriplegia, or dystonia. Some had anemia, and 2 sibs had renal tubular acidosis with renal failure. Brain imaging showed abnormal signals in the white matter and spinal cord, as well as calcifications of the brain and spinal cord. Laboratory studies showed increased serum lactate and pyruvate. Neuropathologic examination of several patients showed deficient myelination, gliosis, and calcifications affecting both the cerebral white matter and corticospinal tracts.

{8:Vargas et al. (2020)} reported a 6-year-old boy, born of unrelated parents of Colombian origin, with a progressive early-onset leukoencephalopathy. He presented at 6 months of age with global developmental delay and deafness. At 12 months, he had sudden neurologic regression and loss of skills associated with a febrile illness. He was also noted to have visual deterioration with poor fixation. The disorder was progressive, and he developed spastic quadriplegia, impaired swallowing requiring a feeding tube, and onset of focal seizures at age 6 years. He was nonverbal. Brain imaging showed progressive cortical atrophy and T2-weighted signal abnormalities in the splenium of the corpus callosum, deep white matter regions, and cerebellum. {8:Vargas et al. (2020)} suggested that the white matter injury be classified as a primary leukodystrophy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of LEPID in the family reported by {5:McMillan et al. (2015)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sibs, born of unrelated parents, with LEPID, {5:McMillan et al. (2015)} identified compound heterozygous missense in the KARS1 gene (R438W, {601421.0005} and E525K, {601421.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors noted that both mutations occurred in a highly conserved region of the catalytic domain.

In a male infant (patient 459) with deficiencies of mitochondrial complexes I and IV, {3:Kohda et al. (2016)} identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the KARS1 gene: a c.1343T-A transversion (NM_005548), resulting in a val448-to-asp (V448D) substitution, and a c.953T-C transition, resulting in an ile318-to-thr (I318T) substitution. The mutations, which were found by high-throughput exome sequencing of 142 unrelated patients with childhood-onset mitochondrial respiratory chain complex deficiencies, segregated with the disorder in the family. A cDNA complementation assay revealed that mitochondrial KARS, but not the cytosolic form, successfully rescued the enzyme defects and assembly of complexes I and IV. Clinical details of the patient were limited, but he was noted to have developmental delay, seizures, nystagmus, lactic acidosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, suggestive of LEPID.

In 3 unrelated patients with LEPID, {1:Ardissone et al. (2018)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations in the KARS1 gene (see, e.g., {601421.0007}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or next-generation sequencing of a panel, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing and demonstrated to segregate with the disorder in at least 1 family. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. One of the patients (patient A) had been reported by {6:Orcesi et al. (2011)}, who had identified 2 intronic variants in cis in the DARS2 gene ({610956}), which is mutated in a similar disorder (LBSL; {611105}); {6:Orcesi et al. (2011)} could not determine whether this finding was causative of the phenotype.

In a French girl with LEPID, {7:Ruzzenente et al. (2018)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the KARS1 gene (P228L, {601421.0009} and c.1438delC, {601421.0010}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Detailed in vitro functional expression studies of patient fibroblasts showed that cytoplasmic translation was intact, but mitochondrial translation was specifically decreased. There were assembly defects of multiple OXPHOS complexes, which could be rescued by expression of mitochondrial KARS1, but not cytoplasmic KARS1. {7:Ruzzenente et al. (2018)} concluded that inhibition of mitochondrial translation underlies the disease mechanism.

In 7 children from 5 unrelated Japanese families with LEPID, {2:Itoh et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the KARS1 gene (see, e.g., {601421.0012} and {601421.0013}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing; segregation was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance in the 2 families from whom parental DNA was available. KARS1 expression levels were decreased in patient tissue, including liver and brain, and enzymatic activity of both the mitochondrial and cytosolic isoforms was decreased compared to controls. Kars-depleted Xenopus embryos showed developmental defects of the head and eyes, which could be rescued with wildtype KARS, but not by the mutant KARS variants found in the patients.

In a Colombian boy with LEPID, {8:Vargas et al. (2020)} identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the KARS1 gene: R477H ({601421.0007}) and A526V (A498V). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Both were present at very low frequencies in public databases. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because it represents a contiguous gene deletion syndrome involving 1.1 to 12.7 Mb on chromosome 13q33-q34.

description.title: Description
description.content: Chromosome 13q33-q34 deletion syndrome is associated with developmental delay and/or impaired intellectual development, facial dysmorphism, and an increased risk for epilepsy, cardiac defects and additional anatomic anomalies (summary by {4:Sagi-Dain et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Kirchhoff et al. (2009)} reported 5 unrelated individuals, aged 2 to 18 years, with interstitial deletions on chromosome 13q33-q34. All 5 individuals had hypotonia, microcephaly, trigonocephaly, moderately to severely impaired intellectual development, and dysmorphisms, including a high forehead, prominent metopic ridge, deep-set eyes, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, strabismus, dysplastic ears, broad nasal bridge, and prominent and arched upper lip. Limb findings included thenar hypoplasia (5 patients), tapering fingers (5 patients), thumb aplasia or hypoplasia (2 patients) and single palmar crease (2 patients). Additional features included seizures (2 patients), pulmonary valve stenosis (1 patient), and short stature (2 patients).

{3:Reinstein et al. (2016)} reported 5 adult patients with terminal microdeletions on chromosome 13q34. The patients included a 57-year-old mother who had 80% mosaicism for the microdeletion and her 3 affected children, aged 24, 28, and 32 years, and a 35-year old patient from an unrelated family. All 5 patients had delayed growth and development, mild dysmorphisms, intellectual disability, and obesity. Three patients had microcephaly, and patient 1 had an atrial septal defect.

{2:Orsini et al. (2018)} reported a mother and her 2 sons, aged 7 years and 18 months, with a 1.3-Mb deletion on chromosome 13q34. The mother had a borderline IQ and short stature. The older sib had hypospadias, delayed developmental milestones, mildly impaired intellectual development, and seizures. The younger sib had labile attention, delayed development of communication, and seizures. Both sibs had dysmorphisms, including a prominent nose, long nasal bridge, wide and rectangular forehead, small chin, downslanting palpebral fissures, and ptosis. Both also had short stature and microcephaly.

{4:Sagi-Dain et al. (2019)} reported 5 unrelated patients with isolated partial deletions on chromosome 13q33-q34 who were identified from local chromosome microarray databases in Israel. Patient 1 was a 17-year-old boy with developmental delay, microcephaly, speech apraxia, delayed puberty, gynecomastia, and central obesity. Patient 2 was a 5-year-old girl with developmental delay, microcephaly, hypermetropia, and strabismus. Patient 3 had prenatal findings of oligohydramnios and intrauterine growth retardation. At 1 month of age, he had developmental delay, microcephaly, severe failure to thrive, recurrent urinary tract infections due to reflux, thoracolumbar scoliosis, and hypotonia. Patient 4 was a 7-year-old boy with impaired intellectual development, microcephaly, facial dysmorphisms, prominent ears, torticollis, pectus excavatum, and a patent foramen ovale. Patient 5 was a 10-year-old boy with developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, ataxia, dysarthria, ambiguous genitalia, hypospadias, and craniosynostosis. His brain MRI showed atrophy with delayed myelination and a thin corpus callosum.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Lessel-Kreienkamp syndrome (LESKRES) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the AGO2 gene ({606229}) on chromosome 8q24.

description.title: Description
description.content: Lessel-Kreienkamp syndrome (LESKRES) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with intellectual disability and speech and language delay apparent from infancy or early childhood. The severity of the disorder is highly variable: some patients have mildly delayed walking and mild cognitive deficits, whereas others are nonambulatory and nonverbal. Most have behavioral disorders. Additional features, including seizures, hypotonia, gait abnormalities, visual defects, cardiac defects, and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, may also be present (summary by {1:Lessel et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Lessel et al. (2020)} reported 20 patients, including a pair of monozygotic twin sisters and a mother-son duo (patients 9 and 10), with a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with heterozygous mutations in the AGO2 gene. The patients, who were identified through genetic studies, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program and international collaborative efforts. All had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development and speech and language delay. The severity of the neurologic impairment was heterogeneous: some patients had mildly impaired intellectual development and acquired independent ambulation between 2 and 3 years, whereas 4 patients had severe cognitive deficits with inability to speak or walk. IQ, measured in 3 patients, ranged from 47 to 58. Additional common features, seen in about 50% of patients, included hypotonia, neonatal feeding difficulties, gastroesophageal reflux, gait abnormalities, variable skeletal anomalies, such as hip dysplasia, fifth finger clinodactyly, and scoliosis, and behavioral problems manifest as autistic features, ADHD, or aggressive behavior. Eight patients (44%) had seizures, 6 (29%) had visual impairment, 4 (19%) had myopia or hyperopia, and 5 (26%) had abnormal respiration or sleep apnea. Some patients had variable cardiac defects, such as patent foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary valve stenosis, and septal defects. Dysmorphic facial features, which were observed in many patients, included skull deformities, frontal bossing, epicanthal folds, deep-set eyes, strabismus, upslanting palpebral fissures, ear helix defects, broad nasal bridge, open mouth with thin upper lip, and dental anomalies. However, there was no recognizable pattern. Brain imaging in some patients showed white matter abnormalities, thin corpus callosum, or enlarged ventricles.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of LESKRES syndrome in 1 family reported by {1:Lessel et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. However, most of the heterozygous mutations identified in patients with LESKRES occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 20 patients, including a pair of monozygotic twins and an affected mother-son duo, with Lessel-Kreienkamp syndrome, {1:Lessel et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous mutations in the AGO2 gene (see, e.g., {606229.0001}-{606229.0006}). The mutation in the first patient was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing; subsequent patients were identified through the GeneMatcher database and international collaboration gathering patients who had undergone genetic studies. All of the mutations occurred de novo except for the dominant transmission in the mother and son duo. There were 11 missense mutations and 1 in-frame deletion; an additional patient (case 21) had a heterozygous 235.3-kb deletion involving both AGO2 and an adjacent gene. None of the mutations were present in public databases. CRISPR-mediated knockdown of AGO2 in HEK293T cells impaired shRNA-mediated gene silencing that could be rescued by wildtype AGO2, but not fully by mutant AGO2. There were differential effects of the mutations on certain mRNAs that were measured, including SHANK3 ({606230}), DDX1 ({601257}), and delta-catenin (CTNND1; {601045}), suggesting targeted effects on specific mRNAs. There was no evidence for a dominant-negative effect, indicating that the mutations most likely result in a loss of function. Additional functional studies suggested that there was reduced phosphorylation of the AGO2 C-terminal serine cluster in most of the mutants, which coincided with reduced target release and extension of the dwelling time of mutant AGO2 proteins on their target mRNAs. Expression of some of the mutations (L192P, {606229.0001}; F182del, {606229.0005}; and M364T, {606229.0003}) in primary cultured rat hippocampal cells showed that they were associated with increased density of dendritic P-bodies compared to controls, again suggesting delayed dissociation of mutant AGO2 from target mRNAs. Molecular dynamic simulations indicated that a common mechanism may involve altered AGO2 unwinding function. A notable exception was the G733R mutant ({606229.0006}), which exhibited a loss-of-function effect in almost every assay. Finally, transcriptome analysis of fibroblasts derived from 2 unrelated patients showed differential expression of multiple genes involved in mitosis and cell cycle regulation compared to controls. The authors concluded that proper human neurologic development is vulnerable to alterations in gene expression patterns and their regulation, which is mediated by AGO2.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with paroxysmal dyskinesia or seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with paroxysmal dyskinesia or seizures (IDDPADS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDE2A gene ({602658}) gene on chromosome 11q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with paroxysmal dyskinesia or seizures (IDDPADS) is an autosomal recessive complex neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and language delay. In addition, most patients develop a paroxysmal hyperkinetic movement disorder in the first months or years of life manifest as sudden falls or backward propulsion, eye or head deviation, and dystonic limb posturing followed by chorea and dyskinetic movements. The episodes are pharmacoresistant to anticonvulsant medication. EEG may show interictal abnormalities, but are usually not consistent with epilepsy. However, some patients may also develop epileptic seizures or only have seizures without a movement disorder (summary by {1:Doummar et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Salpietro et al. (2018)} reported a 12-year-old boy, born of possibly distantly related parents from the Canary Island of Tenerife, with onset of a movement disorder in early childhood around 2 years of age. He also had global developmental delay with language delay and coordination problems, and later showed poor academic performance with moderate intellectual disability. At 2 years of age, he presented with a complex episodic movement disorder that occurred several times a day and was often triggered by stress. The episodes began with neck extension, backward falling, and dystonic limb posturing, followed by choreic movements, facial grimacing, blinking, and orolingual movements. Video EEG at age 5 confirmed and correlated with the episodic movements, most of which occurred while awake, but there was no clear ictal pattern. EEG showed poorly organized background activity and asynchronous interictal discharges more commonly during sleep. The patient was diagnosed with focal epilepsy, but antiepileptic medications were ineffective. Brain imaging was normal. At 9 years of age, he developed a slowly progressive movement disorder with baseline chronic choreic movements, dystonic posturing, and fluctuating dyskinesia. Deep brain neurostimulation resulted in some clinical improvement of the movement disorder.

{1:Doummar et al. (2020)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with a complex and somewhat variable neurologic disorder. Two sibs (patients 1 and 2), born of consanguineous Moroccan parents, presented in the first months of life with abnormal movements. Fetal sonography of both patients showed an intrahepatic portosystemic venous shunt; 1 required treatment and the other resolved spontaneously. The older sib presented at 7 months of age with tonic limb contractions and upward eye deviation during awakening or falling asleep; this was associated with psychomotor regression. Although treatment with vigabatrin transiently resolved the neurologic abnormalities and she learned to walk, she developed a paroxysmal chorea-dystonic movement disorder at 17 months. These episodes, characterized by backward propulsion, head turning, opening of the mouth, limb extension, and chorea-dystonia, occurred daily, could occur during sleep, and were mostly spontaneous, although could be triggered by movement or sound. Paroxysmal dyskinesia was diagnosed, but treatment was ineffective. EEG showed interictal asymptomatic theta waves and artifacts during paroxysms; epilepsy could not be ruled out. At age 9 years, she had truncal hypotonia, inability to walk, permanent choreic movements of the limbs, dystonic hand posturing, moderate intellectual disability with poor speech, and feeding difficulties. The younger sib, who was 15 months old, developed similar episodic movements at 3 to 4 months of age. Ictal EEG showed epileptic spasms and right frontal seizures; interictal EEG showed slow waves and multifocal spikes. He had an episode of status epilepticus at 5 months of age. Other features included truncal hypotonia, inability to sit, and moderate intellectual disability. Dyskinesia was not observed. Brain imaging was normal in both patients. The third patient was a 26-year-old man who presented with global developmental delay at 3 years of age. At age 7 years, he developed a paroxysmal dystonic movement disorder with axial anteflexion of the trunk, head and eye deviation, and facial grimacing, followed by a choreoathetotic phase with limb involvement. The episodes occurred 30 to 50 times per day and could be triggered by stress or stimuli, but not sudden movements. EEG showed interictal polyspikes, but no ictal abnormalities. Anticonvulsive agents were ineffective and brain imaging was normal. The disorder was persistent and he continued to have episodes as an adult.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{2:Haidar et al. (2020)} reported a pair of sisters, born of consanguineous Iraqi parents, with a neurodevelopmental disorder and childhood-onset seizures. The girls, who were 14 and 10 years of age, had normal early development, but then showed developmental delay and regression. They walked at 18 months of age, had severe speech delay, and learning difficulties. One had significant behavioral abnormalities, including inappropriate laughing and screaming, bruxism, hyperactivity, aggression, and insomnia. Both developed seizures at ages 10 and 4 years, respectively, that were partially controlled by medication. Neither had a movement disorder, chorea, or dyskinesia, but both had hand stereotypies and 1 had ataxia. Mild dysmorphic features included microcephaly and a prominent nose. One sister showed dilated ventricles on brain imaging, whereas the other had normal brain imaging. Both were completely dependent for daily life activities. Before genetic analysis, the girls were diagnosed clinically with atypical Rett syndrome (see {312750}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IDDPADS in the family reported by {3:Salpietro et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 12-year-old boy, born of possibly distantly related parents from the Canary Island of Tenerife, with IDDPADS, {3:Salpietro et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the PDE2A gene (D480G; {602658.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was filtered against public databases and was not found in an in-house exome database. In vitro functional expression studies showed that the mutation caused markedly decreased cGMP and cAMP hydrolysis compared to controls, consistent with a loss-of-function effect, likely leading to increased cAMP and cGMP, which are intracellular signaling molecules. The authors noted that other dyskinetic/chorea movement disorders have been associated with mutations in genes involved in cAMP or cGMP metabolism, suggesting a common pathogenetic mechanism (see, e.g., PDE10A, {610652}). Genetic screening of 62 additional patients with a similar disorder did not identify any PDE2A mutations, suggesting that it may be a rare cause of the disorder.

In 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with IDDPADS, {1:Doummar et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PDE2A gene ({602658.0002}-{602658.0004}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. None were present in public databases, including gnomAD. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but all were predicted to result in a loss of function. Patient fibroblasts showed an abnormal and disorganized mitochondrial network, suggesting an imbalance between mitochondrial fission and fusion mechanisms.

In 2 affected sisters, born of consanguineous Iraqi parents, with IDDPADS, {2:Haidar et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the PDE2A gene ({602658.0005}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not present in public databases. The mutation occurred in a region of shared homozygosity. Aside from the confirmation of the splicing defect, functional studies of the variant were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without early-onset generalized epilepsy

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with or without early-onset generalized epilepsy (NEDEGE) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the NBEA gene ({604889}) on chromosome 13q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without early-onset generalized epilepsy (NEDEGE) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy or early childhood. Affected individuals have variably impaired intellectual development, speech delay, and behavioral abnormalities. About half of patients develop early-onset generalized epilepsy with different seizure types; myoclonic seizures and myoclonic-atonic epilepsy are commonly observed. The seizures may remit with age or remain refractory to treatment. Brain imaging is essentially normal and there are no significant accompanying neurologic or systemic abnormalities (summary by {3:Mulhern et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Mulhern et al. (2018)} reported 23 unrelated patients, ranging from 3 to 23 years of age, with a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with de novo heterozygous mutations in the NBEA gene. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after mutation identification. Two patients (patients 13 and 14) had previously been reported by {2:Bowling et al. (2017)}. All patients had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development and speech or language delay. Two patients were nonverbal at 11 and 19 years of age. IQ, when measured, ranged from 40 to 60, and some were able to attend special schools. About half of patients had autism or autistic features, and others showed ADHD or aggressive behavior. Age at ambulation ranged from 11 months to 3.5 years, although 1 patient (patient 11) was nonambulatory as an adult. A few patients had a wide-based or uncoordinated gait or dystonic movements. Fifteen patients had epilepsy, and 2 had presumed or possible epilepsy. All except 1 had generalized epilepsy with multiple seizure types; 1 patient had focal seizures. Seizure onset was usually in early childhood (infancy to 4 years). Some had cessation of seizures in the first or second decade, whereas others continued to have seizures and remained refractory to treatment. Myoclonic seizures and myoclonic-atonic epilepsy (MAE) were observed in many patients and tended to be more common in patients with loss-of-function mutations. EEG showed variable abnormalities with no consistent pattern, although most had generalized spike and polyspike wave discharges. Most patients had normal brain imaging, although a few had nonspecific white matter abnormalities. Additional more variable features included hypotonia (8 patients), microcephaly (3), recurrent infections (2), and eczema (3).

{1:Boulin et al. (2021)} reported a 6-year-old girl who presented with epilepsy, global developmental delay, and ataxia. Neurologic findings on examination included unilateral ptosis, dysarthria, and appendicular hypotonia. She also had mild to moderate intellectual disability. Brain MRI showed mild cortical atrophy and punctate subcortical white matter hyperintensities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the NBEA gene that were identified in patients with NEDEGE by {3:Mulhern et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 23 unrelated patients with NEDEGE, {3:Mulhern et al. (2018)} identified 23 unique de novo mutations or intragenic deletions in the NBEA gene (see, e.g., {604889.0001}-{604889.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, were absent from the gnomAD database. Most were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. There were 8 nonsense, 5 frameshift, 4 missense, and 1 splice site mutation, as well as 5 intragenic deletions. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but they were predicted to result in haploinsufficiency. An additional patient (patient 19) with a similar disorder had a larger heterozygous multigene deletion including NBEA.

{1:Boulin et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous mutation in the NBEA gene (G1967R; {604889.0006}) in a 6-year-old girl with NEDEGE. The mutation, which was identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was located in the DUF1088 domain. CRISPR knock-in of the corresponding mutation (G1514R) in the orthologous sel2 gene in C. elegans resulted in altered cell fate determination of epidermal cells and decreased trafficking of potassium channels to the tips of sensory dendrites. These results were similar to those seen in sel2 null C. elegans mutants, suggesting that the G1514R mutation results in a strong hypomorph or a loss of function.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that immunodeficiency-76 (IMD76) is caused by homozygous mutation in the FCHO1 gene ({613437}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Immunodeficiency-76 (IMD76) is an autosomal recessive primary immunologic disorder characterized by onset of recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections in early childhood. Laboratory studies show T-cell lymphopenia and may show variable B-cell or immunoglobulin abnormalities. More variable features found in some patients include lymphoma and neurologic features. Although bone marrow transplantation may be curative, many patients die in childhood (summary by {2:Lyszkiewicz et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Calzoni et al. (2019)} reported 5 unrelated children with onset of recurrent infections associated with T-cell lymphopenia in the first months or years of life. The families were of Italian, Turkish, and Algerian descent; 4 were consanguineous. The patients had respiratory, gastrointestinal tract, and skin infections of bacterial, mycobacterial, viral, and fungal origin. Two patients had EBV viremia. P2 and P3 had absent thymic shadows on radiography. Laboratory evaluation showed decreased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in all patients; some also had low B-cell levels and increased or decreased Ig levels with poor antibody response. Two patients (P1 and P2) underwent successful bone marrow transplant, whereas the other 3 died in childhood. P3 presented with diffuse lymphadenopathy and EBV viremia at 8 years of age. Bone marrow biopsy showed hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, and lymph node biopsy revealed an EBV-negative diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. He had both lymphopenia and neutropenia, and died of respiratory failure. P5 developed fever, dyspnea, oral thrush, ataxia, and seizures at 6 years of age. Chest CT showed consolidations and respiratory culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae. Brain imaging revealed cerebellar lesions that were identified as lymphomatoid granulomatosis. Laboratory studies showed CD4+ T-cell lymphopenia, increased IgM, and EBV viremia. She died of respiratory failure. In addition to recurrent infections, including disseminated BCG, P4 experienced neuromotor regression associated with ataxia and tremor in early childhood; she died of respiratory failure at 4 years of age.

{2:Lyszkiewicz et al. (2020)} reported 10 patients from 7 unrelated consanguineous families with IMD76. The families were of German, Turkish, Saudi Arabian, Algerian, and Palestinian origin. All patients had severe bacterial, viral, or fungal infections manifest as recurrent pneumonia, otitis media, diarrhea, stomatitis, candidiasis, gingivitis, and various mycoses. Several patients had failure to thrive. Laboratory studies showed decreased CD4+ T cells. Some patients had combined B- and T-cell lymphopenia, and most had hypogammaglobulinemia. One patient had moyamoya syndrome (see {252350}) with transient left hemiparesis and microcephaly. Two patients developed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and 1 developed EBV+ Hodgkin lymphoma. Patients either underwent or were waiting for hematopoietic stem cell transplant or died of the disease.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IMD76 in the families reported by {1:Calzoni et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 5 unrelated probands with IMD76, {1:Calzoni et al. (2019)} identified homozygous putative loss-of-function mutations in the FCHO1 gene (see, e.g., {613437.0001}-{613437.0003}). Four of the families were consanguineous. The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or candidate gene sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were 2 splice site mutations, 2 frameshift mutations, and an in-frame deletion. All were absent from the gnomAD database. T cells derived from 1 patient (P2) showed impaired proliferation and increased apoptosis upon CD3/CD28 stimulation compared to controls. {1:Calzoni et al. (2019)} noted that clathrin-mediated endocytosis is important for mitosis. Patient cells also showed decreased internalization of the transferrin receptor (TFRC; {190010}), consistent with defective clathrin-mediated endocytosis. In contrast, endocytic internalization of the T-cell receptor (TCR)/CD3, which the authors stated is clathrin-independent, was preserved in activated T cells from P2.

In 10 affected patients from 7 unrelated families with IMD76, {2:Lyszkiewicz et al. (2020)} identified homozygous mutations in the FCHO1 gene (see, e.g., {613437.0002}; {613437.0004}-{613437.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were 2 missense, 2 splice site, a nonsense, and a frameshift mutation. T cells derived from 1 patient (kindred C) with a frameshift mutation designated Stop687 ({613437.0002}) showed impaired proliferation and poor cytokine production after TCR stimulation. Deletion of FCHO1 in a T-cell line disrupted endocytic internalization of the CD3:TCR complex, possibly due to impaired calcium mobilization. These defects could be rescued by wildtype FCHO1, but not mutant FCHO1. Further in vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells transfected with 3 of the mutant proteins showed variable effects depending on the location of the mutation. Two mutations affecting the C-terminal mu-HD domain (R679P and Stop687) reduced the interaction with partner proteins, whereas a mutation affecting the N-terminal F-BAR domain (A34P) resulted in the formation of large aggregates that were not associated with the plasma membrane. None of the mutants colocalized with endogenous clathrin, and all failed to facilitate the formation of clathrin-coated pits and vesicles. Patient fibroblasts showed normal endocytic internalization of the transferrin receptor, suggesting that the mutation does not alter global endocytosis. {2:Lyszkiewicz et al. (2020)} concluded that FCHO1 and clathrin-mediated endocytosis play an important role in T-cell development and function, and that these loss-of-function mutations impair TCR internalization and subsequent signaling during immune responses.

phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 3

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex II deficiency nuclear type 3 (MC2DN3) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the SDHD gene ({602690}) on chromosome 11q23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex II deficiency nuclear type 3 (MC2DN3) is an autosomal recessive multisystemic metabolic disorder with a highly variable phenotype. Some patients may have an encephalomyopathic picture with episodic developmental regression, loss of motor skills, hypotonia, ataxia, dystonia, and seizures or myoclonus. Other patients present in infancy with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which may be fatal. Laboratory studies show increased serum lactate and mitochondrial complex II deficiency in muscle and fibroblasts (summary by {2:Jackson et al., 2014} and {1:Alston et al., 2015}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of MC2DN, see MC2DN1 ({252011}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Jackson et al. (2014)} reported a girl, born of unrelated Swiss parents, with encephalomyopathy and biochemical evidence of isolated mitochondrial complex II deficiency. The patient showed developmental regression with reduced motor development. Thereafter, she showed severely delayed psychomotor development associated with hypotonia, nystagmus, secondary microcephaly, ataxia, dystonia, and deteriorating vision. Laboratory studies were normal, excluding severe catabolic episodes. After 4.5 years of age, she developed seizures and myoclonic movements. During an illness at age 7, the patient underwent laboratory studies that showed lactic acidosis, ketonuria, and Krebs cycle intermediates, suggesting a mitochondrial defect. She also had elevated liver enzymes and increased serum creatine kinase. Biochemical assays of skin fibroblasts and muscle homogenates indicated isolated mitochondrial complex II deficiency (5% residual activity) and defective oxygen consumption; immunoblotting showed impaired complex II assembly. She died at 10 years of age.

{1:Alston et al. (2015)} reported an infant, born of unrelated Irish parents, with fatal cardiomyopathy associated with mitochondrial complex II deficiency. The patient was noted prenatally to have dilated cardiomyopathy with mitral regurgitation and left ventricular systolic dysfunction. He died on the first day of life. Postmortem examination showed noncompaction of the hypertrophic left ventricle and an underdeveloped right ventricle. Patient skeletal muscle sample showed isolated complex II deficiency (30% residual activity), as well as a significant decrease in SDHD protein levels and a decrease in fully assembled complex II.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC2DN3 in the family reported by {2:Jackson et al. (2014)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a girl, born of unrelated Swiss parents, with MC2DN3, {2:Jackson et al. (2014)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the SDHD gene (E69K, {602690.0029} and X164L, {602690.0030}). Each parent was heterozygous for one of the mutations. The variants were not found in 200 control individuals. Cellular complementation studies showed that the SDHD variants were unable to rescue the complex II assembly defect, whereas wildtype SDHD was able to rescue it.

In an infant, born of unrelated Irish parents, with mitochondrial complex II deficiency, {1:Alston et al. (2015)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SDHD gene (D92G; {602690.0031}). The parents were heterozygous for the mutation. Complementation studies in yeast deficient in the homologous SDH4 gene showed that the mutation was unable to rescue the oxidative growth defect, consistent with a loss of function.

phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 36

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 36 (MC1DN36) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NDUFC2 gene ({603845}) on chromosome 11q14.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 36 (MC1DN36) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia, and failure to thrive apparent from infancy or early childhood. Affected individuals usually do not acquire ambulation, show progressive spasticity, and have impaired intellectual development with absent speech. More variable features may include pale optic discs, poor eye contact, seizures, and congenital heart defects. Laboratory studies show increased serum lactate; metabolic acidosis may occur during stress or infection. Brain imaging shows T2-weighted abnormalities in the basal ganglia and brainstem, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of Leigh syndrome (see {256000}). Patient tissue showed isolated mitochondrial complex I deficiency. Death may occur in childhood ({1:Alahmad et al., 2020}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex I deficiency, see {252010}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Alahmad et al. (2020)} reported 3 children from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with a complex mitochondrial disorder. The older sib in family 1 (patient 1), of Saudi Arabian origin, presented at 2 years of age with global developmental delay and inability to walk. Laboratory studies showed increased serum lactate and alanine and increased excretion of fumaric acid. Brain imaging at 21 months of age showed T2-weighted signal abnormalities in the thalami, substantia nigra, and posterior tract of the medulla oblongata, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of Leigh syndrome. There was also loss of white matter volume and periventricular leukomalacia. At age 6 years, she was unable to stand or speak, had spasticity with brisk tendon reflexes, optic disc pallor, and dysmorphic facial features. She did not have seizures or other organ involvement. Her younger sib (patient 2) presented in utero and at birth with mild cardiomegaly, a ventricular septal defect, and left pulmonary artery stenosis. He showed global developmental delay with poor growth and increased serum lactate. Brain imaging showed features of Leigh syndrome, as well as a Dandy-Walker malformation and partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. He developed rapid neurologic deterioration with seizures during an infectious illness, and later required tube feeding. He also showed progressive spasticity. He died at age 3 from pneumonia associated with metabolic acidosis. A male infant (patient 3) in family 2, of Moroccan descent, presented soon after birth with failure to thrive, global developmental delay with poor eye contact, truncal hypotonia, peripheral hypertonia, muscle atrophy, and paucity of spontaneous movements. Brainstem auditory and visual evoked potentials showed severe central conduction abnormalities. He also developed seizures while under anesthesia. Brain imaging was consistent with Leigh syndrome. He died at 8 months of age. Assessment of mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme activities in 2 patients showed isolated complex I deficiency and decreased rates of oxygen consumption in patient fibroblasts and skeletal muscle. Patient fibroblasts also showed decreased levels of complex I subunits compared to controls.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC1DN36 in the families reported by {1:Alahmad et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated probands (patients 1 and 3) with MC1DN36, each born of consanguineous parents, {1:Alahmad et al. (2020)} identified homozygous mutations in the NDUFC2 gene ({603845.0001} and {603845.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-genome or direct sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. The families were identified through the GeneMatcher program. Patient 1 had a complex ins/del mutation resulting in decreased NDUFC2 mRNA expression, whereas patient 3 had a missense variant (H58L) and normal mRNA levels. No samples were available for genetic analysis from a similarly affected sib (patient 2) of patient 1. Fibroblasts derived from patients 1 and 3 showed isolated complex I deficiency (16-19% residual activity compared to controls), an overall reduction in steady-state levels of complex I subunits, and decreased levels of fully assembled complex I. Expression of wildtype NDUFC2 was able to partially correct these abnormalities. Close examination of the complex I assembly intermediates in patient cells showed that the Q module was unaffected, but there were abnormal accumulations of intermediate structures after that stage. Modules ND1 and ND2 were also defective. The findings indicated an essential role for NDUFC2 in the assembly of the membrane arm of mitochondrial complex I.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis-15 (CLN15) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CLCN6 gene ({602726}) on chromosome 1p36.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis-15 (CLN15) is characterized by severe global developmental delay apparent in infancy or early childhood. Affected individuals have hypotonia with impaired motor development, respiratory insufficiency, and feeding difficulties requiring intervention. Intellectual and speech development is also delayed, and most have visual defects, including cortical visual blindness, nystagmus, and esotropia. The disorder is progressive, as manifest by developmental regression consistent with neurodegeneration. Although overt seizures are not observed, some patients may have episodic hypertonia or apnea, and EEG may show nonspecific abnormalities. Brain imaging shows unique diffusion restriction signal abnormalities affecting the brainstem, cerebellum, and corticospinal tracts. Early death may occur (summary by {2:Polovitskaya et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Polovitskaya et al. (2020)} reported 3 unrelated children, ranging in age from 18 months to 6 years, with a similar neurodegenerative disorder associated with a de novo mutation in the CLCN6 gene. The patients, who underwent exome sequencing for undiagnosed diseases, were identified through the GeneMatcher program. One patient (P2) died at 23 months of age. All had severe global developmental delay apparent from infancy, with hypotonia, inability to walk, and impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech. They had hypoventilation with respiratory insufficiency and feeding difficulties requiring tracheostomy and tube feeding, as well as neurogenic bladder (2 patients). Visual abnormalities included cortical blindness, optic disc elevation, nystagmus, esotropia, and strabismic amblyopia. Although none had overt seizures, 2 had EEG abnormalities and 1 had episodes of staring, hypertonia, and oxygen desaturation. Brain imaging showed progressive cortical atrophy and symmetric diffusion restriction involving the corticospinal tracts, cerebellum, and brainstem. Muscle biopsy, performed in all patients, showed evidence of a mild myopathy with variation in fiber types, subsarcolemmal accumulation of mitochondria, and fatty vacuoles. More variable features included insensitivity to pain, hyperhidrosis, abnormal temperature regulation, and sensory peripheral neuropathy with areflexia. Patient 1 had reduced serum copper, trichorrhexis nodosa, and abnormal elastic fibers on skin biopsy. Patient 2, who had cafe-au-lait spots and genetically confirmed NF1 ({162200}), developed involuntary movements with dyskinesia and choreoathetosis.

{1:He et al. (2024)} reported a 10-year-old girl with CLN15 who had developmental delay, epilepsy, microcephaly, behavioral abnormalities, and abnormal visual evoked potentials. A brain MRI showed progressive cerebellar and cerebral atrophy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CLCN6 gene that were identified in patients with CLN15 by {2:Polovitskaya et al. (2020)} and {1:He et al. (2024)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 unrelated children with CLN15, {2:Polovitskaya et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the CLCN6 gene (Y553C; {602726.0001}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Electrophysiologic studies in CHO cells transfected with the mutant protein showed slowed activation currents that reached larger steady-state amplitudes compared to wildtype. Unlike wildtype, mutant channels did not show decreased activity in the presence of low pH, indicating insensitivity to low pH, which further contributes to a gain-of-function effect. HeLa cells transfected with the mutant protein developed abnormally large cytoplasmic vesicles, likely due to enhanced fusion, that were poorly acidified. Bafilomycin treatment abrogated vacuole generation, indicating that H(+)-driven Cl- accumulation osmotically drives vesicle enlargement. Although patient-derived fibroblasts did not showed enlarged vacuoles, the authors speculated that neuronal cells, which express CLCN6, may demonstrate these abnormalities and may also have altered lysosomal function.

In a 10-year-old girl with CLN15, {1:He et al. (2024)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the CLCN6 gene (E200A; {602726.0002}). Expression of CLCN6 with the E200A mutation in HeLa cells resulted in abnormalities in the autophagic-lysosomal pathway, with increased expression of SQSTM1/p62 ({601530}) and an increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, as well as increased free cholesterol levels as detected by Filipin staining. {1:He et al. (2024)} also expressed CLCN6 with the previously identified Y553C mutation ({602726.0001}) in HeLa cells and identified the same abnormalities in the autophagic-lysosomal pathway and increased free cholesterol levels.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant primary microcephaly-26 (MCPH26) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the LMNB1 gene ({150340}) on chromosome 5q23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal dominant primary microcephaly-26 (MCPH26) is characterized by progressive microcephaly beginning at birth and associated with global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development. Some patients may have only mild learning difficulties or speech delay, whereas other are more severely affected with the inability to walk or speak. Additional features may include short stature, spasticity, feeding difficulties requiring tube feeding, and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features. Brain imaging in some patients shows a simplified gyral pattern or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, suggesting abnormal neuronal migration (summary by {1:Cristofoli et al., 2020}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of primary microcephaly, see MCPH1 ({251200}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Cristofoli et al. (2020)} reported 7 patients from 5 unrelated families of various ethnic origins with primary microcephaly. The patients, who ranged from 2 to 11 years of age, had microcephaly (-3.6 SD to -12 SD) and global developmental delay. The severity was highly variable: one patient (P2) and her similarly affected mother had the mildest phenotype with head circumferences measuring -3.6 and -2.5 SD, respectively. The patient walked at age 2 years, had slow language acquisition, and followed special education. She had no brain imaging anomalies besides microcephaly. The mother had a history of learning difficulties. The most severely affected patients had poor overall growth with short stature, feeding problems requiring tube feeding, axial hypotonia, spastic tetraparesis, inability to walk, neurogenic scoliosis, severe intellectual disability with absent language, cortical visual impairment, and seizures. Brain imaging in the more severely affected patients showed a simplified gyral pattern, pachygyria, lissencephaly, and dysgenesis of the corpus callosum. Some patients had nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, including long philtrum, short nose, prominent nasal root, bitemporal narrowing, upslanting palpebral fissures, long palpebral fissures, and gingival hypertrophy.

{2:Parry et al. (2021)} reported 7 unrelated patients (P1-P3, P9-P11, and P13) with MCPH26 confirmed by genetic analysis. The patients were ascertained from 2 large cohorts (the DDD study and the 100,000 Genomes Project) of individuals with microcephaly who underwent exome sequencing. The patients had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, poor or absent language, and delayed walking or inability to walk. Some had failure to thrive with poor feeding. Three patients had seizures and 2 had hypothyroidism. Nonspecific dysmorphic features were sometimes observed: these included sloping forehead, upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, depressed and broad nasal bridge, pointed chin, kyphosis, and overlapping toes. Brain imaging was normal in some patients, but in others showed enlarged ventricles, simplified gyral pattern, or aplasia of the corpus callosum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MCPH26 in 2 families reported by {1:Cristofoli et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance; heterozygous mutations in the LMNB1 gene identified in other patients with the disorder occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 7 patients from 5 unrelated families with MCPH26, {1:Cristofoli et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous mutations in the LMNB1 gene ({150340.0002}-{150340.0006}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing or microarray analysis and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The mutations occurred de novo in 3 patients, whereas 1 was inherited from a mildly affected mother, and in 3 sibs were inherited from an unaffected father who was mosaic for the mutation. There was 1 intragenic deletion, 1 splice site mutation, and 3 missense variants affecting highly conserved residues. In vitro functional expression studies of the 3 missense variants showed that they caused variable abnormalities of the nuclear lamina and/or misshapen nuclei. One was associated with decreased protein expression, and the others caused mislocalization of LMNB1 to the cytoplasm. However, mitotic spindle formation and segregation did not appear to be affected. The authors postulated a dominant-negative effect.

In 7 unrelated patients (P1-P3, P9-P11, P13) with MCPH26, {2:Parry et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous mutations in the LMNB1 gene (see, e.g., {150340.0004} and {150340.0007}). There were 2 recurrent missense mutations and an in-frame deletion; none were present in the gnomAD database. The mutations occurred de novo in all patients for whom parental material was available. The location of the mutations predicted interference with dimer or filament assembly, and in vitro functional expression studies in cells transfected with the mutations showed that they caused abnormal LMNB1 nuclear aggregates and an altered nuclear shape. {2:Parry et al. (2021)} postulated that the mutations may alter the properties of lamin filaments, resulting in fragile nuclei that are susceptible to the mechanical stresses of nuclear and neuronal migration, leading to increased cell death during brain development.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant primary microcephaly-27 (MCPH27) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the LMNB2 gene ({150341}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal dominant primary microcephaly-27 (MCPH27) is characterized by small head circumference apparent in early childhood and associated with global developmental delay manifest as delayed walking, inability to walk, impaired intellectual development, and poor or absent speech. Most patients have variable and nonspecific additional features, including facial dysmorphism, hypotonia, limb hypertonia, poor feeding, and distal skeletal anomalies. Brain imaging may show enlarged ventricles or gyral abnormalities, but most have normal imaging ({1:Parry et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of primary microcephaly, see MCPH1 ({251200}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Parry et al. (2021)} reported 6 unrelated patients (P4-P8, P12), ranging from 5 to 15 years of age, with primary microcephaly. They had moderate to severe developmental delay with delayed walking or inability to walk and impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech. One patient had absence seizures and another had hearing impairment. Less common features observed in only a few patients included hypotonia, tremor, clenched fists, limb hypertonia, brisk reflexes, fifth finger clinodactyly, short broad or tapering fingers, toe anomalies, micropenis, undescended testes, poor feeding, drooping, constipation, hip subluxation, short stature, and joint hypermobility. Variable dysmorphic features included sloping forehead, brachycephaly, deep-set eyes, epicanthal folds, long palpebral fissures, prominent nasal bridge, wide mouth with widely spaced teeth, low-set ears, large earlobes, and retrognathia. Brain imaging was normal in 4 of 5 patients studied; the fifth patient had enlarged ventricles and simplified gyri.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the LMNB2 gene that were identified in most patients with MCPH27 by {1:Parry et al. (2021)} occurred de novo; one patient inherited the mutation from an unaffected mosaic parent.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 unrelated patients (P4-P8, P12) with MCPH27, {1:Parry et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous missense mutations in the LMNB2 gene (E398K, {150341.0006} and N54H, {150341.0007}). E389K was a recurrent mutation, found in 5 of the patients. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, occurred de novo in most patients, but in 1 was inherited from an unaffected mosaic mother. The mutations were not present in the gnomAD database. The location of the mutations predicted interference with dimer or filament assembly, and in vitro functional expression studies in cells transfected with the mutant proteins showed that both caused abnormal LMNB nuclear aggregates and an altered nuclear shape. {1:Parry et al. (2021)} postulated that the mutations may alter the properties of lamin filaments, resulting in fragile nuclei that are susceptible to the mechanical stresses of nuclear and neuronal migration, leading to increased cell death during brain development.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-64 (MRD64) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ZNF292 gene ({616213}) on chromosome 6q14.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-64 (MRD64) is characterized by mildly to severely impaired intellectual development (ID) with speech delays. Most patients also have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Additional features are highly variable but may include motor delay, attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and nonspecific dysmorphic features (summary by {1:Mirzaa et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Mirzaa et al. (2020)} reported 28 unrelated patients (19 males and 9 females) with a nonsyndromic intellectual developmental disorder. The families were identified across 20 institutions in 6 countries with data shared through the MatchMaker Exchange Program. Some of the patients had previously been reported with limited clinical description. Twenty-two patients were aged 10 months to 7 years, and 6 patients were aged 17 to 24 years. Most patients were of European descent, but Chinese, Middle Eastern, Hispanic, and African-American patients were also described. All but 1 patient (17-023) had impaired intellectual development or developmental delay (DD); the exception was a 6-year-old boy diagnosed with ASD and speech delays. Eleven of 27 patients (40%) had mild ID/DD, 6 of 27 (22%) had moderate ID/DD, and 3 of 27 (11%) had severe ID (complicated by severe prematurity in one). Speech delay was present in 26 of 27 patients; some patients were nonverbal or minimally verbal and 2 (17-007 and 17-015) had regression of speech and language development. A confirmed or suspected diagnosis of ASD was present in 17 of 27 patients, and 9 of 27 patients had ADHD. Three of 26 patients had seizures: one, who was born at 25 weeks' gestation, experienced neonatal seizures; one had staring spells; and one was described as having 'possible seizures' at age 3 years. Thirteen of 23 patients had tone abnormalities, including hypotonia, hypertonia, or mixed tone. Brain MRI, performed in 12 patients, showed notable abnormalities in 3: posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus in a patient who was born at 25 weeks' gestation; complex cerebellar abnormalities with hypoplasia of the vermis and hemispheres and marked asymmetry between the hemispheres in another patient; and a lacunar insult in the subcortical white matter of unknown etiology in the third. One person each had ventriculomegaly, callosal abnormalities, and periventricular nodular heterotopias. While there was no evidence of a recognizable facial gestalt, 13 of 27 patients had facial dysmorphisms, most commonly micrognathia and hypertelorism. Eleven of 27 patients had growth abnormalities, including short stature.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in 27 of the 28 families with MRD64 reported by {1:Mirzaa et al. (2020)} occurred de novo. In 1 family, the heterozygous mutation was inherited from a mildly affected mother.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: {1:Mirzaa et al. (2020)} reported 28 unrelated patients with MRD64 and a total of 24 heterozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations in the ZNF292 gene (see, e.g., {616213.0001}-{616213.0007}). The families were identified across 20 institutions in 6 countries with data shared through the MatchMaker Exchange Program. Some of the patients and mutations had previously been reported. The mutations, which were identified by targeted or exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, occurred primarily in the last exon. In 27 patients, the mutations occurred as de novo events; 2 of these mutations were recurrent ({616213.0004} and {616213.0005}). In 1 family (18-003), the mutation ({616213.0006}) was inherited from the mildly affected mother. All but one of the 24 mutations were absent from the gnomAD database (v2.1); the exception ({616213.0007}) was present only once. {1:Mirzaa et al. (2020)} also reported 15 additional patients with missense, nonsense, or frameshift mutations in the ZNF292 gene for whom limited phenotyping, lack of both parents to determine inheritance, or a missense variant with no functional evidence prevented determination of pathogenicity. {1:Mirzaa et al. (2020)} noted that there were 5 predicted loss-of-function variants in the control cohort in gnomAD, suggesting that there may be rare instances of incomplete penetrance for the ID/ASD phenotype caused by pathogenic variants in this gene.

Head: Microcephaly (1 family)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Li-Campeau syndrome (LICAS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the UBR7 gene ({613816}) on chromosome 14q32.

description.title: Description
description.content: Li-Campeau syndrome (LICAS) is an autosomal recessive syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, dysmorphic facial features, hypothyroidism, and variable abnormalities of the cardiac and genital systems. Additional features may include seizures, short stature, hypotonia, and brain imaging anomalies, such as cortical atrophy (summary by {1:Li et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Li et al. (2021)} reported 7 patients from 6 unrelated families with a similar syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder ascertained through exome or genome sequencing. The patients, who ranged in age from 2 to 10 years, had global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, often with hypotonia and sometimes with absent speech. A few had brisk reflexes. Six patients had onset of seizures in the first months or years of life. Five patients had variable cardiac abnormalities, including atrial or ventricular septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, and patent foramen ovale. Four had hypothyroidism, and all 6 males had genital anomalies, mainly cryptorchidism; 1 had a small penis. Five patients had short stature and 2 sibs (P6 and P7) had microcephaly (-4.6 to -5.7 SD). There were various dysmorphic features, including prominent forehead, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, downslanting palpebral fissures, strabismus, thick eyebrows, low-set ears, deep nasal bridge, long philtrum, high-arched palate, and ptosis. Less common features included long fingers, single transverse palmar crease, scoliosis, hypertrichosis, hypoplastic patellae, and gastrointestinal dysmotility. Brain imaging, performed in 4 patients, showed enlarged ventricles, cortical atrophy, thin corpus callosum, delayed myelination, and nonspecific white matter abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of LICAS in the families reported by {1:Li et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 7 patients from 6 unrelated families with LICAS, {1:Li et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the UBR7 gene (see, e.g., {613816.0001}-{613816.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome or genome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The mutations included 2 frameshifts, 1 nonsense, 2 splice site, 1 missense, and an intragenic deletion. All but 1 were absent from the gnomAD database; the 1 frameshift was found in only 1 allele in gnomAD. All of the mutations were predicted to result in a loss of function, although specific functional studies were not performed. Cells derived from 3 patients showed loss of the UBR7 protein. Knockdown of the orthologous gene in C. elegans resulted in developmental defects and was associated with abnormal NOTCH signaling in germline stem cells that likely influenced development and embryo formation.

clinicalSynopsis: Two unrelated consanguineous families have been reported (last curated February 2021)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that progressive myoclonic epilepsy-12 (EPM12) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SLC7A6OS gene ({619192}) on chromosome 16q22.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Progressive myoclonic epilepsy-12 (EPM12) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by onset of tonic-clonic seizures and/or myoclonus in the second decade of life. Affected individuals develop cerebellar ataxia associated with progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy on brain imaging. Most patients lose ambulation and become wheelchair-bound. Additional more variable features include mild cognitive dysfunction or psychiatric manifestations, such as depression or anxiety (summary by {1:Mazzola et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of progressive myoclonic epilepsy, see EPM1A ({254800}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Mazzola et al. (2021)} reported 6 patients, ranging from 22 to 43 years of age, from 2 unrelated families with onset of progressive myoclonic epilepsy between 11 and 21 years of age. Both families, of Portuguese and Turkish origin, respectively, were consanguineous. Four patients presented with tonic-clonic seizures, and 2 presented with myoclonus. All eventually developed myoclonus, and all but 1 developed tonic-clonic seizures. EEG showed generalized polyspike, polyspike-wave, and sometimes spike-wave discharges. Additional features included cerebellar ataxia, often with dysarthria or dysmetria, and a decline in independent ambulation. Four patients became wheelchair-bound between 17 and 30 years of age. Three patients had mild cognitive decline manifest primarily as attentional dysfunction, and several had comorbid psychiatric diagnoses, including depression, anxiety, attention deficit disorder, and addiction. Serial brain imaging in 1 family showed progressive cerebellar and cerebral atrophy. All patients were taking multiple antiseizure medications.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of EPM12 in the families reported by {1:Mazzola et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families of Portuguese and Turkish origin, respectively, with EPM12, {1:Mazzola et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous mutation in the SLC7A6OS gene ({619192.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families. The mutation was predicted to result in a splicing alteration, and analysis of patient-derived cells showed decreased SLC7A6OS transcript and protein levels compared to controls, consistent with a loss-of-function effect. Haplotype analysis suggested a founder effect. Additional functional studies were not performed, but the authors noted that SLC7A6OS is highly expressed in the developing human brain.
