text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that limb-brain ENDOVE syndrome (ENDOVESLB) is caused by homozygous mutation in the EN1 gene ({131290}) on chromosome 2q14. One such patient has been reported.

Deletions and genomic rearrangements involving a topologically associated domain that includes the EN1 gene causes ENDOVE syndrome without brain anomalies (ENDOVESL; {619217}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Limb-brain ENDOVE syndrome (ENDOVESLB) is characterized by marked mesomelic shortening of the lower limbs due to severe hypoplasia of the tibia and fibula. The talus is absent and foot bones are rudimentary. Hands show short and malformed fingers with a missing digit, and nails are absent on some fingers. In addition, there is cerebellar aplasia with hypoplasia of the brainstem ({1:Allou et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Allou et al. (2021)} reported a 3-year-old Brazilian girl (patient 4), born of first-cousin parents, who had marked shortening of the lower limbs below the knees, with anterolateral globular appendages over palpable bony spurs. The talus was absent and feet were very short and verticalized. Her hands had 4 digits, and fingers were short and malformed, with absent nails on the index and fourth fingers. At 2 months of age she developed tonic focal seizures and was noted to have severe hypotonia. Evaluation for multiple urinary tract infections revealed bilateral hydronephrosis and neurogenic bladder, requiring regular catheterization. At 4 months, she developed feeding difficulties requiring insertion of a gastrostomy tube. Brain MRI revealed absence of cerebellum and hypoplasia of the brainstem, with extension of abnormally configured occipital lobes into the posterior fossa. Examination at 3.75 years of age showed microcephaly, poor visual contact, joint laxity, hyperactive reflexes, and generalized hypotonia, with no social smile or purposeful movements. Skeletal radiographs showed triangular-shaped tibiae and fibulae, positioned at right angles with the apices palpable as bony spurs. Foot bones were rudimentary, reduced in size and number; the toes were short and malformed, as were the fingers. The authors designated the disorder 'EN1-related dorsoventral syndrome (ENDOVES), limb-brain type' ({2:Superti-Furga, 2021}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of ENDOVESLB in the consanguineous Brazilian family reported by {1:Allou et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a 3-year-old Brazilian girl (patient 4) who had mesomelia of the lower extremities with hand, foot, and brain anomalies, {1:Allou et al. (2021)} sequenced the EN1 gene and identified homozygosity for a 1-bp duplication ({131290.0001}) for which her asymptomatic mother was heterozygous; DNA analysis was not reported for her unaffected father.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase deficiency (SQORD) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SQOR gene ({617658}) on chromosome 15q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase-deficiency (SQORD) is characterized by a variable phenotype ranging from no clinical symptoms to episodes of encephalopathy and Leigh syndrome-like (see {256000}) brain lesions, with acute symptoms triggered by infections and fasting. Other features may include lactic acidosis and decreased mitochondrial respiratory chain complex IV activity in tissues. Most affected individuals are asymptomatic. Patients with encephalopathy may recover or die in childhood ({1:Friederich et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Friederich et al. (2020)} reported 2 sisters, born to consanguineous Lehrerleut Hutterite parents (family A), and an unrelated Turkish male (family B), born to consanguineous Turkish parents, with sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase deficiency and homozygous mutations in the SQOR gene. One sister (patient A.II-3) presented at age 4 years with an episode of fatigue and emesis, and rapid development of encephalopathy with tonic seizures. Laboratory studies showed lactic acidosis and an elevated anion gap. She developed respiratory distress and multiorgan failure, including liver failure. Brain MRI on the fourth day of hospitalization showed diffuse restriction of the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidi, as well as diffusion restriction in the posterior hippocampi, medial left temporal lobe, posterior inferior thalamus, and mamillary bodies. MR spectroscopy showed a large lactate peak and a depressed N-acetylaspartate peak. Muscle and liver biopsy showed normal histology. With supportive care, the multiorgan failure resolved, but she remained comatose and developed neurostorming episodes. She died shortly after discharge from the hospital. The other sister (patient A.III-2) developed migraine headaches 5 months prior to presentation at age 8 years with fever, nausea, and vomiting. She rapidly became comatose and apneic, requiring intubation. She had lactic acidosis and an anion gap. Brain MRI showed restricted diffusion of the left frontoparietal cortex and right frontal cortex. MR spectroscopy of the right basal ganglia revealed a large lactate peak, increased choline, and reduced N-acetylaspartate peak. She died 3 days later. The Turkish patient (patient B.II-3) presented at age 4 years with encephalopathy that developed after gastroenteritis, diarrhea, and 48 hours of fasting. He had mild hypoglycemia, elevated creatine phosphokinase, and elevated transaminases. MRI showed lesions of the splenium of the corpus callosum. He improved with supportive care; neurologic signs, including ptosis, strabismus, and ataxia, persisted for a few months. MRI lesions resolved after 4 months. He had another encephalopathic episode associated with fever, diarrhea, and fasting at age 5 years, with residual learning difficulties and unilateral hearing loss after recovery. He had a third encephalopathic episode at age 13 years after an episode of headache and anorexia. Brain MRI showed T-2 weighed hyperintense lesions of the caudate nuclei, putamina, and ventromedial thalami. After recovery, he had residual fatigue, learning difficulties, and memory and attention deficits. He had 2 asymptomatic sisters with the same homozygous SQOR mutation.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: In affected members of a Hutterite family with SQORD, {1:Friederich et al. (2020)} confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: In patients with SQORD who develop encephalopathy and Leigh syndrome-like brain lesions, {1:Friederich et al. (2020)} hypothesized that an effective therapeutic approach would be reduction in hydrogen sulfide production, including reduction of dietary cysteine intake and reduction of microbiome hydrogen sulfide production with antibiotics. They recommended avoidance of catabolic episodes by provision of adequate calories and avoidance of fasting. They suggested that administration of hydroxycobalamin via daily preventative dosing to bind hydrogen sulfide and administration of methylene blue be considered.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 Hutterite sibs, born of consanguineous parents (family A), with SQORD with encephalopathy and Leigh syndrome-like brain lesions, {1:Friederich et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous missense mutation (E213K; {617658.0001}) in the SQOR gene. The mutation segregated with the disorder in the family. In one of the sibs, SQOR enzyme function was reduced in liver and muscle tissue. The function of complex IV of the mitochondrial respiratory chain was reduced in muscle tissue, whereas the content and assembly of complex IV was normal, suggesting that hydrogen sulfide accumulation resulting from the deficiency led to disruption of complex IV function. In a Turkish boy with SQORD with encephalopathy and Leigh syndrome-like brain lesions, who was born of consanguineous parents (family B), {1:Friederich et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous 1-bp deletion in the SQOR gene ({617658.0002}). He had 2 asymptomatic sisters who were also homozygous for the mutation. The parents were mutation carriers. Western blot analysis of fibroblasts from the patient showed reduced SQOR protein content, and PBMCs and fibroblasts showed reduced SQOR enzyme activity. The mutations in both families were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

populationGenetics.title: Population Genetics
populationGenetics.content: {1:Friederich et al. (2020)} assessed the carrier rate of the SQOR E213K mutation ({617658.0001}) in 40 Hutterite individuals and identified a carrier frequency of 0.08 +/- 0.04, with an estimated affected incidence of SQORD of 1 in 711. {1:Friederich et al. (2020)} used predictive software to perform untargeted population analysis of SQOR mutations in the gnomAD database and estimated a carrier frequency of 0.0023 (1 in 215), resulting in an affected incidence of 1 in 184,477 for SQOR deficiency.

phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex II deficiency, nuclear type 4

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex II deficiency nuclear type 4 (MC2DN4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the succinate dehydrogenase complex subunit B gene (SDHB; {185470}) on chromosome 1p36.

description.title: Description
description.content: Mitochondrial complex II deficiency nuclear type 4 (MC2DN4) is a severe autosomal recessive disorder characterized by early-onset progressive neurodegeneration with leukoencephalopathy. Acute episodes of neurodegeneration are often triggered by catabolic stress such as infection or fasting.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Alston et al. (2012)} reported an Asian girl, born of consanguineous parents, with neurologic impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and biochemical evidence of mitochondrial complex II deficiency. The patient showed developmental regression beginning at age 1 year. She was hypotonic with joint contractures, and she became wheelchair-bound at age 4 years. Brain MRI showed leukodystrophy in the deep white matter and signal abnormalities in the corpus callosum. MR spectroscopy showed increased lactate and increased succinate in the dystrophic white matter.

{2:Ardissone et al. (2015)} reported a Pakistani girl who presented at 15 months of age with acute psychomotor depression that developed several days after a febrile illness. On evaluation one month later, she had general hypotonia, hyperreflexia, lack of postural control, and irritability. Laboratory studies showed elevated plasma lactate and pyruvate and elevated 2-ketoglutarate in the urine. Brain MRI showed diffuse hyperintensity of the hemispheric white matter and corpus callosum with sparing of the subcortical U-fibers, hyperintensities of the bilateral thalami, and cystic degeneration of the deep white matter. HNMR-spectroscopy revealed succinate and lactate peaks. Visual evoked potential testing showed central conduction abnormalities. Her healthy 11-year-old sib had the same homozygous mutation in the SDHB gene (D48V; {185470.0020}), leading {2:Ardissone et al. (2015)} to hypothesize that triggering stimuli may have been necessary to produce a clinical phenotype.

{7:Vanderver et al. (2016)} reported a Turkish boy (patient LD_0756.0A), born of consanguineous parents, who had motor delays from birth and acutely decompensated at 7 months of age. He had ataxia, hypotonia, and spasticity. Brain MRI at 3.5 years of age showed abnormal signal in the supratentorial white matter with sparing of the U-fibers, a swollen appearance of the corpus callosum, and involvement of the cerebellar white matter of the brainstem.

{5:Helman et al. (2016)} reported clinical and radiologic features in 5 patients, 4 of whom were living (patients 10, 11, 16 and 19) with an age range of 19 months to 9 years, and one of whom died at 1 year of age from respiratory failure (patient 15). Age of onset of symptoms ranged from birth to 18 months. In the 4 patients who had an MRI within the first 2 years of life, all had involvement of the corpus callosum and the thalamic nuclei, 3 had involvement of the middle cerebellar peduncles and pons, 3 had involvement of the spinal cord, 3 had involvement of the corticospinal tracts, and 2 had involvement of the cerebellar white matter. Patient 10 had spastic tetraparesis and normal cognition. Patient 11 had dilated cardiomyopathy with significant hypertrophy and poor function, gross motor impairment with contractures, and intact cognition. Patient 16 had spastic diplegia with severe motor difficulties and severe cognitive impairment. Patient 19 had generalized hypotonia, lack of postural control, irritability, and moderate cognitive impairment.

{4:Gronborg et al. (2017)} reported 2 unrelated patients with complex II deficiency. Patient 1, a Lebanese girl born to consanguineous parents, had slight developmental delay and hypotonia in the first year of life. She then had a progressive loss of developmental milestones starting at age 12 months, which was more pronounced during infections. At age 15 months, she had truncal hypotonia and increased muscle tone and increased reflexes in the limbs. She had slight bilateral optic atrophy, reduced vision, and horizontal nystagmus with opsoclonus. Brain MRI at age 16 months showed signal intensities in the frontal, parietooccipital, and posterior temporal white matter with sparing of the juxtacortical fibers. Laboratory studies showed an increased blood lactate and increased ketones and Krebs cycle intermediates (especially succinate) in the urine. She died at age 25 months of multiorgan failure in the setting of a respiratory infection. Patient 2, a boy born of nonconsanguineous parents, had intrauterine growth retardation, with decreased head circumference, length, and weight at birth. Starting at age 6 months, he had progressive loss of acquired skills, which was worse during infections. At age 9 months, he had pneumonia and respiratory failure necessitating assisted ventilation, and he had further loss of developmental skills. Laboratory studies showed increased blood lactate, increased ALAT and ASAT, increased creatine kinase, and increased INR. He had cardiomyopathy with severe dilatation and hypertrophy of the septum and posterior wall of the left ventricle. MRI at age 11 months showed signal intensities in the frontal, parietooccipital, and posterior temporal white matter with sparing of the juxtacortical fibers. He was stable with some improvement until 1 year of age when he died from multiorgan failure and cardiac arrest.

{6:Kaur et al. (2020)} reported an Indian boy who had regression of milestones at 1 year of age. He developed febrile seizures at age 18 months. On examination, he had increased tone in all limbs and brisk deep tendon reflexes. Ophthalmologic examination revealed bilateral optic atrophy. Brain MRI showed confluent lesions in the periventricular white matter, corpus callosum, dorsomedial thalami, brainstem, and spinal cord. Plasma and CSF lactate were elevated.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC2DN4 in the patients reported by {1:Alston et al. (2012)} and {2:Ardissone et al. (2015)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In an Asian girl, born of consanguineous parents, with neurologic impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and biochemical evidence of mitochondrial complex II deficiency, {1:Alston et al. (2012)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SDHB gene (D48V; {185470.0020}). Her unaffected parents were heterozygous for the mutation. Patient fibroblasts showed decreased amounts of fully assembled complex II and almost complete absence of the SDHB subunit. Complex II activity was also decreased in patient muscle samples.

In a Pakistani girl, born to consanguineous parents, with MC2DN4, {2:Ardissone et al. (2015)} identified homozygosity for the previously reported D48V mutation in the SDHB gene. The mutation was found by sequencing of a panel of 7 genes associated with complex II deficiency. A clinically unaffected sib was also homozygous for the mutation. SDHB protein expression was reduced in patient fibroblasts and lymphocytes as well as in lymphocytes from the clinically unaffected sib. SDHA protein was also reduced in these cells, possibly due to instability of complex II assembly.

In a Turkish boy, born of consanguineous parents, with MC2DN4, {7:Vanderver et al. (2016)} identified homozygosity for the D48V mutation in the SDHB gene.

In 6 patients with MC2DN4, {5:Helman et al. (2016)} identified mutations in the SDHB gene. Five patients had the D48V mutation, 4 (patients 10, 11, 16, and 19) in homozygous state and 1 (patient 15) in compound heterozygous state.

In 2 unrelated children with MC2DN4, {4:Gronborg et al. (2017)} identified mutations in the SDHB gene: a Lebanese girl, born of consanguineous parents, was homozygous for a missense mutation (L257V; {185470.0022}), and a boy, born of nonconsanguineous parents, was compound heterozygous for D48V and another missense mutation (R230H; {185470.0023}). In both patients, SDHB protein content was reduced in patient fibroblasts, muscle fibers showed diffuse and severe lack of SDH staining, and complex II enzyme activity was severely deficient in muscle. The parents of both children were confirmed to be mutation carriers. {4:Gronborg et al. (2017)} noted that the R230H mutation was previously reported in heterozygous state in patients with paraganglioma by several authors, including {3:Cerecer-Gil et al. (2010)}.

In a male infant with MC2DN4, who was born to nonconsanguineous Indian parents, {6:Kaur et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SDHB gene (A102T; {185470.0024}). The parents were heterozygous for the mutation. The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay with dysmorphic facies and dental anomalies

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay with dysmorphic facies and dental anomalies (DEFDA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SATB1 gene ({602075}) on chromosome 3p24.

Heterozygous mutation in the SATB1 gene can also cause a similar but more severe disorder (KTZSL; {619229}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay with dysmorphic facies and dental anomalies (DEFDA) is characterized by generally mild global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, walking by 2 to 3 years, and slow language acquisition. The severity of the disorder ranges from moderate cognitive deficits to mild learning difficulties or behavioral abnormalities. Most patients have dysmorphic facial features, often with abnormal dentition and nonspecific visual defects, such as myopia, astigmatism, and strabismus. Although rare, involvement of other systems, such as skeletal, cardiac, and gastrointestinal, may be present (summary by {1:den Hoed et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Den Hoed et al. (2021)} reported 12 patients (patients 1-12), including an affected father and daughter (patients 9 and 10), with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder associated with heterozygous premature truncating mutations or intragenic deletions in the SATB1 gene. The patients, who ranged in age from 2 to 41 years, were ascertained through international collaborative efforts. All patients had developmental delay manifest as delayed walking by age 2 or 3 years, variably impaired intellectual development, and/or speech delay. Cognitive impairment was mild to moderate, and many had learning difficulties or behavioral abnormalities. Patient 6 was a 25.5-year-old man with normal IQ scores (90-107), autism spectrum disorder, hyperactivity, and verbal regression. Other common features observed in about half of patients included hypotonia, visual abnormalities, dysmorphic facial features, and dental anomalies such as small, malpositioned, or widely-spaced teeth. Dysmorphic facial features included prominent forehead, telecanthus, facial asymmetry, bulbous nasal tip, deep short philtrum, prominent chin, snort philtrum, and prominent chin, although there was no distinct gestalt. Visual defects encompassed myopia, amblyopia, divergent squint, and strabismus. Less common features observed in some patients included skeletal or limb abnormalities (e.g., scoliosis or joint hypermobility), gastrointestinal problems (e.g., reflux, constipation, drooling, or dysphagia), hearing abnormalities, cardiac anomalies, ataxia, and sleep disturbances.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SATB1 gene that were identified in most patients with DEFDA by {1:den Hoed et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. However, in some families, the transmission pattern was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 12 patients (patients 1-12), including an affected father and daughter (patients 9 and 10), with DEFDA, {1:den Hoed et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous mutations in the SATB1 gene (see, e.g., R410X, {602075.0001} and Q694X, {602075.0003}). The mutations included 2 intragenic deletions, 6 frameshifts, 2 nonsense mutations, and 1 splice site mutation. These findings suggested haploinsufficiency as a mechanism; however, some of the mutations were demonstrated to escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Most of the mutations occurred de novo, although some patients inherited the mutations from a mildly affected or unaffected parent, indicating autosomal dominant transmission with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. In vitro studies of some of the mutations showed that they caused altered subcellular localization, forming abnormal nuclear puncta or nuclear aggregates. In vitro luciferase reporter assays revealed that whereas R410X and Q694X caused reduced SATB1 transcriptional repressive activity of some substrates compared to wildtype, the c.1877delC frameshift mutation caused increased repressive activity and the c.2207delA frameshift mutation had no change on transcriptional activity. The authors noted that there may be additional disease mechanisms besides haploinsufficiency at play, particularly for those mutations that escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: Among 41 patients with neurodevelopmental disorders associated with heterozygous mutations in the SATB1 gene, {1:den Hoed et al. (2021)} were able to delineate 2 main phenotypes. Patients with mutations predicted to result in a loss of function and haploinsufficiency or premature termination variants that escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay had a milder phenotype compared to patients with heterozygous missense mutations, particularly those affecting functional domains. In vitro functional studies indicated that the loss-of-function or premature termination mutations mislocalized in the cell nucleus and had variable effects on SATB1 transcriptional activity. In contrast, studies of some of the missense variants showed that they caused stronger chromatin binding and increased transcriptional repression compared to wildtype and to the loss-of-function mutations. Although functional effects were not studied for all variants, these findings suggested that different pathophysiologic mechanisms likely underlie the phenotypic variability observed among patients with mutations in the same gene.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that den Hoed-de Boer-Voisin syndrome (DHDBV) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SATB1 gene ({602075}) on chromosome 3p24.

Heterozygous mutation in the SATB1 gene can also cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with overlapping but less severe features (DEFDA; {619228}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Den Hoed-de Boer-Voisin syndrome (DHDBV) is characterized by global developmental delay with moderately to severely impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, and delayed motor skills. Although the severity of the disorder varies, many patients are nonverbal and have hypotonia with inability to sit or walk. Early-onset epilepsy is common and may be refractory to treatment, leading to epileptic encephalopathy and further interruption of developmental progress. Most patients have feeding difficulties with poor overall growth and dysmorphic facial features, as well as significant dental anomalies resembling amelogenesis imperfecta. The phenotype is reminiscent of Kohlschutter-Tonz syndrome (KTZS; {226750}). More variable features of DHDBV include visual defects, behavioral abnormalities, and nonspecific involvement of other organ systems (summary by {1:den Hoed et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Den Hoed et al. (2021)} reported 29 patients (patients 13 to 41), including 9 patients from 3 families, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder associated with heterozygous missense mutations in the SATB1 gene. The patients, who ranged in age from infancy to mid-adulthood, were ascertained through collaborative international efforts. They had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, delayed walking, and poor speech and language acquisition. Although clinical details were lacking for some, many patients were noted to be nonverbal with profoundly impaired intellectual development and inability to sit or stand. Twenty patients had various types of seizure disorders, about half of which occurred in the first months or years of life and were refractory to medication, consistent with epileptic encephalopathy. Seizure types included absence, generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, tonic, focal, and complex partial; status epilepticus was observed in some patients. EEG studies showed abnormalities, including hypsarrhythmia in a few patients. Brain imaging was normal in many patients, but showed nonspecific abnormalities in others, such as enlarged ventricles and cortical atrophy. Other common features included hypotonia, spasticity, gastrointestinal abnormalities, drooling, dysphagia, poor growth with short stature and microcephaly, sleep disturbances, and visual defects, such as hypermetropia, astigmatism, and visual impairment. Variable involvement of other systems, such as cardiac, skeletal, urogenital, endocrine, and immune, were present in less than half of patients. Most patients had significant dysmorphic facial features, including brachycephaly, prominent forehead, hypertelorism, low nasal bridge, short nose, posteriorly rotated ears, long smooth philtrum, long palpebral fissures, full straight eyebrows, thick lips, and anteverted nostrils. Almost all had dental anomalies, including delayed tooth eruption, yellow teeth, oligodontia, widely spaced teeth, enamel hypoplasia, and amelogenesis imperfecta. Several patients were suggested to have Kohlschutter-Tonz syndrome; 2 sibs (patients 27 and 28) had originally been reported by {2:Donnai et al. (2005)} as having clinical features compatible with KTZS. Four patients died prematurely of various causes.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SATB1 gene that were identified in most patients with DHDBV by {1:den Hoed et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. However, in some families, the transmission pattern was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 28 patients (patients 13 to 40), including 9 patients from 3 families, with DHDBV, {1:den Hoed et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous missense variants in the SATB1 gene (see, e.g., {602075.0003}-{602075.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. The patients were ascertained through collaborative international efforts. Most mutations occurred de novo, although some were inherited from mildly affected parents or through parental mosaicism. In vitro functional expression studies showed that the mutant missense proteins displayed a cage-like clustered nuclear pattern, strongly colocalizing with DNA, and caused increased transcriptional repression of the interleukin-2 (IL2; {147680}) promoter, consistent with stronger binding of the mutant SATB1 transcription factor to its target.

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: Among 40 patients with neurodevelopmental disorders associated with heterozygous mutations in the SATB1 gene, {1:den Hoed et al. (2021)} were able to delineate 2 main phenotypes. Patients with variants predicted to result in a loss of function and haploinsufficiency or premature termination protein variants that escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay had a milder phenotype compared to patients with heterozygous missense mutations, particularly those affecting functional domains. In vitro functional studies indicated that the loss-of-function or premature termination mutations mislocalized in the cell nucleus and had variable effects on SATB1 transcriptional activity. In contrast, studies of some of the missense variants showed that they caused stronger chromatin binding and increased transcriptional repression compared to wildtype and to the loss-of-function mutations. Although functional effects were not studied for all variants, these findings suggested that different pathophysiologic mechanisms likely underlie the phenotypic variability observed among patients with mutations in the same gene.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without autism or seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with or without autism or seizures (NEDAUS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CUL3 gene ({603136}) on chromosome 2q36.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without autism or seizures (NEDAUS) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent in infancy, impaired intellectual development, and speech delay. Some patients develop seizures, and may show regression after onset of seizures. Others have autistic features or behavioral abnormalities. Additional variable systemic features may also be present, such as cardiac defects, failure to thrive, or brain imaging anomalies (summary by {5:Nakashima et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{6:Thiffault et al. (2018)} reported a 3-year-old boy (family 2) with failure to thrive, microcephaly, speech delay, and absent thumb associated with a de novo mutation in the CUL3 gene. He was ascertained from a large cohort of patients with neurodevelopmental disorders who underwent next-generation sequencing and were found to have de novo variants in various genes. Clinical details were limited.

{1:Da Silva Montenegro et al. (2020)} reported a 12-year-old Brazilian girl (F1389-1) with NEDAUS. She had mild motor delay, speech delay, and autism spectrum disorder. She did not have seizures.

{5:Nakashima et al. (2020)} reported 3 unrelated children, ranging from 3 to 10 years of age, with a neurodevelopmental disorder. Two patients (patients 1 and 2), of Japanese and Malaysian origin, respectively, were ascertained from a large cohort of 1,230 individuals with early childhood-onset epilepsy who underwent whole-exome sequencing. Patient 3 was identified through the GeneMatcher program. Patients 1 and 2 had onset of intractable spasms and seizures at 2 and 6 months of age, respectively. EEG in patient 1 showed a suppression-burst pattern, whereas EEG in patient 2 showed hypsarrhythmia, both consistent with a clinical diagnosis of West syndrome. They had delayed motor development and severe intellectual disability with speech delay. Patient 2 had hyperactivity; patient 1 had an atrial septal defect and pulmonary valve stenosis. Patient 3 had poor feeding and mildly delayed psychomotor development with speech delay. Brain imaging showed delayed subcortical myelination. She did not have facial dysmorphism, but did have submucosal palatoschisis and bifid uvula. None of the patients was noted to have autism.

{3:Iwafuchi et al. (2021)} reported a 4-year-old Japanese girl with poor overall growth who presented at age 21 months with status epilepticus after normal early development. After seizure onset, she showed developmental regression with loss of speech and loss of eye contact. She later developed behavioral abnormalities consistent with autism spectrum disorder and reminiscent of Rett syndrome (RTT; {312750}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CUL3 gene that were identified in patients with NEDAUS by {5:Nakashima et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 3-year-old boy (family 2) with NEDAUS, {6:Thiffault et al. (2018)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the CUL3 gene (Y58C; {603136.0008}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based next-generation sequencing, was considered to be pathogenic after curation using a point-based system. Functional studies of the variant were not performed. The authors noted that several large studies had identified de novo mutations in the CUL3 gene in patients with variable neurodevelopmental disorders. For example, {4:Kong et al. (2012)} identified a de novo heterozygous loss-of-function R546X variant in 1 of 44 Icelandic individuals with autism spectrum disorder.

In a 12-year-old Brazilian girl (F1389-1) with NEDAUS, {1:da Silva Montenegro et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous nonsense mutation in the CUL3 gene (S133X; {603136.0009}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was classified as pathogenic according to ACMG criteria.

In 3 unrelated children with NEDAUS, {5:Nakashima et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the CUL3 gene ({603136.0010}-{603136.0012}). There were 2 frameshift mutations and 1 missense mutation. The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the dbSNP (build 153) or gnomAD databases. All were predicted or demonstrated to result in a loss of function and haploinsufficiency. Two patients were ascertained from a cohort of 1,230 individuals with childhood-onset epilepsy who underwent whole-exome sequencing; the third patient was identified through the GeneMatcher program.

In a 4-year-old Japanese girl with NEDAUS, {3:Iwafuchi et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation in the CUL3 gene ({603136.0013}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. The mutation was predicted to lead to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and haploinsufficiency. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Dong et al. (2020)} found that mice with homozygous deletion of Cul3 had reduced body size and brain weight compared with wildtype, and died prematurely. Mice heterozygous for Cul3 deletion (Cul3-deficient mice) had more than 40% reduced levels of Cul3, but were viable and fertile, survived as long as wildtype, and did not show deficits observed in mice with homozygous Cul3 deletion. Cul3-deficient mice exhibited social behavioral deficits and anxiety-like behaviors. Hippocampus of Cul3-deficient mice had increased spine density, neuronal excitability, and synaptic transmission and disrupted excitation-inhibition (E-I) balance in CA1 neurons. Similar deficits were observed in pyramidal neurons with Cul3 deficiency, demonstrating a cell-autonomous role of Cul3 for synaptic function, E-I balance, and behavior. Proteomic analysis identified Eif4g1 ({600495}) as a target of Cul3-dependent ubiquitination. Consequently, Cul3 deficiency increased Eif4g1 level and upregulated Cap-dependent protein synthesis in brain. Inhibition of Cap-dependent translation diminished synaptic and social deficits in Cul3-deficient mice, but it had little effect on anxiety-like behaviors. However, chemogenetic inhibition of pyramidal neuron activity in hippocampus attenuated anxiety-like behavior in mutant mice.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with cerebral atrophy and variable facial dysmorphism

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with cerebral atrophy and variable facial dysmorphism (NEDCAFD) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TTC5 gene ({619014}) on chromosome 14q11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with cerebral atrophy and facial dysmorphism (NEDCAFD) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent from birth. Affected individuals have hypotonia with inability to walk and severely impaired intellectual development with absent language. Most patients have variable dysmorphic facial features including prominent eyes, protruding and low-set ears, and thin upper lip. Brain imaging shows cerebral atrophy, corpus callosum hypoplasia, and a simplified gyral pattern (summary by {2:Rasheed et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Hu et al. (2019)} reported 3 children, ranging from 19 months to 7 years of age, from 2 unrelated consanguineous families of Turkish and Iranian origin with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients had severe global developmental delay with hypotonia, inability to walk or even sit in some cases, and severely impaired intellectual development with absent language. IQ in 1 patient was 30. All also had microcephaly (-3 SD), but consistent dysmorphic facial features were not present. None had seizures. Brain imaging in 1 patient showed agenesis of the corpus callosum, mild ventriculomegaly, bifrontoparietal atrophy, and a mild leukodystrophic pattern.

{2:Rasheed et al. (2021)} reported 8 unrelated patients, ranging from 3 to 12 years of age, from 5 different consanguineous families with NEDCAFD. The patients, who ranged from 3 to 12 years of age, had severe global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and absent language. Most had hypotonia and were unable to sit or stand; about half had microcephaly. Common dysmorphic features included wide forehead, long face, flared or arched eyebrows, pointed chin, low-set ears, long or short philtrum, prominent nose, thin or V-shaped upper lip, and high-arched palate. Rare additional features included dry skin, hirsutism, curly or woolly hair, undescended testes, sleep disturbances, and widely-spaced nipples. One patient had seizures. Brain imaging showed cerebral atrophy with enlarged ventricles, atrophy of the corpus callosum, and simplified gyral pattern.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDCAFD in the families reported by {2:Rasheed et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 children from 2 unrelated families with NEDCAFD, {1:Hu et al. (2019)} identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the TTC5 gene ({619014.0001}-{619014.0002}). The variants were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The patients were part of a large cohort of 404 consanguineous Middle Eastern families in which 2 or more offspring had impaired intellectual development. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 8 patients from 5 unrelated consanguineous families with NEDCAFD, {2:Rasheed et al. (2021)} identified homozygous mutations in the TTC5 gene ({619014.0003}-{619004.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. There were 2 nonsense mutations and 2 missense mutations. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but they were predicted to disrupt TTC5 function, consistent with a loss of function.

clinicalSynopsis: Six girls from 2 unrelated consanguineous families have been reported (last curated March 2021)
Caused by mutation in the coatomer protein complex, subunit beta 1 gene (COPB1,)

Head: Microcephaly (in some patients, range -0.2 to -7.9)
Miscellaneous: Six girls from 2 unrelated consanguineous families have been reported (last curated March 2021)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the coatomer protein complex, subunit beta 1 gene (COPB1,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Baralle-Macken syndrome (BARMACS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the COPB1 gene ({600959}) on chromosome 11p15.

description.title: Description
description.content: Baralle-Macken syndrome (BARMACS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy, difficulty walking or inability to walk, and impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech. Affected individuals develop early-onset cataracts; some may have microcephaly. Additional more variable features may include dysmorphic facial features, metabolic abnormalities, spasticity, and lymphopenia (summary by {1:Macken et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Macken et al. (2021)} reported 6 girls, ranging in age from 11 to 18 years, from 2 unrelated consanguineous families of Roma Polish (family 1) and Saudi (family 2) origin who had a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients presented in infancy with hypotonia and global developmental delay manifest as delayed walking with an unsteady gait (family 1) or inability to walk (family 2). They also had severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech; 1 child was deaf due to a mutation in the GJB2 gene ({121011}). The sisters in family 1 developed cataracts at 13 and 7 years of age, whereas the patients in family 2 had earlier onset of cataracts. Despite these phenotypic similarities, each family had additional unique features. The sisters in family 1 had metabolic abnormalities with insulin resistance, axillary acanthosis, increased BMI, facial hirsutism, skin striae, and early menarche. These sisters also had dysmorphic features, including upslanting palpebral fissures, high narrow palate, tapering fingers, kyphosis, and foot deformities. One had focal seizures that could be controlled. Family history revealed that 3 cousins of the patients in family 1 had microcephaly and developmental delay and died in early childhood. The patients in family 2 were wheelchair-bound with spasticity and dystonia. In addition, they had an immunodeficiency with T-cell lymphopenia and impaired antibody response to stimulation. Dysmorphic features were not noted.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of BARMACS in the families reported by {1:Macken et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 girls from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with BARMACS, {1:Macken et al. (2021)} identified 2 different homozygous mutations in the COPB1 gene, a splice site mutation ({600959.0001}) and a missense mutation (F551V; {600959.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Neither was present in the gnomAD database. Transfection of the missense mutation in HEK293 cells resulted in a mild decrease in mutant protein levels, suggesting instability. Transfection of the missense mutation into retinal RPE cells showed diffuse localization of the mutant protein compared to wildtype, which was seen in a defined pattern at the Golgi. The authors concluded that these findings represent defective Golgi to ER endosomal recycling, with mutant beta-COP being abnormally retained in the Golgi; they postulated a hypomorphic effect of the variants.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Macken et al. (2021)} found that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of the copb1 gene in X. tropicalis caused microcephaly, cataracts, and occasional anophthalmia in mutant animals. Some animals showed mild forebrain abnormalities.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and variable seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and variable seizures (NEDDFAS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the EMC10 gene ({614545}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and variable seizures (NEDDFAS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent in early childhood. Patients have mildly impaired intellectual development, often with speech delay or behavioral abnormalities. Some may have seizures. Most have nonspecific dysmorphic facial features. Additional findings may include brain imaging abnormalities, mild skeletal defects, and renal abnormalities, although the renal anomalies may be unrelated (summary by {2:Shao et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Umair et al. (2020)} reported a brother and sister, born of consanguineous Saudi Arab parents, with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who were 14 and 11 years old, respectively, presented in early childhood with global developmental delay manifest mainly as speech delay. They later developed anxiety with poor sleep and onset of repetitive stereotypic movements and tics, such as blinking, nystagmus, and head nodding. They both attended special schools, but showed deficits in mathematics and memory. IQ was measured at 69 and 76, respectively. One sib had isolated febrile seizures at 3.5 years. They had normal growth parameters with subtle dysmorphic features, including triangular face, frontal bossing, synophrys, crowded teeth, and mild hirsutism. Brain imaging was normal.

{2:Shao et al. (2021)} reported 13 patients from 7 unrelated consanguineous families of Middle Eastern descent with NEDDFAS. The patients were ascertained from various centers through the GeneMatcher Program. Twelve patients were between 5 and 27 years of age; the remaining patient was 3 months old. All had global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and often abnormal behavior with poor social skills. Six patients had variable types of seizures. Brain imaging was abnormal in most patients, although there were different findings, such as thin corpus callosum, cerebellar tonsillar ectopia, Chiari I malformation, delayed myelination, enlarged ventricles, and gray matter heterotopia. Four patients presented with fetal polyhydramnios, and 2 of those had infantile polyuria. Four had medullary nephrocalcinosis, 3 had renal cysts, 2 had hydronephrosis, and a 22-year-old was noted to have end-stage renal disease requiring kidney transplantation. More variable features, observed in about half of patients, included failure to thrive, cubitus valgus, hernia, and arachnodactyly. Dysmorphic facial features were common, although there was no clear pattern. These included long face, pointed chin, and curly hair. Neurologic symptoms appeared to be static or nonprogressive.

{1:Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022)} reported 10 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families with NEDDFAS. The average age of the patients was 9.5 years. All 10 patients had global developmental delay or impaired intellectual development ranging from mild to severe, and 5 patients had microcephaly. Other neurologic findings included axial hypotonia (4/10), peripheral hypotonia (5/10), truncal ataxia (3/10), dysarthria (7/10), and hyperkinetic movements (4/10). Two patients had congenital heart disease. One sib pair had elevated parathyroid hormone levels. The most common facial dysmorphisms included long face, broad chin, synophrys, broad nasal tip, and thick lower lip vermilion.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDDFAS in the families reported by {3:Umair et al. (2020)} and {2:Shao et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Arab parents, with NEDDFAS, {3:Umair et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the EMC10 gene ({614545.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. RT-PCR analysis of patient cells showed decreased EMC10 mRNA levels compared to controls.

In 12 patients from 7 unrelated consanguineous families of Middle Eastern descent with NEDDFAS, {2:Shao et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the EMA10 gene ({614545.0002}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing at various centers, was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregated with the disorder in the families. It was not present in the homozygous state in public databases. Haplotype analysis identified 2 distinct haplotypes among the families, suggesting that the mutation occurred in a hotspot; the deletion was within a homopolymeric repeat sequence that predisposes to DNA replication errors. Studies of cells derived from some patients showed reduced but not absent EMC10 expression, suggesting that the mutation results in an unstable protein. The mutation resulted in a putative truncated protein of 103 amino acids in length and was predicted to abolish the C-terminal region that interacts with core EMC proteins. In vitro functional expression studies in HeLa cells transfected with the mutation showed that the mutant protein was unstable due to proteasomal degradation. {2:Shao et al. (2021)} concluded that the mutation resulted in a loss of EMC10 function, which may have detrimental effects on transmembrane protein dynamics in various cell types.

{1:Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022)} identified homozygous mutations in the EMC10 gene in 10 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families. Five of the mutations were novel ({614545.0003}-{614545.0007}) and one was previously identified ({614545.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. The mutations were either absent or present at a rare allelic frequency in multiple public and private variant databases.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Shao et al. (2021)} noted that Emc10-null mice exhibit neurologic and behavioral abnormalities, including abnormal vocalization, gait, activity, and anxiety-related mannerisms as well as defects in cognitive processes, such as memory and learning.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 37 (MC1DN37) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NDUFA8 gene ({603359}) on chromosome 9q33.

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex I deficiency, see {252010}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Yatsuka et al. (2020)} reported a 26-year-old Japanese man who was born full-term with a low birthweight. In infancy, he had poor weight gain, increased muscle tone, opisthotonos, and developmental delay. At age 2 years, he had severe growth retardation, developmental delay, and hypertonia with rigidity and spasticity. Laboratory studies showed elevated plasma, urine, and CSF lactate. Brain MRI at age 1 year showed cerebral atrophy and enlarged ventricles. Brain MRI at age 19 years showed cerebellar atrophy, thinning of the corpus callosum, and progression of cerebral atrophy. At age 26, the patient had quadriplegia, failure to thrive, hypertonia, short stature, microcephaly, psychomotor retardation, and epilepsy.

{1:Tort et al. (2020)} reported a sister and brother, born to consanguineous Spanish Gypsy parents. The sister (patient 1) had hypotonia, respiratory distress, cyanosis, and lactic acidosis after birth. Laboratory studies showed elevated plasma alanine, lactate, and pyruvate. An echocardiogram showed mild hypertrophy of the left ventricle and slight pulmonary hypertension. Brain MRI showed hyperintensity in the parietal white matter. During the first year of life, she had hypertonia, a slight motor delay, and failure to thrive. Muscle biopsy showed disproportion of fibers, increased citrate synthase activity, severe decrease in complex I activity, and mild reductions in complex II and complex III activities. At age 13 months she had status epilepticus and a stroke-like episode. MRI showed multiple acute infarcts in the temporooccipital regions, the left pallidum, and the left caudate nucleus. At age 9 years, the lactic acidosis normalized and she had no further seizures. She had some muscle hypotrophy, normal motor skills, and delayed speech. Her brother (patient 2) was asymptomatic until age 4 years when he presented with bradycardia, hypotension, and severe pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular dilation after anesthesia induction for hypospadias surgery. Brain MRI revealed mild bilateral cortical atrophy. On follow-up at age 6 years, he had slight failure to thrive and mild speech delay.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: {2:Yatsuka et al. (2020)} and {1:Tort et al. (2020)} confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance of MC1DN37.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 26-year-old Japanese patient with MC1DN37, {2:Yatsuka et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous mutation in the NDUFA8 gene (R47C; {603359.0001}). The mutation, which was identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was present in heterozygous state in the parents. NDUFA8 protein expression, expression of mitochondrial supercomplexes, basal oxygen consumption rate, ATP production, and complex I activity were decreased in patient fibroblasts. Complementation with a lentivirus containing wildtype NDUFA8 rescued these defects in patient fibroblasts.

In 2 sibs, born to consanguineous Spanish Gypsy parents, with MC1DN37, {1:Tort et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the NDUFA8 gene (R98L; {603359.0002}). The mutation, which was identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. NDUFA8 protein expression and complex I steady state expression, enzyme activity, and assembly were reduced in fibroblasts from both sibs. Mitochondrial morphology was also abnormal in fibroblasts from both sibs. Lentiviral transduction of patient fibroblasts with wildtype NDUFA8 rescued the complex I enzyme activity defect.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that CIMDAG syndrome (CIMDAG) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the VPS4A gene ({609982}) on chromosome 16q22. One patient with a homozygous VPS4A variant has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content: CIMDAG syndrome (CIMDAG) is a multisystemic disorder characterized by severely impaired psychomotor development and hematologic abnormalities apparent from early infancy. Affected individuals show poor overall growth with microcephaly, impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, poor eye contact, and motor problems, such as inability to walk, hypotonia, and spasticity. Brain imaging typically shows cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and delayed myelination. The associated hematologic abnormalities are variable, but are mostly consistent with congenital dyserythropoietic anemia (CDA) (summary by {3:Rodger et al., 2020} and {4:Seu et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Hamdan et al. (2014)} reported a 4.5-year-old boy (individual 985.382) with severely impaired intellectual development, acquired microcephaly, central hypotonia, and spasticity. No congenital or cardiac malformations or urogenital abnormalities were present. He did not have epilepsy. Brain imaging showed atrophy, ventriculomegaly, decreased white matter, and thin corpus callosum.

{3:Rodger et al. (2020)} reported 6 unrelated Caucasian patients, ranging from 2 to 29 years of age, with a neurodevelopmental disorder that they named CIMDAG (cerebellar hypoplasia, cataracts, impaired intellectual development, congenital microcephaly, dystonia, dyserythropoietic anemia, and growth retardation). The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher database or other repositories linked to diagnostic genetic testing. Two patients had died at 26 months and 29 years of age. The patients had severe global developmental delay with profound intellectual disability, poor or absent speech, limited eye contact and fixation, and inability to walk. Additional motor abnormalities included hypotonia, spasticity, ataxia, dysmetria, dystonia, and chorea. They had feeding difficulties with poor overall growth and microcephaly (down to -6.8 SD); some patients were tube-fed. Four patients had congenital cataracts, 3 had retinal dystrophy, and 2 had sensorineural deafness. Three patients had seizures. More variable features included hepatosplenomegaly, sleep disturbances, scoliosis, hip dysplasia, and foot deformities. Dysmorphic facial features included long palpebral fissures, long smooth philtrum, broad eyebrows, large ears, long oval face, retrognathia, open mouth, protruding tongue, and gingival hypertrophy. Three patients had hematologic abnormalities, including congenital dyserythropoietic anemia. Brain imaging showed thin corpus callosum, cerebellar or pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and cerebral atrophy; 1 patient had polymicrogyria.

{4:Seu et al. (2020)} reported 3 unrelated children with CIMDAG who were identified through a North American registry for congenital dyserythropoietic anemia. In patients 1 and 2, 6 and 5 years of age, respectively, laboratory analysis and bone marrow studies showed macrocytic hemolytic anemia with reticulocytosis, binucleated erythroblasts, and accelerated iron overload, consistent with ineffective erythropoiesis. Both patients were transfusion-dependent. In addition, both patients had severe global developmental delay with poor overall growth, microcephaly, axial hypotonia, appendicular hypertonia, dystonia, cortical blindness (patient 1), and cataracts (patient 2). One had a seizure disorder. Brain imaging showed delayed myelination, decreased periventricular white matter, global cerebral volume loss, thin corpus callosum, and pontocerebellar atrophy. Patient 3 was a 3-year-old girl, born of consanguineous Arab parents, with a milder hematologic phenotype and anemia requiring fewer transfusions compared to patients 1 and 2. Her laboratory studies and bone marrow analysis indicated ineffective erythropoiesis. Similar to the first 2 patients, she had severe global developmental delay with axial hypotonia and appendicular hypertonia. Brain imaging showed delayed myelination, enlarged ventricles, and thin corpus callosum. Macrocephaly was noted in this child.

{2:Lunati et al. (2021)} reported a 3-year-old boy with CIMDAG. He presented at birth with hemolytic anemia requiring transfusion. Laboratory studies showed increased serum ferritin (see {134790}) and reticulocytes. Myelogram showed erythroblast hyperplasia with only a few features of dyserythropoiesis. He had global developmental delay with axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, choreodystonic movements, facial dyskinesia, microcephaly, and no ocular pursuit. Other features included early-onset cataracts and retinal dysfunction suggestive of Leber congenital amaurosis. Brain imaging showed cerebral atrophy, thin dysplastic corpus callosum, basal ganglia atrophy, and brainstem and cerebellar hypoplasia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The heterozygous mutations in the VPS4A gene that were identified in patients with CIMDAG by {3:Rodger et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

Two of the patients with CIMDAG reported by {4:Seu et al. (2020)} had de novo heterozygous VPS4A mutations. A third patient, born of consanguineous parents, had a homozygous VPS4A variant; the segregation pattern in the latter family was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 4.5-year-old boy (individual 985.382) with severely impaired intellectual development, {1:Hamdan et al. (2014)} identified a possibly pathogenic de novo heterozygous mutation in the VPS4A gene (c.577_597delTCC, NM_013245.2; Ser193del).

In 6 unrelated patients with CIMDAG, {3:Rodger et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the VPS4A gene ({609982.0001}-{609982.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome trio-based sequencing, were not present in public databases, including gnomAD. All affected highly conserved residues in the ATPase domain; 5 mutations occurred at the R284 residue, suggesting a mutational hotspot. Patient fibroblasts showed normal VPS4A protein levels. Expression of the mutations in HeLa cells caused the development of vacuolar endosomal structures. Patient fibroblasts showed similar, but less severe, abnormalities, and loss of VPS4A in human neurons had a similar effect. The authors concluded that the mutations exerted a dominant-negative effect on VPS4A hexamer function. Although localization of the core ESCRT-III complex at endosomes was not significantly affected, there was aberrant accumulation of the atypical protein IST1 ({616434}) on endosomal membranes, suggesting altered endosome dynamics. Detailed analysis of patient fibroblasts showed abnormal morphology of the nuclear envelope, as well as increased DNA damage attributed to the breaking of the nuclear envelope. There was also some evidence of abnormal cilia formation, suggesting that VPS4A is involved in a variety of diverse cellular processes. The authors postulated that the pleiotropic clinical manifestations of CIMDAG reflect the multitude of cellular functions of VPS4A.

In 2 unrelated patients (patients 1 and 2) with CIMDAG, {4:Seu et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the VPS4A gene ({609982.0001}, {609982.0004}). In addition, {4:Seu et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the VPS4A gene (A28V; {609982.0005}) in a 3-year-old girl (patient 3), born of consanguineous Arab parents, with CIMDAG. Her parents, who were heterozygous for the mutation, were unaffected. Peripheral red blood cells derived from all 3 patients showed abnormal expression of CD71 (TFRC; {190010}), the transferrin receptor, indicating impaired maturation of reticulocytes and suggesting defective endosomal sorting and trafficking of CD71. However, the hematologic disorder in the patient with the homozygous mutation was not as severe as that observed in patients with heterozygous mutations. {4:Seu et al. (2020)} suggested that tissue-specific expression of VPS4A may explain the predominance of neurologic and erythroid lineage manifestations of the syndrome.

In a boy with CIMDAG, {2:Lunati et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygosity for the previously identified R284W mutation in the VPS4A gene ({609982.0001}). Functional studies were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that microcephaly, epilepsy, and diabetes syndrome-2 (MEDS2) is caused by homozygous mutation in the YIPF5 gene ({611483}) on chromosome 5q31.

description.title: Description
description.content:
MEDS2 is characterized by severe microcephaly and neonatal/early-onset epilepsy and diabetes ({1:De Franco et al., 2020}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of microcephaly, epilepsy, and diabetes syndrome, see MEDS1 ({614231}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:De Franco et al. (2020)} reported 6 patients from 5 consanguineous families who had microcephaly, epilepsy, and diabetes syndrome (MEDS). All had severe microcephaly, with a median standard deviation of -6.2; epilepsy diagnosed at ages ranging from 1 to 7 months; and neonatal/early-onset diabetes, with age at diagnosis ranging from 4 weeks to 20 months, that was treated with a full replacement dose of insulin. For all 6 patients, birth weight was low, consistent with reduced insulin secretion in utero. The proband from family II died at the age of 1.3 years, and he had 2 sisters and 2 brothers who were also diagnosed with MEDS and died in infancy. Severe developmental delay was reported in 5 patients, whereas neuromotor development was reported to be normal in the 5-year-old proband from family I, who also had resolution of his epilepsy at age 2 years. There was no significant family history of diabetes for any of the patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MEDS2 in the families reported by {1:De Franco et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated boys with severe microcephaly, epilepsy, and neonatal/early-onset diabetes, who were negative for mutation in known neonatal diabetes genes, {1:De Franco et al. (2020)} performed genome sequencing and identified homozygosity for mutations in the YIPF5 gene: patient I, a 5-year-old boy from Turkey, was homozygous for a missense mutation (A181V; {611483.0001}), and patient II, an Indian boy who died at age 1.3 years, was homozygous for an in-frame deletion (K106del; {611483.0002}). The authors then analyzed the YIPF5 gene in a cohort of 187 patients diagnosed with diabetes before the age of 12 months who were negative for mutation in known monogenic diabetes genes, and identified 3 more probands who were homozygous for missense mutations (I98S, {611483.0003}; W218R, {611483.0004}; and G97V, {611483.0005}). The unaffected consanguineous parents in all families were heterozygous for the mutations, none of which were found in the gnomAD database.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with spasticity, cataracts, and cerebellar hypoplasia

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with spasticity, cataracts, and cerebellar atrophy (NEDSCAC) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the MED27 gene ({605044}) on chromosome 9q34.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with spasticity, cataracts, and cerebellar atrophy (NEDSCAC) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay, variably impaired intellectual development, and significant movement abnormalities. More severely affected individuals are nonverbal and do not achieve independent ambulation, whereas others develop some speech and can walk, or show regression later in childhood. Patients have notable motor features, including axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, dystonia, and dyskinesia affecting the limbs and orofacial muscles. Almost all have congenital cataracts, and about half have seizures. Brain imaging usually shows cerebellar atrophy with variable additional abnormalities, such as thin corpus callosum, cerebral atrophy, and hypomyelination. Most patients have either a progressive disease course or regression of acquired skills, suggesting both a neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative aspect to the disorder ({2:Meng et al., 2021}; {1:Maroofian et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Meng et al. (2021)} reported 16 patients from 11 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program, were of various ethnic origins, including Algerian, Turkish, Pakistani, Kuwaiti, Hispanic, Finnish, and European. There were 13 pediatric patients, ranging from 10 months to 13 years of age, and 3 adults ranging from 26 to 42 years of age. Two sibs from family 3 died in childhood, and 1 affected sib in family 10 died in infancy; this latter patient also had a homozygous mutation in the COG6 gene ({606977}) and was excluded from the overall clinical analysis. All patients had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech. Eight severely affected individuals were unable to sit or walk and were nonverbal. Five patients were moderately delayed, but achieved ambulation, sometimes with an unsteady gait, and some expressive language. Two sibs (family 6) were reported to have normal development until 8 or 9 years of age, when both showed progressive walking difficulties, speech articulation problems, and declining school performance. These sibs had progressive neurologic decline and showed moderate intellectual disability in the late teenage years. A few other patients also showed neurologic regression in late childhood. Other common features included hypotonia, appendicular spasticity, dystonia, dysarthria, tongue fasciculations, drooling, and feeding difficulties; 1 patient had a feeding tube. Nine (60%) of 15 patients had onset of variable types of seizures in the first months or years of life. Seizure types included infantile spasms, focal, generalized tonic-clonic, hemifacial clonic, myoclonic, and absence. About half of patients had drug-responsive seizures, whereas seizures were refractory in other patients. Cataracts were found in 10 (67%) of 15 patients, and 4 had microcephaly. Some had variable dysmorphic facial features, although there was no recognizable facial gestalt. Features included large ears, frontal bossing, prominent eyebrows, long eyelashes, upturned nose, flat, broad nose, and micrognathia. Brain imaging showed cerebellar hypoplasia in 87% of patients. Some patient had additional imaging abnormalities, including enlarged ventricles, cerebral atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and hypomyelination.

{1:Maroofian et al. (2023)} identified 39 previously unreported patients from 18 unrelated families with NEDSCAC who had biallelic variants in the MED27 gene. The patients were collected using a genotype-first approach though data mining of DNA sequences from laboratories worldwide. Including information from previously reported patients with the disorder, {1:Maroofian et al. (2023)} analyzed the clinical phenotype of a total of 57 patients from 30 families, 21 (30%) of which were consanguineous. The patients ranged from 2 months to 45 years of age (mean age of 17 years); 9 patients (16%) died between 2 months and 13 years (mean age of 5.9 years). All had global developmental delay with motor delay, often with hypotonia, delayed sitting/walking or inability to sit or walk, variably impaired intellectual development, and speech delay. About half of patients were nonverbal, even up to the teenage years, and many had dysarthria. Less than half were able to perform activities of daily living. Most had either a progressive disease course or regression of acquired skills, suggesting both a neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative aspect to the disorder. Some had poor overall growth, including failure to thrive, decreased height, and microcephaly. Notable motor abnormalities included central hypotonia, gait ataxia, spasticity, hyperreflexia, opisthotonic posturing, and limb and orofacial dystonia and dyskinesia. Of note, it was not possible to assess cerebellar ataxia in about 40% of patients, due to infantile mortality, lack of ambulation, dystonia, and severe cognitive impairment. About half of patients had childhood-onset epilepsy, with various types of seizures that were mostly controllable with medication. Most patients had bilateral cataracts requiring surgery, and many had strabismus. Some had dysmorphic facial features, such as triangular face, micrognathia, low-set ears, deep-set eyes, arched eyebrows, and large open mouth. Many had distal muscle atrophy and limb contractures. Brain imaging results, available for 36 patients, showed cerebellar atrophy in all and pontine hypoplasia in about 50%. About half of patients had atrophy of the basal ganglia with reduced volume of the caudate and putamen, as well as T2-weighted signal abnormalities in the basal ganglia. Other common findings were overall volume reduction, enlarged ventricles, white matter abnormalities, thin corpus callosum, and mild simplification of the gyral pattern.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSCAC in the families reported by {2:Meng et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 16 patients from 11 unrelated families of various ethnic origins with NEDSCAC, {2:Meng et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the MED27 gene (see, e.g., {605044.0001}-{605044.0007}). There were 11 unique mutations, including 3 frameshift, 1 splice site, and 7 missense. The variants occurred throughout the gene; missense variants affected highly conserved residues. Six of the 7 missense variants were in the C-terminal domain. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families from whom genetic material was available. They were either absent or present at a low frequency in the gnomAD databases. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 39 patients from 18 unrelated families with NEDSCAC, {1:Maroofian et al. (2023)} identified homozygous mutations in the MED27 gene (see, e.g., {605044.0004}; {605044.0008}-{605044.0010}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. The mutations were either absent from or found at a very low frequency in gnomAD (v3.1.1). All patients had homozygous missense variants except 1, who had a homozygous in-frame deletion. Combined with previously reported patients, none had biallelic loss-of-function mutations, suggesting that that genotype would be embryonically lethal. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but the authors postulated a partial loss of MED27 function as the pathogenic mechanism.

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: In a large study of 57 individuals from 30 unrelated families with NEDSCAC confirmed by genetic analysis, {1:Maroofian et al. (2023)} discerned 3 levels of phenotypic severity based on the degree of developmental delay and impaired intellectual development, early death, microcephaly, developmental regression, epilepsy, the presence and severity of cerebellar ataxia and dystonia, and the ability of patients to perform activities of daily living. About half (51%) had a 'mild-to-moderate' phenotype, a third (32%) had a 'severe-to-profound' phenotype, and 17% had an intermediate 'moderate-to-severe' phenotype. Although there was inter- and intrafamilial variability among patients with the same mutation, some trends were observed. Homozygous carriers of the most frequent variant (G291S) and those with the P259L variant had a mild-to-moderate phenotype. Patients with the H179P, V242A, and P280L variants had moderate-to-severe or severe-to-profound phenotypes. Four patients who were compound heterozygous for a missense variant and a frameshift or splice site variant had an intermediate moderate-to-severe disease course. One individual with a homozygous in-frame deletion had a severe-to-profound phenotype. Of note, no patients carried 2 predicted loss-of-function alleles, suggesting that that scenario may result in embryonic lethality.

Caused by mutation in the SWI/SNF-related, matrix-associated, actin-dependent regulator of chromatin, subfamily A, member 2 gene (SMARCA2,)

Head: Microcephaly (in some patients)
Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, moderate to severe
