text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that blepharophimosis-impaired intellectual development syndrome (BIS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SMARCA2 gene ({600014}) on chromosome 9p24.

Heterozygous mutation in the SMARCA2 gene can also cause Nicolaides-Baraitser syndrome (NCBRS; {601358}), which shows some overlapping features, but is considered to be a distinct phenotype.

description.title: Description
description.content: Blepharophimosis-impaired intellectual development syndrome (BIS) is a congenital disorder characterized by a distinct facial appearance with blepharophimosis and global development delay. Affected individuals have delayed motor skills, sometimes with inability to walk, and impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech; some patients show behavioral abnormalities. There are recognizable facial features, including epicanthal folds, sparse eyebrows, broad nasal bridge, short nose with downturned tip, and open mouth with thin upper lip. Other more variable features include distal skeletal anomalies, feeding difficulties with poor growth, respiratory infections, and hypotonia with peripheral spasticity (summary by {1:Cappuccio et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Cappuccio et al. (2020)} reported 14 patients with a recognizable neurodevelopmental syndrome who were ascertained through international collaboration after genomic sequencing. Reverse phenotyping was done in order to delineate the clinical features. The patients, who ranged from 3 to 19 years of age, had global developmental delay and variably impaired intellectual development, often with poor or absent speech and behavioral abnormalities. Most patients had delayed walking in the first years of life, although several never achieved independent ambulation. Many had hypotonia, sometimes with progression to peripheral spasticity. Three patients had seizures. Some had poor growth and feeding difficulties with gastroesophageal reflux. Six had microcephaly (down to -4.4 SD). All had a distinctive facial appearance with blepharophimosis, narrow palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, sparse eyebrows and eyelashes, arched eyebrows, broad nasal bridge, and downturned nasal tip. Frontal bossing, tented upper vermilion of the lip, hypertelorism, long or short philtrum, abnormal ears, short nose with small nostrils and hypoplastic alae nasi, chin crease, broad and flat face, open mouth, and pinched nose were also observed. Many patients also had widely spaced teeth or enamel defects. Visual problems were common, including astigmatism, hyperopia, esotropia, myopia, and cortical visual impairment. Three males had cryptorchidism and 1 female had hypoplastic labia. Brain imaging, performed in only a few patients, showed variable anomalies, including enlarged ventricles, pontine hypoplasia, and nonspecific white matter signals. Almost all patients had variable skeletal defects, such as limb contractures, flat feet or foot deformities, long tapering fingers, and clinodactyly. About half of patients had recurrent respiratory infections. {1:Cappuccio et al. (2020)} proposed to name the disorder in these individuals 'blepharophimosis intellectual disability syndrome (BIS).'

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SMARCA2 gene that were identified in patients with BIS by {1:Cappuccio et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 14 patients with BIS, {1:Cappuccio et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the SMARCA2 gene (see, e.g., {600014.0015}-{600014.0019}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. The mutations clustered in 2 regions located outside of the catalytic ATPase helicase domains. Some occurred in exons 8 or 9, corresponding to a region between the HSA and helicase ATP-binding domains, whereas others occurred in exon 19, mapping to the linker region located between DExx helicase ATP-binding and helicase C-terminal domains. Structural analysis of the variants using the yeast homolog (Snf2) showed that the residues mutated in BIS are on an alpha-helix that is likely at the interface with other members of the SWI/SNF complex. Introduction of mutations corresponding to E929V and R937L ({600014.0018} and {600014.0019}) in yeast showed no growth abnormalities, being similar to wildtype. RNA-seq transcriptome analysis of blood derived from 2 patients (patients 1 and 9) showed some differential gene expression profiles compared to cells from patients with NCBRS ({601358}). However, there was a close expression profile shared by BIS and NCBRS compared to controls. Cells from patients with BIS and NCBRS also showed some differences in methylation signature patterns. Additional functional studies of the variants were not performed. The authors concluded that SMARCA2 variants outside of the helicase domain result in a phenotypically and molecularly distinct disorder from NCBRS.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that KINSSHIP syndrome (horseshoe KIdney, Nievergelt ({163400})/Savarirayan ({605274}) mesomelic dysplasia, Seizures, Hypertrichosis, impaired Intellectual development, Pulmonary involvement; KINS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the LAF4 gene (AFF3; 601464) on chromosome 2q11.

description.title: Description
description.content: KINSSHIP syndrome (KINS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by a recognizable pattern of anomalies including developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, seizures, mesomelic dysplasia, dysmorphic facial features, horseshoe or hypoplastic kidney, and failure to thrive (summary by {5:Voisin et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{4:Steichen-Gersdorf et al. (2008)} reported a female infant with mesomelic dysplasia characterized by bilateral fibular agenesis and short, dysplastic, triangulated tibiae. The femurs were of normal size. The forearms were slightly short, and the radial heads were subluxed. The feet were in a marked equinovalgus position with postaxial reduction on the left and abnormally spaced toes on the right. Head MRI demonstrated cortical and subcortical brain atrophy and dilatation of the ventricular system. The infant developed apneic spells and myoclonic jerks, and she died at age 4 months following a prolonged hypoxic episode. Postmortem examination showed malrotation of the colon, a horseshoe kidney, and ambiguous genitalia. The findings were similar to those described by {2:Savarirayan et al. (2000)}, with the addition of central nervous system manifestations and urogenital anomalies.

{3:Shimizu et al. (2019)} described a 2.5-year-old Japanese girl with an unclassified mesomelic dysplasia associated with postaxial toe hypoplasia. She was born at 38 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. At 7 months of age, she was referred for evaluation because of growth failure and developmental delay. Physical examination revealed mesomelic shortening of the upper and lower extremities, left 4th-5th toe syndactyly, and a sacral dimple. Radiologic examination showed mesomelic dysplasia with broad and bowed radii and ulnae, hypoplastic fibulae, 4th-5th toe syndactyly, metatarsal anomalies, and 11 pairs of ribs. Abdominal ultrasound revealed bilateral hypoplastic kidneys. Follow-up at age 2.5 years identified severe growth and developmental delay. She measured 73.1 cm (-4.9 SD), weighed 7.4 kg (-3.5 SD), and could neither control her head nor speak single words. {3:Shimizu et al. (2019)} noted the similarities of their patient with the patient previously reported by {4:Steichen-Gersdorf et al. (2008)} including mesomelic dysplasia with foot malformations with the skeletal phenotype more severe in the microdeletion patient as well as developmental delay and renal anomalies.

{5:Voisin et al. (2021)} described 16 individuals with either de novo missense (15/16 patients) or deletion (1/16) mutations in AFF3 and a recognizable pattern of anomalies, which they called KINSSHIP syndrome, and compared them with the patients described by {4:Steichen-Gersdorf et al. (2008)} and {3:Shimizu et al. (2019)}. All probands presented with severe developmental epileptic encephalopathy along with mesomelic dysplasia (12/18) and failure to thrive (14/18). The skeletal features included short forearms, radial head dislocation/subluxation, triangular and/or short tibia, fibular hypoplasia, hip dislocation, and tarsal and/or metatarsal synostosis resembling Nievergelt ({163400})/Savarirayan ({605274}) mesomelic skeletal dysplasia. Other features included microcephaly (9/18), global brain atrophy and/or ventriculomegaly (13/15), fibular hypoplasia (12/16), horseshoe or hypoplastic kidney (13/17), abnormalities of muscle tone (12/16), gastroesophageal reflux disease (6/16), and other gastrointestinal symptoms (14/17). The patients also shared common dysmorphic facial features such as a bulbous nasal tip (10/15), a wide mouth (10/16) often with a square upper lip, abnormalities of the teeth and gums (12/15), and hypertrichosis (12/15). {5:Voisin et al. (2021)} noted that the constellation of features recalled some features of CHOPS syndrome ({616368}), which is caused by mutations in a related gene, AFF4 ({604417}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the AFF3 gene that were identified in patients with KINSSHIP syndrome by {3:Shimizu et al. (2019)} and {5:Voisin et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
{4:Steichen-Gersdorf et al. (2008)} studied a female infant with mesomelic dysplasia and other anomalies with array comparative genomic hybridization (CGH). CGH demonstrated a heterozygous 500-kb deletion on chromosome 2q11.2 containing the LAF4 gene. De novo occurrence in the patient was confirmed by microsatellite analysis of the patient's and parental DNA using 15 polymorphic markers located within 2q11.2. The paternal allele was deleted in the patient. RNA in situ hybridization studies in mouse embryos showed expression of LAF4 in the developing hindbrain and limb buds.

{1:Kraft et al. (2015)} reevaluated the patient reported by {4:Steichen-Gersdorf et al. (2008)} and determined that the deletion in the LAF4 gene was smaller than previously thought, encompassing only 9 exons of the gene and not the entire genomic region. The breakpoints of the deletion were mapped in introns 3 and 12, thus eliminating exons 4 to 12 without introducing a frameshift. The predicted protein is an 850-residue protein lacking a domain predicted to be involved in transcription activation.

In a 2.5-year-old Japanese girl with KINSSHIP syndrome, {3:Shimizu et al. (2019)} identified a de novo heterozygous mutation in exon 6 of the AFF3 gene, resulting in a missense mutation (A258T; {601464.0002}) in the ALF domain. The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in public databases or in an in-house database.

In 15 patients with KINSSHIP syndrome, {5:Voisin et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the AFF3 gene by exome sequencing and data aggregation of multiple laboratories via GeneMatcher. All of the missense mutations occurred within the degron motif of the ALF domain. The highly conserved 9-amino acid motif mediates the interaction with SIAH E3 ubiquitin ligases (see {602212}) and regulates their degradation. Twelve of the probands carried variants affecting the same codon in exon 6, ala258 ({601464.0001}-{601464.0003}), that was affected in the patient reported by {3:Shimizu et al. (2019)}. Three probands (1, 2, and 15) had missense variants affecting neighboring codons ({601464.0004}-{601464.0006}). {5:Voisin et al. (2021)} also identified an affected individual (proband 16) with a de novo 469-kb deletion that removed exons 3-12 of AFF3, including the ALF domain and its degron.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{1:Kraft et al. (2015)} used CRISPR/Cas to generate structural variants in mice, including the microdeletion first reported by {4:Steichen-Gersdorf et al. (2008)}. A homozygous knockout by targeted recombination of the Laf4 gene in mice did not result in a recognizable phenotype. However, chimeric mice with either the heterozygous or homozygous 353-kb Laf4 deletion had a short zeugopod in the upper limb as well as lower limb abnormalities that recapitulated part of the human phenotype, including a small, triangular ossification center of the tibia and severe hypoplasia of the fibula. The mice also had polydactyly of the feet with incomplete penetrance. {1:Kraft et al. (2015)} concluded that the specific intragenic deletion of Laf4 generated by CRISPR/Cas recapitulated the patient's syndrome and concluded that the truncated protein exerts a dominant-negative effect leading to abnormalities of bone formation.

{5:Voisin et al. (2021)} reassessed mouse models with the deletion originally identified by {4:Steichen-Gersdorf et al. (2008)} and further refined by {1:Kraft et al. (2015)}. Consistent with the phenotype in the deletion patients identified by {4:Steichen-Gersdorf et al. (2008)} and {5:Voisin et al. (2021)}, homozygous animals chimeric for a 353-kb deletion syntenic to the 500-kb human deletion exhibited mesomelic dysplasia (12/12), triangular tibia (12/12), severe hypoplastic fibula (12/12), reduced body size (12/12), and polydactyly of the feet (5/12) at embryonic day 18.5. Chimeric heterozygotes for the 353-kb deletion presented with highly variable features ranging from normal phenotypes to homozygous deletion-like phenotypes. Whereas the heterozygous deletion animals with low chimerism were fertile, they produced no heterozygous offspring, suggesting lethality of the 353-kb deletion. {5:Voisin et al. (2021)} engineered a knockin mouse carrying the most commonly observed missense mutation, A258T ({601464.0001}). Microinjection of a total of 410 C57BL/6NTac zygotes and transfer to allow CRISPR/Cas9 editing resulted in only 13 pups at weaning. A single female showed the targeted A258T knockin but with a very low mosaicism rate of 16.7% in an ear biopsy. None of its offspring from 4 consecutive pregnancies were heterozygous for the mutation, suggesting lethality during gametogenesis or the fetal period.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 14 (PCH14) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PPIL1 gene ({601301}) on chromosome 6p21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 14 (PCH14) is a severe autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by congenital onset of progressive microcephaly and poor or absent psychomotor development with severely impaired intellectual development apparent from birth. Other features may include hypotonia, spastic quadriplegia, and early-onset seizures. Brain imaging shows pontocerebellar hypoplasia, agenesis or partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, and sometimes a simplified gyral pattern. Early death may occur (summary by {1:Chai et al., 2021}).

For a phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of PCH, see PCH1A ({607596}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Chai et al. (2021)} reported 17 patients from 9 unrelated families with PCH14. The patients, who ranged from 2 months to 13 years of age, were ascertained through exome sequencing; several were identified through the GeneMatcher program. Five families were consanguineous, of Egyptian, Pakistani, or Mexican descent. The patients presented at birth with severe microcephaly (-2 to -6 SD), which progressed postnatally (-4 to -8 SD). Most showed essentially no developmental progress, with absent motor skills, no language, severe intellectual disability, and no social skills. Four patients died between 2 and 8 months of age. Several patients had axial hypotonia, and most had spastic tetraplegia with brisk tendon reflexes, sometimes with dystonia. All but 3 developed seizures in infancy, including infantile spasms and focal, myoclonic, and generalized seizures; seizures were often intractable. EEG showed a high-voltage disorganized pattern, and 2 patients had hypsarrhythmia. Brain imaging showed pontocerebellar hypoplasia, agenesis or partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, and brainstem hypoplasia. Seven patients had a simplified gyral pattern, and 3 showed defective myelination.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PCH14 in the families reported by {1:Chai et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 17 patients from 9 unrelated families with PCH14, {1:Chai et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PPIL1 gene (see, e.g., {601301.0001}-{601301.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Most of the mutations were missense variants at conserved residues on the enzymatic face of the protein; in vitro studies showed that all mutations assessed either resulted in decreased protein stability or disrupted the interaction with SKIP (SKIIP; {603055}). There were a few frameshift, splice site, and nonsense mutations, predicted to result in a loss of function. However, no patient carried loss-of-function mutations on both alleles. Knockdown of the PPIL1 gene in human HAP1 cells resulted in a disruption of global alternative RNA splicing, as detected by RNA-seq and RT-PCR studies. The detrimental effect seemed to be most severe toward introns with high GC content. The differential splicing events affected genes involved in neurodevelopment, but not those involved in cancer, cardiac disease, or immune disease. Studies in mutant mouse models showed similar results (see ANIMAL MODEL). {1:Chai et al. (2021)} concluded that disruption of splicing integrity resulting from PPIL1 mutations underlies the neurodegenerative process observed in these patients.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Chai et al. (2021)} found that complete knockout of the Ppil1 gene in mice was embryonic lethal. Mice homozygous for the human A99T mutation ({601301.0001}) died within 24 hours. They had small head size, reduced cerebral and cerebellar volume, and decreased cortical surface area and thickness. Although the cortex showed normal lamination, postmitotic neuronal numbers were severely reduced due to apoptosis. There was also evidence of DNA damage, suggesting genome instability. Upregulation of apoptosis was not observed in other organs, indicating a neuronal-specific effect. Ppil1 protein levels were severely decreased compared to controls. RNA-seq analysis of brain tissue from A99T homozygous mice detected significant differential splicing events affecting genes involved in protein translation, RNA processing, DNA damage response, axon development, and the cell cycle.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 15 (PCH15) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CDC40 gene ({605585}) on chromosome 6q22. One such patient has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 15 (PCH15) is a severe autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by congenital onset of progressive microcephaly and poor or absent psychomotor development with severely impaired intellectual development apparent from birth. Other features may include spastic quadriplegia, early-onset seizures, and chronic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Brain imaging shows pontocerebellar hypoplasia and partial agenesis of the corpus callosum (summary by {1:Chai et al., 2021}).

For a phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of PCH, see PCH1A ({607596}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Chai et al. (2021)} reported a 4-year-old girl, born of consanguineous Egyptian parents (family 10), with PCH15. She showed congenital microcephaly at birth (-3 SD), which progressed to -5 SD. She had severely delayed psychomotor development with almost no skill acquisition, impaired intellectual development, absent speech, and absent social interaction. Intractable myoclonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures began in infancy. She also had mild hypertonia and spastic tetraplegia with brisk deep tendon reflexes. Brain imaging showed pontocerebellar hypoplasia with partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. Additional notable features included chronic anemia and thrombocytopenia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PCH15 in the family reported by {1:Chai et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a 4-year-old girl, born of consanguineous Egyptian parents (family 10), with PCH15, {1:Chai et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the CDC40 gene (F502C; {605585.0001}). The mutation, which was found by direct sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Patient fibroblasts and HEK293 cells transfected with the mutation showed decreased protein levels compared to controls. Knockdown of CDC40 in HEK293 cells caused higher intron retention, suggesting a defect in the regulation of splicing, which could be rescued by wildtype CDC40, but not the F502C variant. Cell viability was also decreased by knockdown of the CDC40 gene. {1:Chai et al. (2021)} concluded that disruption of splicing integrity resulting from the CDC40 mutation underlies the neurodegenerative process observed in this patient.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 1E (PCH1E) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the SLC25A46 gene ({610826}) on chromosome 5q22.

Biallelic mutation in the SLC25A46 gene can also cause HMSN6B ({616505}), which shows some overlapping features, but is much less severe.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 1E (PCH1E) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by severe hypotonia and respiratory insufficiency apparent soon after birth. Virtually all patients die in the first days or weeks of life. Postmortem examination and brain imaging show pontocerebellar atrophy and loss of anterior motor neurons in the spinal cord. Additional more variable features may include optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, dysmorphic features, congenital contracture or foot deformities, and seizures (summary by {3:Braunisch et al., 2018}).

For a phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of PCH, see PCH1A ({607596}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Barth (1993)} reported a Dutch family in which 3 sibs died within the first day of life due to lack of spontaneous respiration and profound muscle weakness. Autopsy was not performed on the first child. The pregnancy of the second affected infant was complicated by polyhydramnios. She died of respiratory failure; autopsy showed a small cerebellum. The third child had congenital contractures, hypotonia, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and pale optic discs; seizures were also noted. Postmortem examination showed anterior horn cell degeneration, pontocerebellar atrophy, and atrophic muscle fibers.

{1:Abrams et al. (2015)} reported a female infant, born of unrelated parents from the United States (family US) who presented at birth with contractures, hypotonia, and respiratory insufficiency. She had significant dysmorphic features, including bitemporal narrowing, upturned nose with bulbous tip, tented upper lip, narrow palate, flat midface, inverted nipples, and tapered fingers. She also had optic atrophy. Brain imaging showed progressive cerebellar and brainstem atrophy. She died at age 15 weeks.

{6:Wan et al. (2016)} reported 4 infants from 2 unrelated consanguineous families who died soon after birth with a profound neurodevelopmental disorder associated with congenital pontocerebellar hypoplasia. Three of the 4 pregnancies were noted to be complicated by polyhydramnios. The patients presented at birth with severe hypotonia and respiratory distress necessitating ventilatory support, areflexia, and occasional myoclonic jerks. EEG in 2 patients showed generalized slowing, but no epileptiform activity, whereas 1 patient developed seizures at 3 weeks of age. Additional features included optic atrophy and severe global developmental delay. EMG and nerve conduction studies in 2 patients were consistent with an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy. Brain imaging of all patients showed a small cerebellum and brainstem, consistent with pontocerebellar hypoplasia. Mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme testing in 2 patients was normal. All patients died between 2 weeks and 3 months of age. {6:Wan et al. (2016)} noted the phenotypic similarities to a female infant from the United States with pontocerebellar atrophy who died at age 15 weeks; this infant was previously reported by {1:Abrams et al. (2015)}.

{4:Janer et al. (2016)} reported a female infant, born of consanguineous French Canadian parents, with a lethal neurologic disorder. She developed a convulsion at 4 hours of age, which did not recur. In the first months of life, she showed irritability, feeding and swallowing difficulties, failure to thrive, and delayed psychomotor development. At age 13.5 months, she presented with a febrile seizure and respiratory failure. Brain imaging at that time showed lesions in the cerebellar white matter, cerebellar peduncles, and brainstem, as well as in the globi pallidi, consistent with a clinical diagnosis of Leigh syndrome. Ophthalmologic examination showed optic atrophy. She had mild spasticity and hyperreflexia; EMG and nerve conduction studies were not performed, but muscle biopsy showed neurogenic atrophy. She died soon thereafter. Laboratory studies showed intermittent lactic acidosis, with mildly increased lactate and pyruvate in the CSF.

{3:Braunisch et al. (2018)} identified 4 infants from 2 unrelated families of German and Italian descent with PCH1E. All died in the first days or weeks of life. Both pregnancies in the German family, which was consanguineous, were complicated by polyhydramnios. All the infants presented at birth with severe hypotonia, no spontaneous movements, and respiratory failure. Postmortem examination or brain imaging showed pontocerebellar hypoplasia; there was loss of motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord in those patients who were studied. The 2 Italian patients also had absent motor responses on EMG and nerve conduction studies, suggesting denervation. Laboratory studies in 1 infant showed increased serum lactate. Family history of both families revealed 2 additional individuals who died soon after birth from hypotonia and pontocerebellar dysplasia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PCH1E in the families reported by {1:Abrams et al. (2015)} and {6:Wan et al. (2016)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a girl, born of unrelated American parents (family US), with PCH1E, {1:Abrams et al. (2015)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC25A46 gene: a frameshift ({610826.0004}) and a missense mutation (P333L; {610826.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variants were not performed.

In 4 sibs from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with PCH1E, {6:Wan et al. (2016)} identified 2 different homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SLC25A46 gene ({610826.0007} and {610826.0008}). Although 1 of the mutations was a missense mutation (L341P; {610826.0007}), in vitro studies showed that it resulted in markedly decreased amounts of protein, suggesting that the clinical severity is inversely correlated with relative stability of the mutant protein.

In a girl, born of consanguineous French Canadian parents, with PCH1E, {4:Janer et al. (2016)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SLC25A46 gene (T142I; {610826.0010}). The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The mutant protein was virtually undetectable in patient fibroblasts, which showed mitochondrial hyperfusion, alterations in endoplasmic reticulum morphology, impaired cellular respiration, and premature cellular senescence.

In 3 infant sibs, born of unrelated Dutch parents, with PCH1E originally reported by {2:Barth (1993)}, {5:van Dijk et al. (2017)} identified compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SLC25A46 gene ({610826.0011} and {610826.0012}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Patient fibroblasts showed absence of the SLC25A46 protein, and there was evidence of decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, suggesting perturbation of mitochondrial dynamics.

In 4 infants from 2 unrelated families with PCH1E, {3:Braunisch et al. (2018)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC25A46 gene ({610826.0013}-{610286.0015}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but they were predicted to result in a loss of function.

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: SLC25A46 mutations that result in greatly decreased levels of the mutant protein compared to wildtype cause PCH1E; see {610826.0004}-{610826.0005} and {1:Abrams et al. (2015)}; {610826.0007} and {610826.0008} and {6:Wan et al. (2016)}; and {610826.0010} and {4:Janer et al. (2016)}.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
In zebrafish, {1:Abrams et al. (2015)} found expression of slc25a46 in retinal ganglion cells and their corresponding neuronal projections in axons of the optic nerve and dendrites of the inner plexiform layer. Morpholino knockdown of the gene resulted in fewer retinal ganglion cell axons that reached the tectum, as well as impairment of these dendrites. Morpholino knockouts had a curly tail morphology and impaired swimming, suggesting dysfunction of neural circuits, and spinal motor neurons had shortened axon tracts due to degeneration of neuronal processes. Mitochondria in the degenerating motor neurons showed incomplete fission, abnormal aggregation, and abnormal cell localization compared to wildtype.

{6:Wan et al. (2016)} found that morpholino knockdown of the slc25a46 gene in zebrafish embryos resulted in a dose-dependent phenotype of brain maldevelopment in the midbrain and hindbrain, as well as loss of spinal motor neurons. Dissociated neurons from mutant animals showed elongated and immotile mitochondria compared to controls, suggesting impaired fission/fusion dynamics.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and cerebellar hypoplasia

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and cerebellar hypoplasia (NEDFACH) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the EXOC2 gene ({615329}) on chromosome 6p25.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and cerebellar hypoplasia (NEDFACH) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay and intellectual disability. The phenotype is variable: more severely affected individuals have poor overall growth with microcephaly, delayed walking, spasticity, and poor or absent speech, whereas others may achieve more significant developmental milestones and even attend special schooling. Brain imaging shows abnormalities of the cerebellum, most commonly cerebellar hypoplasia, although other features, such as thin corpus callosum and delayed myelination, may also be present. Dysmorphic facial features include sloping forehead, upslanting palpebral fissures, and hypertelorism. Additional more variable manifestations may include cardiac ventricular septal defect, spasticity, cataracts, optic nerve hypoplasia, seizures, and joint contractures (summary by {1:Van Bergen et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} reported 2 patients from a large consanguineous Lebanese family with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients presented soon after birth with progressive microcephaly, global developmental delay, and dysmorphic features. One died at 10 years of age. Dysmorphic features included sloping forehead, upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, broad depressed nasal bridge, long flat philtrum, and thin upper lip. They had severely impaired development with spastic quadriplegia, clenched hands with camptodactyly, joint contractures, hip dysplasia, and feeding difficulties. One patient had seizures, cataracts, cardiac ventricular septal defect, and undescended testes; the other patient had hypoplastic optic discs. Brain imaging showed cerebellar hypoplasia and other variable abnormalities, including thin corpus callosum, decreased white matter volume, hypoplastic brainstem, and decreased myelination. The authors also reported an 8-year-old girl (patient 3), born of unrelated Italian parents, with a similar but less severe phenotype. She presented with global developmental delay in infancy, but later showed borderline intellectual function and was able to attend a special school. She had dysmorphic features that resembled those of the other patients; brain imaging showed cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, rhombencephalosynapsis, and the 'molar tooth sign.'

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDFACH in the families reported by {1:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 children (patients 1 and 2) from a large consanguineous Lebanese family (family 1) with NEDFACH, {1:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the EXOC2 gene (R437X; {615329.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. An unrelated Italian girl (patient 3) with a similar disorder associated with compound heterozygous missense mutations in the EXOC2 gene (R130H, {615329.0002} and L580S, {615329.0003}) was subsequently identified through the Matchmaker Exchange database. Cells derived from patient 2 with the nonsense mutation showed decreased EXOC2 protein levels and decreased vesicle fusion rates compared to controls. In contrast, fibroblasts from patient 3, who carried compound heterozygous missense variants, showed normal protein levels and normal vesicle fusion rates. However, cells from both patients demonstrated impaired exocytosis. Although cilia length was similar to controls, cells from both patients showed significantly reduced localization of the EXOC2 interacting protein ARL13B ({608922}) to the cilia. This defective localization could be rescued by expression of wildtype EXOC2. {1:Van Bergen et al. (2020)} noted that the milder phenotype in patient 3 compared to that in the patients from family 1 correlated with the severity of exocytosis defects observed in patient cells. Moreover, brain imaging in patient 3 showed the molar tooth sign, which is often associated with a ciliopathy.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-21 (HLD21) is caused by homozygous mutation in the POLR3K gene ({606007}) on chromosome 16p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-21 (HLD21) is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy with loss of motor, speech, and cognitive milestones in the first decades of life. Affected individuals show cerebellar and pyramidal signs, including nystagmus, ataxia, dystonia, and spasticity, resulting in the loss of ambulation. Other more variable features include feeding difficulties, poor overall growth with microcephaly, optic atrophy, and seizures. Brain imaging shows diffuse hypomyelination of the white matter and atrophy of the cerebellum and corpus callosum. The disorder is progressive and may lead to premature death (summary by {1:Dorboz et al., 2018}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of HLD, see {312080}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Dorboz et al. (2018)} reported 2 unrelated boys, each born of consanguineous parents of Berber origin from Algeria, with a severe neurodegenerative disorder beginning in infancy. They had global developmental delay: patient 1 had hypotonia, acquired sitting at age 18 months, and was nonverbal, whereas patient 2 acquired walking at 12 months with an ataxic gait and only had a few words at age 2 years. Cognitive function was poor in both. The neurologic dysfunction was progressive, resulting in loss of motor skills and the onset of cerebellar and pyramidal signs, including dystonia, spasticity, athetosis, quadriparesis, and dyskinesia. They were able only to hold their heads up by ages 6 and 12 years, respectively. Other common features included feeding difficulties, poor overall growth with microcephaly (-3 SD), nystagmus, and cryptorchidism. Patient 1 had acute episodic metabolic (hypoglycemia, ketosis) and neurologic (seizures, coma) deterioration associated with infection or emotional stress. He also had optic atrophy and hypodontia; patient 2 had hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Brain imaging in both patients showed diffuse hypomyelination associated with progressive atrophy of the cerebellum and corpus callosum. Patient 2 died suddenly at age 18 years; patient 1 was alive but severely impaired at age 12 years. The authors emphasized the digestive dysfunction in these patients, as both were tube-fed.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HLD21 in the families reported by {1:Dorboz et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated boys, each born of consanguineous parents, with HLD21, {1:Dorboz et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the POLR3K gene (R41W; {606007.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families. It was not found in several public databases, including gnomAD, or in 500 ethnically-matched control chromosomes. Patient fibroblasts showed reduced expression of tRNA(imet), 5S rRNA (see {180420}), and 7SL RNA (see {612177}) compared to controls. The findings suggested that disrupted RNA regulation resulting from the mutation contributed to the neurologic dysfunction observed in these patients.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Hiatt-Neu-Cooper neurodevelopmental syndrome (HINCONS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RALA gene ({179550}) on chromosome 7p14.

description.title: Description
description.content: Hiatt-Neu-Cooper neurodevelopmental syndrome (HINCONS) is characterized by global developmental delay with delayed walking or inability to walk and impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech. Affected individuals have axial hypotonia and dysmorphic facies. Additional more variable features may include seizures, autistic or behavioral abnormalities, and brain abnormalities, such as dysplastic corpus callosum or polymicrogyria (summary by {1:Hiatt et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Hiatt et al. (2018)} reported 11 patients, including a pair of monozygotic twins, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder associated with de novo heterozygous mutations in the RALA gene who were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. The patients, who ranged from 16 months to 16 years of age, presented in early infancy with global developmental delay, hypotonia, delayed walking or inability to walk, and moderately to severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech and poor eye contact. They tended to have feeding difficulties with poor overall growth, sometimes with short stature. Several patients were wheelchair-bound, and 2 required feeding tubes. Six patients had various types of seizures, including absence, tonic, and myoclonic, 3 had autism spectrum disorder, and others had variable behavioral abnormalities. Brain imaging was normal in some patients, but showed variable abnormalities in others, including thin or dysplastic corpus callosum, periventricular gliosis, incomplete myelination, and polymicrogyria. Most patients had dysmorphic facial features, including relative macrocephaly or microcephaly, broad prominent forehead, bitemporal narrowing, flat midface, horizontal eyebrows, epicanthal folds, mild ptosis, slanted palpebral fissures, depressed or wide nasal bridge with anteverted nares, short philtrum, thin upper lip, pointed chin, drooling, and low-set or posteriorly rotated ears. Other features included distal skeletal anomalies, such as long thin fingers, fifth finger or toe clinodactyly, and hyperextensible joints.

{2:Okamoto et al. (2019)} reported a 9-year-old Japanese girl with global developmental delay, hypotonia, and severely impaired intellectual development; developmental quotient was 30. She had poor eye contact, esotropia, astigmatism, and myopia. Dysmorphic features included relative macrocephaly, frontal bossing, epicanthal folds, wide nasal bridge, thin upper lip, pointed chin, and low-set, posteriorly rotated ears. She also had aggressive behavior including self-mutilation and restlessness. Brain imaging was normal.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the RALA gene that were identified in patients with HINCONS by {1:Hiatt et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 11 patients, including 2 monozygotic twin boys, with HINCONS, {1:Hiatt et al. (2018)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the RALA gene (see, e.g., {179550.0001}-{179550.0004}). The mutations were found by exome or genome sequencing, and the patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. The mutations were demonstrated to have occurred de novo in all but 1 patient, for whom parental DNA was not available. There were 5 missense mutations, 1 nonsense mutation, and 1 in-frame deletion. All except 1 (R176X) were absent from the gnomAD database, and all except R176X occurred at conserved residues in GTP/GDP-binding domains. R176X was considered to be a variant of uncertain significance. In vitro functional expression studies of selected mutations showed that most of the tested mutations caused a dramatic reduction in GTPase activity and RALA effector binding compared to controls. The S157A variant ({179550.0004}) also impaired GTPase activity, but caused increased RALA effector binding, suggesting a possible constitutive gain-of-function effect. Five patients carried variants in other genes that may have contributed to the phenotype, although the authors concluded that RALA was the most important factor.

In a Japanese girl with HINCONS, {2:Okamoto et al. (2019)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the RALA gene (V25M; {179550.0001}). The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Radio-Tartaglia syndrome (RATARS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SPEN gene ({613484}) on chromosome 1p36.

description.title: Description
description.content: Radio-Tartaglia syndrome (RATARS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, speech delay, and variable behavioral abnormalities. Affected individuals show hypotonia, mild motor difficulties, and craniofacial dysmorphism. Brain imaging may show nonspecific defects; rare patients have seizures or pyramidal signs. A subset of individuals may have congenital heart defects, precocious puberty, and obesity in females. Some of the features are similar to those observed in patients with chromosome 1p36 deletion syndrome ({607872}) (summary by {1:Radio et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Radio et al. (2021)} reported 34 individuals from 33 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder ascertained through genetic analysis. The patients had global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, and poor speech. Behavioral or psychiatric abnormalities, including autistic features, anxiety, aggressive behavior, and ADHD, were noted in 81%; 1 patient (S20) developed schizophrenia. Some patients were able to attend special schools. Other common features included generalized hypotonia (73%), oromotor hypotonia (43%), gait imbalance (52%), and pyramidal signs (25%). Three patients had seizures. Brain imaging showed abnormalities in 14 (64%) of 22 patients studied. Features included polymicrogyria, heterotopia, cerebellar atrophy, periventricular white matter defects, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and tethered cord. There was a characteristic facial appearance with rare microcephaly, broad forehead (26%), frontal bossing (16%), bitemporal narrowing (39%), arched elongated eyebrows (39%), synophrys (33%), telecanthus (26%), epicanthal folds (39%), dysplastic ears (35%), and broad nose with bulbous/prominent nasal tip (52%). Some patients had long philtrum, thin upper lip, tooth abnormalities, high-arched palate, or pointed chin. Extraneurologic features were also present, including congenital heart defects (28%) such as ventricular septal defects, patent foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus, and mitral regurgitation, as well as scoliosis, brachydactyly, toe anomalies, dry skin, and hemangiomas. Precocious puberty was found in a subset of subjects (22%), and affected females tended to have increased BMI or to be obese.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SPEN gene that were identified in most of the patients with RATARS by {1:Radio et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. In 2 families, the transmission pattern was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 34 patients, including 2 sibs, with RATARS, {1:Radio et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous truncating mutations in the SPEN gene ({613484.0001}-{613484.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program and the DECIPHER database. The vast majority of the mutations occurred de novo, although they were inherited from an affected parent in 2 families. The mutations were distributed throughout the coding region of the gene, and there were no obvious genotype/phenotype correlations. In vitro functional expression studies of the variants were not performed, but they were predicted to result in a loss of function with haploinsufficiency. Genomewide methylation profiling did not show a substantial difference between the pattern of cells derived from 11 of the patients compared to controls. However, when restricted to females with SPEN truncating mutations, there was a distinct difference in the X-chromosome epigenetic signature compared to controls, suggesting a role for SPEN in X-chromosome inactivation and X-linked gene silencing. The report defined a paradigm of an X chromosome-specific episignature that underlies specific syndromic traits and could be used to classify individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-6B (DEE6B) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN1A gene ({182389}) on chromosome 2q24.

Heterozygous mutation in the SCN1A gene also causes Dravet syndrome (DEE6A; {607208}), which has overlapping but less severe features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-6B (DEE6B) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by early-infantile seizure onset, profoundly impaired intellectual development, and a hyperkinetic movement disorder. Brain imaging usually shows progressive atrophy and other abnormalities (summary by {4:Sadleir et al., 2017}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Ohashi et al. (2014)} reported a 6-year-old Japanese girl, born of unrelated parents, who presented with multifocal seizures at 2 to 3 months of age. The seizures evolved to frequent episodes of hyperthermia-induced status epilepticus. Around 6 months of age, she developed a hyperkinetic movement disorder with sudden jerky movements resembling chorea and ballismus, as well as hand stereotypies. She had profound developmental delay with poor overall growth, inability to speak, sit, or walk, spastic quadriplegia, and no purposeful hand movements. Brain imaging showed progressive cortical and white matter atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and impaired myelination. She had mild nonspecific dysmorphic features. The authors noted that the phenotype was severe and atypical for Dravet syndrome.

{4:Sadleir et al. (2017)} reported 9 unrelated children, ranging from 3 to 12 years of age, with a severe epileptic encephalopathy. Two of the patients (patients 3 and 4) were previously reported by {1:Dhamija et al. (2014)}. The 9 patients presented with various types of seizures at a mean age of 9 weeks (range 6 to 12 weeks) after normal early development. Seizure types included infantile spasms, tonic-clonic, hemiclonic, myoclonic, and tonic; 8 patients had episodes of status epilepticus. Several had seizures associated with fever or illness; most seizures were intractable to multiple medications. EEG showed multifocal discharges, generalized spike and slow waves, and diffuse background slowing. Brain imaging showed multiple variable abnormalities, including generalized cerebral atrophy, dysmorphic corpus callosum, small hippocampus, and progressive white matter abnormalities. All had profoundly impaired development, with inability to walk independently, absent speech, and poor eye contact; most were tube-fed. Periods of neurologic regression were also observed. Other prominent features included axial hypotonia, limb hypertonia, dystonia, choreoathetosis, orofacial myoclonus or hyperkinesia, nystagmus, ataxia, and generalized or multifocal myoclonic movements. A few patients had nonspecific dysmorphic features, such as microcephaly, hypertelorism, and scoliosis. One patient died at age 10 years. In their paper, {1:Dhamija et al. (2014)} found subtle sleep disturbances in their patients with SCN1A mutations.

{2:Harkin et al. (2007)} reported a 5-year-old patient (patient 78) with onset of seizures at 2 months of age. The patient had severely impaired intellectual development and increased muscle tone. Another patient (patient 61) with DEE6B was noted to have severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy (SMEI)-borderland (SMEB, which refers to patients who lack several of the key features of SMEI such as myoclonic seizures or generalized spike-wave activity), but clinical details were limited.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SCN1A gene that were identified in patients with DEE6B by {4:Sadleir et al. (2017)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 6-year-old Japanese girl with DEE6B, {3:Ohashi et al. (2014)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the SCN1A gene (V422L; {182389.0025}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing, was not present in the Exome Sequencing Project or in 408 in-house Japanese controls. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In 8 unrelated patients with DEE6B, {4:Sadleir et al. (2017)} identified a de novo recurrent heterozygous missense mutation in the SCN1A gene (T226M; {182389.0026}). Another patient (patient 9) carried a de novo heterozygous P1345S mutation ({182389.0027}). Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but the authors speculated a gain-of-function effect.

In a 5-year-old patient (patient 78) with DEE6B, {2:Harkin et al. (2007)} identified a de novo heterozygous T226M mutation in the SCN1A gene. Another patient (patient 61) also carried this mutation. Functional studies of the variant were not performed. The patients were part of a cohort of 188 patients with DEE who were examined for mutations in the SCN1A gene.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that oculogastrointestinal neurodevelopmental syndrome (OGIN) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CAPN15 gene ({603267}) on chromosome 16p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Oculogastrointestinal neurodevelopmental syndrome (OGIN) is characterized by microphthalmia and/or coloboma in association with other congenital anomalies, including imperforate anus, horseshoe kidney, and structural cardiac defects. Hearing loss and severe developmental delay are also observed in most patients ({2:Zha et al., 2020}; {1:Mor-Shaked et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Zha et al. (2020)} reported 5 patients from 4 families with microphthalmia and/or coloboma as well as additional anomalies including hearing loss and delayed growth and development. Patient 1 was a 3.5-year-old girl, born of consanguineous Pakistani parents, who had bilateral iris and chorioretinal coloboma involving the optic disc, right cataract, and left microphthalmia. She had poor weight gain postnatally and underwent nasogastric tube feedings due to swallowing difficulties. Other anomalies included laryngeal cleft, dysphonia, mild hirsutism with low anterior hairline, and sacral dimple. Her mother had experienced multiple miscarriages and stillbirths. Patient 2 was a 26-year-old man with bilateral microphthalmia and iridocorneal adhesions, who also had prominent simple ears and hearing loss, bicuspid aortic valve, and horseshoe kidney. He had severe developmental and cognitive delay with no speech, and autism. Patient 3 was a 7-year-old Arab girl with severe myopia due to increased axial length as well as right inferonasal coloboma of iris and retina. Patients 4 and 5 were French Canadian sibs who had iris and chorioretinal coloboma, sensorineural deafness, developmental delay, and imperforate anus. The 11-year-old brother (patient 4) also exhibited postnatal microcephaly, short stature, and dysmorphic features including left ptosis, left simple ear, and prominent columella, whereas his 6-year-old sister (patient 5) also had vaginal fistula, hemivertebrae, and autism spectrum disorder.

{1:Mor-Shaked et al. (2021)} reported 2 brothers from a multiply consanguineous Muslim Arab family who had profound global developmental delay with almost no developmental milestones, severe growth delay, hypotonia, and seizures. Dysmorphic features included microcephaly, triangular face, microphthalmia, iris coloboma, and beaked nose with hypoplastic alae nasi. In addition, both boys had hearing loss, which was noted to be unilateral and conductive in the proband; cardiac defects, including atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary stenosis, and right aortic arch; renal anomalies, including horseshoe kidneys in both; and imperforate anus. The proband had hypothyroidism, and both patients experienced chronic diarrhea with steatorrhea, suggestive of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, although elastase was not specifically measured. Brain imaging of the brothers showed moderate generalized cortical atrophy, mild ventricular dilatation, and increased periventricular white matter signal indicating dysmyelination. The proband died at age 5 years of respiratory infection; his younger brother had frequent hospitalizations due to recurrent respiratory and urinary tract infections. Family history included a previous termination of pregnancy due to brain malformations and horseshoe kidney in a male fetus, and the extended family history included a male cousin who died 2 hours after birth with abdominal distension, pelvic kidneys, lower limb deformity, and triangular face, as well as a female infant who died at 2 weeks of age with congenital malformations that included imperforate anus. The authors noted overlap with Johanson-Blizzard syndrome (JBS; {243800}) in the combination of poor growth, global developmental delay, dysmorphic features with hypoplastic nasal alae, exocrine pancreatic dysfunction, hypothyroidism, and congenital abnormalities, and stated that the CAPN15-associated ocular anomalies seemed to be a crucial differentiator between that disorder and JBS.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of OGIN in the consanguineous families reported by {2:Zha et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
By whole-exome sequencing (WES) in 55 patients from a UK cohort with developmental eye disorders, {2:Zha et al. (2020)} identified a 3.5-year-old Pakistani girl (patient 1) with unilateral microphthalmia and bilateral coloboma who was homozygous for a missense mutation in the CAPN15 gene (G969S; {603267.0001}). Subsequent WES identified 4 additional individuals with anophthalmia/microphthalmia/coloboma (AMC) spectrum disorders and biallelic missense mutations in the CAPN15 gene, including a 26-year-old man (patient 2) who was compound heterozygous for variants S720F ({603267.0002}) and R800W ({603267.0003}); a 7-year-old Arab girl (patient 3) who was homozygous for a R1028K change ({603267.0004}); and a French Canadian brother and sister (patients 4 and 5) who were homozygous for an S613L variant ({603267.0005}). Unaffected parents and sibs in the families were heterozygous for the respective mutations.

In the older of 2 brothers with OGIN from a multiply consanguineous Muslim Arab family, {1:Mor-Shaked et al. (2021)} performed proband-only exome sequencing and identified homozygosity for a 47-bp deletion involving a splice site in the CAPN15 gene ({603267.0006}). Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation of the mutation with disease in the family. Noting that the 2 brothers appeared to be more severely affected than the patients reported by {2:Zha et al. (2020)}, the authors suggested that biallelic loss-of-function variants might cause a more severe syndromic disorder.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-65 (MRD65) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KDM4B gene ({609765}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-65 (MRD65) is characterized by delayed motor and speech acquisition, variably impaired intellectual development, and behavioral abnormalities. Affected individuals also have dysmorphic facial features. Brain imaging may be normal or may show abnormalities, including cerebellar hypoplasia, poor development of the corpus callosum, dysmorphic hippocampus, and polymicrogyria. Feeding difficulties, hypotonia, and seizures may also be observed ({1:Duncan et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Duncan et al. (2020)} reported 9 unrelated probands, ranging from 13 months to 12 years of age, with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after exome sequencing was performed. All had global developmental delay with variably impaired motor and intellectual development beginning in infancy. Several had feeding difficulties in infancy, but overall growth was normal in all but 1 patient (patient 7), who had the most severe phenotype. Other features included hypotonia, speech delay, behavioral abnormalities, and seizures (3 patients). The most severely affected patient, patient 7, was a 14-month-old girl with hypotonia who was unable to roll over, had no speech, and required a feeding tube. She also had cortical visual impairment, infantile spasms, cleft palate, and atrial septal defect. All patients had dysmorphic facial features, but a common gestalt was not noted. Dysmorphic features included protruding metopic ridge, synophrys, sparse temporal hair, abnormal palpebral fissures, short or long philtrum, broad nasal bridge, short or upturned nose, and downturned corners of the mouth. Short hands and clinodactyly were also sometimes observed. Brain imaging was reportedly normal in 4 patients. The other 5 patients had variable structural brain abnormalities, including cerebellar hypoplasia, partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, dysmorphic hippocampus, and mega cisterna magna; 2 patients had polymicrogyria.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the KDM4B gene that were identified in 7 patients with MRD65 by {1:Duncan et al. (2020)} occurred de novo. In 2 patients, the mutation was inherited from a mildly affected parent, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 9 unrelated patients with MRD65, {1:Duncan et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous mutations in the KDM4B gene (see, e.g., {609765.0001}-{609765.0005}). There were 4 missense, 3 frameshift, and 2 splicing variants; none were present in the gnomAD database. Most occurred de novo, but 2 patients (patients 6 and 9) inherited the variant from a mildly affected parent. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program, and the mutations were found by exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but they were predicted to result in a loss or reduction of function. {1:Duncan et al. (2020)} suggested that the reduction in KDM4B function resulted in suppressed transcription of target genes that regulate brain development and corticogenesis.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Duncan et al. (2020)} found that mice with heterozygous loss of Kdm4B had structural brain abnormalities, including overall decreased brain volume, decreased volume of the hippocampal dentate gyrus, partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, and ventriculomegaly. The mutant mice displayed some hyperactivity, which did not reach statistical significance. Homozygous knockout of Kdm4B was embryonic lethal.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and gingival overgrowth

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and gingival overgrowth (NEDSGO) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TBC1D2B gene ({619152}) on chromosome 15q24.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and gingival overgrowth (NEDSGO) is an autosomal recessive disorder with a highly variable phenotype. Some patients have early normal development with developmental regression apparent in the first years of life, whereas others present with hypotonia or delayed development. Most patients develop significant gingival hypertrophy associated with a prominent mandible or cherubism in the first years of life. Other more variable features may include coarse facial features, optic atrophy, sensorineural hearing loss, ataxia, and seizures. Brain imaging may show cerebellar or cerebral atrophy and enlarged ventricles. There is a wide phenotypic spectrum with features that may develop with age; the disorder appears to comprise a continuum of evolving neurologic manifestations ({1:Harms et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Harms et al. (2020)} reported 4 patients from 3 unrelated families with NEDSGO. Two adult sibs in family 1 (patient 1 and 2) presented around age 5 years with gingival hypertrophy in the absence of medication exposure after normal early development. They then showed developmental regression with behavioral abnormalities, deterioration of scholastic performance at around 12 to 13 years, gait ataxia, tremor, slurred speech, visual loss associated with optic atrophy and retinal pigmentary abnormalities, progressive flexion contractures of the fingers and toes, and coarse facial features with hypertelorism, low hanging columella, and prominent mandible. Both had onset of seizures at age 19 years, and 1 (patient 1) developed sensorineural hearing loss. Brain imaging showed cerebellar atrophy and dilated cisterna magna in both patients. Patient 2 died at age 25 years. Patients 3 and 4 were subsequently identified through the GeneMatcher program. Patient 3 was an 8-year-old girl who presented at age 3 with gingival hypertrophy, prominent mandible, and cherubism, as manifest by multilocular radiolucent lesions in the mandible. She was noted to have mild developmental delay, onset of focal seizures around 18 months of age, and unilateral optic disc pallor. Brain imaging at age 2 years was normal. She was diagnosed clinically with Ramon syndrome ({266270}). Patient 4 was an 8-month-old boy born prematurely at 34 weeks' gestation with macrosomia. He had hypotonia with lack of head control, inability to roll over, and poor eye tracking. At age 3 months, he developed status epilepticus associated with fever, but continued to have nonfebrile seizures. Other features included hypertelorism, large flared eyebrows, and macrocephaly. Brain imaging showed dilated lateral ventricles and diffuse cerebral atrophy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSGO in the families reported by {1:Harms et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients from 3 unrelated families with NEDSGO, {1:Harms et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the TBC1D2B gene ({619152.0001}-{619152.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were 3 nonsense and 2 frameshift mutations. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but cells derived from 2 patients (patients 1 and 4) had no detectable TBC1D2B protein expression. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of TBC1D2B in HeLa cells impaired EGFR ({131550}) endocytosis and resulted in decreased cell viability and increased apoptosis during serum starvation. The authors speculated that TBC1D2B deficiency may lead to enhanced degradation of E-cadherin (CDH1; {192090}), which plays a role in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), abnormalities in which are likely to underlie the gingival overgrowth in older patients. Overall, the findings suggested that the mutations caused a deficit in early endocytic trafficking and increased cell death.

clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, mild to moderate
Caused by mutation in the BRD4-interacting chromatin remodeling complex-associated protein gene (BICRA,)

Head: Microcephaly (in some patients)
Macrocephaly (1 patient)
Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, mild to moderate
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the BRD4-interacting chromatin remodeling complex-associated protein gene (BICRA,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Coffin-Siris syndrome-12 (CSS12) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the BICRA gene ({605690}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Coffin-Siris syndrome-12 (CSS12) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, speech and language delay, and behavioral abnormalities, such as autism or hyperactivity. Affected individuals may have hypotonia and poor feeding in infancy. There are variable dysmorphic facial features, although most patients do not have the classic hypoplastic fifth digit/nail abnormalities that are often observed in other forms of CSS ({1:Barish et al., 2020}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of Coffin-Siris syndrome, see CSS1 ({135900}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Barish et al. (2020)} reported 12 unrelated patients, ranging from 9 months to 28 years of age, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through collaboration and with the help of GeneMatcher and the Undiagnosed Disease Network (UDN). All had global developmental delay with variably impaired motor and intellectual development. Most learned to walk by 2 or 3 years of age and had speech and language delay. A few had hypotonia and early feeding difficulties with failure to thrive and poor overall growth. About half had autistic features or behavioral abnormalities, such as aggression, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. Many of the older patients were able to attend special schools. Two patients had seizures and 1 had sensorineural hearing loss. All had notable, if variable, dysmorphic facial features, including amblyopia or strabismus, microcephaly (4 patients), macrocephaly (1 patient), frontal bossing, bitemporal narrowing, high or low anterior hairline, arched eyebrows, synophrys, long eyelashes, epicanthal folds, small or slanted palpebral fissures, deep-set eyes, low-set ears, posteriorly rotated ears, prominent nasal bridge, bulbous or rounded nasal tip, low columella, thin upper lip, long or short philtrum, high-arched palate, micrognathia, and square or pointed chin. A few had scoliosis or joint laxity, but only 3 had fifth digit/nail hypoplasia. Other features included constipation, gastroesophageal reflux, myopia, and hyperopia. {1:Barish et al. (2020)} stated that the phenotype overlapped with those of classic Coffin-Siris syndrome and other SWI/SNF-related intellectual disability disorders (SSRIDDs), but was also somewhat distinct since classic features, such as fifth digit hypoplasia and coarse facies, were not commonly observed in this cohort.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the BICRA gene that were identified in patients with CSS12 by {1:Barish et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 9 unrelated patients with CSS12, {1:Barish et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the BICRA gene (see, e.g., {605690.0001}-{605690.0005}). There were 7 nonsense or frameshift variants and 2 missense variants; all were absent from the gnomAD database. Three additional patients with the disorder carried intragenic deletions affecting BICRA. The mutations and deletions were found by whole-exome, whole-genome, or array-based sequencing. The mutations occurred throughout the gene and there were no apparent genotype/phenotype correlations. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but all were predicted to result in a loss of function with haploinsufficiency. Based on functional studies in Drosophila, the authors suggested that specific components of the SWI/SNF complex may have unique functions in the genome, which could explain phenotypic variability.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Barish et al. (2020)} generated zebrafish mutants with a frameshift loss-of-function variant in the ortholog of the bicra gene. There was no observable phenotype in animals who were heterozygous for the mutation, and there were no abnormalities in the homozygous mutant offspring of the heterozygotes. However, homozygous offspring of homozygous mutant parents had significant craniofacial defects including shorter head length and disrupted jaw elements. In addition to indicating that BICRA is involved in craniofacial development, the absence of phenotypes in young fish derived from heterozygous mutant parents suggested a role for maternal RNA or protein in regulating these early molecular events.

preferredTitle: CATARACTS, SPASTIC PARAPARESIS, AND SPEECH DELAY; CSPSD
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the fatty acyl CoA reductase 1 gene (FAR1,)

Head: Macrocephaly (in some patients)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the fatty acyl CoA reductase 1 gene (FAR1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Cataracts, spastic paraparesis, and speech delay

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cataracts, spastic paraparesis, and speech delay (CSPSD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the FAR1 gene ({616107}) on chromosome 11p15.

description.title: Description
description.content: Cataracts, spastic paraparesis, and speech delay (CSPSD) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by spastic paraparesis and bilateral congenital/juvenile cataracts. Speech delay is a common feature ({1:Ferdinandusse et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Ferdinandusse et al. (2021)} reported 12 patients, aged 2 to 19 years, who exhibited neurologic symptoms in their first years of life. Six of 12 patients presented with spastic di- or paraparesis and 6 of 12 had truncal hypotonia. In addition, all patients had bilateral cataracts, which were congenital in 5 patients. Seizures occurred in 8 patients, mainly in the first months of life. Speech delay was present in 10 patients, cognitive delay in 3 patients, and growth delay in 1 patient. Eleven patients were ambulatory, but all 11 required walking aids. Five patients reported constipation. Two patients presented with macrocephaly, and brain imaging was within normal limits in 10 of 12 patients. One patient had abnormal temporal lobe morphology and ventricular prominence, and 1 patient had benign enlargement of subarachnoid spaces on brain imaging.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of cataracts, spastic paraparesis, and speech delay in the families reported by {1:Ferdinandusse et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: {1:Ferdinandusse et al. (2021)} identified 3 different heterozygous mutations affecting the R480 residue in the FAR1 gene ({616107.0004}-{616107.0006}) in 12 unrelated individuals with CSPSD. The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing in 11 patients and by an exome-based panel focused on genes associated with cerebral palsy in 1 patient. FAR1 enzyme activity and plasmalogens were increased in fibroblasts from 3 of the patients, 2 with the R480H mutation and 1 with the R480C mutation. Ether phospholipid synthesis was shown to be increased in the 3 cell lines. {1:Ferdinandusse et al. (2021)} concluded that the mutations resulted in loss of plasmalogen-dependent feedback on FAR1 protein levels.

Miscellaneous: Two unrelated Japanese patients have been reported (last curated May 2021)
