text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-96 (DEE96) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the NSF gene ({601633}) on chromosome 17q21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-96 (DEE96) is characterized by onset of seizures in the first days or weeks of life. Affected infants have tonic or myoclonic seizures associated with burst-suppression pattern on EEG. They also have hypotonia with respiratory insufficiency that may result in premature death. Those that survive have profound developmental delay and persistent seizures (summary by {2:Suzuki et al., 2019}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Suzuki et al. (2019)} reported 2 unrelated Japanese infant girls with early infantile epileptic encephalopathy (EIEE). The first patient presented after birth with continuous vomiting and tonic seizures associated with a continuous burst-suppression pattern on EEG. She died of respiratory failure on day 36 of life. The second patient was born prematurely at 33 weeks' gestation; prenatally she had exhibited hydrops, anemia, and failure to thrive. At birth, head circumference was -3.4 SD and she had no spontaneous respiration, requiring mechanical ventilation. She had frequent myoclonic seizures associated with continuous burst-suppression patterns on EEG. At age 3 years, she had profound intellectual disability, severe motor developmental delay, and no spontaneous respiration. The patient continued to have frequent myoclonic seizures and epileptic spasms.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the NSF gene that were identified in patients with DEE96 by {2:Suzuki et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated Japanese girls with DEE96, {2:Suzuki et al. (2019)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the NSF gene (A459T, {601633.0001} and P563L, {601633.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were absent from the ExAC database and from a cohort of 2,049 Japanese control individuals. Studies of patient cells were not performed. Transfection of the mutations into the Drosophila eye disc resulted in defective eye development with increased cellular apoptosis, suggesting that the gene is involved in neuronal development. Pan-neuronal expression of the mutation was embryonic lethal. The authors postulated a dominant-negative effect. They also noted that the Drosophila 'comatose' mutant, which shows temperature-sensitive paralysis, is caused by mutation in the NSF ortholog ({1:Pallanck et al., 1995}). These findings suggested a role for NSF in synaptic transmission.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Pallanck et al. (1995)} determined that the Drosophila 'comatose' (comt) phenotype is due to mutation in the ortholog of the NSF gene. Mutant flies show temperature-sensitive paralysis that can be rescued by transfection of the wildtype dNSF gene. The findings further supported a role for NSF in synaptic transmission.

clinicalSynopsis: Ridging of the metopic and coronal sutures
Contiguous gene syndrome caused by deletion of 2.9 to 10.3 Mb on chromosome 1p36

Head: Microcephaly
Brachycephaly
Skeletal - Skull: Ridging of the metopic and coronal sutures
Molecular Basis: Contiguous gene syndrome caused by deletion of 2.9 to 10.3 Mb on chromosome 1p36

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because it represents a contiguous gene deletion syndrome on proximal chromosome 1p36.

See also distal chromosome 1p36 deletion syndrome ({607872}), which shows overlapping clinical features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Proximal 1p36 deletion syndrome is a multisystem developmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, poor overall growth with microcephaly, axial hypotonia, and dysmorphic facial features. Most patients have congenital cardiac malformations or cardiac dysfunction. Additional more variable features may include distal skeletal anomalies, seizures, and cleft palate. The phenotype shows some overlap with distal chromosome 1p36 deletion syndrome (summary by {1:Kang et al., 2007}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Kang et al. (2007)} reported 5 unrelated children, ranging from 2 months to 6 years of age, with global developmental delay associated with heterozygous proximal deletion of chromosome 1p36. One patient died at 2 months of age. The patients had poor overall growth with failure to thrive and global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, speech delay, hypotonia, and motor delay with ataxia. Three patients had seizures, and 2 had appendicular hypertonia. All 5 patients had some kind of cardiac malformation or functional defect, including septal defects, patent foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary stenosis, dilated cardiomyopathy, partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (PAPVR) with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, and valve defects. Common dysmorphic features included microcephaly, frontal and parietal bossing, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, broad arched eyebrows, midface hypoplasia, micrognathia, low-set or posteriorly rotated ears, abnormal palpebral fissures, broad nose, flat nasal bridge, anteverted nares, pointed chin, high-arched or cleft palate, short neck, and hirsutism. Several patients had distal skeletal anomalies such as clinodactyly and camptodactyly. {1:Kang et al. (2007)} suggested that the phenotype differed from that of the classic distal 1p36 deletion syndrome, although there was some overlap.

{2:Rudnik-Schoneborn et al. (2008)} reported an 8-month-old girl with global developmental delay associated with monosomy 1p36. She had poor overall growth with microcephaly, long palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, long eyelashes, broad nose, fleshy ears, large mouth, pointed chin, and short neck. Brain MRI at age 5 months revealed a midline defect with agenesis of the anterior commissure and rostral corpus callosum and partial agenesis of the septum pellucidum. The authors stated that this structural brain defect had not previously been described in proximal 1p36 deletion.

{4:Zaveri et al. (2014)} identified 3 unrelated patients (patients 6, 7, and 8) with nonoverlapping heterozygous interstitial deletions of proximal chromosome 1p36. Clinical details were limited, but features included microcephaly, developmental delay, seizures, kyphosis, and failure to thrive. All had variable congenital heart defects, including ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot, and coarctation of the aorta.

{3:Shimada et al. (2015)} reported 5 unrelated patients with interstitial deletions of chromosome 1p36 (patients 1, 14, 47, 48, and 50). They had microcephaly, brachycephaly, epicanthal folds, broad basal root, long philtrum, low-set ears, and pointed chin. Two had a high-arched or cleft palate. All had global developmental delay with severely impaired intellectual development, absent speech, and motor delay. Three had seizures and 3 had congenital cardiac abnormalities, including septal defects. Brain imaging in 3 patients showed enlarged ventricles.

cytogenetics.title: Cytogenetics
cytogenetics.content:
Using array CGH, {1:Kang et al. (2007)} identified different heterozygous interstitial deletions of chromosome 1p36 in 5 unrelated patients with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The deletions in 4 patients ranged from 9.38-14.69 Mb, whereas in 1 patient (patient 4), it was only 2.9 Mb in size. The cytogenetic findings showed that all patients had 5-prime breakpoints within the common 10-Mb deletion syndrome observed in classical monosomy 1p36; however, the deletions in these patients extended more proximally from band 1p36.23 to 1p36.1. The smallest region of overlap (SRO) was about 2.24 Mb in size on chromosome 1p36.22 (chr1:9,058,817-11,297,159, NCBI35) and contains at least 23 known genes.

{2:Rudnik-Schoneborn et al. (2008)} reported an 8-month-old girl with microcephaly and a midline brain malformation who had an interstitial deletion of 1p36 on conventional chromosome analysis; FISH and array CGH analysis documented an 8.7-Mb deletion encompassing 1p36.23-p36.13.

{4:Zaveri et al. (2014)} identified 3 unrelated patients (patients 6, 7, and 8) with nonoverlapping heterozygous interstitial deletions of proximal 1p36. The deletions, which ranged from 2.9 to 7.8 Mb in size, shared no common region of overlap.

{3:Shimada et al. (2015)} reported 5 unrelated patients with interstitial deletions of chromosome 1p36 (patients 1, 14, 47, 48, and 50). The deletions ranged from 0.9 to 10.3 Mb in size.

Head: Microcephaly (-3.2 SD)
Miscellaneous: Two unrelated patients from consanguineous Indian families have been reported (last curated May 2021)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan anchor biosynthesis class F protein gene (PIGF,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Onychodystrophy, osteodystrophy, impaired intellectual development, and seizures syndrome

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that onychodystrophy, osteodystrophy, impaired intellectual development, and seizures syndrome (OORS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PIGF gene ({600153}) on chromosome 2p21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Onychodystrophy, osteodystrophy, impaired intellectual development, and seizures syndrome (OORS) is an autosomal recessive syndromic developmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, dysmorphic facial features, and hypoplastic terminal phalanges and nails. Patients have seizures or tonic posturing. The disorder is associated with a defect in GPI anchoring of membrane-bound proteins (summary by {1:Salian et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of GPI biosynthesis defects, see GPIBD1 ({610293}).

See also DOORS syndrome ({220500}), which shows some overlapping clinical features.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Salian et al. (2021)} reported 2 unrelated children, each born of consanguineous Indian parents, with a similar syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Patient 1 was a 14-year-old boy with developmental delay, severely impaired intellectual development with no effective speech, hypoplastic fingernails, toenails, and terminal phalanges, and dysmorphic facial features, including delayed permanent dentition, small teeth, anteverted nares, low-set pinnae, anteverted earlobes, full lips, and open mouth. Other features included atrial septal defect, refractory generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and precocious puberty. He had no toilet control and displayed head banging and repetitive nonpurposeful rocking movements of the head. Patient 2 was a 13-month-old girl with poor overall growth, microcephaly (-3.2 SD), global developmental delay with poor eye contact, hypoplastic or absent finger and toenails, and triphalangeal thumb. Dysmorphic features included micrognathia, microstomia, coarse face, and short nose. She had tonic posturing without overt seizures. Neither patient had deafness, and brain imaging was normal. Patient 1 had a similarly affected brother who died before 2 years of age. The authors noted the phenotypic overlap with DOORS syndrome ({220500}), with the notable lack of deafness in their patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of OORS syndrome in the families reported by {1:Salian et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated children with OORS syndrome, each born of consanguineous Indian parents, {1:Salian et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the PIGF gene (P172R; {600153.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families. Flow cytometric analysis of patient cells showed defective GPI anchor biosynthesis that could be restored by expression of wildtype PIGF. Additional functional studies in PIGF-deficient CHO cells showed that the mutant enzyme had low-residual activity compared to wildtype, although levels of the mutant protein were normal. The findings were consistent with PIGF deficiency.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH INFANTILE EPILEPTIC SPASMS; NEDIES
clinicalSynopsis: Two unrelated children have been reported (last curated June 2021)
Caused by mutation in the neurochondrin gene (NCDN,)

Miscellaneous: Two unrelated children have been reported (last curated June 2021)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the neurochondrin gene (NCDN,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with infantile epileptic spasms

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with infantile epileptic spasms (NEDIES) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the NCDN gene ({608458}) on chromosome 1p34.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with infantile epileptic spasms (NEDIES) is characterized by onset of severe and frequent epileptic spasms within the first year of life. Affected individuals have global developmental delay with delayed walking and poor or absent speech. More variable features may include poor overall growth, high-arched palate, and delayed myelination on brain imaging (summary by {1:Fatima et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Fatima et al. (2021)} reported 2 unrelated patients, a 3-year-old Chinese boy (family 3) and a 5-year-old Japanese girl (family 4), who developed early-onset frequent epileptic spasms associated with hypsarrhythmia on EEG with the first year of life. The seizures in 1 patient were noted to be focal, whereas they were myoclonic in the other patient. One patient became seizure-free after surgery, and the other responded to medication. Both had moderate to severely impaired intellectual development. The Chinese boy walked at age 3 and spoke a few words at age 2; he also had a high-arched palate. The Japanese girl was nonambulatory and nonverbal at age 5; she also had poor overall growth, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, and esotropia. Brain imaging showed delayed myelination in the Chinese boy, but was normal in the Japanese girl. The patients were ascertained through international collaboration and the GeneMatcher Program.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the NCDN gene that were identified in patients with NEDIES by {1:Fatima et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated children with NEDIES, {1:Fatima et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the NCDN gene (W498R, {608458.0001} and P652L, {608458.0002}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of the NCDN gene in human neuronal cells resulted in shorter neurites and decreased numbers of neurites compared to controls. These defects could be rescued by expression of wildtype NCDN, but not by the missense variants. In vitro studies showed that the mutations were associated with markedly decreased phosphorylation of ERK1 ({601795})/ERK2 ({176948}), suggesting impaired activation of mGluR5 (GRM5; {604102}). Electrophysiologic studies in NCDN-deficient neuronal cells showed resting membrane hyperpolarization and an increased repolarization rate compared to wildtype, consistent with altered electrophysiologic properties that may predispose to seizures. The authors postulated a dominant-negative effect in these cases. An unrelated 13-year-old French boy (family 2) with a less severe neurodevelopmental disorder, with overlapping features but without seizures, was found to carry a heterozygous missense variant in the NCDN gene (R478E; {608458.0003}). {1:Fatima et al. (2021)} also identified 3 sibs, born of consanguineous Pakistani parents (family 1), with a milder phenotype and rare seizures associated with a homozygous missense variant in the NCDN gene (E433Q; {608458.0004}). The transmission pattern in this family was thus consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Neither of these 2 latter variants was able to rescue neurite growth defects in NCDN-null neuronal cells; however, they had no apparent effect on ERK phosphorylation. The authors suggested that these variants may alter NCDN function in a different way. In addition, the authors suggested that E433Q variant may act as a hypomorph, since the heterozygous carrier parents were unaffected.

Caused by mutation in the NFS1 cysteine desulfurase 1 gene (NFS1,)

Muscle/Soft Tissue: Mitochondrial respiratory chain complex II and III defects

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the NFS1 cysteine desulfurase 1 gene (NFS1,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-52 (COXPD52) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NFS1 gene ({603485}) on chromosome 20q11.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-52 (COXPD52) is an autosomal recessive infantile mitochondrial complex II/III deficiency characterized by lactic acidemia, multiorgan system failure, and abnormal mitochondria. Intrafamilial variability has been reported ({1:Farhan et al., 2014}; {2:Hershkovitz et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Farhan et al. (2014)} reported 3 sibs from a consanguineous Old Order Mennonite family with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency. The first sib (patient IV-I) presented at 7 of months of age with lethargy, anorexia, dehydration, and hypoglycemia after an episode of pharyngitis. She developed seizures, metabolic acidosis, respiratory decompensation, and heart failure. Laboratory testing showed elevated blood lactate and liver enzymes. She died of cardiac failure 3 days later. The second sib (patient IV-II) presented with respiratory failure and cyanosis at 6 weeks of age. Laboratory testing showed elevated lactate, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and creatine kinase. At 15 weeks of age he presented with truncal hypotonia, vomiting, and acidosis. He developed cardiorespiratory failure, focal seizures, cerebral infarction, renal failure, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. He was treated with mitochondrial cofactor therapy and had clinical improvement, and he was discharged from the hospital. However, he died at age 7 months after recurrence of symptoms and cardiac failure. The third sib (patient IV-III) had mild hypotonia of the upper and lower limbs in the neonatal period. In infancy, he had hypotonia, lethargy, weight loss, and abnormal lactate levels. He was treated with a mitochondrial cofactor therapy from 6 months until about 11 years of age. He was generally healthy at 12 years of age but had mild gross motor delay, a minor tremor, and overall low energy. Laboratory testing showed elevated blood lactate, AST, and creatine kinase. Postmortem evaluation of the liver in the 2 youngest sibs showed hepatic steatosis.

{2:Hershkovitz et al. (2021)} reported 3 sibs from a consanguineous Arab Christian family with COXPD. All 3 sibs presented with lethargy and hypotonia. Two sibs, who died at age 43 days and 7 months, had hypoglycemia, respiratory failure, cardiac failure, renal failure, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. One of these sibs also had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and adrenal insufficiency. Both sibs had abnormal laboratory values including elevated creatine kinase, serum lactate, and serum AST. The third sib had a single episode of lactic acidosis, elevated creatine kinase, and liver dysfunction during a urinary tract infection at age 1 month. Echocardiogram was normal. At age 6 years, she was healthy with no reported episodes of suggestive of acute exacerbation.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency in the families reported by {1:Farhan et al. (2014)} and {2:Hershkovitz et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 sibs from a consanguineous Old Order Mennonite family with COXPD52, {1:Farhan et al. (2014)} identified a homozygous missense mutation (R72Q; {603485.0001}) in the NFS1 gene. The mutation, which was found by autozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing, segregated with disease in the family. Reduced NFS1 transcript and protein levels were demonstrated in patient fibroblasts. Deficient respiratory chain complex II and III enzyme function was seen in patient liver and muscle tissue from 2 of the sibs.

In 3 sibs from a consanguineous Arab Christian family with COXPD52, {2:Hershkovitz et al. (2021)} identified homozygosity for the R72Q mutation in the NFS1 gene. Haplotype analysis failed to show a shared haplotype between this family and the Old Order Mennonite family reported by {1:Farhan et al. (2014)}, indicating the likelihood of 2 independent mutation events. Molecular modeling suggested that the R72Q mutation may hinder NFS1-ISD11 ({613311}) complex formation.

clinicalSynopsis: Progressive cerebellar atrophy on brain imaging
Iron deposition in the basal ganglia (in some patients)
Caused by mutation in the VPS41 subunit of HOPS complex gene (VPS41,)

Neurologic - CNS: Progressive cerebellar atrophy on brain imaging
Iron deposition in the basal ganglia (in some patients)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the VPS41 subunit of HOPS complex gene (VPS41,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia-29 (SCAR29) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the VPS41 gene ({605485}) on chromosome 7p14.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia-29 (SCAR29) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by delayed motor development in early infancy followed by difficulty walking due to an ataxic gait or inability to walk, hypotonia, and variably impaired intellectual development. Other features include dysarthria, nystagmus, peripheral spasticity, nystagmus, and visual impairment. Brain imaging typically shows atrophy of the cerebellar vermis, but other abnormalities may also be present. Some patients are wheelchair-bound and/or nonverbal (summary by {2:Sanderson et al., 2021})

In a review of the pathogenesis of disorders with prominent dystonia as a feature, {1:Monfrini et al. (2021)} classified SCAR29 as belonging to a group of neurologic disorders termed 'HOPS-associated neurologic disorders' (HOPSANDs), which are caused by mutations in genes encoding various components of the autophagic/endolysosomal system, including VPS41.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Steel et al. (2020)} reported a boy, born of consanguineous parents, who presented in infancy with global developmental delay and generalized dystonia. He attained a few words and voluntary limb movement, but never sat unsupported. Other features included pale optic discs and an axonal neuropathy. From 6 years of age, he had progressive neurodegeneration with reduced motor abilities and alertness. Brain imaging showed atrophy of the superior cerebellar vermis and thinning of the corpus callosum. The boy was found to have a mutation in the VPS41 gene.

{2:Sanderson et al. (2021)} reported 9 patients from 5 unrelated consanguineous families with SCAR29. The patients, who ranged from 2 to 28 years of age, presented in infancy with a delay in gross motor skills, delayed walking, and ataxic gait with postural instability and frequent falls. Other features included dysarthria, lateral-gaze nystagmus, hypotonia, and mild cognitive impairment. Some patients showed dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesis, or abnormal smooth pursuit. A 28-year-old man (patient 9) had progressive spasticity of the lower limbs. Two sibs, ages 7 and 11 years (family 4), had a more severe phenotype with inability to walk or speak, onset of frequent seizures between 5 and 7 years of age, neuroregression, retinal lesions, and spasticity of the lower limbs. Brain imaging in these sibs showed atrophy of the cerebellum and brainstem, thin corpus callosum, and white matter abnormalities suggestive of delayed myelination. One sib had iron deposition in the basal ganglia, and the other had optic atrophy.

{4:Van der Welle et al. (2021)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with SCAR29. Two sibs in the first family presented in early infancy with hypotonia, poor eye contact, and global developmental delay. They later showed ataxia, intention tremor, progressive spasticity of the lower limbs, hyporeflexia, and extensor plantar responses. Dysmorphic features included high forehead with frontal bossing, retrognathia, deep-set eyes, short and pointed nose, and prominent ears. There was some coarsening of the facial features with age, including puffy eyelids, heavy eyebrows, and thick lips. Brain imaging showed a thin corpus callosum and progressive cerebellar atrophy; 1 patient had bilateral hypointensities in the globus pallidus compatible with early iron deposition. An unrelated boy, born of distantly related parents of Jewish descent, presented in infancy with hypotonia and severe global developmental delay. He had recurrent infections during infancy and childhood, photophobia, retinal hypopigmentation, mild sensorineural hearing deficit that required hearing aids, tracheomalacia, and restricted eye movements. He never developed the ability to sit, walk, or speak. From age 5 years, he developed spasticity of the lower limbs that later progressed to spastic tetraplegia with scoliosis and contractures. Other features included pectus carinatum, foot deformities, and short stubby hands with hypoplastic distal phalanges. He also had swallowing problems that led to airway infections. Dysmorphic features included retrognathia, short and upturned nose, relatively large ears, and clinodactyly of both fifth fingers. His facial features coarsened over time with heavy eyebrows, gingival hypertrophy, protruding tongue, thick lips, and thick ear lobes. His skin was soft and thick, and there was hirsutism on his back and legs. Brain MRI showed agenesis of the corpus callosum, bilateral colpocephaly, hypomyelination, a dysplastic cerebellum with polymicrogyria of the upper part, and a dysplastic pons. The overall findings of all the patients were consistent with a neurodegenerative rather than solely malformative brain disease.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SCAR29 in the families reported by {3:Steel et al. (2020)} and {2:Sanderson et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a boy, born of consanguineous parents, with SCAR29, {3:Steel et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the VPS41 gene ({605485.0001}). The variant was found by targeted Sanger sequencing; segregation studies in the family were not reported. Functional studies of the variant were not performed, but electron microscopic analysis of patient cells showed abnormal vacuoles, suggesting lysosomal dysfunction.

In 9 patients from 5 unrelated consanguineous families with SCAR29, {2:Sanderson et al. (2021)} identified homozygous missense mutations in the VPS41 gene (see, e.g., S285P, {605485.0002}; R633P, {605485.0003}; and C791F, {605485.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were demonstrated to segregate with the disorder in all families with available parental genetic material. The mutations occurred throughout the gene and affected different functional domains. Patient cells showed variably decreased levels of the VPS41 protein, suggesting unstable mutant proteins or transcripts. LAMP2 ({309060}) protein was increased compared to controls in both VPS41-null cells and patient cells; this defect could be rescued by expression of wildtype VPS41, but not the mutants.

In 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with SCAR29, {4:van der Welle et al. (2021)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the VPS41 gene ({605485.0002}; {605485.0005}-{605485.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There was 1 missense variant, 1 nonsense variant, and a splice site mutation. The mutations occurred throughout the gene and were found at very low frequencies only in the heterozygous state in the gnomAD database. VPS41 is a component of the homotypic fusion and protein sorting (HOPS) complex, required for lysosomal fusion events. Although the mutant proteins localized to the cytoplasm and to LAMP1 ({153330})- and LAMP2-positive endolysosomes similar to wildtype VPS41, patient fibroblasts and HeLa cells with knockdown of the VPS41 gene contained abnormally small acidified lysosomes that did not have inclusion bodies. The lysosomes were also positive for cathepsin B (CTSB; {116810}). In vitro functional expression studies showed that the S285P ({605485.0002}) and R662X ({605485.0005}) mutations were unable to rescue the endosome-lysosome fusion kinetic defects in VPS41-null cells, consistent with a nonfunctional HOPS complex in the presence of the mutations. Patient cells showed a similar kinetic defect in the transfer of endocytosed cargo to enzymatically active LAMP1-positive lysosomes. Coimmunoprecipitation studies showed that the S285P variant was able to interact with the core HOPS components VPS18 ({608551}) and VPS33A ({610034}), but the R662X mutant was not. However, S285P was unable to rescue the HOPS complex formation defect in VPS41-null HeLA cells. Although both mutant proteins bound other HOPS subunits RAB7 ({602298}) and ARL8B ({616596}) similar to wildtype VPS41, neither could form a functional HOPS complex, causing delayed lysosomal delivery of endocytic and autophagic cargo. Patient cells and VPS41-null cells showed impaired autophagic response to starvation, which could be rescued by wildtype VPS41, but not by the mutant VPS41 constructs. There was perturbation of the mTORC1 (see {601231}) complex axis in VPS41-null cells and patient cells, with cytosolic redistribution of mTORC1, continuous localization of TFE3 ({314310}) to the nucleus, and increased expression of LC3II (see {601242}). The mutant VPS41 proteins lost the neuroprotective effect of wildtype VPS41 in a C. elegans model of Parkinson disease, suggesting that the HOPS complex is involved in neuroprotection. The authors concluded that the VPS41 variants abrogate HOPS function, which interferes with the axis of mTORC1 signaling and causes a defect in the endosome/lysosome system, resulting in a neurodegenerative disease course.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Sanderson et al. (2021)} found that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of the zebrafish vps41 homolog resulted in melanocyte pigmentation defects, decreased body length, and bladder defects associated with abnormalities in surfactant production or distribution, consistent with abnormalities of lysosome-related organelles. Mutant animals also had defects in the optokinetic response and eye movement control system, suggesting cerebellar dysfunction. Microglia from mutant fish showed morphologic abnormalities, with larger or more numerous lysosomal compartments and increased expression of acidic lysosomal markers compared to controls; these changes could be rescued by expression of wildtype VPS41.

clinicalSynopsis: Increased susceptibility of certain cell types to infection with neurotropic viruses
Variable age at onset (range infancy to adult)
Caused by mutation in the small nucleolar RNA, H/ACA box, 31 gene (SNORA31,)

Immunology: Increased susceptibility of certain cell types to infection with neurotropic viruses

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that susceptibility to acute infection-induced (herpes-specific) encephalopathy-10 (IIAE10) is conferred by heterozygous mutation in the SNORA31 gene ({619378}) on chromosome 13q14.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Susceptibility to infection-induced acute encephalopathy-10 (IIAE10) presents as neurologic deficits in response to acute infection, particularly with herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1), which leads to inflammation of the brain and herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE). The age at onset ranges from infancy to adulthood. However, some mutation carriers do not develop encephalopathy even if exposed to the virus, indicating incomplete penetrance (summary by {1:Lafaille et al., 2019}).

For a phenotypic description of herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of susceptibility to acute infection-induced encephalopathy, see {610551}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Lafaille et al. (2019)} reported 5 unrelated patients with HSV encephalitis. None was born of consanguineous parents. Patients P2, of Saudi Arabian origin, and P5, of Portuguese origin, presented with HSV encephalitis at 3 and 4 months of age, respectively. Patient P1 presented at age 3 years, whereas P3 presented at age 20 years, and P4 presented at age 51 years, with a recurrence at age 63. The diagnoses were confirmed by brain imaging and PCR studies. Clinical features were related to acute neurologic deficits, including cognitive or visual impairment, behavioral instability, and seizures. At the time of the acute illness, all 4 patients studied were seropositive against various other viruses, including VZV, CMV, EBV, parvovirus, and others. There were 4 unaffected family members from 3 families who carried the mutation and had HSV-1 antibodies, but did not develop encephalitis. Two unaffected family members from another family with the mutation tested negative for HSV-1 antibodies.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IIAE10 in the families reported by {1:Lafaille et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 unrelated patients with IIAE10 manifest as forebrain herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE), {1:Lafaille et al. (2019)} identified 4 heterozygous mutations in the SNORA31 gene ({619378.0001}-{619378.0004}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, showed incomplete penetrance in family segregation studies. All were present at very low frequencies in the gnomAD database (less than 3 x 10(-4)). In vitro functional studies showed that patient fibroblasts, but not B cells, had increased susceptibility to infection with HSV-1 and other neurotropic viruses compared to controls. Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cortical neurons also showed increased susceptibility to HSV-1 infection. The susceptibility was independent of TLR3 ({603029}), STAT1 ({600555}), and interferon receptor (see IFNAR1, {107450}) pathways. Transcriptome analysis showed alterations in patient-derived neuronal cells compared to control neurons in response to HSV-1 infection. Exogenous beta-interferon (IFNB1; {147640}) rendered SNORA31-mutated neurons resistant to HSV-1, suggesting a unique mechanism. The authors concluded that the pathogenesis involves haploinsufficiency of SNORA31, which may modify the human transcriptome response and control of infection in cortical neurons, resulting in a failure to control HSV-1 infection. The modified transcriptome response may adversely affect the expression of 1 or more immune effectors induced by TLR3 or IFNAR that control viral infections, with a particular disruption of central nervous system (CNS) cortical neuron-intrinsic immunity.

phenotypes.phenotype: Infantile-onset multisystem neurologic, endocrine, and pancreatic disease 2

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that infantile-onset multisystem neurologic, endocrine, and pancreatic disease-2 (IMNEPD2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the YARS1 gene ({603623}) on chromosome 1p35.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Infantile-onset multisystem neurologic, endocrine, and pancreatic disease-2 (IMNEPD2) is an autosomal recessive multisystemic disorder characterized by cholestatic hepatitis, poor feeding associated with poor overall growth, and hypoglycemia apparent from infancy. Most, but not all, patients have variable global developmental delay. Additional common features include sensorineural deafness, retinal abnormalities with visual defects, and hypotonia. Some patients have endocrine abnormalities, including hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, pancreatic dysfunction, hypothyroidism, and primary amenorrhea. Additional features may include hypertriglyceridemia, anemia, proteinuria, increased lactate, and recurrent infections. Brain imaging often shows dysmyelination, thin corpus callosum, cerebral atrophy, and white matter abnormalities. Although the clinical manifestations and severity of the disorder are highly variable, death in early childhood may occur (summary by {4:Williams et al., 2019} and {5:Zeiad et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of IMNEPD, see IMNEPD1 ({616263}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Nowaczyk et al. (2017)} reported 2 sibs, born of nonconsanguineous Polish parents, with a multisystem disease characterized by failure to thrive, hypertriglyceridemia, and developmental delay. The male proband presented at age 2 months with hypotonia, vomiting, and failure to thrive. At age 5.5 months, he had a head circumference at the 25th centile, length at -3 SD, and weight at -4 SD. He had a cherubic face with deep-set eyes, broad nasal bridge, epicanthal and infraorbital folds, prominent cheeks, and facial weakness, as well as hepatomegaly. At age 15 years, he had mild delays and functioned in school at a third grade level; he could speak and understand English and Polish. He showed poor overall growth with height at -4 SD, weight at -3 SD, and head circumference at the 5th centile. He had a relatively normal facial appearance, areflexic hypotonia, and joint hypermobility. Elevated plasma triglycerides were present since infancy. Mitochondrial evaluation was unrevealing, and a muscle biopsy at age 2 years showed focal vacuolar degeneration. Nerve conduction studies and echocardiograms were normal. Liver biopsy in infancy showed microvesicular fatty accumulation with 'marked droplet steatosis,' sparse peroxisomes with normal morphology, and normal mitochondria. Abdominal ultrasound showed heterogeneous hepatomegaly, splenomegaly with an accessory spleen, and lymphadenopathy. At age 9 years, abdominal MRI showed liver lesions, possibly adenomas or hemangiomas, while the sonogram showed infiltrative liver disease with indeterminate liver lesions, splenomegaly, and cystic lung disease. Liver biopsy at age 10 years showed macronodular cirrhotic liver with steatosis and glycogenated nuclei, and a CT scan of the chest showed lung cysts. Head MRIs performed between 2 and 10 years of age showed mild frontal atrophy, cystic changes in the periventricular white matter, and thinning of the corpus callosum. The proband's sister had a birth height and weight in the 50th centile; head circumference was not recorded. She developed vomiting at day 1 and had a course similar to that of her brother. By age 8 weeks, her head circumference, length, and weight were below the 3rd centile. She had large fleshy cheeks, deep-set eyes, flat nasal bridge, and microretrognathia with a high palate. She exhibited both central and peripheral hypotonia and had elevated triglycerides. MRI showed thinning of the corpus callosum. At age 4.5 years, she had no evidence of developmental delays and was doing better than her brother at the same age. She had normal nerve conduction studies. Both parents had normal neurologic evaluations including normal nerve conduction studies with no evidence of motor or sensory demyelinating or axonal neuropathy. The 4-generation pedigree showed no family history of neurologic disease.

{3:Tracewska-Siemiatkowska et al. (2017)} reported a 26-year-old Swedish woman with a complex multisystemic disorder. She had hypoglycemia in the neonatal period, followed by prolonged jaundice and hepatic cholestasis. Other features included profound hearing loss, nystagmus, progressive rod-cone degeneration with impaired vision, poor feeding requiring tube feeding in early childhood, generalized seizures, hypotonia, and primary amenorrhea. Liver biopsies showed nonprogressive fatty liver with minor fibrotic changes; she had no clinical hepatic insufficiency in later years. Plasma lactate was increased. Brain imaging showed agenesis of the corpus callosum. She was considered deaf with severe visual handicaps, including no night vision, reduced visual fields, and low central vision. However, psychomotor development and intelligence were normal.

{4:Williams et al. (2019)} reported 7 children from a large highly consanguineous Amish kindred with a severe multisystemic disorder apparent from birth. About half the patients were born prematurely, and many births were associated with intrauterine growth retardation or placental abnormalities. Four children died between 10 and 25 months due to end-stage liver disease or infection. The patients had global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor speech, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, poor overall growth requiring tube feeding, chronic cholestatic liver disease, and pancreatic insufficiency. They had deep-set eyes; the oldest child had a long forehead, thin hair, low-set ears, and digital clubbing. Other more variable features included nystagmus, visual impairment or retinal dystrophy, intermittent proteinuria/hematuria, frequent bloodstream infections, hypoglycemia, coagulation abnormalities, hypoalbuminemia, and anemia that was sometimes transfusion-dependent. Liver biopsy showed hepatic steatosis, progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and poorly defined mitochondrial cristae. Three children who had brain imaging showed dysmyelination and abnormal T2-weighted signals. Many patients had evidence of inflammation identified by postmortem examination, chest radiographs, liver biopsy, or renal MRI, suggesting that immune dysregulation may be present and contribute to the pathogenesis. Postmortem examination of 1 patient showed hepatic cirrhosis and microscopic evidence of chronic cortical neuronal loss, gliosis, and diffuse vacuolar changes. {4:Williams et al. (2019)} noted that there is significant phenotypic heterogeneity and variable severity. Heterozygous mutation carriers did not have evidence of peripheral neuropathy.

{2:Shaheen et al. (2019)} identified 2 sibs (14DG0613 and 14DG0614), born of consanguineous parents, with microcephalic primordial dwarfism. They had poor overall growth and dysmorphic features, including sloping forehead, large nose, large ears, high-arched palate, and calcaneovalgus deformity. Additional clinical details were limited.

{5:Zeiad et al. (2021)} reported a male African American infant with a complex multisystemic disorder. He presented at 2 months of age with failure to thrive, hyperbilirubinemia, cholestatic hepatitis, and hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. He had ascites, severe coagulopathy, hypoalbuminemia, hepatomegaly, and elevated liver enzymes. Liver biopsy showed lobular cholestasis, steatosis, and fibrosis. Other features included exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, primary hypothyroidism, persistent anemia associated with G6PD deficiency ({300908}), and acute renal failure. He also had recurrent infections, including bacteremia and pneumonia, as well as evidence of inflammation, such as neutrophilic leukocytosis and varying thrombocytosis. He had global developmental delay. Brain imaging showed diffuse cerebral atrophy and lactate peaks in the basal ganglia, and neuropathologic examination showed generalized CNS leukodystrophy. At age 8 months, the patient was hospitalized for acute bronchiolitis, which was complicated by multiorgan failure, leading to death at 12 months of age.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IMNEPD2 in the kindred reported by {4:Williams et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sibs, born to nonconsanguineous Polish parents, with IMNEPD2, {1:Nowaczyk et al. (2017)} identified 'pathogenic-appearing' compound heterozygous missense mutations in the YARS gene (P213L, {603623.0005} and G525R, {603623.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family and were not found in the EVS and ExAC databases. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but they were predicted to disrupt protein structure or function.

In a 26-year-old Swedish woman with IMNEPD2, {3:Tracewska-Siemiatkowska et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the YARS1 gene (F269S; {603623.0007}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 7 affected children from a large highly consanguineous Amish kindred with IMNEPD2, {4:Williams et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the YARS1 gene (P167T; {603623.0008}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the kindred. In vitro functional studies in HeLa cells transfected with the mutation showed that it caused reduced dimerization, which is essential for proper YARS1 function. Yeast complementation assays indicated that the P167T substitution caused poor growth and reduced gene function. The findings were consistent with a hypomorphic loss-of-function allele.

In 2 sibs (14DG0613 and 14DG0614) with microcephalic primordial dwarfism, poor growth, and dysmorphic features, {2:Shaheen et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the YARS1 gene (P263L); functional studies of the variant were not performed. The patients were ascertained from a cohort of patients from 137 families with congenital microcephaly who underwent exome sequencing.

<Subhead> Reclassified Variants

The Y204C variant reported by {5:Zeiad et al. (2021)} has been reclassified as a variant of unknown significance; see {603623.0009}. In a 12-month-old male African American infant with IMNEPD2, {5:Zeiad et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous c.611A-C mutation in the YARS1 gene (Y204C; {603623.0009}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variant were not performed, but the authors postulated that the mutation results in impaired protein synthesis that fails to meet specific organ demands. The patient also carried a mutation in the G6PD gene ({305900}), consistent with G6PD enzyme deficiency. Because of a discrepancy in the article by {5:Zeiad et al. (2021)} between the reported nucleotide and protein changes, this variant has been reclassified as a variant of unknown significance.

High risk of death in childhood

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that familial combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-53 (COXPD53) is caused by homozygous mutation in the C2ORF69 gene ({619219}) on chromosome 2q33.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-53 (COXPD53) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by hypomyelination, microcephaly, liver dysfunction, and recurrent autoinflammation (summary by {1:Lausberg et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Lausberg et al. (2021)} described 8 patients from 5 families with muscle hypotonia, developmental delay, progressive microcephaly, and brain MRI abnormalities. Age at onset ranged from birth to 6 months of age. Six patients had vision impairment, liver abnormalities, inflammation/inflammatory arthritis, and 5 patients had seizures. Three patients demonstrated cardiac abnormalities. Brain MRIs in the 8 patients showed varying degrees of frontotemporal atrophy, hypomyelination, thin corpus callosum, and Dandy Walker variant with hypoplasia of the caudal vermis. Four patients had absent or reduced glycogen branching enzyme (GBE1; {607839}) activity in tissues. Periodic acid-Schiff-positive deposits were observed in myocytes and macrophages in 1 patient and in liver in 3 patients.

{2:Wong et al. (2021)} described clinical features in 12 patients from 8 families with disease onset between birth and 3 months of age. All 12 patients had developmental delay, 9 of 10 patients had secondary microcephaly, 7 of 9 patients had dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, 6 of 7 patients had CNS hypomyelination, 7 of 7 patients had cerebral atrophy, and 11 of 11 patients had seizures. Immune anomalies included recurrent fevers in 8 patients, inflammatory arthritis in 3, septic arthritis in 2, aseptic osteomyelitis in 2, and hypochromic microcytic anemia in 4. Other features included hypotonia in 9 patients, muscle wasting in 8, abdominal distention in 4, spasticity in 4, and hepatomegaly in 2. Ten of 12 patients died between the ages of 9 and 32 months, and the 2 living patients were in critical condition.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of COXPD53 in the families reported by {1:Lausberg et al. (2021)} and {2:Wong et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 6 patients with COXPD53, who were from 4 families (German, Turkish, and 2 Kurdish), {1:Lausberg et al. (2021)} identified the same homozygous mutation ({619219.0001}) in the C2ORF69 gene. In 2 affected Pakistani sibs, {1:Lausberg et al. (2021)} identified a different homozygous mutation in the C2ORF69 gene ({619219.0002}). The mutations, which were identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families.

In 12 patients from 8 unrelated consanguineous families with COXPD53, {2:Wong et al. (2021)} identified homozygous mutations in the C2ORF69 gene ({619219.0001}; {619219.0003}-{619219.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Wong et al. (2021)} used CRISPR/Cas9 editing to produce c2orf62 knockout zebrafish. By 8 months of age, the knockout zebrafish had reduced weight and length compared to wildtype zebrafish, and they died between 8 and 10 months of age from spontaneous seizures. Reduction in latency for seizures induced by pentylenetetrazole (PTZ) was seen in knockout zebrafish larvae at 7 to 11 days postfertilization and in 2- to 3-month-old knockout zebrafish. At 4 months of age, the knockout fish showed signs of sterile CNS inflammation, including increased expression of il1-beta ({147720}), tgf-beta ({190180}), and tnf-alpha ({191160}).

phenotypes.phenotype: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and neurodevelopmental syndrome

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and neurodevelopmental syndrome (FSGSNEDS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TRIM8 gene ({606125}) on chromosome 10q24.

description.title: Description
description.content: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and neurodevelopmental syndrome (FSGSNEDS) is characterized by global developmental delay and renal dysfunction manifest as proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome apparent from infancy or early childhood. Some patients present with renal disease, whereas others present with developmental delay and develop renal disease later in childhood. Renal biopsy shows focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), but the course of the disease is variable: some patients have transient proteinuria and others require renal transplant. Neurodevelopmental features are also variable, with some patients having only mildly impaired intellectual development, and others having a severe developmental disorder associated with early-onset refractory seizures or epileptic encephalopathy. Additional features, including feeding difficulties, poor overall growth, and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, are commonly observed (summary by {1:Assoum et al., 2018} and {6:Weng et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{4:Sakai et al. (2016)} reported a 10-year-old Japanese boy who presented with recurrent refractory focal seizures at 2 months of age. EEG showed atypical hypsarrhythmia. Thereafter, he showed severe global developmental delay, with poor overall growth, microcephaly, limited activity due to being wheelchair-bound, no meaningful eye contact, and no language skills. Other features included small upslanted palpebral fissures, long arched eyebrows, thin lips, large ears, hip dislocation, enuresis, and constipation.

{1:Assoum et al. (2018)} reported 5 unrelated patients, ranging from 2 to 13 years of age, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder associated with early-onset seizures. Patient 2 had previously been reported by the {2:Epi4K Consortium and Epilepsy Phenome/Genome Project (2013)}. The patients had global developmental delay with poor motor and language skills. The severity of the phenotype was variable: more severely affected patients were unable to stand independently, had no language, and showed poor eye contact. However, some acquired walking by age 2 years. Expressive speech was absent or limited to a few words. The developmental delay was associated with stereotypies and autistic features in some cases. Infantile spasms and various types of seizures occurred in all patients between 5 months and 3 years of age. The seizures were refractory to medication in some cases. More variable features included ataxia, gait instability, dysmetria, hypotonia, poor growth, and abnormalities on brain imaging, including myelination defects, nonspecific white matter lesions, and brain atrophy. Only patient 1 had frank nephrotic syndrome with proteinuria, although 2 other patients had some evidence of proteinuria and hematuria. One patient (P4) was 2 years old and may have been too young for renal manifestations, which developed at age 4 years in patient 1. Some patients had variable dysmorphic features, including synophrys, long philtrum, sunken eyes, and gingival overgrowth.

{3:McClatchey et al. (2020)} reported an 8-year-old boy with FSGSNEDS. He had mild global developmental delay, with walking at 18 months, simple words at age 2, and mildly impaired intellectual development. During a concurrent infection at age 2 years, he was noted to have proteinuria in the nephrotic range. Renal biopsy showed features consistent with FSGS. He had 3 generalized seizures at age 5; seizures were well controlled by medication thereafter. The renal disease was progressive, resulting in renal transplant at age 7. He had challenging behavioral issues, but was able to attend a mainstream school with support. {3:McClatchey et al. (2020)} noted that the neurologic features in this patient were relatively mild, suggesting a phenotypic spectrum.

{5:Warren et al. (2020)} reported an 8-year-old Hispanic boy with FSGSNEDS. He had mildly delayed early milestones, with walking at 14 months and first words at 18 months. At age 29 months, he developed focal tonic-clonic seizures. At that time, nephrotic-range proteinuria was detected; renal biopsy showed FSGS. The disorder was progressive: by age 6, he had significant intellectual disability and language delay, multifocal drug-resistant epilepsy, and end-stage renal disease.

{6:Weng et al. (2021)} reported 11 unrelated patients with FSGSNEDS. After the index patient was identified, additional patients were ascertained from large cohorts of patients with FSGS/nephrotic syndrome or epilepsy. All patients had global developmental delay apparent from infancy or early childhood, and all but 1 developed seizures between 6 months and 4.5 years of age. Other features included hypotonia, delayed walking, and poor or absent speech. Behavioral abnormalities were sometimes present. Cerebral atrophy was observed in 6 of 8 patients who underwent imaging studies. All patients presented with proteinuria and hematuria associated with nephrotic syndrome between birth and 13.7 years, generally after the onset of neurologic disease. FSGS was found in 10 of 12 biopsies, whereas diffuse mesangial sclerosis was found in 2. Other renal findings included interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, and hyperechogenic kidneys on imaging. Five patients had renal transplants. More variable features included feeding difficulties, scoliosis, clinodactyly, and dysmorphic facial features, such as broad forehead, low-set ears, high-arched palate, hyperopia, and broad nasal bridge.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the TRIM8 gene that were identified in patients with FSGSNEDS by {1:Assoum et al. (2018)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 10-year-old Japanese boy with early-onset seizures and global developmental delay, {4:Sakai et al. (2016)} identified a de novo heterozygous 1-bp insertion (c.1099_1100insG) in the TRIM8 gene, predicted to result in a frameshift and premature termination (Cys367fs). The variant, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was absent from the dbSNP (build 137) and ExAC databases, as well as from 575 in-house controls. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. Detailed renal function in this patient was not ascertained. {1:Assoum et al. (2018)} described the variant as Cys367TrpfsTer43. {6:Weng et al. (2021)} noted that this variant occurred just before the NLS domain. Since the patient apparently did not have clinically significant renal symptoms, there may be a possible genotype/phenotype correlation. However, {6:Weng et al. (2021)} noted that a heterozygous variant affecting the same codon (c.1101C-A, C367X) was identified in a single patient aged 50 to 55 in the gnomAD database.

In 5 unrelated patients with FSGSNEDS, {1:Assoum et al. (2018)} identified de novo heterozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations in the last exon (exon 6) of the TRIM8 gene (see, e.g., {606125.0001}-{606125.0003}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors speculated that the mutant transcripts may escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and produce a stable protein product with dominant-negative characteristics.

In an 8-year-old boy with FSGSNEDS, {3:McClatchey et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation in the last exon of the TRIM8 gene ({606125.0004}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. The authors noted that the C-terminal region of TRIM8 is highly conserved and has a crucial role in the subcellular localization of the protein. The patient had severe renal disease, necessitating renal transplant at 7.5 years of age. Early in childhood, he had 3 seizures that were well-controlled.

In an 8-year-old Hispanic boy with FSGSNEDS, {5:Warren et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous nonsense mutation in the last exon of TRIM8 (Y460X; {606125.0005}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based next-generation sequencing, was absent from unaffected family members. Patient kidney biopsy showed no significant TRIM8 expression in any cells, suggesting that the mutation might alter normal protein structure and homodimerization. In addition, patient cells showed strong SOCS1 ({603597}) expression, which the authors noted is normally downregulated by TRIM8 through its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity. {5:Warren et al. (2020)} postulated a dominant-negative effect.

In 11 unrelated patients with FSGSNEDS, {6:Weng et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations in the last exon of the TRIM8 gene (see, e.g., {606125.0003}; {606125.0006}-{606125.0008}). The mutation in the first patient (UC-023-1) was found by trio-based exome sequencing. Seven additional patients with mutations were identified from a large cohort of 2,501 children with FSGS or nephrotic syndrome, and all were found to have some sort of developmental delay. Three additional patients were identified from a cohort of 9,057 patients with a broad diagnosis of epilepsy; all 3 developed nephrotic syndrome. These findings established that de novo mutations in the TRIM8 gene are the genetic basis for an early-onset neuro-renal syndrome.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome-4 (RTSC4) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the DPYSL5 gene ({608383}) on chromosome 2p23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome-4 (RTSC4) is characterized by a constellation of congenital anomalies, including dysmorphic craniofacial features and structural brain anomalies, such as Dandy-Walker malformation ({220200}), hindbrain malformations, or agenesis of the corpus callosum, associated with global developmental delay and impaired intellectual development. Congenital cardiac defects have been reported in 1 family (summary by {4:Ritscher et al., 1987} and {2:Jeanne et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome, see RTSC1 ({220210}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{4:Ritscher et al. (1987)} reported 2 sisters with a unique constellation of craniofacial, neurologic, brain, and cardiac abnormalities. They presented at birth with notable craniofacial features, including macrocephaly, a prominent forehead and occiput, open fontanelles and sutures, foramina parietalia, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, short nose with anteverted nostrils, depressed nasal bridge, narrow palate, apparently low-set ears, open mouth with protruding tongue. They also had hypotonia with poor spontaneous movements and poor overall somatic growth with impaired intellectual development. The older sib had a Dandy-Walker malformation ({220200}) with communicating hydrocephalus and aplasia of the posterior portion of the cerebellar vermis. Her sister had a Dandy-Walker variant, with aplasia of the cerebellar vermis and hypoplasia of the hemispheres, large cisterna magna, high insertion of the confluent sinus, but no hydrocephalus. The older sister had congenital heart defects with a common atrioventricular canal; she died at age 3.5 years after cardiac surgery. The younger sister had a successful heart operation on a cleft mitral valve and septum primum defect. Family history revealed a boy who died of asphyxia and multiple congenital anomalies soon after birth, as well as a spontaneous abortion during the third gestational month. The parents were clinically unaffected; {4:Ritscher et al. (1987)} suggested autosomal recessive inheritance. {3:Lauener et al. (1989)} provided follow-up information on the surviving younger sister, who was found to have a humoral immunodeficiency with markedly reduced immunoglobulin levels, especially affecting IgG2 and IgG4 subclasses, and antipolysaccharide antibody formation. Although possibly only coincidence, the authors suggested that the immunodeficiency might be a manifestation of the syndrome. {1:Aldinger et al. (2019)} and {2:Jeanne et al. (2021)} also provided follow-up of the surviving sister from the original family reported by {4:Ritscher et al. (1987)}. They noted that the cardiac defects in these sisters may be part of the spectrum of RTSC4, although they could represent an unrelated condition.

{2:Jeanne et al. (2021)} reported 8 unrelated patients ranging from 2.5 to 33 years of age with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder with structural brain anomalies. The patients had global developmental delay with hypotonia and severe intellectual disability with poor or absent speech. Five patients achieved independent walking between 3 and 7 years of age; 3 patients were nonambulatory. Many patients had swallowing difficulties, stereotypic or choreoathetoid movements, ataxia, or strabismus. Some had behavioral abnormalities, such as aggression or stereotypies. Two patients had seizures, focal and generalized, and another had abnormal movements. Brain imaging showed agenesis of the corpus callosum in all patients. Six had cerebellar hypoplasia, 2 had hippocampal dysplasia, 1 had abnormal myelination, and 1 had Dandy-Walker malformation with encephalocele. Although most patients had dysmorphic craniofacial features, there was no consistent pattern. Features included microcephaly (3 patients), brachycephaly, plagiocephaly, deep-set eyes, prominent eyes, hypotelorism, hypertelorism, short philtrum, narrow palate, large ears, and depressed nasal bridge. Other features included short stature, scoliosis, hip dysplasia or dislocation, joint hypermobility, tapering fingers, and foot malposition. Two patients had micropenis and 1 had cryptorchidism. None had cardiac abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the DPYSL5 gene that were identified in patients with RTSC4 by {2:Jeanne et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In the surviving sister with Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome originally reported by {4:Ritscher et al. (1987)}, {1:Aldinger et al. (2019)} and {2:Jeanne et al. (2021)} identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the DPYSL5 gene (G47R; {608383.0001}). This molecular finding delineated another genetic form of the disorder, designated RTSC4. The transmission pattern was consistent with parental gonadal mosaicism. In 8 additional patients with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder with features of RTSC4, {2:Jeanne et al. (2021)} identified a recurrent de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the DPYSL5 gene (E41K; {608383.0002}). The patients were ascertained through international collaboration and the GeneMatcher Program. The mutations were found by exome sequencing; neither was present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies showed that both the G47R and E41K mutations abolished the inhibitory effect of DPYSL5 on dendritic and neurite outgrowth in transfected primary neurons, suggesting a loss of function. Protein stability and oligomer assembly were likely not affected, but both variants showed altered interaction with complex members MAP2 ({157130}) and TUBB3 ({602661}), which are neuronal cytoskeleton-associated proteins. Disruption of this interaction could allow DPYSL2 ({602463}) to continue promoting neurite outgrowth because of loss of inhibition by DPYSL5, ultimately resulting in brain malformations and abnormal neurodevelopment.
