text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Luo-Schoch-Yamamoto syndrome (LUSYAM) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RNF2 gene ({608985}) on chromosome 1q25.

description.title: Description
description.content: Luo-Schoch-Yamamoto syndrome (LUSYAM) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay and impaired intellectual development apparent from infancy. Affected individuals have delayed walking, early-onset seizures, hypotonia, dysmorphic facial features, and white matter abnormalities on brain imaging ({1:Luo et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Luo et al. (2021)} reported 2 unrelated girls, 11 and 3.5 years of age, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intrauterine growth retardation, global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, feeding difficulties requiring feeding tube in 1 patient, abnormal stereotypic behavior, and early-onset seizures. Around 9 years of age, the older girl (patient 1) showed developmental regression with loss of language and purposeful use of the hands; this was associated with increased seizure frequency. The younger girl (patient 2) showed poor eye contact, was unable to walk, and could only babble. Both patients had variable dysmorphic features, including hypertelorism, upturned nose, short philtrum, strabismus, and exotropia. Patient 1 had depressed nasal bridge, arched eyebrows, deep-set eyes, and prominent wide mouth with widely spaced incisors, whereas patient 2 had almond-shaped eyes, small mouth, and dysplastic ears. Other variable features included small hands and feet, hypotonia, and hyperreflexia. Brain imaging showed delayed myelination and white matter abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the RNF2 gene that were identified in patients with LUSYAM by {1:Luo et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated girls with LUSYAM, {1:Luo et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the RNF2 gene (R70H, {608985} and S82R, {608985.0002}). Both mutations occurred at conserved residues in the zinc finger motif. The mutations, which were found by genome or exome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of patient cells were not performed, but neither mutation was able to rescue lethality in a Drosophila model with knockdown of the orthologous gene (Sce). Further studies in Drosophila indicated that R70H is an amorphic allele, whereas S82R is hypomorphic, consistent with a loss-of-function effect and haploinsufficiency.

preferredTitle: CILIARY DYSKINESIA, PRIMARY, 47, AND LISSENCEPHALY; CILD47
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the tumor protein p73 gene (TP73,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the tumor protein p73 gene (TP73,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that primary ciliary dyskinesia-47 and lissencephaly (CILD47) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TP73 gene ({601990}) on chromosome 1p36.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Primary ciliary dyskinesia-47 and lissencephaly (CILD47) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by onset of recurrent respiratory infections and respiratory dysfunction caused by defective mucociliary clearance in early childhood. Affected individuals also have neurologic features, such as impaired intellectual development and central hypotonia, associated with structural brain abnormalities, most notably lissencephaly and thin or absent corpus callosum. The disorder results from impaired function of motile ciliopathy and can be classified as 'reduced generation of multiple motile cilia' (RGMC). Situs inversus is not observed (summary by {1:Wallmeier et al., 2021}).

For a phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of primary ciliary dyskinesia, see CILD1 ({244400}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Wallmeier et al. (2021)} reported 7 patients from 5 unrelated consanguineous families with CILD47. The patients had chronic disease of the upper and lower respiratory tract characterized by recurrent infections of the airways, productive cough, chronic rhinitis, and otitis media. Several patients presented in the neonatal period requiring ventilatory support; 1 died from respiratory failure at 2 months of age. Chest imaging showed atelectasis, mucus plugging, and bronchiectasis None of the patients had situs inversus. In addition, the patients had similar cortical malformations most consistent with anterior-predominant lissencephaly with thin, hypoplastic, or even absent corpus callosum. This was associated with variably impaired intellectual development and central hypotonia. Two patients had evidence of increased seizure susceptibility.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CILD47 in the families reported by {1:Wallmeier et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 7 children from 5 unrelated consanguineous families with CILD47, {1:Wallmeier et al. (2021)} identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the TP73 gene ({601990.0001}-{601990.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Some of the patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program. All the mutations affected both isoforms and were predicted to result in complete TP73 deficiency. Studies of patient-derived respiratory epithelial cells showed reduced numbers of multiciliated cells, a reduction in ciliary length, and a significant reduction in mucociliary clearance at the air-liquid interface compared to controls. Ultrastructural analysis showed that although there was some mislocalization of the basal bodies, there was not a severe defect in basal body amplification or positioning; axonemal composition and assembly was also normal. Dynamic particle-tracking studies of patient cells confirmed compromised ciliary airway clearance. The overall findings were consistent with a defect in the differentiation of multiciliated cells. Patient cells also showed decreased nuclear expression of the transcription factor-related genes FOXJ1 ({602291}) and RFX2 ({142765}), which are regulated by TP73. Mutations in FOXJ1 cause CILD43 ({618699}).

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Yang et al. (2000)} generated mice deficient in p73 by targeted disruption. Mice functionally deficient for all p73 isoforms exhibited profound defects, including hippocampal dysgenesis, hydrocephalus, chronic infections and inflammation, as well as abnormalities in pheromone sensory pathways. In contrast to p53-deficient mice, however, mice lacking p73 showed no increased susceptibility to spontaneous tumorigenesis. Functional loss of p73 leads to disappearance of the Cajal-Retzius (CR) neurons in the cortical marginal zone and hippocampal molecular layer, and this defect underlies the hippocampal dysgenesis seen in p73 mice. Notably, the loss of CR neurons in the p73 -/- mouse is not accompanied by a cortical lamination defect, as seen in the 'reeler' mouse (see {600514}). The link between the absence of these CR neurons and the striking yet highly site-specific dysgenesis in the p73 -/- brain suggested that CR neurons, widely believed to control cortical neurogenesis, may instead have a critical role in hippocampal development. The p73-deficient male mice lacked both interest in sexually mature females and aggressive responses to other males. p73 -/- male and female mice were reproductively deficient. No structural abnormalities in the reproductive organs of either male or female p73 -/- mice were observed, but the highest level of p73 RNA in the mouse was found in the neuroepithelium of both the embryonic and adult vomeronasal organ, an accessory olfactory structure involved in pheromone detection. These results suggested that additional defects of sensory or hormonal pathways may contribute to the reproductive and behavioral phenotypes of p73-deficient mice.

clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the adaptor-related protein complex 1, gamma-1 subunit gene (AP1G1,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the adaptor-related protein complex 1, gamma-1 subunit gene (AP1G1,)

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant Usmani-Riazzudin syndrome (USRISD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the AP1G1 gene ({603533}) on chromosome 16q22.

Homozygous mutation in the AP1G1 gene causes autosomal recessive Usmani-Riazzudin syndrome (USRISR; {619548}), which shows overlapping clinical features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal dominant Usmani-Riazzudin syndrome (USRISD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and speech delay, hypotonia, and behavioral abnormalities, most commonly aggressive behavior. More variable additional features may include seizures and distal limb anomalies (summary by {1:Usmani et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Usmani et al. (2021)} reported 9 unrelated patients (families 3-11), ranging in age from 22 days to 40 years, with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing, and the phenotype was characterized retrospectively. Two patients had died at 22 days and 4 years. All had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, speech delay, and behavioral abnormalities, including aggression, hyperactivity, autistic features, impulsivity, and compulsive behavior. Four patients had seizures. Most had hypotonia and distal limb anomalies, such as small hands and feet, fifth finger clinodactyly, short or long digits, and flat feet. Less common features, observed in only 1 or 2 patients, included strabismus, esotropia, amblyopia, hearing loss, frontal bossing, spasticity, pectus anomalies, and kyphosis or lordosis.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the AP1G1 gene that were identified in patients with USRISD by {1:Usmani et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 9 unrelated patients with USRISD, {1:Usmani et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the AP1G1 gene (see, e.g., {603533.0001}-{603533.0003}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and the patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program. There were 3 missense mutations in the N-terminal region (R15Q, R35W, and R35Q), a missense mutation in the C-terminal region (P820R), 2 splice site mutations, and 2 frameshift mutations. The variants were absent from public databases, including gnomAD. Expression of the mutations in HEK293 cells showed that some variants increased protein expression, whereas others decreased protein expression. The frameshift mutations caused a loss of AP1G1 protein expression, suggesting haploinsufficiency. The missense variants R15Q, R35W, and R35Q formed abnormal protein aggregates, whereas P820R had diffuse localization throughout the cytoplasm. These findings suggested that the missense mutations may have a toxic dominant-negative effect. {1:Usmani et al. (2021)} found that homozygous loss of the ap1g1 ortholog in zebrafish was embryonic lethal. Expression of wildtype human AP1G1 was able to rescue the survival, whereas expression of R15Q, R35W, and R35Q also caused poor survival with even increased lethality, further suggesting a dominant-negative effect of these variants.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor and speech delay and behavioral abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with motor and speech delay and behavioral abnormalities (NEDMOSBA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TMEM222 gene ({619469}) on chromosome 1p36.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor and speech delay and behavioral abnormalities (NEDMOSBA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent from early childhood. There is significant phenotypic variability: some patients achieve walking and talking after a few years, whereas others develop spastic tetraplegia with inability to walk independently and never gain proper speech. Affected individuals may have variable additional features, including poor overall growth, hypotonia, tremor, ocular anomalies, seizures, and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features (summary by {1:Polla et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Polla et al. (2021)} reported 17 patients from 9 unrelated families with an overlapping neurodevelopmental phenotype. The patients were ascertained from international research or diagnostic centers through the GeneMatcher Program after undergoing exome sequencing. The families were of Turkish, Pakistani, Jordanian, Iranian, Polish, Russian, Arab, and US origin; 7 families were consanguineous. The patients, who ranged from 8 months to 36 years of age, all had global developmental delay with moderate to severely impaired intellectual development, delayed walking, and poor or absent speech. Most had behavioral abnormalities, including shy character, hyperactivity, stereotypic movements, and autistic features. Seven patients had seizures. Some patients had spasticity and inability to walk. Other manifestations included hypotonia, broad-based gait, decreased muscle mass, and poor overall growth. A few patients had microcephaly. More variable features included cortical visual impairment, strabismus, optic nerve atrophy, tremor, axonal polyneuropathy, and foot deformities. Some patients were noted to have nonspecific dysmorphic features, such as deep-set eyes, hypertelorism, large nose, short philtrum, large mouth with full lips, broad toes, and hypoplastic nails. Brain imaging, when performed, was normal in some patients, but showed nonspecific abnormalities in others. A few patients had cerebral atrophy and 1 had a simplified gyral pattern.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMOSBA in the families reported by {1:Polla et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 17 patients from 9 unrelated families with NEDMOSBA, {1:Polla et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the TMEM222 gene (see, e.g., {619469.0001}-{619469.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. The mutations included 1 in-frame deletion, 1 nonsense variant, and 3 missense, 2 frameshift, and 2 splice site variants. None were present in the homozygous state in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the mutations were not performed, but they were predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay or to interfere with proper protein function. Some of the patients had additional variants in other genes that may have contributed to the phenotypic variability that was observed.

preferredTitle: DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY, IMPAIRED SPEECH, AND BEHAVIORAL ABNORMALITIES; DDISBA
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the spectrin, beta, nonerythrocytic, 1 gene (SPTBN1,)

Head: Large head

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the spectrin, beta, nonerythrocytic, 1 gene (SPTBN1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities (DDISBA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SPTBN1 gene ({182790}) on chromosome 2p16.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities (DDISBA) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent from early childhood. Intellectual disability can range from mild to severe. Additional variable features may include dysmorphic facial features, seizures, hypotonia, motor abnormalities such as Tourette syndrome or dystonia, and hearing loss (summary by {1:Cousin et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Cousin et al. (2021)} reported 29 patients from 28 unrelated families (1 sib pair) with DDISBA. The patients, who ranged from 6 months to 26 years of age, were identified through professional collaboration and tools such as the GeneMatcher Program after undergoing genome or exome sequencing. There was significant phenotypic variability, even among patients with the same mutation. All had developmental delay, often with impaired speech and variably impaired intellectual development. Additional features included motor delay, abnormal movements with hypo- or hypertonia, sleep disturbances, hearing impairment (5 patients), and seizures (9 patients). Three showed developmental regression. Almost all patients had behavioral abnormalities, including autistic features, ADD, ADHD, anxiety, obsessive or aggressive behavior, and emotional lability. Seven patients had nonspecific findings on brain imaging, including enlarged ventricles, cerebral or cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and delayed myelination. Many had nonspecific dysmorphic features, such as frontal bossing, hypertelorism, depressed and wide nasal bridge, thick lips, and head size or shape anomalies. Short stature was noted in some patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: In most patients with DDISBA, the heterozygous mutations in the SPTBN1 gene that were identified by {1:Cousin et al. (2021)} occurred de novo; 1 family showed autosomal dominant inheritance through maternal mosaicism.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 29 patients from 28 unrelated families with DDISBA, {1:Cousin et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous mutations in the SPTBN1 gene (see, e.g., {182790.0001}-{182790.0005}). The mutations were found by whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing; almost all were absent from the gnomAD database. The mutations occurred de novo in all patients except for 1 family in which 2 affected sibs inherited a variant from their unaffected mother who was mosaic. One patient (P10) had 2 de novo SPTBN1 variants in the cis configuration. The mutations occurred at conserved residues throughout the gene: about half clustered in the CH2 region in the N-terminal domain, whereas the others occurred in spectrin repeat domains. There were 22 missense, 3 nonsense, and 3 splice site mutations. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells transfected with a subset of the variants demonstrated variable effects. Most resulted in normal protein expression, although some had reduced protein levels. The nonsense mutations yielded protein fragments of the expected size, suggesting that the truncated proteins are structurally stable. Several mutant proteins formed cytosolic aggregates, and some caused abnormal membrane protrusions, suggesting an impact on cytoskeletal structures. Further studies showed that some mutations disrupted normal protein-protein interactions and binding to F-actin and ankyrin-B (ANK2; {106410}). Studies of cortical neurons derived from Sptbn1-null mice showed impaired organization of the axon initial segment (AIS) with reduced axonal growth, dendritic abnormalities, and aberrant lysosome dynamics. These defects could not be fully rescued by expression of some of the mutations found in patients, further suggesting pathogenicity. Heterozygous knockdown of the Sptbn1 gene in mice caused thinning of the corpus callosum consistent with neuronal miswiring or abnormal connectivity. Heterozygous mutant mice demonstrated dysmorphic facial features, hyperactivity, impaired motor abilities, and social deficits, similar to the human phenotype. The authors concluded that some of the mutations resulted in haploinsufficiency, whereas others had a dominant-negative or gain-of-function effect, the latter possibly due to cytosolic aggregates or abnormal membrane morphology.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and thin corpus callosum

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and thin corpus callosum (NEDDFAC) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SUPT16H gene ({605012}) on chromosome 14q11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and thin corpus callosum (NEDDFAC) is characterized by global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech and language, and dysmorphic facial features. Brain imaging tends to show thin corpus callosum and decreased white matter volume. Additional features such as seizures, cardiac defects, and behavioral abnormalities may also occur. The phenotype is variable (summary by {1:Bina et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Bina et al. (2020)} reported 4 unrelated children (patients 1 to 4), ranging from 2 to 12 years of age, with global developmental delay, delayed walking, intellectual disability, and poor or absent speech, sometimes with poor eye contact. Some had early respiratory or feeding difficulties. Two patients had autistic features and sleep disturbances; 1 had simple partial seizures. They had variable dysmorphic facial features, including dolicho- or plagiocephaly, frontal bossing, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, downslanting palpebral fissures, strabismus, dysplastic ears, broad nasal bridge, and tented upper lip. Patient 2, a 12-year-old boy, had precocious puberty. Patient 4, a 2-year-old girl also had mixed hearing loss, torticollis, hydronephrosis, and congenital heart defects, and was tube-fed. Brain imaging, performed in 3 patients, showed thin corpus callosum and decreased white matter volume in 2, and nonspecific cerebral atrophy in the third. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program and the clinical features reviewed retrospectively.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SUPT16H gene that were identified in patients with NEDDFAC by {1:Bina et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 unrelated patients with NEDDFAC, {1:Bina et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous missense variants in the SUPT16H gene (see, e.g., {605012.0001}-{605012.0003}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and occurred throughout the gene, were absent from public databases, including gnomAD. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. The authors postulated that the mutations may result in a loss of function and cause chromatin and transcription deregulation.

preferredTitle: CENTRAL HYPOVENTILATION SYNDROME, CONGENITAL, 2, AND AUTONOMIC DYSFUNCTION; CCHS2
clinicalSynopsis: Early death may occur due to respiratory dysfunction
Three patients in one consanguineous family have been reported (last curated August 2021)
Caused by mutation in the myosin IH gene (MYO1H,)

Three patients in one consanguineous family have been reported (last curated August 2021)

phenotypes.phenotype: ?Central hypoventilation syndrome, congenital, 2, and autonomic dysfunction

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital central hypoventilation syndrome-2 and autonomic dysfunction (CCHS2) is caused by homozygous mutation in the MYO1H gene ({614636}) on chromosome 12q24. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome-2 and autonomic dysfunction (CCHS2) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by shallow breathing and apneic spells apparent in the neonatal period. Affected infants require mechanical ventilation due to impaired ventilatory response to hypercapnia, as well as tube feeding due to poor swallowing, aspiration, and gastrointestinal dysmotility. Some patients have other features of autonomic dysfunction, including bladder dysfunction, sinus bradycardia, and temperature dysregulation. Although mild global developmental delay with learning difficulties and seizures were present in the single family reported, it was unclear if these features were related to the hypoventilation phenotype ({1:Spielmann et al., 2017}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of CCHS, see CCHS1 ({209880}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Spielmann et al. (2017)} reported 3 sibs, born of consanguineous parents with Native American background, with central hypoventilation apparent from early infancy. The patients presented in the neonatal period with alveolar hypoventilation, shallow breathing, and apnea, requiring mechanical ventilation initially during sleeping but later also while awake. They lacked a ventilatory response to high levels of CO2, necessitating tracheostomy. All 3 infants also had feeding difficulties with gastroesophageal reflux, aspiration, autonomic features of esophageal and intestinal dysmotility, and achalasia, requiring tube feeding. One infant died at 11 months of age, whereas the other 2 patients were alive at 8 and 15 years. The oldest patient had additional signs of autonomic dysfunction, including sinus bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, and bladder dysfunction requiring catheterization. She also had kyphoscoliosis with restrictive lung disease, a nonspecific myopathy, strabismus, myopia, and astigmatism. Both older patients had global developmental delay with hypotonia and poor walking, but were able to attend special education schools. These 2 older patients also developed well-controlled seizures at ages 4 and 15, respectively. {1:Spielmann et al. (2017)} noted that these additional findings, such as seizures and developmental delay, may be unrelated to the hypoventilation disorder. A fourth sib, who was heterozygous for the MYO1H mutation, had mild breathing and swallowing difficulties in infancy, but had no admissions to the ICU or evidence of oxygen desaturation; this individual was considered to be unaffected.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CCHS2 in the family reported by {1:Spielmann et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 sibs, born of consanguineous parents of Native American descent, with CCHS2, {1:Spielmann et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the MYO1H gene ({614636.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of linkage analysis and whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not present in the ExAC database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but it was predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and a loss of function. PHOX2B ({603851}) mutations had been excluded in these patients. Mutations in the MYO1H gene were not identified in 23 additional individuals with symptoms of central hypoventilation who were negative for PHOX2B testing, suggesting that MYO1H mutations are not a common cause of the disorder.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Spielmann et al. (2017)} found that homozygous loss of Myo1h in mice caused neonatal feeding problems, cyanosis, and poor respiration, resulting in death within the first 4 hours of birth. This was associated with marked deficits in ventilatory parameters and an attenuated response to hypercapnia compared to controls.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome-8 (AGS8) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the LSM11 gene ({617910}) on chromosome 5q33. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome-8 (AGS8) is a type I interferonopathy characterized by severe developmental delay and progressive neurologic deterioration ending in premature death. Brain imaging shows diffusely abnormal white matter, severe cerebral atrophy, and intracranial calcification ({1:Uggenti et al., 2020}).

For a general phenotypic description and discussion of genetic heterogeneity of Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, see AGS1 ({225750}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Uggenti et al. (2020)} reported 2 Pakistani brothers (family AGS114), born of first-cousin parents, who died at 2 years of age with AGS. The brothers exhibited neonatal irritability and seizures, with severe developmental delay and deterioration of neurologic status before succumbing. Brain imaging showed diffusely abnormal white matter, intracranial calcification involving the basal ganglia, and severe cerebral atrophy that was most prominent in the temporal and frontal lobes. Elevated interferon scores were documented in the younger brother at 4 months and 15 months of age. Both brothers were noted to have small genitalia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of AGS8 in the family reported by {1:Uggenti et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: By whole-exome sequencing in a cohort of individuals exhibiting the typical features of AGS, but who were negative for mutation in known AGS-associated genes, {1:Uggenti et al. (2020)} identified 2 Pakistani brothers who were homozygous for a missense mutation in the LSM11 gene (G211S; {617910.0001}). Their unaffected first-cousin parents were heterozygous for the mutation, which was not found in public variant databases.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome-9 (AGS9) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the RNU7-1 gene ({617876}) on chromosome 12p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome-9 (AGS9) is a type I interferonopathy characterized by severe developmental delay and progressive neurologic deterioration. Patients present in infancy with irritability and spasticity. Brain imaging shows diffusely abnormal white matter, cerebral atrophy, and intracranial calcification. Premature death has been associated with renal and/or hepatic failure ({1:Uggenti et al., 2020}).

For a general phenotypic description and discussion of genetic heterogeneity of Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, see AGS1 ({225750}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Uggenti et al. (2020)} reported 16 patients from 11 families with AGS and mutations in the RNU7-1 gene. Patients exhibited increased tone or spasticity in the neonatal period and developed spastic dystonia, diplegia, or quadriplegia. Many experienced severe motor disability, with no trunk control and inability to sit, and some exhibited pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs. Although some patients had preserved cognition, most had limited or no speech. Elevated liver transaminases were observed, and early death was associated with liver failure in 2 French sibs (family AGS532); other deaths were associated with renal failure (families AGS694, AGS695, and AGS2412) or seizures (in 1 of 3 Japanese sibs, family AGS620). Inter- and intrafamilial variability was observed: a 15-year-old British girl (AGS271) had relatively preserved cognition, whereas a 23-year-old Belgian man with the same mutations (AGS561) had severe developmental delay, and a French boy from a third family with the same mutations (AGS2412) died at age 9 with pericardial effusion and renal and hepatic insufficiency.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of AGS9 in the families reported by {1:Uggenti et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: By whole-genome and targeted Sanger sequencing in a cohort of individuals exhibiting the typical features of AGS, but who were negative for mutations in known AGS-associated genes, {1:Uggenti et al. (2020)} identified 16 patients from 11 families with compound heterozygosity for mutations in the RNU7-1 gene (see, e.g., {617876.0001}-{617876.0006}). The mutations segregated with disease in the respective families, and none of the variants had a frequency greater than 0.005 in the gnomAD database. Noting that neither parental consanguinity nor mutational homozygosity was observed for this phenotype, the authors suggested that it results from the combination of a severe and a mild mutation, with biallelic severe mutations likely resulting in embryonic lethality, and 2 milder variants causing no phenotype or a phenotype not ascertained in their study.

preferredTitle: CONGENITAL DISORDER OF GLYCOSYLATION, TYPE 2v; CDG2V

phenotypes.phenotype: Congenital disorder of glycosylation, type IIv

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital disorder of glycosylation type 2v (CDG2V) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the EDEM3 gene ({610214}) on chromosome 1q25.

description.title: Description
description.content: Congenital disorder of glycosylation type 2v (CDG2V) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by neurodevelopmental delay and variable facial dysmorphisms ({1:Polla et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Polla et al. (2021)} reported clinical features in 12 patients who presented with developmental delay, speech delay, and/or impaired intellectual development. Hypotonia was present in 6 of the 12 patients. Dysmorphic facial features included narrow palpebral fissures (6/12), epicanthal folds (6/12), increased nasal height (8/12), bulbous nasal tip (6/12), hypoplastic alae nasi (9/12), short philtrum (6/12), thin upper lip (9/12), strabismus (3/12), and retrognathia (6/12). Other findings included nevus flameus in 3 patients, ptosis in 3 patients, and low-set ears in 3 patients. Gastroesophageal reflux was reported in 3 patients, and 2 patients had early feeding problems requiring a nasogastric tube. Brain MRI showed a widened cisterna magna in 1 patient and periventricular leukomalacia in another patient.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDG2V in the families reported by {1:Polla et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 12 patients from 7 families with congenital disorder of glycosylation type 2v, {1:Polla et al. (2021)} identified biallelic mutations in the EDEM3 gene ({610214.0001}-{610214.0008}). The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing. Seven patients from 4 families had homozygous mutations, and 5 patients from 3 families had compound heterozygous mutations. All of the mutations were predicted to be protein-truncating, with the exception of compound heterozygous mutations in 1 patient (family 7). Analysis of the N-glycan profile of total plasma glycoproteins from all affected individuals showed decreased levels of M3-M7 glycan species with normal M8 and M9 species (or sometimes mildly increased M9 species) compared to controls. The M3:M4 ratio was reduced in all 12 affected patients tested, consistent with a possible role of EDEM3 in trimming M5 to shorter polymannose glycans.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Polla et al. (2021)} analyzed N-glycan profiles in Edem3 knockout mice. Plasma from the knockout mice showed decreased ratios of M5:M9, M6:M9, and M7:M9 glycan species compared to controls. Plasma proteins also had significantly increased abundance of M8 and M9 glycan species. N-glycan profiles of brain lysate from knockout mice showed increased high-mannose M8 and M9 N-glycan species and decreased ratios of M5:M9 and M6:M9 species. {1:Polla et al. (2021)} concluded that these profiles were consistent with the known role of EDEM3 in trimming M8B.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA AND DYSMORPHIC FACIES; NEDHYDF
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the guanine nucleotide-binding protein, beta-2 gene (GNB2,)

Brachycephaly

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and dysmorphic facies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and dysmorphic facies (NEDHYDF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNB2 gene ({139390}) on chromosome 7q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and dysmorphic facies (NEDHYDF) is characterized by global developmental delay and hypotonia apparent from birth. Affected individuals have variably impaired intellectual development, often with speech delay and delayed walking. Seizures are generally not observed, although some patients may have single seizures or late-onset epilepsy. Most patients have prominent dysmorphic facial features. Additional features may include congenital cardiac defects (without arrhythmia), nonspecific renal anomalies, joint contractures or joint hyperextensibility, dry skin, and cryptorchidism. There is significant phenotypic variability in both the neurologic and extraneurologic manifestations (summary by {3:Tan et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Fukuda et al. (2020)} reported a 7.5-year-old Japanese girl who presented at birth with hypotonia and significant joint contractures consistent with arthrogryposis. She had global developmental delay and impaired intellectual development with independent walking and a few words achieved at age 5 years. Notable dysmorphic features included brachycephaly, micrognathia, thin upper lip, thick eyebrows, prominent chin, exotropia, dental crowding, tapered fingers, hyperextensibility of the finger joints, and hypertrichosis on her back. She had 1 seizure at age 7 years; brain imaging was unremarkable.

{2:Lansdon et al. (2021)} reported a 15-year-old girl with NEDHYDF. She presented at 7 months of age with hypotonia; the mother reported decreased fetal movements. The patient had global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor speech, although she was able to attend a special school. She developed complex partial seizures at age 6. Dysmorphic features included blue sclerae, dolichocephaly, frontal bossing, large jaw, small mouth, high-arched palate, poor dentition, arachnodactyly, and loose skin. She also had rapid growth consistent with generalized overgrowth, although it was unclear whether this was an example of phenotypic variability or reflected an additional diagnosis.

{3:Tan et al. (2022)} reported 11 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 2 to 26 years, with a similar syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through the Matchmaker Exchange program after GNB2 mutations were identified through molecular studies, and the phenotype of the patients was collected retrospectively. All had global developmental delay with variably impaired motor, speech, and intellectual development. Six patients had autism or autistic traits, such as stereotypic behavior. Most had hypotonia with delayed walking by a few years, often with an unsteady or wide-based gait. Speech was also delayed; the more severely affected patients were nonverbal. Three patients (P1, P2, and P3), who had the same mutation (A73T), had a milder phenotype and were able to achieve some developmental milestones and attend special schools. Three patients were noted to have aspiration, including 1 who had apneic episodes in the first year of life. A few required tracheostomy and/or feeding tubes. One patient (P8) had an axonal neuropathy confirmed by electrophysiologic studies. Only 2 had seizures: 1 patient had a single seizure at age 9 years and another had onset of generalized seizures at age 14 years. Brain imaging was essentially normal, although rare patients had nonspecific abnormalities, such as T2-weighted hyperintensities. Most patients had dysmorphic facial features, including tall or large forehead with high anterior hairline, prominent philtrum, long palpebral fissures, deep-set eyes, hypertelorism, exotropia, esotropia, nystagmus, medial flared or straight eyebrows, full cheeks with prominent nasolabial folds, wide mouth, downturned corners of the mouth, micrognathia, and low-set or large ears. Skeletal anomalies included joint hyperextensibility, tapering fingers, and fifth finger clinodactyly; 1 patient had congenital arthrogryposis. Many patients also had chronic dry skin. Three patients had congenital heart defects, mainly septal defects, but none had cardiac arrhythmias. Three patients had nonspecific renal anomalies, such as displaced kidney, nephrocalcinosis, and vesicoureteral reflux. Additional features included constipation and undescended testes. The authors also identified a fetus (P9) with multiple significant congenital anomalies, including cardiac, renal, and head-body discordance, necessitating termination of the pregnancy at 20 weeks' gestation.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the GNB2 gene that were identified in patients with NEDHYDF by {1:Fukuda et al. (2020)}, {2:Lansdon et al. (2021)}, and {3:Tan et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 7.5-year-old Japanese girl with NEDHYDF, {1:Fukuda et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GNB2 gene (G77R; {139390.0002}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the variant was predicted to be detrimental since mutations affecting the homologous Gly77 residue in the GNB1 gene ({139380}) have been reported in patients with an overlapping neurodevelopmental disorder ({616973}).

In a 15-year-old girl with NEDHYDF, {2:Lansdon et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GNB2 gene, resulting in a gly77-to-trp (G77W; {139390.0003}) substitution. The mutation, which was found by trio-based exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 11 unrelated patients with NEDHYDF, {3:Tan et al. (2022)} identified 5 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the GNB2 gene (see, e.g., {139390.0002}; {139390.0004}-{139390.0006}). The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Exchange program and the mutations were found through genome or exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. However, molecular modeling indicated that all of the mutations occurred at conserved residues at different parts of shared interface regions of GNB2, particularly disrupting affinity to the G-alpha subunit. The mutations were predicted to differentially alter binding to various effectors as well, which would influence downstream signaling pathways. {3:Tan et al. (2022)} suggested that the mutations may have subtle functional differences, which may account for phenotypic variability.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Chopra-Amiel-Gordon syndrome (CAGS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ANKRD17 gene ({615929}) on chromosome 4q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Chopra-Amiel-Gordon syndrome (CAGS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by developmental delay and/or impaired intellectual development, speech delay, facial dysmorphism, and variable other features, including recurrent bacterial infections, ophthalmologic abnormalities, and nonspecific brain abnormalities ({1:Chopra et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Chopra et al. (2021)} reported clinical features of 34 patients from 32 families ascertained using GeneMatcher and DECIPHER. The patients ranged in age from 4 months to 34 years. The primary features in 31 patients were global developmental delay and/or impaired intellectual development. The severity was variable, with 19 patients in the moderate to severe range and 12 in the mild or borderline range. Speech development was delayed in 29 individuals, including 6 with absent speech. Less commonly reported developmental features included autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Postnatal microcephaly was reported in 7 patients, and macrocephaly in 4. Epilepsy was reported in 9 patients. Neuroimaging, performed in 23 individuals, identified abnormalities in 11 patients; abnormalities included decreased white matter volume in 3 patients, thinning of the corpus callosum in 2, optic nerve hypoplasia in 2, localized hyperintensity in 2, right temporal sclerosis in 1, dilated Virchow-Robin spaces in 1, and periventricular nodular heterotopia in 1. Ophthalmologic abnormalities were reported in 13 of 23 individuals. Nine patients had recurrent bacterial infections, 1 patient had recurrent viral infections, and another patient had recurrent viral and bacterial infections. A pair of monozygotic twins with discordant phenotypes were included in the patient cohort. In the 24 patients for whom photographs were available, dysmorphic features included a triangular-shaped face in 10; a high anterior hairline in 19; deep-set eyes in 5, almond-shaped eyes in 8; periorbital fullness in 6, thick nasal alae and flared nostrils in 9, full cheeks in 7, and a thin upper lip in 12. The degree of dysmorphism was variable.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in 29 of the 34 patients with CAGS reported by {1:Chopra et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. One patient inherited the disorder from an affected parent, and another patient inherited it from a parent with low-level mosaicism for an ANKRD17 mutation. Parental inheritance was not determined in 3 patients.

cytogenetics.title: Cytogenetics
cytogenetics.content: In a patient (individual 6) with Chopra-Amiel-Gordon syndrome, {1:Chopra et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous 1.16-Mb deletion encompassing 7 genes, including ANKRD17, by array CGH. The other 6 genes in the region were associated with an autosomal recessive pattern of disease inheritance when mutated (ADAMTS3, {605011}; ALB, {103600}; AFP, {104150}) or were not known to be associated with a disease (COX18, {610428}; AFM, {104150}; RASSF6, {612620}). {1:Chopra et al. (2021)} therefore considered ANKRD17 to be the most likely candidate gene underlying the patient's phenotype. Functional studies were not performed.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 34 patients from 32 families with Chopra-Amiel-Gordon syndrome, {1:Chopra et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous mutations in the ANKRD17 gene (see, e.g., {615929.0001}-{615929.0005}). The mutations included 21 truncating or canonical splice site mutations, 9 missense mutations, 1 in-frame indel, and 1 microdeletion including ANKRD17 and 6 other genes. Molecular modeling suggested that most of the missense mutations disrupted the stability of ankyrin repeats.

clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the chloride channel 3 gene (CLCN3,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and brain abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and brain abnormalities (NEDHYBA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CLCN3 gene ({600580}) on chromosome 4q33.

Biallelic mutation in the CLCN3 gene causes NEDSBA ({619517}), a more severe neurodevelopmental disorder with overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and brain abnormalities (NEDHYBA) is characterized by impaired development of motor skills, cognitive function, and speech acquisition beginning in infancy or early childhood. Some affected individuals may have feeding difficulties, seizures, behavioral abnormalities, and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features. Brain imaging shows variable abnormalities, including corpus callosum defects, cerebellar defects, and decreased white matter volume. There is significant phenotypic variability (summary by {1:Duncan et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Duncan et al. (2021)} reported 9 unrelated patients, ranging from 5 to 17 years of age, with a variable neurodevelopmental disorder. One of the patients died at 23 days of age. The patients were ascertained through international collaboration and the MatchMaker Exchange program after exome sequencing identified heterozygous mutations in the CLCN3 gene. All patients had global developmental delay with poor motor, speech, and intellectual development. Many had early feeding issues, which resulted in failure to thrive in a few patients. They had hypotonia with delayed walking and delayed fine motor skills; 2 were unable to walk independently at 7 and 17 years of age. Intellectual disability tended to be moderate to severe (IQ as low as 24), although 1 patient (P4) had mild intellectual disability with an IQ of 71. Many had behavioral abnormalities, including hyperactivity, stereotypies, anxiety, and autism. Four patients had seizures, including myoclonic and tonic-clonic, but the seizures in general were controlled by medication. All but 1 patient had structural abnormalities on brain imaging, including corpus callosum defects, enlarged ventricles, pontine hypoplasia, cerebellar anomalies, decreased white matter volume, and increased gyral folding. Most patients had variable dysmorphic features, although there was not a common gestalt. These included prominent forehead, full cheeks, bushy eyebrows, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, bulbous nasal tip, short or long philtrum, high-arched palate, and micrognathia. Two patients had microcephaly. Common eye abnormalities included strabismus or esotropia; 1 patient had partial optic atrophy and retinal dystrophy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CLCN3 gene that were identified in patients with NEDHYBA by {1:Duncan et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 9 unrelated patients with NEDHYBA, {1:Duncan et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous missense variants in the CLCN3 gene (see, e.g., I607T, {600580.0001} and T570I, {600580.0002}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Electrophysiologic studies in Xenopus oocytes showed that 2 of the missense variants (I607T and T570I) had reduced voltage-dependent current rectification compared to wildtype. I607T also had decreased current amplitude, and both I607T and T570I had reduced or absent large transient currents. Additional in vitro studies demonstrated that I607T and T570I caused increased inward currents at the acidic pH of late endosomes, where CLCN3 is normally localized, possibly resulting from a defect in a feedback mechanism or in the gating process. In contrast, 2 other missense variants tested (V772A and A413V) had current amplitudes and rectification similar to wildtype. {1:Duncan et al. (2021)} stated that although the biologic consequences of electrophysiologic alterations observed in some variants remained unclear, missense variants likely cause a gain-of-function effect. The patient with the I607T mutation had the most severe phenotype and died at 23 days of age, suggesting a possible genotype/phenotype correlation. Studies of patient cells were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: ?Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and brain abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and brain abnormalities (NEDSBA) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CLCN3 gene ({600580}) on chromosome 4q33. One such family has been reported.

Heterozygous mutation in the CLCN3 gene causes NEDHYBA ({619512}), a less severe disorder with overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and brain abnormalities (NEDSBA) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay and onset of seizures in the first months of life associated with structural brain defects on brain imaging. Additional features may include pigmentary retinopathy with poor visual fixation and spasticity (summary by {1:Duncan et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Duncan et al. (2021)} reported 2 brothers (family 10) with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. One was 18 months of age, whereas the other had died at age 14 months. They presented with focal, tonic, myoclonic, and multifocal seizures at 3 months of age. One infant was very restless and the other showed severe spasticity; neither achieved independent ambulation. Both boys had salt and pepper fundus pigmentation and nystagmus with no visual fixation. Brain imaging showed partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, enlarged ventricles, disorganized cerebellar folia, delayed myelination with decreased white matter volume, small hippocampus and amygdala, and dysmorphic dentate nuclei. Other features included microcephaly and thin, tented upper lip. The parents were unaffected.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSBA in the family reported by {1:Duncan et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 sibs (family 10) with NEDSBA, {1:Duncan et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the CLCN3 gene ({600580.0003}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder; each unaffected parent was heterozygous for the mutation. It was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but it was predicted to result in a loss of function. The authors noted the phenotypic similarities to mice with homozygous loss of Clcn3 (see ANIMAL MODEL).

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
CLCN3 is thought to mediate swelling-activated plasma membrane currents, but {2:Stobrawa et al. (2001)} showed that this broadly expressed chloride channel is present in endosomal compartments and synaptic vesicles of neurons. While swelling-activated currents are unchanged in mice with disrupted Clcn3, acidification of synaptic vesicles is impaired and there is severe postnatal degeneration of the retina and hippocampus. Electrophysiologic analysis of juvenile hippocampal slices revealed no major functional abnormalities despite slightly increased amplitudes of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents. Mice almost lacking the hippocampus survive and show several behavioral abnormalities but are still able to acquire motor skills. Clcn3 -/- mice were smaller than their littermates at all ages except immediately after birth. Although they showed overall higher mortality, Clcn3 -/- mice survived for more than a year. The nearly complete loss of hippocampal structures in adult knockout mice was not due to an early developmental defect but rather was caused by a selective degeneration starting about 2 weeks after birth. Clcn3 -/- mice were blind as a consequence of severe retinal degeneration that led to a complete loss of photoreceptors by postnatal day 28. Immunohistochemistry revealed that Clcn3 is concentrated in the inner and outer plexiform layers, the regions of synaptic connections. In summary, {2:Stobrawa et al. (2001)} showed that CLCN3 is an intracellular chloride channel. It is also present on synaptic vesicles, where it contributes to their acidification. The phenotype of Clcn3 knockout mice strongly suggests that CLCN3 is not the only chloride channel of synaptic vesicles, and {2:Stobrawa et al. (2001)} suggested that other CLC channels may have similar roles.

To determine the physiologic role of CLC3, {4:Yoshikawa et al. (2002)} generated Clc3-deficient mice, Clcn3 -/-, by targeted gene disruption. Together with developmental retardation and higher mortality, the null mice showed neurologic manifestations such as blindness, motor coordination deficit, and spontaneous hyperlocomotion. In histologic analysis, the null mice showed a pattern of progressive degeneration of the retina, hippocampus, and ileal mucosa, which resembled the phenotype observed in cathepsin D (CTSD; {116840}) knockout mice. A defect in cathepsin D is responsible for congenital lysosomal storage disease with profound neurodegeneration in sheep ({3:Tyynela et al., 2000}). This defect results in a lysosomal accumulation of ceroid lipofuscin containing the mitochondrial F1F0 ATPase subunit C (ATP5G1; {603192}). In immunohistochemistry and Western blot analysis, {4:Yoshikawa et al. (2002)} found that subunit C was heavily accumulated in the lysosomes of null mice. Furthermore, they detected an elevation in the endosomal pH of the null mice. Results indicated that the neurodegeneration observed in the null mice was caused by an abnormality in the machinery which degrades the cellular protein and was associated with the phenotype of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN1; {256730}).

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that susceptibility to idiopathic generalized epilepsy-18 (EIG18; {619521}) is conferred by heterozygous mutation in the HCN4 gene ({605206}) on chromosome 15q24. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Idiopathic generalized epilepsy is characterized by various types of seizures, including childhood and juvenile absence epilepsy, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, and epilepsy with generalized tonic-clonic seizures upon awakening (EGTCA). EEG often shows spike-wave discharges. EIG18 is an autosomal dominant disorder manifest as myoclonic seizures in infancy. Although the seizures remit, some patients may have later speech or cognitive impairment (summary by {1:Becker et al., 2017} and {2:Campostrini et al., 2018}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of idiopathic generalized epilepsy, see EIG {600669}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Campostrini et al. (2018)} reported 2 brothers, born of unrelated parents, who presented in the first year of life with myoclonic seizures involving all limbs and loss of consciousness. EEG showed generalized epileptiform activity associated with the seizures; brain imaging was normal. Treatment with valproate achieved full remission, and the boys stopped medication around 2.5 years of age with no recurrence. Both had mild language delay, and 1 had mild intellectual disability (IQ of 76). Detailed cardiac workup in the brothers and father, who had an unknown early medical history, showed mildly decreased heart rate bordering bradycardia. None had clinical cardiac manifestations. The authors suggested that the epileptic phenotype may be restricted to infancy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of EIG18 in the family reported by {2:Campostrini et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 brothers with EIG18, {2:Campostrini et al. (2018)} identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the HCN4 gene (R550C; {605206.0011}). Electrophysiologic studies in CHO cells showed that the mutation caused a negative shift in the activation curve compared to wildtype, consistent with a loss of channel function. Neuronal hyperexcitability and increased firing was observed in neuronal cells transfected with the mutation, which exerted a dominant effect when coexpressed with wildtype. {2:Campostrini et al. (2018)} concluded that reduced HCN4 current contribution may affect input membrane resistance and resting membrane potential, causing cell hyperexcitability. The patients were ascertained from a cohort of 88 patients with various types of epilepsy.

{1:Becker et al. (2017)} identified a heterozygous missense variant (E153G) in the HCN4 gene in a girl who had a single generalized tonic-clonic seizures at 17 years of age. The variant, which was found by direct sequencing, was not present in the ExAC database. However, there were 4 additional family members with various types of seizures who did not carry the variant. Electrophysiologic studies showed that the variant caused a hyperpolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of activation, resulting in reduced function at a physiologic relevant voltage range. The authors suggested that the variant alone is unlikely to cause epilepsy, but that it may contribute along with variants in other genes to the polygenic nature of the disorder.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL-CRANIOFACIAL SYNDROME WITH VARIABLE RENAL AND CARDIAC ABNORMALITIES; NECRC
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the zinc finger, MTM-type 2 gene (ZMYM2,)

Head: Microcephaly
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the zinc finger, MTM-type 2 gene (ZMYM2,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental-craniofacial syndrome with variable renal and cardiac abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental-craniofacial syndrome with variable renal and cardiac abnormalities (NECRC) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ZMYM2 gene ({602221}) on chromosome 13q12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental-craniofacial syndrome with variable renal and cardiac abnormalities (NECRC) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by dysmorphic craniofacial features associated with mild developmental delay, mildly impaired intellectual development or learning difficulties, speech delay, and behavioral abnormalities. About half of patients have congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) and/or congenital cardiac defects, including septal defects ({1:Connaughton et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Connaughton et al. (2020)} reported 19 patients from 15 unrelated families with overlapping clinical features associated with heterozygous mutations in the ZMYM2 gene. The first 2 probands were ascertained from 551 individuals with CAKUT who underwent whole-exome sequencing. A third patient with CAKUT was subsequently identified through collaboration. Use of the GeneMatcher Program identified 12 additional unrelated individuals or families with putative loss-of-function ZMYM2 mutations. The phenotype was highly variable. All were reported to have neurologic abnormalities except 1 patient for whom clinical information was not available. Neurologic features included mild developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, speech delay, learning difficulties, and behavioral abnormalities, such as autism and ADHD. Some patients had hypotonia, and at least 2 had seizures. Four individuals had microcephaly. Common dysmorphic facial features included hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, narrow downslanting palpebral fissures, small nose with hypoplastic nares, and low-set or dysmorphic ears. Some patients had additional skeletal anomalies, such as hyperextensible joints, small hands and feet, fifth finger clinodactyly, and hypoplastic nails. Eight unrelated patients had structural kidney or urinary tract defects manifest as renal agenesis, hydronephrosis, hypospadias, incontinence, urethral strictures, vesicoureteral reflux, and malrotated kidneys. Cryptorchidism was also observed. Six patients from 4 families had congenital heart defects, including septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, and bicuspid aortic valve.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: Most of the heterozygous mutations in the ZMYM2 gene in the patients with NECRC reported by {1:Connaughton et al. (2020)} occurred de novo, but some were inherited from an affected parent.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 19 patients from 15 unrelated families with NECRC, {1:Connaughton et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous frameshift, nonsense, or splice site mutations in the ZMYM2 gene (see, e.g., {602221.0001}-{602221.0006}). Mutations in the first few families were found by whole-exome sequencing; subsequent families were identified through the GeneMatcher Program. The mutations, which occurred throughout the gene, mostly occurred de novo, although some were inherited from an affected parent. There was at least 1 instance of mosaicism. All the mutations were predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay with a loss of function. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells transfected with a subset of the predicted truncated proteins showed altered ZMYM2 intracellular localization compared to wildtype, with retention primarily or entirely within the cytoplasm and decreased or absent nuclear localization. Three truncated proteins tested had impaired interaction with FOXP1 ({605515}) and FOXP2 ({605317}) compared to wildtype. Although the findings were most consistent with haploinsufficiency, the authors could not exclude a dominant-negative effect for some of the ZMYM2 variants.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Connaughton et al. (2020)} found that complete knockdown of the zmym2 gene in X. tropicalis resulted in impaired pronephric development that could not be rescued by expression of the truncated mutations tested. In addition, mutant animals developed craniofacial abnormalities. CRISPR-Cas9 technology was used to generate a heterozygous mutant mouse recapitulating a human frameshift Zmym2 mutation ({602221.0003}). Mutant mice showed a spectrum of CAKUT-like defects including hydroureter, duplex kidneys, simplex kidneys, and vesicoureteral reflux. No additional phenotypes were observed in heterozygous mutant mice. Overall, the findings suggested a role for ZMYM2 in renal and perhaps craniofacial development.

Caused by mutation in the multiple inositol polyphosphate phosphatase 1 gene (MINPP1,)

Head: Microcephaly, progressive
Neurologic - CNS: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia seen on brain imaging
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the multiple inositol polyphosphate phosphatase 1 gene (MINPP1,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 16 (PCH16) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MINPP1 gene ({605391}) on chromosome 10q23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 16 (PCH16) is an autosomal recessive severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by hypotonia and severe global developmental delay apparent from early infancy. Although the severity of the disorder is variable, most affected individuals achieve only a few, if any, developmental milestones. Most are unable to walk or speak, have eye abnormalities with poor visual contact, and develop early-onset epilepsy. Other features may include stereotypic movements, spasticity, and progressive microcephaly. Brain imaging shows pontocerebellar hypoplasia, often with thin corpus callosum, atrophy of the thalamus and basal ganglia, enlarged ventricles, and white matter abnormalities (summary by {2:Ucuncu et al., 2020}).

For a phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of PCH, see PCH1A ({607596}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Ucuncu et al. (2020)} reported 8 children from 6 unrelated families with PCH16. The patients, who ranged in age from 18 months to 12 years, presented in the perinatal period with axial hypotonia, distal hypertonia, and spastic tetraplegia, often with extrapyramidal signs and progressive microcephaly (down to -5 SD). Psychomotor development was essentially absent: none of the patients learned to walk or talk, and they had poor social skills. Ophthalmologic findings included nystagmus, abnormal ocular movement, ptosis, and cataracts. Four had optic atrophy and 1 was blind. All but 1 patient had seizures, with onset between 1 day and 7 years of age. Brain imaging showed cerebellar hypoplasia, pontine atrophy, enlarged ventricles, atrophy of the cerebral cortex, thin corpus callosum, hypoplasia of the basal ganglia and thalami, and nonspecific white matter abnormalities. Other features included dysphagia, muscle wasting, joint stiffness, scoliosis, and mild nonspecific facial features, including micrognathia, prominent nose, and low-set ears. Four of the patients (including 2 sibs of probands) died in childhood. {2:Ucuncu et al. (2020)} suggested the title PCH type 14, but that designation had been reserved for another disorder (PCH14; {619301}).

{1:Appelhof et al. (2021)} reported 8 children from 4 unrelated families, 3 of which were consanguineous, with PCH16. The patients presented in infancy with hypotonia and global developmental delay of variable severity. Most were nonverbal, unable to sit, and showed stereotypic movements, stiffness, spasticity, and ataxia. The 3 brothers in family 4 had spastic tetraplegia. Of note, 2 sisters in family 2 were able to walk, but were nonverbal. Many, but not all, had progressive microcephaly (down to -6.6 SD). Six patients had onset of seizures between 6 months and 4 years of age. EEG showed variable abnormalities, including polyspike and wave discharges and continuous generalized slow spike-waves in sleep. One patient had hypsarrhythmia. Four patients had cortical blindness, 1 had nystagmus, and 2 had cataracts. Brain imaging showed pontocerebellar hypoplasia, reduced volume of the thalamus and basal nuclei, thin corpus callosum, enlarged ventricles, and frontal white matter atrophy or abnormalities. Another similarly affected boy from a fifth unrelated family was added in a note. He presented at 12 months of age with global developmental delay, microcephaly (-4.46 SD), epilepsy, laryngomalacia, and hypogonadism. Brain imaging showed pontocerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and white matter abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PCH16 in the families reported by {2:Ucuncu et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 8 patients from 6 unrelated families with PCH16, {2:Ucuncu et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the MINPP1 gene (see, e.g., {605391.0004}-{605391.0007}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were 2 frameshift, a nonsense, and 4 missense variants; most were absent from the gnomAD database. Knockdown of the MINPP1 gene in HEK293 cells resulted in decreased cell proliferation that could be partially rescued by wildtype MINPP1, but not by 2 missense variants that were tested (Y53D, {605391.0005} and E486K, {605391.0007}). Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) showed impaired proliferation and differentiation, suggesting a role for MINPP1 in neuroectodermal development. This was associated with increased apoptosis. The authors concluded that certain neural progenitors may be more vulnerable to the inositol phosphate metabolism defect. Cells expressing the mutations showed poor degradation of inositol polyphosphates IP(6) and IP(5), with lower levels of IP(2) and IP. These findings indicated that MINPP1 is involved in the regulation of the intracellular pool of de novo synthesized IP(6). Further in vitro cellular studies demonstrated that the mutations altered iron metabolism, cation homeostasis, and calcium signaling. {2:Ucuncu et al. (2020)} noted that the metabolic defects associated with the mutations likely adversely affect neural cell signaling and homeostasis.

In 9 patients from 5 unrelated families with PCH16, {1:Appelhof et al. (2021)} identified homozygous mutations in the MINPP1 gene (see, e.g., {605391.0008}-{605391.0010}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the variants were predicted to result in a loss of function.

Caused by mutation in the adaptor-related protein complex 1, gamma-1 subunit gene (AP1G1,)
