text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive Usmani-Riazzudin syndrome (USRISR) is caused by homozygous mutation in the AP1G1 gene ({603533}) on chromosome 16q22.

Heterozygous mutation in the AP1G1 gene causes autosomal dominant Usmani-Riazuddin syndrome (USRISD; {619467}), which shows overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal recessive Usmani-Riazzudin syndrome (USRISR) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and speech delay, hypotonia, spasticity, and behavioral abnormalities, most commonly aggressive behavior. More variable additional features may include seizures, scoliosis, and joint laxity ({1:Usmani et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Usmani et al. (2021)} reported 2 consanguineous families of Italian (family CPBO) and Pakistani (family PKMR328) descent in which 4 individuals were affected with a neurodevelopmental disorder. Two patients had died at ages 2 and 21 years. The patients had global developmental delay with hypotonia, delayed walking, moderately to severely impaired intellectual development, early-onset aggressive behavior, speech delay, joint laxity, and spasticity. Two patients in the Pakistani family had seizures. Dysmorphic features included high palate, prominent supraorbital ridges, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, and low-set, posteriorly rotated ears. One had scoliosis and another had pectus excavatum. In the Pakistani family, 3 of the unaffected father's sibs reportedly had a similar disorder; 2 had died at an early age.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of USRISR in the families reported by {1:Usmani et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with USRISR, {1:Usmani et al. (2021)} identified homozygous missense mutations in the AP1G1 gene (P246H, {603533.0004} and M369V, {603533.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Patient cells were not available for study, but detailed functional studies in cells transfected with the mutations indicated that the P246H variant interfered with proper recruitment of vesicles from early endosomes to late endosomes. The M369V allele interfered with trafficking between the recycling endosomes and plasma membrane. Although neither variant compromised the formation of the AP-1 complex, both impaired its function. Neither variant was able to rescue lethality in ap1g1-null zebrafish, confirming the pathogenic nature of the variants. However, {1:Usmani et al. (2021)} concluded that they act as hypomorphic alleles and may not result in a complete loss of function.

preferredTitle: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, IMPAIRED SPEECH, AND DYSMORPHIC FACIES; IDDHISD
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the transportin 2 gene (TNPO2,)

Head: Microcephaly (in some patients)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the transportin 2 gene (TNPO2,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with hypotonia, impaired speech, and dysmorphic facies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with hypotonia, impaired speech, and dysmorphic facies (IDDHISD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TNPO2 gene ({603002}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with hypotonia, impaired speech, and dysmorphic facies (IDDHISD) is characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech, hypotonia, ophthalmologic abnormalities, and nonspecific dysmorphic features. Some affected individuals have seizures, and a few have involvement of other organ systems ({1:Goodman et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Goodman et al. (2021)} reported 15 unrelated patients, ranging from 4 months to 20 years of age, with a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with de novo heterozygous mutation in the TNPO2 gene. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts after exome sequencing, and the phenotype was then characterized. The patients presented in infancy with hypotonia, poor feeding, and global developmental delay. Many had poor overall growth, and a few had microcephaly or small head circumference. Two patients required tube feeding. Motor development was variable: some patients were able to walk and run, whereas others were wheelchair-bound or had quadriparesis with inability to walk. The patients had impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech and often with behavioral deficits, such as autistic features, attention-deficit disorder, impulsivity, and emotional dysregulation. Six patients had seizures, mostly nonfebrile. Brain imaging, when performed, showed nonspecific abnormalities in 7 patients. Findings included cerebellar hypoplasia, enlarged ventricles, delayed myelination, and white matter volume loss. Most had variable dysmorphic facial features, including myopathic facies, bitemporal narrowing, short or long philtrum, large or low-set ears, retrognathia, broad nasal bridge with upturned nose, and slant irregularities of palpebral fissures. Ocular anomalies included strabismus, esotropia, saccadic eye movements, myopia, and hypermetropia. A few patients had involvement of other systems manifest as cardiac defects, nonspecific renal anomalies, or skeletal findings such as hip dysplasia and scoliosis.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the TNPO2 gene that were identified in patients with IDDHISD by {1:Goodman et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 15 unrelated patients with IDDHISD, {1:Goodman et al. (2021)} identified 15 different heterozygous mutations in the TNPO2 gene (see, e.g., {603002.0001}-{603007.0005}). The patients were gathered through international collaboration, and the mutations were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing (except for 1). None were present in the gnomAD database. All but one of the mutations occurred de novo; 1 was inherited from a mother who was low-level mosaic for the variant. Most of the mutations were missense and distributed throughout the gene, but there were 2 small intragenic in-frame insertion/deletions. Functional studies of patient cells were not performed, but expression of variant cDNA of 6 of the mutations in Drosophila showed that they were unable to rescue the developmental defects in tnpo-null flies despite normal protein levels (see ANIMAL MODEL). In addition, overexpression of 3 of the variants (G28R, D156N, and A546V) caused significant developmental toxicity, consistent with a gain-of-function effect. There was some variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance, suggesting variant-specific effects. Studies of another variant (W727C) suggested a loss-of-function effect. Overall, these observations suggested a pleiotropic effect, consistent with the phenotypic variability, although the precise mechanism remained to be determined. Given the role of the gene in cytoplasmic-nuclear cargo shuttling, {1:Goodman et al. (2021)} postulated that impaired TNPO2 function disrupts multiple pathways important for development and neuronal maintenance, including ciliogenesis, mitotic spindle assembly, and nuclear envelope assembly. Upregulation of the gene may cause an accumulation of the protein intracellularly, resulting in associated toxicity.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Goodman et al. (2021)} found that knockdown of the Drosophila tnpo gene using mutant alleles or RNAi caused dose-dependent developmental abnormalities, including abnormal eye and wing development and embryonic lethality. The eyes were smaller and rough with disorganized ommatidia, and the wings showed notches and blisters. Drosophila tnpo was expressed in neuronal cell bodies of the mushroom body in the brain and in the ventral nerve cord. Loss of tnpo expression in neurons impaired synaptic function. Overexpression of the wildtype gene caused similar developmental abnormalities, consistent with a toxic effect, although there were subtle differences. The findings indicated that tnpo is expressed in multiple tissues and is essential for basic development, particularly of the nervous system.

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the CUGbp- and ELAV-like family, member 2 gene (CELF2,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-97 (DEE97) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CELF2 gene ({602538}) on chromosome 10p14.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-97 (DEE97) is characterized by developmental delay, epileptic encephalopathy, and impaired intellectual development. Other clinical features may include autistic features and hypotonia.

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Itai et al. (2021)} described 4 unrelated patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Individual 1 had normal development until age 7.5 months when he began having seizures. An EEG showed hypsarrhythmia. At age 3 years and 4 months, he was hypotonic, could not walk without support, and had no speech. Individual 2 developed eye blinking, lateral eye deviation, and myoclonic jerks at 2.5 months of age. EEG at age 4 months showed a burst suppression pattern. His seizures decreased in frequency starting at age 2 years and ceased after age 13. He had autistic features and behavioral problems, including hyperactivity and self-injurious behaviors. At age 16, he had no speech, eye contact, or social smile. Individual 3 started having epileptic spasms at 4 months of age, and she was diagnosed with West syndrome after an EEG showed hypsarrhythmia. She had autistic features, hyperactivity, and tantrums since childhood. At age 9 years she was able to walk and could speak in 2-word sentences. Individual 4 had generalized tonic-clonic seizures at 5 and 6 days of age and again at 4 months of age. Ophthalmologic examination showed delayed visual maturation. EEG showed hypsarrhythmia, and brain MRI demonstrated mild bilateral ventricular enlargement. At age 5 years and 3 months, she had severe developmental delay and hypotonia and could not walk. Another individual in this cohort was a 33-year-old man with moderately impaired intellectual development and autistic behavior who did not have a history of seizures. Cardiac ultrasound showed mild mitral valve prolapse.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CELF2 gene in 3 patients with DEE97 reported by {1:Itai et al. (2021)} occurred de novo; in 1 patient the mutation was inherited from his asymptomatic mother, who was mosaic for the mutation.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 unrelated patients with DEE97, {1:Itai et al. (2021)} identified 4 heterozygous mutations in the CELF2 gene ({602538.0001}-{602538.0003}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Transfection studies with the mutations in HEK293T and COS-7 cells demonstrated abnormal cytoplasmic localization of the mutant protein. Another patient (individual 5), who had impaired intellectual development and autistic features, also carried a heterozygous CELF2 variant, but no functional studies were performed.

preferredTitle: CEREBELLAR ATAXIA, BRAIN ABNORMALITIES, AND CARDIAC CONDUCTION DEFECTS; CABAC
clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, mild to severe (in most patients)
Cerebellar hypoplasia seen on brain imaging
Caused by mutation in the exosome component 5 gene (EXOSC5,)

Head: Small head circumference
Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, mild to severe (in most patients)
Cerebellar hypoplasia seen on brain imaging
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the exosome component 5 gene (EXOSC5,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Cerebellar ataxia, brain abnormalities, and cardiac conduction defects

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cerebellar ataxia, brain abnormalities, and cardiac conduction defects (CABAC) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the EXOSC5 gene ({606492}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Cerebellar ataxia, brain abnormalities, and cardiac conduction defects (CABAC) is an autosomal recessive primarily neurologic disorder with variable manifestations. Common features included infantile-onset hypotonia, poor motor development, poor feeding and overall growth, and ataxic gait due to cerebellar ataxia. Other features include dysarthria, nystagmus, variable ocular anomalies, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and nonspecific dysmorphic features. Most, but not all, patients have global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and speech delay. Brain imaging shows cerebellar hypoplasia, often with brainstem hypoplasia, enlarged ventricles, delayed myelination, and thin corpus callosum. A significant number of patients develop cardiac conduction defects in childhood or adolescence, often requiring pacemaker placement (summary by {4:Slavotinek et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Beheshtian et al. (2019)} reported 3 sibs, born of consanguineous Iranian parents (family 5), who presented in infancy with muscular hypotonia and delayed motor milestones. They had ataxic gait, poor feeding, dysphagia, and nystagmus. At ages 27, 17, and 6 years, they showed poor overall growth, myopathic facies, severely impaired intellectual development, speech delay with dysarthria, cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and hyperreflexia. Brain imaging, performed in 1 patient, showed cortical atrophy, pachygyria, and cerebellar hypoplasia. One patient had myopia and strabismus. Beginning around adolescence, all 3 patients were diagnosed with valvular heart disease, right bundle branch block, and bradycardia, requiring cardiac pacemakers. The family was also reported by {3:Hu et al. (2019)} as family M8700013.

{4:Slavotinek et al. (2020)} reported 4 children from 3 unrelated families with cerebellar ataxia. The first 2 patients were ascertained clinically and underwent exome sequencing. An affected sib pair (patients 4 and 5) was subsequently identified through exome sequencing; clinical details of this sib pair were limited. The phenotype was highly variable. Patient 1 was a 10-year-old girl, born of unrelated parents of mixed ethnic origin, who presented with hypotonia and global developmental delay in the first months of life. Brain imaging showed cerebellar hypoplasia and small brainstem. At age 2 years, she was diagnosed with complete heart block necessitating pacemaker insertion. Other features included poor fixation, ocular esotropia, myopia, and astigmatism. There was also optic disc pallor, generalized retinal degeneration, and diffuse cone dysfunction greater than rod dysfunction. She had an ataxic gait, poor speech with dysarthria, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and attended a special school. Minor dysmorphic features, such as ptosis, epicanthal folds, high nasal bridge with broad tip, full cheeks, and mild retrognathia were observed. Patient 2 was a male infant, born of consanguineous Iraqi parents, who had hypotonia with reduced spontaneous movements, weak or absent reflexes, and poor feeding and respiratory insufficiency in infancy requiring gastrostomy and tracheostomy. Dysmorphic features included full cheeks, epicanthal folds, upslanting palpebral fissures, wide-spaced eyes, micrognathia, and pectus carinatum. He also had latent nystagmus, esotropia, uncontrolled eye movements, and poor visual fixation. Brain imaging showed trigonocephaly with craniosynostosis, cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia, enlarged ventricles, hypomyelination, and thin corpus callosum. There was evidence of developmental regression and subacute axonal neuropathy resembling spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). He died at 11 months of age due to recurrent respiratory infection. Echocardiography was normal. The sib pair, who were 7 years and 11 months of age, had mildly impaired overall growth, hypotonia, and ataxic gait without tremor. The older sister had myopia with mild cortical visual impairment; she had a single febrile seizure at age 3 years. These patients were noted to have normal cognition and stable developmental trajectories. Mild dysmorphic features included narrow face with wide-spaced eyes and micrognathia. Brain imaging showed cerebellar hypoplasia, small brainstem, and enlarged ventricles. Cardiac function was not assessed. A fifth patient (patient 3) with a similar phenotype was also reported, but he had a complex paternal isodisomy of chromosome 19 and homozygosity of a region with several candidate recessive genes, suggesting possible contribution of other genes to the phenotype.

{2:Calame et al. (2021)} reported 2 sibs of Mexican descent, 10 and 20 years of age, with CABAC. They had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, small head circumference, myopia, astigmatism, esotropia, and tapering fingers. Brain imaging showed cerebellar hypoplasia and hypomyelination that was progressive, suggesting neurodegeneration. In addition, the sister had dysmetria, hypotonia, and retrognathia; she had mild intellectual disability. Her older brother was more severely affected: he was nonverbal, unable to walk, and had profound intellectual disability. He also had optic atrophy, short stature, dysmorphic facies, camptodactyly, clinodactyly, scoliosis, spasticity, orolingual dyskinesia, and refractory myoclonic epilepsy. Both patients had cardiac conduction and rhythm abnormalities including sinus node dysfunction, intraventricular conduction delay, atrioventricular block, and ventricular tachycardia, necessitating pacemaker placement.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CABAC in the family reported by {1:Beheshtian et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 sibs, born of consanguineous Iranian parents (family 5), with CABAC, {1:Beheshtian et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous missense variant in the EXOSC5 gene (T114I; {606492.0001}). The mutation was found by exome sequencing; functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 4 patients from 3 unrelated families with CABAC, {4:Slavotinek et al. (2020)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the EXOSC5 gene ({606492.0001}-{606492.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing or microarray analysis, segregated with the disorder in the families. In vitro immunoprecipitation studies showed that 2 EXOSC5 missense mutations (T114I and L206H) caused altered interactions with other RNA exosome subunits. Studies of the orthologous mutations in budding yeast resulted in both impaired growth (L206H) or no growth defects (T114I), suggesting that the mutations may have distinct mechanistic consequences. {4:Slavotinek et al. (2020)} concluded that alteration of the RNA exosome could be tissue-specific, potentially underlying diverse clinical presentations.

In 2 sibs of Mexican descent with CABAC, {2:Calame et al. (2021)} identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in exon 3 of the EXOSC5 gene: T114I and T101K ({606492.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {4:Slavotinek et al. (2020)} found that complete knockdown of the zebrafish exosc5 ortholog did not result in viable larvae. Larvae injected with a construct targeting exon 2 of exosc5 showed increased tail curvature, shortening of the tail and body, edema, small eyes and head, abnormal brain morphology, and fin defects. The findings suggested a critical role for EXOSC5 in neurodevelopment.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH IMPAIRED LANGUAGE AND ATAXIA AND WITH OR WITHOUT SEIZURES; NEDLAS
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the glutamate receptor, ionotropic, kainate 2 gene (GRIK2,)

Head: Small head circumference (in some patients)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the glutamate receptor, ionotropic, kainate 2 gene (GRIK2,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired language and ataxia and with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired language and ataxia and with or without seizures (NEDLAS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GRIK2 gene ({138244}) on chromosome 6q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired language and ataxia and with or without seizures (NEDLAS) is characterized by axial hypotonia and global developmental delay apparent in early infancy. Affected individuals have delayed walking with gait ataxia and poor language development. Behavioral abnormalities also commonly occur. The severity is highly variable: a subset of patients have a more severe phenotype with early-onset seizures resembling epileptic encephalopathy, inability to walk or speak, and hypomyelination on brain imaging (summary by {2:Stolz et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Guzman et al. (2017)} reported a 10-year-old girl with severe global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, ataxia, and speech impairment. In infancy, she was noted to be hypotonic with delayed fine and gross motor skills. She walked at 5.5 years with an ataxic gait and poor balance. She also had poor language development and communicated with gestures. Behavioral assessment revealed short attention span, stereotypic behaviors, and happy demeanor. Other neurologic findings included episodes of tongue protrusion, sialorrhea, and mild alterations in sensory response to sound or touch. She did not have seizures, and brain imaging was normal.

{2:Stolz et al. (2021)} reported 10 additional patients with NEDLAS who were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program or through research collaboration after exome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous GRIK2 mutations. Nine patients were between 2 and 15 years of age; one patient was 37 years old. Although the patients had a core phenotype of global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, speech delay, and delayed walking with ataxic gait, there was phenotypic variability and differences in the severity of the manifestations. The data suggested a possible genotype/phenotype correlation. Five patients with the same missense mutation (A657T; {138244.0003}) were noted to have delayed psychomotor development in infancy with hypotonia, delayed walking by age 5 years with an ataxic or uncoordinated gait, speech and language impairment with articulation problems, and behavior features, including happy and social demeanor at a younger age evolving to ADHD, aggression, anxiety, and impulsivity. In contrast, 3 unrelated patients with a T660K missense mutation ({138244.0004}) had a more severe phenotype with early-onset intractable seizures consistent with an encephalopathy and profound developmental delay with inability to walk or speak. Brain imaging in these patients showed decreased white matter volume and hypomyelination; thin corpus callosum and nonspecific white matter abnormalities were also observed. Two patients with a T660R mutation ({138244.0005}) had an intermediate phenotype: one had focal seizures and was able to stand and speak a few words at age 4 years, whereas the other was able to walk and did not have seizures, but was nonverbal at age 12 years. Both of these patients also had hypomyelination on brain imaging.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the GRIK2 gene that were identified in patients with NEDLAS by {2:Stolz et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 10-year-old girl with NEDLAS without seizures, {1:Guzman et al. (2017)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GRIK2 gene (A657T; {138244.0003}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based exome sequencing, was not present in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. Voltage-clamp electrophysiologic studies in HEK293 cells transfected with the mutation showed slowed desensitization after glutamate application. Mutant A657T receptors showed increased mean currents compared to wildtype. Similar results were observed when coexpressed with heteromeric subunits, suggesting that the mutation causes constitutive activation and a gain-of-function effect with altered gating kinetics.

In 10 unrelated patients with NEDLAS with or without seizures, {2:Stolz et al. (2021)} identified 3 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the GRIK2 gene: A657T ({138244.0003}), T660K ({138244.0004}), and T660R ({138244.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. All occurred at conserved residues in the pore-forming M3 transmembrane domain that is critical for function. In vitro cellular studies showed that the levels of mutant protein expression at the surface membrane was decreased compared to controls. In vitro electrophysiologic studies of HEK293 cells transfected with the variants showed that they caused a slowing of deactivation and slower entry into desensitization compared to wildtype. Decreased mean amplitudes were also observed. These findings suggested that the mutations alter channel kinetics, resulting in a greater likelihood of channel opening and a tonic current in the presence of even low levels of glutamate. {2:Stolz et al. (2021)} postulated that the A657T mutation has a gain-of-function effect, whereas the T660 mutations may have a partial loss of function with subtle differences in KAR biophysical function; these differences may underlie clinical variability. The authors concluded that KAR signaling plays an important role in early development of the central nervous system.

preferredTitle: DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY, HYPOTONIA, MUSCULOSKELETAL DEFECTS, AND BEHAVIORAL ABNORMALITIES; DEHMBA
clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, mild to severe
Caused by mutation in the SNF2-related CBP activator protein gene (SRCAP,)

Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, mild to severe
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the SNF2-related CBP activator protein gene (SRCAP,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay, hypotonia, musculoskeletal defects, and behavioral abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay, hypotonia, musculoskeletal defects, and behavioral abnormalities (DEHMBA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SRCAP gene ({611421}) on chromosome 16p11.

Heterozygous mutation in the SRCAP gene also causes Floating-Harbor syndrome (FLHS; {136140}). Patients with FLHS have truncating mutations within a specific region of the gene, namely exons 33 and 34, whereas patients with DEHMBA have truncating mutations either proximal or distal to the 'FLHS region' of the SRCAP gene.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay, hypotonia, musculoskeletal defects, and behavioral abnormalities (DEHMBA) is an early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by these features. Affected individuals also have nonspecific and variable dysmorphic facial features that do not constitute a recognizable gestalt. Although the disorder is caused by truncating mutations in the SRCAP gene as is FLHS, the DEHMBA phenotype is clinically distinguishable from FLHS by the lack of short stature, brachydactyly, and delayed bone age, as well as absence of a specific facial appearance. There are some overlapping features between the 2 disorders, mainly impaired intellectual development and speech delay (summary by {1:Rots et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Rots et al. (2021)} reported 33 patients with a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized mainly by global developmental delay with or without impaired intellectual development, behavioral and psychiatric problems, nonspecific facial features, musculoskeletal issues, and hypotonia. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts after genetic analysis identified de novo heterozygous truncating mutations in the SRCAP gene that were proximal to the FLHS region (in 28 patients) or distal to the FLHS region (5 patients). None of the patients had a clinical diagnosis of FLHS, and the features were considered to be distinct from FLHS. Most notable were the absence of short stature and delayed bone age, lack of broad thumbs/fingertips and brachydactyly, and absence of the characteristic dysmorphic facial gestalt that is usually associated with FLHS. The patients with DEHMBA had speech and motor delay with hypotonia. Most had mildly impaired intellectual development and required special schooling, although a few had more severely impaired cognition. Behavioral abnormalities included autism spectrum disorder (in about half of patients), challenging behavior, anger, anxiety, ADHD, tics, Tourette syndrome (in 4), and psychosis (in 4). Skeletal anomalies included joint hypermobility, chronic musculoskeletal pain, scoliosis, and pectus defects; short stature and brachydactyly were not present. Rare patients had seizures (in 3), genitourinary abnormalities (in 3), or gastroesophageal reflux in infancy. Dysmorphic facial features were variable and nonspecific. Many had a long face and long philtrum, prominent forehead, thin vermilion upper lip with everted lower vermilion, and wide mouth. Other features included narrow palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, periorbital fullness, wide nasal bridge, prominent ears, and retro- or prognathia. About 40% of patients had myopia or hypermetropia. Use of a facial recognition algorithm also indicated that patients with DEHMBA could not be discriminated from controls; they did not have a unifying facial gestalt, and the features were distinct from those of FLHS. Those with a mutation proximal to the FLHS region did not differ significantly from those with a mutation distal to the FLHS region.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SRCAP gene that were identified in patients with DEHMBA by {1:Rots et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 33 unrelated patients with DEHMBA, {1:Rots et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous truncating mutations in the SRCAP gene (see, e.g., {611421.0008}-{611421.0011}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, occurred de novo in those from whom parental DNA was available, which was the majority of patients. None were present in the gnomAD database. The mutations occurred proximal to the FLHS region in 28 individuals and distal to the FLHS region in 5 individuals. None of the mutations were recurrent. DNA methylation (DNAm) analysis of 8 patients with FLHS, 9 with proximal SRCAP variants, and 5 with distal SRCAP variants showed distinct methylation signatures, suggesting diverse pathogenicity of these variants. {1:Rots et al. (2021)} hypothesized that truncating mutations proximal to the FLHS region may be subject to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and cause haploinsufficiency.

preferredTitle: FETAL AKINESIA, RESPIRATORY INSUFFICIENCY, MICROCEPHALY, POLYMICROGYRIA, AND DYSMORPHIC FACIES; FARIMPD
clinicalSynopsis: Malformations of cortical development seen on brain imaging
Necrotic areas in the basal ganglia
Caused by mutation in the ATPase, Na+/K+ transporting, alpha-2 polypeptide gene (ATP1A2,)

Head: Microcephaly (down to -8 SD)
Neurologic - CNS: Malformations of cortical development seen on brain imaging
Necrotic areas in the basal ganglia
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the ATPase, Na+/K+ transporting, alpha-2 polypeptide gene (ATP1A2,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Fetal akinesia, respiratory insufficiency, microcephaly, polymicrogyria, and dysmorphic facies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that fetal akinesia, respiratory insufficiency, microcephaly, polymicrogyria, and dysmorphic facies (FARIMPD) is caused by homozygous mutation in the ATP1A2 gene ({182340}) on chromosome 1q23.

description.title: Description
description.content: Fetal akinesia, respiratory insufficiency, microcephaly, polymicrogyria, and dysmorphic facies (FARIMPD) is an autosomal recessive syndrome characterized by hypotonia in utero resulting in fetal akinesia with generalized joint contractures and arthrogryposis at birth. Affected newborns have severe respiratory insufficiency at birth requiring ventilation and significant dysmorphic facial features; seizures may also occur. Brain imaging shows variable malformations of cortical development, most commonly polymicrogyria or other gyral anomalies. Death in infancy usually occurs (summary by {3:Monteiro et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Monteiro et al. (2020)} reported 3 newborns from 2 unrelated families who had a similar syndromic congenital disorder with features apparent in utero. The pregnancies were complicated by diminished fetal movements, polyhydramnios, generalized edema associated with hydrops fetalis, and generalized joint contractures consistent with fetal akinesia deformation sequence. In utero seizures were suspected in 2 cases, and postnatal seizures occurred in the third case. At birth, the patients had severe hypotonia with insufficient respiratory drive necessitating ventilatory support. They had clenched hands, clubfeet, multiple limb contractures, camptodactyly, and overlapping toes. Dysmorphic facial features included severe microcephaly (down to -8 SD), low anterior hairline, hirsutism, hypertelorism, periorbital fullness, prominent cheeks, large dysmorphic ears, anteverted nares, micrognathia, everted lower lip, and short neck. Brain MRI showed malformations of cortical development, including pachygyria, polymicrogyria, and lissencephaly, cortical calcifications, attenuation of white matter, and enlarged ventricles. One patient had a hypoplastic corpus callosum and cerebellum, overfolded gyri, and glioneuronal heterotopia. Other features observed included umbilical and inguinal hernia, bell-shaped thorax, posterior diaphragmatic hernia, patent foramen ovale, right cardiac ventricular hypertrophy, and congenital hypothyroidism. Both sibs from family 1 died of septic shock and multiorgan failure at 2 months of age. The female infant from family 2 died of respiratory insufficiency soon after birth. The mother in family 1 reported migraine without aura and the mother in family 2 had mild intellectual disability that ran in her family. The fathers had no neurologic symptoms or complaints.

{1:Chatron et al. (2019)} reported 4 patients from 2 unrelated families with a lethal syndromic form of polymicrogyria. Three sibs, born of consanguineous Algerian parents (family A), presented prenatally with polyhydramnios, microcephaly, and smooth cortex. The first 2 affected infants died after a few hours of life from respiratory distress; the third affected pregnancy was terminated after prenatal ultrasound showed abnormalities. A 35-week-old affected fetus (patient 4), born of consanguineous Pakistani parents (family B), had microcephaly with unique brain malformations and inguinal hernia; the pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios. This patient had previously been reported by {4:Squier and Jansen (2014)}. Postmortem examination of 2 patients from family A and patient 4 showed features of fetal hypokinesia, including hand contractures and rocker-bottom feet. Neuropathologic studies of 2 patients from family A and patient 4 showed a complex brain malformation pattern with irregular cortical surface, dentato-olivary dysplasia, necrotic and calcified areas in the basal ganglia, and calcified leptomeningeal arteries. The abnormal gyral patterns were consistent with diffuse polymicrogyria. There was also hypoplasia/agenesis of the pyramidal tracts. Family history was notable for monthly migraines in the mother of family A and migraine in both parents of patient 4.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of FARIMPD in the families reported by {3:Monteiro et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 infants from 2 unrelated families with FARIMPD, {3:Monteiro et al. (2020)} identified homozygous frameshift mutations in the ATP1A2 gene ({182340.0016} and {182340.0017}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Neither were present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but both were predicted to result in a complete loss of ATP1A2 function. All 3 patients died in the perinatal period.

In 3 sibs, conceived of consanguineous Algerian parents, and an unrelated infant, born of consanguineous Pakistani parents, with FARIMPD, {1:Chatron et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous frameshift and nonsense mutation, respectively, in the ATP1A2 gene ({182340.0018} and {182340.0019}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Both were absent from the gnomAD database. No ATP1A2 immunostaining was detected in brain samples from 2 patients, confirming complete absence of the protein and a loss-of-function effect. Functional studies of the variant were not performed. All patients either died in infancy or the pregnancies were terminated.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Ikeda et al. (2004)} found that homozygous knockout of the Atp1a2 gene in mice was embryonic lethal due to severe motor deficits that also abolished respiration by the medullary respiratory center neurons. Analysis of spinal cord motoneurons in mutant mice showed absence of normal spontaneous rhythmic discharges. This was associated with increased inhibitory GABA levels in the extracellular spaces throughout the brain, as well as increased chloride (Cl-) levels within neurons. {2:Ikeda et al. (2004)} hypothesized that Atp1a2 normally generates a K+ gradient that fuels extrusion of cytosolic Cl- by KCC2 (SLC12A5; {606726}) in respiratory center neurons in the perinatal period. In the absence of this, due to loss of Atp1a2, neurons thus become persistently depolarized and cannot produce action potentials due to the inactivation of fast sodium channels.

clinicalSynopsis: Onset of seizures in the first decade
Caused by mutation in the ATPase, Na+/K+ transporting, alpha-2 polypeptide gene (ATP1A2,)

Miscellaneous: Onset of seizures in the first decade
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the ATPase, Na+/K+ transporting, alpha-2 polypeptide gene (ATP1A2,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-98 (DEE98) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP1A2 gene ({182340}) on chromosome 1q23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-98 (DEE98) is characterized by onset of seizures in the first decade (range infancy to late childhood) associated with variable global developmental delay. Other features may include hypotonia, spasticity, and quadriparesis. Brain imaging may be normal or show nonspecific and variable abnormalities, including polymicrogyria. The severity is variable; some patients may die of refractory status epilepticus (summary by {1:Vetro et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Vetro et al. (2021)} reported 6 unrelated children, ranging from 1 month to 12 years of age, with onset of various types of seizures between 10 days and 8 years of age. Seizure types included focal dyscognitive, clonic, tonic, migrating focal seizures, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Two patients died within the first year of life due to respiratory complications of refractory status epilepticus. EEG was abnormal in all patients, showing slow background with multifocal sharp waves and discharges; 1 patient had a burst-suppression pattern. Brain imaging was normal in 3 patients, and showed variable abnormalities in the other 3. Patient 1 had peritrigonal high signal intensities; patient 2 had a thin corpus callosum, dilated ventricles, and frontal and cerebellar atrophy; and patient 6 had perisylvian polymicrogyria with a thickened corpus callosum. Other features included hypotonia, spasticity, and quadriparesis. All but 1 (patient 5) had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development. Patient 4 also had Down syndrome. Patient 5 was the least affected: she had onset of seizures at age 8 years, no additional neurologic features, and normal brain imaging. Patient 2 was the most severely affected individual. At age 5 years, he was profoundly delayed and nonverbal with severe axial hypotonia and dyskinetic quadriparesis; brain imaging showed cerebral atrophy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the ATP1A2 gene that were identified in patients with DEE98 by {1:Vetro et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 unrelated patients with DEE98, {1:Vetro et al. (2021)} identified 5 de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the ATP1A2 gene (see, e.g., {182340.0020}-{182340.0022}). The mutations, which occurred at conserved residues, were not present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies showed all of the mutations caused variable functional defects in the Na+/(K+)ATPase. Variants with more severe functional deficits were associated with a more severe phenotype. {1:Vetro et al. (2021)} estimated that about 5% of ATP1A2 mutations may be associated with DEE. Polymicrogyria was estimated to occur in about 1% of patients with ATP1A2 mutations.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-99 (DEE99) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP1A3 gene ({182350}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-99 (DEE99) is characterized by onset of seizures in early childhood associated with global developmental delay and severely impaired intellectual development. Other features may include hypotonia, quadriparesis, nystagmus, and apnea. Brain imaging may be normal or show nonspecific and variable abnormalities, including cerebral atrophy and polymicrogyria. The severity is variable; some patients die of refractory status epilepticus (summary by {1:Vetro et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Vetro et al. (2021)} reported 14 unrelated children and one mother/son pair (patients 14 and 15), ranging from infancy to 32 years of age, with onset of various types of seizures between birth and 4 years, although most had onset in early infancy. Seizure types included focal, multifocal, clonic, tonic, migrating focal seizures, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Some had apnea, hypertonic posturing, eye deviation, or dyscognitive seizures. Six patients died in childhood mainly due to respiratory complications of refractory status epilepticus. EEG was abnormal in all patients, demonstrating multifocal discharges and slow background activity. One patient (patient 11) had a burst-suppression pattern. Most patients had severe developmental delay with intellectual disability and hypotonic quadriparesis. Less common features included tube feeding, microcephaly, optic atrophy, nystagmus, poor or absent speech, and dyskinesia. Brain imaging was normal in 4 patients, but showed variable abnormalities in the others, including cerebral atrophy, dilated ventricles, and thin corpus callosum. Polymicrogyria was observed in 9 patients. The only patient without overt seizures was the mother (patient 15): she did have EEG abnormalities, mild intellectual disability, dyspraxia, migraine, and polymicrogyria with a thick corpus callosum on brain imaging.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: Most of the heterozygous mutations in the ATP1A3 gene that were identified in patients with DEE99 by {1:Vetro et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. One mutation was transmitted from an unaffected man to his mildly affected daughter and severely affected grandson, indicating incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 16 patients from 15 families with DEE99, {1:Vetro et al. (2021)} identified 14 heterozygous mutations in the ATP1A2 gene (see, e.g., {182350.0019}-{182350.0021}). The mutations occurred de novo in all except for a mother and son pair (patients 14 and 15). Most mutations were missense, with a few small in-frame deletions or insertions. All occurred at conserved residues, and none were present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies showed that all of the mutations caused variable functional defects in the Na+/(K+)ATPase. Variants with more severe functional deficits were associated with a more severe phenotype. The findings were consistent with a loss-of-function effect. {1:Vetro et al. (2021)} estimated that about 12% of ATP1A3 mutations may be associated with DEE. Polymicrogyria was estimated to be observed in about 5.5% of patients with ATP1A3 mutations.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Galloway-Mowat syndrome-10 (GAMOS10) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the YRDC gene ({612276}) on chromosome 1p34.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Galloway-Mowat syndrome-10 (GAMOS10) is a severe autosomal recessive disorder characterized by onset of symptoms soon after birth. Affected individuals have progressive renal dysfunction with proteinuria associated with diffuse mesangial sclerosis (DMS) on renal biopsy. Other features include global developmental delay, microcephaly, hypothyroidism, arachnodactyly, and dysmorphic facial features. Some patients may have seizures or abnormalities on brain imaging. All reported patients have died in infancy (summary by {1:Arrondel et al., 2019} and {2:Schmidt et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of GAMOS, see GAMOS1 ({251300}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Arrondel et al. (2019)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated families of European descent (families F and G) with GAMOS10. The patients presented with progressive nephrotic syndrome and proteinuria between birth and 2 months of age, and all died between 1.5 and 11 months. Renal biopsy showed diffuse mesangial sclerosis (DMS) with effacement of foot processes. Other features included microcephaly, nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, arachnodactyly, and congenital hypothyroidism. Brain imaging showed progressive cerebellar and cortical atrophy with myelination defects in 1 patient, and a frontal simplified gyral pattern with myelination delay in another. One patient also had hypotonia and myoclonus.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{2:Schmidt et al. (2021)} reported a male infant, born of distantly related Iraqi parents, with a severe congenital syndromic disorder resulting in death at 12 days of age. He was born with microcephaly (-3.6 SD) and developed tonic-clonic seizures and primary liver and renal dysfunction with proteinuria soon after birth. He had a striking progeroid appearance with loss of subcutaneous fat, wrinkled skin, low-set and large ears, micro- and retrognathia, and long smooth philtrum. He also had congenital hypothyroidism, intestinal malrotation, hypertrichosis, and arachnodactyly. Family history revealed a similarly affected sib who died soon after birth; the mother also had a previous miscarriage.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of GAMOS10 in the families reported by {1:Arrondel et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 patients from 2 unrelated families (families F and G) with GAMOS10, {1:Arrondel et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous hypomorphic or amorphic mutations in the YRDC gene ({612276.0001}-{612276.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. None were present in the gnomAD database. Studies of patients cells and in vitro studies in yeast showed that the mutations were unable to fully rescue growth defects and caused decreased t6A levels and lack of t6A modification. Knockdown of YRDC in a human podocyte cell line resulted in decreased protein synthesis, decreased cell proliferation, and decreased cell survival. These authors did not find alterations of telomere length in patient fibroblasts.

In a male infant, born of distantly related Iraqi parents, with GAMOS10, {2:Schmidt et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the YRDC gene (I221T; {612276.0004}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not present in the gnomAD database. Patient fibroblasts showed normal YRDC protein levels and protein localization, but global t6A levels showed a significant decrease of 16.3% compared to wildtype. Q-FISH analysis in patient cells showed 26% telomere shortening of chromosomes compared to controls; this was associated with increased cellular senescence. RNA sequencing of patient cells showed differential expression of genes involved in DNA damage response and repair. Patient cells showed increased susceptibility to genotoxic agents compared to controls, consistent with DNA repair defects. These findings suggested that YRDC may have additional functions besides being a member of the KEOPS complex.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hearing loss and spasticity (NEDHLS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the SPATA5L1 gene (AFG2B; {619578}) on chromosome 15q21.

Biallelic mutation in the SPATA5L1 gene can also cause nonsyndromic hearing loss (DFNB119; {619615}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hearing loss and spasticity (NEDHLS) is characterized by hearing loss, global developmental delay/impaired intellectual development, spastic-dystonic cerebral palsy, focal or generalized epilepsy, and microcephaly. Some children present with hypotonia ({1:Richard et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Richard et al. (2021)} described 25 individuals from 18 families with mild to severe hearing loss and global developmental delay/impaired intellectual development. Cognitive impairment ranged from severe to profound. Sixteen of the patients had spastic-dystonic cerebral palsy, and 15 had cortical visual impairment. Most patients had movement disorders, including spasticity (17/25), dystonia (15/25), or a combination of the two (13/25). Seizures were diagnosed in 13 of 18 patients, and seizure types included infantile spasms, absence focal, and generalized. Microcephaly was present in 13 of 25 patients. Facial dysmorphisms included downslanting palpebral fissures, low frontal hairline, large ears, tooth malformations, bitemporal narrowing, depressed nasal bridge, and micrognathia, among other findings. Common neuroimaging findings included diminished cerebral volume, periventricular leukomalacia, widened sylvian fissures, anterior temporal hypoplasia, and hypoplastic corpus callosum. Quantitative volumetric analysis of brain MRIs revealed a significant decrease in white matter volume compared to controls.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of neurodevelopmental disorder with hearing loss and spasticity in the families reported by {1:Richard et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 25 individuals from 18 families with neurodevelopmental disorder with hearing loss and spasticity, {1:Richard et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the SPATA5L1 gene (see, e.g., {619578.0001}-{619578.0002}; {619578.0005}-{619578.0010}). None of the identified variants were found in homozygous state in the gnomAD database.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and gross motor and speech delay (NEDHMS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the UBE4A gene ({603753}) on chromosome 11q23.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and gross motor and speech delay (NEDHMS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe global developmental delay apparent from infancy. Affected individuals have axial hypotonia and limited ability to walk, including some who are nonambulatory with lower limb spasticity, impaired intellectual development, and poor or absent speech and language. Additional more variable features may include seizures, behavioral problems, distal skeletal anomalies, and dysmorphic facial features ({2:Melo et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Melo et al. (2021)} reported 8 patients, ranging in age from 5 to 20 years, from 4 unrelated consanguineous families of various ethnic backgrounds with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who were of Brazilian, Hispanic/Guatemalan, and Arab descent, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the UBE4A gene. Family C had previously been reported by {1:Anazi et al. (2017)} as family 16DG0294. All had global developmental delay apparent from infancy with severely impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech. All but 1 had hypotonia, and 5 patients showed lower limb spasticity with hyperreflexia. Five patients were nonambulatory, either never having achieved the skill or losing it, 1 could walk with support, and 2 walked at around age 5. Five patients had generalized tonic-clonic seizures in the first years of life. Many had behavioral problems, including autistic features, attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder, and aggressive behavior. The patients from family C were dependent, but able to attend special schooling. Additional more variable features included poor eye contact, cortical visual impairment, cataracts, obesity, small hands and feet, joint contractures, and nonspecific white matter changes on brain imaging. Some patients had dysmorphic features, including coarse features, small head circumference, brachycephaly, flat nasal bridge, broad nasal tip, prominent nose, narrow and upslanted palpebral fissures, prominent teeth, creased earlobes, deep-set eyes, horizontal eyebrows, short philtrum, and large lips.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDHMS in the families reported by {2:Melo et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 patients from 4 unrelated consanguineous families of various ethnic origins with NEDHMS, {2:Melo et al. (2021)} identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the UBE4A gene ({603753.0001}-{603753.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were no homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the UBE4A gene in the gnomAD database. Fibroblasts derived from a patient in family A showed significantly decreased UBE4A mRNA levels and absent protein, consistent with a loss-of-function effect. Fibroblasts from the patient in family D also showed decreased mRNA levels. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but the findings implicated a role for UBE4A in proper neurodevelopment.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Melo et al. (2021)} found that homozygous mutant mice with a frameshift mutation in the Ube4a gene (Cys425PhefsTer) mimicking a mutation found in human patients ({603753.0002}) developed bilateral early cataracts and retinal dysplasia, decreased limb muscle strength, and behavioral abnormalities, suggesting a role for the gene in neurodevelopment. There was some evidence of sexual dimorphism in the studies.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Hengel-Maroofian-Schols syndrome (HEMARS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the BCAS3 gene ({607470}) on chromosome 17q23.

description.title: Description
description.content: Hengel-Maroofian-Schols syndrome (HEMARS) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by severe global developmental delay apparent from infancy or early childhood. Affected individuals have delayed walking or inability to walk, impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, pyramidal signs manifest as lower limb spasticity, poor overall growth often with short stature and microcephaly, and dysmorphic facial features. Some patients develop seizures. Brain imaging shows thinning of the posterior part of the corpus callosum, delayed myelination, and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy ({1:Hengel et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Hengel et al. (2021)} reported 15 patients from 8 unrelated families with a similar syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. After the first 3 families were characterized, the other families were subsequently ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after exome or genome sequencing was performed. The families were of various ethnic origins, including Iranian, Arab, Turkish, Saudi, Albanian, and European; 6 families were consanguineous. The patients, who ranged in age from 19 months to 19 years, had global developmental delay and severely impaired intellectual development (IQ as low as 45) apparent from infancy or early childhood. They had poor overall growth with short stature (in 80%), microcephaly (-3.1 to -6.7 SD, in 85%), delayed walking by several years or inability to walk, and poor or absent speech. All patients had lower limb spasticity with a spastic gait and hyperreflexia, and some had additional movement disorders, including dystonia and dyskinetic movements. Some of the older patients showed regression of motor abilities in the second decade. Seven patients developed various types of seizures, but the severity ranged from 1 febrile seizure at age 3 years in one patient to pharmacoresistant tonic seizures at age 10 years in another. The patients had notable dysmorphic facial features, including prominent and full eyebrows, synophrys, hypertelorism, full lips with everted lower lip, short philtrum, long face with open mouth, and large, widely spaced teeth. Other features included joint contractures, strabismus, visual impairment, nystagmus, and ptosis. Brain imaging showed thin posterior corpus callosum, impaired myelination, and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. A 14-year-old girl from family 9 had a similar phenotype, but the phase of the mutations could not be determined conclusively.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HEMARS in the families reported by {1:Hengel et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 15 patients from 8 unrelated families with HEMARS, {1:Hengel et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the BCAS3 gene (see, e.g., {607470.0001}-{607470.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were nonsense, missense, frameshift, and splice site mutations that occurred throughout the gene. All mutations were either absent from or present at a low frequency in the gnomAD database. Studies of fibroblasts derived from 2 unrelated patients showed undetectable BCAS3 protein levels compared to controls, suggesting a loss-of-function effect. Patient fibroblasts did not show cell migration abnormalities and the patients did not have angiogenesis defects. The findings suggested an essential role for BCAS3 in neurodevelopment.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Hengel et al. (2021)} noted that homozygous loss of the Bcas3 gene in mice is embryonic lethal. They found that RNAi-mediated knockdown of the corresponding Drosophila 'rudhira' gene by use of panneuronal drivers in Drosophila also caused embryonic lethality or paralyzed flies that died on the first day after eclosion. Further genetic studies of mutant flies showed that loss of rudhira reduced longevity and caused severe locomotion defects and an abnormal wing phenotype. Overall, the findings indicated that knockdown of this gene can cause developmental defects in neuronal and nonneuronal tissues in a dose-dependent manner.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that immunodeficiency-91 and hyperinflammation (IMD91) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ZNFX1 gene ({618931}) on chromosome 20q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Immunodeficiency-91 and hyperinflammation (IMD91) is an autosomal recessive complex immunologic disorder characterized by both immunodeficiency and recurrent infections, often to viruses or mycobacteria, as well as by hyperinflammation with systemic involvement. Affected individuals present in infancy with variable features, including fever, infection, thrombocytopenia, renal or hepatic dysfunction, recurrent infections, or seizures. Most patients eventually develop hepatic or renal failure, compromised neurologic function, lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, and multiorgan failure resulting in death. More variable features may include intermittent monocytosis, features of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and serologic evidence of hyperinflammation. The disorder is thought to result from dysregulation of the interferon response to viral stimulation in the innate immune system (summary by {1:Le Voyer et al., 2021}; {2:Vavassori et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Le Voyer et al. (2021)} reported 4 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families (kindred A from Iran, kindred B from Morocco) with intermittent monocytosis and susceptibility to mycobacterial infection. The proband in kindred A developed disseminated mycobacteriosis at 3 months of age after BCG vaccination at birth. He recovered with treatment, but later developed recurrent respiratory infections, including CMV-associated pneumonia with interstitial lung disease. His sister died at 2 months of age from gastroenteritis and renal failure. Kindred B lived in Belgium and BCG vaccination was not given. The proband presented at 18 days of age with failure to thrive, peripheral lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, edema, rash, thrombocytopenia, and monocytosis. He had similar recurrent episodes, and later developed seizures and showed global developmental delay. At age 12 years, he had multiorgan failure associated with possible disseminated Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection, and at 13, he had disseminated TB. Other features included interstitial lung disease, thrombocytopenia, neutrophilia, persistent monocytosis, and high C-reactive protein ({123260}) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Three sibs (kindred B) were affected with a similar disorder: 1 died of atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome at age 5 years, another had recurrent thrombocytopenia and monocytosis without severe infections, and a third died at 14 months of age from disseminated TB. {1:Le Voyer et al. (2021)} stated that the patients did not have severe viral illnesses, despite seropositivity for multiple viruses.

{2:Vavassori et al. (2021)} reported 15 patients from 8 unrelated families of various ethnic origins who presented in the first months or years of life with abnormal susceptibility to viral infections as well as systemic inflammation. They had early-onset, severe, systemic acute inflammatory disease associated with major dysfunction of the liver, brain, kidneys, and lungs. The severe infections were caused by RNA viruses that tended to be negative ssRNA (influenza, parainfluenza, RSV), positive ssRNA (norovirus), and DNA viruses (rotavirus, HSV, adenovirus, and CMV). The patients had variable presentations, including failure to thrive, thrombocytopenia, anemia, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, seizures, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure, fever, respiratory distress, increased white cell count, and recurrent infections. Sometimes an infectious agent, usually viral, could be identified, but not always. Severe hepatic disease was common, manifest by elevated liver enzymes, hepatomegaly, coagulopathy, and sometimes hepatic encephalopathy. Three patients had acute liver failure. Ten patients developed features of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), including 6 who met the diagnostic criteria. Ten patients had neurologic involvement, including recurrent seizures and developmental regression. Other common features included chronic polyarthritis, interstitial pneumonitis, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy on renal biopsy, nephrotic syndrome with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, renal failure, gastroenteritis, necrotizing encephalitis, and multiorgan failure. Several patients had cardiovascular and respiratory failure requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Some patients showed progressive disease manifestations even after infectious agents were cleared. At least 2 patients developed acute systemic hyperinflammation with fever, leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and liver dysfunction after childhood vaccination; vaccine strain measles and varicella zoster (VZV) viruses were detected. One patient underwent stem cell transplantation with resolution of immune dysregulation, although he still had developmental delay and autism. Eleven patients died in childhood, with 7 deaths occurring before 3 months of age. The mean age at death was 3.6 years, and causes included inflammatory episodes with hepatitis or cytopenia, sepsis, and necrotizing aspergillosis 5 years after lung transplantation (1 patient). The patients that survived had delayed development or autistic features. The central nervous system involvement in these patients was thought to result from either HLH-like inflammatory activity or poor control of viral infections.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IMD91 in the families reported by {2:Vavassori et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with IMD91, {1:Le Voyer et al. (2021)} identified homozygous mutations in the ZNFX1 gene ({618931.0001} and {618931.0002}), both of which resulted in premature termination and a loss of function. The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Patient cells and HeLa cells transfected with the mutations showed that 1 resulted in production of a truncated protein, whereas the other caused nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and absence of the protein. However, patients had normal development of major lymphocyte subsets, lymphocytes showed normal production of gamma-interferon (IFNG; {147570}), and other cells showed normal responses to IFNG. Myeloid cells were not studied. {1:Le Voyer et al. (2021)} speculated that ZNFX1 may affect the production of IFNG-inducing cytokines, particularly in myeloid cells. The authors postulated a pathogenetic mechanism by which a mutant protein (ZNFX1) binds to RNA and disrupts IFNG-related immunity.

In 13 patients from 8 unrelated families with IMD91, {2:Vavassori et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the ZNFX1 gene (see, e.g., {618931.0003}-{618931.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were 1 nonsense, 5 frameshift, and 5 missense mutations. The mutations occurred throughout the gene, and all missense variants occurred at highly conserved residues. All but 1 were absent from the gnomAD database. ZNFX1 could not be detected in fibroblasts derived from 2 patients with biallelic frameshift or nonsense mutations. Low levels of the protein were detected in cell extracts from a patient who was compound heterozygous for a frameshift and a missense variant. Stimulation of monocytes derived from 1 patient with synthetic double-stranded nucleic acids was associated with less efficient clearing of vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) compared to controls. Stimulation of fibroblasts derived from several patients caused increased expression of ISGs (interferon-stimulated genes) compared to controls. Further studies showed that ISG mRNAs were more stable in the absence of ZNFX1, suggesting altered posttranscriptional regulation, although the precise mechanism remained elusive. Fibroblasts from patients with biallelic missense variants were not included in functional studies, so conclusions were limited for these variants. The authors emphasized that this genetic defect promotes interferon-associated inflammation, but also interferes with the mechanisms of antiviral response. The findings implicated ZNFX1 as an important regulator of the interferon response to double-stranded nucleic acids following viral infections and showed that it acts as a buffer to keep a balanced interferon response, thereby giving it a role in the innate immune response.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Zaki syndrome (ZKS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the WLS gene ({611514}) on chromosome 1p31.

description.title: Description
description.content: Zaki syndrome (ZKS) is characterized by developmental delay, progressive microcephaly, and short stature, as well as dysmorphic features including sparse scalp hair, cupped ears, wide nose and mouth, short philtrum, and high-arched palate. Other variable features have been observed, including ocular, skeletal, cardiac, and renal anomalies ({1:Chai et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Chai et al. (2021)} reported 10 children from 5 families with delayed global milestones, short stature, progressive microcephaly, and mutation in the WLS gene. There were 5 affected sibs in a consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates (family 1), who shared similar dysmorphisms including cupped ears, sparse scalp hair, and partial toe syndactyly. MRI in 1 child showed cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and enlarged fourth ventricle. Additional features in 2 sisters born of first-cousin Egyptian parents (family 2) included visual impairment, iris coloboma, cupped ears, and sparse hair. MRI in both revealed corpus callosum hypoplasia, as well as cerebellar vermis hypoplasia in the younger sister. An affected Native American girl (family 3) showed bilateral iris coloboma and congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and a Brazilian girl (family 4) had renal agenesis and hydronephrosis, as well as hypoplasia of the corpus callosum and cerebellar vermis and enlarged fourth ventricle on brain MRI; information on dysmorphic features was unavailable for those 2 patients. The proband in family 5 was an Indian girl who had normal intelligence but delayed gross and fine motor milestones, and also showed cupped ears and sparse scalp hair and eyebrows. Skeletal anomalies included toe syndactyly in 5 patients and ectrodactyly in 1, broad distal phalanges in 4, long fingers in 3, and hypoplasia of toe phalanges and toenails in 2. The authors noted that features were overlapping but not identical among the 10 patients, which they attributed to genetic modifiers or environmental factors. They designated the phenotype 'Zaki syndrome.'

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of Zaki syndrome in the families reported by {1:Chai et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

mapping.title: Mapping
mapping.content: In a consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates (family 1) with Zaki syndrome, {1:Chai et al. (2021)} performed parametric linkage analysis of genomewide SNP arrays by genotyping blood-derived DNA from both parents and all 5 affected children. A homozygous peak with a lod score of 3.00 was obtained at chromosome 1, in a region containing the WLS gene.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: By exome sequencing in a consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates with Zaki syndrome mapping to chromosome 1 (family 1), {1:Chai et al. (2021)} identified homozygosity for a missense mutation in the WLS gene (Y392C; {611514.0001}) that segregated fully with disease and was not found in the gnomAD database. Homozygous missense mutations in WLS were then identified in affected individuals from 4 additional families with Zaki syndrome: a Y478C substitution ({611514.0002}) in 2 Egyptian sisters (family 2) and a Native American girl (family 3), an I531T change ({611514.0003}) in a Brazilian girl (family 4), and an R536C variant ({611514.0004}) in an Indian girl (family 5). The mutations segregated with disease in the respective families.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Chai et al. (2021)} generated knock-in mice carrying the Wls Y392C ({611514.0001}) or Y478C ({611514.0002}) mutations. Heterozygotes were healthy and viable, but homozygous mutants showed perinatal lethality. Nearly all mutants in both lines had defects in caudal neural tube closure, with severely reduced or absent tail buds and reduced numbers of caudal vertebrae. Cystic medullary hydronephrosis was observed in both lines, as well as reduced numbers of forelimb and hindlimb digits. Mutants in both lines also showed a notably reduced brain size, with severely defective hippocampal dentate gyrus, decreased numbers of cortical neurons, and cobblestone-like penetration of neurons through the disrupted pial basement membrane. The authors noted that the findings in the knock-in mice recapitulated the major defects observed in patients with Zaki syndrome. Intraperitoneal administration of a pharmacologic Wnt agonist during embryogenesis resulted in partial rescue of the phenotype, including increased tail length and number of caudal vertebrae, reduction in incidence of hydronephrosis, and increase in brain size.
