phenotypes.phenotype: Congenital heart defects, multiple types, 8, with or without heterotaxy

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that multiple types of congenital heart defects-8 with or without heterotaxy (CHTD8) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SMAD2 gene ({601366}) on chromosome 18q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Multiple types of congenital heart defects-8 (CHTD8) is characterized by cardiac septal defects, double-outlet right ventricle, unbalanced complete atrioventricular canal, and valvular anomalies, as well as vascular anomalies including dextroposition of the great arteries, anomalous pulmonary venous return, and superior vena cava to left atrium defect. Patients may also exhibit laterality defects, including dextrocardia, atrial isomerism, dextrogastria, left-sided gallbladder, and intestinal malrotation ({2:Zaidi et al., 2013}; {1:Granadillo et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Zaidi et al. (2013)} reported 2 unrelated patients who had complex congenital heart disease with heterotaxy and mutation in the SMAD2 gene. Patient 1-02020 had dextrocardia, unbalanced complete atrioventricular canal (CAVC), pulmonary stenosis, double-outlet right ventricle (DORV), dextroposition of the great arteries (DTGA), and atrial septal defect (ASD), as well as asplenia. Height and weight were at the 95th and 10th percentile, respectively, and neurologic development was normal. Patient 1-02621 had dextrocardia, unbalanced right-dominant CAVC, pulmonary stenosis, DORV, superior vena cava to left atrium defect, and partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (APVR), as well as abnormal nose, foot syndactyly, and gut malrotation. Height and weight were at the 50th percentile for each; information on neurodevelopment was not available.

Using GeneMatcher, {1:Granadillo et al. (2018)} ascertained 3 individuals, a 2-year-old girl (patient 1), a 10-year-old girl (patient 2), and a female fetus (patient 3), who had complex congenital heart defects with other congenital anomalies and mutation in the SMAD2 gene. All 3 had ASD and ventricular septal defect (VSD); additional defects included DORV and valvular anomalies in patients 1 and 2, DTGA in patient 1, and unbalanced CAVC, APVR, and hypoplastic left ventricle in the fetus. The fetus also exhibited laterality defects, including dextrocardia, atrial isomerism, dextrogastria, and left-sided gallbladder. Other features in patients 1 and 2 included short stature, poor weight gain, developmental delay, and seizures, as well as dysmorphic features including midface hypoplasia, high-arched palate, micrognathia, and dental crowding.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SMAD2 gene that were identified by {2:Zaidi et al. (2013)} and {1:Granadillo et al. (2018)} in patients with congenital heart defects occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
From a cohort of 362 parent-offspring trios in which a child had severe congenital heart disease but no first-degree relative with structural heart disease, {2:Zaidi et al. (2013)} identified 2 unrelated patients with congenital heart defects and heterotaxy who were heterozygous for de novo mutations in the SMAD2 gene: patient 1-02020 had a splice site variant ({601366.0001}) and patient 1-02621 had a missense variant (W244C; {601366.0002}).

In 3 patients with complex congenital heart defects, including 1 with heterotaxy, {1:Granadillo et al. (2018)} identified heterozygous mutations in the SMAD2 gene: a nonsense mutation (E159X; {601366.0007}) in patient 1, a missense mutation (C312S; {601366.0008}) in patient 2, and a splice site mutation ({601366.0009}) in patient 3. None of the mutations were found in public variant databases. In patients 2 and 3, the mutations were shown to have occurred de novo; the father of patient 1 was unavailable for testing. In patient 1, who also exhibited a single central incisor, analysis of a holoprosencephaly panel revealed a known HPE-associated variant (see HPE4, {142946}) in the TGIF1 gene (Q107L; {602630.0006}).

Disease course can be acute and result in early death

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids-2 (HDLS2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the AARS1 gene ({601065}) on chromosome 16q22. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids-2 (HDLS2) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive and executive dysfunction, psychiatric disturbances, and neurologic symptoms, such as gait abnormalities, paresis, seizures, and rigidity. Symptom onset is usually in adulthood, although earlier onset has been reported. Some patients have an acute encephalopathic course with severe neurologic decline resulting in early death, whereas other patients have a more protracted and chronic disease course. Neuropathologic examination shows a leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and myelination defects (summary by {3:Sundal et al., 2012}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of HDLS, see HDLS1 ({221820}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Axelsson et al. (1984)} reported a large multigenerational Swedish family in which multiple members had a progressive neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by various combinations of psychiatric, neurologic, and somatic symptoms. The age at onset ranged from 8 to 60 years (mean of 36 years); some had rapidly progressive dementia and died within a few months or years, whereas others had a more prolonged and protracted course. The most common first and predominant manifestations were psychiatric, including depression and anxiety with later onset of disorientation, amnesia, psychotic symptoms, executive dysfunction, and aggression. Neurologic symptoms included seizures (in 4 patients), gait or balance disturbances, ataxia, and extrapyramidal signs. Somatic symptoms included gastrointestinal problems, arthritis, and weight loss with emaciation. Severe dementia occurred in the late stages. Two patients committed suicide, and several had alcoholism. Neuropathologic examination showed foci of demyelination in the cerebral white matter with preservation of U fibers. {1:Axelsson et al. (1984)} proposed the term 'hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids' (HDLS) to describe the disorder.

{3:Sundal et al. (2012)} reported follow-up of the Swedish family studied by {1:Axelsson et al. (1984)}, noting that there was intrafamilial variability. {3:Sundal et al. (2012)} identified 2 additional affected family members. One had an subacute multisystem encephalopathy resulting in death 1.5 years after presentation at age 33 years. Features included mental deterioration, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and bladder paresis that progressed to a vegetative state with tetraparesis and rigidity. Neuropathologic examination showed axonal spheroids in the cerebral white matter. The other patient was a 48-year-old man who presented with a more chronic course of cognitive decline and executive dysfunction. He had increased muscle tone and dysdiadochokinesis, but the psychiatric and cognitive dysfunction were predominant. Brain imaging showed T2-weighted white matter changes.

{2:Sundal et al. (2019)} also studied the Swedish family reported by {1:Axelsson et al. (1984)}, noting that the initial phase of the disease is dominated by frontal lobe symptoms that develop into a progressive encephalopathy characterized by pyramidal, extrapyramidal, and optic tract symptoms. Median survival is less than 10 years. Clinical details of 2 patients were provided. They had onset of personality changes and frontal lobe syndrome at 46 and 34 years of age. Other manifestations included deep sensory ataxia, gait difficulties, and dystonic and ballistic movements that progressed to a generalized pyramidal syndrome with rigidity and loss of visual fields. Both patients had a rapid disease course and became uncommunicative in a vegetative state; both died of the disease within several years. Postmortem examination showed liquefaction of the white matter, gliosis, axonal spheroids, and severe loss of myelin.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HDLS2 in the family reported by {1:Axelsson et al. (1984)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 affected members of a large multigenerational Swedish family with HDLS2 originally reported by {1:Axelsson et al. (1984)}, {2:Sundal et al. (2019)} identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the AARS1 gene (C152F; {601065.0010}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in unaffected family members, consistent with segregation of the mutation with the disorder in the family. The mutation was not found in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant, which occurred in the aminoacylation domain, were not performed.

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the protein kinase, cAMP-dependent, regulatory, type I, beta gene (PRKAR1B,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Marbach-Schaaf neurodevelopmental syndrom (MASNS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PRKAR1B gene ({176911}) on chromosome 7p22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Marbach-Schaaf neurodevelopmental syndrom (MASNS) is characterized by global developmental delay with speech delay and behavioral abnormalities, including autism spectrum disorder and ADHD. Affected individuals also show movement disorders, such as dyspraxia and apraxia. More variable features include high pain tolerance, sleep disturbances, and variable nonspecific dysmorphic features (summary by {1:Marbach et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Marbach et al. (2021)} reported 6 unrelated patients, ranging from 3 to 16 years of age, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay with speech delay, behavioral abnormalities, hypotonia, and movement disorders, including dyspraxia, apraxia, and clumsiness. One patient had tremor and dystonia. Two patients showed regression of language skills, including 1 who became nonverbal by age 7. All patients were diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Four had ADHD and several had aggressive behavior or arm flapping. More variable features included high pain tolerance, sleep disturbances or sleep apnea, and hyperphagia resulting in increased BMI. One patient had seizures; the patient's mother also had a seizure disorder. A few patients had nonspecific dysmorphic features, including upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, flat nasal bridge, and downturned mouth.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the PRKAR1B gene that were identified in patients with MASNS by {1:Marbach et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 unrelated patients with MASNS, {1:Marbach et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous missense mutations in the PRKAR1B gene ({176911.0002}-{176911.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, occurred de novo in 5 patients; parental DNA from the sixth patient was not available. Four patients carried the same mutation (R335W; {176911.0002}), suggesting a potential mutational hotspot, and all mutations were absent from the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells transfected with the mutations showed that all caused significantly decreased basal PKA enzymatic activity compared to controls, consistent with a loss of function.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and neonatal cholestasis

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and neonatal cholestasis (NEDMSC) is caused by homozygous mutation in the VPS50 gene ({616465}) on chromosome 7q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and neonatal cholestasis (NEDMSC) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severely impaired global development apparent from infancy, progressive microcephaly, and neonatal cholestasis manifest as jaundice and elevated liver enzymes. The liver disease resolves, but affected individuals show feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, hyperkinetic movements, irritability, and poor eye contact or vision, and achieve almost no motor or cognitive developmental milestones. Brain imaging demonstrates agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum. Death in early childhood may occur (summary by {1:Schneeberger et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Schneeberger et al. (2021)} reported 2 unrelated male infants who presented soon after birth with irritability, jaundice, and hepatomegaly due to neonatal cholestasis. Laboratory studies showed elevated liver enzymes, increased total and direct serum bilirubin, and increased alkaline phosphatase. Liver biopsy of patient 2 showed intralobular cholestasis with multinucleation and rosetting of hepatocytes and scant fibrosis. Other histologic abnormalities included disruption of bile canaliculi, displacement of tight junction profiles, and disordered canalicular antigen distribution. The jaundice and liver abnormalities gradually improved and resolved over several months in both patients. In addition, the patients showed failure to thrive with progressive microcephaly (down to -10 z), hypotonia with no head control, inability to sit, walk, or speak, poor or absent visual fixation, poor vision, poor social smile, and poor feeding. They achieved almost no developmental milestones. One required a feeding tube. Patient 1 had opisthotonic posturing and developed infantile spasms at 6 months of age; EEG showed epileptiform activity and was suggestive of focal seizures. He also had severe myopia and auditory pathway dysfunction on audiometry testing. Brain imaging showed a hypoplastic corpus callosum. A similarly affected sister died of aspiration pneumonia at 15 months of age. She developed seizures at 7 days, could not hold up her head, did not fix or follow, and attained no cognitive or motor developmental milestones. Brain imaging showed agenesis of the corpus callosum. Patient 2 had episodes of hyperkinetic irritability with autonomic dysfunction, dehydration, and respiratory decompensation. By age 25 months, he had developed a hyperkinetic movement disorder with multifocal twitching, as well as generalized tonic seizures with eye deviation, screaming, and apnea. Brain imaging showed hypoplastic corpus callosum and generalized brain atrophy. He died at age 32 months in palliative care.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMSC in the families reported by {1:Schneeberger et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated children with NEDMSC, {1:Schneeberger et al. (2021)} identified homozygous mutations in the VPS50 gene ({616465.0001} and {616465.0002}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families. Neither were present in the gnomAD database. Patient-derived fibroblasts showed normal VPS50 mRNA levels, but almost no VPS50 protein was detectable, suggesting that the mutant proteins are unstable or degraded. Protein levels of VPS50-interacting partners in the EARP complex were also decreased, indicating compromised EARP function. Although endocytosis of the transferrin receptor (TFRC; {190010}) was normal in patient cells, there was defective and delayed recycling of TFRC, consistent with impaired function of the EARP complex. Lysosomal function was normal in patient cells.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Brunet-Wagner neurodevelopmental syndrome (BRUWAG) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RBL2 gene ({180203}) on chromosome 16q12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Brunet-Wagner neurodevelopmental syndrome (BRUWAG) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by infantile hypotonia and severely impaired development affecting both motor and cognitive skills. Affected individuals either do not achieve independent ambulation or walk with an unsteady gait; those who walk may lose the ability due to spasticity of the lower limbs. They have absent language, poor or absent social skills, and behavioral abnormalities. Most have variable ocular findings, including nystagmus, strabismus, optic atrophy, myopia, or hypermetropia (summary by {1:Brunet et al., 2020} and {2:Samra et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Brunet et al. (2020)} reported 2 sibs, born of unrelated parents, with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder apparent from early childhood. The patients, who were 17 and 15 years of age, had hypotonia in early infancy and began crawling around 2 years of age, but never achieved independent ambulation. They had severe developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, no social interaction, absent speech, and stereotypic and autoaggressive behavior. Both had nystagmus; additionally, the older sister had strabismus and the younger brother had optic atrophy. The younger brother had a more severe clinical course, showing developmental regression associated with the onset of refractory myoclonic seizures at age 10 years. Minor dysmorphic features, including hypertelorism, thin eyebrows, and full lips, were observed. Brain imaging showed supra- and infratentorial atrophy and hyperostosis of the skull; the brother had a thin corpus callosum. They did not have microcephaly.

{2:Samra et al. (2021)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families of Druze and Kurdish descent, respectively, with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients presented in infancy with hypotonia and global developmental delay. They achieved walking with an unsteady, but not ataxic, gait between 2 and 9 years of age. Two patients from family 1 developed lower limb spasticity and became wheelchair-bound at 6 and 30 years, respectively. The patients had profound intellectual disability with only a few words or absent speech. Two patients had onset of well-controlled seizures at 4 and 20 years. There were variable ocular abnormalities, including strabismus, hypermetropia, corneal clouding, myopia, anisometropia, and astigmatism. Hearing was normal. Two unrelated patients had progressive microcephaly (down to -4.7 SD). Other features included sleep disturbances and irritability.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of BRUWAG syndrome in the family reported by {1:Brunet et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sibs, born of unrelated parents, with BRUWAG syndrome, {1:Brunet et al. (2020)} identified compound heterozygous putative loss-of-function mutations in the RBL2 gene ({180203.0001} and {180203.0002}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 3 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with BRUWAG syndrome, {2:Samra et al. (2021)} identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the RBL2 gene ({180203.0003} and {180203.0004}) that segregated with the disorder in both families. The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Detailed studies of fibroblasts derived from patients in family 1 did not reveal abnormal expression of DNA methyltransferases, did not show DNA methylation abnormalities compared to controls, and did not indicate changes in telomere length or growth characteristics, suggesting that the pathogenesis of the disorder is likely due to another specific function of the RBL2 gene.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay with variable neurologic and brain abnormalities (DENBA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the LMBRD2 gene ({619490}) on chromosome 5p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay with variable neurologic and brain abnormalities (DENBA) is characterized most often by motor and speech delay apparent from early childhood. Most patients have delayed walking and variably impaired intellectual development. Additional neurologic features may include seizures, spasticity, and ocular abnormalities. Brain imaging often shows thin corpus callosum and may show white matter atrophy, myelination abnormalities, or enlarged ventricles. The severity of the disorder and clinical manifestations are highly variable (summary by {1:Malhotra et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Malhotra et al. (2021)} reported 10 unrelated individuals, ranging in age from 21 months to 25 years, with variable developmental or neurologic deficits. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after exome or genome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the LMBRD2 gene. There was a range of phenotypic features, with all but one patient showing developmental delay of motor, speech, and usually cognitive skills. The patients had poor head control in infancy, followed by delayed sitting and walking; some patients later developed hypertonia, spasticity, and hyperreflexia. Five patients had seizures, and 1 was deaf. Seven patients were noted to have a small head circumference, sometimes associated with thin corpus callosum on brain imaging. Brain imaging also showed white matter atrophy, myelination defects, or enlarged ventricles in some patients. About half of patients showed variable ocular anomalies, including congenital esotropia, astigmatism, amblyopia, hyperopia, and nystagmus. Some patients had variable dysmorphic features, including prominent supraorbital ridge, downslanting palpebral fissures, long palpebral fissures, broad nose, and micrognathia. Of note, patient 6 was a 16-year-old Swiss boy who presented with congenital cataract and microphthalmia at birth, but did not have developmental delay or growth defects. He had dysmorphic facial features, including upslanting palpebral fissures, anteverted nares, cupid arc of the lip, micrognathia, corneal calcifications, and tooth hypoplasia. Sloping shoulders and testicular hypoplasia were also observed. Congenital cataract and ocular malformation gene panels were tested and negative in this patient.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the LMBRD2 gene that were identified in patients with DENBA by {1:Malhotra et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 10 unrelated patients with DENBA, {1:Malhotra et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous missense variants in the LMBRD2 gene (see, e.g., R483H, {619490.0001} and W123R, {619490.0002}). The variants, which were found by exome sequencing, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing in most cases. All variants were absent from the gnomAD database. Three patients carried the R483H variant and 2 patients carried W123R. Patient 6, who had no developmental issues and presented with microphthalmia, congenital cataracts, and dysmorphic features, carried a de novo heterozygous K274E variant in the LMBRD2 gene. None of the variants were present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not reported.

text.title: Text
text.content: The existence of a monogenic disorder caused by mutation in the OGDHL gene ({617513}), designated Yoon-Bellen neurodevelopmental syndrome, which was reported by {3:Yoon et al. (2017)} and {2:Yap et al. (2021)}, has been called into question by {1:Lin et al. (2023)}.

description.title: Description
description.content: Yoon-Bellen neurodevelopmental syndrome (YOBELN) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized mainly by global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development. The manifestations and severity of the phenotype are highly variable. Additional neurologic features may include hypotonia, spasticity, ataxia, hearing loss, visual problems, seizures, and nonspecific anomalies on brain imaging (summary by {2:Yap et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Yoon et al. (2017)} reported a 15-year-old girl with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patient had developmental delay apparent in the first year of life, with inability to walk, spasticity, ataxia, microcephaly, and language problems. She did not have seizures. Brain imaging showed hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, cerebellar volume loss, and enlarged ventricles. A similarly affected sib died at age 28 years after being bedridden for many years.

{2:Yap et al. (2021)} identified 9 patients from 8 unrelated families of different ethnic origins with variable early-onset features affecting multiple neurologic domains. The patients, who ranged in age from 2.5 to 27 years, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the OGDHL gene. The families were of Italian, German, Iranian, Pakistani, Syrian, and Ukrainian descent; 6 were consanguineous. The phenotype was highly variable both in manifestations and severity. Most patients began to show symptoms in the first year of life, although 2 (P3 and P4), who had the mildest phenotype, had onset of symptoms at ages 6 and 8 years after normal early development. Common features included developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, speech delay, hypotonia, delayed walking, gait ataxia, or inability to walk due to spasticity, Three patients, including 2 sibs (P1 and P2) had profound hearing loss, and a fourth (P9) had hearing deficits. Five patients had seizures. The seizures in 4 of these patients were severe and consistent with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), including infantile spasms, status epilepticus, and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome with hypsarrhythmia on EEG. The most severely affected patients had continued seizures, were unable to sit or walk independently, were nonverbal, had poor social interactions, and had visual and/or hearing impairment. Patients with less severe manifestations were able to walk, often with ataxia and/or spasticity, and had learning disabilities sometimes with language delay. About half of patients had ocular anomalies, including retinopathy, myopia, central visual impairment, optic atrophy, and nystagmus. Additional variable features included dysarthria, dysphagia, tremor, dysmetria, clonus, pyramidal signs, and sensorimotor neuropathy. Some patients had nonspecific dysmorphic features, including microcephaly, scaphocephaly, high-arched palate, ptosis, downslanting palpebral fissures, and large mouth. Scoliosis, hip dysplasia, and pes cavus were also noted. Brain imaging, performed in a subset of patients, was normal in 3 and showed T2-weighted lesions, thin corpus callosum, and global atrophy in others. One patient had a glioma that was treated successfully.

{1:Lin et al. (2023)} reported a cohort of 14 individuals from 12 unrelated families with a range of phenotypes of variable severity similar to those in the patients reported by {3:Yoon et al. (2017)} and {2:Yap et al. (2021)} with mutation in the OGDHL gene and, in the majority of them, likely pathogenic mutations in another gene (see MOLECULAR GENETICS), 'potentially accounting for a blended phenotype and complicating phenotypic understanding.' The phenotypes included neurodevelopmental disorders, neurodegeneration, infantile-onset epileptic encephalopathy, skeletal dysplasia, childhood-onset epilepsy, multiple congenital anomalies, dysmorphism, nonsyndromic hearing loss, neuromuscular disorders, and congenital heart defects.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of YOBELN in the families reported by {3:Yoon et al. (2017)} and {2:Yap et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 15-year-old girl (BAB4852), born of consanguineous Turkish parents, with YOBELN, {3:Yoon et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the OGDHL gene (S778L; {617513.0001}). The mutation, which was identified in a large database of patients who underwent exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Studies using mutant Drosophila with loss of Ogdh ({613022}), orthologous to human OGDHL, indicated that the OGDHL variant resulted in a loss of function.

In 9 patients from 8 unrelated families of various ethnic descent with YOBELN, {2:Yap et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the OGDHL gene (see, e.g., {617513.0002}-{617513.0006}). Most of the mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing; the mutations segregated with the disorder in the families. There was 1 frameshift, 1 nonsense, and 1 splice site mutation; the remaining mutations were missense variants affecting conserved residues throughout the gene. The patient from family 1 with a P852A mutation ({VAR c.2554C-G, NM_018245}) in OGDHL also carried a homozygous R2064H mutation in the DCHS1 gene ({603057}), but the authors stated that only the OGDHL mutation segregated with disease in the family. Detailed in vitro studies of the orthologous OGDHL missense mutations expressed in Drosophila indicated that some caused a loss of function with decreased protein levels, whereas others conferred normal protein levels. None of the missense variants were able to rescue the lethality of Ogdh-null Drosophila, indicating that they are loss-of-function alleles. In addition, some of the variants tested were unable to rescue lethality in flies with neuronal-specific expression of the mutations, whereas others caused mild behavioral defects in flies. The overall findings indicated that some of the missense mutations resulted in severe functional OGDHL deficiency, whereas others had a less severe effect and acted as hypomorphic alleles. Loss of OGDHL in human neuroblastoma cells resulted in defects in the Krebs cycle and mitochondrial metabolism.

{1:Lin et al. (2023)} reported a cohort of 14 individuals from 12 unrelated families with highly variable phenotypes similar to those in the patients reported by {3:Yoon et al. (2017)} and {2:Yap et al. (2021)} with mutation in the OGDHL and, in the majority of them, likely pathogenic mutations in another gene, e.g., ADARB1 ({601218}), SELENON ({606210}), CYFIP2 ({606323}), NDUFS1 ({157655}), EIF2B3 ({606273}), CDC14A ({603504}), SOX10 ({602229}), and GALNS ({612222}), 'potentially accounting for a blended phenotype and complicating phenotypic understanding.'

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Bryant-Li-Bhoj neurodevelopmental syndrome-1 (BRYLIB1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the H3F3A gene ({601128}) on chromosome 1q42.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Bryant-Li-Bhoj neurodevelopmental syndrome-1 (BRYLIB1) is a highly variable phenotype characterized predominantly by moderate to severe global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, and delayed motor milestones. Most patients have hypotonia, although some have peripheral hypertonia. Common features include abnormal head shape, variable dysmorphic facial features, oculomotor abnormalities, feeding problems, and nonspecific brain imaging abnormalities. Additional features may include hearing loss, seizures, short stature, and mild skeletal defects (summary by {1:Bryant et al., 2020}).

<Subhead> Genetic Heterogeneity of Bryant-Li-Bhoj Neurodevelopmental Syndrome

See also BRYLIB2 ({619721}), caused by heterozygous mutation in the H3F3B gene ({601058}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Bryant et al. (2020)} reported 33 unrelated patients with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder who were ascertained through exome or genome sequencing from several clinical and research centers. Most of the patients were children, although there were a few teenagers and 1 patient was 32 years of age. All had moderate to severe global developmental delay and impaired intellectual development, usually with hypotonia, delayed walking or inability to walk, and poor or absent speech. Rare patients showed developmental regression. Three patients died in the first years of life. About of a third of patients had poor overall growth and short stature. Feeding problems, such as gastroesophageal reflux, were sometimes observed, and 10 patients required a feeding tube. Laryngomalacia was observed in 4 patients. Some patients had hypertonia or peripheral spasticity; the oldest patient had spastic paraplegia. Ten patients had unilateral or bilateral hearing loss. Seventeen patients had various types of seizures, including generalized, myoclonic, tonic, complex partial, and focal. The severity was variable: some had only a single seizure or febrile seizures that were well-controlled, whereas a few had refractory seizures. Most (22) patients had nonspecific abnormalities on brain imaging, including enlarged ventricles, hypoplastic or thin corpus callosum, and hypomyelination. About half of patients had an abnormal head shape with craniosynostosis, microcephaly or macrocephaly, brachycephaly, plagiocephaly, and dolichocephaly. Dysmorphic facial features were common, although there was not a distinct gestalt. Notable findings included prominent forehead, sloped forehead, bitemporal narrowing, flat midface, hypertelorism, deep-set eyes, epicanthal folds, low-set or posteriorly rotated ears, arched or thick eyebrows, flat or depressed nasal bridge, small or large nose, abnormal philtrum, slanted palpebral fissures, micrognathia, retrognathia, open mouth, and thin or tented upper lip. More than half of patients had oculomotor abnormalities, mainly strabismus, exotropia, and nystagmus; a few had tracking problems. Some patients had skeletal anomalies, including distal defects of the hands and feet, scoliosis, kyphosis, joint contractures, and bell-shaped thorax. Less common features included atrial septal defects, cryptorchidism, and chronic constipation. None of the patients developed cancer.

{2:Okur et al. (2021)} reported the clinical details of 4 unrelated patients (patients 1-4), ranging from 4.5 to 28 years of age, with global developmental delay, abnormal ataxic or wide-based gait, speech delay, and hypotonia. Three patients showed failure to thrive in infancy. All had short stature, 3 had microcephaly, and 1 had macrocephaly. Two patients had spasticity of the lower limbs and 2 had seizures. Three were reported to have a happy demeanor. Brain imaging, performed in 2 patients, showed abnormalities in 1: decreased white matter, hypomyelination, and enlarged ventricles. Three patients had variable dysmorphic facial features, including facial asymmetry, upslanting palpebral fissures, esotropia, strabismus, midface hypoplasia, synophrys, hypotelorism, open mouth with full lips, low-set ears, pointed chin, and prognathia. Skeletal anomalies included camptodactyly, small hands and feet, joint hypermobility, pes planus, and scoliosis. Two had chronic constipation. The patients were described retrospectively after exome sequencing identified mutations in the H3F3A gene.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the H3F3A gene that were identified in patients with BRYLIB1 by {1:Bryant et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 33 unrelated patients with BRYLIB1, {1:Bryant et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the H3F3A gene (see, e.g., {601128.0001}-{601128.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or genome sequencing, occurred throughout the gene. All but 1 were absent from the gnomAD database. In vitro studies of lymphoblasts or fibroblasts derived from a subset of patients showed that the distribution of posttranslational modification (PTM) histone abundances was similar to that in controls. The overall histone PTM variation was slightly increased in controls compared to patients. Nonetheless, some histone PTMs were altered in patients compared to controls. The findings suggested that mutant histones can be incorporated into the nucleosome and cause local deregulation of the chromatin state with modest alterations in the control of histone modification. This could affect multiple histone functions, including gene expression, chromatin stability, DNA damage repair, and differentiation. RNA sequencing of a subset of pooled patient cells showed upregulation of genes involved in mitosis, and in vitro studies of pooled patient fibroblast lines showed increased cellular proliferation compared to controls; viability of patient cells was similar to controls. In silico molecular modeling of the mutations suggested 3 broad scenarios for the variants' impact: disruption of H3.3 DNA binding; disrupted formation of the histone octamer or binding with other histones; and disruption of histone-protein binding to chaperones or other interacting proteins. There were no genotype/phenotype correlations.

In 6 unrelated patients with BRYLIB1, {2:Okur et al. (2021)} identified 6 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations at highly conserved residues in the H3F3A gene (see, e.g., {601128.0003}; {601128.0004}; {601128.0006}-{601128.0007}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were absent from the gnomAD database. Expression of a subset of variants in HEK293 cells showed that some resulted in decreased protein levels, whereas 1 (R41C; {601128.0006}) increased protein levels compared to controls. Additional functional studies of some of the variants showed that 1 (R129H; {601128.0007}) had a significantly stronger interaction with DAXX ({603186}) compared to controls, which might lead to aberrant transcription. The mutant proteins localized normally to the nucleus. Molecular modeling suggested that some, but not all, mutations might alter the PTMs of histone H3.3. The possible molecular pathomechanism of other mutations was unclear.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Bryant et al. (2020)} noted that zebrafish with a dominant D123N mutation in the h3f3a gene developed craniofacial abnormalities. Homozygous knockdown of the h3f3a gene resulted in a loss of neural crest-derived jaw cartilages. There was also a partial reduction in Foxd3 ({611539})-derived cranial glia, melanocytes, and xanthophores; those injected with dominant-negative h3f3a showed a further reduction in these cell types.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Bryant-Li-Bhoj neurodevelopmental syndrome-2 (BRYLIB2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the H3F3B gene ({601058}) on chromosome 17q25.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Bryant-Li-Bhoj neurodevelopmental syndrome-2 (BRYLIB2) is a highly variable phenotype characterized predominantly by moderate to severe global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, and delayed motor milestones. Most patients have hypotonia, although some have peripheral hypertonia. Common features include variable dysmorphic facial features, oculomotor abnormalities, feeding problems, and nonspecific brain imaging abnormalities. Additional features may include hearing loss, seizures, short stature, and mild skeletal defects (summary by {1:Bryant et al., 2020}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of Bryant-Li-Bhoj neurodevelopmental syndrome, see BRYLIB1 ({619720}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Bryant et al. (2020)} reported 13 patients (patients 34-46), ranging from 7 months to 18 years of age, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder who were ascertained through exome or genome sequencing from several clinical and research centers. All had moderate to severe global developmental delay with delayed walking or inability to walk, impaired intellectual development, and poor or absent speech. Five patients had short stature or failure to thrive, whereas 2 had macrosomia. Most had hypotonia, and about half had peripheral hypertonia with spasticity. The severity was highly variable: patient 44 was nonverbal and unable to walk at age 18 years, whereas patient 46 had normal development and IQ, but demonstrated an expressive language disorder and had onset of seizures at age 10 years. Three patients had evidence of disease progression. In all, 7 patients had variable types of seizures, which were refractory and severe in a few patients. Brain imaging showed cortical atrophy, hypomyelination, and thin corpus callosum in some patients. Many patients had abnormal head shape, including microcephaly, macrocephaly, brachycephaly, plagiocephaly, and dolichocephaly. Most, but not all, had dysmorphic facial features, including midface hypoplasia, protruding chin, downslanting palpebral fissures, low-set, posteriorly rotated, or large ears, prominent forehead, open mouth expression, low or high nasal bridge, low columella, deep-set eyes, bushy eyebrows, and anteverted nostrils. Some had skeletal anomalies, including scoliosis, hemivertebrae, flat feet, and joint defects. A few patients had cryptorchidism; 2 had hypothyroidism.

{2:Okur et al. (2021)} reported 6 unrelated patients (patients 5-10), ranging from 5 to 33 years of age, with BRYLIB2. The patients had hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and global developmental delay. Most had short stature. Three had microcephaly, 2 had gait abnormalities, and 2 had seizures. Brain imaging was normal in 3, but patient 5 had leukoencephalopathy, and patient 8 had cortical dysplasia with hypoplasia of the corpus callosum and cerebellum. Dysmorphic features included plagiocephaly, dolichocephaly, prominent forehead, flat facial profile, midface hypoplasia, deep-set eyes, downslanting palpebral fissures, long eyelashes, thin upper lip, dental anomalies, depressed nasal bridge, micro- or prognathia, bitemporal narrowing, smooth philtrum, and large posteriorly rotated ears. Despite the facial findings, there was not a clear facial gestalt. Ocular anomalies included strabismus, nystagmus, esotropia, myopia, and retinal degeneration with dysplastic optic nerve. One patient had laryngomalacia and sensorineural hearing loss. Variable skeletal findings included foot deformities, high-arched palate, scoliosis, joint contractures, and joint hypermobility. Two patients had constipation. Two had hypothyroidism, 1 had type I diabetes mellitus, 1 had precocious puberty, and 2 had advanced bone age.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the H3F3B gene that were identified in patients with BRYLIB2 by {1:Bryant et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 13 unrelated patients with BRYLIB2, {1:Bryant et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the H3F3B gene (see, e.g., {601058.0001}-{601058.0004}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or genome sequencing, occurred throughout the gene. All but 1 were missense variants, and all were absent from the gnomAD database. In vitro studies of lymphoblasts or fibroblasts derived from a subset of patients showed that the distribution of posttranslational modification (PTM) histone abundances was similar to controls. The overall histone PTM variation was slightly increased in controls compared to patients. Nonetheless, some histone PTMs were altered in patients compared to controls. The findings suggested that mutant histones can be incorporated into the nucleosome and cause local deregulation of the chromatin state with modest alterations in the control of histone modification. This could affect multiple histone functions, including gene expression, chromatin stability, DNA damage repair, and differentiation. RNA sequencing of a subset of pooled patient cells showed upregulation of genes involved in mitosis, and in vitro studies of pooled patient fibroblast lines showed increased cellular proliferation compared to controls; viability of patient cells was similar to controls. In silico molecular modeling of the mutations suggested 3 broad scenarios for the variants' impact: disruption of H3.3 DNA binding; disrupted formation of the histone octamer or binding with other histones; and disruption of histone-protein binding to chaperones or other interacting proteins. There were no genotype/phenotype correlations. None of the patients developed cancer.

In 6 unrelated patients with BRYLIB2, {2:Okur et al. (2021)} identified 6 different de novo heterozygous mutations at highly conserved residues in the H3F3B gene (see, e.g., {601058.0001} and {601058.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were absent from the gnomAD database. Expression of a subset of variants in HEK293 cells showed that some resulted in decreased protein levels. The mutant proteins localized normally to the nucleus. Molecular modeling suggested that some, but not all, mutations might alter the PTMs of histone H3.3. The possible molecular pathomechanism of other mutations was unclear.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable movement or behavioral abnormalities (NEDMAB) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KCNN2 gene ({605879}) on chromosome 5q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable movement or behavioral abnormalities (NEDMAB) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by mildly to severely impaired intellectual development and, in some patients, movement abnormalities consisting of tremors, cerebellar ataxia, or extrapyramidal symptoms. Movement abnormalities have onset in childhood or adolescence. Other variable features include autism spectrum disorder or autistic features and epilepsy.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Mochel et al. (2020)} described 10 unrelated patients with impaired intellectual development (IID), 6 of whom had early-onset movement abnormalities. The IID was mild in 4 patients, moderate in 3, and severe in 2; 1 patient, aged 2 years, had motor and language delays. The movement abnormalities included tremors (5 patients), cerebellar ataxia (4 patients), and extrapyramidal symptoms (4 patients), including myoclonus dystonia, bradykinesia with cogwheel rigidity, and dyskinesia with parkinsonism and choreic movements. The 4 patients without movement abnormalities were under the age of 16 years at the time of study. Autism spectrum disorder was seen in 2 patients, and autistic features were seen in 4. The 2 oldest patients, aged 30 and 60 years, had psychotic episodes in adulthood, suggesting that psychiatric findings might be a feature of the disorder. Epilepsy was seen in 2 patients. Brain MRI data were available for 6 patients, 3 of which showed white matter abnormalities. In 1 patient, her mother had similar findings (mild intellectual disability, a dyskinetic movement disorder with dystonia, and an unspecified psychiatric disorder) and the mother's brother had similar symptoms but was unavailable for genetic testing. The other 9 patients were the first in their family to be affected. The first patient studied was recruited from a series of individuals with leukoencephalopathies of unknown origin and the other patients were found through GeneMatcher.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the KCNN2 gene that were identified in 9 of the 10 patients with NEDMAB reported by {2:Mochel et al. (2020)} occurred de novo; one patient inherited the mutation from her mother.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 10 unrelated patients with NEDMAB, {2:Mochel et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous mutations in the KCNN2 gene (see, e.g., {605879.0002}-{605879.0004}). Nine of the mutations occurred de novo and one, a missense mutation, was inherited from an affected mother. The de novo mutations included 1 nonsense, 5 missense, 1 splice site, and 2 in-frame deletions. The mutations clustered in or near functional SK domains, and the missense mutations occurred at highly conserved residues. The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. To assess the functional consequences of the KCNN2 mutations, the authors tested SK2 channel function in 5 of the variants and showed that all resulted in loss of function of the SK2 channels. {2:Mochel et al. (2020)} suggested haploinsufficiency as the pathogenic mechanism. ({2:Mochel et al. (2020)} excluded a heterozygous missense mutation in the KCNN2 gene (E30Q) identified in another patient (patient 11) they studied because it was located in the N-terminal domain, did not affect a conserved residue, and did not result in a loss of function of the SK2 channels; this mutation was classified as a variant of uncertain significance.) {2:Mochel et al. (2020)} noted that the mutation they identified in patient 3 (I288S) corresponds to the I289N mutation found in Trdk rats, which also show significantly reduced SK2 currents ({1:Kuramoto et al., 2017}).

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-86 (SPG86) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ABHD16A gene ({142620}) on chromosome 6p21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-86 (SPG86) is a complex neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent from early childhood combined with early-onset progressive spasticity mainly affecting the lower limbs, but also affecting the upper limbs. Affected individuals have hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses, pyramidal signs, and difficulty walking or inability to walk. Some may have joint contractures and foot or ankle deformities. Patients with SPG86 have impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, often with behavioral abnormalities. Brain imaging shows thin corpus callosum and white matter abnormalities. Rare patients may have seizures. The disorder is thus a complicated form of SPG (summary by {3:Yahia et al., 2021}, {2:Miyake et al., 2022}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia, see SPG5A ({270800}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Yahia et al. (2021)} reported 4 children, ranging from 7 to 10 years of age, from 2 unrelated consanguineous Sudanese families with a complex neurodevelopmental disorder apparent from infancy. They had global developmental delay, delayed walking, severely impaired intellectual development with absent language, and spastic paraplegia of the limbs with hyperreflexia. There was some phenotypic variability. The brothers in family F37 showed regression of motor skills and became wheelchair-dependent later in childhood. They had lower limb stiffness, spasticity, foot or ankle deformities, and distal muscle weakness; one brother had bilateral upgoing plantar responses. Both also had choreoathetosis, suggesting extrapyramidal involvement. Behavioral abnormalities, including irritability, crying bouts, emotional lability, hand clapping, and head banging, were present. Brain imaging showed thin corpus callosum and subcortical and periventricular white matter high signals. The sibs in family F69 were first noted to have developmental regression in early infancy following a febrile illness. Later they were able to walk with support, but they had severe intellectual disability and were nonverbal. One child had 2 febrile seizures. Other features included spasticity of the upper and lower limbs, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, scoliosis, and foot deformities. Brain imaging was not performed.

{1:Lemire et al. (2021)} reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated families with complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia. The patients, who ranged from 5 to 21 years of age, were of various ethnic descents, including French Canadian, Armenian, mixed European, Egyptian, and Pakistani; 3 families were consanguineous. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts. The patients presented in early childhood with global developmental delay, delayed walking, impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, progressive spasticity of the lower and often the upper limbs, hyperreflexia, and ankle clonus. Most patients had joint contractures, particularly of the ankles, and/or foot deformities. Five patients had mild scoliosis. The severity of the disorder was variable: some patients were able to walk with difficulty, whereas others needed support or used a wheelchair. Some were able to communicate effectively, whereas others had difficulties. Two patients had seizures, including 1 with early-onset myoclonic seizures and another patient with a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Three patients had evidence of a peripheral axonal or mixed neuropathy, and some had mild extrapyramidal signs. A few patients had nonspecific dysmorphic features. Brain imaging showed a thin corpus callosum and periventricular and deep white matter abnormalities.

{2:Miyake et al. (2022)} reported 2 sibs, 15 and 11 years of age and born of unrelated Chilean parents, with SPG86. They presented in infancy with global developmental delay and pyramidal signs in the lower limbs. The older sib walked with an unstable gait at age 2 years, lost this ability at age 4, and was wheelchair-bound at age 8. Although he had muscle weakness, hyperreflexia, and positive Babinski sign, lower limb spasticity waned in childhood. However, the spasticity spread to affect the upper limbs, and hyperreflexia remained. His younger sister had a similar disease course with loss of ambulation by age 5. The patients had intellectual disability with poor or absent speech and did not achieve sphincter control. The also had behavioral and psychiatric disturbances, including happy demeanor, autistic behavior, hyperactivity, screaming, and sleep disturbances. Additional features included nodular and hyperpigmented skin lesions and cafe-au-lait spots, as well as facial dysmorphism, such as narrow forehead, thick eyebrows, deep-set eyes, low-set ears, full cheeks, short philtrum, large mouth, and high palate. Both had foot deformities. Brain imaging showed thin corpus callosum in both and white matter abnormalities in the older sib.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SPG86 in the families reported by {3:Yahia et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 4 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous Sudanese families with SPG86, {3:Yahia et al. (2021)} identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the ABHD16A gene (R114X, {142620.0001} and R457Q, {142620.0002}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Patient fibroblasts showed lack of ABHD16A expression. The levels of phosphatidylserine substrates were increased, and the levels of lysophosphatidylserine were decreased compared to controls, suggesting that the variants caused a loss of ABHD16A enzyme function. {3:Yahia et al. (2021)} hypothesized that low levels of lysophosphatidylserine, which participates in cellular signaling and neuronal growth, could contribute to the neurologic dysfunction in the brain. The pathogenic mechanism may also be related to altered phosphatidylserine metabolism.

In 11 patients from 6 unrelated families with SPG86, {1:Lemire et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the ABHD16A gene (see, e.g., {142620.0003}-{142620.0005}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing; the families were ascertained through collaborative efforts. The mutations segregated with the disorder in all families. There were 4 missense, 1 nonsense, and 1 frameshift mutation, which were located throughout the gene. Immunoblot analysis of patient fibroblasts showed little to no ABHD16A protein compared to controls. These cells showed a broad range of proliferation compared to controls. Lipidomic studies in patient fibroblasts and plasma showed increased phosphatidylserine levels, but did not show a clear change in lysophosphatidylserine levels compared to controls. However, other lipidomic changes were observed. The authors noted that lipidomic changes may be different in neuronal cells, which were not studied. The findings demonstrated the critical role of lipid metabolism and homeostasis in maintaining the nervous system.

In 2 sibs, born of unrelated Chilean parents, with SPG86, {2:Miyake et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the ABHD16A gene ({142620.0006}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the variant was predicted to result in a loss of function. The authors noted that the gene is expressed in various human tissues which can explain the complex phenotype.

text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-54 (COXPD54) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PRORP gene ({609947}) on chromosome 14q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-54 (COXPD54) is an autosomal recessive disorder with pleiotropic multisystem presentations resulting from a disruption in mitochondrial transcription and translation. The phenotype is highly variable. Many patients have early-onset sensorineural hearing loss, sometimes in isolation, and sometimes associated with global developmental delay or primary ovarian failure. Other features may include peripheral hypertonia, seizures, muscle weakness, behavioral abnormalities, and leukoencephalopathy on brain imaging. Serum lactate may or may not be elevated (summary by {1:Hochberg et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Hochberg et al. (2021)} reported 8 patients from 4 unrelated families with variable systemic abnormalities associated with biallelic variants in the PRORP gene. Family 1 was initially studied by the authors; families 2 through 4 were identified through the GeneMatcher Program and the 100,000 Genomes Project. The phenotype was highly variable. In family 1, which was consanguineous, 3 adult sisters had profound sensorineural hearing loss since infancy and primary amenorrhea with absence of ovarian tissue and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism on hormonal examination. These features were consistent with a clinical diagnosis of Perrault syndrome (see {233400}). They also had mild intellectual disability; brain imaging was not performed. The 9-year-old boy in family 2 had mild to moderate hearing loss with delayed speech and language skills as a result of the hearing loss. No other neurologic involvement or involvement of other organ systems was noted. Brain imaging was normal. There were no other affected family members. The 3-year-old boy in family 3 had a severe phenotype. He presented soon after birth with appendicular hypertonia and mild dysmorphic facial features. He had severe feeding difficulties requiring tube feeding and was noted to have global developmental delay with acquired mild microcephaly. Plasma lactate was consistently elevated. At age 3 years, testing was consistent with an auditory neuropathy and sensorineural hearing loss. Brain imaging showed periventricular nodular heterotopia, dysplastic corpus callosum, and subcortical white matter loss. No other family members were affected. Family 4 was consanguineous and consisted of a mother and her 2 children. None had hearing loss. The proband was a 19-year-old man with a history of childhood psychosis, autistic traits, learning disabilities, and seizures. He had an increased lactate/pyruvate ratio, although plasma lactate was normal. His 15-year-old younger sister had global developmental delay, poor overall growth, seizures, and tremor. She had hyperglycemia, but lactate was normal. Their mother presented with optic neuritis at age 39 years. She subsequently developed asthenia, distal muscle weakness with areflexia, myalgia, memory loss, and headaches. She had 2 episodes of left hemiparesis that resolved, as well as repetitive episodes of lower limb thrombophlebitis. There was no evidence of ovarian insufficiency. Brain imaging in all 3 patients showed a leukoencephalopathy.

{2:Smith et al. (2023)} reported a 7-year-old boy (family 2) with COXPD54 who presented at 3 years of age with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, developmental delay, spastic diplegia, and hypotonia. A brain MRI did not show white matter lesions.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of COXPD54 in the families reported by {1:Hochberg et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance with variable expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 8 patients from 4 unrelated families with COXPD54, {1:Hochberg et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PRORP gene (see, e.g., {609947.0001}-{609947.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were 5 missense variants affecting highly conserved residues in the metallonuclease domain and 1 frameshift variant. Analysis of fibroblasts derived from 2 unrelated families showed decreased levels of the PRORP protein, an accumulation of unprocessed mitochondrial transcripts, and decreased levels of mitochondrial-encoded proteins. These defects could be rescued by wildtype PRORP in vitro. Additional in vitro studies of the recombinant mutant missense proteins showed that the variants caused variably diminished processing of mitochondrial tRNA, with a more severe reduction associated with a more severe phenotype.

In 2 unrelated patients with COXPD54, a 7-year-old boy of Mexican background and the daughter of consanguineous Arab parents, {2:Smith et al. (2023)} identified homozygous mutations (T387A, {609947.0006} and A414V {609947.0007}, respectively) in the PRORP gene. Purified PRORP with each of the mutations demonstrated reduced pre-tRNA Ile processing compared to wildtype.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1I (CMT1I) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the POLR3B gene ({614366}) on chromosome 12q23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1I (CMT1I) is a neurologic disorder characterized predominantly by delayed motor development in the first years of life associated with gait abnormalities, sensory ataxia, hyporeflexia, and distal sensory impairment due to a sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy that mainly affects the lower limbs. The disorder is progressive, and some may have upper limb involvement. A subset of patients has central nervous system involvement that manifests as global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and speech difficulties. Other features may include spasticity, hyperreflexia, tremor, dysmetria, seizures, or cerebellar findings. Brain imaging may be normal or show nonspecific abnormalities, such as white matter signal changes and delayed myelination (summary by {1:Djordjevic et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1, see CMT1B ({118200}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Djordjevic et al. (2021)} reported 6 unrelated patients, ranging from 4 to 22 years of age, with a complex neurologic disorder. They presented in the first years of life with motor delay and walking between 18 months and 3.5 years of age. Walking was impaired by wide-based gait, awkward in-toed gait, or ataxia. Five patients had impaired intellectual development with speech delay and dysarthria. IQ, when measured, ranged in the 50s. One patient (patient 3) had normal cognitive development and attended school. Four patients had progressive spasticity of the upper and lower limbs associated with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses. Five patients had EMG evidence of a peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy, usually demyelinating, but sometimes with secondary axonal features. Clinical muscle strength and sensory examinations were difficult to perform. A few showed signs of cerebellar dysfunction, including ataxia, tremor, and dysmetria. Three patients had onset of various types of seizures in the first months or years of life; seizures were refractory in 2 patients. Brain imaging showed nonspecific findings in 3 patients, including cerebellar atrophy, white matter abnormalities, and delayed myelination. A fourth patient had a Chiari I malformation that was thought to be coincidental. Patient 2 had gross motor delay, abnormal gait, and speech delay with dysarthria. He developed seizures at age 3 years, but did not have electrophysiologic evidence of peripheral neuropathy at age 4; the authors suggested that neuropathy may develop with age, as he was the youngest patient in the group.

{2:Xue et al. (2021)} reported a 19-year-old Chinese man who developed classic features of CMT beginning around 5 years of age. He had progressive lower limb weakness and atrophy with walking difficulties, including a steppage gait. He developed pes cavus; ankle reflexes were absent. The upper limbs became involved showing claw hands and distal muscle atrophy. He also had distal sensory impairment. Electrophysiologic studies were consistent with a sensorimotor demyelinating polyneuropathy with secondary axonal loss. Sural nerve biopsy showed loss of myelinated nerve fibers. He had normal cognition, no evidence of central nervous system involvement, and normal brain imaging.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the POLR3B gene that were identified in patients with CMT1I by {1:Djordjevic et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 6 unrelated patients with CMT1I, {1:Djordjevic et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the POLR3B gene (see, e.g., {614366.0009}-{614366.0012}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Affinity purification coupled with mass spectrometry performed on HEK293 cells transfected with the variants showed that 5 of the 6 impaired the association of POLR3B with 1 or more of the other RNA pol III subunits; the sixth variant showed disrupted association of POLR3B with multiple proteins. These findings suggested that the most of the mutations would render the enzyme inactive. All of the variants localized properly to the nucleus. Western blot analysis of fibroblasts from 1 patient showed normal protein expression. The authors postulated a dominant-negative effect, but noted that more studies were needed to confirm the pathogenetic mechanism.

In a 19-year-old Chinese man with CMT1I, {2:Xue et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous R1046H mutation at a highly conserved residue in the POLR3B gene. The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing, was absent from public databases, including gnomAD. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. He had normal cognition and no evidence of central nervous system involvement.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-55 (COXPD55) is caused by homozygous, compound heterozygous, or heterozygous mutations in the POLRMT gene ({601778}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-55 (COXPD55) is characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia, short stature, and impaired intellectual development with speech disabilities in childhood. Indolent progressive external ophthalmoplegia phenotype has been described in 1 patient (summary by {3:Olahova et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Bowden et al. (2013)} described a 10-year-old girl who presented at 1 year of age with genu valgum and laboratory findings of low serum phosphorus, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and elevated parathyroid hormone. She was treated with ergocalciferol without improvement. Laboratory testing at 3 years of age was consistent with a proximal tubulopathy or a renal Fanconi syndrome. On evaluation at age 5 years, she had mild developmental delay and hypotonia. Laboratory testing showed generalized aminoaciduria, elevated urine lactate, and elevated plasma alanine and proline. Respiratory chain analysis in muscle tissue demonstrated deficient activity of complexes I and III. Brain MRI showed thinning of the corpus callosum. Treatment with elemental phosphorus, calcitriol, and sodium citrate resulted in improvement of genu valgum and a normal growth rate.

{3:Olahova et al. (2021)} described clinical features in 8 patients, including 1 sib pair and the patient (patient 1) previously described by {1:Bowden et al. (2013)}. Five of the patients presented in infancy or childhood and 3 patients presented in adulthood. Five patients had developmental delay, 6 had hypotonia, 1 had seizures, and 4 had brain MRI abnormalities including thinning of the corpus callosum in 1, nonspecific FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the frontoparietal white matter in 1, ventriculomegaly in 1, and cavum septum pellucidum in 1. Eye findings included movement abnormalities in 4 patients, ptosis in 2, and vision problems in 3. Skeletal findings included short stature in 4 patients and hypophosphatemic rickets in 1. Muscle symptoms included facial muscle weakness/wasting in 2 patients, neck wasting/weakness in 1, and limb-girdle myopathy in 3.

{2:Fassad et al. (2026)} reported 6 patients, including a sib pair (family 2) with COXPD55. One of the sibs from family 2 was previously reported by {3:Olahova et al. (2021)}. The patients presented between birth and age 7 years. Two patients reportedly had normal motor development and 3 patients had motor delays. One patient had severely impaired intellectual development, 1 patient had moderately to severely impaired intellectual disability, 1 patient had expressive language delay, 1 patient had no speech and only some sounds at 19 months of age, 1 patient had borderline intelligence, and 1 patient had normal intelligence. Two patients experienced speech regression. Three patients had seizures, and 3 had sleep problems. Behavioral features included irritability and aggressiveness in 1 patient and autism in 1 patient. Muscle hypotonia was identified in 5 patients, and 1 patient had muscle weakness and cramps. Feeding difficulties were reported in 3 patients. Three patients had short stature and 1 patient had tall stature.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: Of the 7 unrelated families with COXPD55 reported by {3:Olahova et al. (2021)}, the transmission pattern was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance in 2 and with autosomal recessive inheritance in 5.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 8 patients from 7 unrelated families with oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-55, {3:Olahova et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous, homozygous, or compound heterozygous mutations in the POLRMT gene ({601778.0001}-{601778.0011}). The mutations were identified by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing or by sequencing of a panel of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes. Functional studies of recombinant POLRMT carried out in all but 2 of the mutations indicated abnormalities in transcription initiation and elongation.

In 5 patients with COXPD55, {2:Fassad et al. (2026)} identified mutations in the POLRMT1 gene: biallelic mutations in 4 (P2, P4, P5, P6) and a de novo heterozygous mutation in 1 (P3). One of the patients (P2) was the sib of a patient previously reported by {3:Olahova et al. (2021)}. Functional studies in patient cells were not performed. An additional patient (P1) studied by {2:Fassad et al. (2026)} with biallelic mutations in the POLRMT1 gene also carried an m.3243A-G mutation.
