text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Tessadori-Bicknell-van Haaften neurodevelopmental syndrome-1 (TEBIVANED1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the H4C3 gene ({602827}) on chromosome 6p22.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Tessadori-Bicknell-van Haaften neurodevelopmental syndrome-1 (TEBIVANED1) is characterized by poor overall growth with short stature, microcephaly, hypotonia, profound global developmental delay often with poor or absent speech, and characteristic dysmorphic facial features, including hypertelorism and abnormal nose. Other variable neurologic and systemic features may also occur ({2:Tessadori et al., 2017}).

<Subhead> Genetic Heterogeneity of Tessadori-van Haaften Neurodevelopmental Syndrome

See also TEBIVANED2 ({619759}), caused by mutation in the H4C11 gene ({602826}); TEBIVANED3 ({619950}), caused by mutation in the H4C5 gene ({602830}); and TEBIVANED4 ({619951}), caused by mutation in the H4C9 gene ({602833}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Tessadori et al. (2017)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder associated with heterozygous mutations in the HIST1H4C gene identified by exome sequencing. Patient 1 was a 9-year-old girl with poor overall growth, short stature, and distinctive facial features noted from birth, including hypertelorism, ptosis, exorbitism, upslanting palpebral fissures, bifid nasal tip, pseudo-cleft of the upper lip, wide mouth, preauricular skin tags, and fair hair. Postnatal microcephaly and hand and foot skeletal ray anomalies were also observed. She had hypotonia with profound global developmental delay and absent speech. She crawled at age 7 years and could pull to stand, yet was able to ride a horse unaided. Other features included myopia, atrial septal defect, small kidneys with lack of corticomedullary junction and small cysts (renal function was normal), and poor feeding necessitating a PEG tube to assist. Brain imaging showed decreased white matter. Patient 2 was a 14-year-old girl with growth delay, microcephaly (-4 SD), hypotonia, and global developmental delay with an IQ of 60. She developed seizures at age 4 years that were controlled with medication, and she later showed psychosis with auditory hallucinations at age 14 years. Brain imaging was normal. Dysmorphic features included hypertelorism, upslanting palpebral fissures, broad nasal tip, low-set ears, lordosis, cutis marmorata, and small feet with ray anomalies. Other features included ocular anomalies with strabismus, recurrent otitis and respiratory tract infections, and umbilical hernia. This patient had an older sister with similar features who died in early infancy of hypertension, thrombosis, and heart and liver failure.

{1:Tessadori et al. (2022)} reported 6 unrelated patients (P1-P6), ranging from 5 to 14 years of age, with a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with de novo heterozygous missense variants in the H4C3 gene that were identified through exome sequencing. P4, P5, and P6 all carried the same mutation (K91Q; {602827.0001}) and appeared to have a more severe phenotype compared to patients P1, P2, and P3, who carried different heterozygous variants (P32A and P32L). P4-P6 had hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and poor overall growth with microcephaly (-2 to -4 SD). All had global developmental delay with variable motor and speech delay; P4 was nonverbal at age 13 years. Two had autism or autistic features and 1 had borderline low intellect. P4 had cortical visual impairment, P5 had seizures, and P6 had conductive hearing loss. P1-P3 had hypotonia, ataxia, mild developmental and speech delay, and variable behavioral problems. Two had myopia or hypermetropia. Five of the patients had variable dysmorphic facial features, including brachycephaly, dolichocephaly, smooth philtrum, wide philtrum, large mouth, hypertelorism, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, round eyes, prominent or wide nasal bridge, round nasal tip, thin upper lip, strabismus, dental crowding, and widely spaced teeth.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of TEBIVANED1 in 1 family reported by {2:Tessadori et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance due to parental mosaicism. The heterozygous mutation in the HIST1H4J gene in another patient with the disorder occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with TEBIVANED1, {2:Tessadori et al. (2017)} identified heterozygous missense mutations affecting a highly conserved residue in the HIST1H4C gene: K92Q ({602827.0001}) and K92R ({602827.0002}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing, occurred de novo in 1 patient and was inherited from an unaffected father who was mosaic in the other 2 patients, who were sibs. Studies of patient fibroblasts showed that the mutant proteins were incorporated into the nucleosome, but posttranslational marks, such as acetylation and ubiquitination, on K91 were absent in the fraction of mutated histone H4 molecules. RNA-seq analysis of patient fibroblasts showed differential expression of multiple genes, including histone genes, genes involved in chromosome organization and DNA packaging, and numerous cell cycle-related genes.

{1:Tessadori et al. (2022)} identified a de novo heterozygous K91Q mutation in the H4C3 gene ({602827.0001}) in 3 unrelated male patients (P4-P6) with TEBIVANED1. The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. The variant was located in the C-terminal domain of the protein. Expression of the mutation in zebrafish embryos induced severe developmental defects, suggesting that it is pathogenic. The authors postulated a dominant effect. Three additional individuals (P1-P3) with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder were found to carry de novo heterozygous variants affecting the same conserved residue in the core globular domain (P32A and P32L). Neither variant was present in the gnomAD database. However, expression of the P32A variant in zebrafish embryos induced only some developmental defects that did not reach significance compared to wildtype; functional studies of P32L were not performed.

<Subhead> Associations Pending Confirmation

For discussion of possible associations between Tessadori-van Haaften neurodevelopmental syndrome and variation in the H4C4 and H4C6 genes, see {602823.0001} and {602824.0001}.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Tessadori et al. (2017)} found that expression of the human HIST1H4C K92Q and K92R mutations in zebrafish resulted in severe embryonic developmental defects, including underdeveloped brain and eyes, defective body axis growth, and a dysmorphic tail. These findings recapitulated some of the features observed in patients carrying the mutations. Analysis of mutant embryos showed an accumulation of double-stranded DNA breaks, genomic instability, increased cell apoptosis and nuclear fragmentation in the head and tail, and disrupted cell cycle progression. There was also evidence of abnormal H4K92 acetylation and ubiquitination compared to controls. The findings suggested an important role for histone H4K92 in early embryonic development.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cerebellar dysfunction, impaired intellectual development, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CDIDHH) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PRDM13 gene ({616741}) on chromosome 6q16.

description.title: Description
description.content: Cerebellar dysfunction, impaired intellectual development, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CDIDHH) is characterized by delayed motor development, ataxia, severe progressive scoliosis, moderate to severe intellectual disability, and delayed sexual development. Cerebellar hypoplasia has been observed in some patients ({1:Whittaker et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Whittaker et al. (2021)} reported a Maltese brother and sister (patients 1 and 2) and an unrelated Maltese man (patient 3) with cerebellar dysfunction, impaired intellectual development, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and mutation in the PRDM13 gene. All 3 patients showed developmental delay in infancy, with generalized hypotonia and hyporeflexia, as well as wide-based ataxic gaits. The 2 sibs ambulated with walkers, whereas patient 3 was wheelchair-dependent by age 12 years. Brain imaging in patients 1 and 3 showed cerebellar hypoplasia, whereas imaging in patient 2 had been reported as normal. All 3 patients had progressive severe scoliosis requiring surgical fixation. In addition, delayed or absent puberty became apparent in adolescence, associated with low gonadotropin levels. Both male patients had a small penis and cryptorchidism, and underwent orchidopexy. The patients responded to testosterone or estrogen supplementation with development of secondary sexual characteristics. Neurologic evaluation in the second and third decades of life showed generalized hypotonia, markedly reduced power, symmetric hyporeflexia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesis, and past-pointing. Patient 3 also exhibited nystagmus. Intellectual deficits were present in all 3, which were reported as moderate in the 2 sibs and severe in patient 3.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDIDHH in the families reported by {1:Whittaker et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: By whole-exome sequencing in a Maltese brother and sister (patients 1 and 2) with cerebellar dysfunction, impaired intellectual development, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, {1:Whittaker et al. (2021)} identified homozygosity for a 13-bp deletion in the PRDM13 gene ({616741.0001}). Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation and demonstrated heterozygosity for the variant in their unaffected third-cousin parents. In a similarly affected unrelated Maltese man (patient 3), the authors sequenced the PRDM13 gene and identified homozygosity for the same 13-bp deletion, for which his unaffected parents were heterozygous. Analysis of 42 Maltese controls revealed 1 heterozygous carrier of the 13-bp deletion. Genomewide microarray analysis in the 3 patients and the unrelated Maltese carrier revealed that the 3 patients shared an identical 1.6-Mb region of homozygosity that encompassed the deletion; the heterozygous carrier shared a smaller (0.2-Mb) nested region of homozygosity, also encompassing the deletion.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Kury-Isidor syndrome (KURIS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the BAP1 gene ({603089}) on chromosome 3p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Kury-Isidor syndrome (KURIS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder with a highly variable phenotype. It is characterized mainly by mild global developmental delay apparent from infancy or early childhood with walking delayed by a few years and speech delay, often with language deficits. Intellectual development may be mildly delayed, borderline, or even normal; most patients have behavioral problems, including autism. Additional variable systemic features may include poor overall growth, hypotonia, distal skeletal anomalies, seizures, and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features (summary by {1:Kury et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Kury et al. (2022)} reported 8 unrelated patients (patients 1-4 and 7-10), ranging from 2 to 16 years of age, who were ascertained through collaborative efforts such as the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous missense variants in the BAP1 gene. Clinical details were limited and the phenotype was highly variable. Most patients presented with mild global developmental delay manifest mainly as delayed walking by a few years and speech delay or speech difficulties. Most also had behavioral abnormalities, including autistic features, sensitivity, and attention deficits. Patient 3 was a 14-year-old girl with more significant behavioral problems, including hyperactivity, tantrums, impulsivity, aggression, and skin picking. Patient 4 was a 6-year-old boy who had speech delay and autism spectrum disorder, but an IQ of 97. Five patients had a history of early seizures that were controlled or resolved. Additional variable features included feeding difficulties with poor overall growth, distal skeletal anomalies, and eye abnormalities, including strabismus, astigmatism, and myopia. Variable nonspecific dysmorphic facial features were sometimes observed: these included frontal bossing, relative macrocephaly, brachycephaly, square-shaped face, coarse facies, long philtrum, low-set simple ears, short nose with anteverted nares, hypertelorism, and downslanting palpebral fissures. Brain imaging, when performed, was normal.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the BAP1 gene that were identified in patients with KURIS by {1:Kury et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 unrelated patients (patients 1-4 and 7-10) with KURIS, {1:Kury et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the BAP1 gene (see, e.g., {602089.0011}-{601089.0014}). All the mutations occurred at conserved residues in the catalytic ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase domain; none were present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies in BAP1-null HAP1 cells showed that some of the variants tested (P12T, {603089.0011}; C91R, {603089.0013}; and H169R, {603089.0014}) were unable to rescue BAP1 activity, as measured by increased BAP1 H2AK119ub substrate levels. Rescue with another variant (P12A; {603089.0012}) was similar to controls for that particular substrate. All variants tested, including P12A, were unable to rescue the expression of BAP1 target genes TMSB4X ({300159}) and S100A11 ({603114}) in a BAP1-null cell line, whereas wildtype BAP1 was able to restore expression of these genes. These data suggested that the BAP1 mutations were unable to compensate H2A deubiquitination of substrates in BAP1-null cells, consistent with a loss-of-function effect. Of note, all the BAP1 variants localized properly to the nucleus in transfected cells. T cells derived from 2 patients carrying the P12T and C91S mutations showed that steady-state levels of ubiquitinated H2A were substantially increased compared to controls, again consistent with a loss-of-function effect for BAP1. CHIP-seq analysis indicated that the variants induced genomewide chromatin state alterations in the 2 patient cell lines; there was also some evidence of proteosome perturbation. {1:Kury et al. (2022)} concluded that BAP1 missense variants alter chromatin remodeling through abnormal histone ubiquitination, leading to transcriptional dysregulation of developmental genes. None of the patients developed tumors. The authors noted that BAP1 mutations that predispose to tumor syndrome are truncating or splice-site mutations; the missense mutations identified in patients with KURIS are loss-of-function and may disrupt the deubiquitinase activity without altering other protein-protein interactions. Some of the patients, including 3 additional patients (patients 5, 6, and 11) with variable developmental abnormalities associated with de novo missense BAP1 variants identified in the study, had additional genetic variants of uncertain significance that may have contributed to the phenotype.

clinicalSynopsis: Dysmorphic facial features, variable, nonspecific (in most patients)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-100 (DEE100) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the FBXO28 gene ({609100}) on chromosome 1q42.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-100 (DEE100) is a severe neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay and onset of variable types of seizures in the first months or years of life. Most patients have refractory seizures and show developmental regression after seizure onset. Affected individuals have ataxic gait or inability to walk and severe to profoundly impaired intellectual development, often with absent speech. Additional more variable features may include axial hypotonia, hyperkinetic movements, dysmorphic facial features, and brain imaging abnormalities (summary by {2:Schneider et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Schneider et al. (2021)} reported 10 unrelated patients with DEE100 associated with heterozygous FBXO28 mutations who were ascertained through international collaborative efforts with research and diagnostic genetic testing laboratories. Patient 3 had previously been reported by {1:Balak et al. (2018)}. The patients ranged from 11 months to 25 years of age: 2 died at 25 years (P5) and 15 years (P8). All patients had developmental delay before the onset of seizures between 8 months and 5 years of age; 6 showed developmental regression after seizure onset. Seizure type at onset varied and included infantile spasms, febrile, focal, generalized tonic-clonic, absence, and myoclonic. The seizures were ongoing in all, often daily in frequency, and refractory to treatment in most patients. EEG showed variable abnormalities, including disorganized background activity, multifocal spikes and continuous spike-wave activity in sleep, multifocal and generalized spike-wave discharges, paroxysmal responses, and modified hypsarrhythmia. The patients had severe to profound intellectual disability with inability to walk or walking only with assistance and absent speech. They had axial hypotonia, drooling, and dysphagia, sometimes with aspiration; 6 were tube-fed. Eight patients were noted to have abnormal movements, including ataxia, myoclonus, hyperkinetic movements, dystonia, chorea, dyskinesia, and stereotypies. More variable features included limb hypertonia, limb contractures, scoliosis or kyphosis, spastic quadriparesis, absent reflexes, and central apnea sometimes requiring oxygen supplementation. Brain imaging was abnormal in most patients, although the findings were variable. Findings included cerebral volume loss or atrophy with enlarged ventricles, delayed myelination, thin corpus callosum, and loss of white matter; P1 and P2 had simplified gyral pattern with polymicrogyria and pachygyria. About half of patients had nonspecific and variable dysmorphic features, such as acquired microcephaly, micrognathia, short palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, hypertelorism, strabismus, large low-set ears, flat nasal bridge, full lips, and high-arched palate.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the FBXO28 gene that were identified in most patients with DEE100 by {2:Schneider et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. Two patients inherited a mutation from an unaffected parent who was low-level mosaic for the mutation.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 3-year-old girl with DEE100, {1:Balak et al. (2018)} identified a de novo frameshift mutation in the last exon (exon 5) of the FBXO28 gene, predicted to result in a frameshift and premature termination (Arg325GlufsTer3; {609100.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors postulated that the mutant transcript would escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and produce a truncated protein that may exert a dominant-negative effect.

In 9 patients with DEE100, {2:Schneider et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous mutations in the FBXO28 gene (see, e.g., {609100.0002}-{609100.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing or gene panel sequencing at various research and diagnostic genetic testing laboratories, were not present in the gnomAD database. All but 2 of the mutations occurred de novo; these were inherited from unaffected parents who had low-level mosaicism. Including the mutation in the patient reported by {1:Balak et al. (2018)}, there were 4 missense variants and 5 frameshift or nonsense mutations. Seven mutations, including 2 missense and all 5 frameshift or nonsense mutations, occurred in the final exon. The latter were predicted to escape nonsense-mediated mRNA, suggesting an alternative mechanism to haploinsufficiency. Two other missense variants (L64R, {609100.0002} and A66P) occurred in the F-box domain, implicating a second pathogenic region of the gene. There was some evidence of a genotype/phenotype correlation, with a more severe phenotype associated with truncating mutations compared to missense mutations. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome-20 (MTDPS20), which manifests as a neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy (MNGIE), is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the LIG3 gene ({600940}) on chromosome 17q12.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome-20 (MTDPS20) is an autosomal recessive multisystem disorder with variable manifestations and severity. Most patients develop symptoms in childhood, although the onset can range from infancy to the teenage years. Prominent features include severe gastrointestinal dysmotility often requiring parenteral nutrition, neurogenic bladder, and muscle weakness and atrophy. Neurologic involvement manifests as headaches, stroke-like episodes, seizures, pyramidal signs, and learning difficulties or cognitive decline. Brain imaging usually shows diffuse leukoencephalopathy and may show cerebellar atrophy. The disorder results from a defect in the maintenance and repair of mitochondrial DNA, resulting in mtDNA depletion and impaired mitochondrial function (summary by {1:Bonora et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mtDNA depletion syndromes, see MTDPS1 ({603041}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Bonora et al. (2021)} reported 3 unrelated families with MTDPS20. Three brothers, born of unrelated Italian parents (family 1), presented in childhood with profound gut dysmotility, recurrent pseudoobstructive episodes, skeletal muscle wasting, and leukoencephalopathy. Gastrointestinal features included vomiting, alternating constipation and diarrhea, abdominal distension, and malnutrition due to delayed gastric emptying. The patients underwent gastric decompression with placement of a terminal ileostomy between 10 and 16 years. Other features included headache with motor deficits and pyramidal signs. The 2 older patients had neurogenic bladder, repetitive behaviors, and macular degeneration. One had tonic-clonic seizures and stroke-like episodes. Brain imaging showed leukoencephalopathy in all patients, cerebellar atrophy in 1, and thin corpus callosum in 1. All 3 boys required teaching support. Two Dutch sisters in family 2 presented in the teenage years with migraines and neurologic symptoms including hemiparesis. One sister had normal schooling and the other had learning difficulties. Both had progressive gastrointestinal symptoms and were diagnosed with chronic intestinal pseudoobstruction (CIPO) at 18 years of age. The older sister underwent colectomy, but later required an ileostomy at age 33, and the younger had ileocecal resection and subtotal colectomy in her early twenties and later became dependent on parenteral nutrition. Other features included seizures, stroke-like episodes with persistent neurologic deficits, cognitive impairment, and onset of macular degeneration around age 40 years. Brain imaging in 1 sister showed progressive diffuse leukoencephalopathy. Two Japanese brothers in family 3 had a severe phenotype and presented with refractory seizures in the first months of life. They had hypotonia, abnormal jerky movements, abdominal distension, and hepatomegaly, and were fed by nasogastric tube. They met almost no developmental milestones; 1 died at 2 years of age. The other had intestinal pseudoobstruction and a neurogenic bladder; he also required a tracheostomy. At age 3 years, he had marked developmental delay with no head control, language, or eye pursuit, cataracts, severe growth impairment (height -6.5 SD, weight -11.0 SD), and neurosensory hearing loss. Brain imaging showed leukoencephalopathy and cerebellar atrophy. The lactate/pyruvate ratio in the CSF was increased in both patients, suggesting mitochondrial dysfunction.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{2:Invernizzi et al. (2021)} reported 2 sibs, born of unrelated Italian parents, with neonatal onset of a rapidly fatal myopathy. The older sib presented at birth with severe hypotonia and cardiorespiratory distress associated with increased lactate levels. She died at 17 days of age. Muscle biopsy showed lipid vacuoles, decreased activities of mitochondrial complexes I, III, IV, and V, and marked mtDNA depletion. Her younger sib presented at birth with a similar condition, resulting in death within hours. Amniocytes showed decreased complex IV activity (56% of controls). Neither patient had signs of gastrointestinal dysmotility, but they had severe muscle weakness and were not able to breathe autonomously. The report expanded the phenotype associated with biallelic LIG3 mutations to include significant myopathy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MTDPS20 in the families reported by {1:Bonora et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 7 patients from 3 unrelated families with MTDPS20, {1:Bonora et al. (2021)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the LIG3 gene ({600940.0001}-{600940.0006}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were 3 missense, 2 nonsense, and 1 splice site mutation. None of the patients carried 2 truncating mutations. The mutations mapped to conserved domains in the gene; several affected functional regions. In vitro studies of patient fibroblasts, skeletal muscle, and cells transfected with some of the mutations showed that the mutations decreased LIG3 protein expression, disrupted mitochondrial morphology and function, impaired mtDNA ligase activity and mtDNA proliferation, and resulted in mtDNA depletion.

In 2 sibs, born of unrelated Italian parents, with MTDPS20, {2:Invernizzi et al. (2021)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the LIG3 gene ({600940.0007} and {600940.0008}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. LIG3 transcripts were reduced and protein levels were about 56% of controls. Patient fibroblasts showed impaired recovery of induced mtDNA depletion.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Bonora et al. (2021)} found that disruption or silencing of the zebrafish lig3 ortholog resulted in multiple abnormalities, including decreased cerebellar area, abnormal gut peristalsis, decreased intestinal goblet cells, reduced swim bladder area, decreased expression of mitochondrial markers, and eye abnormalities.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with central hypotonia and dysmorphic facies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with central hypotonia and dysmorphic facies (NEDCHF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the HDAC4 gene ({605314}) on chromosome 2q37.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with central hypotonia and dysmorphic facies (NEDCHF) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, seizures, distinctive facial features, scoliosis, delayed closure of the anterior fontanel, and nonspecific brain abnormalities ({1:Wakeling et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Wakeling et al. (2021)} reported 7 unrelated patients, aged 2 to 20 years, with a neurodevelopmental disorder. All 7 patients had impaired intellectual development, 3 were nonverbal, 3 had single words only, and 1 had fluent speech but required speech therapy. Only 1 patient was able to walk independently. All 7 patients had central hypotonia, 3 of 6 patients were reported to have seizures, and 2 of 3 patients had a movement disorder. MRIs were abnormal in 5 of 7 patients, and abnormalities included cerebellar atrophy in 2 and ventricular enlargement in 2. Facial dysmorphisms included hypertelorism (4/5 patients), full lower lip (5/6 patients), widely spaced teeth (4/6 patients), frontal upsweep of the hair (4/7 patients), long palpebral fissures (5/6 patients), and large ears (3/5 patients). Other features included drooling in 6 of 6 patients, sleep disturbances in 3, kyphosis and/or scoliosis in 4, congenital hip dislocation in 2, and delayed closure of the anterior fontanel in 2.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the HDAC4 gene that were identified in patients with NEDCHF by {1:Wakeling et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 7 unrelated patients with NEDCHF, {1:Wakeling et al. (2021)} identified 4 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations ({605314.0003}-{605314.0006}) in the HDAC4 gene. The mutations, which were identified by whole-exome sequencing, were predicted to result in reduced HDAC4 affinity for 14-3-3 proteins (see {113508}), leading to reduced sequestration of HDAC4 in the cytoplasm by the 14-3-3 proteins and increased levels of HDAC4 in the nucleus.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant severe congenital neutropenia-9 (SCN9) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CLPB gene ({616254}) on chromosome 11q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal dominant severe congenital neutropenia-9 (SCN9) is characterized by onset of neutropenia in the first years of life. Most patients have recurrent infections; bone marrow examination shows a myeloid maturation arrest. Rare patients may exhibit additional features such as seizures, learning difficulties, or cataracts, which are more commonly observed in patients with MGCA7 ({616271}). However, patients with SCN9 do not have 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, and most have normal neurologic function ({1:Warren et al., 2022}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of severe congenital neutropenia, see SCN1 ({202700}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Warren et al. (2022)} reported 10 unrelated patients with severe congenital neutropenia associated with heterozygous missense mutations in the CLPB gene. The patients were ascertained from several large patient cohorts who underwent exome sequencing. All patients were diagnosed by 2.5 years of age, and most had recurrent infections. Most received G-CSF therapy. Bone marrow examination showed a myeloid maturation arrest in all patients. Three patients had neurologic involvement, including epilepsy, learning difficulties, and developmental delay. One adult patient had cataracts. One patient developed a myeloid malignancy and died. None of 5 patients tested had 3-methylglutaconic aciduria.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CLPB gene that were identified in 2 patients with SCN9 by {1:Warren et al. (2022)} were demonstrated to have occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 10 unrelated individuals with SCN9, {1:Warren et al. (2022)} identified 6 different heterozygous missense mutations in the CLPB gene (see, e.g., {616254.0014}-{616254.0016}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. In 2 patients, the mutations occurred de novo; family studies were not available for the other patients. All of the mutations occurred at conserved residues in the C-terminal ATP-binding pocket of CLPB. Knockdown of CLPB in CD34+ hematopoietic cells resulted in significantly fewer mature neutrophils and increased numbers of granulocyte precursors, indicating that CLPB is required for normal granulocyte differentiation. In vitro studies in transfected CD34+ cells showed that the CLPB variants tested impaired granulocytic differentiation and enhanced apoptosis without affecting the cell cycle or causing ER stress. Mixing studies indicated a dominant-negative effect of the mutations on CLPB ATPase activity and disaggregase activity. Additional studies showed that the tested ATP-binding pocket variants impaired mitochondrial respiration, suggesting a possible mechanistic link between mitochondrial dysfunction and defective granulopoiesis. In addition, 3 patients with cyclic neutropenia were found to carry a heterozygous R628C variant in the CLPB gene; functional studies of this variant were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-101 (DEE101) is caused by homozygous mutation in the GRIN1 gene ({138249}) on chromosome 9q34.

Homozygous mutation in the GRIN1 can also cause autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with or without hyperkinetic movements and seizures (NDHMSR; {617820}).

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-101 (DEE101) is a severe autosomal recessive disorder characterized by early infantile epileptic encephalopathy and severe global developmental delay (summary by {1:Blakes et al., 2022}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Lemke et al. (2016)} reported 3 sibs, born of consanguineous parents (family 5), with severe neonatal epileptic encephalopathy. All developed intractable seizures on the first day of life and died between 5 days and 5 months of age. One patient was reported to have microcephaly; none had developmental progress.

{1:Blakes et al. (2022)} reported a Pakistani patient who presented on the second day of life with difficulty feeding, abnormal tone, and seizures associated with oxygen desaturation and apnea. Serial EEGs were consistent with myoclonic encephalopathy. At 35 days of life, he developed profound bradycardia with episodes of asystole, and an EKG showed episodic complete heart block. An echocardiogram was normal. He had abnormal oromotor coordination and required nasogastric feeding. At 12 months of age, he had multiple daily seizures and gastrointestinal reflux, and he required nasogastric feeding. He had axial hypotonia and limb contractures. He did not babble or smile, lacked head control, and had no purposeful limb movements.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE101 in the families reported by {2:Lemke et al. (2016)} and {1:Blakes et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 infants (family 5) with DEE101, {2:Lemke et al. (2016)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the GRIN1 gene (Q556X; {138249.0009}). In vitro functional expression studies showed that the mutation rendered the channel nonfunctional, with no response to glycine or glutamate, resulting in a complete loss of function. The unaffected parents were heterozygous for the mutation, suggesting that heterozygous truncating mutations and haploinsufficiency for GRIN1 does not result in a neurologic phenotype.

In a Pakistani infant, born to consanguineous parents, with DEE101, {1:Blakes et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the GRIN1 gene ({138249.0013}). Functional studies were not reported.

preferredTitle: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER, AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE 75, WITH NEUROPSYCHIATRIC FEATURES AND VARIANT LISSENCEPHALY; MRT75
clinicalSynopsis: Onset in infancy or early childhood

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal recessive 75, with neuropsychiatric features and variant lissencephaly

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-75 with neuropsychiatric features and variant lissencephaly (MRT75) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PIDD1 gene ({605247}) on chromosome 11p15.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-75 with neuropsychiatric features and variant lissencephaly (MRT75) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy or early childhood and moderate to profoundly impaired intellectual development. Most affected individuals have behavioral abnormalities, including aggression and ADHD; a few have psychiatric manifestations, including psychosis. More variable additional features include well-controlled seizures and dysmorphic facial features. Brain imaging often shows frontal predominant pachygyria or other gyri/sulci abnormalities, consistent with a variant of lissencephaly and a malformation of cortical development (MCD) (summary by {4:Zaki et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Harripaul et al. (2018)} reported 2 consanguineous Pakistani families (families AS110 and AS105) with autosomal recessive nonsyndromic intellectual disability associated with a homozygous nonsense mutation in the PIDD1 gene (Q863X; {605247.0001}). {3:Sheikh et al. (2021)} provided detailed clinical reports of 2 patients from family AS110 and 2 from family AS105 originally reported by {1:Harripaul et al. (2018)}. The patients, who ranged from 5 to 30 years of age, had delayed milestones and severe to profound intellectual disability. Most patients had behavioral abnormalities, including aggression, inability to learn, ADHD, and self-injurious behavior, such as hand or nail biting. Two had seizures that were controlled. All needed help with self-care. Brain imaging from 1 patient in family AS110 showed subtle lissencephaly that was most pronounced in the frontal lobes. One of the patients from family AS105 had mildly decreased volume of the body and splenium of the corpus callosum. {4:Zaki et al. (2021)} stated that a review of the brain imaging of the patient from AS105 showed mildly thickened gyral pattern frontally, consistent with pachygyria, in addition to the corpus callosum abnormalities. There was another patient in family AS105 that had a similar phenotype, but genetic analysis could not be confirmed.

{2:Hu et al. (2019)} reported 5 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families (M278 and M8700004) with intellectual disability and mutation in the PIDD1 gene. The patients, who ranged from 18 to 26 years of age, had global developmental delay apparent from early childhood. The 2 brothers in family M278 had onset of seizures at 12 and 14 years, respectively, which were controlled by medication. The 3 sibs in family M8700004 developed generalized seizures in infancy that were controlled by medication. The sibs in family M278 had normal speech development with IQ measurements of 50 and 55, respectively, whereas the sibs in the other family had poor speech that was slurred and IQ measurements between 24 and 33; these sibs also had features of psychosis. All patients had normal gait and no dysmorphic features. Brain imaging studies were not reported.

{4:Zaki et al. (2021)} reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families with MRT75. The families were of Egyptian, Pakistani, Palestinian, and Colombian descent, and the patients ranged from 8 to 24 years of age, except for the single patient from family 5, who was 8 months old. The patient from family 5 also carried a pathogenic variant in the CCDC39 gene ({613798}) that likely contributed to the phenotype. All patients had developmental delay and variably impaired intellectual development. IQ, when measured, ranged from 42 to 68. Most had hypotonia, delayed walking up to 4 years, and delayed speech acquisition with only a few words and short sentences. A few had gait instability or brisk reflexes. Most had behavioral abnormalities, including ADHD (6 patients), autism spectrum disorder (ASD, 4 patients), aggressive behavior, and self-injury, mainly head banging and hand biting. Two patients developed psychosis requiring antipsychotic treatment. Four patients had seizures, including 3 with onset in the second decade, that were well-controlled or remitted. Brain imaging, performed in 10 patients, showed cortical anomalies, mainly consistent with anterior-predominant pachygyria (8 patients) and dysgyria or a simplified gyral pattern (2 patients). About half of patients had corpus callosum abnormalities, mostly thinning of the corpus callosum. Most patients had variable dysmorphic features, including high or broad forehead, long face, bitemporal narrowing, downslanting palpebral fissures, thick eyebrows, short philtrum, full lips, and thin upper lip.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MRT75 in the families reported by {1:Harripaul et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 10 affected members of 2 consanguineous Pakistani families with MRT75, {1:Harripaul et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the PIDD1 gene (Q863X; {605247.0001}). Functional studies of the variant or studies of patient cells were not reported. The patients were ascertained from a cohort of 192 consanguineous families from Pakistan and Iran with autosomal recessive intellectual disability who underwent whole-exome sequencing.

In affected members of 2 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families (M278 and M8700004) with MRT75, {2:Hu et al. (2019)} identified homozygous mutations in the PIDD1 gene (c.2275-1G-A, {605247.0002} and R815W, {605247.0003}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The families were part of a large cohort of 404 consanguineous families, mostly Iranian, in which 2 or more offspring had impaired intellectual development. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

{3:Sheikh et al. (2021)} performed functional analysis of the 3 PIDD1 mutations identified by {1:Harripaul et al. (2018)} and {2:Hu et al. (2019)}, demonstrating that all disrupted the death domain, abrogated the interaction of PIDD1 with CRADD ({603454}), and failed to activate caspase-2 (CASP2; {600639}), consistent with a loss of function. The authors noted that mutations in the CRADD gene cause a similar intellectual developmental disorder with variant lissencephaly (MRT34; {614499}). {3:Sheikh et al. (2021)} also identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the PIDD1 gene (R637X; {dbSNP rs578222814}) in a 10-year-old Indian girl (Manipal-1) with MRT75. She had an IQ of 75, ADHD, and brain imaging features suggestive of pachygyria. Her 17-year-old brother had normal development, and IQ of 104, no behavioral problems, and normal brain imaging. It was not clear in the paper whether or not the brother carried the mutation. Functional studies of the R637X variant were not performed.

In 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families with MRT75, {4:Zaki et al. (2021)} identified 5 different homozygous mutations in the PIDD1 gene (see, e.g., {605247.0004}-{605247.0006}). There were 4 frameshift or nonsense mutations, predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and a loss of function, and 1 missense variant (R862W; {605247.0004}) that occurred in the death domain and was predicted to destabilize the interaction of PIDD1 with CRADD. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Sheikh et al. (2021)} found that Pidd1-null mice were similar to wildtype at 3 and 12 months of age. Mutant mice did not show significant changes from wildtype, although there was some evidence for decreased anxiety-like behavior.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with neuromuscular and skeletal abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with neuromuscular and skeletal abnormalities (NEDNMS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NRCAM gene ({601581}) on chromosome 7q31.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with neuromuscular and skeletal abnormalities (NEDNMS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy or early childhood. The severity of the disorder is highly variable. Affected individuals show impaired intellectual development and motor delay associated with either severe hypotonia or hypertonia and spasticity. Most affected individuals have skeletal defects and dysmorphic facial features. Some may have ocular or auditory problems, peripheral neuropathy, behavioral abnormalities, and nonspecific findings on brain imaging ({1:Kurolap et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Kurolap et al. (2022)} reported 8 patients from 7 unrelated families with variable neurodevelopmental phenotypes associated with biallelic mutations in the NRCAM gene. The patients, who ranged in age from 21 months to 41 years, were ascertained through international collaborative efforts facilitated through the GeneMatcher Program. The families were of various origins, including Muslim Arab, Amish, European, and Libyan Jewish; 3 families were consanguineous. The patients had developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, motor delay, walking difficulties, and either hypotonia with hyporeflexia or hypertonia with spasticity and dystonia. Ocular findings included optic atrophy, hyperopia, abnormal visual evoked potentials (VEP), retinal detachment, cataract, myopia, optic cupping, astigmatism, and strabismus. Skeletal findings included congenital hip dysplasia, scoliosis, foot deformities, and tapering fingers. Some patients had hearing loss, behavioral abnormalities, or epilepsy (1 patient). Brain imaging was normal in 3 patients and showed nonspecific abnormalities in others, including enlarged ventricles, thin corpus callosum, delayed myelination, white matter abnormalities, and subependymal nodular gray matter heterotopia. About half of patients had nonspecific dysmorphic features, including large forehead, long face, bitemporal narrowing, bushy eyebrows, depressed nasal bridge, tented mouth, micrognathia, and high-arched palate. The 2 most severely affected patients (patients 1 and 2), each born of consanguineous parents of Muslim-Arab descent, presented at birth with severe hypotonia and respiratory insufficiency requiring ventilatory assistance. Both showed failure to thrive, feeding problems necessitating tube-feeding, and dysmorphic facial features. P1 had hydrocephalus (treated with a shunt), microcephaly (-3.5 SD), demyelinating sensorimotor neuropathy, optic atrophy, abnormal VEP and auditory potentials, and skeletal abnormalities. At age 5 years, he was able to walk with assistance, but did not speak. P2 patient had laryngomalacia, respiratory difficulties, little development, and mild hearing loss; she died at age 21 months. Patient 7 had an unusual phenotype with neonatal difficulties, hypotonia, contractures, and motor delay, but later showed improvement of his neuromuscular symptoms and showed no signs of intellectual disability at age 5 years.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDNMS in the families reported by {1:Kurolap et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 patients from 6 unrelated families with NEDNMS, {1:Kurolap et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the NRCAM gene (see, e.g., {601581.0001}-{601581.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were nonsense, missense, splice site, and frameshift mutations. Several mutations occurred in the third fibronectin type III domain, suggesting a deleterious effect on protein function. However, functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. The authors noted that the neurologic features of the patients support a role for NRCAM in nervous system development.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Kurolap et al. (2022)} found that loss-of-function mutation of the nrcama gene in zebrafish did not result in gross morphologic defects, but immunostaining of the brain showed a trend toward increased amounts of alpha-tubulin fibers in the dorsal telencephalon, increased thickness of ascending fiber tracts, and alterations in white matter tracts and projections. Mutant larvae showed increased swimming motion during darkness compared to wildtype. The authors concluded that loss of nrcama has neurologic and behavioral effects in zebrafish.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type VIIA (MGCA7A) is caused by heterozygous dominant-negative mutation in the CLPB gene ({616254}) on chromosome 11q13.

Biallelic loss-of-function mutation in the CLPB gene causes an autosomal recessive form of the disorder (MGCA7B; {616271}), which shows overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content:
3-Methylglutaconic aciduria (MGCA7) is an inborn error of metabolism characterized primarily by increased levels of 3-methylglutaconic acid (3-MGA) associated with variable neurologic deficits and neutropenia. The phenotype is highly variable: most patients have infantile onset of a severe progressive encephalopathy with various movement abnormalities and delayed psychomotor development. Other common variable features include seizures, recurrent infections due to neutropenia, anemia, and brain imaging abnormalities ({1:Wortmann et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, see MGCA1 ({250950}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Wortmann et al. (2021)} identified 6 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 19 months to 12.5 years, with neurologic deficits, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, and neutropenia (in 5 patients) associated with de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the CLPB gene. The patients presented in early infancy with either seizures and developmental delay or recurrent infections and neutropenia. All eventually showed global developmental delay, although the severity was highly variable. Most patients had impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, axial hypotonia, limb spasticity, and difficulty walking or inability to walk. Five patients had variable types of seizures, and 3 showed developmental regression with loss of skills, suggesting neurodegeneration. All patients had brain imaging abnormalities, including cerebral atrophy, cerebellar atrophy, periventricular white matter alterations, thin corpus callosum, and delayed myelination. Four patients had secondary microcephaly. The least affected individual (P6) had mild speech delay and no seizures, whereas the most severely affected individual (P2) had early-onset seizures and essentially no development and died of respiratory failure at age 19 months. Cataracts were notably absent in all patients. All patients except P1 had neutropenia, and several had mild anemia. Two patients underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplant at age 15 months and 5 years, respectively. {1:Wortmann et al. (2021)} noted the phenotypic similarities to patients with MGCA7B who have biallelic mutations in the CLPB gene.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CLPB gene that were identified in patients with MGCA7A by {1:Wortmann et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 unrelated patients with MGCA7A manifest as neutropenia and neurologic dysfunction, {1:Wortmann et al. (2021)} identified 4 different de novo heterozygous missense variants in the CLPB gene (see, e.g., {616254.0011}-{616254.0013}). The mutations, which were found by exome or genome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies using a luciferase assay showed that the mutations caused a variable reduction in ATPase activity and impaired the renaturation and disaggregase activity of CLPB. When mixed with wildtype CLPB, the mutations demonstrated a dominant-negative effect. In control fibroblasts, HAX1 ({605998}) migrated predominantly as a monomer, whereas patient samples showed multiple HAX1 peaks comigrating at higher molecular masses with CLPB. These findings suggested a longer-lasting interaction between CLPB and HAX1; HAX1 is mutated in SCN3 ({610738}).

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Chilton-Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (CHOCNS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CDC42BPB gene ({614062}) on chromosome 14q32.

description.title: Description
description.content: Chilton-Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (CHOCNS) is characterized mainly by global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development and occasional speech delay. Most patients have behavioral abnormalities, including autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and aggression. About half of patients have dysmorphic facial features, and about half have nonspecific brain abnormalities, including thin corpus callosum. Rare involvement of other organ systems may be present. At least 1 child with normal development at age 2.5 years has been reported ({1:Chilton et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Chilton et al. (2020)} reported 14 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 2 to 29 years, who were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the CDC42BPB gene. One patient (individual 4) was a male fetus with cystic hygroma and progressive ventriculomegaly found on prenatal ultrasound; the pregnancy was terminated at 27 weeks' gestation. All except 1 (individual 8) of the other 13 patients had global developmental delay, often with impaired intellectual development, speech delay, and behavioral abnormalities, including ADHD, aggressive behavior, anxiety, and repetitive or stereotypic movements. Eight were diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, including a 14-year-old boy with Asperger syndrome (individual 2). Several patients had hypotonia or unsteady gait, 3 had seizures, and 1 had EEG abnormalities. One of the patients with seizures (individual 7) was unable to walk at age 12 years and had severe speech delay with only a few words. Four patients had ophthalmologic findings, including ptosis, strabismus, esotropia, amblyopia, refractory errors, and septooptic dysplasia with optic atrophy (1 patient). Brain imaging showed nonspecific abnormalities in 4 patients, including cerebellar hypoplasia, thin or absent corpus callosum, white matter loss, and enlarged ventricles. Brain imaging was normal in other patients tested. About half of individuals had dysmorphic facial features, including macrocephaly, abnormal head shape, broad or high forehead, sparse scalp hair, sparse eyebrows, low-set ears, up- or downslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, high nasal root, flat nasal bridge, broad nasal tip, short philtrum, large mouth, thin upper lip, and widely spaced teeth. A few had distal skeletal anomalies of the hands and feet or pectus abnormalities. Less common features included cryptorchidism, constipation, recurrent otitis media, micropenis, kidney abnormalities, and joint hypermobility. Rare features observed in a single patient each included acquired microcephaly, congenital diaphragmatic hernia with intestinal malrotation, patent foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus, and scoliosis.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CDC42BPB gene that were identified in patients with CHOCNS by {1:Chilton et al. (2020)} were confirmed to be de novo in all patients for whom parental DNA was available.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 14 unrelated patients with CHOCNS, {1:Chilton et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous mutations in the CDC42BPB gene (see, e.g., {614062.0001}-{614062.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, occurred de novo in all patients for whom parental DNA was available. All but 1 of the mutations were absent from gnomAD. There were 9 missense mutations, including 2 recurrent mutations, and 3 frameshift or nonsense mutations predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and a loss of function. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, and there were no genotype/phenotype correlations. The phenotype was highly variable, even in patients with the same mutation (see {614062.0004}). Six individuals had additional genetic variants of uncertain significance that may have contributed to the phenotype. {1:Chilton et al. (2020)} noted that mutations in the CDC42BPB gene have been reported in large cohorts of patients with autism and neurodevelopmental delay (see, e.g., {2:O'Roak et al., 2012}). Moreover, CDC42BPB is a major downstream effector of CDC42 ({116952}), which is mutated in another neurodevelopmental disorder (TKS; {616737}).

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that childhood-onset neurodegeneration with progressive microcephaly (CONPM) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the DTYMK gene ({188345}) on chromosome 2q37.

description.title: Description
description.content: Childhood-onset neurodegeneration with progressive microcephaly (CONPM) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy. The phenotype is highly variable: the most severely affected individuals have severe and progressive microcephaly, early-onset seizures, lack of visual tracking, and almost no developmental milestones, resulting in early death. Less severely affected individuals have a small head circumference and severely impaired intellectual development with poor speech and motor delay. Additional features may include poor overall growth, axial hypotonia, limb hypertonia with spasticity, undescended testes, and cerebral atrophy with neuronal loss ({1:Lam et al., 2019} and {2:Vanoevelen et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Lam et al. (2019)} reported 2 Chinese brothers, born of unrelated parents, with a neurologic disorder apparent from infancy. The patients, who were 25 months and 7 years of age, had neonatal hypotonia, global developmental delay, and mild congenital microcephaly. The younger brother developed febrile seizures with status epilepticus at 7 months of age, followed by developmental regression, cortical blindness, sensorineural hearing loss, and dysphagia requiring tube feeding. Other features included mixed spastic quadriplegia with hypertonia, dystonic cerebral palsy, laryngomalacia, and undescended testes. Brain imaging showed marked cerebral atrophy with increased lactate peak on MR spectroscopy. The older brother did not have seizures, could walk independently, and spoke a few words, but he had severe intellectual disability and lower limb dystonia. He also had a single episode of sudden-onset coma with respiratory failure of unknown origin at age 7. Vision, hearing, and brain imaging were normal in this patient. Serum lactate and alanine were intermittently increased in both patients. Blood from the more severely affected younger brother showed a mild decrease in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) at 65% of controls. {1:Lam et al. (2019)} noted the intrafamilial phenotypic variability.

{2:Vanoevelen et al. (2022)} reported 2 unrelated infants, 1 born of unrelated Dutch parents and another born of consanguineous Egyptian parents, with a severe early-onset neurodegenerative disease resulting in death at 18 and 32 months, respectively. The Dutch patient was conceived by in vitro fertilization. Both appeared normal at birth, but developed severe progressive microcephaly and a puffy appearance over the first few months of life. They had very poor overall growth, microcephaly at -7.6 and -7.4 SD, hypotonia, no eye contact, and essentially no developmental progress. One had recurrent febrile seizures and the other had myoclonic jerks. Other features included spasticity, opisthotonus, limb hypertonia with hyperreflexia, clonus, and extensor plantar responses. The Egyptian boy had microcytic hypochromic anemia requiring transfusion, elevated liver enzymes, micropenis, and undescended testes. Brain imaging in patient 1 showed progressive and profound atrophy of the cerebral hemispheres that was associated with a massive loss of neurons and astrogliosis on postmortem examination. The basal ganglia and striatum also showed atrophy with loss of neurons and gliosis. There was a paucity of myelin throughout the brain and loss of oligodendrocytes. The cerebellum, although of normal size, also showed loss of neurons in the granular and Purkinje cell layer. Brain imaging in the Egyptian patient showed profound generalized cerebral atrophy with small basal nuclei, with sparing of the brainstem and cerebellum. Extensive workup for mitochondrial abnormalities showed no defects, in particular no mtDNA depletion.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CONPM in the families reported by {1:Lam et al. (2019)} and {2:Vanoevelen et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 brothers, born of unrelated Chinese parents, with CONPM, {1:Lam et al. (2019)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the DTYMK gene ({188345.0001} and {188345.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In 2 unrelated patients with CONPM, {2:Vanoevelen et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the DTYMK gene (P81L, {188345.0003} and D128N, {188345.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Both were present at low frequencies only in the heterozygous state in public databases. Fibroblasts derived from 1 patient showed barely detectable DTYMK activity, consistent with the mutations conferring a loss-of-function effect with impaired biosynthesis of deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP). Accordingly, patient fibroblasts showed impaired DNA replication with few cells in S phase compared to controls. The findings linked thymidine biosynthesis to genome integrity and postnatal neuronal viability.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Vanoevelen et al. (2022)} found that homozygous knockout of the dtymk ortholog in zebrafish resulted in small eyes and edema of the pericardium, intestine, and brain. Mutant embryos showed a small head size and twitching movements, possibly suggestive of seizures. At 5 dpf, more than 40% of mutant embryos had died. Detailed brain analysis of mutant zebrafish showed empty spaces indicative of neurodegeneration, severe aberrant and underdevelopment of the eyes, and increased numbers of apoptotic cells in the forebrain compared to controls. Dtymk enzyme activity in the mutant embryos was barely detectable and was predicted to block the biosynthesis of dTTP. Accordingly, there was a severe defect in DNA replication and cell proliferation in the forebrain compared to controls. There was also evidence of a nucleotide pool imbalance with increased incorporation of ribonucleotides that led to genomic fragility. Mutant embryos were more susceptible to DNA damage and breakage following UV irradiation compared to controls, consistent with defective DNA repair mechanisms.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-24 (HLD24) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP11A gene ({605868}) on chromosome 13q34. One such patient has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-24 (HLD24) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by global developmental delay and neurologic deterioration ({1:Segawa et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of HLD, see {312080}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Segawa et al. (2021)} reported a patient who developed epilepsy at 2 weeks of age, followed by global developmental delay, hypothyroidism, and cataracts. At 2 years of age he was able to laugh and had eye tracking. He was able to walk with a walker until he started elementary school when he lost his developmental milestones. He also had frequent infections, including aspiration pneumonia. By 18 years of age, he required mechanical ventilation and was nonambulatory. He had tongue fasciculations, flexion contractures of the limbs, and lack of deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory testing demonstrated a reduction in CD19+ B lymphocytes. Serial MRIs showed nonprogressive severe cerebral atrophy, ventriculomegaly, hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. Nerve conduction velocity testing was suggestive of an axonal neuropathy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HLD24 in the patient reported by {1:Segawa et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a patient with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-24, {1:Segawa et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous mutation in the ATP11A gene (Q84E; {605868.0003}). The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. {1:Segawa et al. (2021)} stably transfected ATP11A with the Q84E mutation into W3 cells. Mutant ATP11A was shown to have flippase activity against phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine, and phosphatidylcholine, whereas the wildtype ATP11A had flippase activity only against phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylserine. Examination of incorporation of labeled lipids into the cell membrane showed that the mutant ATP11A led to increased sphingomyelin and decreased phosphatidylcholine in the outer leaflet of the cellular plasma membrane.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Segawa et al. (2021)} developed a mouse model with a heterozygous knock-in Q84E mutation ({605868.0001}) in the Atp11a gene. The mutant mice had slower growth compared to wildtype mice and early death that was preceded by neurologic abnormalities. Brain MRIs of 11-week-old mutant mice showed a reduction in brain size and dilated ventricles. Microscopic examination of brain tissue from the mutant embryos and mouse pups demonstrated tissue degeneration. Brains from the mutant mouse embryos had increased sphingomyelin content compared to wildtype.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities (NEDHISB) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAI1 gene ({139310}) on chromosome 7q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities (NEDHISB) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent since infancy or early childhood, hypotonia with delayed motor development, impaired intellectual development with significant speech delay or absent speech, and variable behavioral abnormalities, such as autism, repetitive actions, or aggression. About two-thirds of patients have early-onset seizures that range from intractable to self-limiting. More variable features include nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, distal skeletal anomalies, and brain imaging abnormalities. The phenotypic manifestations and severity are highly variable ({2:Muir et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
Through exome sequencing of thousands of individuals with developmental delay, the {1:Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study (2017)} identified 8 unrelated individuals with de novo heterozygous mutations in the GNAI1 gene. These patients had global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech. More variable features included hypotonia, rare hypertonia, poor motor coordination, behavioral abnormalities, sleep disturbances, and hypoplasia of the cerebrum. Some patients had nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, including microcephaly or macrocephaly, abnormal facial shape, high forehead, downturned corners of the mouth, hypertelorism, deep-set eyes, epicanthus, heterochromia iridis, synophrys, anteverted nares, and tented upper lip. Common skeletal anomalies included tapered fingers, fifth finger clinodactyly, foot deformities, and joint hypermobility.

{2:Muir et al. (2021)} reported 24 unrelated patients, ranging from 3 to 18 years of age, with a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with de novo heterozygous mutations in the GNAI1 gene identified through exome sequencing. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher Program. Thirteen of the patients (P2, P3, P7-P11, P14, P16, P18-20, and P24) had previously been reported (see, e.g., the {1:Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study, 2017}). All patients had global developmental delay ranging from mild (15%) to profound (55%). Speech was particularly affected, with language delays reported in 91% of individuals: 16 patients were nonverbal, including P5 who was 16 years old and P24 who was 18 years old. Hypotonia was common, and motor skills such as sitting and walking were delayed in most patients. Nine patients were nonambulatory, including P22 who was 14 years old and P24 who was 18. Rare patients had hypertonia or spasticity. Behavioral problems, including aggression, temper tantrums, hypersensitivity, impulsivity, and hand stereotypies were observed in the majority of patients. Seven were diagnosed with autism. Seventeen patients (74%) had seizures that were highly variable in severity and type, including absence, focal, myoclonic, and generalized tonic-clonic. Most had onset of seizures in infancy, and the response to treatment varied. Nonspecific brain imaging abnormalities were observed in about a third of patients: these included global cerebral atrophy, enlarged ventricles, delayed myelination, and choroid plexus or arachnoid cysts. One patient had bilateral mesotemporal sclerosis. However, brain imaging was normal in a significant number of individuals. About two-thirds (76%) of patients had dysmorphic features, although there was not a common gestalt. Features included brachycephaly, plagiocephaly, macrocephaly, round face, broad forehead, downslanting palpebral fissures, broad nose, short upturned nose, flat midface, maxillary hypoplasia, thick eyebrows, synophrys, short philtrum, hypotonic open mouth, thin or tented upper lip, and prominent lower lip. Skeletal defects included small hands and feet, tapered fingers, short fifth digits, clinodactyly, camptodactyly, long halluces, wide feet, foot deformities, and scoliosis. Less common features included feeding difficulties (9 patients), hyperphagia with obesity (7 patients), constipation, and cryptorchidism.

{3:Wayhelova et al. (2022)} reported a pair of 15-year-old monozygotic twin boys with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The twins were born by C-section at 29 weeks' gestation and were in the neonatology unit for 6 weeks. They had global developmental delay with walking at around 21 months, impaired intellectual development, severe dysphasia with very poor speech with only a few syllables, and cerebral palsy with clumsy motor skills. The boys were able to attend a specialized school; they had no apparent facial abnormalities, no seizures, and normal brain imaging. Twin B was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia at age 5, which was in remission after chemotherapy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: Most of the heterozygous mutations in the GNAI1 gene that were identified in patients with NEDHISB by {2:Muir et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. One was inherited from an unaffected parent who was mosaic for the mutation.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 8 unrelated patients with NEDHISB, the {1:Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study (2017)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the GNAI1 gene (see, e.g., {139310.0001}). There were 5 missense mutations and 3 in-frame intragenic deletions. The patients were ascertained from large cohorts of thousands of individuals with developmental delay who underwent exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variants were not performed.

In 24 unrelated patients with NEDHISB, {2:Muir et al. (2021)} identified 16 different heterozygous mutations in the GNAI1 gene (see, e.g., {139310.0001}-{139310.0005}). The patients were ascertained through international collaboration after exome sequencing identified the mutations. Thirteen of the patients had previously been reported (see, e.g., {1:Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study, 2017}). There were 12 missense mutations, 3 small in-frame deletions, and 1 frameshift mutation; none were present in the gnomAD database. The frameshift mutation was predicted to escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay as it occurred in the penultimate exon. The mutations occurred de novo in all except 1 patient who inherited it from an unaffected mosaic mother. Although functional studies of the variants were not performed, structural modeling predicted that most would affect guanine nucleotide (GDP and GTP) binding motifs in GAI1 and disrupt proper GAI1 function. There were no obvious genotype/phenotype correlations.

In a pair of monozygotic twin boys with NEDHISB, {3:Wayhelova et al. (2022)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GNAI1 gene (D272G; {139310.0006}). The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing; it was classified as pathogenic according to ACMG criteria. Functional studies of the variant were not performed. The authors noted that the GNAI1 gene is expressed in multiple fetal and postnatal brain structures and that disruption of gene function may lead to impaired neural development.
