text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that childhood-onset remitting leukodystrophy (CORLK) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the FBP2 gene ({603027}) on chromosome 9q22. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content: Childhood-onset remitting leukodystrophy (CORLK) is a very rare autosomal dominant disorder characterized in some patients by onset of a metabolic crisis at the end of the first year of life that leads to widespread demyelination and leukodystrophy on brain imaging and a dramatic loss of developmental abilities. Affected children recover over the following several months, regaining normal development accompanied by remyelination. Not all patients have documented acute episodes of metabolic demyelination in infancy, but individuals with the FBP2 mutation show persistent white matter abnormalities on brain imaging that resemble the abnormalities observed in infants with the acute crisis. Other neurologic disturbances that may or may not be related to the FBP2 mutation have been observed, including psychiatric manifestations, seizures, and mild learning difficulties ({1:Gizak et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Gizak et al. (2021)} reported a family in which 7 individuals spanning 3 generations had leukodystrophy on brain imaging. Three index patients, all girls, from the family presented with a remitting form of infantile-onset leukodystrophy. After normal early development, the infant girls had a rapid loss of developmental milestones between 10 and 13 months of age. The acute decompensation was associated with cough, fever, and viral infections. The infants were irritable, socially withdrawn, and unable to sit or stand; 2 required tube feeding for several weeks or months. Cerebral MRI at the time of crisis revealed dramatic leukodystrophy of various brain regions. White matter changes on T2-weighted images increased for several months despite clinical improvement, but later showed resolution with subsequent remyelination over a period of 1 to 2 years. A gradual improvement in the white matter abnormalities correlated with the patients regaining their developmental skills. Proton MR-spectroscopy and myelin sensitive imaging indicated mitochondrial failure and demyelination during the acute phase, with subsequent remyelination over months to years. Laboratory studies showed variably increased serum lactate. Skin and muscle biopsies from 1 patient showed moderately reduced activities of mitochondrial complexes III and IV in fibroblasts and reduced activities of complexes II, III, and IV in muscle. Ragged-red fibers were not observed. The 2 older female index patients, who were working at ages 24 and 25 years, had mild gait abnormalities and residual gliotic lesions affecting the corpus callosum and periventricular white matter. The third affected infant, who was the daughter of 1 of the older patients, was regaining her developmental skills at age 21 months. None of the index patients experienced a second attack, indicating that there may be a phase of vulnerability in brain development around the end of the first year of life. Besides these 3 individuals, there were 5 additional family members who carried the mutation and did not have a documented metabolic crisis, but there was enrichment for psychiatric disorders, including anorexia nervosa, psychosis, and drug addiction. Two mutation carriers developed seizures in childhood, including 1 patient who developed epilepsy following a viral illness with high fever. She had normal development with no metabolic crises, and was seizure-free and in a normal school at age 14.5. A 6-year-old mutation carrier had mildly delayed speech development and ADHD.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CORLK in the family reported by {1:Gizak et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 members of a 3-generation family with CORLK, {1:Gizak et al. (2021)} identified a heterozygous missense variant in the FBP2 gene (V115M; {603027.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was found once in a European male in the gnomAD database (frequency of 4.0 x 10(-6)). In vitro functional expression studies of the recombinant mutant V115M protein showed that it had reduced activity, thermal stability, and substrate affinity compared to controls. Fibroblasts derived from 1 of the patients showed granular localization of FBP2 in only cell bodies, as compared to nuclear and diffuse cytoplasmic localization in controls. The mutant protein did not colocalize with mitochondria in patient fibroblasts. In addition, patient cells showed disturbances in the mitochondrial membrane network associated with increased production of ROS both in the cytoplasm and mitochondria. Transfection of wildtype cells with V115M led to colocalization of the mutant protein, but not the wildtype protein, to the ER, presumably for degradation through the ER-to-lysosome-associated degradation system (ELRAD). The authors speculated that coexpression of wildtype with mutant FBP2 would form heteromers with reduced enzyme activity and stability, consistent with a dominant-negative effect. The nearly complete neurologic recovery in the patients suggested to the authors that neuronal damage was not occurring, but that the primary affected cells in this disorder may be oligodendrocytes. {1:Gizak et al. (2021)} noted that FBP2 has a role in gluconeogenesis in the brain, which may have contributed to the phenotype, although disruption of noncanonical functions of the FBP2 gene could not be excluded.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Parenti-Mignot neurodevelopmental syndrome (PMNDS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CHD5 gene ({610771}) on chromosome 1p36.

description.title: Description
description.content: Parenti-Mignot neurodevelopmental syndrome (PMNDS) is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder frequently characterized by impaired intellectual development, speech delay, motor delay, behavioral problems, and epilepsy ({1:Parenti et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Parenti et al. (2021)} reported a cohort of 16 patients, 7 females and 9 males, with a neurodevelopmental disorder and mutations in the CHD5 gene. The patients ranged in age from 3 to 24 years. Common clinical features included speech delay (13/16), behavioral disturbances (11/16), epilepsy (10/16), facial dysmorphism (11/16), motor delay (9/16), impaired intellectual development (9/14), hypotonia (7/14), and craniosynostosis (3/7). The level of intellectual disability, assessed in 6 patients, was moderate in 2 and severe in 4. Facial features, which were variable and nonspecific, included low-set and posteriorly rotated ears, prominent nasal bridge and tip, short philtrum, thin upper lip, and upslanting palpebral fissures. Three patients had craniosynostosis. Three patients (patients 1, 4 and 6) inherited their CHD5 mutation from a parent and also had one or more additional affected family members with the mutation. Disease expression was highly variable within the families.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of Parenti-Mignot neurodevelopmental syndrome in the families reported by {1:Parenti et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. Thirteen of the 16 identified mutations occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 16 unrelated patients with Parenti-Mignot neurodevelopmental syndrome, {1:Parenti et al. (2021)} identified 16 different heterozygous mutations in the CHD5 gene (see, e.g., {610771.0001}-{610772.0005}). The mutations included 11 missense, 2 nonsense, 2 splicing, and 1 single basepair duplication. All of the missense mutations affected highly conserved residues. All of the mutations were either absent from the gnomAD database or present with an allele frequency of less than 0.0001%. Thirteen of the mutations occurred de novo and 3 were inherited from a parent. The inherited mutations, including 1 missense mutation (R193W) and 2 nonsense mutations (E314X, {601771.0003}; R596X), segregated with a variably expressed neurodevelopmental phenotype in each of the families.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, hypotonia, nystagmus, and seizures (NEDMHS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CPSF3 gene ({606029}) on chromosome 2p25.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, hypotonia, nystagmus, and seizures (NEDMHS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay and impaired intellectual development apparent from infancy. Affected individuals have hypotonia with poor or absent motor skills, feeding difficulties with poor overall growth, microcephaly, mild dysmorphic features, and early-onset seizures. Additional variable features, such as nystagmus, cortical blindness, and spasticity, may also occur. Patients with this disorder tend to have recurrent respiratory infections, likely due to aspiration, that may lead to death in childhood ({1:Arnadottir et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Arnadottir et al. (2022)} reported 6 patients from 3 unrelated families with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder apparent from early infancy. Patients A-D were of Icelandic descent (patients C and D were sibs and part of the extended family of patient A), and patients G and H were from a large family of Mexican descent. Two additional unrelated Icelandic patients (patients E and F) with a similar disorder were also identified, but they died early and genetic material was only available from the parents. Of the 8 patients reported, 5 died of pneumonia or respiratory failure between 1 and 7 years of age. The 3 living patients (patients B, G, and H) were 12 to 13 years of age. All patients had global developmental delay with severely impaired intellectual development, hypotonia, muscle atrophy, and feeding difficulties, often with failure to thrive and poor overall growth. All but 1 (patient F) had early-onset seizures, but patient F died at 1 year of age. A few patients had peripheral spasticity or 'cerebral palsy.' Additional variable features included nystagmus, strabismus, esotropia, gastroesophageal reflux, and constipation. Dysmorphic features included microcephaly, long face, high-arched palate, short upturned nose, and protruding teeth. Some patients were suspected to be blind. Brain imaging, when performed, showed nonspecific features, such as cerebral atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and cerebellar hypoplasia. Five patients had recurrent infections. Patients G and H, from the same Mexican family, developed seizures at 7 and 4 months of age. They had severe developmental delay with hypotonia, no head control, inability to sit, absent language, and minimal interaction with surroundings at 12 and 13 years of age. Other features included swallowing difficulties requiring tube feeding, peripheral neuropathy, spasticity, optic nerve atrophy, cortical blindness, nystagmus, osteopenia, and progressive hip contractures. Brain imaging in these patients showed progressive white matter loss, thin or atrophic corpus callosum, and T2-weighted hyperintensities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMHS in the families reported by {1:Arnadottir et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients (patients A-D) from 2 Icelandic families with NEDMHS, {1:Arnadottir et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the CPSF3 gene (G468E; {606029.0001}). The mutation was initially found by analyzing whole-genome data from a large cohort of over 153,054 adult Icelandic individuals for a deficit of carriers of homozygous missense variants in different genes. The affected individuals with NEDMHS were then identified from a clinical cohort of Icelandic patients with various disorders who had undergone whole-genome sequencing. Samples from 2 additional deceased affected children of Icelandic descent (patients E and F) were not available, but the phenotype was similar to the other patients and the unaffected parents were heterozygous carriers. Western blot analysis of cells derived from patient B confirmed that the mutant protein was produced at normal levels, suggesting that the mutation causes a functional defect. The variant had a frequency of 0.41% in Iceland. Two further patients (G and H) from a large Mexican family with a homozygous missense variant in the CPSF3 gene (I354T; {606029.0002}) were identified through the GeneMatcher program. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but they were both predicted to disrupt the pre-mRNA cleavage mechanism, resulting in the accumulation of unprocessed pre-mRNA in cells, which would in turn activate a cellular stress response.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Dentici-Novelli neurodevelopmental syndrome (DENNED) is caused by homozygous mutation in the ZNF526 gene ({614387}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Dentici-Novelli neurodevelopmental syndrome (DENNED) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development apparent from infancy. The severity of the phenotype is highly variable: more severely affected individuals have axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, microcephaly, early-onset seizures, brain imaging abnormalities, and are unable to walk or speak. Those with a less severe phenotype may achieve some developmental goals and show less severe intellectual disability ({2:Dentici et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Dentici et al. (2022)} reported 4 patients (P1 to P4) from 3 unrelated consanguineous families of Italian, Northern European/French Canadian, and Syrian origin, with severe global developmental delay apparent from early infancy. The patients, who ranged from 3 to 7 years of age, were identified through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified homozygous frameshift mutations in the ZNF526 gene. One patient died at 5 years of age. Features included axial hypotonia with poor head control and appendicular hypertonia with spasticity and dystonia, resulting in difficulty walking or inability to walk. They had severely impaired intellectual development with absent speech, poor eye contact, and feeding difficulties; 3 of the 4 were tube-fed. Other features included progressive microcephaly (down to -8 SD) with accompanying dysmorphic features, including sloping forehead, upslanting palpebral fissures, high nasal bridge, large ears, thin upper lip, and pointed chin, and progressive cataracts. Two sibs (P3 and P4) in family 3 had hearing loss. All had onset in the first years of life of various types of seizures, which were refractory in most; EEG in P2 showed hypsarrhythmia. Brain imaging showed cerebral hypoplasia, enlarged ventricles, thin corpus callosum, mild hypomyelination, and simplified gyral pattern.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{2:Dentici et al. (2022)} reported a 6-year-old girl (P5), born of consanguineous Algerian parents, who carried a homozygous missense variant in the ZNF526 gene identified through exome sequencing. She presented in infancy with hypotonia and poor eye contact and later showed motor delay with walking at age 2.5 years. She had significant language delay with only a few words, as well as behavioral problems, such as emotional dysregulation and angry outbursts. Growth parameters were normal (head circumference of -2 SD). Other features included progressive bilateral cataracts and strabismus. She did not have seizures, and brain imaging was normal at 17 months of age. {2:Dentici et al. (2022)} noted that the phenotype was milder compared to patients with frameshift ZNF526 mutations.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DENNED in the families reported by {2:Dentici et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 5 patients from 4 unrelated consanguineous families of various ethnic origins with DENNED, {2:Dentici et al. (2022)} identified homozygous mutations in the ZNF526 gene ({614387.0001}-{614387.0003}). The patients were gathered through the GeneMatcher Program after homozygous mutations were identified in the first patient (P1) through whole-exome sequencing. The mutations segregated with the disorder in all the families. Four patients (P1 to P4) with a more severe phenotype had homozygous frameshift mutations, whereas 1 (P5) with a less severe phenotype had a missense variant (H409Q; {614387.0003}). Fibroblasts derived from P1 with a frameshift variant showed normal expression levels of ZNF526, suggesting that the variant escapes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Expression array analysis of this patient's cells showed upregulation of genes involved in epithelial cell proliferation and downregulation for genes involved in the WNT signaling pathway and midbrain dopaminergic neuron differentiation. Additional functional studies or studies of patient cells were not performed.

{2:Dentici et al. (2022)} noted that {1:Alazami et al. (2015)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the ZNF526 gene (K160T; {614387.0004}) in a patient, born of consanguineous Arab parents, with intellectual disability (patient 12DG0685). The family was part of a large cohort of 143 multiplex consanguineous families with various neurodevelopmental disorders who underwent whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. Clinical details were limited, but the patient was noted to have intellectual disability, Noonan-like facies, and pulmonary stenosis. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. In addition, {3:Najmabadi et al. (2011)} had identified 2 different homozygous missense variants in the ZNF526 gene in patients with autosomal recessive impaired intellectual development: 4 affected members of family M025 had an R459Q missense mutation, and a patient from family 8500156 had a Q539H mutation. The mutations were found by next-generation sequencing in 136 consanguineous families (over 90% Iranian and less than 10% Turkish or Arab) segregating syndromic or nonsyndromic forms of autosomal recessive intellectual disability. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Dentici et al. (2022)} found that knockdown of the znf526 ortholog in zebrafish resulted in a spectrum of malformations of the head, spine, and eyes, including curved spine, ocular fusion, and incomplete development of the eyes. Seizure-like activity was also observed. Head malformations made head size analysis difficult, and few mutant animals survived. The authors suggested that the features were on the holoprosencephaly spectrum, and concluded that znf526 is involved in the development of the nervous system.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with poor growth and skeletal anomalies (NEDGS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PCDHGC4 gene ({606305}) on chromosome 5q31.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with poor growth and skeletal anomalies (NEDGS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay and impaired intellectual development apparent from infancy. Affected individuals have hypotonia, delayed walking, poor or absent speech, and variable skeletal anomalies. More variable features include seizures, nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, oculomotor apraxia, and nonspecific brain imaging abnormalities ({1:Iqbal et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Iqbal et al. (2021)} reported 19 patients from 9 unrelated consanguineous families of various ethnic origins with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who ranged from 12 months to 30 years of age, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program after genetic analysis identified homozygous mutations in the PCDHGC4 gene. The families originated from Iran, Iraq, Turkey, Morocco, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Sudan, and Jordan. Affected individuals had global developmental delay with hypotonia, delayed walking (as late as 10 years), usually with an unsteady or ataxic gait, and mild to moderate intellectual disability with poor or absent speech. A few had neonatal hypertonicity, exaggerated startle response, or peripheral spasticity. Some had behavioral problems, including hyperactivity, aggressive behavior, and echolalia. Several patients achieved basic skills, such as toilet training and recognizing letters, and were able to attend special schools. Most had poor overall growth with short stature and progressive microcephaly (down to -5.5 SD). Ten patients had seizures, ranging from a single or a few nonfebrile seizures to generalized seizures; 1 patient died due to status epilepticus. Dysmorphic facial features were commonly observed, although there was not a consistent gestalt. Findings included craniosynostosis, sloping forehead, long face, high nasal bridge, epicanthal folds, low-set or dysplastic ears, synophrys, esotropia, long or short philtrum, high narrow palate, prognathia, micrognathia, thick lips, and everted lower lip. Several patients had oculomotor apraxia. Brain imaging, when performed, showed nonspecific abnormalities, including cortical atrophy, enlarged ventricles, and thin corpus callosum. Skeletal and joint anomalies were common: these included scoliosis, kyphosis, hyperextensible joints, and valgus deformities. Many had distal skeletal anomalies, such as clinodactyly, broad thumbs, clubhands, swan neck deformity, and clubfeet. A few patients had generalized joint contractures consistent with arthrogryposis.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDGS in the families reported by {1:Iqbal et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 19 patients from 9 unrelated consanguineous families with NEDGS, {1:Iqbal et al. (2021)} identified homozygous mutations in the PCDHGC4 gene (see, e.g., {606305.0001}-{606305.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. There were 5 nonsense, frameshift, or splice site mutations, predicted to result in premature termination and a loss of function, and 3 missense mutations at highly conserved residues. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but molecular modeling of the missense variants suggested that they would interfere with calcium binding, which is critical for proper function. The authors postulated a loss-of-function effect.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-102 (DEE102) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC38A3 gene ({604437}) on chromosome 3p21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-102 (DEE102) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay and severe to profoundly impaired intellectual development with inability to walk or speak. Most patients have onset of variable types of seizures within the first year of life, and the seizures tend to be refractory. Additional features include progressive microcephaly, visual impairment, axial hypotonia, peripheral hypertonia, and nonspecific brain imaging abnormalities ({1:Marafi et al., 2022}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Marafi et al. (2022)} reported 10 children from 7 unrelated families with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. The families were from 6 different countries, including Azerbaijan, Egypt, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, USA, and Yemen; 5 families were consanguineous. The patients, who ranged from 13 months to 8 years of age, were ascertained through international collaborative efforts after exome sequencing or other genetic analyses identified biallelic mutations in the SLC38A3 gene. One of the patients (family 3) had previously been reported by {2:Monies et al. (2019)} as having a homozygous SLC38A3 mutation in the context of a large gene discovery cohort. All patients had global developmental delay, were nonverbal, and had moderate to severe axial hypotonia, rendering them nonambulatory or unable to walk independently. They had severe to profound intellectual disability, usually with inability to fix or follow, and visual problems, including cortical visual impairment, cone-rod dystrophy, and hyperopic astigmatism. Eight patients had onset of seizures of various types in the first year of life. Most seizures were refractory to treatment, consistent with epileptic encephalopathy. EEG tended to show multifocal epilepsy, focal seizures, myoclonic discharges, and slowed background activity; hypsarrhythmia was sometimes seen. Individuals with seizures had a more severe phenotype compared to the 2 patients who did not have seizures (the 4-year-old patient in family 4 and a 15-month-old in family 6). Most patients had feeding and swallowing difficulties resulting in failure to thrive, poor overall growth, and progressive microcephaly; several patients required tube feeding or could only eat pureed food. Gastrointestinal reflux and constipation were common. Other more variable movement abnormalities included peripheral hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus, dyskinesias, and chorea. Some patients developed joint contractures. Brain imaging, when performed, was normal in some and showed nonspecific abnormalities in others, including cerebral atrophy, cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, under-opercularization, and delayed myelination.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE102 in the families reported by {1:Marafi et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 10 patients from 7 unrelated families with DEE102, {1:Marafi et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC38A3 gene (e.g., {604437.0001}-{604437.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families; none was present in the gnomAD database. There were 4 missense mutations and 4 putative truncating or loss-of-function mutations. Functional studies of the variants were not performed. Of note, the patient with the mildest phenotype (family 4), who did not have seizures or brain imaging abnormalities, carried a homozygous missense variant (R208G). Biochemical studies showed increased plasma ammonia levels in 4 children and intermittently increased serum lactate in 8. Metabolome analysis of 3 patients, including 2 sibs, showed some evidence of perturbations of glutamate, histidine, and nitrogen metabolism, although no consistent pattern was observed. {1:Marafi et al. (2022)} noted that SLC38A3 is a major regulator of the glutamate/GABA-glutamine cycle in the brain and postulated that the disorder results, at least in part, from alterations in the homeostasis of certain neurotransmitters in the brain.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that holoprosencephaly-14 (HPE14) is caused by homozygous mutation in PLCH1 gene ({612835}) on chromosome 3q25.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Holoprosencephaly-14 (HPE14) is an autosomal recessive condition characterized by severe developmental delay secondary to brain malformations within the holoprosencephaly spectrum ({1:Drissi et al., 2022}).

For general phenotypic information and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of holoprosencephaly, see HPE1 ({236100}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Drissi et al. (2022)} reported 2 sib pairs from unrelated consanguineous families with holoprosencephaly. In family 1, a female child was born with hydrocephalus and macrocephaly. Brain MRI demonstrated a posterior fossa cyst, atrophy of the cerebellum, partial agenesis of the vermis, hemispheric heterotopias, and abnormal ventricles with absent septum pellucidum, suggestive of holoprosencephaly. She also had a ventricular septal defect, bilateral cleft lip, and cleft palate. She died from complications after a surgery. A male sib was also born with hydrocephalus and macrocephaly. Brain MRI showed agenesis of the corpus callosum, a subependymal cyst, ventriculomegaly, periventricular heterotopias, and an enlarged cisterna magna. At 5 years of age he had epilepsy and severe developmental delay. In family 2, a male patient was prenatally diagnosed with alobar holoprosencephaly on ultrasound at 20 weeks' gestation. He died shortly after birth. His clinical features included alobar holoprosencephaly, cyclopia, cleft lip, microcephaly, and cardiac anomalies including a double outlet right ventricle and ventricular septal defect. A female sib had holoprosencephaly and hydrocephalus. She died shortly after birth. Her clinical features included absence of eyes, a proboscis, and ears joined together under the chin.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HPE14 in the families reported by {1:Drissi et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with holoprosencephaly-14, including a sib pair from family 2, {1:Drissi et al. (2022)} identified homozygous mutations in the PLCH1 gene (R689X, {612835.0001} and c.3235delT, {612835.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the phenotype in both families, although a similarly affected sib of the patient in family 1 died in infancy and did not have genetic testing. Transfection of PLCH1 into HEK293 cells showed that PLCH1 with the c.3235delT mutation had a primarily nuclear localization, whereas wildtype PLCH1 had a cytoplasmic localization.

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the T-cell lymphoma invasion and metastasis 1 gene (TIAM1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with language delay and seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with language delay and seizures (NEDLDS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TIAM1 gene ({600687}) on chromosome 21q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with language delay and seizures (NEDLDS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay with mild to severely impaired intellectual development and speech delay with poor or absent language. Affected individuals develop early-onset seizures that are usually well-controlled with medication. Additional features may include axial hypotonia, peripheral hypertonia, hypothyroidism, and nonspecific dysmorphic features or brain imaging abnormalities ({1:Lu et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Lu et al. (2022)} reported a pair of 35-year-old monozygotic twin brothers (family 1) with global developmental delay and autism diagnosed at 3 years of age due to delayed language acquisition and difficulties in social interactions. They received special education and speech therapy and lived in a group home. Both were verbal, but had limited language abilities; they also demonstrated ADD and ADHD. The patients developed seizures at 7.5 and 13 years of age, respectively; seizures were controlled with medication. In addition, both had hypothyroidism and 1 had Addison disease. Family history was significant for 2 distant cousins with reported autism, although genetic analysis of these patients was not performed. Three additional probands with a similar disorder were identified through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the TIAM1 gene. Two of the 3 additional families were consanguineous. These 3 patients, who ranged from 3 to 7 years of age, had global developmental delay with severely impaired intellectual disability and speech delay; one patient was nonverbal at age 7. All had early-onset seizures. Additional features included axial hypotonia and peripheral hypertonia, undescended testes, subclinical hypothyroidism (in 1), and hypomagnesemia (in 1). One patient had dysmorphic facial features, including frontal bossing, short philtrum, and anteverted nares. Brain imaging in 1 patient showed cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and hypomyelination. Family history revealed several possibly affected individuals in 2 of the families; genetic studies of these relatives were not performed.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDLDS in the families reported by {1:Lu et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 patients from 4 unrelated families with NEDLDS, {1:Lu et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations in the TIAM1 gene ({600687.0001}-{600687.0006}). Mutations in the first family were identified through exome sequencing; subsequent families were identified through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing detected TIAM1 mutations. The mutations segregated with the disorder in the families; the mutations were either absent from or present only in the heterozygous state at a low frequency in the gnomAD database. The mutations occurred throughout the gene. Detailed studies of 3 of the variants (R23C, L862F, and G328V) in Drosophila showed variable loss-of-function effects that may have been limited by toxicity, but the findings supported the hypothesis that the mutant alleles are partial loss-of-function variants with a dosage effect.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: In Drosophila, {1:Lu et al. (2022)} found expression of the TIAM1 ortholog 'sif' within neurons in the central nervous system of both larvae and adult animals. It was not expressed in glial cells. Knockdown of sif in Drosophila resulted in variably decreased survival, climbing defects, and seizure-like behavior. Moreover, knockdown of the sif gene specifically in neurons mimicked the phenotype of ubiquitous knockdown, indicating that the defects were caused by neuronal loss of sif. Expression of wildtype TIAM1 partially rescued the survival rate, but not neurologic deficits, of mutant flies, although this was limited by toxicity of TIAM1 expression. Expression of 3 of the variants (R23C, L862F, and G328V) in mutant flies showed that only R23C was associated with reduced survival rate compared to wildtype; survival rate for L862F and G328V were similar to wildtype, suggesting that they may be functional proteins. In addition, comparative survival analysis upon expression of the variants in flies showed they varied in severity with respect to toxicity, supporting the hypothesis that they are partial loss-of-function variants.

Head: Microcephaly (in some patients)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 17 (PCH17) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PRDM13 gene ({616741}) on chromosome 6q16.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 17 (PCH17) is a severe autosomal recessive developmental disorder characterized by neonatal hypotonia, severe feeding difficulties, and respiratory insufficiency. Brain imaging shows cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia. Most affected individuals die in infancy. Those who survive show variable developmental delay. Other features of the disorder include distal hypertonia, poor overall growth, visual defects, autonomic problems, dysmorphic features, and seizures ({1:Coolen et al., 2022}).

For a phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of PCH, see PCH1A ({607596}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Coolen et al. (2022)} reported 4 unrelated families in which 6 children and 2 fetuses were affected with posterior fossa abnormalities apparent in utero. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts including the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified mutations in the PRDM13 gene. Three families were consanguineous and of Northern African (families 1 and 2) or Omani (family 4) descent; the nonconsanguineous family (family 3) was of Pakistani origin. Four children died between 22 days and 25 months of age; 2 affected pregnancies were terminated after prenatal examination showed cerebellar hypoplasia and/or brainstem abnormalities. The patients presented at birth with profound hypotonia and swallowing and feeding difficulties, often requiring tube feeding. Most had respiratory insufficiency with episodes of desaturation, apnea, and altered consciousness likely of central origin. Two had bradycardia. The patients who were delivered and died early had poor overall growth and made little, if any, developmental progress. Other common features included distal hypertonia, spastic tetraplegia, posterior cleft palate (in 2 patients), suspected poor visual function, variable dysmorphic features, and seizures (in 3 patients). Brain imaging showed cerebellar vermis hypoplasia with abnormal foliation and brainstem hypoplasia or dysgenesis, particularly of the inferior olivary nuclei. Supratentorial brain regions appeared normal. The 2 affected sisters in family 3, 4.5 years and 11 months of age, had a milder disorder and were the only patients alive at the time of the report. They had neonatal hypotonia, respiratory distress, PCH on brain imaging, and episodes of dysautonomia, including bradycardia and temperature instability. Other features included hypertension and hypoglycemia. They had developmental delay, with 1 sister more severely affected than the other.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PCH17 in the families reported by {1:Coolen et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 affected individuals, including 6 children and 2 fetuses, from 4 unrelated families with PCH17, {1:Coolen et al. (2022)} identified homozygous mutations in the PRDM13 gene (see., e.g., {616741.0002}-{616741.0004}). There were 3 frameshift mutations, predicted to result in a loss of function, and 1 missense variant (H619L). All 6 affected individuals (4 infants and 2 fetuses) from 3 families with frameshift mutations died in the first days or months of life, or the pregnancies were terminated based on prenatal findings of PCH. The 2 sibs (family 3) with the missense variant had a milder phenotype and were alive at 4.5 years and 11 months, respectively, suggesting that the missense mutation resulted in a partial loss of PRDM13 function. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. {1:Coolen et al. (2022)} noted that PRDM13 is a known target of PTF1A ({607194}), which also plays a role in hindbrain neural stem cell fate specification. The overall findings suggested that defects in transcriptional regulation during neurodevelopment can lead to disorders of the brainstem and cerebellum.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: In zebrafish, {1:Coolen et al. (2022)} found expression of the prdm13 gene during hindbrain development. Prdm13-null zebrafish demonstrated increased larval lethality, abnormal body curvature, and abnormal lower jaw morphology. The number of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum was significantly reduced in mutant fish compared to wildtype, and there was also absence of the inferior olivary nuclei.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-66 (MRD66) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP2B1 gene ({108731}) on chromosome 12q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-66 (MRD66) is characterized by global developmental delay with mildly to moderately impaired intellectual development and mild speech delay. The phenotype and severity are highly variable. Some patients have behavioral problems or autism spectrum disorder, and about 50% have variable types of seizures. Additional features may include nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, tall or short stature, and mild skeletal anomalies ({1:Rahimi et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Rahimi et al. (2022)} reported 12 unrelated patients, 11 ranging from 3 to 21 years of age and another who was 51 years of age, with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts, such as the GeneMatcher Program, after exome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the ATP2B1 gene. All were referred for global developmental delay and variably impaired intellectual development, mild (58%), moderate (25%), or severe (17%). Most had mild motor delay with a median age at walking of 20 months and speech delay with a median age at first words of 26 months. However, a 5-year-old Chinese boy (patient 12) was nonambulatory and nonverbal. Of note, the most severely affected patient was a 3-year-old boy (patient 6) who was nonambulatory and nonverbal, had treatment-resistant epilepsy, cortical visual impairment, sensorineural hearing loss, and was tube-fed. This patient carried a missense variant (R789C) that was found once in the gnomAD database. Behavioral problems were common in the cohort: 5 had autism spectrum disorder and 3 had additional behavioral abnormalities, including compulsive behavior or anxiety. The oldest patient (patient 9) was a 51-year-old man who had mild nonprogressive developmental delay with mild intellectual disability (IQ of 73) and high functioning autism since early childhood. He was able to attend a special school, live on his own, and hold a job. He had a marfanoid habitus with mild aortic root dilatation. Six (50%) patients had variable types of seizures, including infantile spasms, febrile seizures, myoclonic seizures, and absence seizures. One patient was diagnosed with West syndrome. Two patients had short stature and 2 (including the 51-year-old) had a marfanoid habitus with arachnodactyly and scoliosis. Some patients had nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, but there was not a common gestalt. These variable features included retrognathia, wide nasal bridge, large ears, dysmorphic ears, sparse hair, epicanthus, esotropia, and high-arched palate. Many patients had additional congenital abnormalities, including congenital heart defects, cryptorchidism, and digital defects.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the ATP2B1 gene that were identified in patients with MRD66 by {1:Rahimi et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 12 unrelated patients with MRD66, {1:Rahimi et al. (2022)} identified heterozygous mutations in the ATP2B1 gene (see, e.g., {108731.0001}-{108731.0005}). The mutations were proven to occur de novo in 9 patients, and suspected to be de novo in the other 3. There were 9 missense variants and 3 nonsense variants. All but 1 missense variant (R789C) were absent from the gnomAD database; R789C was found once (frequency of 4.0 x 10(-6)). Mutations occurred throughout the gene, and there were no genotype/phenotype correlations. In silico modeling of the missense variants predicted adverse effects on protein structure that may affect stability or function. In vitro functional expression studies in transfected HEK293 cells showed that all 9 missense variants impaired ATP2B1 calcium transport activity compared to wildtype. In addition, 3 missense variants (e.g., T264I, {108731.0002}) showed altered cellular localization with a shift from the membrane to the cytoplasm. The findings indicated that the ATP2B1 mutations resulted in a loss-of-function effect with haploinsufficiency, although a dominant-negative effect could not be excluded. {1:Rahimi et al. (2022)} noted that ATP2B1 is expressed in the early stages of neurodevelopment and has a significant role in calcium homeostasis in the central nervous system.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with language impairment and early-onset DOPA-responsive dystonia-parkinsonism

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with language impairment and early-onset dopa-responsive dystonia-parkinsonism (IDLDP) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the NR4A2 gene ({601828}) on chromosome 2q24.

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with language impairment and early-onset dopa-responsive dystonia-parkinsonism (IDLDP) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay affecting motor, cognitive, and speech domains apparent in early childhood or infancy. Some patients may have normal early development in infancy before symptom onset. There is phenotypic heterogeneity and the severity is highly variable; less severely affected individuals have only mild deficits and are able to attend special schools. About half of patients develop various types of seizures that may be refractory or responsive to treatment. Most patients also show movement abnormalities, often hypotonia early in the disease course with later development of dopa-responsive dystonia or parkinsonism ({3:Ramos et al., 2019}, {6:Wirth et al., 2020}; {5:Singh et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Ramos et al. (2019)} reported a 9-year-old boy with normal growth and motor development, but who had delayed speech and mild intellectual disability (IQ of 52-63) with learning disabilities. He attended a special school. At age 5, he developed seizure activity during sleep with an EEG pattern that was consistent with rolandic epilepsy. He also had focal seizures, but showed good control with medication. Brain imaging was normal.

{6:Wirth et al. (2020)} reported 2 unrelated patients with a history of mild developmental delay from early childhood who developed dopa-responsive dystonia as young adults. P1 had a history of significant language delay, mild intellectual disability with an IQ of 56, and onset of generalized tonic-clonic seizures at age 26 years. At 29, he presented with paroxysmal dystonia of the limbs that progressed to involve the face and trunk and resulted in difficulties talking and swallowing. He also developed a permanent parkinsonism syndrome with akinesia, rigidity, and tremor associated with reduced dopamine metabolites in the CSF and impaired dopamine uptake on functional brain imaging. Brain MRI was normal. P2 had a history of mild intellectual disability with preserved speech who presented at age 30 with left-hand tremor and behavioral changes, including clumsiness. The motor disorder progressed to dystonia and parkinsonism; brain imaging showed thinning of the substantia nigra and reduced dopamine uptake. The dystonia and movement abnormalities in both patients responded well to treatment with L-dopa. {6:Wirth et al. (2020)} noted the phenotypic expansion of the disorder and concluded that patients with mutations in the NR4A2 gene may present with mild intellectual disability in childhood and develop dopa-responsive dystonia later in early adulthood.

{5:Singh et al. (2020)} reported 8 unrelated patients with neurodevelopmental deficits who were ascertained through collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher Program, after exome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the NR4A2 gene. The patients, who ranged from 2 to 19 years of age, had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development ranging from mild to severe. Two patients had normal early development prior to the onset of symptoms. Five patients were noted to have speech and language impairment, including speech apraxia and dyslexia, and 4 had behavioral problems, including autism, ADHD, hyperactivity, tantrums, anxiety, and hyposensitivity to temperature and pain. Various types of seizures were present in 5 patients: these included tonic clonic, generalized, absence, infantile spasms, and rolandic epilepsy. Most had movement abnormalities, most commonly hypotonia, but also dystonia, ataxia, and choreoathetoid movements. Brain imaging was normal in 4 of 7 patients studied, whereas 3 had nonspecific abnormalities, including cerebellar atrophy, enlarged ventricles, and pontine hypoplasia. The most severely affected patient (P6) was a 2-year-old boy with poor growth, global developmental delay, and abnormal eye movements apparent in early infancy. He developed focal seizures at age 6 months that progressed to infantile spasms and evolved to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome with refractory tonic and myoclonic seizures. Other features in this patient included hypotonia, disordered sleep, and feeding difficulties requiring tube feeding. Brain imaging showed pontine hypoplasia, enlarged ventricles, and delayed myelination.

{1:Jesus et al. (2021)} reported a 30-year-old man with persistent dystonia-parkinsonism and motor tics. He started walking with support at age 13 months, but had frequent falls. He also had speech delay with articulation difficulties, attention deficit, and learning disabilities requiring special schooling (IQ of 77). At age 16 years, he presented with trichotillomania and motor tics. At 28, he had slowness with walking difficulties, abnormal craniocervical posture, jaw dystonia, and features of parkinsonism. Nonmotor symptoms included gastrointestinal and sleep-related problems; mobility and communication issues affected quality of life. Brain imaging showed impaired dopamine uptake in the striatum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the NR4A2 gene that were identified in patients with IDLDP by {6:Wirth et al. (2020)} and {5:Singh et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

cytogenetics.title: Cytogenetics
cytogenetics.content:
{4:Reuter et al. (2017)} reported a 10.5-year-old girl with mild global developmental delay and significant speech and language delay associated with a de novo heterozygous 89-kb deletion on chromosome 2q24 that affected only the NR4A2 gene. She attended a special needs school and had a friendly demeanor; IQ was 60. Growth parameters were normal and she did not have dysmorphic features. The findings were consistent with haploinsufficiency of NR4A2 being responsible for the disorder, although functional studies of the variant were not performed.

{2:Levy et al. (2018)} reported 2 unrelated patients, P1 aged 17 years and P2 aged 8 years, with mild global developmental delay, mildly impaired intellectual development (IQ of 64 in P1), and significant speech delay. P1 had autism spectrum disorder, and P2 was noted to be restless in early childhood. Both patients required special education services. Genetic analysis in both patients identified de novo heterozygous deletions (122 kb and 75 kb) on chromosome 2q24.1 that encompassed only the NR4A2 gene. Functional studies and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the findings suggested that haploinsufficiency of the NR4A2 gene was responsible for the phenotype.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 9-year-old boy with IDLDP, {3:Ramos et al. (2019)} identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation in the NR4A2 gene ({601828.0003}). The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but it was predicted to result in a loss of function.

In 2 unrelated patients with IDLDP, {6:Wirth et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous frameshift mutations in the NR4A2 gene (see, e.g., {601828.0003}). The mutation was proven to occur de novo in 1 case; parental DNA from the other case was not available. The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 8 unrelated patients with IDLDP, {5:Singh et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous mutations in the NR4A2 gene (see, e.g., {601828.0004}-{601828.0006}). The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher Program, after exome sequencing identified NR4A2 mutation. None of the variants was present in the gnomAD database. The mutations, which were demonstrated to have occurred de novo in all 7 patients for whom parental DNA was available, included 1 frameshift, 1 splice site, 1 nonsense, and 5 missense mutations; 4 missense mutations occurred in the DNA-binding domain. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the variants were predicted to result in a loss of function with haploinsufficiency.

In a 30-year-old man with IDLDP, {1:Jesus et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the NR4A2 gene (R319Q; {601828.0007}). Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-103 (DEE103) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KCNC2 gene ({176256}) on chromosome 12q21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-103 (DEE103) is characterized by onset of various types of seizures in the first year of life, most of which are refractory to treatment. Affected individuals show global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development ranging from mild to severe. Additional features may include hypotonia, ataxia, and behavioral abnormalities, including autism and hyperactivity ({3:Schwarz et al., 2022}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{4:Vetri et al. (2020)} reported an 8-year-old boy, born of unrelated parents, who presented with tonic spasms on the second day of life. EEG showed diffuse bursts of high voltage spike-wave complexes during wakefulness, and an almost continuous burst-suppression pattern during sleep. The infant had poor spontaneous movements, lacked head control, and was unable to respond to light or follow objects. The seizures continued to be refractory to multiple medications, and he developed severe global developmental delay, spastic tetraplegia with abnormal posturing, episodes of opisthotonus, and status dystonicus during a febrile infection. A feeding tube was placed at age 5 years. Brain imaging showed hypotrophic frontal lobes and hypomyelination. At age 8, he continued to have daily seizures with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, drooling, and microcephaly (z score of -4).

{1:Rademacher et al. (2020)} reported a 7-year-old girl (patient 3) with genetically confirmed NF1 ({162200}) who presented with infantile spasms at 1 month of age. EEG at age 4 months showed hypsarrhythmia, consistent with West syndrome. The seizures were refractory to treatment, and follow-up EEG showed multifocal discharges and slowed background activity, leading to a clinical diagnosis of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Brain imaging showed 2 arachnoid cysts and progressive brain atrophy. She had moderate to severe intellectual disability, but was able to walk.

{2:Rydzanicz et al. (2021)} reported a 2-year-old Polish girl, born of unrelated parents, who presented with epileptic spasms on the second day of life. Thereafter, she showed hypotonia and severely delayed motor and cognitive development with inability to sit or walk and no cognitive skills. The seizures occurred every 1 to 2 days and were resistant to treatment. EEG was abnormal, showing multifocal, generalized, and continuous spikes, polyspikes, and spike and wave discharges.

{3:Schwarz et al. (2022)} reported 8 unrelated patients, ranging from 7 to 30 years of age, with DEE. The patients, who were collected through clinical and research collaboration, all carried de novo heterozygous missense variants in the KCNC2 gene identified by exome sequencing. Patient 3 had previously been reported by {1:Rademacher et al. (2020)}. All patients had onset of various types of seizures in the first year of life: these included absence, tonic, clonic, focal, generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, and febrile seizures, as well as infantile spasms. EEG abnormalities were also variable, mostly showing generalized epileptic activity; 3 patients had polyspike wave discharges and 2 had continuous spikes and waves during sleep (CSWS). The seizures were refractory to treatment in most cases, although 2 patients eventually became seizure-free on valproate. All 8 patients had impaired intellectual development, ranging from mild to severe. A few had additional findings, including autism spectrum disorder, hyperactivity, language problems, ataxia, and hypotonia. Brain imaging was normal in all patients except patient 3 ({1:Rademacher et al., 2020}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the KCNC2 gene that were identified in patients with DEE103 by {3:Schwarz et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In an 8-year-old boy with DEE103, {4:Vetri et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation KCNC2 gene (V471L; {176256.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the dbSNP, 1000 Genomes Project, or ExAC databases. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In a 7-year-old girl with DEE103, in the context of genetically confirmed neurofibromatosis (NF1; {162200}), {1:Rademacher et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the KCNC2 gene (D167Y; {176256.0002}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing, was not present in public databases. In vitro functional expression studies in Xenopus oocytes showed that the mutation resulted in decreased mean K+ current, consistent with a loss-of-function effect. There was no evidence for a dominant-negative effect. However, cells transfected with the mutation also showed a shift in voltage dependence of activation to more hyperpolarized potentials, suggesting a gain-of-function effect. The findings suggested a complex modifying effect of the variant on the neuronal network.

In a 2-year-old girl with DEE103, {2:Rydzanicz et al. (2021)} also identified a de novo heterozygous V471L mutation in the KCNC2 gene. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by deep sequencing; functional studies were not performed. The patient also carried a heteroplasmic m.15294T-C transition in the MTCYB gene ({516020}) at a high-level (70%) that was inherited from the unaffected mother who had low level heteroplasmy (3%); it was unclear whether this variant played a role in the phenotype.

In 8 unrelated patients with DEE103, including the patient reported by {1:Rademacher et al. (2020)}, {3:Schwarz et al. (2022)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the KCNC2 gene (see, e.g., {176256.0003}-{176256.0006}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in public databases, including gnomAD. In vitro functional expression studies in Xenopus oocytes of a subset of the mutations showed that they had variable effects on current amplitude, but all caused a shift in the activation curve and membrane potential to a more hyperpolarized potential and prolonged the deactivation time compared to controls, consistent with a gain-of-function effect. The authors suggested that impaired function of inhibitory neurons due to KCNC2 mutations likely plays an essential role in seizure development.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with dystonia and seizures (NEDDS) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the SHQ1 gene ({613663}) on chromosome 3p13.

Biallelic mutation in the SHQ1 gene has also been reported in childhood-onset dystonia-35 (DYT35; {619921}), a less severe disorder with overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dystonia and seizures (NEDDS) is a severe autosomal recessive disorder characterized by hypotonia and dystonic posturing apparent from early infancy. Affected individuals show global developmental delay with inability to walk or speak and have profoundly impaired intellectual development, often with behavioral abnormalities. Additional features may include other extrapyramidal movements, seizures or seizure-like activity, and cerebellar hypoplasia on brain imaging ({2:Sleiman et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Sleiman et al. (2022)} reported 2 sisters, born of unrelated parents of European origin (family 1), who presented in the first months of life with hypotonia, dystonic posturing, and global developmental delay. Both showed intractable extrapyramidal movement disorders with diffuse chorea, athetosis, and ballism, with worsening dystonia. The girls also showed severe self-injurious behavior, anxiety, and autonomic dysfunction, including temperature instability, excessive sweating, and constipation. Both were wheelchair-bound and nonverbal. One of the sisters developed seizures at age 10 years, resulting in sudden death. The other sister had staring episodes with a photoparoxysmal response on EEG and was treated with antiseizure medication. Brain imaging of the sister who died showed subtle cerebellar atrophy; brain imaging in the other sister was normal. Neuropathologic analysis of the deceased sister showed loss of neurons and decreased neuronal pigmentation in the substantia nigra.

{1:Bizarro and Meier (2017)} reported a 2-year-old boy who was born at 29 weeks' gestation by cesarean section due to intrauterine growth retardation and sparse fetal movements. He had feeding difficulties, lack of acquisition of developmental milestones, a severe seizure disorder, spastic quadriplegia, and cerebellar hypoplasia and cortical atrophy on brain imaging. He was in a vegetative state. No mucocutaneous findings were reported, and there was no additional information on movement abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDDS in the family reported by {2:Sleiman et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sisters, born of unrelated parents of European descent (family 1), with NEDDS, {2:Sleiman et al. (2022)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the SHQ1 gene (c.828_831del, {613663.0001} and E292K, {613663.0003}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. RT-PCR and Western blot analysis of patient cells showed decreased SHQ1 transcript and protein levels compared to controls. Expression of the variants in the yeast homolog (yShq1) showed that the E292K missense variant slowed cell growth compared to controls, whereas the frameshift mutation abolished growth completely. Further in vitro functional expression studies in yeast showed that the mutation resulted in depletion of H/ACA snoRNAs and caused ribosome biogenesis defects. Immunoprecipitation studies showed that the E292K variant had weakened interaction with Cbf5, the yeast homolog of DKC1 ({300126}). These multiple impacts on SHQ1 function corresponded to the severe phenotype observed in the patients.

In a 2-year-old male infant with spastic quadriplegia, intractable epilepsy, and cerebellar hypoplasia, {1:Bizarro and Meier (2017)} identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the SHQ1 gene (R335C and A426V). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The R335C variant was found 4 times in only heterozygous state in the ExAC database; A426V was not present in ExAC. Both mutations occurred in the SSD domain, which interacts with NAP57 (DKC1; {300126}), and in vitro binding studies showed that both variants reduced the binding to NAP57 (reduced to about 59% of normal values). The authors suggested that the phenotype was reminiscent of the most severe variant of dyskeratosis congenita (DKC), known as Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome (HHS; see {305000}). However, the patient had no mucocutaneous findings and telomere length was not assessed.

preferredTitle: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER, AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT 67; MRD67
clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, mild to severe
Caused by mutation in the glutamate receptor, ionotropic, AMPA 1 gene (GRIA1,)

Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, mild to severe
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the glutamate receptor, ionotropic, AMPA 1 gene (GRIA1,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-67 (MRD67) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GRIA1 gene ({138248}) on chromosome 5q33.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-67 (MRD67) is characterized by global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development apparent from infancy or early childhood. Additional features may include behavioral abnormalities, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and ADHD, as well as language and sleeping difficulties. Brain imaging is normal ({4:Ismail et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:De Ligt et al. (2012)} reported a girl (patient 2) with global developmental delay, severely impaired intellectual development, and absent speech with a heterozygous mutation in the GRIA1 gene. Brain imaging was normal; she did not have seizures. {4:Ismail et al. (2022)} also reported this patient (as patient 2), noting that she was still nonverbal at age 6 years and that she had recurrent airway infections.

{3:Geisheker et al. (2017)} reported 3 unrelated patients with MRD67. A review of phenotypic information from these patients and the patient reported by {1:de Ligt et al. (2012)} indicated that all had global developmental delay with mild to moderate intellectual disability and variable speech delay. All had ASD, and most had other behavioral abnormalities, including ADHD, OCD, and motor tics. One patient had seizures between ages 2 and 5. Brain imaging was normal.

{4:Ismail et al. (2022)} reported 4 unrelated patients (patients 2, 3, 4, and 6) ascertained through collaborative clinical and research efforts after genetic analysis identified de novo heterozygous missense variants in the GRIA1 gene. Patient 2 had previously been reported by {1:de Ligt et al. (2012)}. Patients 3, 4, and 6 were 13, 26, and 21 years of age, respectively, at the time of the report. All had global developmental delay with mildly delayed walking and moderate to severe intellectual disability. Speech was delayed or impaired; P3 was nonverbal. Two were diagnosed with ASD, 2 with ADHD, and 1 with anxiety and tantrums. Two had sleep disturbances. P6 showed early developmental regression, bipolar disorder, hypothyroidism, and polycystic ovary syndrome. P3 and P4 had squint and hypermetropia, respectively. None had seizures or brain imaging abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the GRIA1 gene that were identified in patients with MRD67 by {4:Ismail et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a girl (trio 2) with MRD67, {1:de Ligt et al. (2012)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the GRIA1 gene (A636T; {138248.0001}) by exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant were not performed. The patient was ascertained from a cohort of 100 patients with severe intellectual disability who underwent exome sequencing.

{3:Geisheker et al. (2017)} identified a recurrent heterozygous A636T mutation in the GRIA1 gene in 3 unrelated patients with MRD67. The mutation was demonstrated to occur de novo in 1 patient; paternal DNA was not available for the other 2 patients, but the mutation was not present in either mother. The mutation, which occurred within a highly conserved region in the M3 transmembrane domain, was not present in the ExAC database. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells transfected with the mutant protein showed presence of a constitutive current, consistent with a gain-of-function effect, although a dominant effect of the mutation was not observed when cotransfected with wildtype GRIA1. The authors suggested that the mutation may cause a defect in early synaptic development. The study of {3:Geisheker et al. (2017)} included a large cohort of over 17,000 patients with a diagnosis of ASD or developmental delay who underwent genetic studies. {3:Geisheker et al. (2017)} noted that {2:De Rubeis et al. (2014)} had identified a de novo A636T mutation in a patient from a large cohort of patients with ASD who underwent exome sequencing. Clinical details of that individual were not provided.

{4:Ismail et al. (2022)} identified a de novo heterozygous A636T mutation in the GRIA1 gene in 2 unrelated patients (P3 and P4) with MRD67. The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Xenopus oocytes expressing the A636T mutation showed a 10-fold increased current, impaired desensitization, increased sensitivity towards glu, and increased channel-opening ability compared to controls. These findings were consistent with a gain-of-function effect. In a 21-year-old woman (patient 6) with MRD67, {4:Ismail et al. (2022)} identified a different de novo heterozygous missense variant in the GRIA1 gene (G745D; {138248.0002}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies showed that the G745D variant resulted in decreased current amplitudes compared to controls, suggesting a loss-of-function effect. However, there was also evidence for decreased desensitization and increased kainate/glu ratio of the mutant channel, which would suggest increased current. {4:Ismail et al. (2022)} also reported a patient (P5, who was originally reported by {3:Geisheker et al., 2017} as patient 25431) with MRD67 associated with a de novo heterozygous I627T variant in the GRIA1 gene. The variant was not present in gnomAD and showed decreased current amplitude compared to wildtype consistent with a loss of function, but other significant functional defects were not observed. Of note, {3:Geisheker et al. (2017)} reported that this individual also carried a maternally inherited 18p11.32 duplication and an Xq26.1 duplication. Both of his sisters, each of whom carried one of the duplications, and his mother all had learning difficulties. Lastly, {4:Ismail et al. (2022)} reported a patient (P7) of unknown sex and age with a missense variant (R345Q) in the GRIA1 gene. The patient was identified through the ClinVar database; other than intellectual disability, clinical information was limited. The variant was present in the gnomAD database (1.24 x 10(-5)). Moreover, multiple in vitro functional expression studies in Xenopus oocytes transfected with R345Q showed similar receptor activation properties, currents, and formation of heteromeric receptors as the wildtype protein, suggesting that this variant does not have a functional impact and is benign.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-76 (MRT76) is caused by homozygous mutation in the GRIA1 gene ({138248}) on chromosome 5q33. One such patient has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-76 (MRT76) is characterized by impaired intellectual development, absent speech, poor sleep, abnormal EEG with seizures, normal brain imaging, and precocious puberty ({2:Ismail et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Ismail et al. (2022)} reported a 10-year-old girl (patient 1), born of consanguineous parents, with global developmental delay, severely impaired intellectual development, absent speech, sleep disturbances, feeding difficulties necessitating a feeding tube, toe walking, and self-injurious behavior. She had onset of refractory seizures at 6 months of age. EEG showed diffuse background slowing with frequent spike-wave discharges. Other features included divergent squint, constipation, and precocious puberty. Brain imaging was normal.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MRT76 in the family reported by {2:Ismail et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a 10-year-old girl (patient 1), born of consanguineous parents, with MRT76, {2:Ismail et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the GRIA1 gene (R377X; {138248.0003}). Each parent was heterozygous for the mutation, which was not present in the gnomAD database. {1:Baralle (2024)} stated that the mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing (WES) and that the parents were unaffected. In vitro functional expression studies showed that the mutation truncates the protein, prevented proper subunit assembly and function, and did not produce any current response to glu stimulation, resulting in a complete loss of function. Expression of a homozygous loss-of-function mutation similar to R377X in Xenopus tadpoles using CRISPR/Cas9 techniques resulted in early transient motor deficits and some behavioral abnormalities that could be consistent with seizures. Although mutant animals had no obvious or consistent craniofacial or structural brain abnormalities, they showed impaired spatial memory in an alternative choice search pattern assay. These findings suggested that disruption of glutamatergic signaling impairs normal behavior and possibly affects cognition in vertebrates.
