text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that immunodeficiency-106 (IMD106) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the IFNAR1 gene ({107450}) on chromosome 21q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Immunodeficiency-106 (IMD106) is an autosomal recessive immunologic disorder characterized by increased susceptibility to viral infections beginning in infancy or early childhood. Some patients present with recurrent respiratory infections or other viral infections. In many cases, the susceptibility to viral infections due to IMD106 only becomes apparent after initial vaccination with live attenuated viral (LAV) vaccines, most notably MMR and yellow fever. A subset of IMD106 patients who demonstrate adverse reactions to MMR or other LAV vaccinations develop a severe acute hyperinflammatory response reminiscent of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and may show encephalopathy, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and multiorgan failure. However, some patients with IMD106 tolerate MMR vaccination without sequelae. IFNAR1 deficiency may also predispose to severe respiratory infection with SARS-CoV-2 and to herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV1) encephalitis (HSE). The disorder results from an impaired type I interferon signaling response ({2:Bastard et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{5:Hernandez et al. (2019)} reported 2 unrelated children who presented with a hyperinflammatory response soon after vaccination with live attenuated vaccines for MMR and yellow fever, respectively. Neither showed features of immunodeficiency before vaccination. P1 was a 9-year-old boy born of consanguineous Iranian parents who presented at about 12 months of age with disseminated vaccine-strain measles after vaccination with MMR. He had fever, neurologic symptoms consistent with encephalitis, and leukocytosis in the CSF. He had previously received hepatitis B virus, BCG, and influenza vaccines without adverse effect. Antibodies against measles and mumps were at the low limits of normal, whereas responses to pneumococcal and hepatitis B were normal. He had frequent upper respiratory infections, but had normal development and was in good health at 9 years of age. A sister had died in infancy of meningoencephalitis after receiving MMR vaccine. P2 was a 14-year-old girl, born of unrelated Brazilian parents, who presented at age 12 years with fever, encephalitis, acute renal and hepatic failure, and leukocytosis following vaccination for yellow fever. She made a full recovery and was healthy at age 14. She had previously received 2 MMR vaccines and oral live poliovirus and BCG in early childhood without incident. {6:Khanmohammadi et al. (2022)} reported follow-up of P1, who presented with a severe COVID-19 respiratory infection requiring hospitalization at age 13 years. In addition to MMR-associated meningitis in infancy, he had a history of recurrent hospitalizations due to infection with influenza virus. Treatment with gamma-interferon (IFNG; {147570}) resulted in clinical improvement, and he was eventually discharged. These findings indicated that patients with INFAR1 deficiency may be predisposed to severe COVID-19 infections.

{4:Gothe et al. (2022)} reported a previously healthy 15-month-old boy, born of consanguineous parents, who developed a severe fatal hyperinflammatory response to MMR vaccination. He met the diagnostic criteria for HLH and died 6 months later. Analysis of serum and CSF did not showed vaccine-strain viral replication, but low-level EBV was detected.

{3:Bastard et al. (2021)} reported a girl, born of consanguineous Palestinian parents, who had recurrent viral infections in infancy and developed HSV encephalitis (HSE), resulting in death around 20 months of age. Prior to this, she had developed a fever following MMR vaccination, but it resolved spontaneously. A first cousin of the patient (P3) died at age 12 months following a severe adverse reaction to MMR vaccination. P2, who was the sib of P3, had episodes of aseptic meningitis in infancy that may have been related to HSV. At age 14 years, P2 developed parotiditis followed by bilateral hearing loss. This episode was strongly suspected to be due to mumps infection; he had not received MMR vaccination per the family's request. Serum analysis of P2 showed the presence of antibodies to various viruses, including HSV1, VZV, CMV, EBV, measles, and mumps.

{2:Bastard et al. (2022)} reported 7 patients from 5 unrelated families of western Polynesian origin who presented in the first months or year of life with severe life-threatening viral infections. Six of the 7 patients developed an acute adverse systemic hyperinflammatory reaction within days to weeks after vaccination with live attenuated MMR vaccine. Features included fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, encephalopathy, and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Most of these patients also developed thrombocytopenia, anemia, hyperferritinemia, dyslipidemia, coagulopathy, and increased levels of soluble CD25 (IL2RA; {147730}) with evidence of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Vaccine-strain measles and mumps were detected in tissue from some of the patients. Three patients (P1-P3) died in infancy of multiorgan failure soon after the MMR vaccination, whereas a fourth patient (P4) initially recovered, but died of RSV infection several months later. P5, the brother of P4, was a 7-year-old boy who developed aseptic meningoencephalitis and features of hyperinflammation initially diagnosed as Kawasaki disease ({611775}) 17 days after his first MMR vaccine at age 16 months. He recovered and tolerated the second MMR dose without complications. P5 had no neurocognitive deficits, but demonstrated unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, possibly a sequela of mumps infection. P6 had recurrent viral pneumonia in the first year of life and showed an acute inflammatory reaction to MMR with viral encephalitis at age 14 months. He subsequently had multiple viral respiratory infections, including RSV and parainfluenza virus, necessitating extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO); thereafter he demonstrated bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, global developmental delay, and autism spectrum disorder. Four of the 6 patients with a severe reaction to MMR were noted to have viral infections prior to the first MMR vaccine, including respiratory infections with bronchiolitis (P4 and P5), recurrent viral pneumonia (P6), and enteroviral meningoencephalitis (P3). However, 2 sibs from family A (P1 and P2) were healthy before MMR vaccination at age 12 months and tolerated live attenuated vaccination with BCG and oral polio. P7 presented at 10 months of age with hemophilus influenza type B (Hib) bacteremia and meningitis complicated by seizures, and later developed RSV-associated respiratory insufficiency and multiorgan failure requiring ECMO. P7 received MMR vaccine at ages 4 and 4.5 years without complications; she was the only patient of the cohort who tolerated MMR vaccination. She also had developmental delay that may have been unrelated to the IMD phenotype.

{1:Abolhassani et al. (2022)} reported a 3-year-old girl, born of consanguineous Iranian parents, who presented around 8 months of age with chronic sinusitis and oral thrush and later developed severe mucormycosis of the nose and paranasal sinuses. She had no adverse reaction to vaccination with LAV, including BCG, oral polio, and MMR. At age 3 years, she presented with a severe SARS-CoV-2 infection complicated by pneumonia and multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C). Features included fever, respiratory insufficiency, hypotension, lymphadenopathy, anemia, leukocytosis, elevated transaminases, metabolic acidosis, and evidence of myocardial injury. Despite intensive care, she died of cardiorespiratory failure. This patient was also reported by {7:Zhang et al. (2022)} as patient P12 in a study of an international cohort of 112 children less than 16 years of age who were hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IMD106 in the families reported by {2:Bastard et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 unrelated patients with IMD106 manifest as adverse reaction to MMR and yellow fever vaccinations, {5:Hernandez et al. (2019)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the IFNAR1 gene ({107450.0001}-{107450.0003}). There were 2 splice site and 1 nonsense mutations, suggesting a loss of function. The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. None were present in the 1000 Genomes Project or gnomAD databases. Western blot analysis of patient-derived fibroblast and lymphoid cells showed complete lack of IFNAR1 expression, suggesting nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Patient cells showed impaired type I interferon (IFN) signaling, as evidenced by lack of phosphorylation of the downstream targets STAT1 ({600555}) and STAT2 ({600556}) in response to stimulation. Patient cells also had impaired type I IFN immunity to viruses compared to controls. Transduction of patient cells with wildtype IFNAR1 was able to rescue these defects.

In a 21-month-old boy with IMD106 manifest as a fatal hyperinflammatory response to MMR vaccination, {4:Gothe et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the IFNAR1 gene (Q308X; {107450.0005}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. There was no detectable IFNAR1 protein in patient-derived cells, consistent with a complete loss of function. In vitro functional expression studies of patient cells showed impaired signaling responses to stimulation with alpha or beta-interferon (see, e.g., IFNA2, {147562}), but intact responses to gamma-interferon (IFNG; {147570}). Patient cells were susceptible to infection with the picornavirus EMCV and the Zika virus, and this defect could be rescued by treatment with IFNG, but not IFNA2. Expression of wildtype IFNAR1 in patient cells restored induction of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) and the overall antiviral state in response to IFNA2. The patient developed features of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) following MMR vaccination in infancy, but vaccine-strain viral particles were not detected, consistent with 'sterile autoinflammation' and suggesting an immunoregulatory role for IFNAR1 towards other cytokines.

In 2 members (P1 and P2) of a consanguineous Arab family with IMD106, {3:Bastard et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous deletion in the IFNAR1 gene ({107450.0006}). The mutation, which was found by analysis of copy number variants and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the phenotype in the family. It was not present in multiple public databases, including gnomAD. Analysis of patient cells showed that the deletion resulted in aberrant splicing predicted to generate a protein with a C-terminal truncation lacking residues known to be critical for the interaction of IFNAR1 with TYK2 ({176941}). Patient-derived fibroblasts showed low levels of IFNAR1 mRNA, suggesting nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, although a truncated protein was expressed on the cell surface. Patient cells showed no signaling response or induction of interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) expression in response to stimulation with IFNA2 ({147562}) or IFNB ({147640}). The cellular response to IFNG was normal. The signaling defects could be rescued by expression of wildtype IFNAR1. Patient cells also showed enhanced susceptibility to infection and increased viral replication when exposed to several viruses, including HSV1 and measles, compared to controls. In this family, P1 died of HSV1-associated encephalitis, whereas P2 had a less severe phenotype with recurrent viral infections, suspected to include HSV1 and mumps. The findings highlighted a critical role for IFNAR1 immunity and the type I interferon response to protect against HSV1 infection in the CNS.

In 7 patients from 5 unrelated families of Western Polynesian origin with IMD106, {2:Bastard et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the IFNAR1 gene (E386X; {107450.0007}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. The mutation was found once in the heterozygous state in the gnomAD database. The carrier frequency of the mutation was estimated at 1.25% in the Samoan population, with lesser frequencies in some, but not all, other Pacific Island populations. In vitro functional studies in HEK293 cells transfected with the E386X mutation showed presence of a truncated IFNAR1 protein that was not detected at the plasma membrane. Transfected cells showed a total absence of luciferase reporter activity in response to IFNA2, consistent with a loss of function and complete IFNAR1 deficiency. Cells derived from 1 patient (P3) showed no detectable IFNAR1 at the cell surface, absence of a signaling response to stimulation with IFNA2, an overall defective response to type I IFNs, and impaired induction of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). Expression of wildtype IFNAR1 rescued these defects.

In a 3-year-old girl, born of consanguineous Iranian parents, with IMD106 manifest as a severe inflammatory response to SARS-CoV-2 infection resulting in death, {1:Abolhassani et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous deletion in the IFNAR1 gene ({107450.0008}) resulting in frameshift. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Patient cells were not available for study, but in vitro expression studies of cells transfected with the mutation showed almost undetectable IFNAR1 surface expression as well as impaired functional signaling response to stimulation with certain interferons. These findings were consistent with complete IFNAR1 deficiency, and indicated that a type I IFN response is essential for protective immunity against SARS-CoV-2 in the respiratory tract. This patient was also reported as patient P12 by {7:Zhang et al. (2022)} in a study of an international cohort of 112 children less than 16 years of age who were hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia. {7:Zhang et al. (2022)} did not identify any other children with mutations in the IFNAR1 gene.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Tessadori-Bicknell-van Haaften neurodevelopmental syndrome-3 (TEBIVANED3) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the H4C5 gene ({602830}) on chromosome 6p21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Tessadori-Bicknell-van Haaften neurodevelopmental syndrome-3 (TEBIVANED3) is characterized by global developmental delay with poor overall growth, impaired intellectual development, and speech difficulties. More variable features include hypotonia, microcephaly, and dysmorphic facies. The severity and manifestations of the disorder are highly variable ({1:Tessadori et al., 2022}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of Tessadori-Bicknell-van Haaften neurodevelopmental disorder, see TEBIVANED1 ({619758}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Tessadori et al. (2022)} reported 17 unrelated patients (P8-P24) with variable neurodevelopmental abnormalities associated with de novo heterozygous missense variants in the H4C5 gene that were identified through exome sequencing. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts and the phenotypes reviewed. Most of the patients ranged from 11 months to 21 years of age; P14 was 52 years old. Many had feeding difficulties with poor overall growth, including short stature in 5 and microcephaly (down to -4.6 SD) in 10. All had some degree of global developmental delay with delayed walking, impaired intellectual development, and poor or absent speech. Some had behavioral abnormalities. Additional more variable features included hypotonia, limb hypertonia, ataxia, spasticity, and ocular findings, such as strabismus and myopia. Three patients had seizures and 1 had absence-like episodes. Brain imaging, when performed, was essentially normal. Skeletal anomalies, including scoliosis, tapering fingers, and foot abnormalities, were sometimes observed. Most patients had variable and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, including broad nasal bridge, prominent nose, broad nasal tip, low-set ears, abnormal philtrum, high-arched palate, deep-set eyes, and thick or thin lips. The oldest patient (P14) was noted to have premature aging.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the H4C5 gene that were identified in patients with TEBIVANED3 by {1:Tessadori et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 17 unrelated patients with TEBIVANED3, {1:Tessadori et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the H4C5 gene (see, e.g., {602830.0001}-{602830.0005}). The patients were ascertained through international collaboration after the mutations were identified by exome sequencing. Some of the variants (e.g., R46C; {602830.0004}) were recurrent; none were present in the gnomAD database. The mutations occurred at conserved residues and tended to cluster in the core globular domain or the C-tail domain. Expression of some of the mutations in zebrafish embryos induced developmental defects, suggesting that they are pathogenic. The authors postulated a dominant effect. Of note, 4 patients (P12-P15) carried the same R41C missense variant, which was not present in gnomAD but did not induce significant developmental defects when expressed in zebrafish embryos. All patients had global developmental delay, but the severity and manifestations were highly variable, even in those with the same genotype. {1:Tessadori et al. (2022)} stated that there were inherent limitations in the zebrafish assays.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Dworschak-Punetha neurodevelopmental syndrome (DWOPNED) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PLXNA1 gene ({601055}) on chromosome 3q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Dworschak-Punetha neurodevelopmental syndrome (DWOPNED) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized mainly by global developmental delay and mildly impaired intellectual development (IQ range 77 to 85), often with behavioral abnormalities, including autism spectrum disorder and hyperactivity. Some affected individuals may have only speech delay or behavioral manifestations. More variable additional features include optic disc hypoplasia, ptosis, hypo- or hyperpigmented skin lesions, nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, and brain imaging abnormalities of the ventricles or corpus callosum. Of note, not all patients exhibit all features, and there is significant inter- and intrafamilial phenotypic variability ({1:Dworschak et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Dworschak et al. (2021)} reported 7 patients, ranging from 21 months to 12 years of age, from 4 unrelated families (families A, C, D, and E) with variable neurodevelopmental abnormalities. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the PLXNA1 gene. Two families were consanguineous: family D of Turkish descent, and family E of Pakistani descent. Six individuals showed global developmental delay from infancy, and 1 (the patient from family E) had normal development until about 2.5 years of age when he showed speech regression and autistic features. Several other patients also had autistic features or hyperactivity, including ADHD. Six patients had mildly impaired intellectual development; IQ ranged from 77 to 85 in 3 patients who underwent testing. One patient was nonverbal at age 4, but she also had unilateral hearing loss. The 2 sibs in family D had optic disc hypoplasia, strabismus, and mild ptosis. Nystagmus was observed in 1 other patient and ptosis in 1 other patient. Three patients had no ocular anomalies. One patient had seizures in early childhood. Brain imaging was abnormal in 4 individuals: 2 had defects of the corpus callosum, including agenesis of the corpus callosum and colpocephaly in 1 patient, 1 had dysmorphic ventricles, and another had subcortical white matter abnormalities. Three individuals, including 2 sibs, had nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, and 3 had skin pigmentary anomalies.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DWOPNED in the families reported by {1:Dworschak et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 7 children from 4 unrelated families (families A, C, D, and E) with DWOPNED, {1:Dworschak et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PLXNA1 gene ({601055.0001}-{601055.0006}). The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the PLXNA1 gene. There were 4 missense variants, 1 nonsense variant, and 1 frameshift; all affected the extracellular domain of the protein. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the variants segregated with the disorder in the families and were absent or rarely present in the gnomAD database. The authors hypothesized a loss-of-function effect.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: In developing zebrafish, {1:Dworschak et al. (2021)} found expression of plxna1 in the optic vesicle, neural retina, optic tectum, optic chiasm, hypothalamus, medulla oblongata, forebrain, and ventricle. Morpholino knockdown of plxna orthologs in zebrafish embryos resulted in neurodevelopmental defects including hydrocephalus in the midbrain and hindbrain ventricles, generalized hypopigmentation, reduced head size and eye diameter, and slightly increased mortality. Mutant animals showed hypoplasia of the telencephalon, mesencephalon, and cerebellum, as well as dilatation of the ventricles. There was also a reduction in migrated dorsal root ganglia in the spinal cord and impaired axon outgrowth of somites compared to controls. Some of these abnormalities could be rescued by expression of wildtype human PLXNA1.

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities, with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities, with or without seizures (DEDISB) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ARFGEF1 gene ({604141}) on chromosome 8q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay, impaired speech, and behavioral abnormalities, with or without seizures (DEDISB) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by variably impaired skill acquisition apparent from infancy or early childhood. Affected individuals have predominant language delay with mild fine and gross motor deficits, although they usually are ambulatory by around 3 years of age. Most patients have mildly to moderately impaired intellectual development and behavioral abnormalities, including aggression, hyperactivity, and autism spectrum disorder. About half of individuals develop various types of seizures that may be refractory in some. More variable features include dysmorphic facial features, mild ocular anomalies, and nonspecific findings on brain imaging ({2:Thomas et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Teoh et al. (2020)} reported a 3-year-old boy who developed infantile spasms at 6 months of age that evolved to generalized convulsions as well as myoclonic, tonic, and atonic seizures that were refractory to treatment. EEG showed hypsarrhythmia, generalized slow spike-and-wave activity, and multifocal epileptiform discharges superimposed on a high-amplitude disorganized background. He had global developmental delay with absent speech and axial hypotonia with motor difficulties.

{2:Thomas et al. (2021)} reported 13 individuals from 11 unrelated families with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who ranged from 3 months to 32 years of age, were ascertained through international collaborative efforts after exome sequencing identified heterozygous mutations in the ARFGEF1 gene. Six patients (1-6) had no family history and inherited the mutations de novo. Five patients from 3 families (patients 7-11) inherited the mutation from a mildly affected father. The inheritance pattern in 2 unrelated patients (12 and 13) could not be determined. All had variable developmental delay, and most had mild to moderate intellectual disability. Marked speech delay was particularly common. Almost all individuals demonstrated variable behavioral problems, including agitation, aggression, ADHD, hyperactivity, and autism spectrum disorder. About half had variable motor abnormalities, including cerebellar ataxia, limited fine motor skills, balance disorders, and action tremor; 2 had dysarthria. Six patients had variable types of seizures, including febrile, focal, generalized, myoclonic, atonic, and absence. Seizures were noted to be refractory in 2 patients. More variable features included hyperopia, astigmatism, strabismus, and dysmorphic facial features. These included high forehead, frontal bossing, long face, low-set ears, large ears, wide mouth, and bulbous nasal tip. Brain imaging was abnormal in several patients who were studied, although the features were not consistent: findings included thin corpus callosum, mild myelination delay, cerebellar abnormalities, and subcortical white matter signals.

{3:Xu et al. (2022)} identified 5 unrelated Chinese patients (4 boys and 1 girl) with developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, and epilepsy. All 5 had speech and motor delay (ranging from mild to severe), impaired intellectual development, and epilepsy. The authors did not observe dysmorphic facial features. Behavioral issues were seen in 2 patients, including 1 with autism spectrum disorder. One patient had microcephaly (age of onset not specified) and brain MRI was reportedly abnormal in another (no details were provided about MRI findings).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the ARFGEF1 gene that were identified in some patients with DEDISB by {2:Thomas et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. In other families with DEDISB, the transmission pattern was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 3-year-old boy with DEDISB, {1:Teoh et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous nonsense mutation in the ARFGEF1 gene (C1455X; {604141.0001}). The mutation was predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and haploinsufficiency. Functional studies of the mutation and studies of patient cells were not performed, although a haploinsufficient mutant mouse model showed some overlapping features (see ANIMAL MODEL).

In 6 unrelated patients (patients 1-6) with DEDISB, {2:Thomas et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the ARFGEF1 gene (see, e.g., {604141.0002}-{604141.0004}). Heterozygous mutations were also found in 2 unrelated individuals (patients 12 and 13) with a similar phenotype, although parental DNA was not available for segregation studies in these patients. In addition, 5 patients (7-11) from 3 unrelated families carried heterozygous ARFGEF1 mutations that were each inherited from a mildly affected father (e.g., {604141.0005}, {604141.0006}), consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance. Patients in the cohort were ascertained through international collaborative efforts after exome sequencing identified heterozygous mutations in the ARFGEF1 gene. There was 1 missense mutation, 1 splice site mutation, 6 nonsense mutations, and 3 frameshift mutations. Fibroblasts derived from the patient with the missense mutation showed decreased ARFGEF1 protein levels compared to controls, suggesting that the variant encodes an unstable protein that undergoes degradation. Otherwise, functional studies of the mutations and studies of patient cells were not performed. Since most of the mutations were predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and a loss of function, the authors postulated haploinsufficiency as the pathogenetic mechanism.

By trio exome sequencing in 5 unrelated Chinese patients with developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, and epilepsy, {3:Xu et al. (2022)} identified 5 heterozygous mutations in the ARFGEF1 gene, including 1 missense mutation (I1180R; {604141.0007}), 2 splice site mutations (c.2850+2T-A and c.917-1G-T), and 2 frameshift mutations (c.4951delG and c.2923_2924delCT). All 5 mutations were absent from the gnomAD (v2.1.1), dbSNP (build 153), and ESP6500 databases. Four of the mutations were de novo, with 1 splicing mutation inherited from the patient's mildly affected mother. Only one of the mutations (a frameshift) occurred in a girl, and she also had a de novo missense mutation in the MECP2 gene ({300005}). A likely pathogenic mutation in the MECP2 gene was also seen in a boy (proband 3) with a splicing mutation and his mildly affected mother, leading the authors to raise the possibility of digenic inheritance in females affected with the condition.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Teoh et al. (2020)} found that heterozygous Arfgef1 +/- mice, generated from a frameshift mutation in the Arfgef1 gene, exhibited signs of developmental delay as demonstrated by impaired motor and vocal behavior. Although heterozygous mutant mice did not demonstrate spontaneous seizures, they had a decreased threshold for induced seizures, consistent with increased susceptibility to epilepsy. Neuropathologic studies showed morphologic defects in the brain and neurons, such as dysregulated growth in the dentate gyrus lining of the hippocampus and abnormal dendritic filaments. There was a decrease in synaptic GABA-A receptor (see GABRA1, {137160}) density along the dendritic surface, which was associated with disrupted distribution of trafficking vesicles containing GABA-A receptors. There was an abnormal accumulation of GABA-A receptors in neuronal lysosomes, consistent with decreased expression at the neuronal surface. The findings indicated that haploinsufficiency for Arfgef1 alters endosomal composition and functioning in neurons and that this affects the synapse. {1:Teoh et al. (2020)} postulated that reduction of GABA-A receptor-associated inhibitory signaling may result in seizure susceptibility.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-104 (DEE104) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP6V0A1 ({192130}) on chromosome 17q21.

Biallelic mutation in the ATP6V0A1 gene can cause neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and brain atrophy (NEDEBA; {619971}).

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-104 (DEE104) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by developmental delay in the first few months of life and drug-resistant focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures (summary by {2:Bott et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Aoto et al. (2021)} described 2 unrelated Japanese patients (patients 1 and 2), aged 24 and 15 years, respectively. Patient 1 presented with developmental delay at 5 months of age and developed intractable seizures starting at 7 months of age. She had profoundly impaired intellectual development and microcephaly at 6 years of age. Patient 2 presented with developmental delay at 5 months of age and developed infantile spasms and generalized tonic seizures starting at 6 months of age. At 14 years of age, he had profoundly impaired intellectual development, autism, hyperactivity, and self-injurious behaviors.

{2:Bott et al. (2021)} reported 12 unrelated patients, with an average age at symptom onset of 5.8 +/- 4.2 months. The patients had developmental encephalopathy, treatment-refractory seizures, and severely impaired intellectual development after a period of apparently normal development with delay or loss of milestones. Six patients had ataxia and 2 had myoclonus. Craniofacial features included microcephaly in 5 patients, prognathism in 2 patients, micrognathia in 2 patients, bitemporal narrowing in 1 patient, and hypertelorism in 1 patient. Other features included scoliosis in 2 patients, ameliogenesis imperfecta in 1 patient, and optic atrophy in 1 patient. Brain MRI showed cerebellar and cerebral atrophy in 1 patient, a simplified gyral pattern in 1 patient, and white matter gliosis in 1 patient. A brain biopsy from a stillborn infant showed neuroaxonal dystrophy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-104 in the families reported by {1:Aoto et al. (2021)} and {2:Bott et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. Most of the mutations were confirmed to be de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
By trio whole-exome sequencing in 2 unrelated patients with DEE104, {1:Aoto et al. (2021)} identified heterozygosity for the same mutation in the ATP6V0A1 gene (R741Q; {192130.0001}). The mutation, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. HEK293FT cells transfected with ATP6V0A1 containing the R741Q mutation had impaired lysosomal acidification. Homozygous mutant mice harboring the R741Q mutation in the Atp6v0a1 gene had embryonic lethality.

In 12 patients from 4 families with DEE104, {2:Bott et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the ATP6V0A1 gene ({192130.0006}-{192130.0009}). The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and brain atrophy

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and brain atrophy (NEDEBA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in ATP6V0A1 gene ({192130}) on chromosome 17q21.

Heterozygous mutation in the ATP6V0A1 gene can cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-104 (DEE104; {619970}).

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and brain atrophy (NEDEBA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by early-onset progressive myoclonus epilepsy with ataxia (summary by {2:Bott et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Aoto et al. (2021)} reported 2 unrelated patients (patients 3 and 4), aged 7 and 8 years. Patient 3 had prenatal findings of polyhydramnios starting at 26 weeks of gestation. Soon after birth, poor feeding and obstructive apnea were noted. He developed seizures at 27 days of life with a burst suppression pattern on EEG. He required a tracheostomy and gastrostomy in infancy. At 6 years 11 months of age, he had profoundly impaired intellectual development, spastic quadriplegia, and joint contractures. Brain MRI showed enlarged lateral ventricles and hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis at 10 days of life and progressively severe brain atrophy at 6 months and 3 years of life. Patient 4 presented with seizures at 5 weeks of age. He had significant global developmental delay including motor, language, and learning delays. He walked independently and spoke 10 words at 26 months of age. He had ADHD in childhood. Brain MRI at 3 years of age showed mild cerebellar atrophy, and brain MRI at 6 years of age showed severe atrophy of the brainstem and cerebellum.

{2:Bott et al. (2021)} reported 4 patients from 1 Italian family (family I), previously reported by {3:Coppola et al. (2005)}, and 1 unrelated Italian patient. The average age of onset of initial symptoms (seizures) was 11.8 +/- 7.5 years. All 5 patients had myoclonus, ataxia, and impaired intellectual development. Brain MRI in all patients showed cerebellar atrophy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and brain atrophy in the families reported by {1:Aoto et al. (2021)} and {2:bott et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
{1:Aoto et al. (2021)} identified compound heterozygosity for 2 mutations in the ATP6V0A1 gene ({192130.0002}-{192130.0004}) in 2 unrelated patients (patients 3 and 4) with neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and brain atrophy. Each patient had one missense mutation and one likely loss-of-function allele. The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. HEK293FT cells transfected with ATP6V0A containing each of the 2 identified missense mutations, A512P or N534D, had impaired lysosomal acidification.

{2:Bott et al. (2021)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the ATP6V0A1 gene ({192130.0010}-{192130.0011}) in 4 Italian patients from 1 family (family I) and an unrelated Italian patient with NEDEBA. The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Functional studies were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with severe motor impairment, absent language, cerebral hypomyelination, and brain atrophy

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with severe motor impairment, absent language, cerebral hypomyelination, and brain atrophy (NEDMLHB) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TAF8 gene ({609514}) on chromosome 6p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with severe motor impairment, absent language, cerebral hypomyelination, and brain atrophy (NEDMLHB) is characterized by the onset of these features soon after birth or in early infancy. Affected individuals make almost no developmental progress, are unable to sit or walk, do not acquire speech, have poor visual fixation, and show poor overall growth associated with feeding problems. Some may have a progressive disease course, suggesting neurodegeneration. Additional more variable features include seizures, spasticity, and joint contractures. Brain imaging shows hypomyelination, thin corpus callosum, and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy ({2:Wong et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:El-Saafin et al. (2018)} reported a 4.5-year-old girl, born of unrelated Hispanic parents, with poor overall growth, small head circumference (-2 SD), and severe global developmental delay. She was unable to sit or speak and developed progressive spasticity and equinovarus foot deformities. She did not have seizures. Other features included brachycephaly, a sloping forehead, tented mouth, unilateral ptosis, and long philtrum. Brain imaging showed reduced myelination, small cerebellar vermis, and partial absence of the corpus callosum.

{2:Wong et al. (2022)} reported 7 patients from 4 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The families were of various ethnic origins, including Caucasian, Mexican, Moroccan, and Iranian, and 3 of the families were consanguineous. The patients, who ranged from 2.5 to 19 years of age, had profound global developmental delay with almost no skill acquisition. They had hypotonia with inability to walk or speak and severe intellectual disability; a few were able to roll over. The patients had feeding difficulties with dysphagia and gastroesophageal reflux resulting in poor overall growth, short stature, and microcephaly. Most required tube-feeding. Other features included visual impairment with poor fixation, spasticity, and inability to grasp objects with the hands, indicating absence of fine motor skills. Six patients had seizures. Brain imaging showed hypomyelination, thin corpus callosum, and enlarged ventricles. Two sisters from family 1 were documented as having progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy in 1 patient showed a markedly reduced tNAA peak compared to controls, a sign of reduced vital neuronal tissue.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMLHB in the families reported by {2:Wong et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 4.5-year-old girl, born of unrelated Hispanic parents, with NEDMLHB, {1:El-Saafin et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the TAF8 gene (c.781-1G-A; {609514.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing, was inherited from each unaffected parent who was heterozygous for the mutation. The variant was found in the heterozygous state in 10 individuals in the gnomAD database, including 5 of Hispanic origin (10 of 277,264 alleles). Analysis of patient cells showed that the variant caused a splicing defect, a frameshift, and premature termination, and that the mutant mRNA was subject to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Mutant TAF8 mRNA was only mildly reduced by about 30% compared to controls. The predicted truncated protein would lack the C-terminal nuclear localization signal, but Western blot analysis did not detect a mutant protein, suggesting that it is unstable and prone to degradation, most likely by the proteasome. These findings suggested a loss-of-function effect. {1:El-Saafin et al. (2018)} noted that knockdown of the Taf8 gene in mice causes blastocyst death in early development at around embryonic day 4 due to apoptosis of the inner cell mass. In vitro functional cellular expression studies confirmed that deletion of Taf8 in mouse embryonic stem cells resulted in increased cell death that was associated with transcriptional defects. Patient fibroblasts showed evidence of impaired assembly of the TFIID complex. However, patient fibroblasts demonstrated normal recruitment of RNA polymerase II to active promoters and overall transcription rates that were similar to those of controls. {1:El-Saafin et al. (2018)} speculated that the mutation did not cause a complete loss of function since the patient survived embryonic development.

In 5 patients (patients 3-7) from 3 unrelated consanguineous families with NEDMLHB, {2:Wong et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous c.781-1G-A transition in the TAF8 gene. The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families. Functional studies of this variant were not performed. In addition, 2 German sisters (patients 1 and 2) with the disorder were found to be compound heterozygous for 2 splice site mutations in the TAF8 gene ({609514.0002} and {609514.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed aberrant transcripts related to 1 of the mutations, a 70% reduction of TAF8 mRNA transcripts, and a significant reduction in TAF8 protein compared to controls. TAF8 immunoreactivity was decreased in patient fibroblasts, particularly in the nucleus.

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 105 with hypopituitarism

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-105 with hypopituitarism (DEE105) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the HID1 gene ({605752}) on chromosome 17q25.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-105 with hypopituitarism (DEE105) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by the onset of seizures and pituitary insufficiency in the first weeks or months of life. Affected individuals have profoundly impaired development with almost no acquisition of skills. They are hypotonic, unable to sit or speak, and have poor or absent visual fixation. Endocrine workup shows central pituitary dysfunction with low hormone levels. Brain imaging shows cerebral atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and small pituitary gland ({1:Schanzer et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Schanzer et al. (2021)} reported 6 patients from 5 unrelated families with epileptic encephalopathy associated with combined pituitary hormone deficiency. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts after exome sequencing identified biallelic variants in the HID1 gene. The families were from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Spain, and Pakistan; 4 were consanguineous. The patients, who ranged from 3 months to 4 years of age, presented with severe hypotonia and variable types of seizures soon after birth or in the first months of life. Two sibs from family 1 died within the first years of life due to respiratory complications or intractable seizures. Patient 4 (family 3) died at the age of 2 years ({2:Weber, 2022}). All patients showed global developmental delay and achieved almost no developmental progress: none were able to speak, roll over, or sit independently, and they had poor visual fixation. Seizure types included generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, complex partial, tonic, and autonomic. The seizures were difficult to treat in most patients. EEG showed generalized slowing and focal or multifocal sharp slow waves; the 2 sibs from family 1 showed hypsarrhythmia. Additional features observed in some patients included respiratory insufficiency, feeding difficulties requiring tube feeding, and poor overall growth. All patients developed clinical symptoms related to hypopituitarism and hormone deficiencies within the first months of life, including central hypothyroidism, low serum cortisol, low IGF1 ({147440}), and low antidiuretic hormones. Several patients had hypoglycemia, and 3 had hyperinsulinemia. Brain imaging showed cerebral atrophy, thin or absent corpus callosum, and small pituitary gland. Most patients had variable dysmorphic features, including hypertelorism, epicanthus, synophrys, long eyelashes, long philtrum, depressed nasal bridge, and short nose, and high-arched or cleft palate. Male patients had variable genital anomalies, including cryptorchidism, micropenis, hypospadias, and phimosis.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{1:Schanzer et al. (2021)} reported a 24-year-old man (P3), born of consanguineous Tunisian parents (family 2), who was diagnosed with panhypopituitarism at 3 months of age. He had poor overall growth with failure to thrive, dysmorphic features, global developmental delay with absent speech and language, and spasticity with brisk reflexes. He learned to walk with aids at the age of 11 years and was able to communicate with pictograms. He did not have seizures. Brain imaging showed a small posterior pituitary lobe. This patient carried compound heterozygous mutations in the HID1 gene (Q130X and L533P). Functional studies of these variants were not performed.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE105 in the families reported by {1:Schanzer et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 patients from 5 unrelated families with DEE105, {1:Schanzer et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the HID1 gene (see, e.g., {605752.0001}-{605752.0003}). The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts after exome sequencing identified biallelic HID1 mutations. Four patients carried homozygous missense mutations, 1 carried a homozygous frameshift mutation, and another was compound heterozygous for a splice site and frameshift. The mutations occurred throughout the gene and segregated with the disorder in the families. Fibroblasts derived from 2 unrelated patients showed no differences with regard to degree of HID1 expression or expression pattern compared to controls or to heterozygous mutation carriers. However, postmortem neuropathologic examination of 1 patient showed decreased expression of HID1 in the cerebellum and striatum, as well as liver, compared to controls. Patient fibroblasts showed decreased extracellular acidification when stimulated by KCl compared to controls, indicating impaired function of the trans-Golgi network. This defective extracellular acidification was also observed in cultured PC12 HID1-knockout cells.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with speech delay and variable ocular anomalies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with speech delay and variable ocular anomalies (NEDSOA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the THUMPD1 gene ({616662}) on chromosome 16p12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with speech delay and variable ocular anomalies (NEDSOA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor speech acquisition apparent from infancy. Most affected individuals have dysmorphic facial features with notable ocular anomalies, including exotropia, strabismus, hypo- or hypertropia, and refraction problems. Additional features may include febrile seizures, sensorineural hearing loss, and behavioral abnormalities. Brain imaging is usually normal, but abnormalities of the corpus callosum have been reported ({1:Broly et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Maddirevula et al. (2019)} reported a 23-year-old man (15DG1395), born of consanguineous parents, with intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, hypertension, and diabetes. He also had increased muscle tone with cogwheeling and slow gait initiation. Dysmorphic features included large skull, sparse hair, upslanting palpebral fissures, prognathism, tapering fingers, and thick skin. Ophthalmologic examination showed exotropic strabismus, esotropia, hypertropia, and restricted eye movements. The patient had a 16-year-old brother (reported by {1:Broly et al., 2022}) with intellectual disability, speech delay, and psychotic changes; he did not have dysmorphic features.

{1:Broly et al. (2022)} reported 13 patients from 8 unrelated families, including the family reported by {2:Maddirevula et al. (2019)}, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who ranged from 2 to 23 years of age, were ascertained through collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher Program, after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the THUMPD1 gene. Four of the families were consanguineous. All patients had global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, speech delay or absent speech, and mildly delayed walking (median of 1.5 years of age). Several had poor overall growth, including 3 patients with short stature and 2 with microcephaly (down to -3.74 SD). Variable ophthalmologic abnormalities were identified in most patients: these included eye position defects, strabismus, hypermetropia, esotropia, myopia, nystagmus, zonular cataract, pale optic disc, and astigmatism. Mild to severe sensorineural hearing loss was detected in 5 patients. Six had early-onset febrile seizures that tended to resolve. Many patients had behavioral problems, including hyperactivity, aggressive behavior, and angry outbursts. Brain imaging, performed in 7 patients, was normal in 4 and showed corpus callosum abnormalities in the 3 others, including 1 patient with agenesis of the corpus callosum. Many patients had dysmorphic facial features, including up- or downslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthus, ptosis, hypo- or hypertelorism, wide sparse eyebrows, high nasal root, hypoplastic columella, broad and flat philtrum, thin upper lip, prognathism, wide mouth, low-set ears, sparse hair, scaphocephaly, frontal bossing, and discolored dentition. Some patients had mild skeletal defects.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSOA in the families reported by {1:Broly et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 23-year-old man (15DG1395), born of consanguineous parents, with NEDSOA, {2:Maddirevula et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the THUMPD1 gene (Q236X; {616662.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing of a cohort of over 2,500 patients with various mendelian phenotypes, was present in the heterozygous state at a low frequency (2 x 10(-5)) in gnomAD. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 13 patients from 8 unrelated families, including 2 sibs from the family reported by {2:Maddirevula et al. (2019)}, {1:Broly et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the THUMPD1 gene (see, e.g., {616662.0001}-{616662.0005}). The mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing and demonstrated to segregate with the disorder in the 6 families from whom parental DNA was available. All were absent from or present at a low frequency in the gnomAD database. Knockdown of the THUMPD1 gene in HEK293T and HeLa cells led to a complete loss of N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) modifications of small RNAs and tRNA(Ser), similar to that observed in cells derived from 1 patient. {1:Broly et al. (2022)} hypothesized that lack of postranscriptional tRNA acetylation due to loss of THUMPD1 function disrupts key cellular processes during neurodevelopment.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with intention tremor, pyramidal signs, dyspraxia, and ocular anomalies

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with intention tremor, pyramidal signs, dyspraxia, and ocular anomalies (NEDITPO) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SMG9 gene ({613176}) on chromosome 19q13.

Homozygous mutation in the SMG9 gene can also cause heart and brain malformation syndrome (HBMS; {616920}), a more severe neurodevelopmental disorder.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with intention tremor, pyramidal signs, dyspraxia, and ocular anomalies (NEDITPO) is an autosomal recessive multiple congenital anomaly syndrome characterized by mild to moderate intellectual disability, dysmorphic facial features, intention tremor, dyspraxia, and vertical strabismus ({1:Rahikkala et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Rahikkala et al. (2022)} reported 5 males, ranging in age from 24 to 56 years, from 3 unrelated Finnish families with intention tremor, pyramidal signs, dyspraxia, and ocular manifestations. Patients had mildly or moderately impaired intellectual development with markedly delayed language development; motor development was mildly delayed. Oromotor dyspraxia was seen in all patients. Dysmorphic facial features included prominent forehead, broad nasal bridge, and high-arched palate. Two patients had hypotonia during childhood. Four patients had strabismus, with vertical strabismus in 3. One patient had short stature; growth parameters were otherwise normal. One patient had a complex congenital heart defect consisting of transposition of the great arteries, ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, and hypoplastic right atrium. All patients had hypertonia and clonic or very brisk reflexes in their lower limbs, with intention tremor and slow diadochokinesis. Four patients were described as ataxic in childhood, and 3 patients had planovalgus. Three patients had abnormalities on EEG, but none were diagnosed with epilepsy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of neurodevelopmental disorder with intention tremor, pyramidal signs, dyspraxia, and ocular anomalies in the families reported by {1:Rahikkala et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 men from 3 unrelated Finnish families with neurodevelopmental disorder with intention tremor, pyramidal signs, dyspraxia, and ocular anomalies, {1:Rahikkala et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SMG9 gene (V184A; {613176.0003}). The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The authors noted the milder phenotype in patients with this homozygous missense mutation compared to patients with loss-of-function mutations in SMG9 who have heart and brain malformation syndrome ({616920}). RNA sequencing showed that the V184A mutation did not affect splicing or the expression level of SMG9 gene products, and allele-specific expression analysis did not find evidence of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Differential gene expression analysis identified an overall pattern of increased gene expression in several genes among affected patients. The authors speculated that SMG9 may have an inhibitory effect on gene expression, with this variant causing transcriptional upregulation. The V184A variant had an overall minor allele frequency of 0.0001627 in the gnomAD database, but the allele frequency was 34 times higher in Finnish than in non-Finnish Europeans. Haplotype analysis in the 3 Finnish families showed that the mutation lies on a shared ancestral haplotype with a median length of 1.7 Mb, suggesting that this is a Finnish founder variant.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with spasticity, seizures, and brain abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with spasticity, seizures, and brain abnormalities (NEDSSBA) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NSRP1 gene ({616173}) on chromosome 17q11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with spasticity, seizures, and brain abnormalities (NEDSSBA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent in infancy, axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity, and early-onset seizures of various types and severity. Affected individuals have delayed walking or are unable to walk and show impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech. Brain imaging may show developmental defects of the operculum, cerebellum, and corpus callosum. Death in early childhood may occur ({1:Calame et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Calame et al. (2021)} reported 6 patients from 3 unrelated families with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who ranged from 2 to 13 years of age, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified homozygous mutations in the NSRP1 gene. Two families, of Egyptian (family 1) and Iranian (family 2) origin, were known to be consanguineous; family 3, of Pakistani origin, did not report consanguinity, but genetic analysis indicated distant relations between the parents. All patients had global developmental delay with impaired motor and intellectual development and poor or absent speech. Other features included axial hypotonia and peripheral spasticity, usually with hyperreflexia. More severely affected patients were unable to walk, whereas others did achieve walking. Three patients had flexion contractures or foot deformities, and 3 had dysphagia. The 3 patients from families 1 and 2 had onset of intractable seizures between 5 and 6 months of age. Seizure types included tonic, clonic, myoclonic, and generalized tonic-clonic. The 3 other patients from family 3 had early onset of milder seizures that ranged from apneic/cyanotic episodes to focal or generalized tonic-clonic seizures. EEG was abnormal in all patients, showing epileptiform discharges in 5 and diffuse background slowing in the sixth patient. Brain imaging, performed in 4 patients, showed variable abnormalities, including simplified gyral pattern, underopercularization, hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, thin brainstem, and delayed myelination. Four patients were noted to have variable and nonspecific facial features, including microcephaly (in 3 patients), long face, high forehead, long or short philtrum, prominent chin, large, simple, and low-set ears, hypertelorism, sparse eyebrows, downslanting palpebral fissures, depressed nasal bridge, upturned nose, tented mouth, and high-arched palate. Two patients died at 2 and 4 years of age; one of these patients (family 1) had a deceased sib who was similarly affected, but DNA was not available for study.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSSBA in the families reported by {1:Calame et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 patients from 3 unrelated consanguineous families with NEDSSBA, {1:Calame et al. (2021)} identified homozygous frameshift or nonsense mutations in the NSRP1 gene ({616173.0001}-{616173.0003}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. The 2 frameshift mutations occurred in the last exon and would likely escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and disrupt the nuclear localization signal. The nonsense mutation was predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and result in a loss of function. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but they were predicted to be hypomorphic since the children survived after birth, although 2 died in early childhood.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with muscle tone abnormalities and distal skeletal defects

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with muscle tone abnormalities and distal skeletal defects (IDDMDS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the LGI3 gene ({608302}) on chromosome 8p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with muscle tone abnormalities and distal skeletal defects (IDDMDS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay apparent in infancy manifest as speech delay and late walking by a few years. Affected individuals have hypertonia or, more rarely, hypotonia; a notable common feature is facial myokymia with corresponding EMG findings. Additional features include distal skeletal defects such as joint contractures, hypo- or areflexia, and hernia ({2:Marafi et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Marafi et al. (2022)} reported 16 patients from 8 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who ranged from 3 to 22 years of age, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the LGI3 gene. The families had various origins, including Pakistan, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Guinea, Iraq, and Japan; 7 were consanguineous. Family 4 had previously been reported as family 10 by {1:Froukh (2017)}. The patients had global developmental delay with mild to moderately impaired intellectual development, learning disabilities, speech delay, and delayed walking by a few years. A few had behavioral abnormalities, such as autism spectrum disorder or ADHD, and several attended special schools. Most patients had variable distal skeletal anomalies, including hip dysplasia, contractures of the hips, knees, and ankles, foot deformities, tapered fingers, contractures of the fingers, and fisted hands. Muscle tone was abnormal in most patients, but varied from hypotonia to hypertonia with stiffness; hypo- or areflexia was commonly present. Facial myokymia with near continuous movement was a notable clinical feature in 7 patients, 6 of whom had a small mouth with restricted opening. The facial myokymia was observed as early as 3 months of age. Myokymic discharges, fasciculations, and fibrillations were observed in 5 of 8 patients who underwent EMG studies, suggesting motor nerve hyperexcitability. However, muscle biopsy in 2 patients did not show significant abnormalities, and nerve conduction studies in 6 of 7 patients were normal. Less common features included diaphragmatic or umbilical hernia, gait abnormalities, muscle atrophy of the lower limbs, and tongue fasciculations. Two patients had seizures. All 4 patients in family 5 had poor overall growth. Brain imaging was normal in all except 2 patients, one who had suspected mild frontal hypoplasia and the other who had a small pituitary hypophysis associated with growth hormone deficiency ({262400}). {2:Marafi et al. (2022)} classified this disorder as a peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndrome (PNHS).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IDDMDS in the families reported by {2:Marafi et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 16 patients from 8 families with IDDMDS, {2:Marafi et al. (2022)} identified biallelic mutations in the LGI3 gene (see, e.g., {608302.0001}-{608302.0005}). The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program, and the mutations were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The mutations segregated with the disorder in the families and were absent from or present at a low frequency in the heterozygous state in gnomAD. There were 3 frameshift variants, 2 splice site, 1 nonsense, 1 intragenic deletion, and 2 missense variants; the mutations occurred throughout the gene. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells showed that the mutant missense proteins (L141H and D331N, {608302.0003}) accumulated in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), induced ER stress, and were secreted at severely reduced levels, suggesting that they are functionally null alleles. Functional studies of the other variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Marafi et al. (2022)} observed that Lgi3-null mice are fertile, have a normal lifespan, and do not show obvious behavioral abnormalities. However, loss of Lgi3 resulted in reduced expression and mislocalization of potassium channel complexes that infringe on the paranodal domain. This mislocalization of potassium channel complexes was exacerbated following nerve injury. The authors speculated that these alterations may affect electrophysiologic characteristics and contribute to axonal hyperexcitability.

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay, hypotonia, and impaired language

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay, hypotonia, and impaired language (DEDHIL) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the FBXW7 gene ({606278}) on chromosome 4q31.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay, hypotonia, and impaired language (DEDHIL) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by variably impaired intellectual development usually with hypotonia, mild motor delay, and language difficulties. Affected individuals may also have nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, gastrointestinal problems, and abnormalities on brain imaging ({1:Stephenson et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Stephenson et al. (2022)} reported 35 patients from 32 unrelated families with variable neurodevelopmental abnormalities who were ascertained through global gene matchmaking databases after exome or genome sequencing identified heterozygous mutations in the FBXW7 gene. The phenotype was subsequently delineated. Most of the patients were children between 22 months and 16 years of age, although the affected father in 1 family (patient 6) was 44 years old. All but 1 patient (patient 13) had global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development ranging from borderline normal to severe. Many individuals had delayed speech and a few were nonverbal. Although some patients had early feeding difficulties, growth parameters were essentially normal, with the exception of macrocephaly (in 28.6%) and microcephaly (in 5.7%). Eight (22.9%) patients had seizures of various types. Many patients had dysmorphic facial features, although there was no recognizable gestalt. Features included deep-set eyes with periorbital fullness, midface retraction, tall forehead, high or cleft palate, hypertelorism, depressed nasal bridge, thin upper lip, and strabismus. Additional less common features included cardiac abnormalities, cryptorchidism, and ocular refraction anomalies. Brain imaging showed variable abnormalities in 13 (76.5%) of 17 patients imaged: findings included abnormal or thin corpus callosum, abnormal cerebellum, and delayed myelination. A thick brainstem and polymicrogyria were observed in 2 patients each.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: Most of the heterozygous mutations in the FBXW7 gene that were identified by {1:Stephenson et al. (2022)} in patients with DEDHIL occurred de novo. However, the transmission pattern in 2 families was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 35 individuals from 32 families with DEDHIL, {1:Stephenson et al. (2022)} identified heterozygous mutations in the FBXW7 gene (see, e.g., {606278.0001}-{606278.0005}). The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts after the mutations were identified through genome or exome sequencing. There were nonsense, frameshift, splice site, and missense variants throughout the gene, although many affected the WD40 domain. Two individuals had deletions that encompassed the FBXW7 gene. The majority of the mutations occurred de novo; 2 were inherited from a mildly affected parent. None were present in the gnomAD database. Studies of patient cells were not performed. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293T cells transfected with some of the missense variants showed that they impaired the ability of FBXW7 to ubiquitinate and degrade substrates CCNE1 ({123837}) and CCNE2 ({603775}) to variable degrees. Mutations in the WD40 domain tended to have a more detrimental impact on this function compared to mutations outside of the WD40 domain, although there was variability and some of the differences did not reach statistical significance. The authors proposed haploinsufficiency as the most likely pathogenic mechanism, and suggested that FBXW7 mutations may alter the binding affinity to substrates. There were no genotype/phenotype correlations. Knockdown of the FBXW7 ortholog 'archipelago' (ago) in Drosophila was embryonic lethal. Neuronal-specific knockdown of ago resulted in deficits in habituation learning, as demonstrated by the light-off reflex habituation assay. {1:Stephenson et al. (2022)} concluded that FBXW7 plays a role in neurodevelopment.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with autism and dysmorphic facies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with autism and dysmorphic facies (IDDADF) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PDZD8 ({614235}) on chromosome 10q25.

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with autism and dysmorphic facies (IDDADF) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by moderate to severely impaired cognitive development associated with behavioral abnormalities, including autism spectrum disorder. Affected individuals have variable dysmorphic facial features ({1:Al-Amri et al., 2022})

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Al-Amri et al. (2022)} reported 3 sibs, born of consanguineous Omani parents (family A), and another unrelated boy, born of consanguineous parents from the United Arab Emirates, with cognitive impairment. The patients in family A ranged from 17 to 30 years, whereas the boy in family B was 4 years of age. All had global developmental delay with moderate to severe intellectual disability and mild autistic features. One had ADHD and another had OCD. Of note, autistic features were also observed in the father and a brother of the patients in family A, each of whom was a heterozygous carrier for the pathogenic PDZD8 mutation. All patients in family A had moderate to severe intellectual disability, autistic features, and dysmorphic facial features, such as hypertelorism, malar flattening, open mouth, and high-arched palate. In addition, all patients and both parents in family A had mild myopathy and reduced facial expression, which may be have been related to a concurrent homozygous R328W mutation in the ANKRD2 gene ({610734}) that segregated in this family. The patient in family B presented with delayed speech, moderate intellectual disability, autistic features with stereotypies and poor eye contact, ADHD, and dysmorphic features with low-set ears with simple helix and bilateral ptosis. Less common and variable features included seizures (2 patients), congenital heart defects, marfanoid habitus, scoliosis, cleft palate, myopia, and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IDDADF in the families reported by {1:Al-Amri et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous Middle Eastern families with IDDADF, {1:Al-Amri et al. (2022)} identified homozygous frameshift ({614235.0001}) and nonsense ({614235.0002}) mutations in the PDZD8 gene. The mutations, which were found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. Neither was present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. Based on animal studies (see ANIMAL MODEL), the authors postulated that the mutations resulted in neuronal synaptic defects that would lead to neurodevelopmental abnormalities.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: In Drosophila, {1:Al-Amri et al. (2022)} found expression of the PDZD8 ortholog (CG10632) in the head, eye, brain, and thoracico-abdominal ganglion. RNAi-mediated knockdown of CG10362 resulted in long-term memory deficits in the courtship conditioning assay. Pdzd8-null mice showed poor overall growth and about a 7% decrease in total brain volume as assessed by structural brain MRI. However, the relative volume of certain regions was increased (cerebellum, olfactory bulb, hippocampus, and retrosplenial cortex) or decreased (thalamus, pallidum, superior colliculus, and corpus callosum). These findings were suggestive of structural brain alterations. Mutant mice demonstrated increased spontaneous repetitive stereotypic motor movements and decreased anxiety-like behavior compared to controls. Further behavioral assays suggested impaired hippocampal-dependent spatial memory that was associated with diminished long-term potentiation (LTP) in electrophysiologic studies performed on hippocampal slices from the mutant mice. These findings suggested that loss of Pdzd8 results in reduced synaptic plasticity; the authors postulated that a defect in calcium mobilization and uptake involving the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria may play a role in disrupting the synapse.
