text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures (NEDMIMS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CHKA gene ({118491}) on chromosome 11q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures (NEDMIMS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe global developmental delay apparent from infancy, impaired intellectual development, progressive microcephaly, and early-onset seizures that may be refractory to treatment. Affected individuals have poor overall growth and may have various movement abnormalities, including hypo- and hypertonia. Behavioral problems may also be observed ({1:Klockner et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Klockner et al. (2022)} reported 6 children from 5 unrelated families of various ethnic origins with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients, who ranged from 2 to 11.5 years of age, were ascertained through international collaborative efforts after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the CHKA gene. Four families were consanguineous, from Iran, India, Egypt, and Bangladesh; the last family was nonconsanguineous and of German descent. The patients presented in the first months of life with severe global developmental delay, failure to thrive with poor overall growth, and progressive microcephaly (down to -7 SD). Various types of seizures occurred before 3 years of age and were often refractory to treatment. The individuals had severe cognitive impairment with absent speech, as well as motor abnormalities, including hypertonia, hypotonia, hyperreflexia, and inability to walk in most patients. Nystagmus was present. Three had abnormal movements, including dyskinesia, rigidity, and choreoathetosis. There was phenotypic variability: a 2-year-old boy (family 3) had significant ocular abnormalities, including cortical visual impairment and poor visual acuity associated with retinal pigmentary changes and retinal dysfunction. A pair of affected dizygotic twins in family 1 both had the disorder, but 1 sib had severe motor weakness and was unable to walk, whereas the other could walk with assistance around 3 years of age. Many had behavioral abnormalities, including aggression, self-mutilating actions, and sleep disturbances. Brain imaging was normal in 3, showed transient hypomyelination in another, and demonstrated hypomyelination and thin corpus callosum in another patient. More variable features included scoliosis and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features in some patients. The proband in family 2 had a significant family history of 3 similarly affected sibs with seizures and lack of speech who died between 18 months and 17 years; there was also a spontaneous abortion in this family.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMIMS in the families reported by {1:Klockner et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 patients from 5 unrelated families with NEDMIMS, {1:Klockner et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the CHKA gene ({118491.0001}-{118491.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families from whom parental DNA was available. There were 3 missense variants, 1 frameshift, and 1 mutation that disrupted the initiation codon. Studies of patient cells were not performed, but expression of the missense variants in yeast showed that they caused decreased CHKA enzymatic activity (range 15 to 50% of normal values), consistent with a loss-of-function effect. The authors concluded that the disorder resulted from impairment of the Kennedy biochemical pathway of phospholipid synthesis.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH SEIZURES, MICROCEPHALY, AND BRAIN ABNORMALITIES; NEDSMBA

Hypsarrhythmia seen on EEG (in some patients)
Global developmental delay/intellectual disability and epilepsy seen in all patients MOLECULAR BASIS Caused by mutation in PFIA-binding protein 1 gene (PPFIBP1,)

Head: Microcephaly, primary and/or progressive
Neurologic - CNS: Seizures (onset in infancy, refractory in some patients)
Hypsarrhythmia seen on EEG (in some patients)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, microcephaly, and brain abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, microcephaly, and brain abnormalities (NEDSMBA) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PPFIBP1 gene (PPFIBP1; {603141}) on chromosome 12p11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, microcephaly, and brain abnormalities (NEDSMBA) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a core phenotype of moderate to profound developmental delay, progressive microcephaly, epilepsy, and periventricular calcifications (summary by {1:Rosenhahn et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Shaheen et al. (2019)} reported 3 sibs who were born with microcephaly, congenital heart disease, kidney abnormalities, and intractable seizures. The proband had an atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, and a single kidney. Chromosome breakage analysis showed breaks in 90% of cells. A younger sib had negative breakage studies. Brain imaging showed metopic synostosis, demyelination, and periventricular leukomalacia. One sib died at 6 days of age.

{1:Rosenhahn et al. (2022)} reported 16 individuals from 12 unrelated families. The patients ranged in age from 5 months to 19 years. Developmental features included global developmental delay/intellectual disability in 16 patients, absent speech in 15, motor delay in 15, failure to thrive in 8, and feeding difficulties in 7. Sixteen patients had seizures, which were focal in 11, epileptic spasms in 7, generalized in 7, and myoclonic in 6. Ten patients had hypertonia and 6 had spastic tetraplegia. Microcephaly was described in 15 patients, and 9 patients were small for gestational age. Congenital heart defects were observed in 7 patients. Abnormal brain findings included ventriculomegaly in 11 patients, white matter abnormalities in 11 including paucity of white matter in 5, bilateral intracranial calcifications in 9, thin corpus callosum in 7, cortex abnormalities in 7, and gyral abnormalities in 4.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSMBA in the family reported by {2:Shaheen et al. (2019)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 sibs, born to consanguineous parents, with neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, microcephaly, and brain abnormalities, {2:Shaheen et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the PPFIBP1 gene ({603141.0001}). The patients were identified from a cohort of 150 patients from 104 families with congenital microcephaly.

In 16 patients from 12 unrelated families with NEDSMBA, {1:Rosenhahn et al. (2022)} identified 8 homozygous mutations in the PPFIBP1 gene, including 5 nonsense and 3 frameshift mutations (see, e.g., {603141.0001}-{603141.0006}). The parents in 10 families were confirmed to carry the mutation in heterozygous state. A fetus with severe intrauterine growth retardation, microcephaly, and intracranial calcifications in an additional family (family 13) had a homozygous missense mutation (G726V) in the PPFIBP1 gene; the pregnancy was terminated at about 22 weeks' gestation. The G726V mutation was present in heterozygous state in the parents.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Rosenhahn et al. (2022)} generated a C. elegans PPFIBP1/hlb-1 knockout model. The mutant worm had abnormalities in spontaneous and light-induced behaviors and demonstrated a dose-dependent resistance to the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor aldicarb. This resistance to aldicarb provided evidence for presynaptic defects in the mutant worms.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH MICROCEPHALY, SHORT STATURE, AND SPEECH DELAY; NEDMISS
clinicalSynopsis: Two unrelated consanguineous Pakistani families have been reported (last curated September 2022)
Caused by mutation in the trafficking protein particle complex, subunit 10 gene (TRAPPC10,)

Head: Microcephaly (down to -7.46 SD)
Miscellaneous: Two unrelated consanguineous Pakistani families have been reported (last curated September 2022)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the trafficking protein particle complex, subunit 10 gene (TRAPPC10,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, short stature, and speech delay

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, short stature, and speech delay (NEDMISS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TRAPPC10 gene ({602103}) on chromosome 21q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, short stature, and speech delay (NEDMISS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay with severely impaired intellectual development usually accompanied by behavioral abnormalities. Other features may include hypotonia, abnormal gait, mild dysmorphism, and seizures ({1:Rawlins et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Santos-Cortez et al. (2018)} reported 2 brothers, 20 and 26 years of age and born of consanguineous Pakistani parents (family MR107), who had severely impaired intellectual development (IQ of 30) with poor speech and aggressive behavior. {1:Rawlins et al. (2022)} provided follow-up of this family, noting that the affected brothers also had microcephaly/borderline microcephaly (-4.2 and -2.5 SD), short stature (-3.92 and -5.29 SD), and mild dysmorphic features.

{1:Rawlins et al. (2022)} reported a large highly consanguineous Pakistani kindred (family 1) in which 8 individuals ranging from 4 to 18 years of age had global developmental delay with severe intellectual disability, only a few words or absent speech, and behavioral abnormalities, including autistic features and aggressive episodes. All patients had hypotonia, and walking was delayed to about 3 to 4 years of age, sometimes with a waddling gait. All but 1 had microcephaly (range -1.32 to -7.46 SD), and most had short stature (range -1.78 to -5.09); a few had low body weight. Four patients had seizures. Mild dysmorphic features, including synophrys and upslanting palpebral fissures, were also present. Brain imaging performed in 1 patient showed thinning of the corpus callosum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMISS in the families reported by {1:Rawlins et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Pakistani parents (family MR107), with NEDMISS, {2:Santos-Cortez et al. (2018)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the TRAPPC10 gene (P929L; {602103.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family; it was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In 8 affected members of a consanguineous Pakistani family (family 1) with NEDMISS, {1:Rawlins et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the TRAPPC10 gene ({602103.0002}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies in yeast showed that the frameshift mutation and the P929L mutation identified by {2:Santos-Cortez et al. (2018)} reduced the interaction of TRAPPC10 with TRAPPC2L ({610970}) compared to controls. Neither mutation was able to fully rescue Golgi membrane trafficking defects in TRAPPC10-null HEK293 cells, whereas expression of wildtype TRAPPC10 could rescue the phenotype. The findings were consistent with the mutations causing partial functional defects.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Rawlins et al. (2022)} found that Trappc10-null mice had smaller total brain area compared to wildtype, with specific reductions in the size of the corpus callosum, regions of the hippocampus, anterior commissure, and internal capsule. Only white matter structures were affected. There was loss of myelination in these regions, but oligodendrocyte numbers were normal. These findings recapitulated the microcephalic phenotype observed in human patients with mutations in the TRAPPC10 gene.

clinicalSynopsis: Poor or absent gross motor skills
Onset of seizures in the first year of life
Seizures usually occur multiple times a day
Caused by mutation in the UFM1-specific peptidase 2 gene (UFSP2,)

Head: Small head circumference (in some patients)
Neurologic - CNS: Poor or absent gross motor skills
Miscellaneous: Onset of seizures in the first year of life
Seizures usually occur multiple times a day
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the UFM1-specific peptidase 2 gene (UFSP2,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-106 (DEE106) is caused by homozygous mutation in the UFSP2 gene ({611482}) on chromosome 4q35.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-106 (DEE106) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by the onset of various types of frequent, often refractory, seizures within the first year of life. Affected individuals demonstrate profound global developmental delay with limited ability to move and severely impaired intellectual development with absent speech. Nonspecific brain abnormalities may be observed on MRI ({1:Ni et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Ni et al. (2021)} reported 8 children from 4 unrelated families of Pakistani or Afghan origin with a severe epileptic encephalopathy. The patients, who ranged in age from 1 to 11 years, presented with seizures between 2 days and 7 months of age. Seizure types included infantile spasms, tonic, tonic-clonic, focal-clonic, and generalized epilepsy. Most patients had multiple seizures per day; 1 had several seizures per month. The patients showed profound global developmental delay with motor deficits; most were unable to roll over, sit, or walk. They had impaired intellectual development with absent speech, although some patients vocalized. Other common features included poor overall growth, sometimes with small head circumference, hypotonia, convergent squint, and esotropia. Two patients had dystonic movements. Brain imaging, when performed, showed variable abnormalities, including thin corpus callosum, delayed myelination, underopercularization of the Sylvian fissures, small optic nerves, thinning of the deep periventricular white matter, cerebral atrophy, and cerebellar hypoplasia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE106 in the families reported by {1:Ni et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 patients from 4 unrelated families from Pakistan and Afghanistan with DEE106, {1:Ni et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the UFSP2 gene (V115E; {611482.0004}), which occurred at a highly conserved residue close to the N-terminal domain. The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families; all of the parents were heterozygous for the mutation and asymptomatic. The variant was present at a low overall frequency (0.00013) in the gnomAD database (v2.1.1). Studies of patient-derived fibroblasts showed decreased protein levels of UFSP2 and enhanced levels of UFM1-conjugated proteins. Ectopic expression of wildtype UFSP2, but not the mutant, normalized the levels of UFMylated proteins in these cells. The findings were consistent with a loss of UFSP2 function towards de-UFMylation. There was no evidence of activation of the ER stress response.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, LANGUAGE DELAY, AND SKELETAL DEFECTS WITH OR WITHOUT SEIZURES; NEDHLSS
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the calcium channel, voltage-dependent, L type, alpha-1C subunit gene (CACNA1C,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the calcium channel, voltage-dependent, L type, alpha-1C subunit gene (CACNA1C,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, language delay, and skeletal defects with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, language delay, and skeletal defects with or without seizures (NEDHLSS) is caused by heterozygous missense mutation in the CACNA1C gene ({114205}) on chromosome 12p13.

Individuals with truncating variants in the CACNA1C gene have also been described; see below.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, language delay, and skeletal defects with or without seizures (NEDHLSS) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy. Affected individuals show severe hypotonia with delayed walking or inability to walk, poor or absent speech, and impaired intellectual development with behavioral abnormalities. Most patients have early-onset seizures, mild skeletal defects that are usually distal, and nonspecific dysmorphic features. More severely affected individuals have additional congenital abnormalities; however, cardiac involvement is rare (summary by {3:Rodan et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Kosaki et al. (2018)} reported a 5-year-old Japanese girl with postnatal growth failure, developmental delay, joint contractures, and cutaneous syndactyly. She had spells of loss of consciousness as well as some convulsions thought to be seizures, but these episodes were later attributed to pulmonary hypertension. At age 5 years, she was able to crawl and make eye contact; she had no meaningful words. Dysmorphic features included round face, frontal bossing, narrow mouth, low-set ears, depressed nasal bridge, thin upper lip, and thin scalp hair. She did not have prolongation of the QT interval.

{1:Bozarth et al. (2018)} reported an 18-month-old girl, born of unrelated parents, with poor overall growth, feeding difficulties, and dysmorphic features, including micrognathia, downturned corners of the mouth, frontal bossing, scant hair, and inverted nipples. She had multiple congenital anomalies, including laryngomalacia, gastroesophageal reflux, constipation, anal stenosis, and optic nerve hypoplasia with inability to track visually. Distal skeletal defects included clubfeet, finger and toe syndactyly, and camptodactyly. She had severe hypotonia and made almost no developmental progress; she required a feeding tube. Other features included disturbed sleep cycle and onset of various types of refractory seizures soon after birth. Brain imaging and cardiac workup were normal.

{3:Rodan et al. (2021)} reported 14 unrelated patients (P1-P14) with a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with de novo heterozygous nontruncating mutations (13 missense and 1 in-frame deletion) in the CACNA1C gene. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified the mutations. The patients, who ranged in age from 10 months to 24 years, had global developmental delay with hypotonia, motor delay, and variably impaired intellectual development, although more than half were noted to be severely affected. Nine patients were nonverbal and 6 who were old enough to walk were nonambulatory. The others showed mildly delayed walking, sometimes with an unsteady gait. Two individuals (P2 and P3) were noted to have learning disabilities and dyslexia, suggesting milder cognitive impairment. More than half had behavioral problems, most commonly stereotypic behaviors, abnormal social development, and aggression. All 11 patients from whom information was available developed seizures between 2 months and 8 years of age. Seizure types included focal, absence, generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, fever-sensitive seizures, and infantile spasms; 2 patients had West syndrome. EEG showed variable abnormalities, including focal, multifocal, or generalized discharges, spike and polyspike-and-wave discharges, and diffuse paroxysmal activity; 1 patient showed hypsarrhythmia. The seizures were refractory in some patients, but could be managed in others. Brain imaging was essentially normal. Most patients had distal skeletal defects, including joint hypermobility, foot deformities, hip dysplasia or dislocation, kyphoscoliosis, tapering fingers, adducted thumbs, and finger or toe syndactyly. About half of the patients had nonspecific dysmorphic features, such as high-arched palate, abnormal ears, or deep-set eyes, and many had ocular anomalies, including myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, strabismus, and esotropia; 1 had cortical visual impairment. Cardiac involvement was not present in the majority of patients, but a few had variable findings: P13 had a prolonged QT interval, P14 had a borderline QT interval, P12 had possible ventricular conduction delay with trace valvular regurgitation, and P4 had a small atrial septal defect.

<Subhead> Individuals with Heterozygous Truncating Variants

{3:Rodan et al. (2021)} reported 11 individuals (P15-P22C) from 8 unrelated families with variable neurologic deficits associated with heterozygous truncating variants in the CACNA1C gene identified through exome sequencing. The individuals were identified through the GeneMatcher Program. The individuals had essentially normal early motor development and achieved ambulation, but almost all had expressive language delay. Cognition ranged from normal to moderately impaired. Most had behavioral abnormalities, including autism (in 5), ADHD, anxiety, shyness, social problems, echolalia, aggression, and emotional lability. Less common features included hypotonia, poor balance, tremor, paroxysmal movement disorders, minor dysmorphic features, and recurrent infections. One individual had transient seizures. None had cardiac involvement. In 3 families, the mutation was paternally inherited with variable penetrance and expressivity.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous nontruncating mutations in the CACNA1C gene that were identified in patients with NEDHLSS by {3:Rodan et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 5-year-old Japanese girl with NEDHLSS, {2:Kosaki et al. (2018)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense variant in exon 24 of the CACNA1C gene (R1024G). The variant was found by exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In an 18-month-old girl, born of unrelated parents, with NEDHLSS, {1:Bozarth et al. (2018)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the CACNA1C gene (V1363M; {114205.0011}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based exome sequencing, was not present in public databases, including gnomAD. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 14 unrelated patients (P1-P14) with NEDHLSS, {3:Rodan et al. (2021)} identified de novo heterozygous nontruncating mutations (13 missense and 1 in-frame deletion) in the CACNA1C gene (see, e.g., L614P, {114205.0012}; L657F, {114205.0013}; and L1408V, {114205.0014}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing was performed. Electrophysiologic patch-clamp voltage studies in HEK293 cells transfected with a subset of the mutations showed no or variable effects on the channel current, both increased and decreased. The authors noted that their studies used the canonical transcript, but that the CACNA1C gene undergoes extensive splicing and interacts with multiple accessory subunits. They postulated a dominant-negative effect rather than haploinsufficiency.

<Subhead> Heterozygous Truncating Variants

{3:Rodan et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous putative truncating mutations in the CACNA1C gene in 11 individuals (P15-P22C) from 8 unrelated families with variable neurologic deficits. The phenotype was not as severe as in those with missense mutations. In 3 families with truncating variants, the variant was paternally inherited with variable penetrance and expressivity. Variants occurred de novo in the other individuals. The variants (nonsense, frameshift, and splice site) occurred throughout the gene; all were predicted to result in premature termination and all but one were predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. None of the variants were present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. The authors postulated haploinsufficiency as a possible pathogenetic mechanism, but noted that this gene undergoes complex alternative splicing, which presents a challenge in interpreting the effect of the variants.

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: Among 25 individuals from 22 families with heterozygous variants in the CACNA1C gene, {3:Rodan et al. (2021)} found that the neurologic phenotype associated with de novo nontruncating variants was more severe than that associated with de novo or inherited truncating variants. The pathogenetic mechanism was difficult to determine due to the extensive alternative splicing of CACNA1C, but could result in a dominant-negative effect or haploinsufficiency.

clinicalSynopsis: Onset of seizures in the first months of life
Caused by mutation in in the NSF attachment protein beta gene (NAPB,)

Head: Progressive microcephaly
Miscellaneous: Onset of seizures in the first months of life
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in in the NSF attachment protein beta gene (NAPB,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-107 (DEE107) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NAPB gene ({611270}) on chromosome 20p11.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-107 (DEE107) is a severe autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by onset of seizures in the first months of life and severe global developmental delay, profound intellectual disability, progressive microcephaly, and hypotonia ({1:Conroy et al., 2016}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Conroy et al. (2016)} reported a girl, born to consanguineous parents of Irish Traveller descent, who had an early infantile epileptic encephalopathy. She presented with tonic and/or clonic seizures at age 5 months. Neurodevelopment and physical examination were normal at 5 months, but slowing of development was noted by 8 months of age. At 6 years of age, severe progressive microcephaly was noted (from the 9th to less than the 0.4th centile). The patient also had profound intellectual disability, global developmental delay, axial and peripheral hypotonia, limb tremulousness, and stereotypies. Somatic growth was normal. MRI of the brain was normal at presentation and at age 2 years.

{2:Reuter et al. (2017)} reported a male (patient ER53330), born to distantly consanguineous Turkish parents, who had seizures, profound intellectual disability, microcephaly, muscular hypotonia, impaired vision, and feeding difficulties in infancy.

{3:Zhao et al. (2021)} described a 13-year-old girl and her 8-year-old brother, born of nonconsanguineous Chinese parents, who had multifocal seizures beginning at age 6 months and 2 months, respectively. Other findings included profound intellectual disability, global developmental delay, muscular hypotonia, and severe microcephaly (occipitofrontal head circumference Z score less than -3 SD). Both patients had birth weight and length that were appropriate for gestational age. EEG at age 7 years in the female sib showed multifocal epileptic discharges in the centroparieto-occipital or frontotemporal regions, and MRI of the brain was normal.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE107 in the family reported by {1:Conroy et al. (2016)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 6-year-old girl, born of consanguineous parents of Irish Traveller descent, with early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, {1:Conroy et al. (2016)} identified a homozygous ser160-to-ter (S160X) substitution in the NAPB gene (S160X; {611270.0001}). Each parent was heterozygous for the mutation.

Using autozygosity mapping in 152 consanguineous families with at least 1 offspring with intellectual disability, followed by exome sequencing of the index patients, {2:Reuter et al. (2017)} identified a male patient with a homozygous trp58-to-ter substitution in the NAPB gene (W58X; {611270.0002}).

In a 13-year-old girl and her 8-year-old brother with multifocal seizures, profound intellectual disability, and global developmental delay consistent with early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, {3:Zhao et al. (2021)} used exome sequencing to identify a novel homozygous splicing variant in the NAPB gene ({611270.0003}). The unaffected parents and unaffected sib were heterozygous for the variant, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The variant was not present in public variant databases.

clinicalSynopsis: One consanguineous Saudi family has been reported (last curated September 2022)
Caused by mutation in the programmed cell death 6-interacting protein gene (PDCD6IP,)

Head: Microcephaly (-4.5 SD)
Miscellaneous: One consanguineous Saudi family has been reported (last curated September 2022)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the programmed cell death 6-interacting protein gene (PDCD6IP,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive primary microcephaly-29 (MCPH29) is caused by homozygous mutation in the PDCD6IP gene ({608074}) on chromosome 3p22. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal recessive primary microcephaly-29 (MCPH29) is characterized by small head circumference apparent at birth and associated with global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, speech delay, and behavioral abnormalities. Affected individuals also have poor overall growth with short stature, mild dysmorphic facial features, and seizures ({1:Khan et al., 2020}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of primary microcephaly, see MCPH1 ({251200}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Khan et al. (2020)} reported 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Saudi parents, with microcephaly and impaired intellectual development. The patients, who were 19 and 10 years of age, had global developmental delay with speech delay, inability to perform simple tasks, poor self-care, poor communication skills, and behavioral abnormalities, including mood instability and hyperactivity. They had microcephaly (-4.5 SD), short stature (-5 to -6 SD), and dysmorphic facial features, including short or high forehead, deep-set eyes, thick eyebrows, hypoplastic philtrum, squint, and strabismus. Both had seizures. The older patient was able to attend special schooling. Brain imaging of the older brother confirmed microcephaly and showed a mildly simplified gyral pattern. He also had a unilateral atrophic kidney without evidence of renal dysfunction.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MCPH29 in the family reported by {1:Khan et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 brothers from a consanguineous Saudi family with MCPH29, {1:Khan et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the PDCD6IP gene ({608074.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not present in multiple public databases, including gnomAD. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

preferredTitle: DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY, BEHAVIORAL ABNORMALITIES, AND NEUROPSYCHIATRIC DISORDERS; DEDBANP
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor L1 gene (ADGRL1,)

Head: Large head circumference (in some patients)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor L1 gene (ADGRL1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay, behavioral abnormalities, and neuropsychiatric disorders

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay, behavioral abnormalities, and neuropsychiatric disorders (DEDBANP) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ADGRL1 gene ({616416}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay, behavioral abnormalities, and neuropsychiatric disorders (DEDBANP) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by mild global developmental delay and normal or variably impaired intellectual development. Most individuals have behavioral or neuropsychiatric disorders, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and executive functioning deficits. Additional features may include speech delay, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, sleep disturbances, and seizures ({2:Vitobello et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Vitobello et al. (2022)} reported 10 patients from 9 unrelated families with DEDBANP. The patients, who ranged from 3 to 43 years of age, were ascertained through international collaborative efforts and programs such as GeneMatcher after exome sequencing identified heterozygous ADGRL1 mutations. Retrospective phenotyping of the 10 individuals delineated a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by mild global developmental delay, normal or variably impaired intellectual development, ASD, and ADHD. Most patients had mild motor delay with walking between 11 and 30 months and mild speech delay with first words between 12 and 36 months. Five individuals had mild to moderate intellectual disability, 1 had borderline intelligence, and 3 had average IQs. Five presented with neuropsychiatric disorders, including AHDH, ASD, and Asperger syndrome. Some also had learning difficulties, impulsivity, and executive functioning deficits. Two of 9 individuals had EEG abnormalities associated with epileptic seizures and epileptic aphasia, respectively. Dysmorphic features were commonly observed: these included macrocephaly, broad nasal tip, deep philtrum, thin upper lip, and downslanted palpebral fissures. Other more variable features included hypotonia, sleep disturbances, joint hypermobility, distal skeletal anomalies, and increased weight. Brain imaging was normal in 4 of 5 individuals, whereas it showed nodular heterotopia in 1 individual.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: Most of the heterozygous mutations in the ADGRL1 gene that were identified in patients with DEDBANP by {2:Vitobello et al. (2022)} occurred de novo. However, the transmission pattern of DEDBANP in 2 of the families reported by {2:Vitobello et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 10 patients from 9 unrelated families with DEDBANP, {2:Vitobello et al. (2022)} identified heterozygous mutations in the ADGRL1 gene (see, e.g., {616416.0001}-{616416.0005}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and the patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts. There were 4 nonsense, 1 frameshift, and 4 missense variants. Seven mutations occurred de novo, whereas 2 were inherited from a mildly affected parent. In vitro functional studies of some of the variants indicated that they caused alterations in protein expression, membrane localization, and intracellular calcium signaling; the authors postulated haploinsufficiency as the pathogenetic mechanism. One of the patients had previously been reported by {1:Guo et al. (2019)}.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Vitobello et al. (2022)} found that homozygous loss of Adgrl1 in mice on a nonpermissive genetic background was embryonic lethal. Heterozygous Adgrl1+/- mice showed neurodevelopmental abnormalities, including uncoordinated movement, impaired righting reflex, and poor suckling resulting in failure to thrive. Some developed seizures. Homozygous loss of Adgrl1 in a different mouse strain with a compensatory and permissive genetic background allowed for survival. Homozygous Adgrl1-null mice on the permissive background showed a host of aberrant behaviors, most notably persistent maternal, and lesser paternal, infanticide due to deliberate acts of aggression. {2:Vitobello et al. (2022)} hypothesized that Adgrl1-null mice are in a state of hypervigilance with parturition overloading the sensory endurance of the mother, leading her to experience intense distress from a feared stimuli (her own litter), indicating a defect in sensory processing. There was no adaptation with consecutive parturitions, suggesting impaired learning and cognitive dysfunction. These animals also showed aberrant social and sexual behavior in a bimodal pattern, which could suggest a bipolar affective disorder or bimodal cognitive impairment, such as schizophrenia. Adgrl1-null mice showed both increased and decreased locomotion, impaired sensory gating, and increased startle response in prepulse inhibition (PPI) testing. Treatment with the antipsychotic risperidone increased the PPI from 10 to 45% in Adgrl1-null mice and from 40 to 60% in wildtype mice. The Argrl1-null mice on the permissive background and the heterozygous Adgrl1 +/- mice on the nonpermissive background demonstrated persistent stereotypic behaviors, such as self-grooming, particularly in response to stressful situations. Synapses from Adgrl1-null mice showed increased spontaneous release of glutamate and dopamine in the prefrontal brain areas and of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junctions. In contrast, loss of Adgrl1 in dissociated neuronal cultures led to impaired synapse formation and activity.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cerebral atrophy, and visual impairment

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cerebral atrophy, and visual impairment (NEDMVIC) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the DOHH gene ({611262}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cerebral atrophy, and visual impairment (NEDMVIC) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, facial dysmorphism, and microcephaly ({1:Ziegler et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Ziegler et al. (2022)} described 5 patients from 4 families, including 1 sib pair, with clinical features including developmental delay and/or impaired intellectual development (5/5), microcephaly (5/5), seizures (3/5), nystagmus (3/5), strabismus (3/5), and cortical visual impairment (1/5). Three patients had congenital heart malformations including an incomplete AV canal, atrial septal defect (ASD) and ventricular septal defect (VSD) in patient 2, AV block and reduced ventricular function in patient 3, and aortic coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve, ASD, VSD, and tricuspid valve insufficiency in patient 5. All 5 patients had an abnormal brain MRI, including diffuse atrophy (3/5) and hypomyelination (2/5). One patient had severe scoliosis requiring surgery. Three patients had recurrent infections including pneumonia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cerebral atrophy, and visual impairment in the families reported by {1:Ziegler et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 patients from 4 families, including 1 sib pair, with NEDMVIC, {1:Ziegler et al. (2022)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the DOHH gene ({611262.0001}-{611262.0007}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, were present in heterozygous state in all of the parents. DOHH protein levels were reduced in fibroblasts from patients 1, 3, and 4, with increased eIF5A levels in the unhydroxylated and deoxyhypusine-containing form, compared to controls. No fibroblasts were available from patients 2 and 5, who were deceased.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2II (CMT2II) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SLC12A6 gene ({604878}) on chromosome 15q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2II (CMT2II) is an autosomal dominant neurologic disorder characterized by a slowly progressive sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy affecting mainly the lower limbs, resulting in distal muscle weakness and atrophy and subsequent walking difficulties. Some patients may have upper limb involvement with atrophy of the intrinsic hand muscles. The age at onset is highly variable, ranging from infancy to adulthood. Electrophysiologic studies are usually consistent with an axonal process, although some may show intermediate or even demyelinating values ({4:Park et al., 2020}; {1:Ando et al., 2022}). One family with possible autosomal recessive inheritance has been reported ({2:Bogdanova-Mihaylova et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of axonal CMT, see CMT2A1 ({118210}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Kahle et al. (2016)} reported a 10-year-old boy with onset of a progressive motor-predominant axonal peripheral neuropathy apparent since 9 months of age, when he demonstrated foot dragging followed by foot drop and frequent falls when walking. The disorder was progressive, and he was unable to walk independently by 9 years of age. Physical examination showed distal muscle weakness and atrophy affecting the upper and lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were absent, but there were no sensory deficits. Nerve biopsy showed mild loss of myelinated fibers and mild axonal loss, and muscle biopsy was indicative of denervation. Electrophysiologic studies were consistent with a sensorimotor axonal neuropathy with secondary demyelinating features. Brain imaging and cognitive development were normal.

{4:Park et al. (2020)} reported 3 unrelated patients, who ranged from 11 to 15 years of age, with onset of a slowly progressive peripheral neuropathy in the first years of life. They had delayed motor development with delayed walking, frequent falls, foot dragging, foot drop, and distal muscle weakness and mild atrophy. Ankle contractures or foot deformities were also present. There was involvement of the upper limbs, manifest as distal muscle weakness and difficulties using the hands; 1 patient had hand deformities and scoliosis. Sensation was variably impaired. Reflexes were decreased in 2 patients, whereas 1 patient (P3) had brisk reflexes and also showed spasticity. Electrophysiologic studies showed an 'intermediate' neuropathy with mixed axonal and demyelinating features. One patient had mild hemolytic anemia and another had EEG abnormalities without clinical seizures. Brain imaging and cognitive development was normal in all patients.

{5:Shi et al. (2021)} reported a 31-year-old Chinese man who developed progressive distal muscle weakness and atrophy at 27 years of age. He had episodic muscle cramps, foot drop, loss of the ability to run, steppage gait, and distal sensory impairment. Other features included claw hands, high foot arches, and decreased or absent reflexes. Serum creatine kinase was mildly increased. Nerve conduction studies showed a sensorimotor neuropathy with both axonal and demyelinating features, indicating 'intermediate' CMT. Cognitive development and brain imaging were normal.

{1:Ando et al. (2022)} reported 11 patients from 7 unrelated Japanese families with CMT. Clinical details were provided for the 7 probands. The age at onset was highly variable, ranging from 1 to 40 years of age. Patients had frequent falls, difficulty running, steppage gait, and foot deformities. Physical examination showed distal muscle weakness, often accompanied by distal muscle atrophy, variable sensory disturbances, and decreased or absent reflexes. Electrophysiologic studies in most patients were consistent with an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, although the results in some individuals indicated an intermediate or demyelinating type of neuropathy. One patient became wheelchair-bound in her forties. Four patients had evidence of central nervous system involvement: P1 had poor vision, P2 had poor school performance, P3 had mild intellectual disability (IQ of 71), and P7 had cognitive impairment (IQ of 46) and seizures, as well as hemolytic anemia. Five of the probands had a family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance of the disorder, although clinical details and genetic studies were not performed on many of these family members. The disorder occurred sporadically in the probands from families 1 and 7.

<Subhead> Autosomal Recessive CMT2II

{2:Bogdanova-Mihaylova et al. (2021)} reported a pair of 27-year-old fraternal twins with onset of a length-dependent sensorimotor axonal peripheral neuropathy in the first decade. Features included difficulty walking and running, difficulty in using the hands, foot deformities, ankle contractures, and decreased reflexes. Brain imaging showed a normal corpus callosum. Targeted next-generation sequencing identified a heterozygous splice site mutation in the SLC12A6 gene (c.1592-2A-G) that was absent in gnomAD and inherited from the unaffected father, and a heterozygous 1.8-Mb deletion of 15q13.3-q14 encompassing multiple genes, including SLC12A6, that was inherited from the unaffected mother. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. These authors noted that the phenotype was not consistent with the more severe autosomal recessive disorder ACCPN ({218000}), but was consistent with a pure neuropathy. The report expanded the phenotypic and genetic spectrum associated with SLC12A6 mutations.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of in some of the families reported by {1:Ando et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. In addition, heterozygous mutations in the SLC12A6 gene that were identified in some patients reported by {1:Ando et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 10-year-old boy with CMT2II, {3:Kahle et al. (2016)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the SLC12A6 gene (T991A; {604878.0011}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in public databases, including dbSNP, Exome Variant Server, and ExAC. In vitro functional expression studies in patient fibroblasts and HEK293 cells transfected with the T991A mutation showed about 50% reduced phosphorylation of thr991, which in the phosphorylated state inhibits SLC12A6 transporter activity. Cells with the mutation demonstrated increased transporter activity compared to controls, and showed a compromised swelling response to acute hypotonic stress. These findings were consistent with a gain-of-function effect. {3:Kahle et al. (2016)} suggested that these alterations could lead to impaired cell volume homeostasis in peripheral nerves that may result in secondary axonal degeneration or loss, as well as altered neuronal excitability.

In 3 unrelated patients with CMT2II, {4:Park et al. (2020)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations at highly conserved residues in the SLC12A6 gene (R207H; {604878.0012} and Y679C {604878.0013}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based exome sequencing, were not present in public databases, including gnomAD. In vitro functional expression studies in transfected Xenopus oocytes showed that both mutations impaired K+ influx under hypotonic shock compared to controls, consistent with a loss-of-function effect. R207H resulted in a complete loss of function, whereas Y679C caused a partial loss of function.

In a 31-year-old Chinese man with CMT2II, {5:Shi et al. (2021)} identified a heterozygous R207H mutation in the SLC12A6 gene. Functional studies of the variant were not performed, but molecular modeling suggested that it may interfere with homo- or heterodimer formation and cause a dominant-negative effect.

In 11 patients from 7 unrelated Japanese families with CMT2II, {1:Ando et al. (2022)} identified heterozygous mutations in the SLC12A6 gene (see, e.g., {604878.0012}; {604878.0014}-{604878.0015}). There were 3 missense variants and 1 in-frame deletion. The mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregated with the disorder in 2 families in which genetic material was available from affected individuals. The mutations occurred de novo in 2 of the families. The mutations occurred throughout the gene, affected highly conserved residues, and were absent from the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. The patients were ascertained from a cohort of 2,598 individuals with clinically suspected CMT who underwent genetic studies.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Kahle et al. (2016)} used CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing to express the T991A human mutation in mice. Fibroblasts from heterozygous mice had increased cellular K+ influx due to constitutive activation of the SLC12A6 transporter. Heterozygous mutant mice did not show impaired motor performance, but homozygous mutant mice had significant motor deficits. Electrophysiologic studies showed motor and sensory conduction defects, and peripheral nerve biopsy showed myelination defects, particularly in homozygous mutant animals.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH SHORT STATURE, PROMINENT FOREHEAD, AND FEEDING DIFFICULTIES; NEDSFF
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in diphthamide biosynthesis protein 5 gene (DPH5,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in diphthamide biosynthesis protein 5 gene (DPH5,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with short stature, prominent forehead, and feeding difficulties

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with short stature, prominent forehead, and feeding difficulties (NEDSFF) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the DPH5 gene ({611075}) on chromosome 1p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with short stature, prominent forehead, and feeding difficulties (NEDSFF) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by distinct craniofacial features, multisystem dysfunction, profound neurodevelopmental delays, and neonatal death ({1:Shankar et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Shankar et al. (2022)} reported 5 patients from 3 families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. Sibs 1A and 1B from family A had global developmental delays and profoundly impaired intellectual development at 10 and 8 years of age, respectively. They had dysphagia and failure to thrive and required tube feeding. Both had dysmorphic features, including a broad forehead, sparse eyebrows, epicanthal folds, and poor dentition. A brain MRI in the older sib showed brain atrophy at 1 year of age and was normal in the younger sib at 5 years of age. Patients 2A and 2B from family B had global developmental delay, absent speech, and intellectual disability at 9 and 1 years of age, respectively. Both had seizures, appendicular hypertonia, central hypotonia, and extensible skin. Brain MRI in the older sib showed a white matter lesion in the left inferior frontal gyrus, vertically oriented hippocampi, and a prominent ventricular system. Brain MRI in the younger sib showed diffuse paucity of white matter and cerebellar vermian hypoplasia. Patient 3A from family 3 was born prematurely and weighed 800 grams at birth. She had a ventricular septal defect, pulmonary stenosis, pericardial effusion, and brachycephaly. Dysmorphic facial features included broad forehead with bitemporal narrowing, epicanthal folds, and downturned corners of the mouth. She died from a bowel perforation at 11 days of life. Brain MRI showed an enlarged cisterna magna, normal myelination and gyration.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of neurodevelopmental disorder with short stature, prominent forehead, and feeding difficulties in the families reported by {1:Shankar et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 patients from 3 families with neurodevelopmental disorder with short stature, prominent forehead, and feeding difficulties, {1:Shankar et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the DPH5 gene (see, e.g., {611075.0001}-{611075.0003}). DPH5-null MCF7 cells transfected with the DPH5 R207X ({611075.0002}) or 1-bp duplication (c.521dupA) had absent or reduced ADP-ribosylation activity, respectively. Yeast cells mutant H247R or N111S mutation in Dph5, corresponding to the human H260R ({611075.0001}) and N110S ({611075.0003}) mutation, respectively, demonstrated increased growth inhibition when exposed to hygromycin, a diphthamide-indicative translation inhibitor, compared to wildtype.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and skeletal and brain abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and skeletal and brain abnormalities (NEDDFSB) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the HNRNPR gene ({607201}) on chromosome 1p36.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and skeletal and brain abnormalities (NEDDFSB) is a multisystemic developmental disorder characterized by feeding difficulties, poor overall growth, and global developmental delay with moderate to severely impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech. Affected individuals have dysmorphic facial features and skeletal defects, mainly affecting the distal extremities. More variable additional findings include hypotonia, seizures, and ocular defects. Brain imaging tends to show structural defects of the corpus callosum and cerebellar hypoplasia ({1:Duijkers et al., 2019}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Duijkers et al. (2019)} reported 4 unrelated patients, ranging from 3 to 12 years of age, with a multisystemic developmental disorder associated with de novo heterozygous mutations in the HNRNPR gene. The patients were ascertained through international collaboration after exome sequencing identified the mutations. They had feeding difficulties, sometimes requiring tube feeding, and poor overall growth with small head circumference. Two patients had laryngomalacia and 1 had a cardiac ventricular defect. All had moderate to severe developmental delay with hypotonia, delayed walking by a few years, and impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech. One required a tracheostomy. Behavioral problems included ADD and stereotypic movements. Three of the 4 had seizures and 3 had hypotonia. One had cryptorchidism and micropenis, whereas another had hypoplastic labia. Dysmorphic features were common, including brachycephaly, small head circumference, abnormal head hair, bitemporal narrowing, round face, ear abnormalities, upslanted and/or short palpebral fissures, abnormal nasal bridge, micrognathia, short neck, tooth abnormalities, and hirsutism. Variable ocular anomalies were also observed, such as strabismus, pale retina, oculomotor defects, nystagmus, myopia, esotropia, and hypermetropia. The patients had variable skeletal defects, including short hands and feet, pes valgus, brachydactyly, broad thumb or big toe, clinodactyly, hypoplastic end phalanges, 11 pairs of ribs, hip dysplasia, and scoliosis. Two patients had precocious puberty or suspected precocious puberty. Brain imaging showed short or hypoplastic corpus callosum and small cerebellar vermis. A fifth patient was also identified (patient 115 in {2:Helbig et al., 2016}), but clinical information was limited. This infant had epileptic encephalopathy, mild facial dysmorphism, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and cerebellar vermis hypoplasia. {1:Duijkers et al. (2019)} noted that although there were clinical similarities among the patients, it was difficult to delineate a recognizable phenotype.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the HNRNPR gene that were identified in patients with NEDDFSB by {1:Duijkers et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 unrelated patients with NEDDFSB, {1:Duijkers et al. (2019)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the last exon of the HNRNPR gene ({607201.0001}-{607201.0004}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, were not present in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. There were 2 frameshift, 1 nonsense, and 1 missense mutation. The frameshift and nonsense mutations all occurred in the RGG domain, whereas the missense variant (R588H) was in the C-terminal QN domain. Immunoblot analysis of cells derived from P1 and P2 and HeLa cells transfected with their frameshift mutations ({607201.0001} and {607201.0002}) showed production of the corresponding truncated HNRNPR proteins. Patient fibroblasts showed proper nuclear localization of HNRNPR and did not demonstrate stress granules. Although oxidative stress induced the formation of stress granules that colocalized with HNRNPR both in control cells and in patient cells, patient cells had persistent visible stress granules at the end of the recovery period compared to controls. RNA sequencing of patient fibroblasts showed that these HNRNPR variants caused significant changes in the expression of several homeobox genes, as well as other transcription factors, such as LHX9 ({606066}), TBX1 ({602054}), and multiple HOX genes that are considered fundamental regulators of embryonic development. Given that the mutated mRNAs appeared to escape nonsense-mediated decay and produce mutant proteins, the authors postulated a dominant-negative or gain-of-function effect.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with facial dysmorphism, absent language, and pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with facial dysmorphism, absent language, and pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly (NEDFLPH) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TMEM147 gene ({613585}) on chromosome 19q32.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with facial dysmorphism, absent language, and pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly (NEDFLPH) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay with severely impaired intellectual development. Affected individuals often have behavioral abnormalities and may have variable findings on brain imaging, such as thin corpus callosum. Laboratory studies show nuclear lobulation defects in a subset of neutrophils, indicating a pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly (see {169400}) and suggesting defects in the integrity of the nuclear envelope, where TMEM147 localizes ({1:Thomas et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Thomas et al. (2022)} reported 23 patients from 15 unrelated families with a unique neurodevelopmental disorder associated with biallelic mutations in the TMEM147 gene. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts including the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified the mutations. Most patients (87%) were born of consanguineous parents. The patients, who ranged in age from 1 to 16 years, all had global developmental delay with severely impaired intellectual development (IQ range, 20-50) and absent speech or only a few words. Gross and fine motor skills were also delayed, although most achieved walking by around 5 years of age. Behavioral problems were common and included hyperactivity, aggression, outbursts, and self-injury. Some patients had poor overall growth; a few had microcephaly. The patients had consistent facial dysmorphism characterized by coarse facies, prominent forehead, long face, broad and depressed nasal root, smooth philtrum, downslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, synophrys, tented upper lip with open mouth, and low-set ears. The authors noted that some clinicians had initially suspected a RAS-associated disorder based on the facial features. Some patients had normal brain imaging, whereas others showed thin corpus callosum, cortical atrophy, enlarged ventricles, cerebellar atrophy, white matter hyperintensities, and myelination defects. Less common features included seizures (in 2), hypotonia, and distal skeletal anomalies, such as clinodactyly. Laboratory studies showed frequent nuclear lobulation defects in neutrophils with forms of hypolobulation reminiscent of Pelger-Huet anomaly. These cytologic abnormalities were observed in about 15 to 25% of neutrophils and less commonly in eosinophils.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDFLPH in the families reported by {1:Thomas et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 25 patients from 15 unrelated families with NEDFLPH, {1:Thomas et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the TMEM147 gene (see, e.g., {613585.0001}-{613585.0005}). Twelve different mutations were identified, including nonsense (3), frameshift (4), splice site (2), and missense (3). The mutation occurred throughout the gene and there were no genotype/phenotype correlations. All but one of the nonsense, frameshift, and splice site mutations were predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, consistent with a loss of function. Fibroblasts derived from 3 patients, 1 with compound heterozygous nonsense and frameshift mutations and 2 with a homozygous missense variant (R166W; {613585.0005}) showed abnormal upregulation of ER markers and morphologic changes in the ER. In addition, LBR ({600024}) was evenly distributed throughout the nucleus, which was different from controls in which LBR localized to the nuclear envelope. These findings suggested nuclear instability, which corresponded to neutrophil nuclear lobulation defects observed in a subset of patients. Based on gene coexpression analysis, {1:Thomas et al. (2022)} concluded that the mutations result in a loss of function. Based on gene expression data, the authors noted that the disorder should be considered an encephalopathy rather than a leukoencephalopathy.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with craniofacial dysmorphism and skeletal defects (NEDCDS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the HNRNPH1 gene ({601035}) on chromosome 5q35.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with craniofacial dysmorphism and skeletal defects (NEDCDS) is characterized by global developmental delay, severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, characteristic facial features, and variable skeletal abnormalities. Additional features include feeding difficulties, inability to walk or walking with an abnormal gait, and cerebellar or other abnormalities on brain imaging ({2:Reichert et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Pilch et al. (2018)} reported a 13-year-old boy, born of unrelated parents, with striking dysmorphic facial features, gastroesophageal reflux with poor feeding and severe failure to thrive, short stature, microcephaly, and lack of developmental progress. He had severely impaired intellectual development with absent speech and was unable to sit unsupported. Brain imaging showed asymmetry of the frontal lobes, enlarged ventricles, features of colpocephaly, abnormal corpus callosum, and hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis. There was a complex developmental defect of the skull base and a cervical vertebral anomaly, resulting in craniofacial abnormalities. Dysmorphic features included high forehead, long face, arched eyebrows, blepharophimosis, downslanting palpebral fissures, squint, exotropia, high nasal root, thin nasal ridge, long hanging columella, small alae nasi, malar hypoplasia, short and smooth philtrum, open bite with dental crowding, high-arched palate, retrognathia, and low-set dysplastic ears. Physical examination and radiographs detected other skeletal abnormalities, including scoliosis, chest deformity, hypermobile joints, hip and elbow dislocations, knee contractures, pes planus, arachnodactyly, clinodactyly, and clubbed fingers and toes. Radiographs showed abnormal metaphyses of the long bones, delayed development of ossification centers that were dysplastic and defective, and osteopenia. Other features included hypospadias, muscle weakness, incoordination, and dyspraxia. {1:Pilch et al. (2018)} noted the similarities to Schilbach-Rott syndrome (SBRS; {164220}).

{2:Reichert et al. (2020)} reported 6 unrelated patients (1,2, 4-7) with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder who were ascertained through clinical networks and the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the HNRNPH1 gene. Four patients ranged between 5 and 23 years of age, 1 died at age 10.5 months, and another was a 30-week-old fetus. All living patients and the patient who died at 10.5 months showed global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech. Three had feeding difficulties requiring tube feeding. Several had hypotonia. The patients were either nonambulatory or had an wide-based ataxic gait or dystonia. Some had self-injurious or aggressive behavior; 2 had seizures. Variable skeletal defects were observed, including scoliosis, lordosis, joint laxity, short stature, hip dysplasia, clubfoot, camptodactyly, arachnodactyly, clinodactyly, clubbed fingers, clenched fists, and wrist flexures. Brain imaging was abnormal in 5 patients, but there were not consistent findings. Features included tethered cord, anomaly of the clivus and atlantooccipital joint, stenosis of the foramen magnum, white matter abnormalities, cerebellar abnormalities, dysmorphic brainstem, and delayed myelination. One had cryptorchidism and another had horseshoe kidney and hypospadias. Dysmorphic features included long face, hypotelorism, blepharophimosis, downslanting palpebral fissures, arched eyebrows, long prominent nose, hypoplastic alae nasi, low hanging columella, small mouth, open mouth, micrognathia, posteriorly rotated hypoplastic ears, and cleft palate. Ocular features included strabismus, myopia, hypermetropia, and squint.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the HNRNPH1 gene that was identified in patient with NEDCDS by {1:Pilch et al. (2018)} and {2:Reichert et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 13-year-old boy with NEDCDS, {1:Pilch et al. (2018)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the HNRNPH1 gene (R206W; {601035.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in public databases, including gnomAD. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. The authors noted that the same mutation in the HNRNPH2 gene (R206W; {300610.0001}) had been found in patients with the Bain type of X-linked syndromic intellectual developmental disorder (MRXSB; {300986}), which shows overlapping clinical features.

In 6 unrelated patients with NEDCDS, {2:Reichert et al. (2020)} identified 5 de novo heterozygous mutations in the HNRNPH1 gene (see, e.g., {601035.0001}-{601035.0004}). The mutations were found by exome sequencing and the patients were ascertained by international collaboration through the GeneMatcher Program. There were 2 missense variants affecting the same codon (R206W, {601035.0001} and R206Q, {601035.0003}), 2 frameshift variants, and an in-frame deletion. The 2 missense variants were predicted to disrupt the nuclear localization sequence (NLS) and have a detrimental effect on HNRNPH1 function. Patients with mutations affecting codon R206 had a more severe phenotype with early onset of symptoms. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors postulated haploinsufficiency as the most likely pathogenetic mechanism. Another patient (case 3) with a similar phenotype had a large duplication encompassing both the HNRNPH1 and RUFY1 ({610327}) genes.

phenotypes.phenotype: Intellectual developmental disorder with ocular anomalies and distinctive facial features

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that intellectual developmental disorder with ocular anomalies and distinctive facial features (IDDOF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the MTSS2 gene ({616951}) on chromosome 16q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Intellectual developmental disorder with ocular anomalies and distinctive facial features (IDDOF) is characterized by global developmental delay, mildly impaired intellectual development, ophthalmologic anomalies, microcephaly or relative microcephaly, hearing loss, and characteristic facial features ({1:Huang et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Huang et al. (2022)} reported 5 patients from unrelated families with an intellectual developmental disorder. The patients ranged in age from 14 months to 42 years, including only 1 adult. Neurodevelopmental issues included mild global developmental delay or mild intellectual disability, with IQs ranging from 55 to 69. Two patients had autism spectrum disorder and 2 patients had attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Two patients had microcephaly, whereas the other 3 had relative microcephaly with head circumferences low compared to their heights. All 5 patients had ophthalmologic findings (nystagmus, optic nerve atrophy) and 2 patients had hearing loss. Distinctive facial features included long, upslanting palpebral fissures, bitemporal narrowing of the forehead, arched eyebrows, and epicanthal folds. Late onset of optic atrophy and seizures in the adult patient suggested that the condition might have a slowly progressive course.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IDDOF in the families reported by {1:Huang et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 patients from unrelated families with IDDOF, {1:Huang et al. (2022)} identified the same de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the MTSS2 gene (R671W; {616951.0001}). The variant was not present in the gnomAD database. PCR analysis showed that the MTTS2 transcript level was reduced in fibroblasts from 2 patients compared to controls, but Western blot analysis showed variable levels of protein within the normal range in patient fibroblasts.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Huang et al. (2022)} modeled the MTSS2 R671W variant ({616951.0001}) identified in patients with IDDOF in Drosophila. The fly ortholog gene mim was widely expressed in most neurons and in some glia of the developing larval central nervous system and adult brain. Expression was particularly enriched in the neurons that mediate learning and memory. Loss of the mim gene in Drosophila led to reduced life span, impaired locomotor behavior, and reduced synaptic transmission in adult flies. Expression of the human reference cDNA for MTSS1L rescued the phenotype, whereas the c.2011C-T variant had reduced rescue ability, suggesting that it is a loss-of-function allele. Elevated expression of the reference cDNA did not affect life span or locomotor activity, but elevated expression of the variant in flies led to similar defects as with mim loss of function, suggesting that the variant may act as a dominant-negative allele in flies.

Head: Small head circumference (in some patients)
Neurologic - CNS: Pontine hypoplasia seen on brain imaging
Laboratory Abnormalities: Combined mitochondrial oxidative respiratory chain complex (OXPHOS) deficiencies

Progressive disorder, may be rapid or slow
