phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodegeneration, childhood-onset, with multisystem involvement due to mitochondrial dysfunction

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that childhood-onset neurodegeneration with multisystem involvement due to mitochondrial dysfunction (CONDMIM) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the LETM1 gene ({604407}) on chromosome 4p16.

description.title: Description
description.content: Childhood-onset neurodegeneration with multisystem involvement due to mitochondrial dysfunction (CONDMIM) is an autosomal recessive syndromic disorder characterized primarily by neurologic deficits. Patients show global developmental delay and variably impaired intellectual development with speech delay apparent from infancy. Affected individuals have hypotonia, poor feeding, poor overall growth, and respiratory distress early in life. Other features include visual impairment due to optic atrophy, sensorineural hearing loss, and neuromuscular abnormalities. The severity is highly variable. The disorder is progressive; about half of patients show developmental regression with loss of previous skills. Features suggestive of a mitochondrial disorder include cataracts, cardiomyopathy, diabetes mellitus, combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, and increased lactate. Some patients develop seizures, some have dysmorphic facial features, and some have nonspecific abnormalities on brain imaging. Death in childhood may occur ({1:Kaiyrzhanov et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022)} reported 18 patients from 11 unrelated families with a similar disorder suggestive of mitochondrial disease associated with biallelic mutations in the LETM1 gene. The patients were ascertained through international collaboration and data sharing via the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified the mutations. The families were from various geographic regions, including Europe, Chechnya, Pakistan, Egypt, Mexico, and Kuwait; 7 of the families were consanguineous. Nine patients from 4 families died of various causes between infancy and 8 years of age, and 9 patients, ranging in age from 1 to 39 years, were still living at the time of the report. Most of the patients (78%) had infantile onset of disease manifestations, whereas some (22%) presented in the first 2 years of life. Common early features included feeding difficulties with failure to thrive, respiratory distress, hypotonia, unsteady gait, and global developmental delay. Many had poor overall growth with low weight and short stature. Most had impaired intellectual development, often with speech delay or absent speech. Almost all patients had impaired vision, usually with optic atrophy, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Cognitive and motor regression was common, with loss of independent ambulation in the first decade and loss of language skills. Variable neurologic or neuromuscular features were also observed in about half of patients. These included spasticity or spastic ataxic gait, myopathy, muscle atrophy, cerebellar ataxia, nystagmus, hyperkinetic movement disorders, brisk tendon reflexes, extensor plantar responses, and peripheral neuropathy. Ten patients (67%) developed epileptic seizures by a median age of 5 years. Seizure types were variable and included infantile spasms, myoclonic jerks, and absence, focal, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Features suggestive of mitochondrial dysfunction included cataracts (45%), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (36%), often with pericardial effusion, and diabetes mellitus (27%). About 40% of patients had dysmorphic facial features, including small head circumference, long and thin face, prominent nose, low-set ears, micrognathia, high-arched palate, and dental abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed that most patients had increased serum lactate and that some patients had elevated plasma amino acids, mainly alanine. Nine patients had increased urinary excretion of 3-methylglutaconic acid. Muscle biopsy showed internal nuclei, prominent mitochondrial patterns, ragged-red fibers, and COX-deficient fibers. Respiratory chain enzyme analysis showed isolated or combined mitochondrial oxidative respiratory chain deficiencies in all patients studied. Brain imaging available for 6 patients showed nonspecific and variable abnormalities such as optic nerve atrophy, chiasm atrophy, pontine hypoplasia, cerebellar atrophy, and mild ventricular dilatation. The severity of the disorder was highly variable. Half of the patients showed rapid disease progression resulting in death, 4 (22%) had moderate progression, and 5 (28%) demonstrated slow progression.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CONDMIM in the families reported by {1:Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 18 patients from 11 unrelated families with CONDMIM, {1:Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the LETM1 gene (see, e.g., {604407.0001}-{604407.0005}). There were 6 missense mutations, all within the conserved LETM domain, an in-frame deletion in the LETM domain, and 3 frameshift mutations affecting the C-terminal domain. Most of the variants were absent from the gnomAD database, although a few were present at a low frequency in only heterozygous state. Some, but not all, of the variants resulted in variably decreased LETM1 protein levels. {1:Kaiyrzhanov et al. (2022)} noted that previous studies had demonstrated that cellular LETM1 deficiency leads to uncompensated mitochondrial electrophoretic K+ uptake and loss of volume homeostasis, which causes mitochondrial fragmentation, matrix swelling, and disorganized cristae. Fibroblasts derived from a subset of their patients showed variable mitochondrial morphologic abnormalities, including increased fragmentation, irregular polarization patterns of mitochondrial network tubules, and shortened tubules. These abnormalities were associated with reduced inner membrane potential. Further studies of some patient fibroblasts and skeletal muscle samples showed variably decreased levels of OXPHOS complex proteins as well as cellular proliferation defects. Some of these mitochondrial defects could be rescued by using nigericin, a mitochondrial K+/H+ exchanger (KHE), illustrating the connection between mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired K+ homeostasis. Functional compensation studies in letm1-null yeast showed that the LETM1 mutations had variably impaired ability to rescue KHE activity, whereas wildtype could rescue KHE activity, thus demonstrating an adverse functional impact of the mutations.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH EYE MOVEMENT ABNORMALITIES AND ATAXIA; NEDEMA
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the FERM domain-containing protein 5 gene (FRMD5,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the FERM domain-containing protein 5 gene (FRMD5,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with eye movement abnormalities and ataxia

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with eye movement abnormalities and ataxia (NEDEMA) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the FRMD5 gene ({616309}) on chromosome 15q15.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with eye movement abnormalities and ataxia (NEDEMA) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy. Affected individuals show delayed walking with an unsteady gait, variably impaired intellectual development, learning disabilities, and speech difficulties. Abnormal eye movements, which are often noted in early childhood, include opsoclonus, nystagmus, and strabismus. Some patients have seizures, which may be refractory ({1:Lu et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Lu et al. (2022)} reported 8 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 3 to 27 years, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder and de novo heterozygous mutations in the FRMD5 gene. The patients presented in infancy with global developmental delay and showed delayed walking, variably impaired intellectual development, and poor or absent speech. Those that achieved walking had an unsteady gait, and most had hypotonia and ataxia; a few demonstrated spasticity. Some patients had dyslexia or learning disabilities. Six patients had seizures or evidence of seizures, including 2 patients who were diagnosed in infancy with refractory epilepsy and West syndrome. All patients had eye movement abnormalities, ranging from strabismus and intermittent esotropia to opsoclonus and nystagmus. Two were visually impaired and had myopia or hypermetropia. Brain imaging was normal in most patients, but one had pachygyria and another had delayed myelination. A few patients had additional features such as myoclonus, dystonia, dyskinesia, and behavioral problems.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the FRMD5 gene that were identified in most patients with NEDEMA by {1:Lu et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 unrelated patients with NEDEMA, {1:Lu et al. (2022)} identified 7 different heterozygous missense mutations in the FRMD5 gene ({616309.0001}-{616309.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. The mutations occurred de novo in 6 patients; paternal DNA was not available for the other 2 individuals, but the mother did not carry the mutation in either case. Five of the mutations clustered within a few amino acids (349-354) in the FA domain. Studies of patient cells were not performed, but functional studies of some of the mutations in CG5022-null Drosophila demonstrated that they cause a partial loss-of-function effect with a dominant-negative effect (see ANIMAL MODEL).

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Lu et al. (2022)} found that loss of the orthologous FRMD5 gene in Drosophila, CG5022, resulted in heat-induced seizures. Mutant flies were unable to climb properly and showed wing fluttering, leg twitching, and abdominal muscle contractions. These defects could be rescued by expression of the wildtype gene, but not by 3 missense mutations (S351G, {616309.0002}; C352R, {616309.0003}; and Y546C, {616309.0005}) that were identified in humans with NEDEMA. Mutant flies also showed defective responses to light, with electroretinogram (ERG) studies indicating defects in synaptic transmission between presynaptic photoreceptors and postsynaptic lamina cells in an age-dependent manner. This phenotype was fully rescued by wildtype FRMD5, but not by 2 of the human missense mutations (S351G and Y546C). In addition, overexpression of the wildtype gene was toxic to the flies, but overexpression of selected human variants was not as toxic, again illustrating that they result in a partial loss of function. The human mutations acted in a dominant-negative manner.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH GROWTH RETARDATION, DYSMORPHIC FACIES, AND CORPUS CALLOSUM ABNORMALITIES; NEDGFC
clinicalSynopsis: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum
Caused by mutation in the FRA10A-associated CGG repeat 1 gene (FRA10AC1,)

Head: Microcephaly (in most patients)
Neurologic - CNS: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the FRA10A-associated CGG repeat 1 gene (FRA10AC1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with growth retardation, dysmorphic facies, and corpus callosum abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with growth retardation, dysmorphic facies, and corpus callosum abnormalities (NEDGFC) is caused by homozygous mutation in the FRA10AC1 gene ({608866}) on chromosome 10q23.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with growth retardation, dysmorphic facies, and corpus callosum abnormalities (NEDGFC) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by these cardinal features apparent from infancy. There is phenotypic variability both in disease manifestations and severity. More severely affected individuals are unable to walk independently, are nonverbal, and may have other anomalies, including congenital heart defects, feeding difficulties, or skeletal defects, whereas others show mildly delayed motor and speech acquisition with mild or borderline intellectual disability (summary by {3:von Elsner et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Von Elsner et al. (2022)} reported 5 patients from 3 unrelated consanguineous Arabic families (families 1, 2, and 3) with a neurodevelopmental disorder who were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after genetic analysis identified homozygous mutations in the FRA10AC1 gene. Common features included global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development, hypotonia, dysmorphic facial features, clinodactyly of the fingers or toes, and corpus callosum abnormalities on brain imaging. All had poor overall growth with short stature (-2.8 to -4.8 SD) and microcephaly (-2 to -4.8 SD), although 2 patients from family 3 were noted to have growth hormone deficiency. The 2 unrelated girls from families 1 and 2 had a more severe phenotype than the 3 sibs from family 3. Patient 1 was a 3-year-old girl with systemic features, including complex congenital heart defect, caudally located left kidney, echogenic kidneys, punctate echogenic signals in the liver, feeding difficulties requiring tube feeding, onset of seizures at 2 months of age, and various skeletal defects. She was unable to walk or speak. Patient 2 was a 9-year-old girl with feeding difficulties, delayed walking at age 3 years, absent speech, and no sphincter control. Her IQ was 35. The 3 brothers in family 3, ranging from 7 to 15 years, showed mildly delayed walking and borderline to mild intellectual disability (IQ range 68 to 77) with speech delay. All patients had notable dysmorphic facial features, including facial nevi, bitemporal narrowing, high forehead, broad and medial flaring of the eyebrows, upslanted and narrow palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, prominent nose, smooth philtrum, large mouth, thick lips, high-arched palate, retrognathia, full cheeks, and low-set posteriorly rotated ears. With age, the shape of the face became triangular with a pointed chin. Brain imaging showed agenesis of the corpus callosum in patient 1, partial agenesis of the corpus callosum in patient 2, and thinning of the corpus callosum in the sibs from family 3.

{2:Banka et al. (2022)} reported 3 female patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. Two sisters, 23 and 21 years of age, had mildly delayed walking and speech acquisition in early childhood, as well as poor overall growth. Dysmorphic features included wide forehead, bushy eyebrows, blepharophimosis, epicanthus, long eyelashes, low-set ears, flat face, small nose, micrognathia, open mouth, and short neck. They had distal skeletal anomalies of the hands and feet, such as tapering fingers, brachydactyly, short palms, fifth finger clinodactyly, and flat feet. Both had myopia. One sister had cleft palate, whereas the other had congenital cardiac septal defects and hearing loss. A 12-year-old girl from family 2 had intrauterine growth retardation, cardiac septal defects, global developmental delay, late walking, unsteady gait, poor speech, hypotonia, and dysmorphic features. She also had feeding difficulties requiring a feeding tube and absence seizures since age 9 years. Brain imaging was not performed in these 3 patients.

{1:Alsaleh et al. (2022)} reported 2 sibs, born of consanguineous parents, with a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by failure to thrive, poor growth, hypotonia, and global developmental delay. The older sister had short stature (-6.47 SD), microcephaly (-3.92 SD), poor vision, right lower pulmonary vein stenosis, profound intellectual disability, inability to walk, and severe oropharyngeal dysphagia requiring a feeding tube. She also had recurrent hospitalizations with metabolic decompensation; she died of septic and hypovolemic shock at 6 years of age. Brain imaging showed enlarged ventricles and thinning of the corpus callosum. Her 15-month-old brother had mild cardiac defects, hypotonia, nystagmus, feeding difficulties, and had not yet achieved independent sitting or speech. Dysmorphic features included plagiocephaly, frontal bossing, high forehead, medial flaring of the eyebrows, epicanthus, strabismus, anteverted nares, pointed chin, and prominent ears. There was a positive family history of 3 cousins with a similar disorder, but those individuals were not available for testing.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDGFC in the families reported by {3:von Elsner et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 5 patients from 3 unrelated consanguineous Arabic families with NEDGFC, {3:von Elsner et al. (2022)} identified 3 different homozygous mutations in the FRA10AC1 gene ({608866.0001}-{608866.0003}). The mutations were absent from gnomAD and segregated with the disorder in each family. Patients from 2 families carried an intragenic deletion ({608866.0001}) and a frameshift mutation ({608866.0002}), respectively, and fibroblasts derived from these patients showed reduced FRA10AC1 transcript and protein levels compared to controls, suggesting that the mutations trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and result in a loss of function. Three sibs in the third family carried an in-frame deletion of 1 residue (Glu165del; {608866.0003}), which was demonstrated in vitro to cause a reduction of FRA10AC1 levels, although the mutant protein localized normally to the nucleus. These findings indicated a milder adverse impact of this mutation on protein function. The sibs in this family also had a less severe phenotype compared to the patients in the other 2 families, suggesting a possible genotype/phenotype correlation. An in vitro splicing reporter assay using patient fibroblasts (families 1 and 2) showed that FRA10AC1 deficiency did not suppress missplicing events caused by mutations in highly conserved splice sites. Transcriptome analysis of patient fibroblasts did not show a significant disturbance in alternative splicing integrity. {3:Von Elsner et al. (2022)} suggested that there may be a cell type-specific function of FRA10AC1, such that neurons may be more susceptible to splicing alterations, especially during development. In addition, FRA10AC1 may have additional cellular functions, such as coupling of transcription and splicing reactions.

In 3 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with NEDGFC, {2:Banka et al. (2022)} identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the FRA10AC1 gene ({608866.0004} and {608866.0005}). RNA-seq analysis of fibroblasts derived from 1 patient showed a significant number of differentially expressed genes, including those that encode developmental transcription factors, compared to controls. However, there were not major changes in splicing. The study supported the conclusions reached by {3:von Elsner et al. (2022)}.

In 2 sibs, born into a highly consanguineous Arab family, with NEDGFC, {1:Alsaleh et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the FRA10AC1 gene (R161X; {607766.0006}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but it was predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and result in loss of function.

One family (family A) with a milder phenotype had an inherited mutation
Three unrelated patients and 1 family (family A) have been reported (last curated November 2022)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with speech impairment and with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with speech impairment and with or without seizures (NEDSIS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1I gene ({608230}) on chromosome 22q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with speech impairment and with or without seizures (NEDSIS) is a phenotypically heterogeneous neurologic disorder whose severity appears to depend on the functional effect of the CACNA1I mutation. Severely affected individuals present in infancy with profound global developmental delay, hypotonia, delayed or absent walking, absent speech, feeding difficulties, cortical visual impairment, and onset of hyperexcitability and seizures in the first months or years of life. They achieve little or no developmental progress and may be tube-fed. Mutations in these individuals occurred de novo. In contrast, a milder phenotype associated with an inherited mutation has been found in a family with mild to moderate cognitive impairment and mild speech delay, usually without seizures ({1:El Ghaleb et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:El Ghaleb et al. (2021)} reported 3 unrelated children (P1, P5, and P6) with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia with inability to walk or delayed walking (8 years in P6), absent speech, feeding difficulties requiring tube feeding in 2 patients, cortical visual impairment, and early-onset seizures. P1, who had almost no developmental progress by 8 years of age, showed EEG abnormalities and hyperexcitability in infancy, followed by the onset of refractory myoclonic and generalized seizures. Brain imaging in P1 at 2 years of age showed frontal brain atrophy, flat brainstem, and mildly delayed myelination. Brain imaging in P5 was normal at 12 months of age; brain imaging in P6 showed hypogenesis of the corpus callosum at 5 years of age. Two of the patients had short stature, including 1 with growth hormone deficiency.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{1:El Ghaleb et al. (2021)} identified a family (family 2) in which a woman and her 2 adult children had mild to moderate intellectual disability associated with a heterozygous missense mutation in the CACNA1I gene identified through exome sequencing and the GeneMatcher program. The mother had an IQ of 70-85 and developed well-controlled seizures at age 58 years; brain CT scan was normal. Her 28-year-old son (P3) had an IQ of 50-70 and her 31-year-old daughter showed speech delay and an IQ of 36-51. Neither of the 2 children had seizures.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: {1:El Ghaleb et al. (2021)} found that targeted treatment of a patient with refractory myoclonic seizures (P1) using a nonselective T-type channel blocker (ethosuximide) resulted in improved control of seizures.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the CACNA1I gene that were identified in 3 unrelated patients with NEDSIS by {1:El Ghaleb et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. The transmission pattern of NEDSIS in 1 family with the disorder was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 unrelated children (P1, P5, and P6) and affected members of a family (family 2, P2, P3, and P4) with NEDSIS, {1:El Ghaleb et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous missense mutations in the CACNA1I gene ({608230.0001}-{608230.0004}). The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after exome sequencing identified the mutations. None of the mutations were present in the gnomAD database. The mutations in patients P1, P5, and P6, who had a more severe phenotype, were shown to be de novo in P1 and P5, and absent from the mother of P6, whose father was not available for testing. In contrast, the 3 patients from family 2 had a less severe phenotype. All the mutations affected highly conserved residues at the cytoplasmic end of respective transmembrane helices, which form part of the channel's activation gate. In vitro electrophysiologic studies in HEK293 cells transfected with the mutations showed that they altered the gating properties of the channel to different extents, causing increased activation time, decreased inactivation kinetics, and a left-shift in the voltage dependence for activation, all consistent with a gain-of-function effect. Further studies indicated that the mutations resulted in variably increased calcium influx in the steady state as well as during depolarization and repolarization, which was postulated to cause neuronal hyperexcitability and possibly cellular toxicity. {1:El Ghaleb et al. (2021)} suggested that neuronal hyperexcitability could contribute to seizures and that calcium toxicity could underlie the neurodevelopmental phenotype.

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: {1:El Ghaleb et al. (2021)} identified 2 different heterozygous mutations affecting the same codon in the CACNA1I gene within the activation gate of the channel that resulted in different phenotypes. A girl (P1) with severe disease manifestations, early-onset refractory seizures, and almost no developmental progress carried a de novo I860N mutation ({608230.0001}), whereas 3 affected members of a family (family 2) with mild disease manifestations with or without seizures carried an inherited I860M mutation ({608230.0002}). Molecular modeling indicated that the I860N mutation formed strong hydrogen bonds and stabilized the linker region, whereas I860M resulted in weaker bonds that would still allow for flexibility in this region. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells transfected with the mutations and in mouse chromaffin cells demonstrated that the I860N mutation had a stronger adverse effect on channel function compared to I860M. Thus, the magnitude of the functional impact of the CACNA1I mutation correlated with phenotypic severity.

Onset of seizures before 2 years of age
Seizures may be triggered by fever
Caused by mutation in the microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase 3 gene (MAST3,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-108 (DEE108) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the MAST3 gene ({612258}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-108 (DEE108) is characterized by the onset of multiple types of seizures in the first 2 years of life. Affected individuals often have normal early development before the onset of seizures, after which they show developmental regression with loss of skills, particularly language; most are nonverbal or speak only a few words. Other features included mildly delayed walking, unsteady gait, hypotonia, and behavioral abnormalities, such as ADHD or autism ({2:Spinelli et al., 2021}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Spinelli et al. (2021)} reported 11 unrelated individuals, ranging from 7 to 44 years of age, with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. The patients were ascertained through international collaboration and the GeneMatcher program after exome sequencing identified heterozygous missense mutations in the MAST3 gene. Most patients had normal early development before the onset of seizures between 2 months and 2 years of age, and thereafter showed developmental regression of motor and language skills. Seizure types were highly variable and included febrile, atonic, myoclonic, absence, generalized tonic-clonic, and focal with impaired awareness. The seizures were often triggered by fever, and most patients had episodes of status epilepticus. EEG studies were unremarkable at seizure onset in most patients, but later showed mild background slowing and disorganization without burst suppression or hypsarrhythmia. A few patients showed epileptiform discharges. Most patients had refractory seizures, although 2 patients became seizure-free by 2.5 years of age. The patients showed global developmental delay with mildly delayed walking, often with an unsteady gait, severely impaired intellectual development, absent or very poor language skills, and behavioral abnormalities, including impulsivity, hyperactivity, aggression, sleep difficulties, and autistic features. Brain imaging performed in 5 patients showed thin corpus callosum and/or small pituitary. More variable features observed in only a few patients included nonspecific dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, hypothyroidism (2 patients), and gastrointestinal difficulties.

{1:Shu et al. (2022)} reported 2 unrelated Chinese boys (patients 3 and 4) with DEE108. P3 was a 10-year-old boy with onset of infantile spasms at 3 months of age. The seizures continued and he was diagnosed with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS). He had global developmental delay and could not walk or speak. P4 was a 12-year-old boy who developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures at 11 months of age. He had developmental delay with normal motor skills and impaired language development. Both had EEG abnormalities, but brain imaging was normal in both patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the MAST3 gene that were identified in patients with DEE108 by {2:Spinelli et al. (2021)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 11 unrelated patients with DEE108, {2:Spinelli et al. (2021)} identified 5 different heterozygous missense mutations that all occurred in the highly conserved STK domain ({612258.0001}-{612258.0005}). All but 1 were proven to have occurred de novo; segregation studies were not available for a 44-year-old man (patient 8). None of the mutations were present in the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies of 4 of the variants in HEK293 cells showed that all resulted in slightly decreased protein levels compared to wildtype, but maintained sufficient phosphorylation of the MAST3 substrate ARPP16 (see {605487}). When expression levels were normalized, the variants showed increased phosphorylation activity compared to wildtype, consistent with a possible gain-of-function effect. {2:Spinelli et al. (2021)} postulated that increased phosphorylation of ARPP16 would affect downstream signaling through PP2A (see {176915}) in cortical excitatory neurons.

In 2 unrelated Chinese boys (patients 3 and 4) with DEE108, {1:Shu et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the MAST3 gene. The mutations occurred in the STK domain and were the same as 2 of the mutations identified by {2:Spinelli et al. (2021)} (G515S, {612258.0003} and L516P, {612258.0004}). The mutations were found by trio-based exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

preferredTitle: PSEUDOHYPOALDOSTERONISM, TYPE IB3, AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE; PHA1B3
clinicalSynopsis: Severe neurodevelopment delay after cardiac arrest (some patients)
Episodes of salt wasting, recurrent severe
Cardiac issues due to hyperkalemia common
Caused by mutation in sodium channel, epithelial 1, gamma subunit (SCNN1G,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in sodium channel, epithelial 1, gamma subunit (SCNN1G,)

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive pseudohypoaldosteronism type IB3 (PHA1B3) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gamma subunit of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), SCNN1G ({600761}), on chromosome 16p12.

Mutation in the alpha ({600228}) and beta ({600760}) subunits of ENaC cause PHA1B1 ({264350}) and PHA1B2 ({620125}), respectively.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal recessive pseudohypoaldosteronism type IB3 (PHA1B3) is characterized by renal salt wasting and high concentrations of sodium in sweat, stool, and saliva. The disorder involves multiple organ systems and is especially threatening in the neonatal period. Laboratory evaluation shows hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and increased plasma renin activity with high serum aldosterone concentrations. Respiratory tract infections are common in affected children and may be mistaken for cystic fibrosis (CF; {219700}). Aggressive salt replacement and control of hyperkalemia results in survival, and the disorder appears to become less severe with age (review by {3:Scheinman et al., 1999}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Bandhakavi et al. (2021)} reviewed the hospital experiences of children with pseudohypoaldosteronism over a 37-year period, including 6 with homozygous mutations in the SCNN1G gene. All 6 were born of consanguineous parents of Indian or Yemeni origin and presented at 5 to 12 days of age with life-threatening hyperkalemia and hyponatremia. One patient, a sib of an index case, had electrolyte monitoring postnatally, leading to an earlier diagnosis. Cardiac issues related to severe hyperkalemia were common; 4 of the children sustained cardiac arrest and 2 patients developed cardiac arrhythmias as well. Two children developed substantial neurodevelopmental sequelae from hypoxic brain injury following cardiac arrest. Two children had normal neurologic development despite prior cardiac arrest. Nasogastric feeding or gastrostomy and long-term feeding problems were seen in all 6 patients. Excessive salt in tears caused blepharoconjunctivitis in 3 patients. One patient had a successful pregnancy leading to the birth of a growth-retarded infant.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of PHA1B3 in the families reported by {4:Strautnieks et al. (1996)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 families with PHA type I showing linkage to chromosome 16p, {4:Strautnieks et al. (1996)} demonstrated a homozygous mutation in the SCNN1G gene ({600761.0002}) that resulted in incorrect splicing of the transcript.

In a Japanese patient with sporadic PHA type I, {1:Adachi et al. (2001)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the SCNN1G gene ({600761.0003}-{600761.0004}).

Myelination defects seen on brain imaging (in some patients)
Caused by mutation in the fizzy and cell division cycle 20-related protein 1 gene (FZR1,)

Head: Small head circumference (in some patients)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-109 (DEE109) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the FZR1 gene ({603619}) on chromosome 19p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-109 (DEE109) is characterized by the onset of various types of seizures in the first months or years of life. Affected individuals show developmental delay before and concurrent with the onset of seizures. Features include impaired intellectual development with poor speech, ataxic gait, coordination problems, and behavioral abnormalities ({1:Manivannan et al., 2022}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Rodriguez et al. (2019)} identified a 4-year-old boy, born of unrelated Spanish parents, with intrauterine growth retardation, poor overall postnatal growth with failure to thrive, and microcephaly (less than -3 SD). He developed refractory seizures in the first days of life, including hemiclonic seizures, focal seizures, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. EEG showed polymorphic focal seizures with continuous migratory ictal foci. Brain imaging was normal. He had severe psychomotor retardation with profound intellectual disability, axial hypotonia, and peripheral spasticity. At age 4, he was unable to walk, had no speech, and showed poor interaction with his environment.

{1:Manivannan et al. (2022)} reported 3 unrelated patients with DEE109. The patients, who were 3, 15, and 17 years of age, presented with generalized tonic-clonic seizures around 3 to 4 years of age after demonstrating early developmental delay of motor and language skills. All developed other types of seizures, including myoclonic, atonic, and absence. EEG showed a slowed background and generalized and focal epileptiform activity. Patient 1 was a 17-year-old Turkish boy whose seizures responded to medical treatment, and he eventually became seizure-free at age 4.5 years, although EEG abnormalities remained. He had impaired intellectual development with poor speech, ataxic gait, orofacial coordination problems, and behavioral abnormalities (hyperactivity and inattention). Patient 2 was a 15-year-old girl of Moroccan descent whose seizures were refractory to treatment. She had severely impaired intellectual development with poor speech and behavioral abnormalities on the autism spectrum. Brain imaging showed delayed myelination that resolved on subsequent studies. Patient 3 was a 3-year-old girl, born of consanguineous Afghan parents, with refractory seizures, hypotonia, coordination problems, ataxic gait, and a feeding tube. Brain imaging showed mild frontotemporal volume reduction and myelination defects.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the FZR1 gene that were identified in patients with DEE109 by {1:Manivannan et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 4-year-old boy, born of unrelated Spanish parents, with DEE109, {2:Rodriguez et al. (2019)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the FZR1 gene (D187G; {603619.0001}). In vitro functional studies in HEK293 cells and in cultured mouse cortical cells showed that the mutant protein failed to arrest the cell cycle and caused abnormalities in cell cycle progression, consistent with impaired activation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) and a loss-of-function effect. The patient was part of a cohort of 390 individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders who were screened for mutations in the FZR1 gene through whole-exome sequencing.

In 3 unrelated patients with DEE109, {1:Manivannan et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations affecting the WD40 domain of the FZR1 gene. One mutation (D187N; {603619.0002}) occurred at the same residue as the mutation reported by {2:Rodriguez et al. (2019)}, whereas the other 2 mutations yielded the same substitution even though the nucleotide changes were different (N333K; {603619.0003} and {603619.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome or panel-based sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Expression of the mutations in HEK293 cells showed that they caused a reduction in FZR1 protein levels by about 40% compared to controls. None of the mutations was able to rescue the abnormal neurodevelopmental phenotype in fzr mutant Drosophila, indicating that that they cause a partial loss-of-function effect and are likely hypomorphic alleles.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: In Drosophila, {1:Manivannan et al. (2022)} found expression of the orthologous fzr gene in larval brains and eye imaginal discs, consistent with a developmental role in these tissues. Loss-of-function mutations in the fzr gene resulted in a rough eye phenotype and defects in ERG responses. Mutant flies showed an aberrant pattern of photoreceptors in the retina, ERG defects indicating abnormalities in synaptic transmission, and defects in neuronal patterning in the CNS, and abnormal migration of glial cells. These findings suggested that fzr is involved in the development and function of the fly visual system and likely plays a role in overall neurodevelopment. Homozygosity for a null allele was embryonic lethal.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-110 (DEE110) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CACNA2D1 gene ({114204}) on chromosome 7q21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-110 (DEE110) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by profound global developmental delay and hypotonia apparent in infancy followed by onset of seizures in the first months or years of life. Affected individuals achieve almost no developmental milestones and show impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, inability to walk or grasp objects, peripheral spasticity, and poor eye contact. Brain imaging shows hypoplastic corpus callosum and cortical atrophy ({1:Dahimene et al., 2022}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Dahimene et al. (2022)} reported 2 unrelated 4-year-old boys who presented in infancy with hypotonia, severe global developmental delay, small head circumference, poor head control, and cortical visual impairment with limited eye contact. Patient 1 had suspected absence seizures at 9 months of age that later developed into generalized seizures, whereas patient 2 had onset of epilepsy at 11.5 months of age. Brain imaging showed hypoplastic corpus callosum and progressive cortical atrophy in both patients. They also had feeding problems requiring a gastrostomy tube, failure to thrive, inability to sit or roll over, absent language, sleep disturbances, peripheral spasticity, hyperkinetic choreiform movements, dystonic movements, orofacial dyskinesia, and insensitivity to pain. One patient had nystagmus and the other had disconjugate gaze. Dysmorphic features included bitemporal narrowing, low-set and large ears, and facial hypotonia with open mouth and tented upper lip; 1 had a high-arched palate.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE110 in the families reported by {1:Dahimene et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 unrelated boys with DEE110, {1:Dahimene et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the CACNA2D1 gene ({114204.0001}-{114204.0003}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families. Patient 1 was homozygous for a frameshift allele, and patient 2 was compound heterozygous for a frameshift and a missense allele. Studies of patient fibroblasts and in vitro functional studies of cells transfected with the missense variant (G209D; {114204.0003}) indicated that the variants resulted in a loss-of-function effect on calcium channel function.

preferredTitle: HYPOMAGNESEMIA 7, RENAL, WITH OR WITHOUT DILATED CARDIOMYOPATHY; HOMG7
clinicalSynopsis: Variable age at onset (range infancy to young adult)
Caused by mutation in the RAS-related GTP-binding protein D gene (RRAGD,)

Miscellaneous: Variable age at onset (range infancy to young adult)
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the RAS-related GTP-binding protein D gene (RRAGD,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Hypomagnesemia 7, renal, with or without dilated cardiomyopathy

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that renal hypomagnesemia-7 with or without dilated cardiomyopathy (HOMG7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RRAGD gene ({608268}) on chromosome 6q15.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Renal hypomagnesemia-7 with or without dilated cardiomyopathy (HOMG7) is characterized primarily by renal salt wasting resulting in hypomagnesemia with secondary effects such as hypokalemia or hypocalcemia. Many patients develop nephrocalcinosis, although renal function is generally well-preserved. The age at onset is highly variable, ranging from infancy to young adulthood. A subset of patients develop severe dilated cardiomyopathy as early as in infancy, which may require heart transplant ({1:Schlingmann et al., 2021}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of hypomagnesemia, see {602014}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Schlingmann et al. (2021)} identified 8 unrelated patients with onset of hypomagnesemia and a complex renal tubulopathy between 6 months and 6 years of age, although 1 patient (F6) presented at 14 years of age. Three patients had accompanying muscle spasms, tetany, or seizures. Additional more variable renal features included polyuria, hypokalemia, hypochloremia, hypocalcemia, hypercalciuria, medullary nephrocalcinosis, and metabolic alkalosis. Renal evaluation confirmed renal magnesium wasting consistent with a salt-losing tubulopathy affecting the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle and the distal convoluted tubule. Two patients were noted to have a prenatal course complicated by polyhydramnios. Six patients developed dilated severe cardiomyopathy between 6 months and 14 years of age, including 3 with heart failure who required a heart transplant. Clinical signs of cardiac insufficiency in these individuals included feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, vomiting, sweating, tachycardia, and tachypnea. Family history of the proband of family 4 revealed that the father had similar renal abnormalities and died of dilated cardiomyopathy at 41 years of age; his DNA was not available for study. The proband in family 7 had a similarly affected sister who died in infancy of dilated cardiomyopathy. DNA was not available from the sister, but the mother, who did not have cardiomyopathy, was found to be mosaic for an RRAGD mutation. The authors also identified a family (F9) in which 8 individuals spanning 3 generations had hypomagnesemia without dilated cardiomyopathy. The phenotype was generally milder in this family, with onset of symptoms between 10 and 24 years of age and preserved renal and cardiac function.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the RRAGD gene that were identified in 6 patients with HOMG7 by {1:Schlingmann et al. (2021)} occurred de novo. The transmission pattern of HOMG7 in another family with the disorder (F9) was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 8 unrelated patients (F1 to F8) and 8 affected members of a family (F9) with HOMG7, {1:Schlingmann et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous missense mutations in the RRAGD gene (see, e.g., {608268.0001}-{608268.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, direct Sanger sequencing, or whole-genome sequencing, occurred de novo in the majority of individuals and was inherited in family F9. One family (F4) may have shown autosomal dominant inheritance, but DNA from the affected deceased father of the proband was not available. The proband in another family (F7) had a similarly affected sister who died in infancy, but DNA from the sister was not available; the unaffected mother was mosaic for the mutation (at 17%), suggesting autosomal dominant inheritance. The mutations occurred at conserved residues in GTP-binding domains. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells transfected with the mutations showed that they all increased binding of RRAGD to RPTOR ({607130}) and MTOR ({601231}). All mutants resulted in increased phosphorylation of the downstream molecule S6K1 ({608938}) compared to controls, indicating constitutively activated MTOR signaling. Interactome analysis of a recurrent mutation (S76L; {608268.0001}) demonstrated increased binding to components of the mTORC1 signaling complex at the lysosomal membrane. The findings suggested a critical role for RRAGD in renal electrolyte handling and cardiac function.

clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, severe to profound
Hypoplasia of the corpus callosum on brain imaging
Caused by mutation in the SET domain-containing protein 2 gene (SETD2,)

Head: Small head circumference
Microcephaly, progressive
Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, severe to profound
Hypoplasia of the corpus callosum on brain imaging
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the SET domain-containing protein 2 gene (SETD2,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Rabin-Pappas syndrome (RAPAS) is caused by a specific heterozygous missense mutation (R1740W) in the SETD2 gene ({612778}) on chromosome 3p21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Rabin-Pappas syndrome (RAPAS) is a multisystemic disorder characterized by severely impaired global development apparent from infancy, feeding difficulties with failure to thrive, small head circumference, and dysmorphic facial features. Affected individuals have impaired intellectual development and hypotonia; they do not achieve walking or meaningful speech. Other neurologic findings may include seizures, hearing loss, ophthalmologic defects, and brain imaging abnormalities. There is variable involvement of other organ systems, including skeletal, genitourinary, cardiac, and possibly endocrine ({1:Rabin et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Rabin et al. (2020)} reported 12 unrelated patients (group 1), ranging from 1 month to 12 years of age, with a multisystemic neurodevelopmental disorder associated with a specific de novo heterozygous mutation in the SETD2 gene (R1740W; {612778.0005}). The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts after the mutation was identified, and the phenotype was delineated retrospectively. Nine patients were born prematurely, and 4 mothers of the preterm infants had preeclampsia. All had feeding difficulties and failure to thrive, and most required tube-feeding. None had signs of overgrowth; several had small head circumference or frank microcephaly (down to -4 SD). Respiratory insufficiency, such as hypoventilation, aspiration, or sleep apnea, was commonly observed. The patients had severe global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, hypotonia, inability to walk independently, and absent language. Seven patients had seizures, many of which were refractory to treatment. Brain imaging showed structural abnormalities in all patients, such as hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, shallow sulci, enlarged ventricles, and pontocerebellar hypoplasia. All patients over 2 months of age developed ophthalmic abnormalities, including telangiectasia of the retina with exudates resembling Coats disease, retinal detachment, optic nerve coloboma, and cataracts. Eight had mixed hearing loss. Common dysmorphic features included hypertelorism, micrognathia, small upturned nose, biparietal narrowing, small forehead, flat face, short palpebral fissures, upslanting palpebral fissures, arched eyebrows, strabismus, wide nasal bridge, broad nasal tip, low hanging columella, maxillary and mandibular hypoplasia, and forward facing ears. Distal skeletal abnormalities of the hands and feet were also observed: these included proximally implanted triphalangeal thumbs and halluces, hypoplastic distal phalanges and nails, and camptodactyly. Other skeletal anomalies included hip dysplasia, contractures, thoracic dysplasia, scoliosis, and craniosynostosis. Almost all had involvement of other organ systems, including genitourinary tract anomalies (cryptorchidism, dysplastic or cystic kidneys) and/or congenital heart defects (mainly septal defects). Eight patients had hyponatremia in infancy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SETD2 gene that were identified in patients with RAPAS by {1:Rabin et al. (2020)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 12 unrelated patients (group 1) with RAPAS, {1:Rabin et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the SETD2 gene (R1740W; {612778.0005}). The mutation, which was found through clinical genetics services, was not present in the gnomAD database. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts, and the phenotype determined retrospectively. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. The patients had a severe phenotype with intellectual disability, inability to walk or speak, and involvement of multiple organ systems, which was considered to be different from that of patients with other SETD2 mutations, including those with a different mutation at the same codon (see R1740Q, {612778.0006}).

preferredTitle: CORTICAL DYSPLASIA, COMPLEX, WITH OTHER BRAIN MALFORMATIONS 11; CDCBM11
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the kinesin family member 26A gene (KIF26A,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the kinesin family member 26A gene (KIF26A,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Cortical dysplasia, complex, with other brain malformations 11

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations-11 (CDCBM11) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the KIF26A gene ({613231}) on chromosome 14q32.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations-11 (CDCBM11) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by dilated ventricles and reduced white matter and associated with axonal developmental defects ({1:Qian et al., 2022}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of CDCBM, see CDCBM1 ({614039}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Qian et al. (2022)} reported 5 unrelated patients with complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations. The proband from family A presented with microcephaly, dysmorphic features, and ileus with megacolon. A brain MRI at 3 months of age showed reduced white matter, ventriculomegaly, and a thin corpus callosum. Several other sibs of the patient had similar clinical features and died in infancy but did not undergo genetic testing. The patient from family B was diagnosed prenatally with bilateral schizencephaly at 21 weeks' gestation. Other abnormalities included shortened corpus callosum, a high-arched palate and long philtrum, and absence of a stomach bubble on ultrasound. An MRI after pregnancy termination showed bilateral schizencephaly and abnormal gray-white matter differentiation. The patient from family C had mild developmental delay and learning disabilities. A brain MRI at 18 years of age showed agenesis of the corpus callosum with an enlarged anterior commissure, absent hippocampal commissure, colpocephaly, and decreased white matter volume. The patient from family D had polymicrogyria and hydrocephalus. The patient from family E had growth retardation and developmental delay. A brain MRI at 18 months of age showed a thin corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, and polymicrogyria.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDCBM11 in the families reported by {1:Qian et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 5 unrelated patients with complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations-11, {1:Qian et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the KIF26A gene ({613231.0001}-{613231.0006}). The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing. {1:Qian et al. (2022)} developed KIF26A knockout iPSCs and differentiated them into cortical excitatory neurons. The KIF26A knockout neurons had shorter neurites compared to wildtype, consistent with a possible microtubule instability. {1:Qian et al. (2022)} then generated forebrain organoids from the KIF26A knockout iPSCs, which demonstrated abnormal migration consistent with stalled or arrested radial migration.

preferredTitle: MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY, CONGENITAL, WITH OR WITHOUT SEIZURES; MYOS

phenotypes.phenotype: Muscular dystrophy, congenital, with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital muscular dystrophy with or without seizures (MYOS) is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the GOSR2 gene ({604027}) on chromosome 17q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Congenital muscular dystrophy with or without seizures (MYOS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe muscle hypotonia apparent from birth, as well as developmental delay. Laboratory studies show increased serum creatine kinase and muscle biopsy shows nonspecific dystrophic features. Most patients develop seizures or have abnormal epileptiform findings on EEG studies; other variable findings may include feeding difficulties, nystagmus, myopathic facies, areflexia, and brain atrophy on MRI (summary by {2:Larson et al., 2018} and {1:Henige et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{4:Tsai et al. (2013)} reported a boy who was born with mild hypotonia and subsequently found to have severe developmental delay and optic atrophy. Muscle biopsy showed severe nonspecific dystrophic changes, and serum creatine kinase was elevated. Immunostaining showed normal levels of glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan (DAG1; {128239}). At 28 months of age, he developed seizures, including 1 episode of status epilepticus. Brain imaging showed periventricular white matter loss, enlarged ventricles, and thin corpus callosum. The authors concluded that this phenotype represented a novel form of congenital muscular dystrophy.

{2:Larson et al. (2018)} reported 2 sisters (patients 2 and 3) who presented in early infancy with hypotonia and elevated serum creatine kinase. The older sister had progressive muscle weakness with areflexia and myopathic facies. Fine nystagmus was also noted. She developed absence seizures at 2 years of age; brain imaging was normal. She died of respiratory failure at age 5. Her 6-year-old younger sister (patient 3) also had progressive severe muscle weakness and developed intractable focal and generalized seizures at 2.5 years of age. Brain imaging showed diffuse volume loss with enlarged ventricles. Skeletal muscle biopsy of patient 3 showed an active dystrophic process with hypoglycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan detected by Western blot analysis and immunofluorescent studies. Glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan was normal in patient fibroblasts.

{1:Henige et al. (2021)} reported a 22-month-old Caucasian girl who presented at 4 months of age with hypotonia and increased serum creatine kinase. Decreased fetal movements were noted during the pregnancy. She had subtle arthrogryposis and developed respiratory distress necessitating oxygen supplementation shortly after birth. She was unable to lift her head or arms against gravity, showed myopathic facies with areflexia, and had feeding difficulties with poor growth requiring a feeding tube. She also had profound developmental delays and nystagmus. EEG showed epileptic discharges in the absence of clinical seizures. Muscle biopsy was not performed, but serum O-glycan analysis was normal.

{3:Stemmerik et al. (2021)} reported a 48-year-old patient who presented at 4 years of age with frequent falling. She developed progressive hearing loss at 5 years of age, myoclonic epilepsy at 7 years of age, and ataxia at 13 years of age. She then developed insulin dependent diabetes at age 25. She developed dysarthria in her thirties and dysphagia at age 45. She also had mild cognitive decline affecting her short-term memory starting at 46. At age 46, she also became wheelchair-bound. On examination at age 48, she had scanning speech, saccadic eye movements, generalized areflexia, and proximal muscle weakness. She had successfully been treated with valproic acid and had not had a seizure in the previous 15 years.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MYOS in the family reported by {1:Henige et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 36-month-old boy with congenital muscular dystrophy with MYOS, {4:Tsai et al. (2013)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the GOSR2 gene: a splice site mutation ({604027.0003}) and G144W ({604027.0001}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing; functional studies of the variants were not performed.

In a 6-year-old girl (patient 3) with MYOS, {2:Larson et al. (2018)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the GOSR2 gene (M1R, {604027.0004} and G144W). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing; functional studies of the variants were not performed.

In a 22-month-old girl with MYOS, {1:Henige et al. (2021)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the GOSR2 gene: G144W and Q28X ({604027.0005}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based exome sequencing, were in trans and inherited from asymptomatic parents. Functional studies of the variants were not performed. The Q28X mutation was predicted to result in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay or protein truncation, causing a severe functional defect, whereas G144W most likely retained partial function. {1:Henige et al. (2021)} postulated that there may be a genotype/phenotype correlation based on residual GOSR2 protein function, with more detrimental mutations resulting in a more severe phenotype manifest as congenital muscular dystrophy.

In a 48-year-old woman with MYOS, {3:Stemmerik et al. (2021)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the GOSR2 gene (c.204-7A-G, {604027.0006}; R107X, {604027.0007}). cDNA analysis in patient muscle tissue showed that 40% of the GOSR2 transcripts were abnormally spliced and that membrin protein staining was reduced in muscle tissue. Additionally, alpha-dystroglycan was hyperglycosylated. The patient had a relatively milder phenotype compared to other patients with MYOS, which {3:Stemmerik et al. (2021)} hypothesized was due to residual normal splicing of MYOS.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-57 (COXPD57) is caused by compound heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the CRLS1 gene ({608188}) on chromosome 20p12.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-57 (COXPD57) is an autosomal recessive multisystem mitochondrial disease with varying degrees of severity from premature death in infancy to permanent disability in young adulthood ({1:Lee et al., 2022}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Lee et al. (2022)} reported 4 patients from 3 families with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency and a mutation in the CRLS1 gene. The patient in family 1 (subject 1), who was born small for gestational age, had nonimmune hydrops fetalis and bilateral pleural effusions after birth. Echocardiogram at 2 days of life showed left ventricular noncompaction and biventricular systolic dysfunction, which evolved to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy by 7 weeks of age. She had central hypotonia and myoclonus and became encephalopathic with bulbar dysfunction at 8 weeks of age following a cardiac arrest. She also developed bull's eye maculopathy, bilateral auditory neuropathy, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and autonomic instability. She had progressive neurologic deterioration and died at 3.5 months of age. Brain MRI and MRS at 6 and 10 weeks of age were normal. Two sibs were affected in family 2. Patient II:1 presented with feeding difficulties and apnea at 10 days of life. He was also hypotonic and had bilateral auditory neuropathy and vocal cord palsy. He experienced progressive neurodegeneration with epileptic encephalopathy, bulbar dysfunction, myoclonus, central hypoventilation, dystonia, auditory neuropathy, bull's eye maculopathy, central diabetes insipidus, and autonomic dysfunction. Serial brain MRIs showed progressive cerebral atrophy with preservation of the brainstem and cerebellum. He died at 10 months of age. His sib (patient II:3) was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit at 2 days of life. An echocardiogram demonstrated severe biventricular dysfunction, which subsequently improved. He developed RSV bronchiolitis at age 9 weeks and became progressively encephalopathic with seizures, bulbar dysfunction, and dystonia. He also developed bull's eye maculopathy, auditory neuropathy, autonomic instability, and diabetes insipidus. He died at 4 months of age. The patient in family 3 (subject 2) presented at 3 months of age with hypotonia, congenital nystagmus, and sensorineural hearing loss. Somatosensory evoked potential, visual evoked response, and brainstem auditory evoked response were abnormal. He had global developmental delay, slowly progressive encephalopathy, acquired microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, and impaired vision. Brain MRI at 2.5 years of age demonstrated cerebral atrophy. At 19 years of age he was totally dependent for all aspects of his care.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of COXPD57 in the families reported by {1:Lee et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients from 3 families with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-57, {1:Lee et al. (2022)} identified biallelic mutations in the CRLS1 gene: a Lebanese patient from a nonconsanguineous family (subject 1, family 1) and 2 Lebanese sibs from an apparently unrelated, consanguineous family (family 2) were homozygous for a missense mutation (I209N; {608188.0001}), and a Caucasian patient (subject 2, family 3) was compound heterozygous for missense mutations (A172D, {608188.0002} and L217F, {608188.0003}). Lipidomics in fibroblasts from 2 patients demonstrated that cardiolipin was reduced, cardiolipin acyl side chains had an abnormal distribution, and substrates of CRLS1 were abnormally elevated, including an elevation of phosphatidylglycerol. Mitochondrial morphology in fibroblasts from 2 patients was abnormal, demonstrating a role for CRLS1 in maintaining mitochondrial membranes. Proteomics analysis in fibroblasts from the patient in family 1 demonstrated disturbances in proteins associated with the endoplasmic reticulum stress response.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Atelis syndrome-2 (ATELS2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the SMC5 gene ({609386}) on chromosome 9q21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Atelis syndrome-2 (ATELS2) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by poor overall growth with microcephaly and short stature, dysmorphic facial features, and congenital cardiac defects. Additional more variable features may include hematologic abnormalities, variable ocular abnormalities, motor delay, and anxiety. Patient cells exhibit a unique chromosomal instability phenotype consisting of segmented and dicentric chromosomes with mosaic variegated hyperploidy ({1:Grange et al., 2022}).

See also ATELS1 ({620184}), caused by mutation in the SLF2 gene ({610348}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of MVA, see MVA1 ({257300}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Grange et al. (2022)} reported 4 patients (P7, P8, P9-1, and P9-2) from 3 unrelated families with poor overall growth, microcephaly (down to -7.67 SD), short stature (down to -5.68 SD), dysmorphic facial features, and congenital heart defects. The patients, who ranged from 5 to 10 years of age, showed mild motor delay and anxiety; some had learning difficulties and attention problems. One patient had 2 seizures before 3 years of age that resolved. The patients had variable cardiac abnormalities, such as persistent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary stenosis, septal defects, and heart murmur. Dysmorphic features included frontal bossing, triangular facies, bulbous nasal tip, small mouth, micrognathia, high palate, and dental abnormalities. Three patients had hematologic abnormalities, including anemia, lymphopenia, neutropenia, and increased eosinophils; 1 developed myelodysplastic syndrome. Two patients had persistent fetal vasculature of the eye resulting in blindness; 1 also had retinal detachment and cataracts. Two patients had sacral dimples, and 2 patients had mild distal skeletal defects, such as clinodactyly, brachydactyly, pes planus, and single plantar creases. One patient died at 10 years of age.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of ATELS2 in the families reported by {1:Grange et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

nomenclature.title: Nomenclature
nomenclature.content: {1:Grange et al. (2022)} named this disorder 'Atelis syndrome' after the Greek word for 'incomplete' to indicate the importance of atelic or segmented chromosomes as a diagnostic marker of the disorder.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients (P7, P8, P9-1, and P9-2) from 3 unrelated families with ATELS2, {1:Grange et al. (2022)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the SMC5 gene ({609386.0001}-{609386.0003}). The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families from whom parental DNA was available. The mutations were either absent from gnomAD or present at a low frequency. Coimmunoprecipitation studies in patient cells showed that the mutations disrupted the ability of SMC5 to be recruited to sites of DNA damage induced by laser microirradiation. Patient-derived lymphoblastoid cells and fibroblasts showed a significant increase in spontaneous DNA replication fork stalling and fork asymmetry compared to controls, indicating replication stress. Cells with the H990D mutation ({609386.0003}) showed a moderate reduction in replication fork speed. Patient cells showed increased levels of chromosome aberrations, such as gaps, double-strand breaks, radial formation, lagging chromosomes, and large increases in chromosome numbers, which the authors termed 'mosaic variegated hyperploidy (MVH).' Other features of chromosome instability included loss of sister chromatid cohesion, chromosome missegregation, and centrosome amplification, suggesting mitosis-associated cellular pathologies. There was also a specific defect in resolving G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures during replication. These chromosomal abnormalities could be rescued by expression of wildtype SMC5. {1:Grange et al. (2022)} concluded that the replication defects associated with SMC5 mutations trigger cell death in highly proliferative tissues such as the developing brain, thus resulting in the clinical features of the disorder.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Grange et al. (2022)} found that knockdown of the smc5 gene in zebrafish using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing or morpholino suppression resulted in a reduction in head size and aberrant craniofacial patterning in the pharyngeal skeleton. These defects could be rescued by wildtype human SMC5, but not by 3 human mutations identified ({609386.0001}-{609386.0003}), indicating that they have a loss-of-function effect. Analysis of the mutant zebrafish embryos showed increased apoptosis, suggesting that disruption of the RAD18-SLF1/2-SMC5/6 pathway is required for normal brain development. The authors concluded that compromising this pathway triggers a G2/M cell cycle arrest and apoptosis leading to microcephaly.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, dysmorphic facies, and skin abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, dysmorphic facies, and skin abnormalities (NEDHFS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PGM2L1 gene ({611610}) on chromosome 11q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, dysmorphic facies, and skin abnormalities (NEDHFS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and poor or absent speech. Affected individuals have dysmorphic facies, including large abnormally shaped ears and strabismus, hypotonia, and dry skin with keratosis pilaris. Some patients develop seizures. Metabolic studies are unremarkable ({1:Morava et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Morava et al. (2021)} reported 4 unrelated children (PT1-4) with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder who were identified through the GeneMatcher program after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the PGM2L1 gene. Three patients were around 7 years of age; 1 was 30 months. The patients had severe global developmental delay with hypotonia, delayed walking or inability to walk, and impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech. Two patients had ataxia and 1 had pyramidal signs. Three patients had seizures, including tonic-clonic and absence seizures. PT1 developed status epilepticus and afterwards showed severe developmental regression with a complete loss of motor skills. Brain imaging was normal in 2 patients and showed nonspecific abnormalities (frontal atrophy, signal abnormalities) in the other 2. All patients had facial dysmorphism, although the features were somewhat variable. These included large prominent ears with overfolded helices, downslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, high-arched and narrow palate, flat nasal bridge with prominent nasal tip, thin upper lip, pointy chin, long philtrum, and dental caries. All patients had exotropia or strabismus; 1 had hypermetropia (PT3) and another (PT1) had visual loss. Other features included feeding difficulties (in 2), dry skin with keratosis pilaris or eczema, joint hypermobility, and small hands and feet. Three patients developed early obesity. Laboratory studies, including transferrin glycoform analysis and metabolic studies, were unremarkable in all patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDHFS in the families reported by {1:Morava et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 unrelated patients with NEDHFS, {1:Morava et al. (2021)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PGM2L1 gene ({611610.0001}-{611610.0005}). The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after exome sequencing identified the mutations. Patient fibroblasts showed significantly reduced (90% decrease) glucose-1,6-bisphosphate levels compared to controls. Despite the decrease of hexose/pentose-bisphosphates, levels of nucleoside diphosphate (NDP) sugars were not affected, suggesting that protein glycosylation was not affected. The findings were consistent with a loss-of-function effect of the mutations. The authors postulated that PGM2L1 may have a regulatory role in sugar metabolism in the brain, which may explain the clinical features observed in these patients.
