text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with poor growth, large ears, and dysmorphic facies (NEDGEF) is caused by homozygous mutation in the ZNF668 gene ({617103}) on chromosome 16p11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with poor growth, large ears, and dysmorphic facies (NEDGEF) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by these features as well as hypotonia and global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development. The severity is variable, even within families. Death in early childhood has been reported in 1 family ({1:Alsaif et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Alsaif et al. (2021)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families from the Middle East with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder. Patient 1 (family 1) had previously been reported by {2:Shaheen et al. (2016)} as patient 13DG0784. Patient 1 died at 13 months of age; he had a similarly affected sib who died at age 3 weeks, although DNA was not available from the sib. This patient had feeding difficulties and severe growth delay with microcephaly (-7.2 SD) and loss of subcutaneous fat, hypotonia, global developmental delay, and dysmorphic features, most notably very large, simple ears and deep-set eyes. He also had a large nose, micrognathia, and broad thumbs and toes. Additional congenital abnormalities in this patient included chorioretinal coloboma, atrial septal defect, polysplenia, hydronephrosis, and osteopenia. Brain imaging showed brain atrophy, thin corpus callosum, hypomyelination, and malformations of cortical development, including abnormal gyration and sulcation and nodular heterotopia. The sibs in family 2, aged 34 and 33 years, were born prematurely at 34 weeks' gestation. Both had feeding difficulties with failure to thrive, small head circumference or microcephaly, and loss of subcutaneous fat. They had hypotonia, global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, and seizures. Dysmorphic features were similar to those observed in patient 1, including very large ears, large nose, micrognathia, and large big toes; 1 had deep-set eyes. Both also had a high-arched palate. One sib had lower limb spasticity and the other had hepatomegaly and hepatic steatosis. Brain imaging in 1 sib showed nodular and laminar heterotopia, whereas brain imaging in the other sib was normal in infancy.

nomenclature.title: Nomenclature
nomenclature.content: {1:Alsaif et al. (2021)} proposed the designation ZMAND syndrome (ZNF668-related brain malformation, microcephaly, abnormal growth, neurodevelopmental delay, and dysmorphism) for this disorder.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDGEF in the families reported by {1:Alsaif et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a male infant (patient 13DG0784), born of consanguineous Saudi Arabian parents, with NEDGEF, {2:Shaheen et al. (2016)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the ZNF668 gene (Q319X; {617103.0001}). The mutation was found by autozygosity mapping and exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Turkish parents (family 2), with NEDGEF, {1:Alsaif et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the ZNF668 gene (R371X; {617103.0002}). Fibroblasts derived from 1 of these patients and the patient reported by {2:Shaheen et al. (2016)} showed impaired DNA damage and repair as well as decreased cellular viability after irradiation compared to controls. The findings indicated that the disorder was due to abnormal function of the DNA damage and repair machinery.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIy (CDG2Y) is caused by compound heterozygous mutations in the GET4 gene ({612056}) on chromosome 7p22. One such patient has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIy (CDG2Y) is an autosomal recessive multisystemic congenital disorder characterized by poor overall growth and global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development. Other features may include hypotonia, seizures, brain imaging abnormalities, dysmorphic features, and various skeletal defects. Laboratory studies show a subtle type II glycosylation defect of serum transferrin ({1:Tambe et al., 2020}).

For a general discussion of CDGs, see CDG1A ({212065}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Tambe et al. (2020)} reported an 11-year-old boy, born of unrelated Hispanic parents, with a complex multisystemic congenital disorder apparent from infancy. He presented with global developmental delay and walked with a trainer by age 3, but never achieved independent ambulation or speech. At age 8 months, he presented with tonic-clonic seizures associated with multifocal epileptiform discharges and a poorly organized background on EEG. The seizures were difficult to control and he had episodes of status epilepticus. By age 10 years, he showed poor overall growth with malnutrition and microcephaly; tube-feeding was recommended. He was hypotonic with dysmorphic features, including brachycephaly, bitemporal narrowing, deep-set eyes, synophrys, open mouth, hindfoot valgus, curved toes, and smooth soles. Skeletal survey showed delayed bone age, subluxation of the hips, scoliosis, and osteopenia. Other features included sleep disturbances, spasticity, and an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy. On brain imaging, he had cortical atrophy, enlarged ventricles, brainstem atrophy, basal ganglia volume loss, optic nerve atrophy, and thin corpus callosum; transient delayed myelination was also observed. Laboratory studies revealed generalized aminoaciduria and a subtle serum transferrin glycosylation defect consistent with a type II pattern. Glycosylation was normal in patient fibroblasts.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDG2Y in the family reported by {1:Tambe et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In an 11-year-old boy (CDG-0381), born of unrelated Hispanic parents, with CDG2Y, {1:Tambe et al. (2020)} identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the GET4 gene that affected highly conserved residues (R122H, {612056.0001} and I279M, {612056.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Patient fibroblasts showed an 80 to 90% reduction in GET4 protein levels with a corresponding reduction in GET5 (UBL4A; {312070}) and BAG6 ({142590}) compared to controls. These findings were consistent with these 3 proteins forming a stable complex that was disrupted by the mutations. Although total levels of STX5 ({603189}) were normal in CDG-0381 cells, there was a 2-fold increase of STX5 in the cytosolic fraction compared to the Golgi, indicating mislocalization. In vitro transport studies in patient fibroblasts showed impaired retrograde ER-Golgi transport, although anterograde transport was normal. The proteasome inhibitor bortezomib restored GET4/5 and BAG6 protein levels to normal and also corrected STX5 mislocalization in patient fibroblasts. These findings indicated that the mutations affected the components of the transmembrane domain recognition (TRC) complex and impaired TRC pathway function.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIz (CDG2Z) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CAMLG gene ({601118}) on chromosome 5q23. One such patient has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIz (CDG2Z) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by poor overall growth, severe global developmental delay, seizures, contractures, hypotonia, spasticity, and brain imaging abnormalities. Serum transferrin shows a type 2 pattern of glycosylation abnormalities with a combined N- and O-glycosylation defect ({1:Wilson et al., 2022}).

For a general discussion of CDGs, see CDG1A ({212065}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Wilson et al. (2022)} reported a 14-year-old boy, born of consanguineous Turkish parents, with a congenital disorder with prominent neurologic features. He showed global developmental delay in infancy with lack of head control. At age 1 year, he developed seizures that were controlled, but were associated with developmental regression. He was unable to sit independently, was nonverbal, had contractures, and required tube feeding and intermittent respiratory support. He had poor overall growth with small head circumference, dolichocephaly, contractures, axial hypotonia, and limb spasticity. Brain imaging showed thin corpus callosum, atrophic brainstem, severe cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and diffuse hypomyelination. Serum transferrin isoelectrofocusing showed a type 2 pattern, consistent with CDG. More detailed studies identified combined O- and N-linked glycosylation defects, suggesting dysfunction of the transmembrane domain recognition complex (TRC) pathway.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDG2Z in the family reported by {1:Wilson et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a 14-year-old boy, born of consanguineous Turkish parents, with CDG2Z, {1:Wilson et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the CAMLG gene ({601118.0001}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based whole-genome analysis, was inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Analysis of patient fibroblasts showed that the mutation caused the skipping of exon 2 and absence of the CAMLG protein. Serum studies identified a combined defect in N- and O-linked glycosylation characterized mostly by undersialylation, indicating late Golgi disruption and suggesting dysfunction of the TRC pathway. Knockdown of the CAMLG gene in HeLa cells led to disorganization of the Golgi. Patient fibroblasts and CAMLG-null HeLa cells showed an increase in STX5 ({603189}) mislocalization to the cytoplasm, also indicating dysfunction of the TRC pathway. Levels of BET1L ({615417}), another related SNARE protein, were also decreased.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia-33 (SCAR33) is caused by homozygous mutation in the RNU12 gene ({620204}) on chromosome 22q13. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia-33 (SCAR33) is a neurologic disorder characterized by delayed motor development apparent in infancy, unsteady ataxic gait, intention tremor, nystagmus, and speech delay with dysarthria. Some patients have seizures and/or learning difficulties. Brain imaging shows cerebellar hypoplasia ({1:Elsaid et al., 2017}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Elsaid et al. (2017)} reported 6 patients from 1 large consanguineous kindred from Qatar with onset of spinocerebellar ataxia before 2 years of age. The patients, who ranged from 10 to 25 years of age, showed hypotonia and delayed motor milestones in infancy with an inability to sit until 1 year of age and walking achieved between 2 and 8 years of age. They showed an ataxic gait with tendency to fall, head nodding, slowed finger dexterity, intention tremor, nystagmus (in 3), learning difficulties (in 4), and poor speech with dysarthria. Four patients had seizures, including 3 with febrile seizures and 1 with complex partial seizures. Brain imaging showed cerebellar hypoplasia with an enlarged cisterna magna and fourth ventricle; there was also evidence of cerebellar degeneration.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SCAR33 in the family reported by {1:Elsaid et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 6 affected members of a consanguineous kindred from Qatar with SCAR33, {1:Elsaid et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous C-to-T transition at position 43,011,333 on chromosome 22 within the RNU12 gene ({620204.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of whole-genome sequencing and homozygosity mapping and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The mutation affected a highly conserved area within the basepairing region at the base of the third stem-loop structure (SLIII) in this snRNA. RT-PCR of patient mononuclear blood cells showed increased levels of RNU12 in the patients, suggesting a transcriptional compensatory mechanism due to functionally defective U12 snRNA. Further studies of patient cells showed significant minor intron retention of U12-type genes, indicating splicing abnormalities. Transcriptome analysis showed differential expression of multiple RNA transcripts compared to controls, including several associated with cerebellar ataxia (e.g., ATXN10, {611150} and SLC9A6, {300231}). The findings suggested that altered transcriptome processing is the likely pathogenetic mechanism of this disorder.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and ischiopubic hypoplasia

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and ischiopubic hypoplasia (NEDFIH) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NAE1 gene ({603385}) on chromosome 16q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and ischiopubic hypoplasia (NEDFIH) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by these features and moderate to severe global developmental delay. Affected individuals show episodic regression during periods of stress, including seizures or infection, the latter of which may be associated with lymphopenia. Brain imaging shows diminished white matter volume, enlarged ventricles, and thin corpus callosum ({1:Muffels et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Muffels et al. (2023)} reported 3 unrelated patients ascertained through the GeneMatcher program who had a similar syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder associated with biallelic mutations in the NAE1 gene identified through exome sequencing. The patients, who were 12, 19, and 4 years of age, had moderate to severe developmental delay and mild growth delay with a variable disease course. At 1 year of age, patient 1 was admitted to the ICU for a lower respiratory infection that was followed by a loss of developmental milestones and profound drug-resistant epilepsy. Laboratory studies showed leukopenia, lymphopenia, and decreased Ig levels. At age 12 years, she could not sit without support and was nonverbal. Other features included congenital heart defects and craniofacial dysmorphism. Patient 2 had normal development until 14 months of age when he was admitted to the ICU with pneumonia and thereafter showed developmental regression; he acquired walking at age 2.5 years. Laboratory studies showed mild leukopenia and low Ig levels with lymphocytopenia during infections. Other features included craniofacial dysmorphism and cleft palate. He did not have seizures. At age 19 years, he could sit, walk, and communicate verbally. Patient 3 presented in infancy with plagiocephaly, sleeping difficulties, hyporeflexia, hypotonia, and epileptic spasms associated with developmental regression. He also had dysmorphic facial features. At 2.5 years of age, he could roll, sit with support, vocalize, and recognize his parents. The epilepsy was effectively treated. Common dysmorphic features include broad forehead, downslanting and almond-shaped palpebral fissures, telecanthus, round face with prominent cheeks, broad nasal tip, pointed chin, full lower lip, and asymmetric or cleft palate. All patients had skeletal abnormalities, most notably ischiopubic hypoplasia, decreased bone density, and hyperextensible joints with joint dislocation. Brain imaging in all patients showed diminished white matter volume, enlarged ventricles, and thin corpus callosum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDFIH in the families reported by {1:Muffels et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 unrelated patients (patients 1-3) with NEDFIH, {1:Muffels et al. (2023)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations in the NAE1 gene ({603385.0001}-{603385.0003}) affecting highly conserved residues. The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing, were demonstrated to segregate with the disorder in 1 of the families (individual 1). Western blot analysis of fibroblasts from 2 patients showed an almost 80% reduction in NAE1 levels compared to controls; the parents of patient 1 had about 50% NAE1 abundance. Patient cells showed a reduction in the ratio of neddylated to non-neddylated cullin (e.g., CUL1, {603134}), suggesting that NAE1 deficiency adversely affects function. Transcriptome analysis of patient fibroblasts showed evidence of proteasomal dysfunction with compensatory upregulation of alternative cellular protein degradation pathways. There was also a significant downregulation of genes involved in cartilage development, ossification, and chondrocyte differentiation, including SOX9 ({608160}) and RUNX2 ({600211}), which the authors postulated may result in altered endochondral bone development as observed in the patients. Patient CD3+ T cells showed perturbed NFKB (see {164011}) signaling in response to stimulation, which may explain the infection-induced lymphopenia observed in some of the patients. Patient fibroblasts showed increased cellular toxicity and cell death when exposed to proteosome or neddylation inhibitors. Collectively, these data suggested that patients with NAE1 deficiency cannot adequately upregulate neddylation during periods of stress, which could explain the episodic stress-induced neurodegeneration observed in the patients.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia-8 (HHF8) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SLC25A36 gene ({616149}) on chromosome 3q23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia-8 (HHF8) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by protein-related hypoglycemia and persistent mild hyperammonemia (summary by {3:Shahroor et al., 2022}).

For a phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, see HHF1 ({256450}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Jasper et al. (2021)} described a girl who presented at 5 months of age with hyperammonemia and hypoglycemia in the setting of pneumonia. She had a second episode of hyperammonemia and hypoglycemia with hyperinsulinism at 11 months of age. Despite treatment with diazoxide, she developed hypoglycemia-induced seizures. She had growth delay, and primary hypothyroidism was diagnosed at 13 months of age. At 4 years of age she was diagnosed with developmental delay, and at 6 years of age she was diagnosed with ADHD. A brain MRI showed mild volume loss in the frontal regions, and an EEG was normal. A thyroid ultrasound showed a small left lobe.

{3:Shahroor et al. (2022)} reported 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Pakistani parents, with HHF8. The 5-year-old brother presented with tonic-clonic movements at several months of age, which were associated with hypoglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, and elevated ammonia. Between episodes, blood glucose was normal, but ammonia remained elevated. Protein loading was performed at 2 years of age, which resulted in hypoglycemia. At 4 years of age, his growth parameters and development were normal. The 6-year-old brother had similar episodes at 8 months of age, typically associated with hypoglycemia and hyperammonemia, and usually preceded by a meal that included protein. He was treated with a low protein diet and sodium benzoate. At 6 years of age, his development was age appropriate. He had a muscle biopsy, which demonstrated normal respiratory chain enzymatic activity.

{2:Safran et al. (2023)} reported 4 patients with HHF8 from a consanguineous Israeli Bedouin family. Three of the patients had borderline low birthweight. Three of the patients presented with hypoglycemic seizures at 6 months of age, and 1 patient presented with hypoglycemia in the setting of gastroenteritis at 10 weeks of age. All 4 patients had elevated ammonia at presentation. Three of the patients later developed nonhypoglycemic seizures. The patients had normal development and were not dysmorphic.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content:
{1:Jasper et al. (2021)} treated a child with familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia-8 with oral uridine, which resulted in improvement of thyroid function, thyroid gland size, obstipation, growth, and development. No side effects were observed.

{2:Safran et al. (2023)} reported hypoglycemia management in 4 patients from a consanguineous family. Two patients were treated with diazoxide and uncooked cornstarch, 1 patient was treated with diazoxide, uncooked cornstarch, and a low protein diet, and 1 patient was treated with diazoxide, uncooked cornstarch, a low protein diet treated, and overnight feeds.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HHF8 in the family reported by {1:Jasper et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a girl, born of consanguineous Turkish parents, with HHF8, {1:Jasper et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the SLC25A36 gene (c.803dupT; {616149.0001}). SLC25A36 expression was absent in patient fibroblasts. SLC25A36 with this mutation was assayed in liposomes and had absent CTP transport activity.

In 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Palestinian parents, with HHF8, {3:Shahroor et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the SLC25A36 gene (c.284+3A-T; {616149.0002}). When SLC25A36 with the c.284+3A-T mutation was expressed in E. coli and assayed in liposomes, there was reduced nucleotide transport activity.

In 4 patients from a consanguineous Israeli Bedouin family with HHF8, {2:Safran et al. (2023)} identified homozygosity for the splice site mutation in the SLC25A36 gene ({616149.0002}) that had previously been identified by {3:Shahroor et al. (2022)}. The mutation, which was identified by a combination of linkage analysis, whole-exome sequencing, and Sanger sequencing, segregated with disease in the family. Analysis of mRNA from patient blood cells demonstrated overexpression of a SLC25A36 transcript missing exon 3. Protein expression in patient fibroblasts was normal.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, dysmorphic facies, and skeletal anomalies, with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, dysmorphic facies, and skeletal anomalies, with or without seizures (NEDFSS), is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TRPM3 gene ({608961}) on chromosome 9q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, dysmorphic facies, and skeletal anomalies, with or without seizures (NEDFSS), is characterized by these features and global developmental delay with delayed or absent walking, moderate to severely impaired intellectual development, and poor or absent speech acquisition. Affected individuals may also have behavioral abnormalities. About half of patients develop various types of seizures that are usually well-controlled with medication. Rare patients are noted to have heat intolerance or insensitivity to pain ({4:Lines et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Dyment et al. (2019)} reported 7 unrelated patients, ranging from 6 to 38 years of age, with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder who were ascertained through the GeneMatcher database after exome sequencing identified a recurrent de novo heterozygous mutation in the TRPM3 gene (V837M; {608961.0001}) in all patients. From infancy, they showed mild overall growth impairment and global developmental delay with hypotonia, delayed walking by around 5 years (2 patients were nonambulatory at 6 and 28 years of age), moderately to severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, and lack of toilet training in most. Four were noted to have autistic features. All had epilepsy and/or various types of seizures confirmed by EEG with onset in early childhood. Dysmorphic craniofacial features included broad forehead, deep-set eyes, bulbous nasal tip, long nose, short or long philtrum, strabismus, and micrognathia. Most patients had variable skeletal anomalies, including scoliosis, foot or finger deformities, hip dysplasia, plagiocephaly, and/or pectus excavatum. One had torticollis and another showed athetoid movements in infancy. Brain imaging showed cortical atrophy/enlarged ventricles in 2 patients, but was normal in the other patients.

{1:De Sainte Agathe et al. (2020)} reported a 5-year-old French girl with NEDFSS associated with the recurrent de novo heterozygous V837M mutation in the TRPM3 gene ({608961.0001}) identified through trio-based whole-exome sequencing. She presented with bilateral hip and patellar dislocations necessitating surgical intervention, and was also noted to have hypotonia, global developmental delay with walking at age 5 years, absent speech, and behavioral abnormalities, including aggression, high frustration, and stereotypies. Dysmorphic facial features included broad prominent forehead, synophrys, low-set ears, bulbous nasal tip, short philtrum, and short neck. She had a diminished pain threshold and her mother reported her to have heat intolerance. Additional features included dysarthria, dysphagia, and gastrointestinal reflux. Brain imaging showed mildly enlarged ventricles and nonspecific periventricular white matter hyperintensities. She did not have seizures and EEG studies were normal. {4:Lines et al. (2022)} reported follow-up of this patient, noting that she still had not developed seizures at 7.5 years of age.

{3:Gauthier et al. (2021)} reported a 7-year-old boy, born of unrelated parents of African and Portuguese origin, with NEDFSS associated with the recurrent de novo heterozygous V837M mutation in the TRPM3 gene. He presented in early childhood with axial hypotonia, global developmental delay with inability to walk and absent language, and behavioral abnormalities with autistic-like features, stereotypies, and temper tantrums. At age 7 years, he developed eye-blinking episodes and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Brain imaging showed cerebellar atrophy and enlarged ventricles. Dysmorphic features included broad forehead, strabismus, low-set ears, prognathia, dental malocclusion, open mouth, and pectus excavatum. Other notable findings included trigonocephaly, macrocephaly, and decreased sensitivity to pain.

{4:Lines et al. (2022)} reported 7 unrelated patients, ranging from 5 months to 15 years of age, with NEDFSS associated with the recurrent de novo heterozygous V837M mutation in the TRPM3 gene who were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. The patients showed congenital hypotonia, global developmental delay, delayed walking, and moderate to severe intellectual development with poor or absent speech, although 4 individuals were younger than 36 months of age. Only 2 patients had seizures in early childhood: 1 had a single febrile seizure and another had generalized tonic-clonic seizures that were well-controlled. However, EEG abnormalities were found in a total of 4 patients. Most patients had variable skeletal anomalies, including hip dysplasia, talipes equinovarus or other foot deformities, torticollis, tapering fingers, and scoliosis. Dysmorphic facial features were noted in all patients, although there was not a specific recognizable gestalt. These included brachycephaly, plagiocephaly, broad forehead, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, hypertelorism, strabismus, deep-set eyes, low-set ears, small mouth, downturned corners of the mouth,, and small or prominent chin. Brain imaging was normal in 2 individuals and showed nonspecific abnormalities in others, such as small brain, delayed myelination, enlarged ventricles, occipital arachnoid cyst, and thin corpus callosum. One patient had gray matter heterotopia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the TRPM3 gene that were identified in patients with NEDFSS by {2:Dyment et al. (2019)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
By trio-based exome sequencing in 7 unrelated patients with NEDFSS, {2:Dyment et al. (2019)} identified a recurrent de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the TRPM3 gene (V837M; {608961.0001}). The mutation, which occurred in the highly conserved S4-S5 linker region of one of several reported protein isoforms, was not present in the gnomAD database. The substitution was proposed to produce a conformational change during gated channel opening and thus have functional significance. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. {2:Dyment et al. (2019)} also reported an 8-year-old girl (patient 8) with a similar disorder who carried a de novo heterozygous P937Q variant in the TRPM3 gene that was found once in the gnomAD database (frequency of 3.98 x 10(-6)). Patient 8 also carried a de novo heterozygous splice site variant in the DDB1 gene ({600045}) that was considered a variant of uncertain significance; de novo heterozygous mutations in the DDB1 gene cause a different neurodevelopmental disorder ({619426}).

In a 5-year-old French girl with NEDFSS, {1:De Sainte Agathe et al. (2020)} identified the recurrent de novo heterozygous V837M mutation in the TRPM3 gene through trio-based whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies were not performed.

By trio-based whole-exome sequencing of a 7-year-old boy with NEDFSS, {3:Gauthier et al. (2021)} identified the de novo recurrent V837M mutation in the TRPM3 gene. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

{4:Lines et al. (2022)} identified the recurrent de novo heterozygous V837M mutation in 7 additional unrelated patients with NEDFSS identified through exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

<Subhead> Variant Function

{6:Zhao et al. (2020)} performed in vitro functional expression studies of the V837M mutation (also known as V990M and V992M) and the P937Q variant (also known as P1090Q and P1092Q) in the TRPM3 gene in transfected Xenopus oocytes and HEK293 cells. They found that the disease-associated mutations render the TRPM3 channel overactive, possibly via different mechanisms, and the authors postulated that increased neuronal excitability and/or calcium-induced neuronal damage may underlie disease pathogenesis.

In HEK293 cells, {5:Van Hoeymissen et al. (2020)} found that TRPM3 variants V990M and P1090Q resulted in increased channel current densities compared to wildtype, both in the basal state and when stimulated by agonists. Their overall findings indicated that the mutations caused altered functional properties of the channel, and the authors hypothesized that increased calcium influx and depolarizing channel activity is the basis of seizure development and neurodevelopmental symptoms in patients carrying these mutations.

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay with hypotonia, myopathy, and brain abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay with hypotonia, myopathy, and brain abnormalities (DEDHMB) is caused by homozygous mutation in the GOLGA2 gene ({602580}) on chromosome 9q34.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay with hypotonia, myopathy, and brain abnormalities (DEDHMB) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay and muscle weakness apparent in infancy. Affected individuals show severe motor delay and may not achieve independent walking due to central hypotonia and skeletal muscle myopathy. Some have poor overall growth with microcephaly, subtle dysmorphic features, and delayed language acquisition. Brain imaging shows cerebral atrophy, thinning of the corpus callosum, and delayed myelination ({3:Shamseldin et al., 2016}; {1:Kotecha et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Shamseldin et al. (2016)} reported a 10.5-month-old infant girl, born of consanguineous Saudi parents, who was noted to have microcephaly, hypotonia, failure to thrive, and strabismus at around 4 months of age. At age 6 months, she developed infantile spasms associated with a febrile illness, and EEG showed hypsarrhythmia that normalized after treatment. Physical examination at age 10.5 months showed poor overall growth with progressive microcephaly (-4.2 SD), developmental delay, motor delay with inability to sit, and subtle dysmorphic features, including tented upper lip, micrognathia, and brachycephaly. Brain imaging showed cerebral volume loss, delayed myelination, and thinning of the corpus callosum. Serum creatine kinase was persistently elevated, and muscle biopsy showed mild muscle fiber atrophy. The parents of the proband had had 2 first trimester miscarriages.

{2:Maddirevula et al. (2019)} reported an 11-year-old girl (patient 17-1853), born of consanguineous parents, with global developmental delay, microcephaly, hypotonia with poor motor development (she only achieved sitting), brisk tendon reflexes with clonus, and profound language delay. Motor weakness affected the lower limbs more than the upper limbs, although flexion contractures developed in the upper limbs. She had stereotypic movements, but no seizures. Serum creatine kinase was elevated and skeletal muscle biopsy showed dystrophic changes. Brain imaging showed brain atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and delayed myelination.

{1:Kotecha et al. (2021)} reported a 2-year-old girl, born of consanguineous Indian parents, who demonstrated central hypotonia and developmental and motor delay with absent eye contact that was noted around 6 months of age. She also had focal seizures that resolved. She had poor overall growth with a small head circumference (-2 SD), but moved from a supine to prone position around 9 months of age, developed eye contact, and began cooing. Dysmorphic features included prominent forehead with bitemporal narrowing, depressed nasal bridge, long smooth philtrum, and bowed upper lip. Neuroimaging showed cortical atrophy with thinning of the corpus callosum. {1:Kotecha et al. (2021)} noted the phenotypic similarities to the patient reported by {3:Shamseldin et al. (2016)}.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEDHMB in the families reported by {3:Shamseldin et al. (2016)}, {2:Maddirevula et al. (2019)}, and {1:Kotecha et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 10.5-month-old girl, born of consanguineous Saudi parents, with DEDHMB, {3:Shamseldin et al. (2016)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the GOLGA2 gene ({602580.0001}). The mutation was found by a combination of autozygosity mapping and exome sequencing. Analysis of patient cells did not show evidence of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, but immunoblot studies failed to identified a truncated GOLGA2 protein, indicating that the mutation is null at the protein level.

In an 11-year-old girl (patient 17-1853), born of consanguineous parents, with DEDHMB, {2:Maddirevula et al. (2019)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the GOLGA2 gene ({602580.0002}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In a 2-year-old girl, born of consanguineous Indian parents, with DEDHMB, {1:Kotecha et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the GOLGA2 gene (Q751X; {602580.0003}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was present in the heterozygous state in each unaffected parent. It was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Shamseldin et al. (2016)} found that morpholino knockdown of the golga2 gene in zebrafish resulted in skeletal muscle defects consistent with a myopathy and smaller brains compared to controls, suggesting microcephaly. Skeletal muscle was disorganized in mutant animals, and they showed impaired mobility consistent with overall muscle weakness. In addition, golga2 morphant fish died early, suggesting a crucial role for GOLGA2 function in survival. Expression of human wildtype GOLGA2 was able to rescue these defects.

clinicalSynopsis: Susceptibility conferred by variation in the SWI/SNF-related, matrix-associated, actin-dependent regulator of chromatin, subfamily C, member 1 gene (SMARCC1,)

Molecular Basis: Susceptibility conferred by variation in the SWI/SNF-related, matrix-associated, actin-dependent regulator of chromatin, subfamily C, member 1 gene (SMARCC1,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that susceptibility to congenital hydrocephalus-5 (HYC5) is conferred by heterozygous mutation in the SMARCC1 gene ({601732}) on chromosome 3p21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Congenital hydrocephalus-5 (HYC5) is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by hydrocephalus associated with aqueductal stenosis apparent from birth. Some patients may have neurodevelopmental delay, seizures, or structural brain abnormalities ({1:Furey et al., 2018}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of congenital hydrocephalus, see {233600}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Furey et al. (2018)} reported 5 unrelated children with congenital hydrocephalus due to aqueductal stenosis associated with heterozygous variants in the SMARCC1 gene identified through exome sequencing. Clinical details were limited, but 3 of the 5 patients showed neurodevelopmental delay and epilepsy. Two patients exhibited schizencephalic clefts and possibly other structural brain abnormalities, suggesting abnormal brain development.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HYC5 in the families reported by {1:Furey et al. (2018)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. A de novo mutation occurred in the proband from one of the families.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 unrelated children with HYC5, {1:Furey et al. (2018)} identified heterozygous variants in the SMARCC1 gene ({601732.0001} and {601732.0002}). The variants were identified by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. One variant (a missense variant) occurred de novo in the patient, whereas the other variant (a frameshift variant) was inherited from an unaffected father. Three additional heterozygous putative loss-of-function variants in the SMARCC1 gene were identified in 3 additional probands with HYC5 due to aqueductal stenosis. However, in 2 cases, the variant was inherited from an unaffected parent; parental studies were not performed in the third. None of the variants were present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. Overall, these findings were consistent with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. Based on the expression pattern of SMARCC1, the authors suggested that this form of hydrocephalus is related to impaired or disrupted neurogenesis rather than active CSF accumulation. The patients were part of a cohort of 88 probands with communicating hydrocephalus and 89 probands with hydrocephalus associated with aqueductal stenosis who underwent whole-exome sequencing.

In 6 patients from 5 unrelated families with HYC5, {2:Jin et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous putative loss-of-function variants in the SMARCC1 gene (see, e.g., {601732.0003} and {601732.0004}). The variants were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. One of the variants occurred de novo, 3 were inherited from unaffected parents, and the inheritance pattern in 1 individual could not be determined. These findings were consistent with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. Clinical details were not provided.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-25 (HLD25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TMEM163 gene ({618978}) on chromosome 2q21.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-25 (HLD25) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by horizontal nystagmus, hypotonia, and global developmental delay apparent soon after birth or in infancy. Most patients show gradual clinical improvement over time with resolution of the nystagmus in early childhood. Many achieve developmental milestones and may have normal cognition, although the severity of the disorder varies and some patients may have persistent neurologic deficits, such as ataxia or intellectual disability. Brain imaging shows hypomyelination that may also improve with time ({2:Yan et al., 2022}; {1:do Rosario et al., 2022}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of HLD, see {312080}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Yan et al. (2022)} reported 2 unrelated children, a 7-year-old boy and a 3-year-old girl, both born of nonconsanguineous Chinese parents, with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. Both presented in infancy with horizontal nystagmus that resolved at 8 months of age in the boy and by 3 years of age in the girl. They had mild global developmental delay, hypotonia, and delayed walking with an unsteady gait. Language and cognition were relatively spared in the boy, who improved gradually and attended a regular school at age 7. He also had abnormal brainstem auditory evoked potentials. The girl showed a mild impairment in language development and social and adaptive skills, but had no regression and was learning to speak in sentences. In the boy, a single brain MRI at 7 months of age showed delayed myelination; subsequent scans were not performed. In the girl, a diffuse myelin deficit was observed at age 4 months with no improvement at age 13 months. The authors noted the amelioration of clinical symptoms over time.

{1:Do Rosario et al. (2022)} reported 4 unrelated children (S1, S2, S3, and S4), ranging from 3 to 10 years of age, with HLD25. The manifestations and severity of the disorder varied widely, even in 2 patients (S1 and S2) who had the same mutation (L76P; {618978.0001}). All patients presented with nystagmus at birth or in early infancy. The nystagmus resolved between 7 months and 4 years of age in 3 of the patients; only patient S2 still had nystagmus at age 7 years. Patient S1 was a 7-year-old Indian girl with global developmental delay and hypotonia who achieved independent walking around 7 years of age. She had speech delay, learning difficulties, and delayed toilet training, but improved and was able to attend a regular school. She also had seizures in the first 2 years of life that resolved. Other features included poor growth with microcephaly (-3.5 SD), blue sclerae, mild dysarthria, and ataxic gait. Serial brain imaging showed dysmorphic corpus callosum and hypomyelination that demonstrated some improvement with time. Patient S2 was a 7-year-old Caucasian girl who had onset of dystonia in infancy, followed by epilepsy, although seizure freedom was achieved by 2 years. At age 7, she had hypotonia and was nonambulatory with severe intellectual disability and no expressive language. Nystagmus was persistent. Brain imaging at age 4 months showed hypomyelination that showed some improvement by age 5 years. Patient S3 was a 10-year-old boy who presented in infancy with mild developmental delay, jittery and tremulous movements, hypotonia, and poor eye contact. Brain imaging showed diffuse hypomyelination. He did achieve developmental milestones and had normal cognition; he was attending regular school at age 10. Patient S4 was a 3-year-old girl who had mild developmental delay, gait ataxia, and a single febrile seizure. She developed well thereafter and did well in kindergarten with some concentration problems. Brain imaging showed hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. Of note, she inherited the TMEM163 mutation (H146R; {618978.0004}) from her father, who had a possible early history of nystagmus and showed some white matter abnormalities on brain imaging, but had normal development and was employed.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The heterozygous mutations in the TMEM163 gene that were identified in patients with HLD25 by {2:Yan et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

The transmission pattern of HLD25 in 1 family reported by {1:do Rosario et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity. Mutations identified in 3 other patients occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 unrelated children, each born of nonconsanguineous Chinese parents, with HLD25, {2:Yan et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations affecting the same nucleotide and residue in the N-terminal cytoplasmic domain of TMEM163 (L76P, {618978.0001} and L76R, {618978.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in public databases, including gnomAD. In vitro functional expression studies in HeLa cells showed that the L76P variant resulted in increased zinc efflux compared to controls, whereas L76R resulted in decreased zinc efflux compared to controls.

In 2 unrelated girls (patients S1 and S2) with HLD25, {1:do Rosario et al. (2022)} identified a de novo heterozygous L76P mutation in exon 2 of the TMEM163 gene. Another boy with the disorder (S3) carried a different de novo heterozygous mutation (R138C; {618978.0003}). Finally, a girl with HLD25 (S4) was found to carry a heterozygous missense variant (H146R; {618978.0004}) that was inherited from her possibly affected father, suggesting variable expressivity. The mutations were found by exome sequencing; most were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. All mutations occurred in the cytoplasmic domain and were absent from the gnomAD database. In vitro functional expression studies in HEK293 cells demonstrated that the mutations caused reduced zinc efflux from the cells compared to controls. Protein localization was not altered by the mutations. Expression of the mutations in a murine oligodendroglial cell line caused reduced expression of major myelin genes, reduced number of branches, and increased rates of cell death compared to controls. Of note, there was not an increased cell death rate in HEK293 cells transfected with the mutations, suggesting that oligodendrocytes are uniquely susceptible to the pathogenic effects of TMEM163 mutations. {1:Do Rosario et al. (2022)} suggested that reduced zinc efflux could be toxic to oligodendrocytes. The mutations may have a dominant-negative effect since TMEM163 functions as a dimer. The findings implicated a role for zinc homeostasis in oligodendrocyte development and myelin formation.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {2:Yan et al. (2022)} found that morpholino knockdown of the tmem163 gene in zebrafish embryos resulted in severely disrupted development of the central nervous system with morphologic changes, locomotor defects, myelin deficits, and decreased survival. Expression of the human L76P and L76R mutations resulted in similar developmental and myelination defects with a dominant-negative effect. Further studies showed that downregulation of tmem163 in zebrafish reduced the number of oligodendrocytes and caused increased apoptosis and reduced cellular proliferation in the head region compared to controls. These findings suggested a critical role for tmem163 in neuronal development.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, spasticity, and complete or partial agenesis of the corpus callosum

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, spasticity, and complete or partial agenesis of the corpus callosum (NEDSSCC) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the HECTD4 gene ({620209}) on chromosome 12q24.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures, spasticity, and partial or complete agenesis of the corpus callosum (NEDSSCC) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by axial hypotonia and global developmental delay apparent from the first days or months of life. Affected individuals often have feeding difficulties and develop early-onset seizures that tend to be well-controlled. Other features include peripheral spasticity with hyperreflexia, variable dysmorphic features, impaired intellectual development, behavioral abnormalities, and hypoplasia or absence of the corpus callosum on brain imaging ({1:Faqeih et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Faqeih et al. (2023)} reported 7 patients from 5 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder associated with biallelic mutations in the HECTD4 gene identified by exome sequencing; some of the patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. Four patients, ranging in age from 1.25 to 8 years, from 3 consanguineous Middle Eastern families (families 1-3) showed a severe phenotype, presenting soon after birth or in infancy with axial hypotonia, delayed motor development, swallowing dysfunction, seizures that were mostly controlled, and global developmental delay. They had moderately to severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech and aggressive behavior. All except the youngest showed peripheral spasticity with hyperreflexia. Two sibs from family 1 had conductive hearing loss with absence of the external auditory canal. Brain imaging showed complete or partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. Exome sequencing in these families identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the HECTD4 gene ({620209.0001}-{620209.0003}). {1:Faqeih et al. (2023)} also reported 3 patients, between 4.5 and 27 years of age, from 2 unrelated nonconsanguineous families (families 4 and 5) with a similar disorder due to compound heterozygous missense mutations in the HECTD4 gene (see, e.g., {620209.0004}-{620209.0005}). These 3 patients presented slightly later, between 4 and 30 months of age, with hypotonia, global developmental delay, delayed walking, and speech impairment. All developed seizures that were controlled. They also had behavioral problems, including aggression, autistic behavior, and anxiety. The 4.5-year-old boy was noted to have limb hypertonia, mild stiffness of the lower limbs, wide-based gait, and hyperkinetic movements. More variable features included feeding or chewing problems (2 patients), oculomotor apraxia (1 patient), dyspraxia (1 patient), and scoliosis (1 patient). Brain imaging showed complete agenesis of the corpus callosum and cerebellar hypoplasia in 1 patient and mild enlargement of the temporal horn of the right lateral ventricle in another; brain imaging was normal in 1 of the patients from family 5. Variable dysmorphic features were noted in all patients, but there was not a common gestalt. Features included large head circumference, frontal bossing, hypertelorism, upslanting palpebral fissures, long or short philtrum, large or small ears, retrognathia, micrognathia, wide mouth with thick lips, small mouth, and abnormal teeth.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSSCC in the families reported by {1:Faqeih et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 7 patients with NEDSSCC from 5 unrelated families, 3 of which were consanguineous and of Middle Eastern origin, {1:Faqeih et al. (2023)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the HECTD4 gene (see, e.g., {620209.0001}-{620209.0005}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. They were either absent from or present at a low frequency in the gnomAD database (v2.1.1). Homozygous nonsense or frameshift mutations were found in the 3 consanguineous families (families 1-3), whereas compound heterozygous missense mutations were found in the 2 remaining families (families 4 and 5). Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but cells from 1 of the patients with a nonsense mutation showed a marked reduction in HECTD4 expression compared to controls, suggesting that that mutation undergoes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and causes a loss of function. The other mutations were predicted to cause a loss of function or to disrupt protein structure or function.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with absent speech and movement and behavioral abnormalities (NEDSMB) is caused by homozygous mutation in the UBE3C gene ({614454}) on chromosome 7q36. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with absent speech and movement and behavioral abnormalities (NEDSMB) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay and severely impaired intellectual development with aggressive behavior. Mild dysmorphic features and hypodontia are also present ({1:Faqeih et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Faqeih et al. (2023)} reported 2 sisters, born of consanguineous Saudi Arabian parents (family 6), with hypotonia and global developmental delay apparent from early infancy and a mutation in the UBE3C gene. The girls, aged 12 and 10 years, had severely impaired intellectual development, absent speech, mutism, tremor, ataxia, and limb dystonia. Both had significant behavioral disturbances, including self- and hetero-aggression and autistic features; 1 had sleep disturbance. Other features included conductive hearing loss, myopia, and mild dysmorphic features, such as macrostomia, large mandible, hypodontia, and open-mouthed expression. One had seizures and the other had transient obesity in childhood. Brain imaging was unremarkable in both girls. The phenotype was reminiscent of Angelman syndrome (AS; {105830}).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDSMB in the family reported by {1:Faqeih et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 sisters, born of consanguineous Saudi parents (family 6), with NEDSMB, {1:Faqeih et al. (2023)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the UBE3C gene ({614454.0001}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was present in heterozygous state in each unaffected parent. Patient cells showed a marked reduction in UBE3C expression compared to controls, suggesting that the mutant transcript undergoes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and causes a loss-of-function effect. A 20-year-old man, born of consanguineous Turkish parents (family 7), was recruited through the GeneMatcher Program after identification of a homozygous 185-kb deletion affecting the first 17 exons of the UBE3C gene. DNA was not available from the parents for segregation studies, and functional studies of the variant were not performed. This patient had global developmental delay and severely impaired intellectual development with absent speech and behavioral abnormalities, including self- and hetero-aggression. Other features included hypodontia, myopia, mild peripheral motor neuropathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, insulin-dependent diabetes, hypertriglyceridemia, and advanced bone age. He did not have seizures. Brain imaging showed short and thin corpus callosum and cerebellar hypoplasia.

phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 23

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 23 (MC4DN23) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COX11 gene ({603648}) on chromosome 17q22.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 23 (MC4DN23) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by infantile-onset encephalopathy ({2:Rius et al., 2022}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) deficiency, see {220110}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Rius et al. (2022)} reported 2 unrelated patients, born to consanguineous parents, with mitochondrial complex IV deficiency. Patient X1 presented with congenital sensorineural hearing loss. At 6 weeks of age she had hypotonia, poor feeding, and seizures. Brain MRI at that time was normal. At 3 months of age, she had progression of seizures, developmental stagnation, visual impairment, and poor feeding. Repeat brain MRI demonstrated lesions in the cerebellar peduncles. Laboratory testing showed elevated cerebrospinal and plasma lactate. She developed a dyskinetic movement disorder, and a brain MRI at 7 months of age showed progressive brain atrophy, dentate nucleus lesions, and diffuse white matter disease. Her neurologic symptoms worsened and she died at 9 months of age. Patient X2 was born to a pregnancy complicated by intrauterine growth restriction. After birth, she had feeding intolerance, gastrointestinal tract dysmotility and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Laboratory testing showed elevated plasma lactate and hypoglycemia. She developed seizures at 7 months of age. At 1 year of age, a brain MRI showed bilateral basal ganglia hyperintensities and brain atrophy. At 3 years of age, she had microcephaly and significant developmental delay; she could not sit or roll over and had no speech.

{1:Caron-Godon et al. (2023)} reported an 11-year-old girl who presented at 17 months of age with developmental delay, cerebellar signs, and pyramidal signs. At 5 years of age, she had dystonia, oro-buccal dyskinesia, exotropia, and pale optic papilla. At 6 years of age, she developed increased muscle tone. She developed episodes of sleep disturbances, apnea, and rigidity at 7 years of age. Brain MRIs demonstrated progressive neurodegeneration with relapsing and remitting abnormal signals in the peridentate white matter, thalami, corpus callosum, and lenticular nuclei.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC4DN23 in the family reported by {2:Rius et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 unrelated patients, born to consanguineous parents, with mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 23, {2:Rius et al. (2022)} identified homozygous mutations in the COX11 gene (A244P, {603648.0001}; c.35_36delinsG, {603648.0002}). The mutations, which were identified by trio whole-exome sequencing, were present in heterozygous state in both sets of parents. Analysis of mitochondria from fibroblasts from patient X1 demonstrated a modest reduction in complex IV assembly and a reduction of respiration-derived ATP. The reduction in respiration-derived ATP was corrected in vitro by treatment with coenzyme Q10.

{1:Caron-Godon et al. (2023)} identified compound heterozygous mutations in the COX11 gene (c.766dupA, {603648.0003} and P247T, {603648.0004}) in a patient with MC4DN23. cDNA analysis in fibroblasts from the patient demonstrated that each mutation resulted in a relative decrease in complex IV function and that neither mutation resulted in nonsense-mediated decay. Studies in patient muscle tissue demonstrated decreased COX11 protein expression. {1:Caron-Godon et al. (2023)} generated S. cerevisiae with compound heterozygous mutations in cox11: a c.238T mutation corresponding to the human P247T mutation and a Y250X mutation to mimic the effects of the human c.766dupA mutation. The Y250X mutation in COX11 resulted in increased sensitivity to oxidative stress and complete respiratory deficiency when grown on glycerol and ethanol carbon sources.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with language delay and behavioral abnormalities, with or without seizures (NEDLBAS), is caused by heterozygous mutation in the AGO1 gene ({606228}) on chromosome 1p34.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with language delay and behavioral abnormalities, with or without seizures (NEDLBAS), is characterized by global developmental delay with variably impaired intellectual development apparent from infancy or early childhood. Affected individuals have significant speech delay, and most demonstrate behavioral abnormalities, including autistic features. About half of patients develop seizures, which may be controlled or refractory. More variable features include hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and subtle facial dysmorphism ({6:Schalk et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Rauch et al. (2012)} reported a 2-year-old Israeli girl (DD15852) with impaired intellectual development associated with a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the AGO1 gene (L190P; {606228.0001}) identified through exome sequencing. Clinical details were limited, but she was noted to have global developmental delay with an estimated IQ range of 20-49. These authors noted that {5:Sanders et al. (2012)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense variant (T355I) in the AGO1 gene in a patient (11740) with autism ascertained from a large cohort of patients who underwent exome sequencing.

{1:Hamdan et al. (2014)} reported a 14-year-old girl (patient 702.278) with moderately impaired intellectual development associated with a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the AGO1 gene (G199S; {606228.0002}) identified through exome sequencing. She had global developmental delay, mildly delayed walking (24 months), and speech delay, although she could speak sentences in both French and Arabic. She developed seizures at age 8, presenting with an episode of status epilepticus, although seizures were well-controlled. Brain imaging showed nonspecific signal abnormalities in the frontal periventricular regions.

{2:Martinez et al. (2017)} reported a girl (patient 30) with syndromic intellectual disability associated with a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the AGO1 gene (E195K; {606228.0003}) identified through next-generation sequencing. Clinical details were limited, but she had global developmental delay, speech delay, hypotonia, mild dysmorphic features (epicanthus, macrotia), kidney anomalies, sleep disturbances, and behavioral abnormalities, including hyperactivity and stereotypic behavior.

{4:Sakaguchi et al. (2019)} reported a 15-year-old Japanese girl with global developmental delay, hypotonia, moderate intellectual disability (IQ of 41), and febrile seizures that evolved to afebrile seizures. Mild dysmorphic features were also observed, including telecanthus, wide nasal bridge with bulbous tip, downslanting palpebral fissures, and round face. Brain imaging showed calcification of the globi pallidi at age 8 years, but was unremarkable at age 13. Exome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous G199S mutation in the AGO1 gene.

{6:Schalk et al. (2022)} reported 28 patients from 26 unrelated families with NEDLBAS. The patients, who ranged from 2 to 20 years of age, were ascertained through international collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher program, after exome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the AGO1 gene. All patients had global developmental delay with motor delay, impaired intellectual development, and speech delay, although there was wide variability in the severity. Most had poor communication skills; 3 were nonverbal. However, some were able to attend special schools or receive therapy. Behavioral abnormalities were common and included autistic features, attention deficits, hyperactivity, anxiety, and aggression. About half of patients had various types of seizures, most of which were controlled, although some patients had refractory seizures with status epilepticus. Many patients had feeding difficulties, some requiring a feeding tube. Additional features included hypotonia, sleep disturbances, and nonspecific dysmorphic features such as thin upper lip, tall forehead, almond-shaped eyes, strabismus, and flat nasal bridge. Two patients had hypothyroidism. Brain imaging showed nonspecific abnormalities in 11 of 24 patients studied: these included thin or absent corpus callosum, cerebral atrophy, and signal abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the AGO1 gene that were identified in patients with NEDLBAS by {6:Schalk et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 2-year-old Israeli girl (DD15852) with NEDLBAS, {3:Rauch et al. (2012)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the AGO1 gene (L190P; {606228.0001}). The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing; functional studies were not performed. The patient was ascertained from a large cohort of 51 patients with intellectual disability who underwent exome sequencing. These authors noted that {5:Sanders et al. (2012)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense variant (T355I) in the AGO1 gene in a patient (11740) with autism ascertained from a large cohort of autistic patients who underwent exome sequencing.

In a 14-year-old girl (patient 702.278) with NEDLBAS, {1:Hamdan et al. (2014)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the AGO1 gene (G199S; {606228.0002}). The mutation was found by exome sequencing; functional studies were not performed. The patient was from a cohort of 41 probands with intellectual disability who underwent exome sequencing. {4:Sakaguchi et al. (2019)} identified a de novo heterozygous G199S mutation in the AGO1 gene in a 15-year-old Japanese girl with

In a girl (patient 30) with NEDLBAS, {2:Martinez et al. (2017)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the AGO1 gene (E195K; {606228.0003}). The patient was part of a large study of 92 patients with intellectual disability who underwent next-generation sequencing of a gene panel. Functional studies were not performed.

{6:Schalk et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the AGO1 gene (see, e.g., {606228.0001}, {606228.0002}, {606228.0004}-{606228.0006}) in 28 patients from 26 families with NEDLBAS. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher program, and the mutations were found by exome sequencing. None of the variants were present in the gnomAD database. Most of the mutations were missense variants occurring at highly conserved residues throughout the gene, although there were several small in-frame deletions and 1 splice site mutation. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. There were no apparent genotype/phenotype correlations. Molecular modeling suggested that the mutations could affect dynamic conformational changes in the protein and thus disrupt function, likely with a dominant effect rather than haploinsufficiency. The phenotype was highly variable, even in those with the same mutation, suggesting that additional genetic or environmental factors modulate the effect of the AGO1 variant.

text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect (NSCT) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SLC31A1 gene ({603085}) on chromosome 9q32.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect (NSCT) is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport characterized by hypotonia, global developmental delay, seizures, and rapid brain atrophy (summary by {2:Dame et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Batzios et al. (2022)} described monozygotic twins who were healthy until 10 weeks of life when they became lethargic with transient eyelid twitching. At 17 weeks of age, they were both diagnosed with complex partial seizures and had temperature instability. Laboratory testing demonstrated mildly elevated serum lactate and more significantly elevated CSF lactate. At 8 months of age, serum copper was in the normal range, but CSF copper was decreased. At 9.5 months of age, the infants were unresponsive and lacked spontaneous vocalization or movements. They had profound truncal hypotonia and appendicular hypertonicity. The patients were treated with copper histidinate and had a modest improvement in serum copper and in development; at 2 years of age they had purposeful smiling and mild improvement in feeding and muscle tone. Copper histinidate was discontinued at 29 months of age with no regression in clinical status. One of the infants required ventriculoperitoneal shunt at 2 years of age due to nonobstructive hydrocephalus. Both twins had a mutation in the SLC31A1 gene.

{2:Dame et al. (2023)} reported a patient with mutation in the SLC31A1 gene who had prenatal ultrasound findings of short femurs, an enlarged heart to thorax ratio, and a wide cisterna magna. After birth, he had severe respiratory distress and required intubation and mechanical ventilation. He had lung hypoplasia, tricuspid regurgitation, and suprasystemic right ventricular pressure. Skeletal features included femoral and tibial metaphyseal enlargement and pes equinovarus. Other findings included enlarged nuchal skin and hypospadias. Brain imaging at 2 weeks of age showed tortuous internal carotid, basilar, and vertebral arteries, and numerous intraaxial hemorrhages in the white and central gray matter of the cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: {1:Batzios et al. (2022)} treated monozygotic twins with neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect with copper histidinate. The patients had a modest improvement in serum copper and mild improvement in feeding and muscle tone. Copper histinidate was discontinued at 29 months of age with no regression in clinical status.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect in the family reported by {1:Batzios et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In monozygotic twins with neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect, {1:Batzios et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous missense mutation (R95H; {603085.0001}) in the SLC31A1 gene. The mutation was identified by whole-exome sequencing. The copper level and mitochondrial respiratory chain function were reduced in patient fibroblasts compared to controls, which was improved with treatment with copper histidinate. SLC31A1 with the R95H mutation was normally localized in patient fibroblasts but the cells had a dilated endoplasmic reticulum.

In a Turkish patient, born to consanguineous parents, with NSCT, {2:Dame et al. (2023)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SLC31A1 gene (L79P; {603085.0002}). The mutation, which was identified by whole-exome sequencing, was present in heterozygous state in the parents. The patient had low serum copper and ceruloplasmin.
