phenotypes.phenotype: Mitochondrial complex V (ATP synthase) deficiency, nuclear type 7

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex V deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC5DN7) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ATP5PO gene ({600828}) on chromosome 21q22.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial complex V deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC5DN7) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by hypotonia and global developmental delay apparent soon after birth. More variable features include poor growth, seizures, dystonia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and brain imaging abnormalities. Some affected individuals die in infancy or childhood ({2:Zech et al., 2022}, {1:Ganapathi et al., 2022}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of mitochondrial complex V deficiency, nuclear types, see MC5DN1 ({604273}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Zech et al. (2022)} reported a girl of European descent (patient 4) with MC5DN7 resulting in death at 6 years of age. She presented in the neonatal period with fever-induced partial seizures, hypotonia, and increased CSF lactate levels. She later showed acquired microcephaly, global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development and speech delay, inability to walk independently, and dystonia. Brain imaging showed progressive brain atrophy, delayed myelination, and hypoplasia of the lower part of the cerebellar vermis. She had neurologic regression with progression of the seizure phenotype, resulting in death from refractory status epilepticus at 6 years of age.

{1:Ganapathi et al. (2022)} reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated families with MC5DN7. Family 1 was consanguineous and of Moroccan descent, whereas family 2 was nonconsanguineous and of Turkish descent. The affected patient in family 1 and 1 of the sibs in family 2 died at 4 and 6 months of age, respectively; the other affected sib in family 2 was alive at 3 years of age. Features included intrauterine growth retardation, hypotonia, neonatal respiratory distress, and global developmental delay. Two patients including the 3-year-old had clinical seizures, with infantile spasms, generalized seizures, and myoclonic seizures consistent with epileptic encephalopathy; the third patient had EEG abnormalities. All patients had progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Brain imaging showed cerebral atrophy with enlarged ventricles and variable other abnormalities in the patients, including periventricular cysts and white matter changes, thin corpus callosum, cavum septum pellucidum, and delayed myelination. One patient showed signal abnormalities in the basal ganglia consistent with Leigh syndrome. Laboratory studies showed increased lactate; 1 patient had elevated urine 3-MGA. Patient fibroblasts and muscle samples showed mitochondrial complex V deficiency. The sibs in family 2 showed mild dysmorphic features, including high forehead, prominent metopic suture, mildly depressed nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, full cheeks, and deep philtrum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MC5DN7 in the family reported by {2:Zech et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 6-year-old girl (patient 4) with MC5DN7, {2:Zech et al. (2022)} identified compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the ATP5PO gene ({600828.0001} and {600828.0002}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were inherited from the unaffected parents. Patient fibroblasts showed reduced ATP5PO levels, and proteomics studies showed significant underexpression of ATP5PO and 4 other ATPase subunits compared to controls, consistent with a loss-of-function effect. ATPase was decreased to about 50% that of controls, and there was evidence for defective ATPase assembly. This patient was ascertained from a large cohort of 2,962 individuals with mitochondrial disease or dystonia who underwent whole-exome sequencing.

In 3 affected patients from 2 unrelated families (family 1 of Moroccan origin and family 2 of Turkish origin) with MC5DN7, {1:Ganapathi et al. (2022)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the ATP5PO gene ({600828.0003}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in both families; it was not present in the gnomAD database. Studies of patient cells and in yeast showed that the mutation decreased ATPase activity, disrupted complex V assembly, and impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with intracranial hemorrhage, seizures, and spasticity

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with intracranial hemorrhage, seizures, and spasticity (NEDIHSS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the ESAM gene ({614281}) on chromosome 11q24.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with intracranial hemorrhage, seizures, and spasticity (NEDIHSS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by prenatal or neonatal onset of intracranial hemorrhage, usually with ventriculomegaly and calcifications, resulting in parenchymal brain damage. Some affected individuals have symptoms incompatible with life and die in utero. Those that survive show profound global developmental delay with almost no motor or cognitive skills, hypotonia, spasticity, and seizures. Other features may include facial dysmorphism, retinal vascular abnormalities, and poor overall growth. The pathogenesis of the disease likely results from dysfunction of vascular endothelial cells in the brain ({1:Lecca et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Lecca et al. (2023)} reported 13 individuals, including 4 fetuses, from 8 unrelated families (families A-H) with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder associated with intracranial hemorrhage apparent in utero or soon after birth. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts and the GeneMatcher program after exome sequencing identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the ESAM gene. All families were consanguineous except for family C, who was from Spain. Families A, B, E, and F originated from the same geographical area in Turkey (southeastern Anatolia), family D was Algerian, and families G and H were of Arab Bedouin descent. Prenatal ultrasound and brain imaging soon after birth showed hydrocephalus, enlarged ventricles, intracranial hemorrhage, and cerebral microangiopathy with cerebral calcifications. Cerebral atrophy, thin corpus callosum, periventricular leukomalacia, and focal white matter lesions were also observed. One stillborn 31-week-old fetus (patient 10) had congenital heart defects, fetal hydrops, foot deformities, and renal medullary hemorrhage. Of the 9 liveborn children, 2 died at 13 months and 5.5 years, respectively; the others were alive and ranged from 19 months and 13 years of age. Some patients had poor overall growth with microcephaly, respiratory distress, and feeding difficulties; 2 older patients (1 and 7) were tube-fed at 10 and 13 years. The surviving patients had axial hypotonia, severe global developmental delay with poor head control, inability to sit or walk, profound intellectual disability with poor or absent speech, epilepsy, and spasticity (usually spastic tetraparesis) with hyperreflexia. Four patients showed retinal hemorrhages or retinal ischemia with increased tortuosity of retinal vasculature. P2 had iris coloboma and retinal detachment, whereas sibs 4 and 5 had cortical blindness. Most patients had variable dysmorphic facial features, including bitemporal narrowing, triangular face, smooth philtrum, high-arched eyebrows, bulbous nasal tip, long eyelashes, abnormal vermilion, high narrow palate, wide nasal bridge, upslanted palpebral fissures, prominent chin, and microretrognathia. {1:Lecca et al. (2023)} noted that the features in this disorder overlap with a clinical diagnosis of cerebral palsy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDIHSS in the families reported by {1:Lecca et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 13 patients, including 4 fetuses, from 8 unrelated families with NEDIHSS, {1:Lecca et al. (2023)} identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the ESAM gene ({614281.0001}-{614281.0004}). The mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregated with the disorder in the families; all were predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and result in a loss of ESAM function. Fetal brain tissue from one of the affected individuals at 31 weeks' gestational age (P10, family A) with the c.155del mutation ({614281.0001}) showed lack of ESAM staining in the capillary endothelial cells. In vitro studies of endothelial progenitor cells derived from patient P1 (also family A) showed aberrant formation of capillary-like tube structures, including defects in proliferation, migration, and tubulogenesis with decreased numbers of branch points and decreased tube length compared to controls and to her heterozygous parents. RT-PCR on P1's cells showed no detectable ESAM expression. Functional studies of the other mutations were not performed. {1:Lecca et al. (2023)} concluded that proper cerebrovascular maturation is important for normal neuronal growth and brain development, and that brain endothelial dysfunction plays a role in neurodevelopmental disorders.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-89 (SPG89) is caused by homozygous mutation in the AMFR gene ({603243}) on chromosome 16q13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-89 (SPG89) is characterized by symptom onset in the first years of life. Affected individuals show delayed motor development with abnormal spastic gait and hyperreflexia of the lower limbs. Some patients may have mildly impaired intellectual development or learning difficulties ({1:Deng et al., 2023}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of autosomal recessive SPG, see SPG5A ({270800}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Deng et al. (2023)} reported 20 patients from 8 unrelated consanguineous families of various origins (Morocco, Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, and Syria) with autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia. The patients were ascertained through international collaboration and the GeneMatcher program after biallelic mutations in the AMFR gene were identified. The patients, who ranged from 5 to 24 years of age, presented with motor delay, but all achieved walking (as late as 7 years) with an unsteady gait due to spasticity of the lower limbs. Hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses, muscle cramps, and reduced hip flexion were also observed. Most patients had a pure form of the disorder, but about half of the patients showed global developmental delay with mildly impaired intellectual development or learning disabilities. Three of 6 patients in family 3 had a severe phenotype with spastic quadriparesis; these individuals also had generalized seizures. Two other patients had febrile seizures, and 1 patient had focal seizures. Five of 9 patients who underwent brain imaging had a thin corpus callosum. The affected sibs in family 1 had normal serum cholesterol levels.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SPG89 in the families reported by {1:Deng et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 20 patients from 8 unrelated consanguineous families with SPG89, {1:Deng et al. (2023)} identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the AMFR gene (see, e.g., {603243.0001}-{603243.0005}). Fibroblasts derived from patients of 2 families (1 and 8) showed complete absence of the main 73-kD AMFR isoform. If expressed, the truncated AMFR proteins would lack important functional domains, causing endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) dysfunction. AMFR-null neural stem cells showed downregulation of lipogenic genes and increased cholesterol synthesis, likely due to the stabilization of HMGCR ({142910}). There was altered lipid metabolism with increased numbers of enlarged lipid droplets; these defects could be rescued by expression of wildtype AMFR. Patient-derived fibroblasts and carrier fibroblasts also showed enlarged lipid droplets in a dose-dependent manner. Although there was no evidence of ER stress, electron microscopic studies showed abnormally dilated ER morphology in mutant cells. These data suggested that altered lipid metabolism and loss of ERAD function are part of the disease mechanism (see ANIMAL MODEL).

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Deng et al. (2023)} found that CRISPR-Cas9-mediated knockdown of the amfra gene in zebrafish resulted in smaller length and dysregulation of lipid homeostasis. There was increased lipid content, downregulation of lipogenic gene expression, and increased cholesterol synthesis. Electron microscopy showed dilated ER morphology. Amfra-null zebrafish demonstrated impaired touch-evoked escape responses associated with decreased axonal branching. Hmgcr ({142910}) was expected to be stabilized by the absence of amfra. Treatment of amfra-null embryos with statins (simvastatin and atorvastatin) resulted in increased length and rescued the abnormal motor behavior. Atorvastatin fully corrected axon branching defects observed in the amfra-null larvae.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-90B (SPG90B) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SPTSSA gene ({613540}) on chromosome 14q13. One such patient has been reported.

Heterozygous mutation in the SPTSSA gene causes autosomal dominant SPG90A ({620416}).

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-90B (SPG90B) is characterized by motor impairment and progressive lower extremity spasticity as well as neurologic findings, cognitive impairment, and hearing loss ({1:Srivastava et al., 2023}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of autosomal recessive SPG, see SPG5A ({270800}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Srivastava et al. (2023)} reported a patient who presented with motor delay, with walking at 2 years of age. He was diagnosed with hearing loss at 3 years of age. He was diagnosed with rolandic seizures at 6 years of age. He developed contractures in his lower extremities and required surgical release of the tendons in the lower extremities at 7 years of age. At 10 years of age he had motor regression and lost the ability to walk. Brain MRI showed mild thinning of the corpus callosum at 12 years of age. At 22 years of age, he had weakness and spasticity more prominent in the lower than in the upper extremities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SPG90B in the family reported by {1:Srivastava et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In a 22-year-old man (patient 3), born to nonconsanguineous Ashkenazi-Jewish parents, with autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-90B, {1:Srivastava et al. (2023)} identified a homozygous 2-bp deletion in the SPTSSA gene (c.171_172del; {613540.0002}). Expression of SPTSSA with the mutation in HEK293 cells led to higher intracellular serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) activity and elevated de novo sphingolipid synthesis compared to cells expressing wildtype SPTSSA. Furthermore, sphingolipid synthesis was less responsive to cotransfection with ORMDL3 ({610075}) in the cells expressing mutant compared to wildtype SPTSSA. {1:Srivastava et al. (2023)} concluded that the mutation in SPTSSA impaired negative regulation of SPTSSA by ORMDLs.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that multiple mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome-7 (MMDS7) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the glycine cleavage system H protein gene (GCSH; {238330}) on chromosome 16q23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome-7 (MMDS7) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a clinical spectrum ranging from neonatal fatal glycine encephalopathy to an attenuated phenotype of developmental delay, behavioral problems, limited epilepsy, and variable movement problems ({1:Arribas-Carreira et al., 2023}).

For a general description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of multiple mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome, see MMDS1 ({605711}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Majethia et al. (2021)} reported 3 patients from 2 families, including a sib pair, with elevated glycine, progressive lethargy, seizures, and mutation in the GCSH gene. Patient 1 presented on day 32 of life with lethargy, poor feeding, and developmental delay. He developed myoclonic seizures and at 3 years of age he had microcephaly. Plasma glycine, CSF glycine, and a plasma/CSF glycine ratio were elevated at 1 year of age. MRI spectroscopy at 1 year of age showed a lactate peak in the putamen. Brain MRI at 45 days of life showed abnormal signal in the putamen and caudate nucleus, and a repeat MRI at 1 year of age showed cystic encephalomalacia in the basal ganglia and brainstem. Patient 2 presented at 48 hours of life with hypotonia, lethargy, and seizures. Brain MRI at 3 months of age showed abnormal signal in the lentiform nuclei, caudate, and thalamus. Laboratory testing demonstrated hypernatremia, elevated lactate, and metabolic acidosis. She died at 22 months of age due to seizures. Patient 3, the sister of patient 2, presented with respiratory acidosis, seizures, hypotonia, and poor respiratory effort on day 3 of life. She died on day 10 of life. Brain MRI at day 4 of life showed restricted diffusion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, corona radiata, parietooccipital gray matter, and posterior tegmental tracts of the brainstem.

{1:Arribas-Carreira et al. (2023)} reported 5 unrelated patients with glycine encephalopathy ranging from lethal to attenuated and mutation in the GCSH gene. Symptom onset ranged from day 1 of life to 3 months of age. Patient 1 presented on day 1 of life with lethargy and hypotonia that progressed to coma and seizures. She also had liver dysfunction and thrombocytopenia. An EEG showed burst-suppression pattern and she died on day 18 of life. Patient 2 presented on day 3 of life with lethargy, hypotonia, and hypoglycemia. He required ventilation from day 4 of life. An EEG showed burst-suppression pattern and paroxysmal epileptic activity. He died on day 7 of life. Patient 3 presented at 2 months of life with infantile spasms and seizures. She also had progressive developmental delay and poor feeding. An EEG showed hypsarrhythmia and multifocal epilepsy. She died at 11 months of age. Patient 5 presented at day 5 of life with apnea and cyanosis and required ventilation for 2 weeks. Moderate global developmental delay and a suspected dystonic movement disorder were observed at 6 months of age. At 20 months of age, he had global developmental delay, generalized dystonia, irritability, and hyperactivity. Brain MRI at 18 months of age showed reduced volume of the caudate nucleus. Patient 6 presented at 3 months of age with partial seizures. Brain MRI showed diffusion restriction of the supratentorial white matter. At 6 months of age he had flexion spasms. At 3 years 7 months of age he had severe global developmental delay.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MMDS7 in family 2 reported by {2:Majethia et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 3 patients, including a sib pair, from 2 Indian families with MMDS7, {2:Majethia et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous mutation (c.1A-G, {238330.0002}) in the GCSH gene predicted to disrupt the methionine start site. Homozygosity mapping demonstrated a 490-kb region of homozygosity on chromosome 16 shared by the 2 families.

In 5 unrelated patients with MMDS7, {1:Arribas-Carreira et al. (2023)} identified biallelic mutations in the GCSH gene ({238330.0002}-{238330.0008}). Analysis of the mutations in patient cells, COS7 cells, and/or yeast cells showed that the mutations had variable effects in glycine exchange and protein lipoylation. Most of the mutations resulted in a hypomorphic effect on both glycine exchange and lipoylation, whereas some mutations affected only 1 function. Patient phenotypes showed some correlation to the enzyme defect of either of the 2 GCSH enzyme functions (glycine exchange or lipoylation).

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor and language delay, ocular defects, and brain abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with motor and language delay, ocular defects, and brain abnormalities (NEDMLOB) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the INTS11 gene ({611354}) on chromosome 1p36.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor and language delay, ocular defects, and brain abnormalities (NEDMLOB) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by the onset of features in infancy or early childhood. Affected individuals show hypotonia, severe motor delay with ataxic gait or sometimes an inability to achieve walking, and impaired intellectual development with speech and language delay. Ocular defects can include optic atrophy, nystagmus, strabismus, and retinal dystrophy. Additional features may include seizures (in some), dysmorphic facial features, poor overall growth, and variable brain imaging abnormalities ({1:Tepe et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Tepe et al. (2023)} reported 15 patients from 10 unrelated families with a neurodevelopmental disorder who were ascertained through collaborative efforts, including communications through GeneMatcher, the Undiagnosed Diseases Network (UDN), and the Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) study after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the INTS11 gene. The patients, who ranged from 2 to 18 years of age, presented in infancy or early childhood with global developmental delay. Five female patients from 2 unrelated families died between 6 and 18 years of age. Several patients showed intrauterine growth retardation or poor overall growth, and about half had microcephaly (down to -4.6 SD). Common features of the disorder included hypotonia, poor head control, delayed walking or inability to walk, severe speech delay or absent speech, and impaired intellectual development. Those that walked had an ataxic unsteady gait with poor coordination. Five patients had seizures, which were refractory in 2 sibs from family 1. These sibs presented at birth with club foot, nystagmus, and optic atrophy. Both developed severe refractory seizures in infancy, showed progressive microcephaly, and did not acquire any milestones. They died at 18 and 6 years of age. Three sibs in family 10 had respiratory distress with stridor, tracheomalacia, and narrowing of the larynx, resulting in death in all by age 13. Most patients had variable ophthalmologic findings, including optic atrophy, nystagmus, strabismus, myopia, hypermetropia, impaired vision, and retinal dystrophy. Dysmorphic features, observed in some patients, included triangular shaped head, high forehead, receding forehead, bitemporal narrowing, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, narrow chin, broad nose, flat nasal bridge, cleft lip or palate, macroglossia, coarse facies, retrognathia, thin upper lip, wide mouth, and low-set ears. Brain imaging showed variable abnormalities, including progressive cerebral atrophy, cerebellar atrophy, pontocerebellar atrophy, simplified gyral pattern, corpus callosum abnormalities, enlarged ventricles, and myelination defects. Less common features included swallowing difficulties, gastroesophageal reflux sometimes requiring tube feeding, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, dyskinesia, athetotic movements, and scoliosis. Some had nonspecific skeletal defects, such as premature closure of the fontanels, shortened long bones, short tapering fingers, broad distal phalanges, vertebral flattening, and joint hyperlaxity.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMLOB in the families reported by {1:Tepe et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 15 patients from 10 unrelated families with NEDMLOB, {1:Tepe et al. (2023)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the INTS11 gene (see, e.g., {611354.0001}-{611354.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, were either not present in the gnomAD database or present at low frequencies in the heterozygous state. There were 14 missense mutations, 2 splice site mutations, 2 frameshifts, and 1 nonsense. The mutations were spread throughout the gene. Studies of patient cells were not performed, but expression of some of the orthologous missense mutations in Ints11-null Drosophila showed that 2 were unable to rescue lethality, consistent with a strong loss-of-function effect, whereas others were able to rescue lethality, but caused a reduction in lifespan, suggesting weak loss-of-function alleles.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Tepe et al. (2023)} found that Ints11 is expressed in larval and adult Drosophila central nervous system (CNS), where it localized to both neuronal and glial cells. Genetically modified Drosophila with a homozygous deletion of the Ints11 gene died prematurely as L2 larvae. Targeted loss of Ints11 in Drosophila neuronal cells did not cause any obvious phenotype, whereas loss of Inst11 in glial cells caused a significant reduction in the number of eclosed flies, as well as impaired climbing speed and a shorter lifespan. These data indicated that fly Ints11 has an important function in the glia of the fly CNS. Expression of human INTS11 did not rescue the lethality associated with the Ints11-null mutant in flies, indicating that the human gene cannot functionally replace fly Ints11.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and movement abnormalities (NEDMIM) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TTI1 gene ({614425}) on chromosome 20q11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly and movement abnormalities (NEDMIM) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, and delayed walking with an abnormal gait. Affected individuals may show hypotonia or hypertonia with spasticity, ataxia, and choreoathetoid movements. Most patients have microcephaly and short stature. Ophthalmic features, behavioral abnormalities, and nonspecific dysmorphic features are commonly observed. Additional more variable features include seizures, brain imaging abnormalities, and skeletal defects ({1:Serey-Gaut et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Serey-Gaut et al. (2023)} reported 11 patients from 9 unrelated families of various ethnic descent with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The patients were ascertained through international collaboration and the GeneMatcher program after biallelic TTI1 mutations were identified; 2 of the families were consanguineous. The patients, who ranged from 3 to 20 years of age, had poor overall growth, including 8 with short stature and 9 with microcephaly (-2.0 to -9.2 SD). All had moderate to severe global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, and delayed walking; 1 patient was nonambulatory at age 8. Variable behavioral abnormalities, including aggressive outbursts, self-mutilation, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and stereotypies, were commonly observed. Most patients received special education, but had limited autonomy. About half of the patients showed movement disorders, including hypotonia, hypertonia with spasticity, ataxic gait, waddling gait, and choreoathetoid movements. Four patients had seizures, including 2 with a clinical diagnosis of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and 1 with infantile febrile seizures. Six of 8 patients showed nonspecific brain abnormalities on MRI, including thin corpus callosum, decreased white matter volume, enlarged ventricles, and cerebral and cerebellar volume loss. Seven patients had ophthalmic abnormalities, including strabismus, esotropia, hypermetropia, and myopia; one patient had nystagmus and cortical visual impairment. Variable dysmorphic features were present in most patients: these included upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthus, short palpebral fissures, smooth or short philtrum, large ears, low-set ears, prominent nose, upturned nose, anteverted nares, micrognathia, wide mouth, widely spaced teeth, and thin upper lip. Seven patients had variable skeletal findings, such as scoliosis, kyphosis, coxa vara, hip dysplasia, genu varum, equinovalgus, tapering fingers, and fifth finger clinodactyly. Five patients had features of hypogonadism (cryptorchidism, amenorrhea, hypoplastic genitalia), and 3 had renal anomalies, including 2 with vesicoureteral reflux.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDMIM in the families reported by {1:Serey-Gaut et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 11 patients from 9 unrelated families with NEDMIM, {1:Serey-Gaut et al. (2023)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the TTI1 gene (see, e.g., {614425.0001}-{614425.0005}). There were 10 missense mutations, 2 nonsense, 2 splice site, and a frameshift. In vitro functional studies were performed on some of the missense mutations: S402P, L767S ({614425.0001}), S838L, and D921N ({614425.0005}). Immunoprecipitation studies showed that the missense mutations studied could interact with the TTT and PIKK complexes, but caused variable alterations in the composition of dimers of mTOR ({601231}) and raptor ({607130}) in the mTORC1 complex. Some mutations caused more stable active mTOR complexes, whereas others formed less active mTOR complexes compared to wildtype. Cells expressing the mutations showed variable alterations in cell-cycle progression, impaired growth recovery after starvation, and altered UV-induced DNA repair damage responses compared to controls. Patient-derived fibroblasts showed variably altered mTORC1 activity and impaired mitochondrial function compared to controls.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts-3 (MLC3) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GPRC5B gene ({605948}) on chromosome 16p12.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts-3 (MLC3) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by increased head circumference in infancy followed by progressive motor and cognitive decline in early childhood. Affected individuals either do not achieve walking or lose independent ambulation in the first or second decades. Cognitive impairment is variable and accompanied by poor speech and dysarthria. Most patients have early-onset seizures, which may be mild or refractory. Brain imaging shows unremitting megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts and swelling of the cerebral white matter ({1:Passchier et al., 2023}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts, see MLC1 ({604004}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Passchier et al. (2023)} reported 3 unrelated patients (P1-P3), ranging from 19 to 27 years of age, who presented with increased head circumference between 6 and 9 months of age. P1 and P2 had delayed motor development, with P2 walking at 3 years of age and P1 never achieving walking. P3 had normal early development and walked at 13 months. Slow motor decline was noted in all patients between 4 and 8 years of age, resulting in loss of independent ambulation and full wheelchair dependency by 6 years in P1 and P2 and 12 years in P3. Motor decline was characterized by clumsiness, spasticity of the upper and lower limbs, trunk and limb ataxia, rigidity, and variable dystonia. Cognitive decline was noted at age 4 in P1, and at 14 to 15 years of age in P2 and P3. Dysarthria was present in all 3, and P2 had dysphagia. The seizure phenotype was variable. P1 developed severe refractory epilepsy at age 4, P2 had mild epilepsy beginning at age 14, and P3 had 2 single seizures after a fall as an adult. At age 19, P1 had limited motor function, marked cognitive deficit, and no speech. At 27 years, P2 could handle objects and use a wheelchair, but had mild cognitive and speech deficits. P3 had mild cognitive deficits and mood problems at age 24. Brain imaging in all patients showed classic unremitting megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with diffusely abnormal and swollen cerebral white matter and subcortical cysts in the anterior temporal and frontal white matter.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the GPRC5B gene that were identified in patients with MLC3 by {1:Passchier et al. (2023)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 3 unrelated patients (P1-P3) with MLC3, {1:Passchier et al. (2023)} identified 2 different de novo heterozygous 3-bp in-frame duplications in the GPRC5B gene ({605948.0001} and {605948.0002}). Both mutations occurred in the fourth transmembrane protein domain. The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Western blot analysis of patient lymphoblasts showed a strong increase in GPRC5B levels compared to controls. Levels of modulator of VRAC current-1 (MLC1; {605908}) were similar to controls, but levels of the cation channel TRPV4 ({605427}) were strongly decreased. In vitro functional studies showed that regulatory volume decrease (RVD) in patient lymphoblasts was reduced following swelling compared to controls. These findings indicated disturbed volume regulation in patient lymphoblasts, potentially due to increased GPRC5B expression. Overexpression of mutant and wildtype GPRC5B in human astrocytoma cells increased volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) function to similar degrees. {1:Passchier et al. (2023)} suggested that increased GPRC5B expression causes chronic white matter edema by disrupting fine tuning of the essential volume-regulating channels VRAC and TRPV4.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that remitting megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts-4 (MLC4) is caused by homozygous mutation in the AQP4 gene ({600308}) on chromosome 18q11. One such family has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Remitting megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts-4 (MLC4) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by macrocephaly in infancy associated with developmental delay, delayed walking, variable cognitive decline, behavioral abnormalities, and early-onset seizures. The severity of neurologic dysfunction is variable, even within a family, but tends to show improvement with time. Brain imaging shows swelling of the cerebral white matter and subcortical cysts in the anterior temporal region, consistent with MLC. Brain imaging abnormalities also tend to improve with time, indicating a remitting disease course ({1:Passchier et al., 2023}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts, see MLC1 ({604004}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Passchier et al. (2023)} reported a brother (P4) and a sister (P5), born of consanguineous parents, who developed macrocephaly in the first 6 months of life; head circumference normalized in the boy and remained just above 2 SD in the girl. Both showed developmental delay and hypotonia, although P4 was more severely affected. He walked at 4-5 years, whereas his sister walked at age 2. Both had seizures from 1 year of age. P4 had frequent status epilepticus, which eventually was controlled, and P5 had epilepsy that was well-controlled. At 16 years of age, P4 had marked cognitive decline with limited language ability. He could walk with difficulty and had limited hand function. Additional features in P4 included truncal and limb ataxia, dystonia, rigidity, and dysarthria. At age 13, P5 had close to normal motor function with mild clumsiness and mild cognitive deficit. Both patients demonstrated behavioral problems in early childhood, including agitation, impulsivity, and hyperactivity, which later improved (P4) or normalized (P5). Brain imaging of P4 at 8 months of age showed diffuse signal abnormalities, mild swelling of the cerebral white matter, and subcortical cysts in the anterior temporal region. Follow-up at age 4 showed normalization of the cerebral white matter, but persistence of small temporal cysts. Brain imaging of P5 showed similar findings, but milder. The brain imaging findings were consistent with remitting MLC.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MLC4 in the family reported by {1:Passchier et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 2 sibs (P4 and P5), born of consanguineous parents, with MLC4, {1:Passchier et al. (2023)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the AQP4 gene (A215T; {600308.0001}) affecting the second NPA motif that forms part of the channel pore. The mutation, which was found by a combination of homozygosity mapping and candidate gene sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Western blot analysis of MDCK cells transfected with the mutation showed no detectable expression of mutant AQP4, suggesting that the mutant protein is unstable and rapidly degraded. Functional studies showed no change in swelling and shrinking rate constants when the cells with the A215T mutation were exposed to hypotonic or hypertonic shock, whereas cells with wildtype AQP4 responded with increased swelling and shrinking under the same conditions. Overexpression of the A215T mutation in HEK293 cells showed detectable, but reduced, AQP4 membrane localization compared to controls. Mutant AQP4 formed large intracellular protein aggregates, and there was a 60% reduction in membrane localization compared to wildtype. Overexpression of mutant AQP4 increased swelling and shrinking in response to shock, but the rates were significantly reduced compared to wildtype. The findings suggested that mutant A215T AQP4 reaching the cell membrane retains some residual water channel function.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-73 (MRD73) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TAF4 gene ({601796}) on chromosome 20q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-73 (MRD73) is a highly variable neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired intellectual development that ranges from mild to severe, speech delay, behavioral abnormalities, and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features ({2:Janssen et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Bertoli-Avella et al. (2021)} reported 2 unrelated patients with neurodevelopmental delay and dysmorphic facial features. Clinical details were limited, but both patients showed global developmental delay from infancy. One had prenatal increased nuchal translucency, premature birth, short stature, and intellectual disability. The other had hypotonia, delayed speech and language development, and triangular face with narrow nasal bridge and deep-set eyes.

{2:Janssen et al. (2022)} reported 8 unrelated patients, ranging from 2 to 18 years of age, with variable neurodevelopmental abnormalities associated with de novo heterozygous putative loss-of-function mutations in the TAF4 gene. The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after genetic analysis identified the mutations. Seven patients had mildly to moderately impaired intellectual development, and 7 had speech delay. P2, who was the only patient without intellectual disability, showed speech improvement over time. P1 and P2 were able to attend mainstream schools. P6 was more severely affected and only spoke 2- to 3-word sentences at age 12 years. Several patients had mild behavioral features, including shyness and autism or autistic features. Three patients had mildly delayed walking by 2-3 years of age, and a few showed gait abnormalities, such as toe-walking. Two patients had febrile seizures, including 1 who also had a single nonfebrile seizure. Dysmorphic facial features were noted in all patients, although there was not a common gestalt. Features included prominent nose, high or low nasal bridge, wide nasal bridge, short or long philtrum, prominent philtrum, abnormal palpebral fissures (short, long, narrow, upslanting, downslanting), arched eyebrows, synophrys, small or large ears, low-set ears, posteriorly rotated ears, prominent midface, retrognathia, and high palate. Two patients had hypermetropia. Some patients had joint laxity, mild flexion contractures of the knees or elbows, scoliosis, kyphosis, or hyperlordosis. Brain imaging, when performed, showed mild cerebellar abnormalities in 2 patients.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the TAF4 gene that were identified in patients with MRD73 by {2:Janssen et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 unrelated patients with MRD73, {1:Bertoli-Avella et al. (2021)} identified different de novo heterozygous putative loss-of-function mutations in the TAF4 gene (see, e.g., Q949X, {601796.0001}). Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors postulated haploinsufficiency as the pathogenetic mechanism. The patients were ascertained from a data repository cohort of over 33,000 patients who underwent exome or genome sequencing.

In 8 unrelated patients with MRD73, {2:Janssen et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous putative loss-of-function mutations in the TAF4 gene (see, e.g., {601796.0002}-{601796.0005}). The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. The mutations, which were found by trio whole-exome or trio whole-genome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but all were predicted to result in a loss of function.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-58 (COXPD58) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TEFM gene ({616422}) on chromosome 17q11.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-58 (COXPD58) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a wide range of clinical presentations including neonatal lactic acidosis, epileptic encephalopathy, developmental delay and impaired intellectual development with nonspecific changes on brain MRI, or mitochondrial myopathy with a treatable neuromuscular transmission defect ({2:Van Haute et al., 2023}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, see COXPD1 ({609060}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {2:Van Haute et al. (2023)} described 7 patients from 5 families with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency with mutation in the TEFM gene. Disease onset ranged from birth to age 5 years. There was significant variability in disease severity, even within families. Patient 1, a 16-year-old boy, had typical developmental milestones until age 5 years, when he developed fatigable muscle weakness of his extremities, drooping eyelids, and fluctuating restriction of eye movements. By 11 years of age he had difficulty in walking. He developed seizures at 12 years of age. His sib, patient 2, presented with fatigable muscle weakness and fluctuating eye movement abnormalities in childhood and developed seizures at 11 years of age. He also had a tremor and impaired intellectual development. Serum lactate was increased in both sibs. Muscle biopsies in patients 1 and 2 demonstrated COX-negative ragged-red fibers and a severe combined defect of complexes I and IV. Patient 3 developed progressive respiratory distress and hypoglycemia on the first day of life. He then developed acute liver failure, increased creatine phosphokinase, and severe lactic acidosis. He died at 1 month of age of liver failure. Patient 4, previously reported by {1:Riley et al. (2020)} as patient 28, presented at 4 weeks of age with poor feeding, myoclonic jerks, and vomiting. She had rapid progression of her disease symptoms and developed seizures. She had feeding difficulties and required a gastrostomy. She died at 17 months of age. Patient 5, a 5-year-old girl, had a history of speech delay and was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder at 4 years of age. She had mild dysmorphic features, including epicanthus, tubular nasal bridge, and protruding columella. Patient 6, an 8-year-old boy, had typical motor development until the age of 2 years, when he developed visual impairment with nystagmus. His cognitive function was mildly delayed and he had learning difficulties, aggressive behavior, and hyperactivity. On examination, he had a wide-based gait and hypotonia. He also had bilateral optic atrophy. A brain MRI demonstrated cerebellar atrophy, abnormal white matter signal in the cerebellum, and thin corpus callosum. His sister, patient 7, had normal motor milestones but delayed speech and mild cognitive delay. Brain MRI demonstrated mild trigonal dysmyelination.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-58 in the families reported by {2:Van Haute et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: {2:Van Haute et al. (2023)} reported that 2 sibs (family 1) with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-58 demonstrated improvement in muscular symptoms (muscle weakness and ambulation) after treatment with salbutamol.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 7 patients from 5 families with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency-58, {2:Van Haute et al. (2023)} identified biallelic mutations in the TEFM gene (see, e.g., {616422.0001}-{616422.0005}), including 4 missense mutations, 1 frameshift mutation, 1 splice site mutation, and 1 in-frame deletion. The mutations were in homozygous state in 2 sib pairs (families 1 and 5) and in compound heterozygous state in the other 3 patients. Run-off transcription assays in purified recombinant TEFM with several of the mutations (Gly162_Arg163del, {616422.0005}; P157A, {616422.0001}, I159K, {616422.0003}; K188R) showed delayed processivity of POLRMT ({601778}) compared with wildtype TEFM. Gene expression analysis in skeletal muscle from 2 patients and fibroblasts from 3 patients demonstrated a decrease in promoter-distal mt-mRNAs, which was consistent with reduced levels of TEFM and likely impaired processivity of mtDNA transcription.

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that juvenile-onset dystonia-22 (DYT22JO) is caused by homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the TSPOAP1 gene ({610764}) on chromosome 17q22.

An adult-onset form of the disorder (DYT22AO; {620456}) is caused by homozygous missense mutation in the TSPOAP1 gene.

description.title: Description
description.content: Juvenile-onset dystonia-22 (DYT22JO) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by progressive, generalized dystonia associated with cognitive decline and cerebellar atrophy on brain imaging ({1:Mencacci et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Mencacci et al. (2021)} reported 4 patients from 2 families (families A and B) with progressive generalized dystonia associated with homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the TSPOAP1 gene. Three sibs from family A, a consanguineous Indian family, and 1 patient from family B had normal early language and motor development with mild learning disabilities presenting in primary school. All 4 patients developed dystonia early in their teenage years, which displayed a craniocaudal gradient. Symptoms included dysphonia, dysarthria, swallowing difficulties, upper extremity dystonia, and progressive gait abnormalities. All 4 patients also had cognitive deterioration. One of the patients also had seizures. Brain MRIs demonstrated cerebellar atrophy with predominance in the vermis.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DYT22JO in the families reported by {1:Mencacci et al. (2021)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients from 2 families with DYT22JO, {1:Mencacci et al. (2021)} identified homozygous putative loss-of-function mutations in the TSPOAP1 gene ({610764.0001}-{610764.0002}). The mutations were identified by homozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but complete loss of the gene in mice resulted in a similar phenotype (see ANIMAL MODEL).

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Mencacci et al. (2021)} generated TSPOAP1 knockout mice. The mutant mice had reduced spontaneous locomotion and signs of abnormal coordination. They also had increased dystonic events when treated with oxotremorine compared to wildtype mice. In the cerebellum of the mutant mice, the Purkinje cells had shortened dendritic trees, reduced excitatory synaptic puncta, and abnormal expression of synaptic markers. The cerebellar abnormalities were shown to be progressive, as they were not present in younger mice but developed with increasing age.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and speech delay, with or without seizures

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and speech delay, with or without seizures (NEDHSS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the EIF4A2 gene ({601102}) on chromosome 3q27. One family with compound heterozygous mutations has been reported.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and speech delay, with or without seizures (NEDHSS) is characterized by global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, and fine and gross motor delay. Most affected individuals are severely affected and may be unable to walk, have feeding difficulties requiring tube-feeding, and develop early-onset seizures. Additional features may include cortical blindness and nonspecific structural brain abnormalities. Rare individuals present only with hypotonia and mild developmental delay ({1:Paul et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
Through international collaborative efforts, including Matchmaker Exchange, {1:Paul et al. (2023)} identified 10 unrelated patients (patients 6-15), ranging from 2 to 9.5 years of age, with variable neurodevelopmental abnormalities associated with de novo heterozygous mutations in the EIF4A2 gene identified through exome sequencing. All patients had global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, which was severe. Common features included hypotonia, delayed gross and fine motor skills, and speech delay. Six patients were nonverbal. At least 1 patient (P11) had no speech and had not acquired sitting by 9.5 years of age. One patient had spastic paraparesis. A few patients had autistic features and variable behavioral abnormalities (head-banging, repetitive motions, limited interaction). Most patients had feeding issues with dysphagia, 6 were tube-fed, and 2 had constipation. Two patients showed hypoventilation and required a tracheostomy. Nine individuals had early-onset seizures of variable severity, including infantile spasms, focal, absence, generalized, and myoclonic. Two were diagnosed with West syndrome and 2 with Lennox-Gastaut. Three patients had cortical blindness. Some had nonspecific dysmorphic features, including macro- or microcephaly, high forehead, long palpebral fissures, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, broad nasal root, short philtrum, and micrognathia. Eight patients had nonspecific findings on brain imaging, including thin or short corpus callosum, decreased cerebral volume, enlarged ventricles, cerebellar hypoplasia, small pons, and gyral abnormalities.

<Subhead> Autosomal Recessive NEDHSS

{1:Paul et al. (2023)} also reported 2 sibs (P4 and P5), 11 and 18 years of age, with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder associated with compound heterozygous mutations in the EIF4A2 gene. Both had hypotonia and failure to thrive with feeding difficulties in infancy and remained tube-fed. They had severe global developmental delay with gross and fine motor delay (1 could not sit), severely impaired intellectual development with absent speech, and early-onset myoclonic seizures. Additional features included hypoventilation, visual impairment or blindness, and hearing impairment. Brain imaging showed multiple abnormalities, such as cerebral volume loss, abnormal brainstem and cerebellum, and gyral abnormalities. The disease course was consistent with a neurodegenerative process. The parents were unaffected.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the EIF4A2 gene that were identified in most patients with NEDHSS by {1:Paul et al. (2023)} occurred de novo. The transmission pattern of NEDHSS in 1 family (P4 and P5) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 10 unrelated patients (P6-P15) with NEDHSS, {1:Paul et al. (2023)} identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the EIF4A2 gene ({601102.0001}-{601102.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. All mutations occurred in 1 of 2 main functional domains, the C-terminal helicase domain or the N-terminal helicase ATP-binding domain, and were predicted to hinder protein function. Studies of patient cells were not performed. Various functional expression studies of 4 of the missense mutations in Drosophila showed that 3 mutations (G364E, L344F, and T243I), all located within or adjacent to the helicase C-terminal domain, resulted in climbing defects and disturbed eye development, and were unable to fully rescue lethality in eif4a2-null flies, consistent with a dominant loss-of-function effect. The fourth mutation (T216I), located in the N-terminal helicase ATP-binding domain, did not affect climbing, but caused defective wing development and was completely unable to rescue lethality, consistent with a toxic gain-of-function effect. Two sibs (P4 and P5) with a severe phenotype were found to be compound heterozygous for a frameshift and an in-frame deletion ({601102.0005} and {601102.0006}). Of note, 3 additional patients (P1, P2, and P3) with a mild phenotype were also identified: however, P1 carried a de novo heterozygous S2C variant that was present in 1 of 251,478 alleles in gnomAD (frequency of 4.0 x 10(-6)) and P3 was mosaic for a frameshift variant. P2, born of consanguineous Syrian parents, was homozygous for an in-frame deletion (D37del) that was found once in the heterozygous state in gnomAD. All 3 of these variants occurred in the N terminus upstream of the functional domains; studies of these variants were not performed. {1:Paul et al. (2023)} suggested that phenotypic variability in patients with mono- or biallelic EIF4A2 variants likely depends on the degree of functional impairment of the mutant protein.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: The Drosophila Eif4a2 gene encodes a negative regulator of decapentaplegic (Dpp) signaling that regulates embryo patterning, eye and wing morphogenesis, and stem cell identity formation. Complete loss of Eif4a2 in the fly results in pupal lethality ({1:Paul et al., 2023}).

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that susceptibility to infection-induced acute encephalitis-12 (IIAE12) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RNH1 gene ({173320}) on chromosome 11p15.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Infection-induced acute encephalitis-12 (IIAE12) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by episodic acute encephalopathy associated with infections and febrile illness. Patients present with neurologic symptoms in the first months or years of life, usually after normal early development. Brain imaging in the acute episodes shows restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and T2-weighted abnormalities in the periventricular and subcortical regions, which progresses to cavitation of previously affected areas. The long-term outcome is highly variable, even within families, ranging from death to severe neurologic deficits to normal outcomes ({2:Shashi et al., 2023}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of susceptibility to acute infection-induced encephalopathy, see {610551}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Hedberg-Oldfors et al. (2023)} reported 2 sibs, born of consanguineous Somali parents, who presented soon after birth with congenital cataracts, hypotonia, and feeding difficulties. They had global developmental delay, poor head control, and clumsy movements. Both had recurrent viral upper respiratory infections with fever, breathing difficulties, and feeding problems beginning at age 4 months and 8 months, respectively. These episodes were associated with macrocytic anemia and increased CSF levels of NEFL ({162280}) and GFAP ({137780}), suggesting neuroaxonal and astroglial injury. At age 7 months, the boy developed seizures and respiratory insufficiency that required ventilator treatment. At 8 months, he had fever and vomiting followed by severe hypotonia, multifocal seizures, and apnea. He became comatose with no spontaneous respiration. Brain imaging showed supratentorial ischemia and cerebral herniation, and he died. From 8 to 17 months of age, his younger sister had similar recurrent viral infections associated with seizures, respiratory insufficiency, and neurologic deterioration with loss of developmental skills. Brain imaging at 8 months of age showed increased T2-weighted signals in the thalamus, globus pallidus, and other cortical/subcortical regions. She was able to walk with aid at age 17 months, but had neurologic stagnation, subtle evidence of a myopathy, and required tube-feeding. She was noted to have exophoria, tent-shaped mouth, and small chin.

{2:Shashi et al. (2023)} reported 8 patients from 4 unrelated families who presented between 3 months and 6 years of age with acute encephalopathy associated with febrile illness or infection, usually viral. All had normal early development before the onset of symptoms. Neurologic features of the acute episodes included seizures, hemiplegia, decreased consciousness, hypotonia, abnormal posturing, feeding problems, and respiratory insufficiency. Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP; {123260}) and cytokines were observed in some patients, consistent with inflammation, and some patients had anemia. One patient developed atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) associated with thrombotic microangiopathy. Three patients died between 3 months and 4 years of age. Brain imaging during the acute episodes showed DWI restriction and T2-weighted abnormalities in the periventricular and deep white matter regions, including the thalami. Some patients had involvement of the brainstem and cerebellum. Later brain imaging showed parenchymal volume loss, ventriculomegaly, and extensive cavitation of previously affected areas. Of the 5 living patients, who ranged from 5 to 22 years of age, 2 had normal neurodevelopment (1 with emotional lability), whereas 3 had profound neurologic and intellectual disabilities. Two sibs in family 4, ages 16 and 22 years, were severely affected with little voluntary movement, diffuse spasticity, ankle clonus, contractures, scoliosis, absent speech, and chronic pigmentary retinopathy; both were tube-fed.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IIAE12 in the family reported by {1:Hedberg-Oldfors et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. In families with IIAE12 reported by {2:Shashi et al. (2023)}, the transmission pattern of the disorder indicated autosomal recessive inheritance with incomplete penetrance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 sibs, born of consanguineous parents of Somali origin, with IIAE12, {1:Hedberg-Oldfors et al. (2023)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the RNH1 gene ({173320.0001}). The mutation, which was found by a combination of whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The mutation was not present in public databases, including dbSNP (build 151), ExAC, Exome Sequencing Project, 1000 Genomes Project, and gnomAD. Western blot analysis of patient muscle tissue showed total absence of the RNH1 protein, consistent with a loss-of-function effect. Patient-derived fibroblasts showed increased sensitivity and increased apoptosis in response to RNase exposure, which was reversed by expression of wildtype RNH1. Noting that RNH1 has been shown to regulate inflammation, the authors hypothesized that the infection-induced deterioration in the patients may have resulted from lack of RNH1-mediated control of inflammasome activation.

In 8 children from 4 unrelated families with IIAE12, {2:Shashi et al. (2023)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the RNH1 gene ({173320.0002}-{173320.0007}). The patients were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after exome or genome sequencing identified the mutations. The mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregated with the disorder in the families; family 3 showed incomplete penetrance, as 2 unaffected family members also had biallelic mutations. There were 4 missense mutations, 1 nonsense, and 1 frameshift. All but 1 of the mutations affected highly conserved residues in LLR domains. Fibroblasts derived from patients in families 1 and 2 showed nearly undetectable RNH1 protein levels, suggesting a loss of function. Functional studies of the mutations were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: Epilepsy, early-onset, 3, with or without developmental delay

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that early-onset epilepsy-3 with or without developmental delay (EPEO3) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP6V0C gene ({108745}) on chromosome 16p13.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Early-onset epilepsy-3 with or without developmental delay (EPEO3) is an autosomal dominant neurologic disorder characterized by the onset of various types of seizures in the first months or years of life. Many patients present with febrile seizures and later develop afebrile seizures. The severity and disease course is highly variable: some affected individuals have global developmental delay or regression with impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, and motor delay, whereas others have normal psychomotor development. More severely affected individuals often show additional features, including hypotonia, gait ataxia, nonspecific dysmorphic features, behavioral abnormalities, and variable anomalies on brain imaging ({3:Mattison et al., 2023}, {5:Zhao et al., 2023}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of EPEO, see {617290}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Carvill et al. (2014)} reported an 8-year-old boy (patient T1911) who had onset of multiple seizure types at 7 months of age. He was noted to show fever sensitivity. EEG showed generalized spike-wave and multifocal discharges. He had severely impaired intellectual development and developmental regression. Brain imaging was normal.

{2:Ittiwut et al. (2021)} reported a 16-year-old girl, born of unrelated Thai parents, who presented at 2 years of age with generalized tonic-clonic seizures during a febrile illness after normal early development. She later developed multiple refractory afebrile seizures. Her intellectual development slowly regressed and then plateaued. At age 16, she could communicate in short sentences, but needed help with grooming and could not do math. The seizures continued despite treatment.

{3:Mattison et al. (2023)} reported 27 unrelated patients, including the patients reported by {1:Carvill et al. (2014)} and {2:Ittiwut et al. (2021)}, with early-onset seizures and neurodevelopmental abnormalities associated with de novo heterozygous ATP6V0C mutations identified through exome or genome sequencing. The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher Program. Almost all of the patients, who ranged from 12 months to 34 years of age, presented in the first months or years of life with various seizure types, including infantile spasms, febrile, generalized tonic-clonic, focal, focal dyscognitive seizures, absence, tonic, atonic, and myoclonic. The seizure status of a few patients was unknown. All patients had global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development that was severe to profound in most, but mild in some. Hypotonia, delayed walking, gait ataxia, and speech delay were also observed; some were nonverbal. Behavioral abnormalities such as head-banging, tantrums, and autism spectrum disorder were common. Many patients had nonspecific dysmorphic features, including microcephaly, micrognathia, retrognathia, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, round face, long palpebral fissures, downslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, deep-set eyes, synophrys, prominent nasal bridge, short nasal bridge, beaked nose, large mouth, high palate, and low-set ears. There did not appear to be a consistent facial gestalt. Thirteen of 21 patients studied had nonspecific variable abnormalities on brain imaging, including agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum or cerebellar vermis and delayed myelination. Four patients had cardiac anomalies and 3 had dental enamel defects. Scoliosis, tapering fingers, and feeding difficulties were present in a few patients.

{5:Zhao et al. (2023)} reported 2 unrelated patients, a 3-year-old boy (patient 1) and a 15-year-old boy (patient 2), who presented with febrile seizures at 7 months and 3 years of age, respectively. P1 developed afebrile seizures at 8 months of age, and EEG showed multifocal spikes and spiky discharges during sleep. Treatment with valproic acid led to control of seizures. He had developmental delay with poor coordination, frequent falls, and speech delay. Brain imaging was normal. P2 had febrile seizures in early childhood followed by the onset of afebrile seizures, including absence and myoclonic seizures, at 11 years of age. EEG showed polyspike and spike slow-wave discharges. At age 15, he had impaired intellectual development and language delay. Brain imaging showed right frontal lobe demyelination.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{4:Tian et al. (2022)} reported 6 individuals from 2 unrelated Chinese families with EPEO3 manifest as self-limited febrile seizures or generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures-plus (GEFS+). The proband in family 1 was a 5-year-old boy with onset of febrile seizures at 8 months of age followed by afebrile seizures, including generalized tonic-clonic and myoclonic. He responded to antiepileptic medication and became seizure-free at 4 years; neurodevelopment and intelligence were normal. His father and 2 older sisters, who also carried the mutation, had febrile seizures from 8 months to 5 years of age. They did not require seizure medication and had normal development and intelligence. The proband in family 2 was a 3-year-old boy who developed febrile seizures at 7 months of age, followed by afebrile seizures. He became seizure-free on valproic acid around 2 years of age. His 30-year-old paternal aunt, who also carried the mutation, had febrile seizures from 8 months to 5 years of age. The proband's unaffected father carried the mutation, indicating incomplete penetrance. All 3 individuals in family 2 had normal development and intelligence. The authors emphasized the favorable prognosis in these individuals.

{5:Zhao et al. (2023)} reported a 6-year-old girl (patient 3) who presented at 2.9 years of age with recurrent generalized tonic-clonic febrile seizures. She later developed atypical absence and myoclonic seizures associated with EEG abnormalities (spike slow-wave discharges). Brain imaging was normal. She was treated with medication and became seizure-free at 6.5 years of age with normal learning, language, and motor abilities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The heterozygous mutations in the ATP6V0C gene that were identified in patients with EPEO3 by {3:Mattison et al. (2023)} occurred de novo. Four patients were mosaic for the mutations.

The transmission pattern of EPEO3 in the families reported by {4:Tian et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In an 8-year-old boy (patient T1911) with EPEO3, {1:Carvill et al. (2014)} identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift mutation in the ATP6V0C gene ({108745.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the Exome Sequencing Project database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In a 16-year-old Thai girl, born of unrelated parents, with EPEO3, {2:Ittiwut et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous stop-loss mutation in the ATP6V0C gene ({108745.0002}) predicted to result in an abnormal extension of 35 residues at the C terminus of the protein (Ter156LeuExtTer35). The mutation, which was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Patient cells showed a 50% decrease in ATP6V0C expression compared to her mother. The findings suggested that the mutant transcript was expressed, but mostly degraded. The authors postulated haploinsufficiency as the most likely mechanism. However, {3:Mattison et al. (2023)} noted that a dominant-negative effect is also possible.

In 27 unrelated patients with EPEO3, including the patients reported by {1:Carvill et al. (2014)} and {2:Ittiwut et al. (2021)}, {3:Mattison et al. (2023)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the ATP6V0C gene (see, e.g., {108745.0003}-{108745.0007}). The patients were ascertained through collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher program, after the mutations were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing. There were 18 unique missense mutations affecting highly conserved residues, 4 frameshifts, and 1 stop-loss variant ({2:Ittiwut et al., 2021}). Four patients were mosaic for their mutation. None of the mutations were present in the gnomAD database. In vitro expression studies in VMA3 (the ortholog of ATP6V0C)-null yeast showed that 9 of 12 missense mutations studied were unable to rescue growth defects to variable degrees, consistent with a loss-of-function effect. Three mutations (G63A, F137L, and L150F) showed intermediate growth defects in the yeast studies. These 3 mutations caused impaired growth, reduced movement, uncoordinated movements, and shortened lifespan when expressed in C. elegans, and the abnormalities were exacerbated by osmotic stress conditions. Worms carrying these 3 mutations were hypersensitive to aldicarb treatment compared to controls, suggesting defects in neuronal synaptic transmission. Overall, the findings were consistent with the mutations resulting in a loss of protein function. However, the authors noted that some of the frameshift mutations are predicted to escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, and suggested that these and the missense mutations may act in a dominant-negative manner, while nonsense mutations may act through haploinsufficiency. {3:Mattison et al. (2023)} hypothesized that disruption of ATP6V0C activity could cause synaptic defects that affect neurotransmitter release, alter trafficking and sorting of neuropeptides and neuropeptide receptors, and perturb lysosomal and autophagy pathways.

In 6 individuals from 2 unrelated Chinese families with EPEO3 manifest as self-limited febrile seizures or generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures-plus (GEFS+), {4:Tian et al. (2022)} identified heterozygous variants in the ATP6V0C gene (A22T, {108745.0008} and c.361_373del, {108745.0009}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the seizure phenotype in both families, although there was 1 unaffected mutation carrier in family 2, suggesting incomplete penetrance. Neither variant was present in gnomAD. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but both were predicted to be damaging. All individuals had normal neurologic development and intelligence.

In 3 unrelated patients with EPEO3, {5:Zhao et al. (2023)} identified 3 different de novo heterozygous mutations in the ATP6V0C gene. P1 and P2, who showed subsequent developmental delay, carried an R119W mutation and an in-frame deletion (V99_S102del), respectively, whereas P3, who had normal development, carried a splice site mutation ({108745.0010}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were absent from the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but molecular modeling predicted that they would interfere with protein function.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Mattison et al. (2023)} found that knockdown of the orthologous Atp6v0c gene in Drosophila resulted in seizure-like behavior.

Head: Plagiocephaly
