phenotypes.phenotype: Cranial dysinnervation disorder, congenital, with absent corneal reflex and developmental delay

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder with absent corneal reflex and developmental delay (CCDDRD) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NEUROG1 gene ({601726}) on chromosome 5q31.

description.title: Description
description.content: Congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder with absent corneal reflex and developmental delay (CCDDRD) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by abnormal development of the proximal cranial sensory ganglia and nerves, mainly CN V (trigeminal nerve) and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve). Affected individuals present at birth or in early infancy with corneal opacities due to absent blinking. Most patients also have sensorineural deafness associated with hypoplastic or malformed cochlea and hypoplasia or agenesis of CN VIII. Developmental delay with poor speech and autistic behavior are also present. Additional features may include expressionless face, feeding or chewing difficulties due to oromotor dysfunction, and dysmorphic facial features ({1:Dupont et al., 2021}; {5:Sheth et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{6:Yavarna et al. (2015)} reported a 12-year-old boy, born of consanguineous Middle Eastern parents, with a syndromic neurocognitive disorder characterized by mild intellectual disability, corneal opacities, and absent corneal reflex. Clinical details were limited.

{1:Dupont et al. (2021)} reported a 12-year-old boy, born of unrelated Portuguese parents, who presented at birth with hypotonia and feeding difficulties and was later found to have profound bilateral sensorineural deafness and keratoconjunctivitis. He showed global developmental delay with walking at 3 years, and did not acquire expressive language. He attended a deaf school and learned sign language; IQ at age 10 was 62. Additional features included insomnia, hyperkinesia, self-injurious behavior, and brief myoclonic seizures. Physical examination at age 10 years showed deafness, apparent loss of facial sensation, oromotor dysfunction, absence of corneal reflexes with normal ocular motility, and unsteady gait. Dysmorphic features included long, asymmetric, and expressionless face with open mouth, long palpebral fissures, high-arched eyebrows, ocular leucoma in the right eye, and arched narrow palate. Brain imaging showed hypoplasia of cranial nerves V and VIII, marked atresia of the internal auditory canal, and hypoplasia of the cochlear labyrinth. EMG was compatible with an axonal sensory neuropathy.

{5:Sheth et al. (2023)} reported 2 sisters, born of Indian parents, with no eye blinking resulting in corneal ulceration and opacities, hearing loss, expressionless face, and developmental delay. The 6.8-year-old older sister, who was more severely affected, had difficulties chewing in infancy, profound developmental delay (walking at 5.5 years, babbling at 4 years), and autistic features, including poor social interaction, perseverative interests, and stereotypic movements. Dysmorphic features included flat occiput, facial asymmetry, ptosis, arched eyebrows, and long palpebral fissures. Brain imaging showed bilateral cochlear hypoplasia with only half basal turns, hypoplastic CN VIII, absent modiolus, narrowing of internal auditory canals, and dilated vestibules. Her 4-year-old younger sister had similar, but less severe, clinical features. Brain imaging in the sister showed cochlear hypoplasia with 1.5 turns, stenotic internal auditory canal, and absent CN VIII. She also had evidence of otitis media.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CCDDRD in the families reported by {1:Dupont et al. (2021)} and {5:Sheth et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

cytogenetics.title: Cytogenetics
cytogenetics.content: {4:Schroder et al. (2013)} reported a 6-year-old Turkish boy, born of consanguineous parents, who presented in infancy with global developmental delay, hypotonia, torticollis, and profound sensorineural deafness. Cranial imaging showed bilateral stenosis of the internal auditory canal and a hypoplastic cochlea with only a single widened cochlear turn (normal is 2.5 turns), consistent with Mondini malformation. The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) was assumed to be aplastic because no nerve structure reaching the cochlea could be detected. He walked at 2.5 years of age. At age 6, he had balance problems, faulty foot posture, hypotonia, increased salivation, and a severe gulp and mouth motor disorder resulting in feeding difficulties. The oromotor dysfunction was attributed to malfunction of CN V. IQ measurements were variable, but consistent with low-normal intelligence. Dysmorphic features included plagioscaphocephaly, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, high-arched eyebrows, elongated palpebral fissures, high and narrow palate, funnel chest, sacral dimple, and hypoplastic genitalia. Genomewide microarray analysis identified a homozygous 115-Mb deletion on chromosome 5q31 that included the NEUROG1, TIFAB ({612663}), and DCNP1 ({609710}) genes. The deletion, which was confirmed by PCR studies, was present in the heterozygous state in the unaffected parents. Based on animal studies (see ANIMAL MODEL), the authors concluded that loss of NEUROG1 was responsible for the main clinical features.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 12-year-old boy, born of consanguineous Middle Eastern parents, with CCDDRD, {6:Yavarna et al. (2015)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the NEUROG1 gene (R116L; {601726.0001}). The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Familial segregation was not reported. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In a 12-year-old Portuguese boy with CCDDRD, {1:Dupont et al. (2021)} identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the NEUROG1 gene (E68X; {601726.0002}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. The authors suggested that the mutation most likely led to production of a truncated protein with a loss of function. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In 2 sisters, born of Indian parents, with CCDDRD, {5:Sheth et al. (2023)} identified a homozygous frameshift mutation in the NEUROG1 gene ({601726.0003}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but the authors suggested that an abnormal protein could be produced. {5:Sheth et al. (2023)} noted that all reported NEUROG1 mutations affected the bHLH domain, likely disrupting its function.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{3:Ma et al. (1998)} generated Ngn1-deficient mice, which failed to generate the proximal subset of cranial sensory neurons. They concluded that Ngn1 is required for the activation of a cascade of downstream bHLH factors and functions in the determination of neuronal precursors.

Using immunocytochemistry, nerve tract tracing, and electron microscopy, {2:Ma et al. (2000)} characterized an abnormal inner ear phenotype in the Ngn1-null mutants generated by {3:Ma et al. (1998)}. In summary, Ngn1-null mutants lack differentiated inner ear sensory neurons. {2:Ma et al. (2000)} hypothesized that efferent and autonomic nerve fibers are lost secondarily to the absence of afferent nerve fibers. The Ngn1 mutant ears develop smaller sensory epithelia with hair cells that are morphologically normal but disorganized and reduced in number. {2:Ma et al. (2000)} concluded that Ngn1 is essential for development of the inner ear sensory neurons.

clinicalSynopsis: Perivascular PAS-positive hyalin deposits in papillary and upper reticular dermis (present but less marked in unexposed skin)
Patients rarely experience acute neuropsychiatric or abdominal attacks
Heterozygous relatives may exhibit cutaneous or neurovisceral attacks
Caused by mutation in the protoporphyrinogen oxidase gene (PPOX,)

Skin - Histology: Perivascular PAS-positive hyalin deposits in papillary and upper reticular dermis (present but less marked in unexposed skin)
Miscellaneous: Patients rarely experience acute neuropsychiatric or abdominal attacks
Heterozygous relatives may exhibit cutaneous or neurovisceral attacks
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the protoporphyrinogen oxidase gene (PPOX,)

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that childhood-onset variegate porphyria (VPCO) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the protoporphyrinogen oxidase gene (PPOX; {600923}) on chromosome 1q23.

Heterozygous mutation in the PPOX gene causes an autosomal dominant form of variegate porphyria (VP; {176200}).

description.title: Description
description.content:
Childhood-onset variegate porphyria (VPCO), also called 'homozygous' variegate porphyria, is a rare disorder of heme biosynthesis characterized by severe PPOX deficiency, onset of photosensitization by porphyrins in early childhood, skeletal abnormalities of the hand, and, less consistently, short stature, impaired intellectual development, and seizures. The term 'homozygous' refers to the presence of mutations on both alleles of the PPOX gene, resulting in earlier onset and more severe manifestations than those seen in variegate porphyria (VP), a low-penetrance disorder inherited as an autosomal dominant trait (summary by {15:Roberts et al., 1998}). Heterozygous family members of VPCO patients are usually clinically silent, but symptomatic heterozygotes have been reported ({12:Mustajoki et al., 1987}; {14:Palmer et al., 2001}; {7:Kauppinen et al., 2001}).

<Subhead> Nomenclature

'Homozygous' variegate porphyria was so designated before the molecular defect in PPOX was elucidated, on the basis of severe reduction in PPOX activity (between 5 and 20% of control values) compared to that seen in variegate porphyria (approximately 50% reduction), in which autosomal dominant transmission had been observed. It is probable that most cases of 'homozygous' variegate porphyria actually result from compound heterozygosity for PPOX mutations ({5:Frank et al., 1998}; {14:Palmer et al., 2001}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
Homozygous variegate porphyria was reported in 2 Czech sibs by {8:Korda et al. (1984)} and {9:Korda et al. (1985)} and in 2 unrelated English patients by {11:Murphy et al. (1986)}. In the family of {8:Korda et al. (1984)} and the first case of {11:Murphy et al. (1986)}, both parents were, by the biochemical evidence, heterozygotes. Photosensitivity dating from the first year or so of life, growth retardation, and raised red cell protoporphyrin concentration with 60 to 70% zinc chelation were the seemingly characteristic features. The Czech sibs also had mental retardation and nystagmus.

{12:Mustajoki et al. (1987)} described a 2.5-year-old Finnish boy with variegate porphyria, who was later found to have biallelic mutations in the PPOX gene ({7:Kauppinen et al., 2001}). The proband developed a severe bullous skin disease a few days after birth, followed by increased fragility and keloid scarring of exposed skin in spring and summer. The patient had high concentration of protoporphyrin in red cells, and lymphocyte protoporphyrinogen oxidase was very low in the patient and half-normal in his first-cousin parents, suggesting that the patient had homozygous variegate porphyria. Both grandmothers, who were sisters, had high fecal porphyrin content; and 1 grandmother was mildly affected, experiencing vesicular dermatitis in the summer followed by minor scarring on the exposed areas. {7:Kauppinen et al. (2001)} provided follow-up on the proband, noting that from 5 years of age, the proband had no severe acute photo reactions, but blistering and fragility with deep erosions complicated by bacterial infections had occurred. His fingers were markedly shortened with flexion impairment, and early closure of the phalangeal epiphyses was detected on radiography. Electroneuromyography (ENMG) and sensory evoked potentials revealed sensory polyneuropathy, primarily in the upper extremities. Fine motor coordination disturbances were accompanied by minor verbal and visuospatial deficiencies, and he also had elevated intraocular pressure and myopia. IgA nephropathy (see {161950}) was confirmed by renal biopsy.

{2:Coakley et al. (1990)} described an unusual form of variegate porphyria in a young girl with epilepsy, mental retardation, and premature adrenarche. Symptoms of porphyria commenced about the age of 12 years and death occurred about 18 months later. The patient had a very low level of protoporphyrinogen oxidase activity in her cultured fibroblasts, whereas both parents had half-normal activity of the enzyme in lymphocytes. {2:Coakley et al. (1990)} suggested the patient was homozygous. Two of the subjects with homozygous VP described by {8:Korda et al. (1984)} were similar to this patient in that they had severe neurologic symptoms which included convulsions and mental retardation. The ratio of 5-beta to 5-alpha steroids in urine suggested a defect in hepatic 5-alpha-reductase activity in the patient of {2:Coakley et al. (1990)}. This presumed defect as well as anticonvulsant therapy may have contributed to the severity of the patient's condition. Noting that the proband described by {2:Coakley et al. (1990)} had no photosensitivity and had a normal stool protoporphyrin with markedly elevated coproporphyrin, {6:Hift et al. (1993)} stated that this was incompatible with VP and suggested that the diagnosis might be incorrect.

{13:Norris et al. (1990)} reported a 14-year-old girl with variegate porphyria, who was later found to have biallelic mutations in the PPOX gene ({5:Frank et al., 1998}). From the age of 18 months, the proband experienced recurrent blisters and erosions associated with sun exposure, and increased skin fragility was noted from age 5 years, with mild flexural atopic eczema from age 6. In addition, she experienced 2 seizures in the first year of life and had impaired intellectual development. Examination revealed crusts, erosions, milia, and superficial scars on the skin of the face, hands, and knees, with perioral radial linear scarring. She also exhibited fifth-finger clinodactyly and brachydactyly, and flexion deformities of the other fingers. Stool porphyrin concentrations were elevated, with protoporphyrin higher than coproporphyrin, and the urinary porphyrin profile was also compatible with variegate porphyria. Fluorescence-emission spectroscopy of patient plasma showed a large porphyrin peak at 624 nm; her mother showed a very small peak at 625 nm and her father showed no abnormality. {13:Norris et al. (1990)} noted that both parents were asymptomatic, with normal fecal porphyrin concentrations, despite half-normal protoporphyrinogen oxidase (PO) activity.

Homozygous variegate porphyria was also described by {4:D'Alessandro Gandolfo et al. (1991)}.

{6:Hift et al. (1993)} described the first South African case of autosomal homozygous VP, a 6-year-old Afrikaner girl with severe symptoms who was later found to have biallelic mutations in the PPOX gene ({10:Meissner et al., 1996}). She developed severe blistering of the face and hands within days of birth. Examination showed markedly foreshortened stubby fingers and toes, resulting in such severe functional impairment that she could not hold a pencil or use scissors. X-rays showed brachydactyly with broad short metacarpals and phalanges, and a delayed bone age. She had severe skin disease, manifested by blistering, erosions, crusting, hyperpigmentation, and milia. Skin in nonexposed areas was also abnormally thickened and infiltrated. Histology showed perivascular PAS-positive hyalin deposits in papillary and upper reticular dermis of exposed skin; similar but less marked changes were present in unexposed skin. Acute and chronic photodamage was evident, with basket-weave hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy with necrotic keratinocytes, and marked dermal solar elastosis. She also had severe myopia, pendular nystagmus, and developmental delay. From the age of 3 years, she had infrequent complex partial seizures; electroencephalogram was normal. At age 4, she developed sensory neuropathy of the hands and feet, confirmed by electrophysiologic studies showing a reduced amplitude of conduction in the right and left median sensory nerves; sural nerve biopsy showed features of early segmental demyelination. No motor abnormalities were detected. PPO activity assays in patient lymphoblasts showed no detectable activity; lymphoblasts from her mother and father showed 50% and 70% of normal activity, respectively. {6:Hift et al. (1993)} also reported a male infant, born to consanguineous parents, who developed seizures at 5 months of age and had developmental delay, nystagmus, and clinodactyly. He exhibited skin manifestations at 6 months of age. Examination at age 6 years showed blistering and fragility of skin of hands, face, and ears, with hypertrichosis, hyperpigmentation, scarring, and milia in those areas. His PPO activity was approximately 5% of normal levels; his parents were unavailable for testing. He had no neuropathy, and nerve conduction studies were normal.

{3:Corrigall et al. (2000)} reported 2 severely affected probands from 2 unrelated South African families with variegate porphyria. In family 1, of Afrikaner origin, the proband was a 7-year-old girl who first presented at age 10 months with severe skin disease and the typical urine and stool porphyrin excretion profile of VP. Examination showed fragile skin with blisters, scars, and milia most marked in sun-exposed areas, although even her unexposed skin was abnormal. She had brachydactyly, photo-onycholysis, nystagmus, myopia, sensory neuropathy, and problems with concentration. She had never experienced an acute attack. In family 2, the proband was a 26-year-old South African woman of mixed-race origin who presented at age 19 years with symptoms suggestive of a porphyric acute crisis; biochemical analysis confirmed VP. She subsequently experienced 2 milder acute attacks, and also manifested an unusually severe form of skin disease with chronic blistering of the face and hands, hypertrichosis, and photomutilation of the hands with progressive shortening of the fingers and deformities of the joints of the fingers. Her affected 25-year-old sister exhibited typical skin disease of VP and a typical porphyrin excretion pattern.

{14:Palmer et al. (2001)} reported a 36-year-old British woman with variegate porphyria and mutation in the PPOX gene. Skin fragility, blisters, and scarring developed at 9 months of age on sun-exposed skin. At 4 years of age, she experienced a febrile seizure associated with an upper respiratory tract infection; an electroencephalogram was normal. At age 19, her bone age was estimated at 16 years, and she had short stature. Dysmorphic features included a small face with flattened nose, and accentuated skin creases with perioral radial linear furrowing. There was hyperpigmentation, milia, scarring, and crusted erosions in a photosensitive distribution. Her hands were small, with brachydactyly, clinodactyly, fixed flexion deformities, and variable nail dystrophy. X-rays revealed short misshapen terminal phalanges. The proband's mother experienced 3 acute neuroabdominal episodes, 2 related to drug ingestion, and she had no cutaneous manifestations. The proband's deceased father was reported to be asymptomatic.

{1:Cho et al. (2021)} reported a 33-year-old Chinese man, born of consanguineous parents, who at 3 months of age developed itchiness, rash, and blistering skin lesions, followed by atrophic scar formation, only on exposed skin of the face and forearms. Skin biopsy findings were consistent with porphyria, and biochemical testing of urinary and fecal porphyrins showed a pattern suggestive of variegate porphyria that was not observed in his unaffected parents and sibs.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of childhood-onset variegate porphyria in the family studied by {5:Frank et al. (1998)}, originally reported by {13:Norris et al. (1990)}, was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a girl of Afrikaner origin with photosensitivity, severe brachydactyly, seizures, developmental delay, sensory neuropathy, and an abnormal porphyrin excretion pattern, who was originally described by {6:Hift et al. (1993)}, {10:Meissner et al. (1996)} identified compound heterozygosity for missense mutations in the PPOX gene: an R59W substitution ({600923.0003}) and an R168C substitution ({600923.0004}). Her mother, who met the criteria for VP, was heterozygous for the R59W mutation, and her father, who had normal porphyrin biochemistry and a 25% reduction in PPO activity, was heterozygous for the R168C variant. The authors also detected the R59W mutation in 43 of 45 patients with autosomal dominant VP ({176200}) from 26 of 27 South African families; genealogic analysis of 1 of the South African families demonstrated relatedness to the original South African VP family tree, suggesting a founder effect. Functional analysis of the R59W mutation demonstrated that the mutant enzyme had an almost undetectable catalytic rate but a relatively invariant K(m), consistent with the 50% reduction in PPO activity seen in the proband's mother.

In a 20-year-old woman with variegate porphyria, impaired intellectual development, and hand deformities, who was originally described by {13:Norris et al. (1990)}, {5:Frank et al. (1998)} sequenced the PPOX gene and identified compound heterozygosity for missense mutations: a G169E substitution ({600923.0014}) and a G358R substitution ({600923.0015}). Her asymptomatic parents, who both exhibited approximately half-normal levels of PPO activity, were each heterozygous for 1 of the mutations, neither of which was found in 50 unrelated controls.

{15:Roberts et al. (1998)} confirmed the molecular characterization of the rare homozygous variant of variegate porphyria. They identified biallelic PPOX mutations in 5 of the 11 unrelated patients with apparent autosomal recessive VP reported to that time. Two patients were homozygous for missense mutations (D349A, {600923.0007} and A433P), whereas 2 were compound heterozygous for a G358R substitution and either a G169E substitution or a splice site mutation, respectively, and the remaining patient was compound heterozygous for a 12-bp insertion and another splice site mutation. Functional analysis by prokaryotic expression showed that the D349A and A433P mutations and 1 missense mutation in each of the 3 compound heterozygous patients (G538R in 2 patients and c.657ins12) preserved some PPOX activity (9.5-25% of wildtype). Mutations on the other allele of the compound heterozygous patients abolished or markedly decreased activity. There was no relation between genotype assessed by functional analysis and the presence or severity of noncutaneous manifestations. All the mutations found in the homozygous patients were absent from 104 unrelated patients with autosomal dominant VP. The authors concluded that mild PPOX mutations occur in the general population but have a very low or no clinical penetrance in heterozygotes.

In a 7-year-old girl of Afrikaner origin (family 1) with severe photosensitivity, brachydactyly, and sensory neuropathy, {3:Corrigall et al. (2000)} identified compound heterozygosity for the recurrent R59W mutation in the PPOX gene, and a Y348C mutation ({600923.0016}). Testing of 10 additional family members revealed heterozygosity for the R59W mutation in the proband's asymptomatic mother and 12-year-old sister; the mother showed a fecal porphyrin excretion pattern typical of VP, but the sister was biochemically negative. The proband's asymptomatic father, half brother, and half sister were heterozygous for the Y348C mutation; her father had a normal fecal porphyrin excretion profile but showed a small peak at 625 nm on plasma fluoroscanning, her half brother had a typical VP fecal porphyrin excretion pattern but normal plasma fluoroscan, and her half sister was biochemically negative. In 2 South African sisters of mixed-race origin (family 2), 1 of whom experienced acute porphyric attacks and severe cutaneous photosensitivity and the other of whom showed typical VP skin disease, {3:Corrigall et al. (2000)} identified compound heterozygosity for R59W in PPOX and a R138P mutation ({600923.0017}). None of the mutations was found in 50 ethnically matched controls.

In a 36-year-old British woman with severe cutaneous manifestations of variegate porphyria and brachydactyly, {14:Palmer et al. (2001)} sequenced the PPOX gene and identified compound heterozygosity for mutations in the PPOX gene: an in-frame 12-bp insertion ({600923.0010}) and a splice site mutation ({600923.0011}). The proband's mother, who was heterozygous for the splice site mutation, experienced 3 neuroabdominal episodes, 2 of which followed drug ingestion; she had no cutaneous manifestations. A maternal first cousin, who also carried the splice site mutation, was asymptomatic. DNA was unavailable from the proband's deceased father, who was reported to be asymptomatic.

In a follow-up study of the Finnish boy with apparent homozygous variegate porphyria reported by {12:Mustajoki et al. (1987)}, {7:Kauppinen et al. (2001)} identified compound heterozygosity for 2 missense mutations in the PPOX gene: an I12T substitution ({600923.0012}) and a P256R substitution ({600923.0013}). Affected members of another Finnish family were compound heterozygous for the same mutations, suggesting a common ancestor. One heterozygous carrier in each family was mildly symptomatic.

In a 33-year-old Chinese man with childhood-onset variegate porphyria, {1:Cho et al. (2021)} sequenced the PPOX gene and identified homozygosity for a missense mutation (V270L; {600923.0018}) at the first base of exon 8 of the PPOX gene. His unaffected consanguineous parents were heterozygous for the mutation. Functional analysis revealed that the mutation affected splicing, resulting in exon skipping that was predicted to result in a truncated protein.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH IMPAIRED LANGUAGE, BEHAVIORAL ABNORMALITIES, AND DYSMORPHIC FACIES; NEDLBF
clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, borderline to severe
Onset in infancy or early childhood
Caused by mutation in the ubiquitin-associated protein 2-like gene (UBAP2L,)

Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, borderline to severe
Miscellaneous: Onset in infancy or early childhood
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the ubiquitin-associated protein 2-like gene (UBAP2L,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired language, behavioral abnormalities, and dysmorphic facies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired language, behavioral abnormalities, and dysmorphic facies (NEDLBF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the UBAP2L gene ({616472}) on chromosome 1q21.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired language, behavioral abnormalities, and dysmorphic facies (NEDLBF) is characterized by global developmental delay, speech delay, variably impaired intellectual development, behavioral abnormalities, and dysmorphic facial features. The phenotype and severity of the disorder is heterogeneous, ranging from borderline to severe. Brain imaging is usually normal. More variable additional features include early feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, short stature, mild visual impairment, hypotonia, seizures (particularly febrile), and distal skeletal defects of the hands and feet ({1:Jia et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Jia et al. (2022)} reported 12 unrelated individuals with variable neurodevelopmental concerns associated with de novo heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the UBAP2L gene identified through exome sequencing. The patients, who ranged from 4 to 16 years of age, were ascertained through international collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher program. All patients were referred for neurodevelopmental concerns, including delayed development, speech delay, variably impaired intellectual development, motor delay, hypotonia, and various behavioral abnormalities. Some had early feeding difficulties with failure to thrive or short stature. Intellectual disability ranged from borderline to severe, and all had some type of speech/language problem. Behavioral abnormalities included autism spectrum disorder, autistic features, ADHD, repetitive behavior, anxiety, and aggression. Seven patients had seizures, often febrile, but only 3 had a formal diagnosis of epilepsy. A few had visual impairment with ocular anomalies such as esotropia, exotropia, myopia, hypermetropia, and astigmatism. Brain imaging was essentially normal in the patients studied. Most individuals had variable dysmorphic facial features, including round face, flat face, long face, high broad forehead, microretrognathia, deep-set eyes, abnormal palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, strabismus, deep and prominent concha, synophrys, broad nasal bridge, bulbous nose, long philtrum, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, and thin upper lip. Some patients had skeletal anomalies, including scoliosis/kyphosis, joint stiffness, brachydactyly, fifth finger clinodactyly, nail hypoplasia, broad halluces, flat feet, and finger joint contractures.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the UBAP2L gene that were identified in patients with NEDLBF by {1:Jia et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 12 unrelated individuals with NEDLBF, {1:Jia et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the UBAP2L gene (see, e.g., {616472.0001}-{616472.0005}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. There were 6 nonsense, 3 frameshift, and 3 splice site mutations. UBAP2L is involved in the assembly of stress granules, which are formed to shut down gene translation in cells under stress conditions and thus play a role in gene expression. Fibroblasts derived from 2 patients showed decreased UBAP2L protein levels and reduced stress granule formation after oxidative stress compared to controls. A similar decrease in stress granule formation after oxidative stress was observed in vitro in UBAP2L-null HeLa cells transfected with 4 of the mutations. {1:Jia et al. (2022)} concluded that UBAP2L haploinsufficiency perturbs stress granule dynamics during early brain development, resulting in neurodevelopmental abnormalities.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Jia et al. (2022)} found that homozygous deletion of the Ubap2l gene in mice was embryonic lethal. Heterozygous mice were viable with no morphologic abnormalities, but showed behavioral abnormalities and cognitive impairment. Heterozygous mice showed lower preference for social novelty, mild repetitive behavior, anxious-like behavior, and abnormal spacial working memory compared to controls. The brains of heterozygous mice showed disordered cortical development and lamination, decreased cortical thickness, and decreased numbers of proliferating progenitor radial glial cells compared to controls. The intensity and number of stress granules in the developing cortex were decreased in mutant animals compared to controls under normal physiologic conditions and after oxidative stress.

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with language delay and variable cognitive abnormalities

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with language delay and variable cognitive abnormalities (NEDLC) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GABBR1 gene ({603540}) on chromosome 6p22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with language delay and variable cognitive abnormalities (NEDLC) is a phenotypically heterogeneous neurologic disorder. Affected individuals may show early motor delay, speech and language delay, impaired intellectual development, learning disabilities, and/or behavioral abnormalities, although the severity and manifestations vary widely. Repetitive behavior and sleep difficulties are commonly present. More severe features include seizures, hypotonia, ocular abnormalities, dysmorphic features, and psychiatric comorbidities ({1:Cediel et al., 2022}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Cediel et al. (2022)} reported 4 unrelated individuals, ranging from 2.5 to 17 years of age, with variable neurodevelopmental abnormalities associated with de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the GABBR1 gene identified by exome sequencing and through the GeneMatcher program. P1 was a 2.5-year-old girl with global developmental delay, delayed walking at 17 months, speech delay with regression to being nonverbal, axial hypotonia, peripheral hypertonia, and stereotypic behaviors. She also had constipation and periodic fevers without focus. P2, a 4.5-year-old girl, was profoundly impaired with severe intellectual disability, inability to walk or speak, generalized hypotonia, absent language, poor hand function, a history of generalized febrile seizures, absence seizures, learning disabilities, stereotypic movements, and sleep problems. She also had optic nerve hypoplasia, cortical visual impairment, nystagmus, and hypermetropia. Additional findings included long philtrum, epicanthus, broad nasal root, fifth finger clinodactyly, tooth hypoplasia, and scoliosis. Brain imaging showed progressive cerebellar atrophy. P3 was a 13-year-old boy with delayed walking at 36 months, impaired intellectual development (IQ of 58), poor speech, repetitive behavior that resolved, ADHD, sleeping difficulties, and encopresis. He had no seizures and brain imaging was normal. P4 was a 17-year-old girl who did not have intellectual disability, but showed behavioral and psychiatric disorders, including severely rigid autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, borderline personality disorder, oppositional defiant disorder, social anxiety, daytime sleepiness, and mood swings. She had early speech delay, but was later fluent; motor development was normal. Additional features included constipation, skin and nail abnormalities, and mild skeletal abnormalities.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the GABBR1 gene that were identified in patients with NEDLC by {1:Cediel et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 unrelated individuals with NEDLC, {1:Cediel et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous missense variants in the GABBR1 gene that were absent from the gnomAD database ({603540.0001}-{603540.0004}). The variants occurred in the GB1b subunit, which is generated by alternative promoter usage in the GABBR1 gene. Two of the variants (E368D, {603540.0002} and A397V, {603540.0003}) were in the Venus flytrap domain (VFTD) containing the orthosteric GABA-binding site, one (A535T; {603540.0001}) localized to the linker region between VFTD and transmembrane domain 1, and one (G673D; {603540.0004}) localized to transmembrane domain 3. Detailed in vitro functional expression studies of the variants in HEK293 cells showed that they had differential detrimental effects on GABA-B receptor function. There was impaired transport of the variant receptors assembled with E368D and G673D to the plasma membrane, whereas receptors assembled with A397V and A535T demonstrated close to normal cell surface expression. G673D was not trafficked to the cell surface, so it did not respond to GABA stimulation and was completely inactive. In response to GABA stimulation, the E368D variant receptor exhibited decreased constitutive activity, a reduced Emax, and a nearly 100-fold increased EC50, illustrating reduced potency and efficacy of GABA at the receptor. The A397V and A535T variants resulted in a decrease in Emax, but similar constitutive activity and GABA potency as the wildtype receptor. The authors hypothesized that these variants interfered with coupling of agonist binding to G protein activation. No overt dominant-negative effects were observed. Overall, the data suggested that all 4 variants are loss-of-function mutations that most likely tip the excitation/inhibition balance in the central nervous system towards more excitation.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-111 (DEE111) is caused by homozygous mutation in the DEPDC5 gene ({614191}) on chromosome 22q12.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-111 (DEE111) is an autosomal recessive severe neurologic disorder characterized by early-onset refractory seizures, global developmental delay, hypotonia, impaired gross motor development, impaired intellectual development, and absent speech. Most patients have macrocephaly. Brain imaging shows frontal, parietal, and perisylvian polymicrogyria, dysmorphic basal ganglia and corpus callosum, and hypoplastic pons. Additional features may include feeding difficulties, poor vision with ocular anomalies, congenital cardiac abnormalities, and recurrent infections associated with neutropenia. Death in early childhood may occur ({1:Ververi et al., 2023}).

For a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Ververi et al. (2023)} reported 9 children from 5 unrelated families with an early-onset severe neurologic disorder. Families 1-3 were of Irish Traveller origin (family 1 was consanguineous), family 4 was a consanguineous Tunisian family, and family 5 was a consanguineous Lebanese family. Five of the 6 affected Irish Traveller patients died in early childhood: P2 died of congenital heart disease on the first day of life, whereas P1, P4, and P5 died between 15 and 37 months of age from respiratory-related illnesses; clinical information from deceased patient 9 was not available, although he reportedly had a similar phenotype. The living children were between 10 months and 6 years of age. All patients except 1 were born prematurely between 28 and 36 weeks' gestation due to intrauterine growth retardation or maternal preeclampsia, and several had neonatal hypotonia, respiratory insufficiency, and/or feeding difficulties. Almost all were noted to have macrocephaly with frontal bossing, and a few had dysmorphic features, such as hypertelorism, midface hypoplasia, bushy eyebrows, low-set ears, and capillary malformations. The patients had severe global developmental delay with hypotonia, inability to sit or walk, poor head control, absent speech, and variably impaired visual fixation and tracking; tube-feeding was sometimes required. All patients had onset of seizures in the first weeks, months, or years of life, including infantile spasms, febrile seizures, multifocal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and status epilepticus; the seizures were often refractory to medication. Some patients showed developmental regression after seizure onset. About half had ocular abnormalities, including rod-cone dystrophy, hypopigmented retina, amblyopia, and nystagmus. Brain imaging showed extensive frontal, perisylvian, or diffuse polymicrogyria, dysmorphic corpus callosum and basal ganglia, large frontal lobes, and hypoplastic pons. Enlarged ventricles and cerebellar abnormalities were found in some. Four patients had cardiac findings, including hypoplastic left heart syndrome, pulmonary artery stenosis, arrhythmia, hypertension, and ventricular hypertrophy, 2 had umbilical or inguinal hernia, and 3 had recurrent infections or sepsis associated with neutropenia.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of DEE111 in the families reported by {1:Ververi et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 9 patients from 5 unrelated families with DEE111, {1:Ververi et al. (2023)} identified homozygous missense mutations in the DEPDC5 gene: T337R ({614191.0016}) and R806C ({614191.0017}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families and were not present in the gnomAD database. Molecular modeling predicted that the mutations would result in a loss of protein stability and adversely affect protein function. Functional studies of the variants were not performed, but immunohistochemical studies of a skin sample from 1 of the patients with the T337R mutation was consistent with an overall increase in mTOR ({601231}) activity. Since heterozygous carriers in the families were unaffected, {1:Ververi et al. (2023)} postulated that these missense mutations resulted in a partial loss of function.

phenotypes.phenotype: Xerosis and growth failure with immune and pulmonary dysfunction syndrome

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that xerosis and growth failure with immune and pulmonary dysfunction syndrome (XGIP) is caused by homozygous mutation in the DBR1 gene ({607024}) on chromosome 3q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Xerosis and growth failure with immune and pulmonary dysfunction syndrome (XGIP) is characterized by premature birth, intrauterine and postnatal growth retardation, and collodion membrane or collodion-like skin at birth with dry skin thereafter. Patients also exhibit bronchopulmonary disease and thrombocytopenia and neutropenia. Variable features include cardiac anomalies, seizures, encephalopathy, and cholestasis, and cataract has been observed. Affected individuals die within the first year of life ({1:Shamseldin et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Shamseldin et al. (2023)} described 4 unrelated Saudi children, born prematurely of first-cousin parents (pedigrees A to D), who had an ichthyosis-like presentation with red, shiny collodion skin or collodion membrane at birth followed by dry peeling skin, and mutation in the DBR1 gene. All exhibited severe intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) with postnatal growth retardation, and all died in the first year of life. Other common features included thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, with 1 proband (D) experiencing persistent pancytopenia; and all 4 had bronchopulmonary disease requiring long-term supplemental oxygen. The probands displayed variable cardiac abnormalities, including atrial septal defect, dilated right atrium, mild to moderate left ventricular hypertrophy, mild dilation of left ventricle, and mild regurgitation of the tricuspid, mitral, and/or pulmonary valves. Two of the probands (B and C) had seizures, and proband A had epileptic activity seen on EEG. Probands B and C also had encephalopathy and cholestasis. Dysmorphic features included ectropion in probands A, C, and D, and eclabium in A and D. Skin biopsy in the proband from pedigree B showed unremarkable epidermis, no inflammation, and no features suggestive of congenital ichthyosis. Proband A died at age 5 months, having never left the neonatal intensive care unit; proband B died at age 4 months with respiratory distress, progressive bradycardia, and cardiac arrest; proband C died at age 6 months of multiorgan failure and cerebral edema attributed to septic shock; and patient D died at age 1 year due to sepsis. In 3 of the families (A, C, and D), there were other children who had died in infancy or childhood, but only limited information was available regarding those children.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of XGIP in the families reported by {1:Shamseldin et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: From the CENTOGENE biodatabank, {1:Shamseldin et al. (2023)} identified 6 families in which probands had a similar phenotype consisting of intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction with a collodion-like presentation, and all were homozygous for the same missense mutation in the DBR1 gene (Y67C; {607024.0005}). The authors noted that only 4 of the families agreed to participate in their study. The mutation segregated fully with disease in those 4 families, which shared a haplotype extending at least 2.27 Mb around the founder variant.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Fliedner-Zweier syndrome (FZS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCAF4 gene ({616023}) on chromosome 21q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Fliedner-Zweier syndrome (FZS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by variable manifestations including mild intellectual disability, seizures, behavioral abnormalities, and various skeletal and structural anomalies ({2:Fliedner et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Fliedner et al. (2020)} reported 8 patients, aged 20 months to 16 years, with FZS and mutation in the SCAF4 gene. All had developmental delay and intellectual disability, which was mostly in the mild range. In general, speech development was more significantly affected than motor development. Five patients had behavioral concerns including autistic features, hyperactivity, and aggressive behavior. Four patients had seizures. Brain MRI was performed in 5 patients and demonstrated nonspecific white matter anomalies in 3 patients and pontocerebellar hypoplasia and a thin corpus callosum in 1 patient. Other features included skeletal anomalies in 4 patients, renal abnormalities in 3 patients, and cardiac abnormalities in 3 patients. One patient had a tracheoesophageal fistula, and 1 patient had a tethered spinal cord.

{1:Carvalho et al. (2023)} reported a 16-year-old Brazilian boy with FZS and mutation in the SCAF4 gene who presented at age 4.4 years with microcephaly and speech delay. Brain MRI, head CT, and kidney ultrasound were normal. At 6 years of age he had surgery to correct a congenital atrial communication. He developed seizures at 8 years of age. On exam at 16.6 years of age, he had dysmorphic facial features including strabismus, epicanthus, prominent nasal bridge, long philtrum, and long ears. He also had intellectual disability, anxiety, and aggressiveness.

{3:Lin and Chen (2024)} reported a 12-year-old Chinese boy (patient 1) with FZS and mutation in the SCAF4 gene who presented with seizures at 4 years of age. He had a history of spinal myelomeningocele, bifid spine, and tethered cord identified at birth. He had moderate neurodevelopmental and intellectual disability. Dysmorphic facial features including a deep nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, and a deep philtrum.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the SCAF4 gene identified in all but 1 patient with FZS by {2:Fliedner et al. (2020)}, {1:Carvalho et al. (2023)}, and {3:Lin and Chen (2024)} occurred de novo. The heterozygous mutation in 1 patient reported by {2:Fliedner et al. (2020)} was inherited from his healthy mother.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
{2:Fliedner et al. (2020)} identified heterozygous mutations in the SCAF4 gene in 8 patients with Fliedner-Zweier syndrome (e.g., {616023.0001}-{616023.0003}). The mutations included 2 splice-site and 6 truncating mutations. All but 1 mutation were shown to have occurred de novo. None of the SCAF4 variants were present in the gnomAD database. All patients except 1 (patient 6) carried additional heterozygous or biallelic variants in other genes, including several genes associated with neurologic disorders, such as NSD1 ({606681}), SLC4A4 ({603345}), PI4KA ({600286}), SHANK2 ({603290}), and EPM2A ({607566}). Paired-end RNA sequencing in blood from 4 patients, all of whom also carried variants in other genes, and 8 controls demonstrated a large number of differentially expressed as well as differentially spliced genes, with an increased fraction of short transcripts in affected individuals. {2:Fliedner et al. (2020)} concluded that impaired SCAF4 function resulted in altered mRNA processing and splicing.

{1:Carvalho et al. (2023)} identified a heterozygous frameshift mutation ({616023.0004}) in the SCAF4 gene in a 16-year-old Brazilian boy with Fliedner-Zweier syndrome. The mutation was identified by whole-exome sequencing and shown to have occurred de novo by Sanger sequencing. Functional studies were not performed.

{3:Lin and Chen (2024)} identified a heterozygous nonsense mutation (R471X; {616023.0005}) in the SCAF4 gene in a 12-year-old Chinese boy (patient 1) with Fliedner-Zweier syndrome. The mutation was identified by whole-exome sequencing and shown to have occurred de novo by Sanger sequencing.

Caused by mutation in the small nuclear RNA-activating protein complex, polypeptide 4 gene (SNAPC4,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor regression, progressive spastic paraplegia, and oromotor dysfunction

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with motor regression, progressive spastic paraplegia, and oromotor dysfunction (NEDRSO) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the SNAPC4 gene ({602777}) on chromosome 9q34.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor regression, progressive spastic paraplegia, and oromotor dysfunction (NEDRSO) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by onset of progressive motor abnormalities in early childhood after normal early development. Affected individuals show regression of motor function with axial hypotonia, appendicular spasticity, and ataxic gait or loss of ambulation; some never achieve walking. Additional features include poor coordination, dystonia, oromotor dysfunction, poor speech with dysarthria, ocular defects (in about half), and variably impaired intellectual development. Short stature and small head circumference or microcephaly are observed. Brain imaging often shows progressive cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with other findings such as basal ganglia abnormalities ({1:Frost et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Frost et al. (2023)} reported 10 patients from 8 unrelated families with a neurodevelopmental and neuroregressive disorder characterized mainly by early-childhood onset of significant gross movement abnormalities, loss of previously acquired skills, and progressive spasticity. The patients, who ranged from 4.5 to 25 years of age, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after genetic analysis identified biallelic mutations in the SNAPC4 gene. Most patients had normal development in the first months or years of life, but presented between 6 and 36 months of age with progressive motor abnormalities, including motor regression, axial hypotonia, peripheral spasticity with hyperreflexia (sometimes with extensor plantar responses), appendicular hypertonia, muscle weakness, easy fatigue, dystonia, poor coordination, athetotic or choreic movements, dysmetria, and tremor. Six had spastic quadriparesis. The patients also had oromotor dysfunction with slowed speech, dysarthria, and drooling. Many had delayed walking, frequent falls, and ataxic gait, and some lost the ability to walk. Three patients never achieved independent ambulation. A few patients had limited volitional movements and/or feeding difficulties requiring tube-feeding. Cognitive development was variable, but appeared to be delayed: most could follow simple instructions, but others were noted to have mild to severely impaired intellectual development, and a few were able to attend special schools. Speech and language difficulties were common; 2 were nonverbal. Three patients had seizures that were a single episode, mild, and self-limited or easily controlled. About half of the patients had ocular abnormalities, such as nystagmus, optic nerve pallor, strabismus, esotropia, hypermetropia, astigmatism, oculomotor apraxia, and retinopathy; P8 became blind at age 10 years. Short stature and small head circumference or microcephaly were commonly observed; 5 patients were underweight and 2 were overweight. More variable features included hip dysplasia, coxa valga, genu valgum, kyphosis, scoliosis, constipation, and mild dysmorphic features. Six of 9 patients studied showed brain imaging abnormalities, including progressive cerebellar atrophy (5 patients), cerebral volume loss (3 patients), thin posterior corpus callosum (1 patient), basal ganglia abnormalities (2 patients), and posterior periventricular white matter abnormalities (2 patients). Three individuals (P3, P4, and P5) had normal brain imaging.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of NEDRSO in the families reported by {1:Frost et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 10 patients from 8 unrelated families with NEDRSO, {1:Frost et al. (2023)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous putative loss-of-function mutations in the SNAPC4 gene (see, e.g., {602777.0001}-{602777.0007}). The mutations, which were found by trio-based whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in all families and were absent from or present at a low frequency in the gnomAD database. SNAPC4-deficient HeLa cells showed a nonsignificant reduction in overall snRNA expression by about 50% compared to controls. However, expression of RNU4-1, RNU4ATAC ({601428}), and RNU5A-1 ({180691}) were significantly reduced compared to controls. RNA-seq analysis detected 7,496 differentially spliced alternative splicing events in SNAPC4-deficient cells compared to controls, and Gene Ontology (GOBP) analysis indicated that affected genes were involved in RNA splicing, transport, and processing, as well as microtubule regulation during mitosis. Similar to SNAPC4-deficient HeLa cells, patient fibroblasts and lymphoblastoid cells showed an overall decrease in SNAPC4 mRNA and protein expression, and fibroblasts showed decreased expression of certain snRNAs (particularly RNU2-1 ({180690}) and RNU5A-1); other RNU species were variably decreased compared to controls. RNA-seq analysis of patient fibroblasts detected 5,523 differentially spliced alternative splicing events compared to controls, also with involvement of genes involved in RNA dynamics and microtubule cytoskeleton organization involved in mitosis. The findings in both cell models suggested that SNAPC4 mutations impair snRNA transcription and have broad consequences on alternative splicing throughout the transcriptome.

phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay, dysmorphic facies, and brain anomalies

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay, dysmorphic facies, and brain anomalies (DEVDFB) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the U2AF2 gene ({191318}) on chromosome 19q13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Developmental delay, dysmorphic facies, and brain anomalies (DEVDFB) is characterized by global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, speech delay, nonspecific dysmorphic facial features, hypotonia, and impaired overall growth with small head circumference. Most affected individuals have early-onset seizures that are variable in severity. Brain imaging typically shows hypoplasia of the corpus callosum and/or delayed myelination ({1:Hiraide et al., 2021}; {3:Kuroda et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Hiraide et al. (2021)} reported a 7.5-year-old Japanese girl with global developmental delay, poor overall growth, microcephaly (-3.9 SD), impaired intellectual development (IQ of 61), and mild speech delay. She had hypotonia and walked at 21 months. Febrile seizures were noted at 2 and 3 years of age, followed by afebrile seizures that were controlled with medication. Additional features included pes planus, broad eyebrows, smooth philtrum, dental crowding, ptosis, and exotropia. Brain imaging showed hypoplasia of the corpus callosum.

{4:Wang et al. (2023)} reported a 6-year-old Chinese boy who developed febrile seizures at 1 year of age and later had afebrile focal seizures that were difficult to control. He had a history of congenital hypothyroidism and showed poor overall growth with small head circumference (-2.8 SD). He had global developmental delay with walking at 16 months, impaired language acquisition, and poor communication skills. Dysmorphic features included small low-set ears, dental anomalies, cleft palate, and mandibular protrusion with underbite. Brain imaging showed hypoplastic corpus callosum.

{2:Kittock et al. (2023)} reported a 4-year-old Caucasian boy who presented in infancy with poor feeding, poor growth, laryngomalacia with obstructive sleep apnea, hypotonia, and dysmorphic features, including pointed ears, short palpebral fissures, short nose, smooth philtrum, and flexion contractures of the fingers. He showed global developmental delay with speech delay. At age 2 years, he had a single complex febrile seizure and later had afebrile seizures with impaired awareness and a tonic motor component. Additional features included recurrent upper respiratory infections, asthma, intolerance to formula, and gastroesophageal reflux. Brain imaging showed mega cisterna magna.

{3:Kuroda et al. (2023)} reported a 2-year-old Japanese girl who presented soon after birth with vertical nystagmus and hypotonia. She later showed global developmental delay with inability to roll over at 21 months, absent speech, hypersensitivity, poor ocular fixation, choreic involuntary movements, ballismus, and limb hypertonia. Brain imaging showed delayed myelination, white matter abnormalities, features of hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, midbrain, and pons. She also had dysmorphic features, including hirsutism, upslanting and long palpebral fissures, depressed nasal bridge, prominent nasal alae, prominent philtrum, small mouth, and retrognathia. Seizures were not reported.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the U2AF2 gene that were identified in patients with DEVDFB by {1:Hiraide et al. (2021)} and {4:Wang et al. (2023)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 7.5-year-old Japanese girl with DEVDFB, {1:Hiraide et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the U2AF2 gene (R149W; {191318.0001}). The mutation, which was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

By trio-based whole-exome sequencing, {2:Kittock et al. (2023)} identified a de novo heterozygous R149W mutation in the U2AF2 gene in a 4-year-old boy with DEVDFB. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed.

In a 6-year-old Chinese boy with DEVDFB, {4:Wang et al. (2023)} identified a de novo heterozygous single-base mutation in the U2AF2 gene ({191318.0002}) that resulted in aberrant splicing and deletion of exon 6. The mutation, which was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD, ExAC, or 1000 Genomes Project databases. Patient cells showed a 50% reduction in wildtype U2AF2 mRNA and decreased expression of the normal 65-kD protein compared to controls. A smaller 55-kD band corresponding to expression of the abnormal protein with the in-frame deletion was detected. The mutation significantly inhibited the proliferation of patient immortalized lymphocytes in vitro, showing a slightly increased proportion of cells in the G1/G0 phase and a slightly decreased proportion of cells in the G2/M phase compared to controls.

{3:Kuroda et al. (2023)} reported a de novo heterozygous missense variant (P157L) in the U2AF2 gene in a 2-year-old Japanese girl with global developmental delay identified through exome sequencing. She did not have seizures. The variant was not present in the gnomAD database; functional studies of the variant were not performed. The patient also carried de novo heterozygous variants in 3 additional genes.

clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the potassium channel, voltage-gated, subfamily H, member 5 gene (KCNH5,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the potassium channel, voltage-gated, subfamily H, member 5 gene (KCNH5,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-112 (DEE112) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the KCNH5 gene (KCNH5; {605716}) on chromosome 14q23.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-112 (DEE112) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by a wide range of seizure types, including focal and generalized seizures. Cognitive outcomes range from normal intellect to profound impairment (summary by {1:Happ et al., 2023}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of DEE, see {308350}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{5:Veeramah et al. (2013)} reported a 13-year-old boy with epileptic encephalopathy who had a mutation in the KCNH5 gene. The patient had normal development until 6 months of age, when he developed intractable generalized tonic-clonic seizures. He later showed developmental regression and was nonverbal with limited comprehension, autism, and hypotonia.

{4:Minardi et al. (2020)} reported a 61-year-old man (patient 25) who developed seizures within the first month of life and had a history of cognitive motor slowing. A brain MRI showed multiple white matter hyperintensities on T2-weighted images. The patient also had macroglossia. He was found to have a mutation in the KCNH5 gene.

{2:Hu et al. (2022)} reported 3 unrelated Chinese patients, aged 2 to 4 years, with DEE112. Patient 1, a 4-year-old boy, presented at 8 months of age with seizures. He also had autism-like symptoms. Patient 2, a 4-year-old girl, presented with seizures at 6 months of age and was diagnosed with infantile spasms. Brain MRI was normal. She had good seizure control until 2 years of age, when she had recurrence of seizures and was diagnosed with West syndrome. At 4 years of age, she had developmental delay, particularly in language. Patient 3, a 4-year-old boy, presented with seizures at 7 months of age. A brain MRI and EEG were normal. At age 8 months, he was treated with valproic acid for 2 months, after which he remained seizure-free.

{1:Happ et al. (2023)} reported 17 unrelated patients with DEE112. The average age of seizure onset was 6 months, with a range of 1 to 12 months. Seizure types included focal, tonic clonic, myoclonic, and absence seizures, epileptic spasms, and others. Nine patients were seizure free after treatment. Fourteen patients had developmental abnormalities, predominantly affecting language. Cognitive outcomes were reported in 10 patients, of whom 3 had normal cognitive development and 7 had intellectual disability, which was mild in 3, moderate in 2, severe in 1, and profound in 1. Two patients died at age 14 months and 9 years due to respiratory failure and pneumonia, respectively.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The heterozygous mutation identified in a patient with DEE112 by {5:Veeramah et al. (2013)} occurred de novo.

Most of the heterozygous mutations in the 17 patients with DEE112 reported by {1:Happ et al. (2023)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 13-year-old boy with DEE112, {5:Veeramah et al. (2013)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the KCNH5 gene (R327H; {605716.0001}). The mutation was identified by whole-exome sequencing.

In a patient with DEE112, {4:Minardi et al. (2020)} identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the KCNH5 gene (R327H; {605716.0001}). The mutation was identified by whole-exome sequencing.

In an infant (patient 532) with DEE112, {3:Imafidon et al. (2021)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the KCNH5 gene (I463T; {605716.0002}). The mutation was identified by whole-exome sequencing. The patient had hyperekplexia and dysmorphic features.

In 3 unrelated Chinese patients with DEE112, {2:Hu et al. (2022)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the KCNH5 gene: the previously identified R327H mutation, S321N, and an intronic mutation c.2020-4A-G ({605716.0003}). The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing.

{1:Happ et al. (2023)} identified heterozygous mutations in the KCNH5 gene in 17 unrelated patients with DEE12, 3 of whom were previously reported: 9 patients (including 2 previously reported) had the recurrent R327H mutation, 4 patients had an R333H mutation ({605716.0004}), and 1 patient each had different missense mutations K324E, I463T ({605716.0002}), Thr468Pro ({605716.0005}), or F471S ({605716.0006}). The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing and/or sequencing of the KCNH5 gene. The mutation occurred de novo in 14 patients and was inherited from an affected mother in 1 patient (patient 14); in 2 patients, parental testing was not performed.

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: {1:Happ et al. (2023)} identified genotype-phenotype correlations in a cohort of 17 patients with DEE112. The 9 patients with a R327H mutation ({605716.0001}) generally had severe epilepsy, which was drug resistant in some patients, as well as learning difficulties or mild to severe intellectual disability. The 4 patients with an R333H mutation ({605716.0004}) in the second recurrent voltage-sensing domain of KCNH5 tended to have a comparatively milder disease process with drug-responsive seizures, mild developmental delays, and normal cognitive development. Patients with the missense mutations I463T ({605716.0002}) or T468P ({605716.0005}) in or at the S6 transmembrane pore-forming domain had severe disease with drug-resistant seizures and limited developmental progression.

phenotypes.phenotype: Spastic paraplegia 91, autosomal dominant, with or without cerebellar ataxia

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant spastic paraplegia-91 with or without cerebellar ataxia (SPG91) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SPTAN1 gene ({182810}) on chromosome 9q34.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Autosomal dominant spastic paraplegia-91 with or without cerebellar ataxia (SPG91) is a highly variable neurologic disorder characterized by early-onset gait abnormalities due to spastic paraplegia of the lower limbs, sometimes with cerebellar ataxia. The age at onset is highly variable (congenital to young adult), although most patients have symptom onset in the first decade. Some patients present with a spastic paraplegia-predominant phenotype with significant pyramidal signs, whereas others present with an ataxic-predominant phenotype. In addition, although most patients have a more 'pure' phenotype restricted to gait abnormalities without additional features, others have a more 'complicated' phenotype with additional features such as sensory abnormalities, peripheral neuropathy, optic neuropathy, developmental delay, variably impaired intellectual development, and seizures. Many have normal brain imaging, but cerebellar atrophy may be observed in those with prominent cerebellar ataxia ({2:Van de Vondel et al., 2022}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of autosomal dominant spastic paraplegia, see SPG3A ({182600}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Van de Vondel et al. (2022)} reported 15 patients from 7 unrelated families (E-K) with spastic paraplegia. The patients, who ranged from 10 to 57 years of age, had onset of gait difficulties between infancy and 13 years of age. The patients had pyramidal signs and muscle weakness of the lower limbs, mostly distal, but sometimes also proximal. Two also had mild cerebellar ataxia affecting the lower limbs. Many patients had pes cavus, and 4 had sensory deficits associated with an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, sometimes with demyelinating features. One individual had epilepsy and another had febrile seizures. Two had optic neuropathy. None were noted to have delayed development or intellectual disability. Brain MRI was normal in all 7 patients who underwent imaging. All of these patients carried a heterozygous inherited or de novo missense mutation in the SPTAN1 gene (R19W; {182810.0013}).

{1:Morsy et al. (2023)} reported 6 patients from 4 unrelated families (families 1-4) with SPG91 associated with an inherited or de novo R19W mutation in the SPTAN1 gene. The patients, who ranged from 15 to 50 years of age, presented with spastic gait. The age at onset (noted only in 3 patients) ranged from 8 to 10 years. Common features included hyperreflexia of the lower limbs, sometimes with ankle clonus, and weakness of the lower limbs. More variable features included abnormal eye movements such as nystagmus, bladder dysfunction, upper limb weakness, amyotrophy, and impaired vibratory sensation. All but 1 also showed ataxia. Brain imaging, performed in 3 patients, was normal in 2 and showed subcortical white matter hyperintensities in 1. One patient (P5) had onset of generalized seizures at age 10 years that were well-controlled; she also had a learning disability. None of the other patients had developmental delay or intellectual disability.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{2:Van de Vondel et al. (2022)} reported 7 unrelated patients (families A-D, L-N) who presented with cerebellar ataxia and abnormal gait, some of whom also had mild pyramidal signs. These patients, who ranged from 15 to 42 years of age, had a variable age at symptom onset. Five had onset between infancy and 6 years of age, whereas 2 had onset at 17 and 25 years of age. Five of these individuals had developmental delay with impaired intellectual development; 2 had seizures. Additional more variable features included sensory abnormalities, dystonia, paroxysmal dyskinesia, myoclonus, head tremor, and scoliosis. Brain imaging in 2 patients showed hypoplastic cerebellum; 1 of these patients also had parietal polymicrogyria. None of these patients had a family history of the disorder. All carried heterozygous mutations in the SPTAN1 gene, 5 of which were confirmed to have occurred de novo. Four patients (families A-D) carried the same heterozygous in-frame deletion in the SPTAN1 gene (K2083del; {182810.0014}). The other patients (families L, M, and N) carried missense variants (R1098C, R1624C, and Q2205P).

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of SPG91 in several families reported by {2:Van de Vondel et al. (2022)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. Heterozygous SPTAN1 mutations identified in some patients with SPG91 occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In affected members of 7 unrelated families (families E-K) with SPG91, {2:Van de Vondel et al. (2022)} identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the SPTAN1 gene (R19W; {182810.0013}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families from whom parental DNA was available. The mutation in at least 1 case (family F) was demonstrated to have occurred de novo. One large family (family K) contained 10 affected individuals spanning 3 generations who were found to carry the mutation. {2:Van de Vondel et al. (2022)} also identified a recurrent heterozygous 3-bp in-frame deletion (K2083del; {182810.0014}) in the SPTAN1 gene in 4 unrelated patients (families A-D) with SPG91 and more predominant cerebellar ataxia. None of the patients had a family history of the disorder, and the mutations were demonstrated to occur de novo in 2 patients. Three additional patients (families L, M, and N) carried de novo heterozygous missense SPTAN1 mutations (R1098C, R1624C, and Q2205P). These patients had congenital symptom onset, primarily cerebellar ataxia; 2 had impaired intellectual development and epilepsy. None of the mutations were present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed, but molecular modeling suggested that the mutations would result in destabilization of electrostatic interactions at the heterotetramerization site.

{1:Morsy et al. (2023)} reported 6 patients from 4 unrelated families (families 1-4) with SPG91 associated with a heterozygous R19W mutation. The mutation in family 2 (3 affected individuals) showed autosomal dominant transmission. The mutation in the patient from family 4 occurred de novo; the single patients in families 1 and 3 had sporadic disease, but the unaffected parents were not sequenced. Fibroblasts derived from 1 patient showed normal protein levels. However, immunofluorescent studies showed intense irregular expression and aggregation of SPTAN1 throughout the patient cells that was not observed in control cells. Four additional unrelated individuals with SPG and/or cerebellar ataxia (families 5-8) were also found to carry heterozygous variants in the SPTAN1 gene (2 missense variants, 1 in-frame deletion, and 1 splice site variant), but familial segregation studies and functional studies of these variants were not performed.
