phenotypes.phenotype: Developmental delay with or without epilepsy

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay with or without epilepsy (DEVEP) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SPTAN1 gene ({182810}) on chromosome 9q34.

Heterozygous mutation in the SPTAN1 gene can also cause the more severe phenotype DEE5 ({613477}), as well as SPG91 ({620538}), which shows some overlapping features.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Developmental delay with or without epilepsy (DEVEP) is a clinically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by motor delay, speech delay, and variably impaired intellectual development apparent from infancy or early childhood. Hypotonia and behavioral abnormalities are common. About half of affected individuals develop various types of seizures that are not as severe as observed in the allelic disorder DEE5. In general, the phenotype is similar to but milder than DEE5. Some individuals with DEVEP have ataxia or nystagmus associated with cerebellar atrophy on brain imaging, indicating phenotypic overlap with the allelic disorder SPG91 ({1:Morsy et al., 2023}).

In a study of 31 individuals with SPTAN1 mutations, {1:Morsy et al. (2023)} delineated 3 distinct phenotypic subgroups: DEE5; a milder phenotype of developmental delay with or without seizures (DEVEP); and pure or complicated spastic paraplegia/ataxia (SPG91). {2:Syrbe et al. (2017)} similarly emphasized the remarkably broad phenotypic spectrum of neurologic disorders associated with heterozygous SPTAN1 mutations in their cohort study.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Syrbe et al. (2017)} reported 5 unrelated patients (P1-P4 and P15), ranging from 4.5 to 19 years of age, who had developmental delay and/or early-onset seizures. The patients were ascertained through international collaboration after genetic testing identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the SPTAN1 gene. Four (possibly 5) patients developed various types of seizures between 1.5 and 3 years of age. Seizure types included focal, myoclonic, atonic, focal dyscognitive, and febrile. EEG showed focal spikes, multifocal discharges, and generalized spike-wave discharges. Most became seizure-free with medication. P3 was a 10-year-old boy with mild developmental delay and autism spectrum disorder. Table 1 of the report stated that P3 did not have epilepsy, whereas the text stated that he developed epilepsy at 10 years of age. Four patients had developmental delay with mild to moderately impaired intellectual development; 2 had autism and 1 had ADHD. P1 was a 4.5-year-old boy who had onset of focal seizures at 3 years of age, but did not show developmental delay. P4 had a more complicated phenotype with hypotonia, spasticity, and cerebellar atrophy on brain imaging. Brain imaging in 3 other patients was normal.

{1:Morsy et al. (2023)} reported 16 individuals (P11-P26) from 13 unrelated families (families 9 to 21) with developmental delay with or without seizures associated with heterozygous variants in the SPTAN1 gene. The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher Program, after genetic analysis identified the variants. The phenotype was highly variable. Most of the patients were under the age of 10, although 1 was 19 and another was 13. In addition, there were 2 families (families 10 and 13) in which the proband had a mildly affected mother, ages 26 (P14) and 32 (P18). Most of the patients did not have a family history of a similar disorder and were singly affected. All came to attention in infancy or by 2 years of age due to developmental delay, speech delay, hypotonia, or seizures. P11 presented at 15 months of age with ataxia. Nine individuals did not have seizures, and some of those with seizures had only 1 or 2 seizures that remitted. The others had myoclonic, absence, generalized seizures, and infantile spasms; most seizures were controlled with medication. In general, the individuals had impaired intellectual development, motor delay, speech delay, and learning disabilities. A few had microcephaly or mild dysmorphic features. Five patients had ataxia, often with nystagmus or strabismus, and cerebellar atrophy on brain imaging, similar to SPG91. One individual had bladder dysfunction. Other patients did not have ataxia and had normal brain imaging.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The heterozygous mutations in the SPTAN1 gene that were identified in patients with DEVEP by {2:Syrbe et al. (2017)} occurred de novo.

Most of the patients reported by {1:Morsy et al. (2023)} had de novo SPTAN1 mutations, but 2 families showed autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 6 unrelated patients with DEVEP, {2:Syrbe et al. (2017)} identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the SPTAN1 gene (see, e.g., {182810.0016}-{182810.0017}). There were 4 missense mutations and 2 in-frame deletions. Fibroblasts derived from 2 patients did not show abnormal SPTAN1 aggregation, and alpha-2 spectrin was mainly present in the soluble fraction, similar to controls.

In 16 individuals (P11-P26) from 13 unrelated families (families 9 to 21) with DEVEP, {1:Morsy et al. (2023)} identified heterozygous mutations in the SPTAN1 gene (see, e.g., {182810.0018}). The patients were ascertained through international collaborative efforts, including the GeneMatcher Program, after genetic analysis identified the variants. Most of the variants occurred de novo. Most of the variants were nonsense or frameshift; in addition, there were 4 in-frame deletions and 2 missense variants. The mutations occurred throughout the gene, and all but 1 (R2204Q) occurred before the C-terminal alpha/beta dimerization domain. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed.

phenotypes.phenotype: Congenital disorder of glycosylation, type IIbb

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital disorder of glycosylation type 2bb (CDG2BB) is caused by homozygous mutation in the COG3 gene ({606975}) on chromosome 13q14.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIbb (CDG2BB) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by global developmental delay, severely impaired intellectual development, microcephaly, epilepsy, facial dysmorphism, and variable neurologic findings ({1:Duan et al., 2023}).

For an overview of congenital disorders of glycosylation, see CDG1A ({212065}) and CDG2A ({212066}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Duan et al. (2023)} reported sib pairs from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with CDGBB. All 4 patients had developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, seizures, microcephaly, and speech impairment. Age at onset of seizures ranged from 10 months to 2 years. Two of the patients had axial and appendicular hypotonia, and 1 patient had spasticity. Dysmorphic facial features were variable and included long face, prominent nose, long philtrum, and large or low-set ears. Brain MRI findings included cortical volume loss, underopercularization, delayed myelination, thin corpus callosum, and small cerebellar vermis in both sibs from family 1. A similarly affected sib from family 2 was deceased and not tested for mutation.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of CDG2BB in the families reported by {1:Duan et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous families with CDG2BB, {1:Duan et al. (2023)} identified homozygous missense mutations (S42P, {606975.0001} and D37H, {606975.0002}) in the COG3 gene. Both mutations were located in the N-terminal region and were predicted to destabilize the COG lobe A components. COG3 protein expression was reduced in fibroblasts from one of the sibs from family 1. Analysis of glycoproteins from patient fibroblasts demonstrated disturbances in some glycoproteins and Golgi enzymes, suggesting an intra-Golgi membrane trafficking defect. A BFA-induced retrograde transport assay revealed slower retrograde transport in patient cells compared to controls.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that folate-responsive immunodeficiency-114 (IMD114) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SLC19A1 gene ({600424}) on chromosome 21q22.

description.title: Description
description.content: Folate-responsive immunodeficiency-114 (IMD114) is an autosomal recessive immunologic disorder characterized by the onset of oral ulcers and recurrent skin and respiratory infections in early infancy. Affected individuals have lip fissures, skin sores and abscesses, genital dermatitis, chronic diarrhea, and poor overall growth. Laboratory studies show megaloblastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and lymphopenia with decreased Ig levels. Some individuals have global developmental delay, often with brain imaging abnormalities. Treatment with folic acid supplementation results in significant clinical improvement of the hematologic and immunologic abnormalities, although neurologic abnormalities, if already present, do not respond to treatment. Early intervention and treatment with folic acid supplementation may prevent or delay neurologic deficits in affected infants ({1:Gok et al., 2023}; {2:Shiraishi et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Gok et al. (2023)} reported 2 boys, related as first cousins from a consanguineous Turkish family, who presented in early infancy with features of immunodeficiency, including recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, oral mucositis, skin sores, dermatitis, and mild cytopenia with low IgG. Both had poor overall growth; 1 had tooth abnormalities. P1, who was 40 days old at diagnosis, was noted to have fever, hepatosplenomegaly, high triglycerides, low fibrinogen, and high ferritin, suggestive of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). P1 had normal neurodevelopment. P2, who was 2 years old at diagnosis, had recurrent infections since infancy and also showed global developmental delay (sitting at 1.5 years of age); brain imaging showed cerebral and cerebellar atrophy with delayed myelination. Laboratory studies showed mildly decreased T cells, B cells, and IgG, and bone marrow showed megaloblastic changes; serum folate levels were normal. Treatment with folinic acid supplementation resulted in normalization of the hematologic and immunologic parameters in both patients, and severe infections no longer occurred. P2 showed some neurologic improvement and learned to walk with support and speak a few words. Both boys had a mutation in the SLC19A1 gene. P1 had a similarly affected sib who died at 3.5 months of age, and a sib of P2 had died in early childhood of unknown causes; genetic studies were not performed in the sibs.

{2:Shiraishi et al. (2023)} reported 2 boys from a large Turkish family who had severe recurrent respiratory and skin infections, oral lesions, fever, chronic diarrhea since infancy, and a mutation in the SLC19A1 gene. More variable features included atopic dermatitis, lip fissures, food allergies, dental caries, and oral bleeding. Both also developed sparse gray hair, and 1 had discoloration patches on the skin. Laboratory studies showed megaloblastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and lymphopenia with low serum IgG. Red cell folate levels were decreased, although serum folate levels were normal. Both patients had poor overall growth and global developmental delay; P2 had seizures. Brain imaging was abnormal in both patients, showing periventricular white matter abnormalities and delayed myelination in P1, and calcifications affecting the basal ganglia and other brain regions in P2. Folic acid treatment at age 5.5 years (P1) and 3.5 years (P2) led to improvement of the immunologic and hematologic abnormalities and discolored hair, but neurologic deficits persisted. P2 died at 6.5 years of age due to acute neurologic decompensation.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: {1:Gok et al. (2023)} and {2:Shiraishi et al. (2023)} found that folic acid supplementation resulted in significant clinical and laboratory improvement of hematologic and immunologic abnormalities in patients with IMD114.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of IMD114 in the family reported by {1:Gok et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 male first cousins from a large consanguineous Turkish family with IMD114, {1:Gok et al. (2023)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SLC19A1 gene (G348R; {600424.0002}). The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. Patient cells were resistant to apoptosis when exposed to methotrexate, suggesting impaired transporter function of the mutant SLC19A1 protein. Patient T cells showed proliferation defects in vitro when folic acid concentration was reduced. In addition, patient CD4+ T cells showed reduced expression of several cytokine genes involved in antiviral immunity, including IFNA ({147660}), IFNG ({147570}), TNFA ({191160}), and IL6 ({147620}), in reduced folic acid conditions compared to controls. Patient T cells had increased levels of GM-CSF (CSF2; {138960}) and IL10 ({124092}). The findings suggested that patients are vulnerable to infection when folate intake is insufficient, and that presence of the defective folate transporter becomes more apparent during infection when B and T cells undergo clonal expansion and their folate demands are high.

In 2 distantly related boys with IMD114, {2:Shiraishi et al. (2023)} identified homozygosity for the G348R mutation in the SLC19A1 gene. The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family. It was not present in the gnomAD database (v2.1.1). Although serum folate levels were normal, folate levels were reduced in patient red blood cells, indicating impaired cellular folate uptake. Additional in vitro functional studies showed that patient lymphocytes and cells transfected with the mutation had decreased phosphorylation of STING ({612374}) with reduced downstream activation of NFKB (see {164011}) signaling and impaired induction of IFNB ({147640}) transcription compared to controls after stimulation with the cyclic dinucleotide cGAMP. Patient CD4+ T cells, which were decreased in number, showed defective proliferative responses to stimulation. These findings were consistent with reduced transporter activity for both cyclic dinucleotides and folate.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Tan-Almurshedi syndrome (TANALS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the DRG1 gene ({603952}) on chromosome 22q12.

description.title: Description
description.content: Tan-Almurshedi syndrome (TANALS) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intrauterine growth retardation, poor overall growth with short stature and microcephaly, hypotonia, global developmental delay with impaired intellectual development, poor or absent speech, spasticity, and dysmorphic facial features ({1:Westrip et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Westrip et al. (2023)} reported 4 patients from 3 unrelated families with a neurodevelopmental syndrome associated with mutation in the DRG1 gene. The patients, who ranged in age from 6 to 19 years, presented at birth with intrauterine growth retardation, hypotonia, and poor feeding. They showed global developmental delay with walking between 3 and 10 years of age, impaired intellectual development, and poor or absent speech and language. Additional features included spasticity with hyperreflexia in all 4 limbs, absent secondary sexual characteristics into the teenage years, short stature (as low as -6.7 SD), and microcephaly (as low as -5.2 SD). Dysmorphic features included brachycephaly, prominent forehead, hypoplasia of the supraorbital ridges, short palpebral fissures, broad nasal bridge, small, low-set, and posteriorly rotated ears, everted lower lip, widely spaced teeth, exotropia, strabismus, camptodactyly, foot deformities, reduced eyebrows and eyelashes, and eczematous skin lesions. One patient (family 1) had well-controlled generalized tonic-clonic seizures at age 7 years and developed diabetes mellitus at age 17. Another patient (family 3) was born with lumbosacral meningomyelocele and had vertebral abnormalities. Brain imaging in this patient showed mild cerebral volume loss.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of TANALS in the families reported by {1:Westrip et al. (2023)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 4 patients from 3 unrelated families with TANALS, {1:Westrip et al. (2023)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the DRG1 gene ({603952.0001}-{603952.0004}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families. None of the mutations were present in the gnomAD database. There were 3 nonsense mutations and 1 missense mutation. Expression of the mutations in HeLa cells showed that the G54X ({603952.0001}) and R140X ({603952.0004}) proteins were not expressed, likely due to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. The K263X ({603952.0002}) and N248F ({603952.0003}) proteins were detected, but at significantly decreased levels compared to controls. The N248F mutation had a loss of GTPase activity in in vitro studies and compromised binding to the DRG1 protein partner ZC3H15 ({619704}). Overall, the findings were consistent with a loss-of-function effect for all variants.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {1:Westrip et al. (2023)} found that Drg1 is ubiquitously expressed in mouse embryos and is essential for proper development. Homozygous knockout of Drg1 in murine embryos led to significantly decreased survival rates compared to controls.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-80 with variant lissencephaly (MRT80) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CASP2 gene ({600639}) on chromosome 7q35.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-80 with variant lissencephaly (MRT80) is characterized by global developmental delay with mildly to moderately impaired intellectual development and behavioral abnormalities. Speech delay and motor abnormalities, such as hypotonia, may also be present. Brain imaging shows lissencephaly with pachygyria and mild cortical thickening in the frontotemporal lobes ({1:Uctepe et al., 2024}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Uctepe et al. (2024)} reported 7 patients from 5 unrelated families with a similar neurodevelopmental disorder associated with cortical brain malformations. The patients, who ranged in age from 6 to 26 years, were ascertained through the GeneMatcher Program after exome sequencing identified biallelic mutations in the CASP2 gene. Four of the families were consanguineous (of Turkish or Iranian descent). The patients had global developmental delay with mildly to moderately impaired intellectual development, sometimes with speech delay. Most had behavioral abnormalities, including autistic features, ADHD, aggression, and intolerance to frustration. Brain imaging performed in 3 patients showed lissencephaly with bilateral pachygyria and mild cortical thickening in the frontotemporal lobes. One patient had prominent subcortical perivascular spaces and another had hydrocephaly. More variable features included seizures (1 patient), hypotonia, weakness, spasticity (1 patient), abnormal and uncoordinated gait (1 patient), and optic atrophy (1 patient). One patient was noted to have dysmorphic facial features, including synophrys, upslanting palpebral fissures, prominent nasal tip, thin upper lip, and low-set, posteriorly rotated ears.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MRT80 in the families reported by {1:Uctepe et al. (2024)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 7 patients from 5 unrelated families with MRT80, {1:Uctepe et al. (2024)} identified homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the CASP2 gene ({600639.0001}-{600639.0004}). The mutations, which were found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families from whom parental DNA was available. None of the mutations were present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variants were not performed. The phenotype was similar to that observed in patients with biallelic mutations in the other 2 components of the PIDDosome, namely CRADD ({603454}) and PIDD1 ({605247}) (see MRT34, {614499} and MRT75, {619827}), indicating that each component of the PIDDosome complex is critical for normal development of the human cerebral cortex and brain function.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Alfadhel syndrome (AFDL) is caused by homozygous mutation in the RAP1GDS1 gene ({179502}) on chromosome 4q23.

description.title: Description
description.content: Alfadhel syndrome (AFDL) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with features of global developmental delay, hypotonia, and facial dysmorphism ({1:Asiri et al., 2020}, {2:Bertoli-Avella et al., 2021}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Asiri et al. (2020)} reported 2 families in which 4 individuals had developmental delay and dysmorphic facial features. Three of the patients were children, and 1 was 27 years of age. They all presented in infancy with hypotonia and delayed motor development. Walking was delayed, and some showed an unsteady gait. They also had impaired intellectual development with poor expressive speech. The 2 patients from family 1 showed hyporeflexia, and 1 showed behavioral abnormalities. Common dysmorphic features included triangular face, low-set or everted ears, arched eyebrows, bulbous nose, flat philtrum, short philtrum, thin lips, and retrognathia. The patients in family 2 had poor overall growth and clubfeet with dorsal clonus. The 27-year-old developed generalized seizures at age 10 years; he was the only patient with seizures. All 4 patients had mutations in the RAP1GDS1 gene. The authors proposed naming the disorder Alfadhel syndrome.

{2:Bertoli-Avella et al. (2021)} reported 4 patients with a neurodevelopmental disorder and mutations in the RAP1GDS1 gene. {3:Bertoli-Avella (2023)} clarified that 2 of the patients had previously been reported by {1:Asiri et al. (2020)}. The new patients (patients 22 and 23) had global developmental delay and regression, short stature, abnormality of movement, difficulty standing, delayed myelination, generalized hypotonia, joint laxity, stereotypy, and dysmorphic features, including high forehead, highly arched eyebrows, low-set ears, nasal flaring, and hypertelorism.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of AFDL in the families reported by {1:Asiri et al. (2020)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 4 male patients from 2 unrelated consanguineous Saudi Arabian families with Alfadhel syndrome, {1:Asiri et al. (2020)} identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the RAP1GDS1 gene ({179502.0001}). The mutation, which was found by whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the families.

{2:Bertoli-Avella et al. (2021)} reported 4 patients from consanguineous families with Alfadhel syndrome and homozygous mutations in the RAP1GDS1 gene. {3:Bertoli-Avella (2023)} clarified that patients 22 and 23 in their table 1 were females in whom {2:Bertoli-Avella et al. (2021)} had identified the mutations ({179502.0001} and {179502.0002}, respectively) and that patients 24 and 25 were the patients previously reported by {1:Asiri et al. (2020)}.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation-9 (NBIA9) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the FTH1 gene ({134770}) on chromosome 11q12.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation-9 (NBIA9) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent from infancy and progressive neurodegeneration of motor and cognitive skills. Affected individuals have delayed walking or inability to walk, spasticity with hyperreflexia, ataxia, dystonia, and poor or absent language. Additional more variable features include dysphagia, failure to thrive, poor growth, microcephaly, hypotonia, impaired vision, and seizures. Brain imaging shows progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, iron accumulation in the basal ganglia, thin corpus callosum, and pontocerebellar hypoplasia. The disorder can be classified as a neuroferritinopathy (see NBIA3, {606159}) ({1:Shieh et al., 2023}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of NBIA, see NBIA1 ({234200}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Shieh et al. (2023)} reported 5 unrelated patients, ranging from 20 months to 23 years of age and ascertained through the GeneMatcher program, who had global developmental delay with delayed walking or inability to walk, poor or absent speech, dysarthria, and variably impaired intellectual development. They also had movement abnormalities, including spasticity, hyperreflexia, ataxia, dysmetria, dystonia, exaggerated startle, and other involuntary movements. One patient had significant axial hypotonia. Most had dysphagia with feeding difficulties, some had failure to thrive with poor overall growth and microcephaly, and 2 were tube-fed at ages 4 and 14 years. A few patients had poor eye contact, abnormal vision, or cortical visual impairment. Two patients had epilepsy (including 1 with myoclonic seizures) and a third had a single seizure. The symptoms and disease course were progressive, consistent with neurodegeneration. The oldest patients lost ambulation and became wheelchair-bound. Laboratory results of iron studies were variable: serum iron levels were borderline low or normal, and ferritin and transferrin saturation were low in some and normal in others. One patient had mild normocytic anemia. Brain imaging showed progressive supratentorial white matter loss, cerebellar hypoplasia or atrophy primarily affecting the vermis, thinning of the corpus callosum, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and abnormal signals in the basal ganglia, consistent with iron accumulation. The authors noted several brain imaging patterns, including the 'eye of the tiger' sign in the globus pallidus and the 'hot-cross bun' and 'figure-of-eight' signs in those with pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and suggested that the disease has prenatal onset. Neuropathologic examination of P2, who died at 23 years of age, showed diffuse involvement of the brain, brainstem, and spinal cord with patchy destruction of the basal ganglia and midbrain, including the red nucleus and substantia nigra. Intracytoplasmic and intranuclear eosinophilic FTH1-positive inclusions were observed in neurons throughout the brain and cerebellum, and there was extracellular iron deposition in the white matter and basal ganglia. Rare iron deposition was observed in the gastrointestinal system, suggesting that other cells outside of the nervous system may be subtly affected. None of the patients had features of hemochromatosis.

On postmortem testing in the brain of a 78-year-old woman who had died of COVID-19 pneumonia, {2:Umathum et al. (2024)} identified ferritin-containing inclusion bodies, consistent with brain iron accumulation seen in NBIA9 but without neurodegeneration. The patient was without neurologic symptoms prior to her death and had no family history of central nervous system disease. Postmortem brain weight was moderately reduced. The basal ganglia appeared normal, but histologic studies showed a striking number of inclusion bodies caused by enlargement of the nuclei due to ferritin complex accumulation. A few extracerebral inclusion bodies were found in the kidney and liver, suggesting that NBIA9 might be a systemic disease.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the FTH1 gene that were identified in patients with NBIA9 by {1:Shieh et al. (2023)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 5 unrelated patients with NBIA9, {1:Shieh et al. (2023)} identified de novo heterozygous truncating mutations in the last exon (exon 4) of the FTH1 gene. One patient carried an S164X mutation ({134770.0002}) and the 4 other patients carried an F171X mutation ({134770.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Studies of patient fibroblasts showed that both mutations escaped nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and produced a C-terminally truncated protein. Molecular modeling predicted that the mutations would disrupt the ferritin E-helix, alter the pore region that is important for iron retention, and thus likely diminish iron-storage capacity. Patient fibroblasts showed elevated FTH1 and FTL ({134790}) protein levels, abnormal accumulation of cytoplasmic ferritin aggregates, increased susceptibility to iron accumulation, and evidence of increased oxidation and oxidative stress compared to controls. The findings were consistent with a dominant-negative effect. Targeted knockdown of the mutant S164X FTH1 transcript using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) in vitro partially rescued the abnormal cellular phenotype.

In a 78-year-old woman with ferritin-containing inclusion bodies in the brain on postmortem testing, consistent with brain iron accumulation seen in NBIA9 but without neurodegeneration, {2:Umathum et al. (2024)} identified a heterozygous 2-bp deletion (c.409_410delTG) in the last exon of the FTH1 gene ({134770.0004}), resulting in a frameshift and premature stop codon. The variant was not present in the gnomAD, ExAC, and 1000 Genomes Project databases. The patient, who died of COVID-19 pneumonia, had not had neurologic symptoms and had no family history of central nervous system disease.

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-27 (HLD27) is caused by homozygous mutation in the POLR1A gene ({616404}) on chromosome 2p11.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-27 (HLD27) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder characterized by global developmental delay with impaired motor and intellectual development apparent from infancy. Affected individuals have poor or absent speech, ataxic gait or inability to sit or walk, spasticity, and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus, gaze palsy). Some patients have seizures. Disease progression and developmental regression consistent with neurodegeneration is often observed. Brain imaging shows progressive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and thin corpus callosum ({2:Misceo et al., 2023}).

For a general phenotypic description and a discussion of genetic heterogeneity of HLD, see {312080}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{1:Kara et al. (2017)} reported 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Turkish parents, with a severe neurodegenerative disease characterized by global developmental delay, impaired intellectual development, ataxia, spasticity with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses, head titubation, pyramidal signs, optic atrophy, equine foot deformities, and gaze palsy. One brother had an ataxic gait at age 5 and lost ambulation at age 9.5 years. The other brother never achieved head control, sitting, walking, or speech, and developed seizures at 6 years of age. Brain imaging in both patients showed cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, and hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. Neither had abnormal craniofacial features, aside from relative macrocephaly; the younger brother had short stature. {2:Misceo et al. (2023)} noted that the younger brother in the family reported by {1:Kara et al. (2017)} died at 19 years of age.

{2:Misceo et al. (2023)} reported 2 unrelated patients with global developmental delay apparent from infancy. P1 was from a rural part of Scandinavia and demonstrated irritability and increased muscle tone and reflexes since birth. At age 5 years, he could sit and walk only with support, had truncal ataxia, and speak only a few words. Convergent strabismus and vertical nystagmus were noted; cataracts appeared at age 11. He had regression of skills, and later developed dystonia, scoliosis, seizures, and myoclonic seizures that were difficult to treat. At 16.5 years, he had apnea due to cardiac arrest, resulting in death. Serial brain imaging showed progressive brain atrophy, particularly of the cerebellum, thinning of the corpus callosum, brainstem atrophy, and hypomyelination. The basal ganglia was small with abnormal signals mimicking neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation. Overall, the features were consistent with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. P2, born of unrelated parents of European descent, was a 2 year, 10 month-old girl who showed global developmental delay from infancy. She had hypotonia, poor head control, motor delay, poor eye contact, ataxia, dystonia, spasticity with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses, nystagmus, short stature, and brachycephaly. She showed poor overall growth and feeding difficulties requiring a gastrostomy tube. At 3.5 years of age, she was unable to walk and had no speech. Brain imaging showed cerebellar atrophy, thinning of the corpus callosum, enlarged ventricles, and signal changes consistent with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of HLD27 in the family reported by {1:Kara et al. (2017)} was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 2 brothers, born of consanguineous Turkish parents, with HLD27, {1:Kara et al. (2017)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the POLR1A gene (S934L; {616404.0005}). The brothers were also homozygous for a missense variant (R171W) in the OSBPL11 gene ({606739}). The mutations, which were found by a combination of linkage analysis and exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were both heterozygous in each parent. A sister who was neurologically normal also carried the homozygous OSBPL11 variant, but was homozygous wildtype for the POLR1A variant, suggesting that the POLR1A variant was responsible for the phenotype in the brothers. Patient fibroblasts showed decreased nucleolar levels of POLR1A. Molecular modeling suggested that the POLR1A mutation resulted in altered protein conformation and altered intramolecular associations, resulting in decreased function. The findings indicated that defects in noncoding RNA synthesis can compromise neurologic development. Skin fibroblasts from the 2 brothers and the sister who carried the homozygous OSBPL11 variant showed increased cholesterol deposition compared to controls. Similar results were obtained in RNAi studies, suggesting that the OSBPL11 variant is functionally defective and unable to facilitate normal cholesterol trafficking.

In 2 unrelated patients with HLD27, {2:Misceo et al. (2023)} identified a homozygous missense mutation in the POLR1A gene (T642N; {616404.0006}). The mutation, which was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, was found in the heterozygous state in all the unaffected parents. Fibroblasts from patient 1 showed decreased POLR1A protein levels, consistent with reduced stability of the mutant protein. The mutant protein localized normally to the nucleolus, but patient cells had enlarged nucleoli and decreased numbers of nucleoli per cell, suggesting impaired nucleolar homeostasis. Patient cells showed defects in rRNA processing and degradation and abnormal accumulation of DNA:RNA hybrids, suggesting impaired transcription and transcriptional stress due to a loss of RNA polymerase I function. Further studies of patient cells showed dysregulation of protein synthesis and degradation, decreased DNA repair, shortened telomeres, and chronic ER stress leading to constitutive activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR).

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content: {3:Weaver et al. (2015)} generated homozygous polr1a-mutant zebrafish embryos and observed gross morphologic defects beginning at 15 hpf, including noticeably smaller and misshapen heads. By 24 hpf, the eyes and brain were also abnormally shaped as was the shortened tail. At 36 to 48 hpf, the mutant embryos were proportionally smaller than wildtype and exhibited microphthalmia, cerebral hypoplasia, jaw agenesis, perturbed pigmentation, and abnormal morphology of the heart, otolith, and pectoral fin. The mutant zebrafish died by 4 to 5 days postfertilization, and skeletal staining showed reduced neural crest cell (NCC)-derived cartilage, consistent with jaw agenesis. {3:Weaver et al. (2015)} observed reductions in sox9 ({608160})-, sox10 ({602229})-, and dlx2 ({126255})-labeled NCCs in mutant

preferredTitle: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER, AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT 74; MRD74
clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, mild to severe
Caused by mutation in the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C gene (HNRNPC,)

Head: Small head circumference
Microcephaly (in some patients)
Brachycephaly
Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, mild to severe
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C gene (HNRNPC,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-74 (MRD74) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the HNRNPC gene ({164020}) on chromosome 14q11.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-74 (MRD74) is characterized by global developmental delay, including delay of gross and fine motor skills and speech delay, and variable subtle dysmorphic facial features ({1:Niggl et al., 2023}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Niggl et al. (2023)} reported 13 unrelated patients, ranging from 17 months to 15 years of age, with global developmental delay and variably impaired intellectual development who were ascertained through the GeneMatcher program after exome sequencing identified de novo heterozygous variants in the HNRNPC gene. Five individuals (Ind1-Ind5) carried a recurrent de novo heterozygous 9-residue in-frame deletion in the HNRNPC gene ({164020.0001}). These 5 patients had mildly impaired intellectual development (IQ range from 54 to 72 in 2 patients), variable speech delay with articulation problems, and delayed gross and fine motor skill acquisition. Some had early feeding issues and poor overall growth with small head circumference; Ind3 had microcephaly (-3.54 SD). Other features included hypotonia (in 3), hypertonia (in 1), motor tics (in 2), hyposensitivity to pain (in 2), and sleep difficulties (in 4). Most patients had a happy demeanor, often with poor attention span. All had variable subtle dysmorphic features, including brachycephaly, deep-set eyes, hypo- or hypertelorism, prominent nose, smooth philtrum, and thin upper lip. None had seizures or significant brain imaging abnormalities. Another 7 individuals had heterozygous frameshift (4 patients) or missense (3 patients) variants in the HNRNPC gene, and 1 patient (Ind10) had a larger deletion that included the HNRNPC gene and extended into adjacent genes. Overall, these individuals had similar features as Ind1-Ind5, including mild to severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech, hypotonia, delayed walking or inability to walk, poor fine motor skills, and sleep issues. Three patients had seizures. Some had feeding problems, including 3 patients who required a feeding tube. Most also had dysmorphic facial features, including asymmetric head, round face, broad forehead, broad nasal bridge, deep-set eyes, downslanting palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, hypertelorism, micro- or retrognathia, and thin upper lip.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the HNRNPC gene that were identified in patients with MRD74 by {1:Niggl et al. (2023)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: {1:Niggl et al. (2023)} reported 13 unrelated patients with MRD74 associated with heterozygous variants, mostly de novo, in the HNRNPC gene ascertained through the GeneMatcher program. One individual (Ind10) carried a larger deletion that included the HNRNPC gene and extended into adjacent genes. Five individuals (Ind1-Ind5) carried a recurrent de novo heterozygous 9-residue in-frame deletion (HNRNPC(del); {164020.0001}) that affected the C terminus and escaped nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. The 7 other individuals had heterozygous frameshift (4 patients, see, e.g., {164020.0002}) or missense (3 patients) variants. Of note, some of these individuals carried additional variants of uncertain significance in other genes, parental samples were not available for 2 patients, and 2 patients inherited the variants from their unaffected mothers who were mosaic. Four of these variants were confirmed to be de novo. Detailed in vitro cellular studies showed that HNRNPC(del) did not cause a loss-of-function, dominant-negative, or gain-of-function effect, but likely results in haploinsufficiency. In silico computational metaanalysis of published data suggested that loss of HNRNPC results in alternative splicing of multiple target genes, including a subset of genes associated with intellectual disability. RNA-seq analysis of fibroblasts derived from Ind8, who carried a de novo heterozygous frameshift variant ({164020.0002}), showed some evidence of alternative splicing that was similar to that identified in the metaanalysis (about a 52% overlap of alternative exon or ALU sequences). However, iPSCs from Ind1 with the HNRNPC(del) variant did not show splice site alterations in any of the genes identified in the metaanalysis, which the authors attributed to the differences in cell type. ShRNA-mediated knockdown of the Hnrnpc gene in murine primary neuronal cultures resulted in decreased neurite length and arborization compared to controls. Overexpression of both wildtype HNRNPC and HNRNPC(del) caused reduced neuronal soma area, neurite length, and dendrite arborization; moreover, the dendrites in cells overexpressing the wildtype and variant genes deteriorated 5 days posttransfection, while those in control cells developed normally. In utero electroporation of mouse embryos to express HNRNPC shRNAs, HNRNPC isoform 1 (wildtype), and HNRNPC(del) in immature neurons of the subventricular zone all resulted in delayed neuronal migration during early cortical development. The findings indicated that the HNRNPC(del) variant behaves like the wildtype protein and that its pathogenic effect is caused by the reduction of HNRNPC levels. The authors concluded that correct dosage of HNRNPC is critical for normal neuronal development and function.

preferredTitle: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH MOTOR ABNORMALITIES, SEIZURES, AND FACIAL DYSMORPHISM; NEDMSF
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the pumilio RNA binding family member 1 gene (PUM1,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the pumilio RNA binding family member 1 gene (PUM1,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor abnormalities, and facial dysmorphism

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with motor abnormalities, seizures, and facial dysmorphism (NEDMSF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PUM1 gene ({607204}) on chromosome 1p35.

See also chromosome 1p35 deletion syndrome ({617930}), a contiguous gene deletion syndrome that includes the PUM1 gene and has an overlapping phenotype.

description.title: Description
description.content: Neurodevelopmental disorder with motor abnormalities, seizures, and facial dysmorphism (NEDMSF) is characterized by global developmental delay, poor overall growth, early-onset seizures (in most patients), severely impaired motor development with hypotonia and/or ataxia, and dysmorphic facial features. Affected individuals have impaired intellectual development, which can be severe. Brain imaging may show thin corpus callosum, enlarged ventricles, or cerebellar atrophy. All reported mutations have occurred de novo ({2:Gennarino et al., 2018}; {5:Voet et al., 2020}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{2:Gennarino et al. (2018)} reported a 9-year-old girl (P11) who developed intractable generalized seizures at age 5 months, followed by progressive ataxia, hypotonicity of the lower limbs, global developmental delay with cortical visual impairment, and stereotypic hand movements. She also had hypotonia, scoliosis, facial dysmorphism, and low bone mineral density. Dysmorphic features included broad nasal bridge, high-arched palate, almond-shaped eyes, bitemporal narrowing, ptosis, low-set ears, tapering fingers, small hands, toe syndactyly, and abnormal finger and foot pads. Brain imaging showed an enlarged fourth ventricle and shortening of the cerebellar vermis. The authors called the disorder 'Pumilio-1-associated developmental disability, ataxia, and seizure syndrome (PADDAS).'

{1:Bonnemason-Carrere et al. (2019)} described a boy born by cesarean section because of severe intrauterine growth restriction. At birth, his weight, length, and head circumference were all more than 4 SD below the median. He had sparse, thin, fragile hair, with temporal balding, and sparse eyebrows and eyelashes, consistent with hair dysplasia. He had profound axial hypotonia and severe developmental delay. He also had hypospadias and cryptorchidism. At age 3 years he had a generalized nonfebrile seizure, with later development of absence seizures, which were well-controlled with anticonvulsant medications. An EEG showed paroxysmal abnormalities in the central areas. At age 13 years, growth delay remained severe, and dysmorphic features included hypertelorism, ptosis, almond-shaped eyes, epicanthus, broad nasal bridge, bitemporal narrowing, low-set ears, high-arched palate, oligodontia with widely spaced teeth, and bilateral clinodactyly. The presence of ataxia could not be assessed because of the severity of the motor delay. Brain MRI showed a shortened corpus callosum and T2 flair periventricular hypersignal. The patient also developed mild hypothyroidism. No kidney or heart defects were seen on ultrasonography.

{5:Voet et al. (2020)} reported 2 unrelated boys, 15 and 18 years of age, who presented with refractory seizures in infancy (P1) and 14 months of age (P2). The patients had apneic episodes and absence seizures, with occasional tonic-clonic seizures. P1 had episodes of status epilepticus. Both patients had profound developmental delay with poor overall growth, hypotonia, delayed walking, and severely impaired intellectual development with poor or absent speech. P2 had uncoordinated movements and stiffness, but no frank ataxia. Dysmorphic features in both patients included sloping forehead, hypertelorism, abnormal eyebrows, high nasal bridge, prominent nose, low-set columella, prominent mandible, pointed chin, high palate, and clinodactyly of the fingers and toes. P1 also had hypermetropia, exotropia, pectus excavatum, hirsutism on the back, joint hyperlaxity, and unilateral cryptorchidism. Brain imaging in P1 showed hypoplasia of the corpus callosum and cerebral atrophy, whereas brain imaging in P2 was normal at 18 months. Both were noted to have a happy and friendly personality.

{6:Ye et al. (2022)} reported a 3-year-old girl, born of unrelated Chinese parents, who had onset of febrile seizures progressing to refractory status epilepticus at 4 months of age. Profound axial hypotonia and developmental regression with loss of head control was noted after the onset of seizures. The frequency and severity of seizures eventually improved with medication, and she could roll over and smile at age 3 years, but had severely impaired intellectual development and was nonverbal. Dysmorphic facial features included high-arched palate, ptosis, hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, low-set ears, bitemporal narrowing, and almond-shaped eyes. Brain imaging showed enlarged ventricles and thin corpus callosum.

<Subhead> Clinical Variability

{2:Gennarino et al. (2018)} also reported an unrelated 9-year-old girl (P10) who showed chorea, gait ataxia, and fine-motor incoordination from the age of 5 years. She also had dysarthria, spasticity, and ballismus. Clinical details were limited; she was noted to have early motor delay and short stature, but she did not have impaired intellectual development or documented seizures. Brain imaging was normal at age 6.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the PUM1 gene that were identified in patients with NEDMSF by {2:Gennarino et al. (2018)}, {1:Bonnemason-Carrere et al. (2019)}, {5:Voet et al. (2020)}, and {6:Ye et al. (2022)} occurred de novo.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 9-year-old girl (P11) with NEDMSF, {2:Gennarino et al. (2018)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the PUM1 gene (R1147W; {607204.0002}). Another girl (P10) with a milder phenotype carried a different de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the PUM1 gene (R1139W; {607204.0001}), as well as a variant of uncertain significance in the XPR1 gene ({605237}). The PUM1 mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not found in the ExAC database. Cells from P11 showed about 43% residual wildtype PUM1 protein levels, consistent with haploinsufficiency. PUM1 mRNA levels were normal in P11, but mRNA and protein levels of known PUM1 targets, including ATXN1 ({601556}) and E2F3 ({600427}), were abnormally increased, suggesting that the R1147W variant impaired PUM1 repression activity. In vitro transfection studies in HEK293 cells showed that overexpression of the R1139W variant was unable to reduce ATXN1 and E2F3, indicating that it impaired the repression activity of PUM1. {4:Hamosh (2024)} noted that the R1139W variant is present in 2 of 833,094 alleles in the gnomAD database (frequency of 2.4 x 10(-6)).

In a boy with NEDMSF, {1:Bonnemason-Carrere et al. (2019)} identified a de novo heterozygous R1147W mutation in the PUM1 gene. The mutation, which was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing, had previously been identified by {2:Gennarino et al. (2018)}. The boy was also found to carry a heterozygous variant in the GRIA3 gene, which the authors classified as a variant of unknown significance.

In a 15-year-old boy (P1) with NEDMSF, {5:Voet et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous R1147W mutation in the PUM1 gene. The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing, was not present in public databases, including gnomAD. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed. In an 18-year-old male (P2) with NEDMSF, {5:Voet et al. (2020)} identified a de novo heterozygous nonsense variant in the PUM1 gene (R837X). The variant was found by whole-exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant and studies of patient cells were not performed, but it was predicted to result in haploinsufficiency. {5:Voet et al. (2020)} stated that the R837X variant was not present in public databases, including gnomAD. However, {4:Hamosh (2024)} noted that R837X was present in 1 of 628,780 alleles in gnomAD (frequency of 1.59 x 10(-6)).

In a 3-year-old Chinese girl with NEDMSF, {6:Ye et al. (2022)} identified a de novo heterozygous R1147W substitution in the PUM1 gene. The mutation, which was found by trio-based whole-exome sequencing, was not present in the gnomAD database. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{3:Gennarino et al. (2015)} found that heterozygous Pum1 +/- mice had increased levels of Atxn1 mRNA and protein levels in the cerebrum and cerebellum compared to controls, indicating that Pum1 directly regulates Atxn1 levels in the mouse brain. Pum1-null mice were significantly smaller in body and brain size compared to controls and to Pum1 +/- mice. The loss of 1 copy of the Pum1 gene was sufficient to cause progressive motor performance, and the motor incoordination was even more pronounced in Pum1-null mice. Loss of Pum1 resulted in progressive cerebellar dysfunction, manifest as gait and stride ataxia with a spinocerebellar ataxia-like neurodegeneration with gross and fine motor impairment. Neuropathologic examination showed progressive Purkinje cell degeneration and loss of dendritic arborization in mutant mice. The features were similar to those observed in mouse models of SCA1 ({164400}), which is caused by abnormal accumulation of Atxn1 due to an expanded polyglutamine repeat within that gene. The motor phenotype, Purkinje cell degeneration, and dendritic arborization defects could be mitigated by decreasing Atxn1 protein levels using genetic crossing of Pum1 +/- mice with Atxn1 +/- mice. In addition, overexpression of wildtype Pum1 in Atxn1 mutant mice resulted in a reduction of Atxn1 levels in the cerebellum. The findings elucidated a posttranscriptional regulatory mechanism that regulates ATXN1 levels and could putatively play a role in disease.

Follow-up analysis of Pum1-null mutant mice by {2:Gennarino et al. (2018)} showed that they were born at a lower frequency than expected and showed hyperactivity, marked growth defects, spontaneous seizures, abnormal EEG, cerebellar hypoplasia, and Purkinje cell degeneration.

clinicalSynopsis: Giant pigmented hairy nevus, often in lumbosacral distribution
Hair may not be present on the nevus
Relatives with multiple small congenital pigmented nevi
Caused by somatic mutation in the NRAS proto-oncogene, GTPase gene (NRAS,)
Caused by somatic mutation in the HRas proto-oncogene, GTPase gene (HRAS,)

Skin: Giant pigmented hairy nevus, often in lumbosacral distribution
Hair may not be present on the nevus
Miscellaneous: Relatives with multiple small congenital pigmented nevi
Molecular Basis: Caused by somatic mutation in the NRAS proto-oncogene, GTPase gene (NRAS,)
Caused by somatic mutation in the HRas proto-oncogene, GTPase gene (HRAS,)

phenotypes.phenotype: Spitz nevus or nevus spilus, somatic

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because congenital melanocytic nevus syndrome (CMNS) is caused by somatic mutation in the NRAS gene ({164790}) on chromosome 1p13.

Two other forms of benign melanocytic proliferation, nevus spilus and Spitz nevus, are caused by somatic mutation in the HRAS gene ({190020}) on chromosome 11p15.

description.title: Description
description.content:
Congenital melanocytic nevus syndrome is characterized by pigmentary skin defects apparent at birth. Most individuals have 1 or more large or giant lesions greater than 20 cm and up to over 60 cm in diameter, which may cover up to 80% of total body area. These lesions may or may not be hairy. Smaller 'satellite' pigmented lesions numbering in the hundreds may also be present all over the body. Congenital melanocytic nevi (CMN) can be associated with malignant melanoma (see CMM1, {155600}), but the risk appears to be low, ranging from 1 to 2% for all individuals, but rising to 10 to 15% in those with very large nevi (greater than 40 cm). A small subset of patients with CMNS have abnormalities of the central nervous system, known as 'neurocutaneous melanosis' or 'neuromelanosis' ({249400}), which may be symptomatic. Patients with CMNS also tend to have a characteristic facial appearance, including wide or prominent forehead, periorbital fullness, small short nose with narrow nasal bridge, round face, full cheeks, prominent premaxilla, and everted lower lip (summary by {11:Kinsler et al., 2008}; {13:Kinsler et al., 2012}).

Spitz nevi are benign melanocytic melanomas composed of epithelioid or spindle cell melanocytes. They usually present as solitary skin tumors but can occur in multiple patterns, having agminated, dermatomal, and disseminated forms (summary by {15:Sarin et al., 2013}). Nevus spilus, also known as speckled lentiginous nevus, is a congenital hyperpigmented patch that progressively evolves, with affected individuals developing dark macules and papules during childhood and adolescence. Over time, nevus spilus may give rise to common lentigines, melanocytic nevi, Spitz nevi, and melanomas (summary by {14:Sarin et al., 2014}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{8:Hecht et al. (1981)} reported 2 first-cousin infants, a boy and a girl, who were born with giant pigmented hairy nevus (GPHN) of the scalp. The diameter of the nevi in each child approximated half of the scalp area, and the hair was dark in the center and of normal texture. Both infants showed normal development. Biopsies showed no evidence of malignancy.

{10:Ho et al. (1999)} reported a girl with sporadic occurrence of GPHN. At birth, she was noted to have a large patch of dark, coarse, thick hair over the right temporoparietal region of the scalp extending to the right occiput. There was also a separate small 1-cm hairy nevus adjacent to the front fontanel, and 2 epidermal sebaceous nevi on the right temple. CT scan showed an absence of the cranial bone underlying the large hairy nevus, with a size of about 7 x 6 cm. The bony edges of the cranial defect were irregular. The skull defect showed gradual spontaneous regression over the next 2 years, and the patient had normal development and no seizures. {10:Ho et al. (1999)} postulated a dysregulation of growth at the cellular and extracellular matrix level resulting from paracrine effects.

{17:Stojanovic et al. (2000)} reported a 21-year-old woman with extensive GPHN covering 20% of her total body surface. The lesions covered the trunk, upper and lower extremities, and the face. They were congenital, but there had been no changes in color, size, or distribution. Family history was negative.

{6:Foster et al. (2001)} reported follow-up of 46 patients with giant congenital melanocytic nevi, including 42 who underwent MR imaging. MRI abnormalities, consistent with neuromelanosis, were detected in 14 of 42 children, most of whom were under 12 months of age. {6:Foster et al. (2001)} concluded that central nervous system melanosis is not a rare event in patients with giant congenital melanocytic nevi, but that most patients with abnormal findings remain asymptomatic.

{3:De Wijn et al. (2010)} reported 2 unrelated families with recurrence of giant congenital melanocytic nevi. The first patient was a male infant with a typical giant melanocytic nevus (3 x 7 cm) with hairy patches on the occipital region of the head, covering about 1% total body surface area. His sister was born with a larger hairy melanocytic nevus on the back and buttocks, covering about 10% total body surface area. Both patients were otherwise healthy. In a second family, a girl was born with a hairy nevus covering about 30% total body surface area on the abdomen, back, buttocks, and upper legs. She also had 2 hypertrophic masses over the sacrum and mons pubis that were removed and found to contain pale myxoid matrix between nevus cells. Follow-up of this patient was uneventful. Family history revealed that the mother's niece had several large congenital melanocytic nevi covering about 11% body surface area and soft tissue hypotrophy of the affected right arm, as well as multiple satellite lesions all over her body, but no other abnormalities. These 2 familial cases were identified from a larger cohort of 120 patients, suggesting that familial occurrence is rare. {3:De Wijn et al. (2010)} discussed possible involvement of the RAS/RAF/MAPK pathway as well as a disturbance in neural crest cell development due to a postzygotic mutation.

{13:Kinsler et al. (2012)} reviewed facial photographs of 95 Caucasian children with CMNS and concluded that there is a distinctive facial morphology. Most children (74%) in this series had at least 3 typical features, including wide or prominent forehead, apparent hypertelorism, eyebrow variants, periorbital fullness, small/short nose, narrow nasal ridge, broad nasal tip, broad or round face, full cheeks, prominent premaxilla, prominent or long philtrum, and everted lower lip. No association was found between the number of facial features and the severity of the cutaneous phenotype. The findings were consistent with the hypothesis that CMNS results from an abnormality of neural crest development, since the neural crest also contributes to facial development. {13:Kinsler et al. (2012)} proposed the term 'congenital melanocytic nevus syndrome.'

{12:Kinsler et al. (2013)} studied tissue samples from 15 unrelated patients with congenital melanocytic nevi who ranged in age from 2 to 23 years. Three of the patients developed malignant melanoma and died at ages 2, 7, and 10 years. Two of those who died of melanoma had neurologic involvement. The lesions varied in size and number, but most patients had 50 to greater than 100 nevi, with the largest lesion greater than 60 cm.

<Subhead> Spitz Nevus

{15:Sarin et al. (2013)} studied a 25-year-old man who had a 4-year-history of pink papules arising in a large congenital pigmented tan patch on his left lower back. Examination showed a more than 20-cm diameter tan patch speckled with 1- to 2-mm hyperpigmented macules, characteristic of a nevus spilus, and containing 15 to 20 4- to 6-mm pink papules, characteristic of Spitz nevi. The patient was otherwise healthy, with no personal or family history of malignant melanoma. Histopathologic examination of 2 pink papules revealed symmetric, well-demarcated melanocytic proliferations consisting of spindle cell melanocytes with large vesicular nuclei splayed throughout the dermis, consistent with intradermal Spitz nevi.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
{1:Amir et al. (1982)} reported monozygotic twins who were discordant for giant pigmented nevus. At birth, the affected male infant was noted to have extensive areas of the skin over the trunk and thighs covered with a confluent, darkly pigmented nevus. He also had multiple smaller pigmented nevi on the entire body surface, and large tumor masses on the sacrum and scrotum. His twin brother had no detectable abnormalities. The findings argued against classic mendelian inheritance.

Congenital giant pigmented hairy nevus usually occurs sporadically, but familial occurrence has rarely been reported. By studying the families of 3 patients, {7:Goodman et al. (1971)} found that each had relatives with multiple small pigmented nevi. The authors suggested autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity.

{18:Voigtlander and Jung (1974)} observed affected sibs, and {8:Hecht et al. (1981)} reported affected first-cousins with an one instance of male-to-male transmission.

diagnosis.title: Diagnosis
diagnosis.content: {13:Kinsler et al. (2012)} proposed the following diagnostic criteria for congenital melanocytic nevus syndrome: (1) a CMN of greater than 5 cm projected adult size or more than 1 CMN of any size at birth, and (2) neurologic involvement, either clinical or radiologic, and/or 3 or more typical facial features.

clinicalManagement.title: Clinical Management
clinicalManagement.content: {11:Kinsler et al. (2008)} provided a protocol for the management of congenital melanocytic nevi based on the size of the largest CMN and the presence of satellite lesions.

cytogenetics.title: Cytogenetics
cytogenetics.content: By cytogenetic analysis of a giant congenital pigmented nevus, {9:Heimann et al. (1993)} found 74% normal mitoses, 22% polyploids, and 4% mitoses with chromosome rearrangements involving, in particular, chromosomes 1p, 12q, and 19p. Histology showed no signs of malignancy. Constitutional karyotype of the patient was normal. Microscopic examination of the nevus showed an infiltration of the dermis by regular nests or cords of nevus cells extending down to the reticular dermis and subcutaneous tissue. In the deeper part, the nevus cells displayed neuroid differentiation.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
{12:Kinsler et al. (2013)} identified somatic oncogenic missense mutations affecting codon 61 of the NRAS gene in affected cutaneous and neurologic tissues from 12 of 15 patients with CMNS and/or neurocutaneous melanosis. Affected skin samples from 10 of 13 patients carried a somatic heterozygous mutation, including 8 with Q61K ({164790.0008}) and 2 with Q61R ({164790.0002}). The same codon 61 mutation was found in each of the anatomically separate melanocytic nevi from the same patient. In addition, all 11 neurologic samples from 5 patients from whom neurologic tissue was available were positive for a somatic Q61K mutation; this included both melanocytic and nonmelanocytic tissue, such as a choroid plexus papilloma and meningioma. In patients with both neurologic and skin samples available, the same mutation was present in both affected tissues. None of the patients carried an NRAS mutation in the blood. Pre- and post-malignant skin tissue was available from a patient with malignant melanoma, which showed a progression from heterozygosity to homozygosity for the Q61K mutation with the onset of malignancy. Mutations at codon 61 in the NRAS gene affect the guanosine triphosphate-binding site and result in constitutive activation of NRAS. {12:Kinsler et al. (2013)} concluded that multiple congenital melanocytic nevi and neuromelanosis, as well as nonmelanocytic CNS lesions, result from somatic mosaicism, and that the mutation probably occurs in a progenitor cell in the developing neural crest or neuroectoderm. The findings also suggested that these mutations may be lethal in the germline. Three of the original 15 patients with CMNS did not have NRAS mutations.

<Subhead> Nevus Spilus and Spitz Nevus

By exome sequencing in 2 Spitz nevi that arose within the nevus spilus of a 25-year-old man, {15:Sarin et al. (2013)} identified a missense mutation in the HRAS gene (G13R; {190020.0017}) that was not found in the adjacent normal skin. Sanger sequencing revealed the same mutation in 2 more Spitz nevi from the patient. Copy number analysis confirmed amplification of HRAS in 2 of the nevi and polysomy in the melanocytes from a third Spitz nevus. No HRAS amplification was detected in adjacent fibroblasts or epidermal keratinocytes.

{14:Sarin et al. (2014)} analyzed nevi spili biopsy specimens from 8 unrelated patients and identified the G13R mutation in all, implicating the HRAS variant as the predominant causative mutation for nevi spili. Using laser-capture microdissection on 2 nevus spilus samples to isolate DNA from lentiginous melanocytes, junctional melanocytic nests, superficial dermis, and surrounding dermis, the authors demonstrated the presence of the G13R mutation in the melanocyte isolate but not in keratinocytes or dermal fibroblasts. {14:Sarin et al. (2014)} suggested that sporadic nevi spili result from a postzygotic mutation in the melanocytic lineage.

populationGenetics.title: Population Genetics
populationGenetics.content:
In a large population-based study in South America, {2:Castilla et al. (1981)} estimated that the incidence of giant pigmented nevi greater than 10 cm is 1 in 20,455 live births.

The frequency of occurrence of congenital giant pigmented hairy nevus larger than 20 cm in diameter in pediatric patients has been estimated to be 1 in 4,150. Data on possible malignant transformation of these lesions into a melanoma vary from 6 to 12% ({17:Stojanovic et al., 2000}).

history.title: History
history.content: Although it is a common observation that nevi occur in families, probably with dominant transmission, the study by {4:Denaro (1944)} is one of the few that has examined the matter specifically. Multiple pigmented moles are a feature of one chromosomal aberration, the Turner syndrome, as pointed out by {16:Sharpey-Schafer (1941)} in the pre-chromosomal era. {5:Estabrook (1928)} reported affected persons in 5 generations of a family. (His term 'nevus spilus' comes from the Greek 'spilos' for 'spot.')

clinicalSynopsis: 5-10% of patients have a first degree relative with IBD (Crohn or ulcerative colitis)
35% of cases involve ileum only (ileitis), 45% of cases involve ileum and colon (ileocolitis), 20% of cases involve colon alone - rectum spared (granulomatous colitis)
Susceptibility conferred by mutation in the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain protein 2 gene (NOD2,)

Miscellaneous: 5-10% of patients have a first degree relative with IBD (Crohn or ulcerative colitis)
35% of cases involve ileum only (ileitis), 45% of cases involve ileum and colon (ileocolitis), 20% of cases involve colon alone - rectum spared (granulomatous colitis)
Molecular Basis: Susceptibility conferred by mutation in the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain protein 2 gene (NOD2,)

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mutations in the NOD2/CARD15 gene ({605956}) are associated with susceptibility to Crohn disease in families linked to chromosome 16. A promoter polymorphism in the IL6 gene ({147620}) is associated with susceptibility to Crohn disease-associated growth failure.

For information on genetic heterogeneity of IBD, see MAPPING and MOLECULAR GENETICS sections.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
Inflammatory bowel disease is characterized by a chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation. IBD is subdivided into Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis phenotypes. Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis have a combined prevalence of 200 to 300 per 100,000 in the United States. Crohn disease may involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract, but most frequently the terminal ileum and colon. Bowel inflammation is transmural and discontinuous; it may contain granulomas or be associated with intestinal or perianal fistulas. In contrast, in ulcerative colitis, the inflammation is continuous and limited to rectal and colonic mucosal layers; fistulas and granulomas are not observed. In approximately 10% of cases confined to the rectum and colon, definitive classification of Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis cannot be made and are designated 'indeterminate colitis.' Both diseases include extraintestinal inflammation of the skin, eyes, or joints.

Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are commonly classified as autoimmune diseases. The prevalence of inflammatory bowel disease is increased in individuals with other autoimmune diseases, particularly ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, sclerosing cholangitis, and multiple sclerosis. There is strong evidence from twin studies, familial risk data, and segregation analysis that inflammatory bowel disease, especially Crohn disease, is genetic ({113:Yang and Rotter, 1994}; {18:Duerr, 1996}). Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are considered complex genetic traits as inheritance does not follow any simple mendelian models. Both genetic and environmental factors seem to be important in its etiology.

{91:Satsangi et al. (1996)} studied the clinical characteristics (disease type, extent, age of onset, need for surgery, and presence of extraintestinal manifestations) in affected subjects in multiply-affected families with inflammatory bowel disease. They identified 54 families in which 1 parent and at least 1 child were affected (a total of 77 parent-child pairs) and 155 families in which 2 sibs were affected (a total of 190 affected sib pairs). In affected parent-child pairs, parent and child were concordant for 'disease type' (Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis) in 58 of 77 pairs (75.3%), for extent in 63.6%, for extraintestinal manifestations in 70.1%, and for smoking history in 85%. The median age of onset in parents was significantly higher than in offspring (p = less than 0.0001). In 40 pairs (60.6%) the parent was at least 10 years older than the child at age of onset. Sibs were concordant for disease type in 81.6% of the affected sib pairs, extent in 76.0%, extraintestinal manifestations in 83.8%, and smoking history in 81.3%. In contrast with the parent-child pairs, 68.1% of sibs (111 sib pairs) were diagnosed within 10 years of each other. Median age of onset was 24.0 years. {91:Satsangi et al. (1996)} felt that the differences in age of onset between parents and children was not readily explained by a simple cohort effect or ascertainment bias, and may it reflect effects of genetic factors, producing anticipation between generations.

<Subhead> Crohn Disease

About 10% of persons with regional enteritis have 1 or more close relatives with granulomatous disease of the bowel. In 5 persons of Ashkenazi Jewish origin (ancestors from area of Russia-Poland around Vilna), {95:Sheehan et al. (1967)} found red cell glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency associated with regional enteritis or granulomatous colitis. The affected persons were 2 males and 3 females. Regional enteritis and sarcoidosis have been observed in the same family (see {181000}); {35:Gronhagen-Riska et al. (1983)} commented on the association. {94:Schwartz et al. (1980)} found no HLA association in sporadic cases or in familial cases. However, in 5 affected sib pairs, 4 shared both haplotypes (i.e., were HLA-identical) and the 5th shared one haplotype. Only 1 unaffected sib shared both haplotypes with an affected sib. {52:Kuster et al. (1989)} suggested that a recessive gene with incomplete penetrance is responsible for susceptibility to Crohn disease. {61:McConnell (1988)} suggested polygenic inheritance; an individual inheriting few susceptibility genes would develop ulcerative colitis, while someone inheriting a larger number of these genes would develop regional enteritis.

Although controversial, epidemiologic evidence ({34:Greenstein et al., 1988}) suggests that there may be 2 distinct clinical forms of Crohn disease: perforating and nonperforating. Patients with perforating Crohn disease have abscesses and/or free perforations. Perforating Crohn disease is the more aggressive form with a higher reoperation rate. By contrast, nonperforating Crohn disease has a more indolent clinical course and is associated with obstruction and bleeding as the main features. {31:Gilberts et al. (1994)} reasoned that the host immune response may determine which clinical presentation the disease assumes. Leprosy is an incontrovertible example of 2 clinical forms of disease, tuberculous and lepromatous, with the same etiologic factor. Resected intestinal tissue from control patients, as well as perforating and nonperforating Crohn disease patients, was evaluated for mRNA levels of a housekeeping gene (beta-actin; {102630}), a human T-cell marker, CD3-delta ({186790}), and 6 cytokines. Differences were observed with interleukin-1-beta (IL1B; {147720}) and with interleukin-1 receptor alpha (IL1RA; {147810}). Nonperforating Crohn disease, the more benign form, was associated with increased IL1B and IL1RA mRNA expression.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: Prevalence in first-degree relatives has been estimated to be between 4 and 16% ({54:Lewkonia and McConnell, 1976}; {21:Farmer et al., 1980}). {79:Orholm et al. (1991)} found that first-degree relatives of patients with either ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease had a 10-fold increase in the risk of having the same disease as the patients. The risk of having the other of the 2 diseases was also increased, but less so, and the increase in the risk of having Crohn disease was not significant in the relatives of patients with ulcerative colitis. {112:Yang et al. (1993)} found evidence of higher frequency of inflammatory bowel disease among first-degree relatives of Jewish patients than among the relatives of non-Jewish patients. The first-degree relatives of Jewish patients had a lifetime risk for inflammatory bowel disease of 7.8% and 4.5% when probands had Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, respectively. The values for first-degree relatives of non-Jewish probands were 5.2% and 1.6%.

pathogenesis.title: Pathogenesis
pathogenesis.content:
{12:Cattan et al. (2000)} studied the incidence of IBD in non-Ashkenazi Jewish patients with familial Mediterranean fever (FMF; {249100}). The association was 8 to 14 times greater than expected. The prevalence of IBD in non-Ashkenazi Jews is 120 per 100,000, whereas {12:Cattan et al. (2000)} estimated a prevalence of at least 3 per 300 (or 3 per 173 if the calculation is done through probands) in non-Ashkenazi Jews with FMF. They postulated that the inflammatory processes of FMF and IBD are additive, resulting in increased severity of disease in the new patients.

{53:Lawrance et al. (2001)} examined global gene expression profiles of inflamed colonic tissue using DNA microarrays. They identified several genes with altered expression not previously linked to IBD. In addition to the expected upregulation of various cytokine and chemokine genes, novel immune function-related genes such as IGHG3 ({147120}), IGLL2, and CD74 ({142790}), inflammation-related lipocalins HNL and NGAL ({600181}), and proliferation-related GRO genes (see, e.g., {139110}) were overexpressed in ulcerative colitis. Certain cancer-related genes such as DD96, DRAL ({602633}), and MXI1 ({600020}) were differentially expressed only in ulcerative colitis. Other genes overexpressed in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease included the REG gene family (see {167770}) and the calcium-binding S100 protein genes S100A9 ({123886}) and S100P ({600614}). The natural antimicrobial defensin DEFA5 ({600472}) and DEFA6 ({600471}) genes were particularly overexpressed in Crohn disease. Overall, significant differences in the expression profiles of 170 genes identified ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease as distinct molecular entities.
