{8:Smallwood et al. (1996)} identified and characterized 4 novel members of the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) family, including FGF13, which they called FHF2. The genes were identified by a combination of random cDNA sequencing, database searches, and degenerate PCR.

By high-through sequencing of a human ovarian cancer cell library, {4:Greene et al. (1998)} cloned the FGF13 gene, which encodes a 216-amino acid protein with a calculated molecular mass of 22 kD. FGF13 contains an N-terminal hydrophobic region characteristic of a signal sequence and shares 70% similarity with FGF8 ({600483}). Northern blot analysis showed prominent expression of FGF13 in human fetal and adult brain, particularly in cerebellum and cortex.

{3:Gecz et al. (1999)} found that FGF13 showed tissue-specific alternative splicing and alternative transcription starts. Northern blot hybridization showed highest expression in brain and skeletal muscle.

Using in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence staining on human hair follicles in the growth (anagen) stage of the hair cycle, {1:DeStefano et al. (2013)} detected expression of FGF13 in the outer root sheath within the middle and upper portions, as well as in the outer root sheath compartment (trichilemma) of the club hair during the resting stage (telogen). In anagen hairs, FGF13 localized to the outer root sheath and to the companion layer that separates the outer from the inner root sheath. In mice at embryonic day (E) 12.5 to E16.5, {1:DeStefano et al. (2013)} observed strong expression in placodes of newly forming follicles as well as in the dermal condensate beneath the placodes, which becomes the dermal papilla of the hair follicle at E14.5 within the developing whisker pad and guard hair pelage follicles. Immunofluorescence staining of vibrissae follicles during morphogenesis at E16.5 revealed that Fgf13 localizes to the outer root sheath; in postnatal skin, localization to the bulge, isthmus region, and outer root sheath of the hair follicle was observed.

geneStructure.title: Gene Structure
geneStructure.content: {3:Gecz et al. (1999)} determined the structure of the FGF13 gene and identified 2 new exons, including a new 5-prime end exon, designated 1B. FGF13 is a large gene, extending over approximately 200 kb in Xq26.3, and contains at least 7 exons.

mapping.title: Mapping
mapping.content:
By Southern blot hybridization of genomic DNA from rodent/human hybrid cell lines carrying individual human chromosomes, {8:Smallwood et al. (1996)} mapped the FGF13 gene to the X chromosome. By using an interspecific backcross mapping panel, they demonstrated that the mouse gene, Fgf13, shows no recombination with the Cd40lg gene ({300386}), suggesting that the human FGF13 gene is probably located at Xq26.

By use of isotopic in situ hybridization, {5:Lovec et al. (1997)} assigned the FHF2 gene to Xq21.

By cytogenetic, FISH, and database analysis, {3:Gecz et al. (1999)} localized the FGF13 gene within a 400-kb duplication interval on chromosome Xq26.3.

geneFunction.title: Gene Function
geneFunction.content: After membrane depolarization, the majority of voltage-gated sodium channels are rapidly inactivated by a mechanism intrinsic to the channel, but about one-third are inactivated by an 'inactivation particle' contained in the N-terminal domain (residues 2-21) of A-type FHF proteins, including FHF2. Recovery from the intrinsic inactivation mechanism is complete within 10 ms, whereas recovery from FHF-mediated inactivation takes hundreds of ms. Channels may also proceed directly from a closed to an inactivated state. A-type FHF isoforms have inhibitory and excitatory effects on the inactivation mechanisms. Repeated cycles of channel opening promotes accumulation of channels in FHF-mediated long-term block. In addition, A-type FHF isoforms can induce a depolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of sodium channels for steady-state inactivation by slowing intrinsic fast inactivation (summary by {2:Fry et al., 2021}).

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
<Subhead> Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy 90

In 7 patients, including 6 males and 1 female, from 5 unrelated families with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-90 (DEE90; {301058}), {2:Fry et al. (2021)} identified heterozygous or hemizygous missense mutations in exon 1A of the FHF2 gene (R11C, {300070.0001}; R14T, {300070.0002}; and R11P, {300070.0003}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. Segregation studies, when possible, suggested de novo occurrence, although there were 2 families (A and B) with 2 affected sibs, consistent with maternal mosaicism. In vitro electrophysiologic studies in transfected neuronal cells showed that the R11C mutation reduced long-term inactivation of sodium channels compared to wildtype, whereas R14T was completely incapable of promoting long-term inactivation. The sodium channels in cells expressing R11C recovered from long-term activation by 200 ms, compared to 1 s in cells with wildtype FHF2. Sodium channels in cells expressing R14T showed no evidence of long-term inactivation, as channels fully recovered as quickly as in cells lacking FHF2. The mutations did not affect protein expression or binding of FHF2 to the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain of sodium channels. The findings indicated that the mutations disrupted the ability of the FHF2 N-terminal inactivation particle to cause long-term inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels. {2:Fry et al. (2021)} concluded that the mutations have a gain-of-function effect that is likely to increase neuronal excitability.

In a 16-month-old girl with DEE90, {6:Narayanan et al. (2022)} identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in the FGF13 gene (I5S; {300070.0004}). The report provided further evidence for affected females with this condition. The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The variant was not present in the gnomAD database or in an in-house database. The authors noted that all of the variants identified by {2:Fry et al. (2021)} in patients with DEE90 also involved exon 1. Exon 1A codes for the highly conserved N-terminal domain of isoform A of the FGF13 protein and has both proexcitatory and inhibitory effects on voltage-gated sodium channels.

<Subhead> Intellectual Developmental Disorder, X-Linked 110

In 3 unrelated boys with X-linked intellectual developmental disorder-110 (XLID110; {301095}), {7:Pan et al. (2021)} identified 3 unrelated boys with a single-nucleotide substitution (c.-32C-G; {300070.0005}) in the 5-prime untranslated region of FGF13 mRNA. In all 3 families, the variant was inherited from an unaffected mother. The mutation was identified by Sanger sequencing of the FGF13 gene in 100 Han Chinese children with IQs of less than 40. In HEK293 cells and patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells, the variant reduced FGF13 translation, which stabilizes microtubules in developing neurons. The variant also reduced the interaction between the 5-prime untranslated region and PTBP2 ({608449}), which was required for FGF13 translation in cortical neurons.

animalModel.title: Animal Model
animalModel.content:
{9:Wei et al. (2017)} observed Na+ channel dysfunction, but not Ca(2+) channel dysfunction, in mice with an inducible deletion of Fgf13 specifically in heart. Mutant mice exposed to pressure overload induced by transverse aortic constriction developed hypertrophy, but they maintained cardiac function in association with reduced fibrosis and upregulation of adaptive hypertrophic signaling pathways. Proteomic analysis revealed interaction of Fgf13 with cavins (e.g., CAVIN1; {603198}), and Fgf13 functioned as a regulator of cardiomyocyte caveolae density. Biochemical, electron microscopy, and functional analyses demonstrated that Fgf13 knockout in heart increased caveolae density and also enhanced mechanoprotection of cardiomyocytes in the setting of increased ventricular loading. {9:Wei et al. (2017)} concluded that FGF13 is a regulator of caveolae-mediated mechanoprotection and adaptive hypertrophic signaling.

{7:Pan et al. (2021)} found that mice carrying the homologous c.-32C-G mutation in the FGF13 gene ({300070.0005}) found in patients with XLID110 had delayed neuronal migration during cortical development as well as weakened learning and memory.

preferredTitle: CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE, AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT 2; ADCAD2
clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the low density lipoprotein receptor-related protein-6 gene (LRP6,)

Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the low density lipoprotein receptor-related protein-6 gene (LRP6,)

text.title: Text
text.content:
A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that one form of autosomal dominant coronary artery disease with myocardial infarction and metabolic risk factors is caused by mutations in the LRP6 gene ({603507}).

For general background information on autosomal dominant coronary artery disease, see entry {608320}.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: From a screen of patients and families with coronary artery disease (CAD), {1:Mani et al. (2007)} identified an extreme outlier kindred with extraordinary prevalence of early CAD. The kindred, of Iranian ancestry, was ascertained by the proband who presented with myocardial infarction (MI) at the age of 48. His CAD risk factors included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus. He had never smoked, and his body mass index (BMI) was 24. He had critical stenosis of all 3 major coronary arteries, which led to coronary artery bypass grafting. He had progressive atherosclerosis of the grafts and internal carotid arteries. At age 62 he suffered a low impact hip fracture and was found to have severe osteoporosis of unknown cause. He died of a stroke at the age of 72. Among 58 blood relatives of the index case, 28 were diagnosed with early CAD, defined as MI, angina, or sudden cardiac death at or before age 50 in men or 55 in women. Of these, 23 had died from CAD, with a mean age at death of 52 years. In contrast, kindred members without early CAD died at a mean age of 81. Detailed clinical data were obtained for all available kindred members, including 13 affected with early CAD, 5 free of early CAD at or beyond the age threshold, and 9 younger asymptomatic members with a mean age of 35. Cardiac risk factors before or at presentation among affected subjects were surprisingly homogeneous, including high fasting LDL cholesterol in all (mean 176.4 mg/dl, normal less than 130 mg/dl), high fasting triglycerides in 90% (mean 240 mg/dl, normal less than 150 mg/dl), marked hypertension in all (mean 175/103 mm Hg, normal less than 140/90; typically diagnosed after age 40), and type 2 diabetes mellitus (see {125853}) in 77% (fasting blood sugar greater than 126 mg/dl; typically diagnosed after hypertension and hyperlipidemia). Despite high triglycerides, HDL levels were normal in all, and only 1 had a history of smoking.

mapping.title: Mapping
mapping.content: Of the 58 members of the large family segregating autosomal dominant CAD described by {1:Mani et al. (2007)}, 19 were available for genetic studies. Under a stringent model of the trait locus, the maximum multipoint lod score was 4.4 for linkage of CAD within a 2.7-cM interval flanked by SNPs {dbSNP rs2213177} and {dbSNP rs747726}. Within the interval were 6 annotated genes, of which LRP6 ({603507}) was subjected to further analysis.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
{1:Mani et al. (2007)} found that the index case in the large Iranian family with autosomal dominant CAD studied by them carried an arginine-to-cysteine substitution at codon 611 of the LRP6 gene (R611C; {603507.0001}), which lies in the epidermal growth factor-like domain and is conserved among LRP6 orthologs ranging from Xenopus to human. An arginine at this position was also found in mammalian LRP5 ({603506}), LRP2 ({600073}), and LRP3 ({603159}). This mutation precisely cosegregated with early CAD in the kindred and was absent in 400 unrelated Iranian and 3,600 U.S. Caucasian control chromosomes. All 5 mutation carriers studied had low bone density, each with values expected in less than 12.5% of the population (P less than 0.001).

{2:Singh et al. (2013)} screened 200 white Americans with early-onset familial CAD and metabolic syndrome and 2,000 healthy northern European controls for nonconservative mutations in the LRP6 gene, and identified 3 missense mutations ({603507.0002}-{603507.0004}) that cosegregated with the metabolic traits in the kindreds of the affected individuals. No mutations were identified in the controls. The index cases had extreme phenotypes of angiographically documented early-onset CAD, at less than 55 years of age in males and less than 60 years of age in females, with at least 3 risk factors for metabolic syndrome and a strong family history of CAD and metabolic traits.

preferredTitle: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER, AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT 39; MRD39
clinicalSynopsis: Some patients have deletions or duplications of chromosome 2p25.3 encompassing several genes
Caused by mutation in the myelin transcription factor 1-like gene (MYT1L,)

Miscellaneous: Some patients have deletions or duplications of chromosome 2p25.3 encompassing several genes
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the myelin transcription factor 1-like gene (MYT1L,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-39 (MRD39) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the MYT1L gene ({613084}) on chromosome 2p25.3. Some patients with a similar phenotype have deletions or duplications of chromosome 2p25.3 encompassing several genes, including MYT1L.

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:De Rocker et al. (2015)} described 2 unrelated patients with MRD39. Patient 14, originally reported by {2:de Ligt et al. (2012)}, was a girl who presented with neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulties soon after birth, and was noted to have developmental delay around 6 months of age. At age 12 years, she had an IQ of about 45 and showed autistic features. Mild dysmorphic features included broad base and bridge of the nose and a large mouth. Patient 15 was a 13-year-old boy with delayed development, especially affecting language, and autism spectrum disorder. At age 9 years, his IQ was about 50. He had brachycephaly and upwardly slanted narrow eyes.

{1:Blanchet et al. (2017)} reported 9 patients with MRD39. All had developmental delay or impaired intellectual development and gross motor delay. Most (85%) were overweight/obese and 70% had hyperphagia. CNS malformation and minor anomalies were each seen in 42% of patients. Autism and epilepsy were seen in 30% and 15% of patients, respectively. The proportions with impaired intellectual development, gross motor delay, speech delay, autism, overweight/obesity, and hyperphagia among patients with MYT1L haploinsufficiency were similar to those in patients with the 2p25.3 deletion syndrome, suggesting that MTY1L haplosufficiency is responsible for the 2p25.3 deletion phenotype.

{4:Loid et al. (2018)} reported a 13-year-old boy with MRD39 with early-onset obesity. The patient was overweight at age 1 year and obese at age 2 years. He had hyperphagia, speech delay, strabismus, hyperactivity, and neurologic, cognitive, and motor delay. The patient had no dysmorphic features, and his brain MRI was normal.

cytogenetics.title: Cytogenetics
cytogenetics.content:
{6:Stevens et al. (2011)} identified heterozygous deletions of chromosome 2p25.3 in 3 adult sibs and 3 unrelated patients with intellectual disability. The patients were also overweight or obese but had no notable additional features. The deletions ranged in size from 0.37 to 3.13 Mb, and the minimal region of overlap included the MYT1L gene.

{3:De Rocker et al. (2015)} reported 14 patients, including 10 unrelated individuals and 4 members of the same family, with heterozygous deletions of chromosome 2p25.3 ranging in size from 120 kb to 6.07 Mb. All led to either partial or complete deletion of the MYT1L gene. Six additional patients, including 3 members of the same family, had 2p25.3 duplications ranging in size from 170 to 377 kb. These breakpoints were located in MYT1L, very likely leading to an aberrant transcript and loss of function. All patients, including the ones with duplications, had mild to moderate intellectual disability with speech delay, and the majority were overweight or obese. Additional features included behavioral problems, such as autism, aggression, hyperactivity, stereotypic hand movements, and sleep disturbances.

{5:Mayo et al. (2015)} reported a 4.5-year-old girl with a de novo intragenic deletion of MYT1L. She had neonatal hypotonia, microcephaly, delayed psychomotor development, and autistic features. Additional features included strabismus, myopia, recurrent otitis, and seizures; she was not overweight.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The transmission pattern of MRD39 in 2 families reported by {3:De Rocker et al. (2015)} was consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In a 12-year-old girl with autosomal dominant MRD39, {2:de Ligt et al. (2012)} identified a de novo splice site mutation in the MYT1L gene ({613084.0001}). The patient was ascertained from a larger cohort of 100 patients with severe intellectual disability who underwent exome sequencing. Functional studies of the variant were not performed.

In a 13-year-old boy with MRD39, {3:De Rocker et al. (2015)} identified a de novo heterozygous truncating mutation in the MYT1L gene (Y639X; {613084.0002}).

Using trio exome sequencing and a Genematcher-facilitated collaboration, {1:Blanchet et al. (2017)} reported 9 patients with impaired intellectual development and obesity, consistent with MRD39, who had mutations in the MYT1L gene, including 4 loss-of-function and 5 missense (see, e.g., {613084.0003}) mutations. Using a knockout cell line, MYT1L loss of function was shown to result in dysregulated expression of neurodevelopmental genes. A knockdown zebrafish model demonstrated loss of oxytocin expression in the preoptic neuroendocrine area, which might explain how MYT1L mutations result in obesity. MYT1L was shown to be expressed at significantly higher levels in the adult cerebral cortex than in the hippocampus, basal ganglia, and hypothalamus, and in multiple hypothalamic structures at 15 to 16 postconception weeks.

In a 13-year-old boy with MRD39 and early-onset obesity, {4:Loid et al. (2018)} identified a de novo heterozygous frameshift deletion in the MYT1L gene ({613084.0004}). The mutation was identified by whole-genome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The frameshift variant was not present in the 1000 Genomes Project, ExAC, SweGen, or SISu Project databases, but was found in 1 of 8,696 alleles in the African population in the gnomAD database.

preferredTitle: INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER, AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT 61; MRD61
clinicalSynopsis: Impaired intellectual development, mild to moderate
Caused by mutation in the mediator complex subunit 13 gene (MED13,)

Neurologic - CNS: Impaired intellectual development, mild to moderate
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the mediator complex subunit 13 gene (MED13,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-61 (MRD61) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the MED13 gene ({603808}) on chromosome 17q23.

description.title: Description
description.content: Autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder-61 (MRD61) is characterized by global developmental delay apparent in infancy with mildly impaired intellectual development, expressive speech delay, and behavioral abnormalities, including autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Most affected individuals learn to walk on time or with some mild delay. Additional features are highly variable and may include nonspecific dysmorphic features, obstipation, ocular anomalies, and poor overall growth ({1:Snijders Blok et al., 2018}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content: {1:Snijders Blok et al. (2018)} reported 11 unrelated patients and an affected mother-daughter duo (patients B and C) with MRD61. The patients, who were ascertained through collaborative research efforts and the GeneMatcher program, ranged in age from 3 to 19 years, except for the mother who was 32. All patients had some degree of global developmental delay apparent from infancy or early childhood, with most patients having impaired intellectual development ranging from borderline (IQ of 85) or mild to moderate. All had speech delay, particularly in expressive language and often associated with speech apraxia and difficulties in language formulation and articulation. Receptive language was less severely affected. Six patients were diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and/or ADHD, and brain imaging, when performed, was essentially normal. The patients tended to have poor overall growth, but none had short stature or microcephaly. About half achieved walking by age 12 months, whereas about half had mildly delayed walking by about 2 years. Many patients had variable ocular anomalies, including strabismus, astigmatism, nystagmus, and pale optic discs; 2 patients had Duane anomaly and 2 had conductive hearing impairment. Less common features, observed in only a few patients, included hypotonia, kyphosis, scoliosis, laterally deviated halluces, pes cavus, sleep disturbances, chronic obstipation, and mild cardiac defects, such as subaortic stenosis and dilated aortic root. Only 1 patient had drug-resistant myoclonic seizures. Many patients had nonspecific dysmorphic features, such as flat philtrum, widely spaced eyes, narrow palpebral fissures, periorbital fullness, synophrys, broad and high nasal bridge, full nasal tip, and wide mouth with thin upper lip.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content: The heterozygous mutations in the MED13 gene that were identified in 11 unrelated patients with MRD61 by {1:Snijders Blok et al. (2018)} occurred de novo. {1:Snijders Blok et al. (2018)} also reported an instance of autosomal dominant inheritance of MRD61 in a mother and daughter.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content: In 11 unrelated patients and an affected mother-daughter duo with MRD61, {1:Snijders Blok et al. (2018)} identified heterozygous mutations in the MED13 gene (see, e.g., {603808.0001}-{603808.0005}). The mutations, which were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, were not present in the gnomAD database. The mutations occurred de novo in 11 patients; 1 was inherited from an affected mother. There were 3 nonsense, 2 frameshift, and 6 missense variants, and 1 in-frame deletion of a single residue. Analysis of cells derived from a patient carrying an R1400X mutation ({603808.0004}) showed normal levels of MED13 transcript and protein, with no detection of a truncated protein product. The mutant transcript was detected at about a 70% level compared to wildtype. Additional functional studies of the other variants and of other patient cells were not performed. {1:Snijders Blok et al. (2018)} noted that mutations in other genes encoding subunits of the Mediator complex have been associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, which supports the hypothesis that MED13 variants may be responsible for this phenotype.

clinicalSynopsis: Caused by mutation in the chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4 gene (CHD4,)

Head: Macrocephaly
Molecular Basis: Caused by mutation in the chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4 gene (CHD4,)

text.title: Text
text.content: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Sifrim-Hitz-Weiss syndrome (SIHIWES) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CHD4 gene ({603277}) on chromosome 12p13.

description.title: Description
description.content: Sifrim-Hitz-Weiss syndrome (SIHIWES) is an autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder with variable congenital defects affecting other systems, including cardiac, skeletal, and urogenital. Some patients may have short stature, enlarged head circumference, hearing loss, and nonspecific dysmorphic facial features (summary by {3:Sifrim et al., 2016} and {4:Weiss et al., 2016}).

clinicalFeatures.title: Clinical Features
clinicalFeatures.content:
{3:Sifrim et al. (2016)} reported 5 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 1 to 16 years, with a syndrome associated with congenital heart defects. Three had tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) or TOF-like features, 1 had an aortic coarctation, and 1 had a septal defect. All were reported to have early global neurodevelopmental delay, although the 16-year-old had only gait imbalance without apparent intellectual disability. Most had variable and nonspecific dysmorphic features such as coarse facies, abnormal facial shape, epicanthal folds, ptosis, astigmatism, and ear abnormalities. Additional abnormalities observed in some patients included omphalocele, cryptorchidism, ambiguous genitalia, anteriorly placed anus, and vesicoureteral reflux. One patient had skeletal abnormalities manifest as broad and short clavicles, flat acetabular roof, short femoral neck, and fusion of the wrist bones; another patient had postaxial polydactyly, and a third had wormian bones. One patient had hearing impairment and 2 had Chiari malformation.

{4:Weiss et al. (2016)} reported 5 unrelated patients, ranging in age from 5 to 18 years, with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. All had global developmental delay and impaired intellectual development. Common dysmorphic features included macrocephaly, widely spaced eyes, square-shaped face, dysmorphic ears, and palatal anomalies, but these features were nonspecific. Four patients had hearing loss, 2 patients had short stature, and all 3 males had hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with cryptorchidism and/or micropenis. Additional congenital anomalies seen in 2 patients included cervical vertebral fusions, tarsal coalitions, and heart defects, such as patent ductus arteriosus and septal defects. One patient had congenital stroke and moyamoya disease (see {252350}), and 1 had chronic renal insufficiency. Brain imaging showed enlarged ventricles.

From a cohort of 197 probands with moyamoya disease, {2:Pinard et al. (2020)} reported 7 unrelated patients with mutation in the CHD4 gene. All 7 patients had ischemic stroke due to bilateral moyamoya angiopathy and 5 had hypertension. Other features were variable, and the authors concluded that rare variants in the CHD4 gene predispose to moyamoya disease in the presence or absence of developmental delay.

{1:Karimi et al. (2025)} described clinical features in a cohort of 27 patients with SIHIWES. Common findings included impaired intellectual development (19/23), speech delay (26/27), motor delay (27/27), macrocephaly (11/24), heart defects (12/24), abnormal brain imaging (14/23), hypogonadism (11/24), and hearing loss (9/23). Intelligence was in the normal range in 4 patients. Less common recurrent clinical features included optic nerve abnormalities, aortic root dilatation, and gut malrotation.

diagnosis.title: Diagnosis
diagnosis.content: {1:Karimi et al. (2025)} examined the DNA methylation profile in peripheral blood in a cohort of patients with mutations in the CHD4 gene. A characteristic episignature was identified in 14 patients with missense mutations in the SNF2-like ATPase/helicase domain and in 1 patient with a missense mutation near the PHD domain. This episignature differed both from controls and from patients with truncating mutations in the CHD4 gene, and helped to clarify the pathogenicity of variants of unknown significance in the ATPase/helicase domain. The methylation pattern identified in 7 patients with truncating mutations in the CHD4 gene had some overlap with the methylation pattern identified in the ATPase/helicase domain mutation cohort, but was less pronounced.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.content:
The heterozygous mutations in the CHD4 gene that were identified in patients with SIHIWES by {3:Sifrim et al. (2016)} and {4:Weiss et al. (2016)} occurred de novo.

Of the 26 heterozygous mutations in the CHD4 gene that were identified in patients with SIHIWES by {1:Karimi et al. (2025)}, 8 occurred de novo and 7 were inherited; the inheritance was unknown in 11. One patient reported by {1:Karimi et al. (2025)} inherited compound heterozygous CHD4 variants.

molecularGenetics.title: Molecular Genetics
molecularGenetics.content:
In 5 unrelated patients with SIHIWES, {3:Sifrim et al. (2016)} identified 5 different de novo heterozygous mutations in the CHD4 gene (see, e.g., {603277.0001}-{603277.0003}). There were 4 missense mutations and 1 in-frame deletion. Functional studies of the variants and studies of patient cells were not performed. The patients were ascertained from a cohort of 518 trios in which a child had syndromic congenital heart defects who underwent exome sequencing. Statistical analysis indicated that de novo mutations in the CHD4 gene were significantly enriched in patients compared to those expected under a null mutation model (p = 2.28 x 10(-7), Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.05).

In 5 unrelated patients with SIHIWES, {4:Weiss et al. (2016)} identified 4 different de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the CHD4 gene (see, e.g., {603277.0004}-{603277.0006}). The mutations were found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Three of the mutations occurred at highly conserved residues in the C-terminal helicase domain and were predicted to disrupt the ATPase activity of CHD4. Both {3:Sifrim et al. (2016)} and {4:Weiss et al. (2016)} noted phenotypic overlap with CHARGE syndrome ({214800}), which is caused by mutation in the CHD7 gene ({608892}).

genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.title: Genotype/Phenotype Correlations
genotypePhenotypeCorrelations.content: In a cohort of 27 patients with SIHIWES, {1:Karimi et al. (2025)} found that autism was more common in patients with truncating mutations than in those with missense mutations in the CHD4 gene.
